cards.title: The chapter “Fundamentals of Partnership” introduces the legal and accounting…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The chapter “Fundamentals of Partnership” introduces the legal and accounting framework governing partnership firms under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. It defines a partnership as a relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. The chapter covers: (1) key provisions of the Act such as registration, rights, duties, and dissolution; (2) default rules that apply when no partnership deed exists — profit‑sharing ratio, interest on capital, drawings, and remuneration; (3) preparation of the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account to allocate net profit among partners after charging interest on capital, drawings, partner’s salary, commission, and creating reserves; (4) distinction between fixed and fluctuating capital methods and the role of partners’ current accounts; (5) calculation of interest on capital and drawings under various methods; (6) treatment of guaranteed profits to a partner and past adjustments for errors or omissions. These sub‑concepts interlink: the deed (or Act defaults) sets the profit‑sharing ratio, which drives the appropriation account; capital method choice determines whether interest on capital is credited to capital or current accounts; guarantees and past adjustments modify the final distributable profit. Mastery of this chapter is essential because every subsequent partnership accounting topic — admission, retirement, dissolution — builds on these fundamentals.
steps: The chapter equips you with the rulebook and the first accounting tool — the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account — that every partnership firm must master before moving to complex events like admission or dissolution.

Here is why: the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 provides the legal backbone; without a written deed, its default provisions automatically govern profit sharing, interest, and remuneration, so you must know them to avoid…

Fixed versus fluctuating capital decides whether these appropriations adjust the capital account directly or flow through a separate current account — a choice that affects balance‑sheet presentation and interest…

Guarantee of profit ensures a minimum return to a partner, requiring the guaranteeing partners to bear any shortfall, while past adjustments correct prior‑period errors without reopening closed books.

cards.title: The Indian Partnership Act 1932 governs the formation, operation…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Indian Partnership Act 1932 governs the formation, operation, and dissolution of partnership firms in India. Section 4 defines a partnership as “the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.” Three essential elements emerge: (1) an agreement between two or more persons, (2) to carry on a business, and (3) with the intention of sharing profits. The Act establishes mutual agency (Section 13) — every partner is an agent of the firm and can bind it by acts done in the ordinary course of business. Implied authority (Section 19) extends this power to usual transactions such as buying goods, borrowing money, and drawing cheques. Sections 9‑17 enumerate partners’ rights and duties: right to take part in management, access books, share profits equally (Section 13(a) default), indemnity for liabilities incurred in the firm’s business, and duty to render true accounts. Default financial provisions apply only when the partnership deed is silent: no interest on capital (Section 13(b)), no interest on drawings (Section 13(c)), no remuneration for acting in the business (Section 13(d)), and interest at 6% p.a. on advances beyond capital (Section 13(e)). Registration (Sections 58‑69) is optional but unregistered firms suffer disabilities such as inability to sue third parties. Dissolution provisions (Sections 39‑44) cover dissolution by agreement, notice, court order, or on the happening of certain events. These statutory provisions form the legal framework upon which accounting treatments — profit‑sharing ratios, interest calculations, salary, commission, reserves, and guarantee of profits — are built in subsequent nodes.
steps: The Indian Partnership Act 1932 is the statutory skeleton that gives a partnership its legal identity and default operating rules.
Here is why: without the Act, every firm would need a exhaustive deed; the Act supplies gap‑filling provisions that apply automatically when partners are silent.
First, Section 4 crystallises the three pillars — agreement, business, profit‑sharing — distinguishing a partnership from a mere co‑ownership or a Hindu Undivided Family.

Second, mutual agency (Sec 13) makes each partner an agent of the firm; a partner’s act of buying inventory on credit binds all partners, which is why the firm’s books must record such liabilities immediately.
Third, implied authority (Sec 19) limits this power to acts usual in that trade; a partner in a textile firm cannot bind the firm by selling real estate.

Fourth, the default financial clauses (Sec 13(a)‑(e)) are the accountant’s starting point: profits/losses shared equally, no interest on capital or drawings unless the deed says otherwise, no salary for routine work…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Section 13 defines partnership”) reveals confusion between the definition section and the mutual agency provision.

cards.title: When a partnership deed is silent or does not exist…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: When a partnership deed is silent or does not exist, the Indian Partnership Act 1932 supplies a set of default provisions that govern the mutual rights and duties of partners. The key defaults are: (1) profits and losses are shared equally irrespective of capital contribution; (2) no partner is entitled to remuneration (salary or commission) for taking part in the business; (3) no interest is allowed on capital contributed by partners; (4) interest at 6 % per annum is charged on drawings made by partners; (5) interest at 6 % per annum is payable on loans advanced by a partner to the firm beyond his capital; (6) the firm must indemnify a partner for payments made and liabilities incurred in the ordinary conduct of business. These rules apply automatically unless the partners expressly agree otherwise in a written deed. They form the statutory baseline that the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account (next node) will use to allocate the net profit among partners. Understanding these defaults is essential because any deviation — such as agreeing on a 3:2 profit‑sharing ratio or allowing 10 % interest on capital — must be explicitly recorded in the deed to override the Act.
steps: When a partnership deed is absent, the Indian Partnership Act 1932 becomes the governing rule‑book, imposing equal treatment on all partners unless they expressly agree otherwise.
Here is why: the Act assumes that partners who did not bother to write a deed intended a simple, egalitarian arrangement.
First, profits and losses are divided equally — capital size does not matter — because the law treats each partner’s effort and risk as identical.
Second, no partner receives a salary or commission; the Act views management as a collective duty, not a paid service.
Third, interest on capital is disallowed; the capital is seen as the partner’s stake, not a loan to the firm.
Fourth, drawings attract 6 % interest per annum to discourage excessive withdrawals and protect the firm’s liquidity.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “profit is shared in capital ratio”) reveals the misconception that capital contribution automatically determines profit share — confusing the default rule with a common deed provision.

cards.title: The Profit & Loss Appropriation Account is a nominal account prepared after the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Profit & Loss Appropriation Account is a nominal account prepared after the Profit & Loss Account to show how the net profit (or loss) of a partnership firm is allocated among the partners according to the partnership deed or, in its absence, the Indian Partnership Act 1932. It starts with the net profit transferred from the Profit & Loss Account on the credit side. Debit entries include interest on partners’ capital (at the agreed rate), partners’ salaries, partners’ commissions, interest on partners’ drawings (which reduces the amount available for distribution), and transfers to reserves or other appropriations. The balance after all appropriations — called “profit available for distribution” — is then credited to the partners’ capital or current accounts in their profit‑sharing ratio. If the firm incurs a net loss, the loss is debited to the appropriation account and the partners’ capital/current accounts are debited in the profit‑sharing ratio (unless the deed provides otherwise). The account thus links the firm’s overall profitability (from the Profit & Loss Account) to the individual partners’ equity, ensuring that contractual obligations such as interest on capital, remuneration, and reserve creation are honoured before profit sharing. It also provides the basis for preparing the partners’ capital accounts (fixed or fluctuating) and current accounts, which are covered in subsequent nodes.
steps: The Profit & Loss Appropriation Account is the bridge that converts the firm’s net profit into partners’ individual entitlements.
Here is why: every partnership agreement (or the Act) mandates certain charges — interest on capital, remuneration, interest on drawings, reserves — before the remaining profit is split.

cards.title: Fixed capital and fluctuating capital are two methods of maintaining partners’…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Fixed capital and fluctuating capital are two methods of maintaining partners’ capital accounts in a partnership firm. Under the fixed capital method, each partner has a Capital Account that records only permanent contributions (initial capital, additional capital introduced, permanent withdrawals). All recurring transactions — share of profit/loss, interest on capital, interest on drawings, partner’s salary, commission, and drawings — are posted to a separate Current Account. The Capital Account balance therefore remains constant unless the partner explicitly adds or withdraws capital. Under the fluctuating capital method, a single Capital Account per partner records every transaction affecting the partner’s equity: opening capital, additional capital, share of profit/loss, interest on capital, interest on drawings, salary, commission, drawings, and any other adjustments. Consequently, the Capital Account balance fluctuates with each entry. The choice of method is usually stated in the partnership deed; if the deed is silent, the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not prescribe a default, but accounting practice in India favours the fixed capital method for clarity. The fixed method simplifies tracking of permanent capital versus current earnings, while the fluctuating method reduces the number of ledger accounts. Both methods ultimately yield the same total equity for each partner; only the presentation differs. The next node will detail the operation of partners’ current accounts under the fixed capital method.
steps: The fixed capital method isolates permanent capital from current earnings, while the fluctuating capital method merges them into a single account.
Here is why: the partnership deed (or accounting policy) decides the method.
In the fixed method, the Capital Account is credited only with initial and additional capital; it is debited only for permanent withdrawals.
All periodic items — profit share, interest on capital, salary, commission, interest on drawings, and drawings — flow through the Current Account.
This separation lets stakeholders see at a glance how much capital each partner has permanently invested versus how much current profit they have earned or withdrawn.
Consider a firm “Mehta & Shah” with partners Mehta (₹5,00,000) and Shah (₹3,00,000).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Fixed capital means capital cannot be changed at all”) reveals the misconception that the capital balance is frozen, confusing “fixed method” with “fixed amount”.

cards.title: A partner’s current account is a ledger account maintained under the fixed…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A partner’s current account is a ledger account maintained under the fixed capital method to record all transactions that affect a partner’s equity other than permanent capital contributions or withdrawals. While the capital account remains static (showing only the agreed‑upon capital balance), the current account captures interest on capital, partner’s salary, commission, share of profit or loss, drawings, and interest on drawings. The balance of the current account fluctuates each period and is transferred to the partner’s capital account only on dissolution or when the partnership deed permits. Under the Indian Partnership Act 1932, if the deed is silent, the fixed capital method with current accounts is not mandatory; however, most firms adopt it for clarity. The current account is a nominal account in nature but treated as a personal account for each partner. Its closing balance (debit or credit) reflects the partner’s net claim on the firm after appropriating profits and charging drawings. This account links directly to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account (node) and to the Interest on Capital/Drawings (node), Salary (node), Commission (node) and Reserves (node) nodes.
steps: The current account is the only ledger that moves under the fixed capital method; the capital account stays unchanged unless new capital is introduced or permanently withdrawn.
Here is why: the fixed capital method separates permanent investment from operational fluctuations.
Consider a firm “Mehta & Shah” where Mehta contributes ₹10 lakh and Shah ₹8 lakh as fixed capital.
The partnership deed provides Mehta a salary of ₹12,000 per month, Shah a commission of 5 % of net profit before commission, and interest on capital at 10 % p.a.
Both partners draw ₹20,000 per quarter.
At year‑end, net profit before appropriations is ₹6,00,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to record additional capital introduced”) reveals the misconception that current accounts handle permanent capital changes — they do not; only the capital account does.

cards.title: Interest on capital is the return paid to partners for the use of their…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Interest on capital is the return paid to partners for the use of their invested funds, calculated at an agreed rate (or, absent a deed, the rate prescribed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932). It is an appropriation of profit, debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and credited to each partner’s capital or current account. Interest on drawings is the charge levied on amounts withdrawn by partners for personal use; it is credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and debited to the partner’s current or capital account. The calculation method depends on the timing of drawings: (a) if drawings are made at the beginning of each period, interest is charged for the full period; (b) if at the end, for one period less; (c) if at irregular intervals, the product method (amount × months outstanding) is used. Both interests affect the divisible profit and therefore the partners’ share of net profit. The rates, whether fixed or fluctuating capital accounts are used, and the treatment of interest when profits are insufficient are governed by the partnership deed; in its absence, the Act provides default rules (no interest on capital, 6 % p.a. on drawings).
steps: Interest on capital and drawings are two sides of the same appropriation coin: one rewards investment, the other penalises withdrawal.
Here is why: the partnership deed (or the Act) sets the rates; the accounting period determines the time factor; and the method of drawing (regular vs irregular) decides the computation technique.
First, identify each partner’s capital balance at the start of the year and any additional capital introduced during the year.
Multiply each amount by the number of months it remained in the business, sum the products, and apply the annual rate divided by 12 — this yields interest on capital.
Second, list every drawing with its date.
For regular monthly drawings at the beginning of each month, interest = total drawings × rate × 6.5/12; at the end of each month, use 5.5/12; mid‑month uses 6/12.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “10 % because that is a common market rate”) reveals the misconception that the Act follows commercial lending rates rather than its own statutory provision.
remember: State the default rate of interest on drawings prescribed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 when the partnership deed is silent.

cards.title: Partner’s salary is a periodic payment to a working partner for services…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Partner’s salary is a periodic payment to a working partner for services rendered to the firm, authorised solely by the partnership deed. Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, no partner is entitled to remuneration unless the deed expressly provides for it. Salary is an appropriation of profit, not a charge against profit; therefore it is debited to the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account and credited to the partner’s Current Account (under fixed capital method) or Capital Account (under fluctuating capital method). It reduces the divisible profit available for distribution among partners in their profit‑sharing ratio. The amount is fixed or determined by a formula in the deed and is payable even if the firm incurs a loss, unless the deed states otherwise. Salary differs from commission (which is usually a percentage of profit) and from interest on capital (which is a return on invested capital). Proper accounting ensures the appropriation is shown separately in the Appropriation Account and the partner’s account reflects the credit, maintaining transparency in profit allocation.
steps: Partner’s salary is an appropriation of profit, not a charge against profit, and it is payable only when the partnership deed expressly authorises it. Here is why: the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (Section 13) states…
Therefore, the first step in any problem is to verify the deed clause.
If the deed is silent, no salary is recorded, even if a partner works full‑time.

cards.title: Commission in a partnership is an appropriation of profit paid to a partner for…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Commission in a partnership is an appropriation of profit paid to a partner for services rendered (e.g., management, sales) as per the partnership deed. It is not an expense but a distribution of profit, shown in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account. Two bases exist: 1. On profit before commission – Commission = Net Profit × Rate / 100. 2. On profit after commission – Commission = Net Profit × Rate / (100 + Rate). The deed may also fix a lump‑sum amount. Absent a deed, the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 provides no commission; partners share profits equally. Commission is credited to the partner’s current account (fluctuating capital) or capital account (fixed capital) and debited to the Appropriation Account. It ranks after interest on capital and salary but before transfer to reserves. Guarantee of profit to a partner may affect the commission calculation if the guaranteed amount exceeds the share after commission.
steps: Commission is an appropriation of profit, not an expense, and its calculation base (before or after commission) changes the amount a partner receives.
Here is why: the partnership deed decides the basis; if silent, the Act gives none.
Consider a firm with net profit ₹2,00,000 and a 10 % commission to Partner A. 1.
Before‑commission basis – Commission = ₹2,00,000 × 10 / 100 = ₹20,000.
Appropriation Account debits ₹20,000;
Partner A’s current account credits ₹20,000.

cards.title: In partnership accounting, a reserve is an amount of profit retained in the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: In partnership accounting, a reserve is an amount of profit retained in the business rather than distributed to partners. It is created by debiting the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and crediting a Reserve Account (e.g., General Reserve, Workmen Compensation Reserve, or Investment Fluctuation Reserve). Reserves strengthen the firm’s financial position, provide for future contingencies, and may be used for expansion, writing off losses, or meeting legal requirements. Unlike provisions, which are charges against profit for known liabilities, reserves are appropriations of profit and appear on the liability side of the Balance Sheet under “Partners’ Funds”. The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not mandate specific reserves; their creation depends on the partnership deed or a unanimous decision of partners. Reserves affect partners’ capital accounts: under the fixed capital method, the reserve is credited to partners’ current accounts (or shown separately), while under the fluctuating capital method it is added directly to each partner’s capital in the profit‑sharing ratio. Proper treatment of reserves ensures that the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account shows the amount available for distribution after all appropriations (interest, salary, commission, etc.) and reserves.
steps: Takeaway: In partnership accounting, reserves are profits retained in the business, created by appropriating profit, and they appear as a liability under Partners’ Funds while increasing the firm’s financial strength.

Here is why: First, reserves are not expenses; they are distributions of profit decided by partners, so they are debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account (the same account used for interest, salary…
Second, the credit goes to a Reserve Account, which accumulates over years and is shown on the liability side, thereby not reducing partners’ immediate claim but strengthening the firm’s net worth.

Third, under the fixed capital method, the reserve is credited to partners’ current accounts (or shown separately) in the profit‑sharing ratio, whereas under the fluctuating capital method it is added directly to each…

cards.title: A guarantee of profits is a contractual arrangement in a partnership whereby…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A guarantee of profits is a contractual arrangement in a partnership whereby one or more partners assure a specified partner a minimum amount of profit (or a minimum share of profit) irrespective of the firm’s actual earnings. The guarantee may be given by the firm as a whole (i.e., all other partners jointly) or by one or more specific partners in a predetermined ratio. When the guaranteed partner’s calculated share under the profit‑sharing ratio falls short of the guaranteed amount, the deficiency is borne by the guaranteeing partners in the agreed ratio (or equally if no ratio is stated). The guarantee does not alter the profit‑sharing ratio; it only creates an additional appropriation after the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account has distributed profit according to the normal ratio. The accounting treatment involves: (1) preparing the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account in the usual way; (2) computing each partner’s share; (3) comparing the guaranteed partner’s share with the guaranteed amount; (4) debiting the deficiency to the guaranteeing partners’ capital/current accounts in the guarantee ratio; and (5) crediting the guaranteed partner’s account with the guaranteed amount. The guarantee is disclosed in the notes to accounts and is governed by the partnership deed; in its absence the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does not impose any guarantee — it must be expressly agreed.
steps: A profit guarantee creates a secondary appropriation after the normal profit‑sharing ratio has been applied; the shortfall is borne by the guaranteeing partners in their agreed ratio.

Here is why: the partnership deed first distributes profit according to the agreed sharing ratio, after charging interest on capital, salary, commission, etc. Only then does the guarantee clause operate — it compares…
If the allocated share is lower, the difference (deficiency) is transferred from the guaranteeing partners’ accounts to the guaranteed partner’s account.
This two‑step process ensures the profit‑sharing ratio remains unchanged while honouring the guarantee.
Consider a firm with partners A, B and C sharing profits 3:2:1.

cards.title: Past adjustments refer to the rectification of profit‑sharing, interest…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Past adjustments refer to the rectification of profit‑sharing, interest, salary, commission, or guarantee errors that relate to periods before the current accounting year. When a partnership deed is missing, silent, or later amended, the Indian Partnership Act 1932 (Sections 13, 14, 17) supplies default rules: equal profit sharing, no interest on capital, no salary, and no commission. If the actual distribution deviated from these defaults or from a subsequently ratified agreement, the firm must compute the difference for each prior period and pass a single adjusting journal entry. The adjustment touches the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, Partners’ Capital/Current Accounts, and any Guarantee of Profits account. It ensures that each partner’s capital reflects the true economic entitlement up to the date of correction, maintaining the principle of equity among partners.
steps: Past adjustments correct prior‑period profit allocations so that each partner’s capital reflects the agreed or statutory entitlement.
Here is why: the Indian Partnership Act 1932 supplies default rules when the deed is silent; any deviation discovered later must be rectified retrospectively.
First, list every item that was mis‑applied — profit‑sharing ratio, interest on capital, partner’s salary, commission, or guarantee shortfall — for each affected accounting period.
Second, determine the correct amount per period using the ratified agreement or statutory defaults.
Third, compute the difference per partner (Correct − Recorded).
Fourth, aggregate the differences across all prior periods.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ratio follows capital contribution”) reveals the misconception that capital determines profit share by default — confusing company shareholding rules with partnership law.

cards.title: Change in Profit Sharing Ratio (PSR) occurs when existing partners mutually…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Change in Profit Sharing Ratio (PSR) occurs when existing partners mutually agree to alter their profit‑sharing proportions without any admission, retirement, or death. The core steps are: (1) compute the sacrificing ratio (old share – new share) for partners who lose, and the gaining ratio (new share – old share) for partners who gain; (2) adjust goodwill — if goodwill appears in books, it is written off in the old ratio; if not, the gaining partners’ capital accounts are debited and sacrificing partners’ credited with the value of goodwill in the gaining/sacrificing ratio; (3) distribute accumulated reserves, profits, or losses (including P&L credit balance, general reserve, workmen compensation fund, etc.) in the old ratio because they belong to the period before the change; (4) revalue assets and liabilities — any profit or loss on revaluation is also allocated in the old ratio; (5) if partners decide to adjust capitals to reflect the new ratio, they bring in or withdraw cash (or use current accounts) so that capitals become proportionate to the new PSR. All adjustments are routed through partners’ capital (or current) accounts. This concept builds on the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account, fixed/fluctuating capital, and past adjustments covered earlier.
steps: The key takeaway: When partners change their profit‑sharing ratio, the gaining partners must compensate the sacrificing partners for goodwill, and all accumulated reserves, profits, losses, and revaluation effects up to…
Here is why: 1.
Sacrificing and gaining ratios quantify the shift.
If A, B, C share 3:2:1 and change to 1:1:1, A sacrifices 3/6 – 2/6 = 1/6, B sacrifices 2/6 – 2/6 = 0, C gains 2/6 – 1/6 = 1/6.
The gaining partner (C) pays the sacrificing partner (A) for the share of goodwill. 2.
Goodwill adjustment ensures fairness.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “sacrificing ratio is the new ratio minus the old ratio”) reveals the misconception that sacrificing ratio is calculated as new minus old, confusing it with gaining ratio.

cards.title: Goodwill in partnership accounting is an intangible asset representing the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Goodwill in partnership accounting is an intangible asset representing the excess of a firm’s true worth over the net identifiable assets (capital employed) reflected in the books. It arises from factors such as reputation, customer loyalty, advantageous location, efficient management, or special contracts that enable the firm to generate super‑normal profits consistently. Goodwill is not recorded unless there is a change in the partnership—admission, retirement, death, or a change in profit‑sharing ratio—because accounting follows the conservatism principle and only recognises value when objectively measurable. When such events occur, goodwill is valued, brought into the books (or adjusted via partners’ capital accounts), and then either written off or retained according to the agreed treatment. The valuation of goodwill relies on three main methods: (i) Average Profit Method, (ii) Super Profit Method, and (iii) Capitalisation Method. Each method links goodwill to the firm’s maintainable profits and the normal rate of return expected in the industry. Understanding goodwill is essential because it affects the distribution of reserves, the calculation of sacrificing/gaining ratios, and the adjustment of partners’ capital accounts during reconstitution.
steps: The takeaway: Goodwill is valued only when a partnership undergoes a structural change, and its amount depends on the firm’s maintainable profits relative to a normal return, using one of three accepted methods.

Here is why: First, accounting standards prohibit recognising internally generated goodwill unless it is purchased, because its value is subjective; therefore, valuation is triggered only by events that require an…

Second, the average profit method assumes that future maintainable profits will resemble past average profits, and goodwill equals this average multiplied by an agreed number of years’ purchase, reflecting the years…

Third, the super profit method isolates the excess over normal profit (normal profit = capital employed × normal rate of return) and treats goodwill as the present value of that excess, again using years’ purchase.

Fourth, the capitalisation method treats the firm’s average profit as a perpetuity and calculates the capital required to earn that profit at the normal rate; the difference between this capitalised value and actual net…
Consider a firm, “Spice Traders”, with partners A and B sharing profits 3:2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Goodwill is the total capital contributed by partners”) reveals the misconception that goodwill is a tangible, owner‑contributed fund, confusing it with partners’ capital and ignoring its nature as an earned, non‑physical advantage.
remember: State the meaning of goodwill in the context of a partnership firm.
Explain why goodwill is valued only when there is a change in the partnership structure.

cards.title: This node synthesises the entire Chapter 1 – Fundamentals of Partnership – by…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: This node synthesises the entire Chapter 1 – Fundamentals of Partnership – by integrating the statutory framework (Indian Partnership Act 1932, Sections 4, 13, 19, 24‑30), default provisions when a deed is absent, and the accounting mechanics of profit appropriation. It connects the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account (the ledger that distributes net profit) with partner‑level allocations: interest on capital (calculated on opening/closing balances per the deed or at 6 % p.a. under the Act), interest on drawings (charged on amounts withdrawn, using product or average‑period method), partner salary and commission (allowed only if the deed authorises), and transfers to reserves (e.g., General Reserve, Investment Fluctuation Reserve). It distinguishes fixed capital accounts (capital remains constant; current accounts record drawings, interest, share of profit) from fluctuating capital accounts (all transactions directly affect the capital account). The guarantee of profit clause forces the guaranteeing partner(s) to bear any shortfall so the guaranteed partner receives the promised minimum. Past adjustments rectify errors/omissions of prior periods through a Profit & Loss Adjustment Account, impacting current‑year appropriation. Mastery of these inter‑linkages enables a student to construct complete partnership final accounts, answer case‑based ISC questions, and apply the correct statutory defaults when the deed is silent.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that every ISC partnership question ultimately tests whether you can translate the deed (or the Act’s defaults) into a correctly structured Profit & Loss Appropriation Account with…
First, always start by reading the deed clauses: profit‑sharing ratio, interest on capital rate, interest on drawings rate, salary/commission entitlements, reserve policy, and any guarantee.
If a clause is missing, apply the Act’s defaults – equal profit sharing, 6 % p.a. interest on capital, no interest on drawings, no salary/commission, no reserves.
Second, decide the capital method.
Fixed capital means you open a Capital Account (unchanged) and a Current Account for each partner; fluctuating capital merges everything into the Capital Account.
The choice changes where you post interest, drawings, and profit share.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “profit sharing in capital ratio, interest at 12 %”) reveals the misconception that capital contribution determines profit share and that the Act mandates a higher statutory interest rate – confusing the Act with the Companies Act…
remember: State the default profit‑sharing ratio and interest‑on‑capital rate prescribed by the Indian Partnership Act 1932 when the partnership deed is silent.
A partnership deed provides for interest on capital @ 10 % p.a. but is silent on interest on….
Evaluate whether a partner can claim salary for active participation if the partnership deed does not mention salary.

cards.title: Goodwill is an intangible asset representing the future economic benefits…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Goodwill is an intangible asset representing the future economic benefits arising from assets that are not individually identified and separately recognised. It emerges only in a business combination when the purchase consideration exceeds the net fair value of identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed. Under the CISCE ISC syllabus, goodwill is defined as the excess of the purchase price over the aggregate fair value of net assets taken over. It reflects factors such as reputation, customer loyalty, favourable location, efficient management, and synergies expected from the combination. Goodwill is not amortised but is tested annually for impairment in accordance with Accounting Standard (AS) 26 (Intangible Assets) as adopted by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. The concept links directly to the valuation methods covered in subsequent nodes: average profit, super profit, and capitalisation methods each attempt to quantify this excess earning capacity. Goodwill differs from other intangibles (patents, trademarks) because it cannot be sold, licensed, or separated from the business; it exists only as part of the going concern. Recognition criteria require a transaction — either acquisition of a firm or admission/retirement of a partner — that provides objective evidence of its value. Internally generated goodwill, no matter how valuable, is not recorded because it lacks a verifiable transaction price.
steps: Goodwill is the premium paid for a business’s unrecorded earning power — the amount by which purchase consideration exceeds the fair value of identifiable net assets.
Here is why: first, goodwill arises only when a transaction provides an objective market price; without a purchase, there is no verifiable measure.
Second, it captures collective intangible factors — reputation, customer base, location, managerial skill — that individually cannot be valued reliably.
Third, Indian accounting standards (AS 26) prohibit recognition of internally generated goodwill because its value is subjective and cannot be verified by an arm’s‑length transaction.
Fourth, goodwill is inseparable from the entity; it cannot be sold, licensed, or transferred independently, unlike patents or trademarks.
Fifth, once recognised, goodwill is not amortised but is subject to annual impairment review, ensuring the carrying amount does not exceed recoverable amount.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “goodwill is the value of a brand name”) reveals the misconception that any intangible reputation qualifies as goodwill, ignoring the requirement of a purchase transaction and the definition as a residual excess.
remember: Define goodwill in the context of a business combination under Indian GAAP.
Why is internally generated goodwill not recognised in the balance sheet.
Evaluate the statement: “Goodwill can be sold separately like a patent.”.

cards.title: Goodwill is an intangible asset representing the future economic benefits…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Goodwill is an intangible asset representing the future economic benefits arising from assets that are not individually identified and separately recognised. It embodies the collective value of a firm’s brand reputation, customer relationships, skilled workforce, favourable location, proprietary technology, and efficient management. Goodwill arises only on acquisition of a business (purchased goodwill) and is measured as the excess of consideration transferred over the net fair value of identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed. It is non‑separable — it cannot be sold, licensed, or transferred independently of the business. Under ISC accounting standards, purchased goodwill is recognised at cost and subsequently tested for impairment annually; internally generated goodwill is never recognised. The nature of goodwill therefore links three sub‑concepts: (1) intangibility — no physical substance; (2) inseparability — tied to the entity as a whole; (3) acquisition‑dependence — recognised only in a business combination. These features distinguish goodwill from other intangibles such as patents or trademarks, which are identifiable and can be separately valued.
steps: Goodwill is the only intangible asset that cannot exist independently of the business that creates it. Here is why: first, goodwill has no physical form — you cannot store it in a warehouse or display it on a balance…
Consider a family‑owned textile mill in Surat that has supplied premium cotton to loyal retailers for three decades.
Its customer list, supplier goodwill, and skilled weavers generate profits above the industry norm.
When a larger conglomerate acquires the mill, it pays ₹12 crore while the fair value of identifiable net assets (machinery, inventory, land) is ₹8 crore.
The ₹4 crore excess is recorded as purchased goodwill.
If the same mill had simply expanded organically, the extra profit potential would remain unrecognised on its books.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “true, because it cannot be seen”) reveals the misconception that lack of physical substance equates to fictitious status, confusing intangible assets with deferred expenses that are written off over time.
remember: State whether the following statement is true or false: “Goodwill is a fictitious asset because it has no physical existence.”.
Explain why internally generated goodwill is not recognised in the financial statements under ISC accounting standards.
A firm purchases another business for ₹25….

cards.title: Goodwill is an intangible asset that arises when a business earns profits…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Goodwill is an intangible asset that arises when a business earns profits higher than the normal return on its identifiable net assets. Its features are: (1) Intangibility – it has no physical form; (2) Non‑separability – it cannot be sold, transferred, or licensed independently of the business; (3) Arises from reputation – built over time through quality, service, brand name, and customer trust; (4) Dependent on future earnings – its value exists only because the firm is expected to continue generating super‑normal profits; (5) Subjective valuation – no objective market price, so valuation relies on methods such as average profit, super profit, or capitalisation; (6) Inherent to the entity – it attaches to the business as a whole, not to individual assets. These features link directly to the factors that affect its value (location, management efficiency, market position) and to the valuation techniques taught in later nodes.
steps: Goodwill’s features – intangibility, non‑separability, arising from reputation, customer loyalty, location, and efficient management – make it a unique asset that cannot be sold separately and whose value depends on…
First, intangibility means goodwill cannot be touched or seen; it lives in the minds of customers and stakeholders.
Second, non‑separability implies you cannot carve out goodwill and sell it like a machine; it exits only with the business.
Third, reputation‑based origin shows that goodwill is built over years through consistent quality, branding, and service – for example, the “Tata” name commands premium pricing across sectors.
Fourth, earnings dependence ties goodwill to the expectation of super‑normal profits; if a firm’s future earnings fall to normal levels, goodwill evaporates.
Fifth, subjective valuation forces accountants to use estimation techniques (average profit, super profit, capitalisation) because no active market quotes exist.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “goodwill is a tangible asset like machinery”) reveals the misconception that goodwill has physical substance, confusing it with fixed assets.
remember: List any three features of goodwill.
Why can goodwill not be sold separately from the business.
Evaluate the statement: “Goodwill exists only when a firm earns super‑normal profits.”.

cards.title: Goodwill represents the excess value a business commands over its identifiable…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Goodwill represents the excess value a business commands over its identifiable net assets, arising from intangible advantages that generate super‑normal profits. The value of goodwill is not arbitrary; it is shaped by a set of inter‑related factors. Nature of business determines risk and stability — a firm in a regulated, essential‑goods sector (e.g., pharmaceuticals) typically enjoys higher goodwill than a speculative trading concern. Location and infrastructure affect customer access and operational efficiency; a retail outlet in a high‑footfall area of Bengaluru commands a premium. Management competence and personnel quality drive operational consistency; experienced partners and skilled staff reduce earnings volatility. Profitability track record — both average maintainable profits and their trend — directly feeds valuation models such as average‑profit and super‑profit methods. Market share and brand reputation create barriers to entry and pricing power, enhancing future cash flows. Economic and industry conditions (e.g., GST regime stability, RBI interest‑rate cycles) influence expected returns and risk discounts. Future growth prospects — expansion plans, new product pipelines, or favourable demographic shifts — raise the capitalisation rate applied to maintainable profits. These factors interact: strong management can amplify a good location, while adverse industry trends can erode even a historic profit record. Understanding this web of determinants is essential before applying any valuation technique (average profit, super profit, capitalisation) covered in subsequent nodes.
steps: The value of goodwill is driven by a combination of internal strengths and external opportunities that together determine how much extra a buyer will pay over net assets.
First, profitability track record provides the quantitative backbone; consistent, growing maintainable profits signal lower risk and higher capitalisation.
Second, management quality converts resources into profits efficiently; competent partners reduce earnings volatility, a key input for super‑profit calculations.
Third, market position and brand reputation create pricing power and customer loyalty, which sustain future cash flows beyond the current accounting period.
Fourth, location and infrastructure lower operating costs and increase revenue potential — a factory near a port in Gujarat enjoys logistics advantages that a remote unit cannot replicate.
Fifth, future growth prospects such as planned capacity expansion or entry into high‑margin segments raise the expected maintainable profit, directly inflating goodwill under capitalisation methods.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only past profits matter”) reveals the misconception that goodwill is a mechanical multiple of historical profit, ignoring risk and qualitative drivers.
remember: List any four factors that affect the value of goodwill in a partnership firm.
Explain why a firm with consistent profits but poor management may have lower goodwill than a firm with slightly lower profits but strong management.
A firm claims its goodwill is high because it owns a prime location in Mumbai. Critically evaluate this claim considering other factors.

cards.title: The simple average profit method values goodwill by taking the arithmetic mean…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The simple average profit method values goodwill by taking the arithmetic mean of the maintainable profits of a partnership firm over a specified number of past years and multiplying that average by an agreed number of years’ purchase. Maintainable profit excludes abnormal gains/losses, non‑recurring items, and partners’ remuneration not charged to profit and loss. The formula is: Goodwill = (Sum of adjusted profits for n years ÷ n) × Number of years’ purchase. This method assumes future profits will mirror the simple average of past results, ignoring trends or weightage. It is the most basic valuation technique, used when profits are relatively stable and no clear upward or downward pattern exists. The method links directly to the factors affecting goodwill (node 004) — stable earnings, low risk, and consistent management increase the years’ purchase multiplier. It also sets the foundation for the weighted average method (node 006), where recent profits receive higher weights.
steps: The simple average profit method values goodwill by multiplying the arithmetic mean of adjusted past profits by an agreed years’ purchase factor.

Here is why: goodwill represents the extra amount a buyer pays for the firm’s ability to earn above normal returns; when profits are stable, the best proxy for future earnings is the plain average of recent maintainable…
First, gather the profit figures for the chosen number of years (usually 3‑5).
Second, adjust each year’s profit by removing non‑recurring gains (e.g., profit on sale of fixed assets) and adding back abnormal losses (e.g., fire loss not insured).
Also deduct partners’ remuneration if not already charged.
Third, sum the adjusted profits and divide by the number of years to obtain the simple average profit.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Goodwill = Total profit × Years’ purchase”) reveals the misconception that averaging is optional — students confuse total profit with average profit, ignoring the division by the number of years.
remember: State the formula for goodwill under the simple average profit method.
A firm’s profits for three years are ₹1,00,000, ₹1,20,000 and ₹1,40,000. No adjustments are needed. If goodwill is valued at 2 years’ purchase, what is the goodwill amount.
Evaluate whether the simple average profit method is appropriate for a firm whose profits have risen sharply each year: ₹80,000, ₹1,20,000, ₹1,80,000.

cards.title: Weighted average profit method values goodwill by assigning different weights…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Weighted average profit method values goodwill by assigning different weights to profits of past years, reflecting their relevance. Recent years usually receive higher weights because they better represent current earning capacity. The weighted average profit = Σ (Profitᵢ × Weightᵢ) / Σ Weightᵢ. Goodwill = Weighted Average Profit × Number of Years’ Purchase. This method improves on simple average (equal weights) by capturing trends, cyclical fluctuations, or exceptional items. It links directly to the super‑profit and capitalisation methods that follow, as all three start from an adjusted maintainable profit figure. The choice of weights is subjective but must be justified (e.g., 1,2,3,4 for four years). The method assumes profits are comparable after adjustments for non‑recurring items, changes in accounting policy, and capital structure.
steps: The weighted average profit method is the bridge between simple averaging and more sophisticated goodwill models because it lets recent earnings speak louder.
Here is why: goodwill reflects future earning power, and the most recent years are the best proxy for that future.
Consider a partnership that earned ₹2,00,000, ₹2,50,000, ₹3,00,000 and ₹3,50,000 over four years.
Total weights = 1+2+3+4 = 10.
Weighted average profit = ₹30,00,000 / 10 = ₹3,00,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Average Profit = Total Profit / Number of Years”) reveals the misconception that weighted and simple averages are identical — ignoring the role of weights in emphasising recent performance.
remember: State the formula for weighted average profit used in goodwill valuation.
Evaluate the statement: “Weighted average profit method eliminates the need for adjusting profits for non‑recurring items.”.

cards.title: Super profit is the excess of a firm’s average maintainable profit over the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Super profit is the excess of a firm’s average maintainable profit over the normal profit expected on the capital employed at the prevailing normal rate of return. Average profit is derived from past profits (simple or weighted average) after adjusting for abnormal items, non‑recurring incomes/expenses, and partner’s remuneration. Normal profit = Capital Employed × Normal Rate of Return ÷ 100. Capital employed equals net assets (total assets minus outside liabilities) or partners’ capital plus reserves minus fictitious assets. Goodwill under the super‑profit method = Super Profit × Number of Years’ Purchase (the period over which the super profit is expected to continue). This method links goodwill directly to the firm’s ability to generate earnings above the industry benchmark, making it a performance‑based valuation.
steps: Super profit is the extra earning power a firm enjoys over the normal return on its capital, and goodwill equals that super profit multiplied by the agreed years’ purchase.

Here is why: goodwill represents the value of a firm’s reputation, location, customer loyalty, and efficient management — all of which enable it to earn more than a comparable firm with the same capital.

The normal profit is the benchmark return that any investor would expect for the risk undertaken; it is calculated by applying the industry’s normal rate of return to the capital actually employed in the business.
When the firm’s maintainable average profit (after removing abnormal gains/losses and partner’s salary) exceeds this benchmark, the difference is the super profit.
Because super profit is expected to persist for a limited period, the buyer capitalises it for a certain number of years — the years’ purchase — to arrive at the goodwill amount.
Consider a partnership with capital employed ₹10,00,000 and a normal rate of return 12 %.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “super profit is the total profit of the firm”) reveals the misconception that super profit equals total profit, ignoring the benchmark normal return.
remember: Define super profit in the context of goodwill valuation.
A firm’s capital employed is ₹8,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10 %. Its adjusted average profit is ₹1,00,000. Calculate super profit.
Evaluate whether the super‑profit method is appropriate for a start‑up with no profit history.

cards.title: Capitalization methods value goodwill by converting a maintainable profit…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Capitalization methods value goodwill by converting a maintainable profit figure into a capital sum using the normal rate of return (NRR) prevailing in the industry. Two variants exist: 1. Capitalization of Average Profit – Goodwill = (Average Maintainable Profit ÷ NRR) × 100. 2. Capitalization of Super Profit – Goodwill = (Super Profit ÷ NRR) × 100, where Super Profit = Average Maintainable Profit – Normal Profit, and Normal Profit = Capital Employed × NRR ÷ 100. Both methods assume profits will continue indefinitely at the same level and that the NRR reflects the risk of the business. The capitalized value represents the present worth of future profit streams. The methods are linked to the average‑profit and super‑profit approaches (nodes,,) but differ by expressing the result as a capital amount rather than a number of years’ purchase.
steps: Takeaway: Capitalization methods turn a yearly profit figure into a lump‑sum goodwill value by dividing the profit by the normal rate of return and multiplying by 100.
Here is why: Goodwill is the present value of future excess earnings.
If a firm earns ₹2,00,000 average profit and the industry NRR is 12 %, an investor would need to invest ₹16,66,667 (₹2,00,000 ÷ 12 % × 100) to earn that profit at the normal rate.
That invested amount is the capitalized goodwill.
Consider a partnership where capital employed is ₹50,00,000 and NRR is 10 %.
Normal profit = ₹5,00,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “goodwill = average profit × number of years’ purchase”) reveals the misconception that capitalization and years‑purchase are the same method — they differ in that capitalization uses a rate of return, not a purchase multiplier.
remember: Define “capitalization of average profit” in the context of goodwill valuation.
A firm’s average maintainable profit is ₹3,00,000 and the industry NRR is 15 %. Compute goodwill by capitalization of average profit.
Evaluate whether capitalization of super profit will always give a lower goodwill than capitalization of average profit for the same firm.

cards.title: The new profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) is the ratio in which all partners
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The new profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) is the ratio in which all partners (old and newly admitted) will share future profits and losses after a partner is admitted to the firm. It is derived by adjusting each old partner’s original ratio by the amount of share they sacrifice to the incoming partner, while the new partner’s ratio equals the share he acquires. The new PSR therefore reflects the post‑admission ownership structure and serves as the basis for allocating profits, losses, and any subsequent goodwill or revaluation adjustments. It is directly linked to the sacrificing ratio (the proportion of profit given up by existing partners) and the gaining ratio (the proportion gained by the new partner), but in this node we focus only on calculating the new PSR itself, leaving the detailed mechanics of sacrificing/gaining ratios to the sibling nodes.
steps: The new profit‑sharing ratio shows exactly how profits will be divided after a new partner joins.

Here is why: the admission transaction reallocates ownership without dissolving the firm, so each old partner’s claim shrinks by the portion they sell to the newcomer, while the newcomer’s claim equals what he bought.
Step 1 – Identify the old PSR. Suppose A, B and C share profits 3:2:1 (total 6 parts).
Step 2 – Determine the share the new partner buys.
If D is admitted for 1/4 of the future profits, he must acquire that fraction from the existing partners.
Step 3 – Allocate the purchase among the old partners according to their sacrifice ratio (given or assumed equal to old ratio if not specified).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “new PSR = 5:3:1”) reveals the misconception that the new partner’s share is simply appended without reducing the old partners’ shares, ignoring the sacrifice required.
remember: State the new profit‑sharing ratio when X and Y share profits 5:3 and admit Z for 1/5 share, assuming Z acquires his share equally from X and Y.
A firm’s old PSR is 4:3:2. If a new partner is admitted for 1/6 share and the sacrificing ratio among the old partners is 2:1:0, calculate the new PSR.
Evaluate the statement: “The new profit‑sharing ratio after admission is always the old ratio plus the new partner’s share.”.

cards.title: The sacrificing ratio is the proportion in which existing partners surrender…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The sacrificing ratio is the proportion in which existing partners surrender their share of profits to accommodate a newly admitted partner. It is calculated as the difference between each partner’s old profit‑sharing ratio and their new profit‑sharing ratio after admission (Sacrificing Ratio = Old Share – New Share). This ratio is directly linked to the new profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) discussed in the previous node; once the new PSR is known, the sacrificing ratio follows. The sacrificing ratio is the counterpart of the gaining ratio (covered in the next node), which shows how much the remaining partners gain when a partner retires or the PSR changes. In the admission process, the sacrificing ratio determines how much of the incoming partner’s premium for goodwill (or hidden goodwill) is credited to each existing partner’s capital account, and it also guides adjustments to reserves and revaluation accounts. Thus, sacrificing ratio bridges the calculation of the new PSR with the accounting treatments of goodwill, capital, and reserves that appear in later nodes.
steps: The sacrificing ratio shows how much each existing partner gives up in profit share when a new partner is admitted.
Here is why: 1.
It is derived directly from the change in each partner’s share, making it a straightforward arithmetic difference. 2.
It determines the distribution of the incoming partner’s premium for goodwill, ensuring that the sacrifice is compensated. 3.
It is the mirror image of the gaining ratio, so understanding one clarifies the other. 4.
It links the new PSR (already calculated) to the accounting adjustments that follow.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “New Ratio – Old Ratio”) reveals the misconception that the ratio measures gain rather than sacrifice, confusing the direction of change.
remember: State the formula for calculating a partner’s sacrificing ratio on admission of a new partner.
X, Y, and Z share profits in the ratio 4:3:2. They admit W for a 1/4 share. Calculate the sacrificing ratio of X, Y, and Z.
Evaluate the statement: “The sacrificing ratio of a partner can never be zero.”.

cards.title: The gaining ratio is the proportion in which existing partners acquire an…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The gaining ratio is the proportion in which existing partners acquire an additional share of profit when the profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) changes—most commonly on the admission of a new partner or when partners mutually decide to reshare profits. It is computed as the difference between each partner’s new profit‑sharing ratio and his/her old ratio (New – Old). A positive result indicates a gain; a negative result indicates a sacrifice (which is the sacrificing ratio). The gaining ratio is directly linked to the sacrificing ratio: the total gain of the gaining partners equals the total sacrifice of the sacrificing partners, ensuring the total profit share remains unity. In admission problems, the gaining ratio is used to allocate any goodwill premium brought by the incoming partner to the existing partners in proportion to their gains. It also determines how reserves, accumulated profits/losses, and capital adjustments are distributed when the PSR changes without a new partner. Understanding gaining ratio clarifies why the old partners’ capital accounts are credited or debited, and it sets the stage for subsequent topics such as goodwill treatment (AS‑26), revaluation, and hidden goodwill.
steps: The gaining ratio tells us exactly how much each existing partner’s profit share increases when the profit‑sharing ratio changes.
Here is why: 1.
It is derived directly from the definition of profit share—new share minus old share. 2.
It balances the sacrificing ratio, ensuring total profit share remains 100 %. 3.
It serves as the allocation basis for any financial adjustments (goodwill, reserves, capital) that accompany a PSR change. 4.
It distinguishes between partners who gain and those who sacrifice, preventing double‑counting in adjustments. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Old ratio – New ratio”) reveals the misconception that the order of subtraction does not matter, confusing gaining with sacrificing.
remember: State the formula for calculating a partner’s gaining ratio.
If a partner’s gaining ratio comes out negative, what does it indicate about that partner’s position in the PSR change.
Evaluate the statement: “In every admission of a partner, the gaining ratio of the old partners is always positive.”.

cards.title: Under Accounting Standard 26 (AS‑26)…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Under Accounting Standard 26 (AS‑26), goodwill is an intangible asset recognised only when purchased. In a partnership admission, the premium method applies when the incoming partner brings goodwill in cash (or cash equivalent). The cash received is debited to Bank/Cash Account and credited to the old partners’ Capital Accounts in their sacrificing ratio — the proportion of profit share each old partner gives up to accommodate the new partner. This treatment ensures that the premium compensates the old partners for the loss of future profits. If the old partners withdraw the premium, their Capital Accounts are debited and Bank credited. If the premium is retained, it remains as part of the firm’s capital. The method differs from the revaluation method (where goodwill is raised and written off) and from hidden goodwill (where goodwill is inferred from capital contributions). The premium method directly links the cash inflow to the sacrifice made, preserving the integrity of the capital structure and complying with AS‑26’s requirement that purchased goodwill be recognised at cost.
steps: Under AS‑26, goodwill premium brought in cash by an incoming partner is credited to the old partners’ capital accounts in their sacrificing ratio, ensuring the premium reflects the value of the firm’s reputation.
Here is why: the sacrificing ratio quantifies exactly how much each old partner gives up; the premium compensates that sacrifice.
Consider a firm where A and B share profits 3:2.
They admit C for 1/5th share, acquiring it 2/5 from A and 1/5 from B. The sacrificing ratio is 2:1.
If C brings ₹1,00,000 goodwill cash, A receives ₹66,667 and B ₹33,333.
The journal entry: Bank Dr. ₹1,00,000 → A’s Capital Cr. ₹66,667, B’s Capital Cr. ₹33,333.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “goodwill is debited to Goodwill Account”) reveals the misconception that goodwill must always appear as an asset — confusing purchased goodwill with internally generated goodwill, which AS‑26 does not recognise.
remember: What is the premium method of goodwill treatment per AS‑26.
Why is goodwill premium shared in the sacrificing ratio rather than the old profit‑sharing ratio.
A firm admits a partner who brings ₹50,000 goodwill….

cards.title: Hidden goodwill arises on admission of a partner when the capital brought by…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Hidden goodwill arises on admission of a partner when the capital brought by the new partner implies a total firm value higher than the combined capital of all partners after admission. Under AS‑26, goodwill can be recognised only when purchased; hidden goodwill is not recorded as an asset but is adjusted through the partners’ capital accounts. The implied total capital = New Partner’s Capital ÷ New Partner’s Profit Share. Hidden Goodwill = Implied Total Capital – (Old Partners’ Combined Capital + New Partner’s Capital). This goodwill is credited to old partners in their sacrificing ratio (or old profit‑sharing ratio if sacrificing ratio not given) and debited to the new partner’s capital account if the new partner brings less than the proportionate capital. The adjustment ensures that the capital accounts reflect the true economic value of the firm without violating AS‑26’s prohibition on recognising self‑generated goodwill. It links directly to the new profit‑sharing ratio (node), sacrificing ratio, and the premium method of goodwill. Subsequent revaluation and capital adjustments build on this figure.
steps: Hidden goodwill is the unrecorded value of a firm revealed when a new partner’s capital contribution implies a higher total capital than the book values show.
Here is why: when a partner is admitted, the firm’s value is often negotiated informally.

The new partner pays a premium for goodwill, but if that premium is not routed through a goodwill account (as AS‑26 forbids recognising self‑generated goodwill), the excess value stays hidden in the capital accounts.
First, identify the new partner’s share (e.g., 1/5) and the capital they bring (e.g., ₹50,000).
The implied total capital = ₹50,000 ÷ (1/5) = ₹2,50,000.
Next, sum the old partners’ capitals after any revaluation (say ₹1,80,000) and add the new partner’s capital (₹50,000) = ₹2,30,000.

cards.title: The Revaluation Account (also called Profit and Loss Adjustment Account) is a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Revaluation Account (also called Profit and Loss Adjustment Account) is a nominal account prepared at the time of reconstitution of a partnership — specifically on admission of a partner — to ascertain the net effect of revaluing assets and reassessing liabilities. All increases in asset values (e.g., land appreciation, stock revaluation) and decreases in liabilities (e.g., provision for doubtful debts written back) are credited; all decreases in asset values (e.g., depreciation on machinery, bad debts written off) and increases in liabilities (e.g., outstanding expenses recognised) are debited. The balance — Revaluation Profit (credit side > debit side) or Revaluation Loss (debit side > credit side) — is transferred to the old partners’ capital accounts in their old profit‑sharing ratio (PSR). This ensures that the incoming partner does not share in gains or losses arising from events before his admission. The account is temporary; it is closed after the transfer. It links directly to the Capital Adjustment node where revised capitals are worked out, and follows the Goodwill Treatment node (/005) because goodwill may also be recognised through revaluation. The Revaluation Account does not affect the new partner’s capital; it only adjusts the old partners’ capitals.
steps: The Revaluation Account captures every change in asset and liability values at the moment a new partner joins, and the resulting profit or loss belongs solely to the old partners in their old profit‑sharing ratio.
Here is why: the new partner’s capital should reflect only the future earning capacity of the firm, not past unrealised gains or losses.
Therefore, any appreciation of land, revaluation of stock, or write‑back of provisions is credited to the Revaluation Account; any depreciation, bad debts, or newly recognised liabilities is debited.
The net balance is then transferred to the old partners’ capital accounts.

They admit C for 1/5th share.

cards.title: Accumulated profits/losses and reserves
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Accumulated profits/losses and reserves (General Reserve, Profit & Loss Account credit balance, Investment Fluctuation Fund, Workmen Compensation Fund, etc.) belong to the old partners in their old profit‑sharing ratio (old PSR). On admission of a new partner, these balances are not shared with the incoming partner; instead they are distributed (or written off) among the old partners by crediting/debiting their capital/current accounts in the old PSR. Key relationships: - Old PSR (from node) determines each old partner’s share. - Sacrificing ratio (node) is irrelevant here because reserves are not sacrificed; they are fully allocated to old partners. - Revaluation Account (node) deals with asset/liability re‑measurement; reserves adjustment is a separate ledger entry. - Goodwill (nodes, 005) is valued and treated separately; it does not affect reserve distribution. - After reserves are adjusted, the capital accounts reflect the updated balances, which then feed into capital adjustments (node) such as bringing capitals to proportionate amounts or adjusting for goodwill premium. The journal entry for a credit balance (accumulated profit/reserve): `Reserve A/c Dr. → Old Partners’ Capital/Current A/c Cr. (in old PSR)` For a debit balance (accumulated loss): `Old Partners’ Capital/Current A/c Dr. (in old PSR) → Profit & Loss A/c Cr.` No entry involves the new partner’s capital account.
steps: Takeaway: On admission, all accumulated profits, losses and reserves are exclusively allocated to the old partners in their old profit‑sharing ratio; the new partner receives none of these balances.
Here is why: the reserves were built from profits earned before the new partner’s entry, so only those who contributed to those profits — the old partners — are entitled to them.
The new partner’s capital starts afresh, and any future profits will be shared per the new PSR. Supporting arguments: 1.
Legal ownership – Reserves are part of the firm’s net assets belonging to the partners in their profit‑sharing ratio at the time the profits arose.
Admission does not retroactively change that ownership. 2.
Accounting standard – AS‑26 (Intangible Assets) and the Partnership Act require that pre‑admission reserves be distributed before the new partner’s capital is recognised. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “distribute in the new profit‑sharing ratio”) reveals the misconception that admission retroactively changes entitlement to past profits, confusing the timing of profit generation with the new sharing arrangement.

cards.title: Capital adjustments at admission of a partner refer to the process of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Capital adjustments at admission of a partner refer to the process of realigning the capital accounts of all partners (old and new) so that the final capital balances reflect the agreed new profit‑sharing ratio (PSR). This realignment incorporates several elements: the new partner’s capital contribution (cash or assets), the share of goodwill brought in (premium method) or raised (hidden goodwill), the net effect of revaluation of assets and liabilities, and the distribution of accumulated profits or losses (reserves). The adjustment can be effected through (a) cash infusion by the new partner, (b) transfer between partners’ current accounts, or (c) proportionate capital method where each partner’s capital is made proportionate to the new PSR by bringing in or withdrawing cash. Journal entries debit/credit Partner’s Capital Accounts, Cash/Bank, Goodwill, Revaluation Account, and Reserve Accounts. The objective is to ensure that after admission, each partner’s capital bears the same proportion to total capital as their profit‑sharing ratio, maintaining equity and compliance with AS‑26 for goodwill recognition.
steps: Capital adjustment ensures that after a new partner’s admission, every partner’s capital is in the same proportion as the new profit‑sharing ratio.

Here is why: the profit‑sharing ratio determines how future profits and losses are divided; if capital balances are not aligned, a partner with a higher capital share than profit share would effectively subsidise…
First, determine the total adjusted capital of the firm after accounting for goodwill, revaluation profit/loss, and reserves.
This total becomes the base for the new capital structure.
Second, calculate each partner’s target capital by multiplying the total adjusted capital by their new PSR fraction.
Third, compare each partner’s existing capital (after goodwill, revaluation, reserves) with the target.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to increase the firm’s total capital”) reveals the misconception that admission automatically requires raising capital, ignoring that adjustment may involve only reallocation among existing partners.

cards.title: A change in profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) occurs when the existing partners of a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A change in profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) occurs when the existing partners of a partnership firm agree to alter the proportion in which they share future profits and losses. This change may arise on admission, retirement, death, or by mutual agreement without any change in the firm’s constitution. The old ratio is replaced by a new ratio, and the difference between the two determines each partner’s sacrificing ratio (old share − new share, if positive) or gaining ratio (new share − old share, if positive). The reconstitution triggers accounting adjustments: revaluation of assets and liabilities, treatment of goodwill (per AS‑26), distribution of accumulated profits/reserves, and capital account realignment. These adjustments ensure that the partners’ capital balances reflect their revised entitlements. The concept links directly to the sibling nodes on new PSR, sacrificing/gaining ratios, goodwill treatment, hidden goodwill, revaluation account, reserves adjustments, and capital adjustments, but this node focuses on the overarching principle that any change in PSR necessitates a systematic accounting process to maintain equity among partners.
steps: The one thing to remember: Any change in profit‑sharing ratio forces a complete accounting reconstitution so that each partner’s capital reflects the new entitlement.
Here is why: (1) The old ratio no longer represents the economic reality;
(2) Partners who sacrifice deserve compensation (goodwill, revaluation gains);
(3) Partners who gain must contribute to those sacrifices;
(4) Accumulated reserves belong to the old ratio and must be redistributed;
(5) Capital accounts must be realigned to the new ratio to avoid future disputes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “change in PSR only affects new partners”) reveals the misconception that existing partners’ entitlements remain untouched — ignoring that even mutual ratio changes among existing partners trigger reconstitution.
remember: Define “change in profit‑sharing ratio” in a partnership firm and state the two key ratios derived from it.
Explain why the sacrificing ratio is calculated only for partners whose share decreases, and why the gaining ratio is calculated only for partners whose share increases.
Evaluate the statement: “When the profit‑sharing ratio changes, only the goodwill account needs adjustment; revaluation and reserves are irrelevant.”.

cards.title: The new profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) is the proportion in which the continuing…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The new profit‑sharing ratio (PSR) is the proportion in which the continuing partners share future profits after a partner retires or dies. It is derived by adjusting each continuing partner’s old PSR by the share they gain from the departing partner. The gaining ratio expresses how the retiring/deceased partner’s share is distributed among the continuers; it may be agreed upon, based on capital ratios, or equal. Conversely, if a partner is admitted, the existing partners sacrifice a portion of their share, and the sacrificing ratio works similarly but in reverse. The new PSR therefore equals: New PSR = Old PSR + Gaining Ratio (for each continuer). When the departing partner’s share includes goodwill, undistributed profits, or revaluation gains/losses, those amounts are first adjusted via the revaluation account and then transferred to partners’ capital accounts in the new PSR. Thus, the new PSR is the pivotal link that connects gaining/sacrificing ratios, goodwill adjustment (including hidden goodwill), treatment of undistributed reserves, deceased partner’s profit to date, and subsequent capital readjustment. Understanding this ratio ensures correct allocation of all subsequent adjustments in reconstitution.
steps: The new profit‑sharing ratio is the revised share each continuing partner holds after a partner leaves, and it is calculated by adding the partner’s gained portion to their old share.
Here is why: When a partner retires or dies, their share of future profits does not vanish; it must be absorbed by the remaining partners.
The manner of absorption is defined by the gaining ratio, which reflects the agreement (or default rule) on how the departing partner’s share is split.
By adding each continuer’s gained portion to their existing share, we obtain the new PSR that governs all subsequent profit distribution and adjustments.
Consider a firm with partners A, B, and C sharing profits 5:3:2.
C retires, and the partners agree that A and B will gain C’s share in the ratio of their existing capitals, which are ₹4,00,000 and ₹2,00,000 respectively (i.e., 2:1).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the new PSR is the same as the old PSR because the retiring partner’s share is simply removed”) reveals the misconception that the retiring partner’s share disappears, ignoring that it must be absorbed by the continuers.
