Evaluate the statement: “Overdrafts of partners should be added to their capital accounts because they represent extra funds contributed by the partners.”.

cards.title: Dissolution of a partnership firm is the process of winding up the business…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Dissolution of a partnership firm is the process of winding up the business, settling all obligations, and distributing the remaining assets among partners according to their rights. This node synthesises the procedural elements covered in the sibling nodes: the legal framework under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 (which governs the mode of settlement), the memorandum balance sheet (a snapshot of assets and liabilities before realisation), the realisation account (which records the sale of assets and payment of liabilities to ascertain profit or loss on dissolution), partners’ loan accounts (separate from capital, treated as external liabilities), capital accounts (showing each partner’s interest), cash/bank accounts (tracking actual receipts and payments), treatment of reserves (general reserve, workmen compensation fund, etc., transferred to partners’ capital in profit‑sharing ratio), overdrafts (shown as a liability in the memorandum balance sheet and paid off during realisation), and realisation expenses (costs incurred in the dissolution process, debited to the realisation account). By integrating these components, students can prepare a complete set of dissolution accounts, verify that the accounting equation remains balanced, and understand how each element influences the final amount distributable to partners. The synthesis also highlights exam‑oriented patterns: marks are allocated for correct journal entries, ledger postings, working notes, and the final balance sheet or cash‑bank statement.
steps: The key takeaway is that a dissolution problem is solved by systematically converting the memorandum balance sheet into a set of ledger accounts that ultimately reveal the cash available for distribution to partners.

Here is why: first, the memorandum balance sheet provides the opening balances of all assets and liabilities; second, the realisation account captures the profit or loss on turning those assets into cash and settling…
Consider a firm with assets of ₹2,00,000 (including stock ₹80,000, debtors ₹70,000, furniture ₹50,000) and liabilities of ₹1,20,000 (creditors ₹90,000, bank overdraft ₹30,000).
Partners A and B share profits 3:2 and have capital balances of ₹1,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 respectively, plus a partner’s loan of ₹40,000 from A. The memorandum balance sheet lists these figures.

Step 1: Open the realisation account; debit all assets at book value (₹2,00,000) and credit liabilities (creditors ₹90,000, overdraft ₹30,000) and the partners’ loan (₹40,000) as they are to be settled.
Step 2: Record the actual sale of assets: suppose stock realised ₹75,000, debtors ₹68,000, furniture ₹48,000; total realised ₹1,91,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is used to calculate the firm’s goodwill”) reveals the misconception that the memorandum balance sheet measures intangible value, whereas it merely lists existing tangible and financial items at their recorded amounts.
remember: State the purpose of preparing a memorandum balance sheet in the dissolution of a partnership firm.
A firm has a general reserve of ₹60,000 and partners share profits in the ratio 5:3. How is the reserve treated on dissolution.
Explain why partners’ loan accounts are shown as liabilities in the memorandum balance sheet and not as part of capital.

cards.title: The “Issue of Shares” chapter covers the complete life‑cycle of a company’s…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The “Issue of Shares” chapter covers the complete life‑cycle of a company’s equity capital raise under the Companies Act 2013. It begins with the statutory framework that permits a company to issue shares at par (face value) or at a premium (above face value), and the accounting treatment for the premium received in the Securities Premium Reserve. The chapter then examines non‑cash consideration — shares issued to promoters, underwriters, and vendors — and the valuation principles that govern such issues. Subsequent sections deal with the mechanics of call money: calls in arrears (unpaid call amounts) and calls in advance (pre‑paid call amounts) together with the interest provisions prescribed by the Act (typically 10 % p.a. on arrears and 12 % p.a. on advance). The concepts of over‑subscription and under‑subscription are introduced, followed by the pro‑rata allotment method used when applications exceed the offered shares. The chapter concludes with forfeiture of shares for non‑payment of calls, the accounting for re‑issue of forfeited shares at par, premium, or discount, and the disclosure requirements for share capital in the Balance Sheet as per Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013. Together, these sub‑topics form a coherent narrative from capital raising to final financial‑statement presentation.
steps: This chapter teaches how a company raises capital by issuing shares, covering every stage from pricing to balance‑sheet disclosure under the Companies Act 2013.

First, the Act authorises a company to issue shares either at face value (par) or above face value (premium); the premium is not revenue but a capital receipt credited to the Securities Premium Reserve, which can later…

Second, shares may be issued for consideration other than cash — to promoters for their services, to underwriters for underwriting commission, or to vendors for assets purchased — and each requires a fair valuation to…

Third, the company collects the issue price in instalments called “calls”; if a shareholder fails to pay a call, the amount becomes “calls in arrears” attracting interest at 10 % p.a., while early payment creates “calls…

Fourth, when applications exceed the shares offered (over‑subscription), the company may allot proportionately (pro‑rata) and adjust excess application money towards subsequent calls; under‑subscription triggers a…

Fifth, persistent non‑payment leads to forfeiture — the shareholder loses the amount already paid, and the forfeited shares become the company’s property; they can be re‑issued at par, premium, or discount, with any…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “issue, allotment, forfeiture, dividend”) reveals the misconception that dividend declaration is part of the issue process, confusing post‑issue profit distribution with capital‑raising steps.
remember: List the four main stages of share issue covered in this chapter.
Explain why a company might issue shares at a premium rather than at par.
Assess the impact of forfeiture and reissue of shares on the company's equity structure.

cards.title: Issue of shares at par means the issue price equals the nominal (face) value of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Issue of shares at par means the issue price equals the nominal (face) value of the share. No premium or discount arises; the full amount received is credited to the Share Capital Account. Issue of shares at a premium means the issue price exceeds the face value. The excess amount is credited to the Securities Premium Account as mandated by Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013. This account is a capital reserve and cannot be distributed as dividend; it may be applied only for purposes such as writing off preliminary expenses, issue expenses, commission, or for issuing fully paid bonus shares. The journal entry for a premium issue debits Bank with the total issue price, credits Share Capital with the face value, and credits Securities Premium with the premium amount. Disclosure in the Balance Sheet shows Share Capital at face value and Securities Premium under “Reserves and Surplus”. The concept links directly to the later topics of calls in arrears/advance, forfeiture, re‑issue, and balance‑sheet presentation.
steps: When a company issues shares at par, the issue price equals the face value; when issued at a premium, the excess over face value is credited to the Securities Premium Account as per Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013.
Here is why: the Act treats premium as a capital receipt that strengthens the company’s net worth without increasing the nominal capital.
Therefore, it must be kept in a separate reserve and used only for prescribed purposes.
Consider a company with an authorised capital of ₹1 crore divided into 10 lakh shares of ₹10 each.
It issues 2 lakh shares at par. Bank is debited ₹20 lakh, Share Capital credited ₹20 lakh.
No premium account arises.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., crediting the full ₹65,000 to Share Capital) reveals the misconception that premium forms part of nominal capital, ignoring the statutory requirement to keep it separate under Section 52.
remember: A company issues 5,000 shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹3 per share. State the journal entry.
Explain why the Securities Premium Account cannot be used for declaring dividends.
A student argues that issuing shares at a premium increases the authorised capital of the company. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Consideration other than cash: promoters refers to the issuance of shares to…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Consideration other than cash: promoters refers to the issuance of shares to the promoters of a company in exchange for non‑cash assets (land, building, machinery, patents, goodwill, services rendered, etc.) or for the settlement of preliminary expenses incurred before incorporation. Under the Companies Act 2013 (Section 62(1)(c) and Schedule III), such shares may be issued at par (face value) or at a premium (above face value). The transaction is recorded by debiting the relevant asset/expense account and crediting Share Capital (face value) and Securities Premium (if any). The valuation of the non‑cash consideration must be fair and supported by a registered valuer’s report; otherwise the issue may be deemed voidable. This concept links directly to the earlier node on Issue at par and premium and sets the stage for underwriters who may also receive shares for services.
steps: Shares issued to promoters for non‑cash consideration increase both the company’s asset base and its share capital without any cash inflow.
Here is why: promoters often contribute property, intellectual property, or pre‑incorporation expenses to the new company.
The Companies Act 2013 mandates that such consideration be valued by a registered valuer and approved by the board; the shares are then allotted at a price decided by the board (par or premium).
The accounting entry mirrors a cash issue — debit the asset/expense received, credit Share Capital at face value, and credit Securities Premium for any excess.

For example, if a promoter transfers a factory valued at ₹1 crore for 1 lakh shares of ₹10 face value issued at ₹100 each, the company debits Factory ₹1 crore, credits Share Capital ₹10 lakh (1 lakh × ₹10) and…
The same logic applies when promoters are allotted shares for services rendered (e.g., legal fees) — the expense account is debited.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only a board resolution is enough”) reveals the misconception that valuation is optional — confusing promoter issues with cash issues where no external valuation is required.
remember: What is the minimum legal requirement for issuing shares to promoters for non‑cash consideration under the Companies Act 2013.
A promoter transfers a patent valued at ₹40 lakh to a company and receives 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value issued at ₹100 each. Write the journal entry.
Evaluate whether a company can issue shares to promoters at a discount for non‑cash consideration.

cards.title: An underwriter is a financial intermediary
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: An underwriter is a financial intermediary (bank, broker, or institution) that enters into an underwriting agreement with a company issuing shares. The underwriter guarantees subscription of a specified number of shares: if the public applies for fewer shares, the underwriter purchases the shortfall. In return, the company pays an underwriting commission, capped at 5 % of the issue price under Section 40(6) of the Companies Act 2013. The commission is an issue expense, debited to Underwriting Commission Account (or Share Issue Expenses) and credited to Underwriters’ Account. When the underwriter pays the commission or takes up shares, the Underwriters’ Account is settled via Bank or Share Capital (and Securities Premium, if issued at premium). Underwriting differs from firm‑commitment underwriting (where the underwriter buys the entire issue) and from best‑efforts arrangements. The accounting entries ensure the commission is recognised as a cost of raising capital, while any shares taken up by underwriters increase share capital exactly like public subscriptions.
steps: Underwriters guarantee that a company’s share issue will be fully subscribed, earning a commission capped at 5 % of the issue price.
Here is why: the Companies Act 2013 limits the commission to protect shareholders from excessive issue costs.
Consider a company issuing 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2.
The issue price is ₹12.
The maximum commission = 5 % × ₹12 × 1,00,000 = ₹6,00,000.
The company debits Underwriting Commission A/c (or Share Issue Expenses) ₹6,00,000 and credits Underwriters A/c ₹6,00,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “underwriter is a promoter who buys shares at par”) reveals confusion between underwriters and promoters — underwriters are independent intermediaries, not founders.
remember: Define an underwriter in the context of a company’s share issue and state the maximum commission permitted under the Companies Act 2013.
Explain why the Companies Act 2013 restricts underwriting commission to 5 % of the issue price.
A company issues 2,00,000 shares of ₹10 each at a premium of….

cards.title: Issue of shares to vendors occurs when a company acquires assets
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Issue of shares to vendors occurs when a company acquires assets (land, building, machinery, patents, etc.) or services from a vendor and settles the consideration by allotting its own equity shares. Under the Companies Act 2013, the shares may be issued at par, at a premium, or at a discount (subject to Section 53 restrictions). The vendor is treated as a subscriber to the share capital; the transaction is recorded by debiting the relevant asset account at the fair value of the consideration and crediting Share Capital (face value) and Securities Premium (if any). If shares are issued at a discount, the discount is debited to “Discount on Issue of Shares” and later written off. The vendor’s name appears in the Register of Members, and the allotment must comply with the authorised capital limit and any special resolution requirements for issue at discount. This concept links to “Consideration other than cash” (promoters, underwriters) and precedes the treatment of calls in arrears/advance, over‑/under‑subscription, and forfeiture/re‑issue.
steps: Takeaway: When a company pays a vendor with its own shares, the asset acquired is recorded at the agreed purchase consideration and the share capital is increased by the face value of shares allotted, with any premium…
Here is why: the vendor becomes a shareholder, so the transaction is an equity issue, not a cash purchase.
The Companies Act 2013 requires that shares issued for consideration other than cash be valued at the fair value of the asset or service received.
If the issue price exceeds face value, the excess is a premium; if it is below face value, the shortfall is a discount (allowed only under strict conditions).
Consider a company that buys machinery worth ₹10,00,000 from M/s Sharma & Co. and agrees to issue 10,000 equity shares of ₹100 each at a premium of ₹20 per share.

The journal entry: Machinery A/c Dr. 10,00,000 To Share Capital A/c (10,000 × ₹100) 10,00,000 To Securities Premium A/c (10,000 × ₹20) 2,00,000 (Being machinery purchased and shares issued at premium).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., crediting the full ₹75,000 to Share Capital) reveals the misconception that the entire consideration increases share capital, ignoring the distinction between face value and premium.
remember: A company issues 5,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹5 per share to a vendor for machinery valued at ₹75,000. State the correct journal entry.
Explain why a discount on issue of shares to a vendor is debited to “Discount on Issue of Shares” and not directly to the vendor’s account.
A company purchases a building worth ₹20,00,000 from a vendor and issues equity shares of ₹100 each at a discount of 10….

cards.title: Calls in arrears arise when a shareholder fails to pay the amount due on a call…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Calls in arrears arise when a shareholder fails to pay the amount due on a call (e.g., allotment, first call, final call) by the due date. The company may charge interest on the unpaid amount at a rate not exceeding 10 % per annum as per Table F of Schedule I to the Companies Act 2013, unless the Articles prescribe a lower rate. The interest accrues from the due date until actual payment and is credited to the Calls‑in‑Arrears Account (or directly to Interest on Calls‑in‑Arrears). Calls in advance occur when a shareholder pays a call amount before it is due. The company must pay interest on such advance at a rate not exceeding 12 % per annum (Table F) from the date of receipt to the due date of the call. The amount is credited to Calls‑in‑Advance Account and the interest paid is debited to Interest on Calls‑in‑Advance. Both items are disclosed in the Balance Sheet: calls in arrears are deducted from the called‑up capital under “Share Capital”, while calls in advance are shown under “Current Liabilities” as a separate line item. Journal entries for receipt, interest accrual, and payment follow the double‑entry system and are recorded in the Cash Book, Calls‑in‑Arrears/Advance Ledger, and Interest Accounts. The concept links to earlier nodes on share issue (par/premium, vendors, underwriters) and leads into over/under‑subscription and forfeiture.
steps: Takeaway: Calls in arrears and calls in advance are two sides of the same timing mismatch — one penalises late payment, the other rewards early payment — and both are governed by statutory interest ceilings that must be…

Here is why: The Companies Act 2013 (Table F) sets a ceiling of 10 % p.a. on arrears and 12 % p.a. on advances to protect shareholders from excessive charges while giving companies a tool to manage cash flow.

When a call is made, the company debits Call Account and credits Share Capital; if a shareholder does not pay, the unpaid portion moves to Calls‑in‑Arrears (a debit balance) and interest is accrued by debiting Interest…

Conversely, early payment creates a credit balance in Calls‑in‑Advance; the company credits Interest on Calls‑in‑Advance (expense) and debits Calls‑in‑Advance when the call falls due. Consider a company that makes a…
Shareholder A defaults on 200 shares;
Shareholder B pays the call on 150 shares two months early.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “12 %”) reveals confusion with the ceiling for calls in advance, which is 12 % p.a. — students often swap the two ceilings because both appear in the same Table.
remember: What is the maximum rate of interest a company may charge on calls in arrears as per Table F of the Companies Act 2013.
A shareholder pays the second call of ₹30 per share on 500 shares three months before the due….
Evaluate the statement: “Calls in advance are shown as a deduction from share capital in the Balance Sheet.”.

cards.title: Over‑subscription occurs when applications for shares exceed the number of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Over‑subscription occurs when applications for shares exceed the number of shares offered for subscription. Under‑subscription is the opposite: applications received are fewer than the shares offered. Both situations require the company to follow the Companies Act 2013 and SEBI (ICDR) Regulations for allotment. In over‑subscription, the company may (i) reject excess applications and refund money, (ii) make a pro‑rata allotment where each applicant receives shares in proportion to his application, or (iii) combine both. The excess application money is first adjusted towards allotment and call money; any remaining balance is refunded. In under‑subscription, the company must ensure the minimum subscription (90 % of the issue) is received; otherwise the entire issue fails and all money is refunded. Journal entries record application money received, allotment due, calls made, and adjustments/refunds. The concept links directly to pro‑rata allotment (next node) and to calls in arrears/advance (previous node) because excess or short application money influences subsequent call receipts and interest calculations.
steps: Takeaway: Over‑subscription and under‑subscription are the two possible outcomes of a public issue, and the Companies Act 2013 mandates a minimum 90 % subscription; the company must then allot shares either by rejecting…
Here is why: when a company invites the public to subscribe, the number of applications received determines the next accounting steps.
If applications exceed the issue size, the company cannot allot more shares than offered; it must decide a fair basis.

The law permits three routes — outright rejection of excess applications with full refund, pro‑rata allotment where each applicant gets a proportionate number of shares, or a combination where some applicants are…
In every case, the application money already received is first applied towards the allotment money due; any surplus is then adjusted against future calls or refunded.
If applications fall short of the 90 % threshold, the issue fails and the entire application money must be returned within the prescribed period.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “75 %”) reveals the misconception that the threshold is the same as the erstwhile Companies Act 1956 requirement, confusing the old and current law.
remember: State the statutory minimum subscription a public company must achieve under the Companies Act 2013 for an issue to be valid.
A company issues 2,00,000 shares.….
Evaluate the following statement: “In case of over‑subscription, the company must refund the entire excess application money immediately without any adjustment.”.

cards.title: Pro‑rata allotment is the method prescribed under Section 39 of the Companies…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Pro‑rata allotment is the method prescribed under Section 39 of the Companies Act 2013 for distributing shares when applications exceed the number of shares offered (over‑subscription). The company allots shares to each applicant in the proportion (Shares applied for × Shares offered) ÷ Total shares applied for. The excess application money is either refunded or adjusted against subsequent calls (allotment, first call, etc.). This mechanism ensures equitable treatment of all applicants, maintains the company’s capital structure, and complies with SEBI’s ICDR Regulations on minimum subscription and allotment norms. It links directly to the earlier concept of over‑subscription (node) and sets the stage for accounting of calls in arrears/advance (node) and later forfeiture (node).
steps: Pro‑rata allotment is the fair‑share rule that kicks in whenever a public issue is over‑subscribed.
Here is why: the Companies Act 2013 mandates that no applicant can be favoured; each must receive shares in the same ratio as their application bears to total applications.
Consider a company offering 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each.
Applications pour in for 3,00,000 shares.
The pro‑rata factor = 1,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 1/3.
An applicant who applied for 300 shares gets 100 shares (300 × 1/3).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Shares Allotted = Shares Applied ÷ Total Shares Applied”) reveals the misconception that the ratio alone gives the allotment without scaling by shares offered.
remember: State the formula used to determine the number of shares allotted under pro‑rata allotment.
A company offers 50,000 shares. Applications received for 1,50,000 shares. An applicant applied for 9,000 shares. How many shares will be allotted to this applicant.
Explain why excess application money is first adjusted against allotment money before any refund.

cards.title: Forfeiture of shares occurs when a shareholder fails to pay the called‑up…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Forfeiture of shares occurs when a shareholder fails to pay the called‑up amount (call money) within the stipulated period. The company cancels the shares, and the amount already received from the defaulting shareholder is transferred to a Forfeited Shares Account (a capital reserve). The shares then become the property of the company and may be re‑issued. Reissue at par means the forfeited shares are re‑issued at their nominal (face) value. No securities premium arises on reissue because the issue price equals the nominal value. The journal entries are: 1. On forfeiture – debit Share Capital Account with called‑up value of forfeited shares, credit Calls‑in‑Arrears with unpaid amount, and credit Forfeited Shares Account with amount already paid. 2. On reissue – debit Bank with nominal value received, credit Share Capital Account with nominal value. The Forfeited Shares Account balance after reissue represents a capital profit and is eventually transferred to Capital Reserve. This node covers only the at‑par reissue; premium or discount reissues are treated in later nodes.
steps: Takeaway: Forfeiture cancels shares for non‑payment of calls, the paid‑up amount is parked in a Forfeited Shares Account, and reissue at par simply records the nominal value received, moving any surplus in the Forfeited…
Here is why: 1.
Legal basis – Section 61 of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers a company to forfeit shares for non‑payment of calls after giving proper notice. 2.
Accounting logic – The called‑up capital on forfeited shares is reversed; the unpaid call is removed via Calls‑in‑Arrears; the amount already paid is not refunded but held as a capital receipt. 3.

Reissue at par – When the company re‑issues these shares at nominal value, the Share Capital Account is credited with the nominal amount, Bank is debited, and the Forfeited Shares Account is debited for the nominal…
The credit balance left in Forfeited Shares Account is a capital profit. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., debiting Share Capital with only ₹750) reveals the misconception that forfeiture only reverses the paid‑up portion, ignoring the called‑up capital that must be cancelled.
remember: What is the correct journal entry to record forfeiture of 150 shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 called‑up, where the shareholder paid ₹5 per share and the remaining ₹3 per share is in….
Explain why the Forfeited Shares Account is credited on forfeiture and debited on reissue at par.
A company forfeits 300 shares of ₹10 each, ₹7 called‑up, ₹4….

cards.title: Forfeiture and reissue at premium deals with shares cancelled due to…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Forfeiture and reissue at premium deals with shares cancelled due to non‑payment of calls and subsequently re‑issued above their nominal (face) value. Under the Companies Act 2013, when a share is forfeited, the called‑up capital is debited to Share Capital Account, the unpaid calls are credited to Calls in Arrears, and the amount already received is credited to Forfeited Shares Account. On reissue at a premium, the company receives more than the nominal value; the excess is credited to Securities Premium Account (Section 52). The Forfeited Shares Account is debited for any discount allowed on reissue (if reissue price < nominal) and the net balance — forfeited amount minus discount plus premium — is transferred to Capital Reserve. This node focuses exclusively on the premium scenario; reissue at par and at discount are covered in sibling nodes and respectively.
steps: Takeaway: When forfeited shares are reissued at a premium, the premium received is credited to Securities Premium Account and the net gain (forfeited amount minus any discount allowed plus premium) is transferred to…
Supporting arguments: 1.
Forfeiture entry reverses the unpaid calls and parks the paid‑up amount in Forfeited Shares Account. 2.
Reissue at premium brings in cash exceeding nominal value; the excess is a statutory premium under Section 52. 3.
Capital Reserve computation = Amount forfeited – Discount on reissue (if any) + Premium on reissue.
Since reissue is at premium, discount is zero, so Capital Reserve = Forfeited amount + Premium received. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “credit Bank because cash is received”) reveals the misconception that forfeiture involves a cash inflow, confusing it with reissue proceeds.
remember: A student writes the forfeiture entry as: Debit Share Capital ₹1,000; Credit Calls in Arrears ₹500; Credit Bank ₹500. Identify the error and state the correct credit.
Explain why the premium on reissue of forfeited shares is credited to Securities Premium Account and not to Capital Reserve directly.
Evaluate the statement: “If forfeited shares are reissued at a premium, the entire forfeited amount plus the premium becomes Capital Reserve.”.

cards.title: Reissue of forfeited shares at a discount means the company issues again shares…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Reissue of forfeited shares at a discount means the company issues again shares that were previously forfeited for non‑payment of calls, and it sells them at a price below their nominal (face) value. Under the Companies Act 2013, a company cannot originally issue shares at a discount (except sweat equity), but it may reissue forfeited shares at a discount provided the discount does not exceed the amount already received on those shares (the forfeited amount). The discount allowed is debited to the Forfeited Shares Account; the balance of that account after absorbing the discount represents a capital profit and is transferred to Capital Reserve. The maximum permissible discount per share = (Amount already paid by the defaulting shareholder on that share). If the reissue price plus the forfeited amount equals or exceeds the nominal value, the transaction is valid. Journal entries: (1) On forfeiture – debit Share Capital, credit Calls‑in‑Arrears and Forfeited Shares Account with amount received. (2) On reissue at discount – debit Bank with reissue price, debit Forfeited Shares Account with discount allowed, credit Share Capital with nominal value. (3) Transfer of surplus in Forfeited Shares Account to Capital Reserve.
steps: The key takeaway: When forfeited shares are reissued at a discount, the discount per share cannot exceed the amount already forfeited on that share; any excess forfeited amount becomes capital reserve.
Here is why: 1.
Legal safeguard – Section 53 of the Companies Act 2013 prohibits issue of shares at a discount.
The only exception is reissue of forfeited shares, where the discount is effectively funded by the money already paid by the defaulting shareholder. 2.

Maximum discount logic – If a share of ₹10 face value had ₹6 paid (application ₹2, allotment ₹2, first call ₹2) and the shareholder defaulted on the final call of ₹4, the company holds ₹6 in the Forfeited Shares Account.
It may reissue that share at ₹8 (₹2 discount) because the ₹2 discount is covered by the ₹6 forfeited.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹10) reveals the misconception that the discount can equal the face value, ignoring the statutory limit that the discount must be covered by the forfeited amount.
remember: State the maximum discount a company can allow on reissue of a forfeited share of ₹10 face value on which ₹6 has already been paid by the defaulting shareholder.
A company forfeited 100 shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 paid per share. It reissues them at ₹9 per share. Pass the journal entry for reissue.
Evaluate whether a company can reissue forfeited shares at a discount greater than the forfeited amount if it has sufficient reserves.

cards.title: Balance sheet disclosure for share capital requires presenting the authorised…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Balance sheet disclosure for share capital requires presenting the authorised, issued, subscribed, called‑up and paid‑up capital separately. Under Schedule III (Division I) of the Companies Act 2013, the “Share Capital” line item in the Equity & Liabilities section must show: (i) Authorised capital (face value × number of shares authorised), (ii) Issued capital (face value × shares offered), (iii) Subscribed capital (face value × shares applied for), (iv) Called‑up capital (face value × amount called), (v) Paid‑up capital (called‑up capital minus calls in arrears plus calls in advance). Calls in arrears are shown as a deduction from called‑up capital; calls in advance appear under “Other Current Liabilities”. Forfeited shares re‑issued are disclosed at the re‑issue price, with any gain transferred to “Securities Premium Reserve” and any loss debited to “Forfeited Shares Account” (shown as a deduction from share capital). Securities premium received on issue at premium is shown under “Reserves and Surplus” as “Securities Premium Reserve”. All disclosures must follow the vertical format of Schedule III, with notes to accounts providing details of terms of issue, forfeiture, and re‑issue.
steps: The one thing to remember: Every item of share capital — authorised, issued, subscribed, called‑up, paid‑up, calls in arrears, calls in advance, forfeited shares, and securities premium — has a fixed place in the…
Here is why: The Companies Act 2013 mandates a vertical balance sheet where “Share Capital” appears under “Equity and Liabilities”.

The note breaks this single line into its components so that users see the exact amount shareholders have paid versus what is still due. First, list authorised capital (e.g., 10,00,000 shares of ₹10 each = ₹1,00,00,000).
Next, issued capital (e.g., 8,00,000 shares offered = ₹80,00,000).
Then subscribed capital (applications received for 7,50,000 shares = ₹75,00,000).
Called‑up capital is the amount the company has demanded (say ₹8 per share on 7,50,000 shares = ₹60,00,000).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing Paid‑up Capital before Called‑up Capital) reveals the misconception that paid‑up capital is independent of the calling process, ignoring the statutory hierarchy.
remember: State the correct order of share capital components as they appear in the note to the balance sheet under Schedule III.

cards.title: A rights issue is an offer by a company to its existing equity shareholders to…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A rights issue is an offer by a company to its existing equity shareholders to subscribe to additional shares in proportion to their current holdings, usually at a price below the prevailing market price. It is governed by Section 62(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2018 for listed companies. The offer is made via a letter of offer specifying the ratio (e.g., 1:4 means one new share for every four held), the issue price, and the subscription period. Shareholders may accept, renounce (sell their right), or let it lapse. Accounting entries mirror a normal share issue at premium/discount but include a “Rights Issue Account” to track subscriptions. The theoretical ex-rights price (TERP) and value of a right are key valuation metrics. This concept extends the principles of issue at premium/discount, pro-rata allotment, and balance sheet disclosure to a targeted capital-raising method that protects pre-emptive rights.
steps: A rights issue lets existing shareholders maintain their proportional ownership by subscribing to new shares at a discount to market price.
Here is why: it is a cost-effective, pre-emptive capital-raising tool that signals confidence and avoids dilution for participating shareholders.
Consider a company with 10,00,000 shares of ₹10 each, market price ₹50.
It announces a 1:5 rights issue at ₹30.
Each shareholder gets one right for every five shares.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., citing Section 53 or Section 42) reveals confusion between rights issue, issue at discount, and private placement provisions — each has distinct legal requirements and shareholder approval thresholds.
remember: Define a rights issue and state the statutory provision under the Companies Act, 2013 that governs it.
A company with 2,00,000 shares of ₹10 each (market price ₹40) announces a 1:4 rights issue at ₹25. Calculate the Theoretical Ex-Rights Price (TERP) and the value of one right.
Evaluate the statement: “A rights issue always increases the market capitalization of a company.”.

cards.title: This concept node integrates the sequential accounting events that follow the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: This concept node integrates the sequential accounting events that follow the initial issue of shares: over‑subscription leading to pro‑rata allotment, subsequent call money management (arrears with interest under Section 51 and advance with interest under Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013), forfeiture of shares for non‑payment of calls, and reissue of forfeited shares at par, premium or discount. It shows how each event affects the Share Capital, Calls in Arrears, Calls in Advance, Forfeited Shares, and Securities Premium accounts, and how the final position is disclosed in the Balance Sheet as per Schedule III. The node does not re‑teach the mechanics of each sub‑topic (covered in nodes 006‑012) but demonstrates their inter‑linkages through combined journal entries and ledger postings, preparing students for the synthesis node (015).
steps: The key takeaway: A single share issue often triggers a chain of events — over‑subscription, pro‑rata allotment, call money defaults, forfeiture, and reissue — and the accountant must record each link in the correct…
Here is why: when a company issues shares, the subscription list rarely matches the offer exactly.
Over‑subscription forces pro‑rata allotment, which creates advance payments from some applicants and arrears from others.
The Companies Act 2013 mandates interest on calls in arrears (max 10% p.a.) and on calls in advance (max 12% p.a.).
If arrears persist, the board may forfeit shares (Section 61), transferring the paid‑up amount to a Forfeited Shares account.
Those forfeited shares can be reissued at par, premium, or discount (but discount cannot exceed the forfeited amount).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹0 refund) reveals the misconception that excess application money is automatically adjusted to allotment without checking the allotment terms — ignoring the pro‑rata adjustment step.

In the above scenario, after pro‑rata allotment, the excess application money is adjusted towards….

cards.title: This synthesis node integrates every sub‑concept of Chapter 6…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: This synthesis node integrates every sub‑concept of Chapter 6 — issue of shares at par and premium under the Companies Act 2013, issue for consideration other than cash to promoters, underwriters and vendors, accounting for calls in arrears and calls in advance with statutory interest, handling over‑ and under‑subscription with pro‑rata allotment, forfeiture of shares for non‑payment of calls, and reissue of forfeited shares at par, premium or discount — into a unified framework for financial statement preparation. It demonstrates how each transaction flows through journal entries, ledger accounts (Share Capital, Calls‑in‑Arrears, Calls‑in‑Advance, Forfeited Shares, Securities Premium) and finally into the Balance Sheet under “Share Capital” and “Reserves and Surplus” as per Schedule III. The node also maps the typical CISCE ISC question patterns: short‑answer journal entries, long‑answer ledger reconstruction, and case‑based balance‑sheet disclosure. By linking the procedural steps (application, allotment, calls, forfeiture, reissue) with the statutory disclosure requirements, it enables a student to move from isolated concept mastery to integrated problem‑solving and exam‑ready presentation.
steps: The takeaway: mastering this node means you can stitch every share‑issue transaction into a single coherent story that ends in a compliant Balance Sheet.
Here is why: first, the Companies Act 2013 fixes the legal framework — sections 39, 40, 42, 53 govern issue price, calls, forfeiture and reissue — so every entry must reference the correct provision.
Second, the accounting cycle is linear: application money → allotment → calls → possible arrears/advance → forfeiture → reissue; missing a step breaks the trail.
Third, CISCE examiners test the trail through three lenses — journal entries (short answer), ledger reconstruction (long answer), and Balance Sheet note (disclosure).

Fourth, statutory interest on calls in arrears (10 %) and calls in advance (12 %) is a frequent calculation trap; the interest is credited/debited to the respective call account, not to Profit & Loss.
Fifth, reissue of forfeited shares at discount cannot exceed the forfeited amount, a rule that appears in almost every past paper.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “both are 10 %”) reveals the misconception that a single rate applies to both, confusing the debit‑interest on arrears with the credit‑interest on advance.
remember: State the statutory rate of interest on calls in arrears and on calls in advance as per the Companies Act 2013.
A company issues shares at a premium of ₹5 per….
Evaluate the following statement: “When shares are forfeited for non‑payment of calls, the amount already paid by the defaulting shareholder is transferred to Capital Reserve.”.

cards.title: Issue at par refers to the issuance of debentures at their face (nominal) value.
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Issue at par refers to the issuance of debentures at their face (nominal) value. When a company issues debentures at par, the issue price equals the nominal value printed on the debenture certificate. The accounting entry records the full nominal amount as a liability under “Debentures” and the same amount as cash or bank receipt. No “Securities Premium” or “Discount on Issue of Debentures” accounts arise. This concept links directly to the later nodes on issue at premium, issue at discount, and redemption terms. It also underpins the calculation of interest payable and tax deducted at source (TDS) covered in node. Understanding issue at par is essential because it establishes the baseline liability measurement before any premium or discount adjustments.
steps: The takeaway: When debentures are issued at par, the company records the exact face value as both cash inflow and long‑term liability, with no premium or discount accounts involved.
Here is why: 1.
Equal value exchange – The subscriber pays ₹100 for a ₹100 debenture; the company’s obligation matches the cash received. 2.
Simplicity in ledger – Only two accounts are touched: Bank (debit) and Debentures (credit).
This mirrors the cash‑sale of a share at face value taught earlier. 3.
Foundation for premium/discount – Later nodes add Securities Premium or Discount on Issue; mastering the par entry prevents confusion when those extra columns appear. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., debiting Bank ₹2,00,000 and crediting 9% Debentures ₹1,80,000 and Discount on Issue ₹20,000) reveals the misconception that every debenture issue automatically creates a discount account — confusing issue at par with issue at discount.
remember: State the journal entry when a company issues 2,000, 9% debentures of ₹100 each at par.
Explain why “Securities Premium” does not appear in the journal entry for issue at par.
A student argues that issuing debentures at par increases the company’s equity. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Issue of debentures at premium occurs when a company invites subscription for…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Issue of debentures at premium occurs when a company invites subscription for debentures at a price higher than their nominal (face) value. The excess amount is credited to the Securities Premium Account (a capital reserve) and cannot be used for dividend distribution. The premium may be collected with application, with allotment, or in calls as per the prospectus. Accounting treatment: - Bank A/c Dr. (total money received) - To Debenture Application/Allotment/Call A/c (face value portion) - To Securities Premium A/c (premium portion) If premium is received in instalments, each instalment entry splits the amount between the debenture capital and securities premium. The premium is shown under “Reserves and Surplus” in the Balance Sheet (Schedule III, Part I). It is distinct from discount on issue (node 003) and collateral security (node 004). The premium does not affect the interest expense (node 007) but improves the company’s net worth and borrowing capacity.
steps: Takeaway: When debentures are issued at a price above face value, the excess is a capital receipt credited to Securities Premium Account and strengthens the company’s reserves.
Here is why: 1.
Legal nature – The Companies Act, 2013 treats premium as part of share/debenture capital reserves; it cannot be used for dividends. 2.
Accounting split – Every receipt must be allocated between the debenture liability (face value) and the premium reserve. 3.
Timing flexibility – Prospectus may stipulate premium payable with application, allotment, or subsequent calls; each stage requires a separate entry. 4.
Disclosure – Securities Premium appears under “Reserves and Surplus” (Schedule III), not under “Current Liabilities”.
remember: State the account credited when a company receives premium on issue of debentures with application money.
A company issues 2,000, 12 % debentures of ₹100 each at a premium of ₹20, premium payable with allotment. Write the journal entry for allotment money due.
Evaluate: “Securities Premium received on debentures can be used to declare dividends.”.

cards.title: Issue of debentures at discount occurs when a company receives less than the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Issue of debentures at discount occurs when a company receives less than the face (nominal) value of the debentures from subscribers. The difference between the face value and the issue price is debited to Discount on Issue of Debentures Account, a capital loss shown under “Miscellaneous Expenditure” on the asset side of the Balance Sheet until written off. As per the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, discount on debentures is permissible but must be disclosed in the prospectus and the financial statements. The discount is amortised (written off) over the tenure of the debentures, usually through the Statement of Profit and Loss, by debiting Debenture Discount Written Off and crediting Discount on Issue of Debentures. This treatment aligns with the matching principle: the finance cost relating to the borrowing period is recognised in each accounting period. The discount does not affect the redemption amount; debentures are redeemed at face value (or premium, covered in node). Journal entries at issue: Bank A/c Dr., Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c Dr., To Debentures A/c (face value). On write‑off: Debenture Discount Written Off A/c Dr., To Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c. The node focuses solely on discount; premium, collateral, and redemption methods are handled in sibling nodes.
steps: The key takeaway: Discount on issue of debentures is a capital loss recorded at inception and systematically written off over the debenture’s life, never treated as a revenue expense in the year of issue.
Here is why: when a company issues debentures at a price below face value, it effectively pays a higher interest cost than the coupon rate; the discount represents this additional cost.
The Companies Act, 2013 requires such discount to be shown under “Miscellaneous Expenditure” (Asset side) until amortised, ensuring the financial statements reflect the true borrowing cost over time.
First, at issue, the company debits Bank with the cash received, debits Discount on Issue of Debentures with the shortfall, and credits Debentures Account with the face value.
For example, 1,000 debentures of ₹100 each issued at ₹95: Bank Dr. ₹95,000;
Discount on Issue of Debentures Dr. ₹5,000;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., crediting Discount on Issue of Debentures to Profit & Loss) reveals the misconception that discount is a revenue gain rather than a capital loss to be amortised.
remember: What is the correct journal entry when a company issues 2,000, 10% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 5%.
Explain why discount on issue of debentures is shown as an asset (under Miscellaneous Expenditure) in the Balance Sheet until written off.
A company issues debentures at a discount of 10% redeemable at par after 4 years. The accountant writes off the entire discount in the first year. Evaluate this treatment.

cards.title: Collateral security refers to an additional asset pledged by a company to a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Collateral security refers to an additional asset pledged by a company to a debenture holder (or lender) over and above the primary charge on the company’s assets. In the context of debenture issue, the company may offer specific assets — such as land, building, plant, or investments — as a secondary charge to strengthen the debenture holders’ claim. The primary charge remains on the general assets of the company (floating charge), while the collateral charge is a fixed charge on identified assets. The debenture holders have the right to realise the collateral assets only if the company defaults on interest or principal repayment and the primary assets are insufficient. Accounting treatment: the collateral security is not recorded as a liability; instead, a memorandum entry is made in the register of charges, and the assets continue to appear in the balance sheet at their book value. If the company defaults, the debenture holders may enforce the charge, leading to a transfer of the asset to them. The concept links to “Issue at par/premium/discount” (nodes 001‑003) because the terms of issue may specify whether collateral is offered, and it precedes “Consideration other than cash” (node 005) where assets are issued as payment.
steps: Collateral security is an extra asset pledged to debenture holders as a safety cushion, not the main repayment source.
Here is why: the primary charge on a company’s assets is usually a floating charge covering all present and future assets, which ranks after secured creditors.
To make debentures more attractive, the company may offer a fixed charge on specific assets — land, building, or investments — as collateral.
This fixed charge ranks ahead of the floating charge, giving debenture holders a stronger claim.
Consider a company issuing 10,000 debentures of ₹100 each at par, and also pledging its factory building worth ₹15,00,000 as collateral.
The journal entry for the issue records only the debenture liability (Debit Bank ₹10,00,000;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Debit Collateral Security Account, Credit Debentures”) reveals the misconception that collateral creates a separate liability — it does not; it is only a disclosure.
remember: What is the primary accounting entry when a company issues debentures and simultaneously pledges a building as collateral security.
Explain why collateral security is not shown as a liability in the balance sheet.

cards.title: Consideration other than cash refers to the issue of debentures in exchange for…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Consideration other than cash refers to the issue of debentures in exchange for non‑monetary benefits such as acquisition of fixed assets, settlement of creditors, conversion of existing loans, or remuneration to promoters for services rendered. The accounting treatment mirrors a cash issue: the debenture account is credited at the agreed issue price (par, premium or discount) while the corresponding asset, liability or expense account is debited. For example, when debentures are issued to a vendor for machinery, Machinery Account is debited and Debentures Account credited. If issued at a premium, Securities Premium Account is also credited; if at a discount, Discount on Issue of Debentures Account is debited. This node links with the sibling concepts of issue at par, premium, discount (‑003) and collateral security because the same premium/discount logic applies irrespective of the consideration type. The key distinction is the debit entry — Bank is replaced by the relevant non‑cash account.
steps: The takeaway: When debentures are issued for consideration other than cash, the debit entry replaces Bank with the specific asset, liability or expense account, while the credit side follows the same…
Here is why: 1.
Substance over form — The economic substance is the acquisition of a resource or settlement of an obligation; the legal form is the creation of a debenture liability.
Accounting records the substance. 2.
Uniform premium/discount logic — Whether cash or non‑cash, a premium increases Securities Premium and a discount creates a debit to Discount on Issue of Debentures.
This consistency avoids separate rule‑sets. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., debiting Bank for ₹1,90,000) reveals the misconception that non‑cash issues still involve a cash receipt — confusing the consideration type with a cash transaction.
remember: A company issues 2,000 debentures of ₹100 each at a 5% discount to a vendor for supply of raw materials worth ₹1,90,000. Which account is debited and for what amount.
Explain why Securities Premium Account is credited when debentures are issued at a premium for non‑cash consideration.
Evaluate the statement: “When debentures are issued to promoters for services, the debit should be to Promoters’ Account.”.

cards.title: A debenture is redeemable at par when the company repays the holder exactly the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A debenture is redeemable at par when the company repays the holder exactly the face (nominal) value on maturity. It is redeemable at premium when the company repays the face value plus an additional premium amount, which is fixed at the time of issue. The premium on redemption is a capital loss for the company and must be provided for through the Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) and Debenture Redemption Investment (DRI) as per the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations. The premium is recorded in a Premium on Redemption of Debentures Account (a liability) at the time of issue and written off against profits or securities premium over the life of the debenture. Redemption at par involves only the face value; redemption at premium involves face value plus premium. Both types require creation of DRR (minimum 25% of the value of debentures to be redeemed) and investment of at least 15% of the amount due for redemption in specified securities (DRI) before 30 April of the redemption year. The accounting treatment differs: at par, Debenture Account is debited and Bank Account credited; at premium, Debenture Account and Premium on Redemption Account are debited, Bank Account credited. Interest on debentures is paid periodically and is subject to TDS under Section 194A of the Income Tax Act.
steps: The key takeaway: Whether a debenture is redeemable at par or at premium determines the cash outflow at maturity and the accounting treatment of any premium, but both require creation of DRR and DRI as per law. Here is…
Par redemption means the company returns only the face value; the journal entry at redemption is simply debit Debenture Account, credit Bank Account. 2.

Premium redemption adds a fixed premium to the face value; at issue the company credits a Premium on Redemption of Debentures Account (liability) and at redemption debits both Debenture Account and Premium on Redemption…

Statutory compliance is identical for both: Section 71(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates DRR of at least 25% of the nominal value of debentures to be redeemed, and Rule 18(7) of the Companies (Share Capital and…
Premium on redemption is a capital loss; it is written off against Securities Premium Reserve or Statement of Profit and Loss over the debenture life, not at redemption. 5.
Interest payments are unaffected by redemption terms; they are paid periodically and attract TDS under Section 194A.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., crediting Securities Premium instead of Premium on Redemption) reveals the misconception that premium on redemption is a capital receipt like issue premium — it is actually a future obligation.
remember: State the journal entry at the time of issue for 5,000 8% debentures of ₹100 each issued at par and redeemable at 5% premium.
Explain why the premium on redemption of debentures is not debited to the Statement of Profit and Loss at the time of redemption.
A company issues 2,000 10% debentures of ₹100 each redeemable at 10% premium after 4 years. Evaluate whether the DRR requirement is based on face value or redemption value.

cards.title: Interest on debentures is a statutory obligation paid to debenture‑holders at…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Interest on debentures is a statutory obligation paid to debenture‑holders at the coupon rate on the face value for the period the debenture is outstanding. Under Section 194A of the Income‑Tax Act, 1961, the payer (the company) must deduct tax at source (TDS) at the prescribed rate (currently 10 % for resident individuals/HUF, 20 % for non‑residents) on the gross interest amount before payment. The gross interest is debited to Debenture Interest Account (an expense), the TDS amount is credited to TDS Payable Account (a current liability), and the net amount is credited to Bank/Debenture‑holders Account. At the time of filing the TDS return, the company remits the TDS to the government. The debenture‑holder receives a TDS certificate (Form 16A) and claims the credit in his/her income‑tax return. This node covers the accounting entries, the calculation of gross interest, TDS, and net payment, and the disclosure requirements in the financial statements as per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013.
steps: Takeaway: Interest on debentures is an expense recorded at the gross coupon amount; the company must deduct TDS at the statutory rate before paying the holder, creating a liability for the tax deducted.
Here is why: The Companies Act requires the company to recognise the full interest cost in the Statement of Profit and Loss, while the Income‑Tax Act mandates that the payer withhold tax at source.
The two statutes operate simultaneously, so the accounting must reflect both the expense and the tax withheld.
First, compute the gross interest: Face Value × Coupon Rate × (Months Outstanding ÷ 12).
For a ₹10,00,000, 9 % debenture outstanding for 6 months, gross interest = ₹10,00,000 × 9 % × 6/12 = ₹45,000.
Second, calculate TDS: Gross Interest × Applicable TDS Rate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “20 %”) reveals the misconception that the higher rate for non‑residents applies universally, confusing the residency‑based distinction.
remember: What is the TDS rate applicable on interest paid to a resident individual debenture‑holder under Section 194A.
A company issues 12 % debentures of ₹5,00,000 on 1 April….
Evaluate the statement: “TDS on debenture interest is an expense for the company and should be debited to the Profit and Loss Account.”.

cards.title: Redemption out of profits means that a company discharges its debenture…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Redemption out of profits means that a company discharges its debenture liability by appropriating a part of its divisible profits rather than by using capital or fresh issue proceeds. Under Section 71 of the Companies Act 2013, a company must create a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) equal to at least 25 % of the nominal value of debentures to be redeemed before the redemption date. The DRR is built by transferring the required amount from the Statement of Profit and Loss (or Surplus) to a separate reserve account. On redemption, the DRR is transferred back to the General Reserve (or Surplus) and the debenture holders are paid from the company’s bank balance. The process involves three linked journal entries: (1) transfer of profit to DRR, (2) payment to debenture holders, and (3) transfer of DRR back to General Reserve after redemption. This method preserves the company’s capital base, complies with statutory reserve requirements, and reflects a prudent profit‑retention policy. It is distinct from redemption out of capital (where no DRR is required) and from lump‑sum or instalment redemptions, which are covered in later nodes.
steps: Takeaway: Redemption out of profits uses a statutorily mandated Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) funded from profits, leaving the company’s capital intact while satisfying legal requirements.
Supporting arguments: 1.
Statutory compulsion – Section 71 of the Companies Act 2013 obliges every company issuing debentures to create a DRR of at least 25 % of the nominal value before redemption.
This reserve is built solely from divisible profits. 2.
Capital preservation – Because the reserve comes from profits, the paid‑up share capital and other capital reserves remain untouched; the company’s net worth is not eroded by the redemption. 3.

Accounting flow – The process follows three clear journal entries: (a) Profit & Loss A/c Dr → DRR A/c Cr (creation), (b) Debenture Holders A/c Dr → Bank A/c Cr (payment), (c) DRR A/c Dr → General Reserve A/c Cr…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “10 %” or “50 %”) reveals the misconception that the DRR percentage is linked to the coupon rate or to the premium on redemption, whereas the law fixes it at 25 % irrespective of interest or premium.
remember: State the minimum percentage of nominal value of debentures that must be transferred to Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) before redemption under the Companies Act 2013.
A company redeems ₹5,00,000 debentures out of profits. It has already created a DRR of ₹1,25,000. After paying the debenture holders, what journal entry is passed to close the DRR.
Evaluate whether a company can redeem debentures out of profits without creating a DRR if the debentures are redeemable at a premium.

cards.title: Redemption out of capital is a method where a company discharges its debenture…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Redemption out of capital is a method where a company discharges its debenture liability by utilizing its capital base — equity share capital, preference share capital, capital reserves, or proceeds from asset realization — instead of appropriating profits to a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR). Under the Companies Act, 2013 (Section 71), a company may redeem debentures out of capital only if authorised by its articles and a special resolution is passed; the redemption must not reduce the company’s net assets below the sum of its paid‑up capital and reserves. Accounting treatment: (1) On redemption, Debenture Account is debited and Bank Account credited for the nominal value; (2) If redeemed at a premium, Premium on Redemption of Debentures Account is debited and Debenture Holders Account credited, with the premium later written off against Securities Premium Account or Statement of Profit & Loss; (3) No transfer to DRR is required, distinguishing it from redemption out of profits (node). The capital reduction is disclosed in the Balance Sheet under “Share Capital” and “Reserves & Surplus” with appropriate notes. This method is typically chosen when the company has strong capital reserves but insufficient distributable profits.
steps: Redemption out of capital means the company repays debenture holders by drawing on its capital structure rather than earmarking profits.
Here is why: the Companies Act, 2013 permits this route only when the articles authorise it and a special resolution approves the capital reduction, ensuring creditors’ interests are protected.
First, the company must verify that net assets after redemption will not fall below paid‑up capital plus reserves.

Second, journal entries are straightforward: for redemption at par, debit Debenture Account and credit Bank Account; for redemption at premium, additionally debit Premium on Redemption of Debentures Account and credit…
Third, no Debenture Redemption Reserve is created, so the Statement of Profit & Loss remains untouched — unlike redemption out of profits where a DRR transfer is mandatory.
Fourth, the Balance Sheet reflects the reduction in share capital or reserves used, with a note disclosing the capital redemption.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., debiting Profit & Loss instead of Securities Premium) reveals the misconception that premium on redemption is always charged to revenue; however, when securities premium exists, it must be used first as per Section 52 of the Companies…
remember: State the primary legal requirement under the Companies Act, 2013 for a company to redeem debentures out of capital.
A company redeems ₹15,00,000, 10% debentures at a premium of 10% out of….

cards.title: Lump‑sum redemption of debentures means the issuer repays the entire nominal…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Lump‑sum redemption of debentures means the issuer repays the entire nominal value (plus any premium) to debenture holders on a single predetermined maturity date. Under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations, a company must create a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) equal to at least 25 % of the nominal value of debentures outstanding before redemption commences. Additionally, Debenture Redemption Investment (DRI) — investment in specified securities (e.g., government bonds) — must be made to the extent of 15 % of the nominal value of debentures maturing during the year. Accounting entries: 1. Transfer to DRR – Debit Surplus/Profit & Loss, Credit DRR. 2. Investment for DRI – Debit DRI (Bank/Investments), Credit Bank. 3. Redemption – Debit Debenture Holders’ Account (face value + premium), Credit Bank (or Debenture Redemption Fund). 4. Premium on Redemption – Debit Premium on Redemption of Debentures, Credit Debenture Holders. 5. Transfer from DRR to General Reserve after redemption – Debit DRR, Credit General Reserve. The method contrasts with annual instalments (node) where redemption is spread over several years, and with out‑of‑profits vs out‑of‑capital (nodes/009) which describe the source of funds. Lump‑sum redemption is a one‑time cash outflow requiring careful liquidity planning and compliance with DRR/DRI norms.
steps: Takeaway: In lump‑sum redemption the company must set aside 25 % of the debenture nominal value in a Debenture Redemption Reserve and invest 15 % of the maturing amount in specified securities before paying the full…
Here is why: The Companies Act, 2013 (Section 71) and SEBI regulations protect debenture holders by forcing the issuer to build a reserve and a liquid investment cushion.
Without these, a sudden large payment could jeopardise the company’s solvency.
Step 1 – Create DRR. At least 25 % of the nominal value of debentures outstanding must be transferred from Surplus (Profit & Loss) to DRR before redemption starts.
Example: ₹10 crore debentures → DRR ₹2.5 crore.
Step 2 – Make DRI. By 30 April of the year in which debentures mature, the company must invest 15 % of the nominal value maturing that year in government securities or other approved instruments.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “10 %”) reveals the misconception that DRR percentage aligns with the older 10 % rule under the 1956 Act or confuses DRR with the 15 % DRI requirement.
remember: State the minimum percentage of nominal value that must be transferred to Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) before lump‑sum redemption of debentures under the Companies Act, 2013.
A company has ₹20 crore 9 % debentures maturing in….
Evaluate the following statement: “If a company redeems debentures out of capital, it is exempt from creating a Debenture Redemption Reserve.”.

cards.title: Redemption of debentures by annual instalments means the company repays the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Redemption of debentures by annual instalments means the company repays the face value of the debentures in equal (or predetermined) portions each year over the redemption period. Each instalment reduces the outstanding debenture liability. Interest continues to be paid on the outstanding amount at the coupon rate until that portion is redeemed. The method requires creation of a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) and investment of a specified percentage in prescribed securities (Debenture Redemption Investment, DRI) as per the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI guidelines. It differs from lump‑sum redemption (node) where the entire principal is repaid at maturity, and it precedes the detailed DRR/DRI compliance rules covered in node.
steps: Redemption by annual instalments spreads the repayment of debenture principal over several years, reducing the outstanding liability gradually and lowering the interest burden each subsequent year.
Here is why: the company pays a fixed principal portion annually, so the balance on which interest is calculated shrinks.
Consider a company that issued 10,000 debentures of ₹100 each at par, redeemable in 5 equal annual instalments.
The annual principal repayment is ₹10,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹2,00,000.

In Year 1, interest is on ₹10,00,000; after paying ₹2,00,000 principal, the outstanding becomes ₹8,00,000 for Year 2, and so on. The journal entries each year: (1) Debenture Interest A/c Dr. → Bank A/c (interest paid…
An exam trap: forgetting to reduce the outstanding debenture balance before computing the next year’s interest leads to overstated interest expense.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹5,00,000) reveals the misconception that the whole principal is repaid each year instead of being spread over the redemption period.
remember: What is the annual redemption instalment if a company issued 5,000 debentures of ₹100 each, redeemable in 4 equal yearly instalments.
A company redeems debentures by annual instalments. Explain why the interest expense decreases each year.
Evaluate the statement: “Redemption by annual instalments always results in lower total interest cost than lump‑sum redemption.”.

cards.title: The Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) and Debenture Redemption Investment…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) and Debenture Redemption Investment (DRI) are statutory safeguards under the Companies Act 2013 (Section 71) and SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations. - DRR: Every company that issues debentures (except certain private companies) must create a reserve equal to 25 % of the nominal value of debentures issued. The reserve is built out of profits (not capital) and can be used only for redemption of those debentures. It appears under “Reserves and Surplus” in the Balance Sheet. - DRI: At least 15 % of the nominal value of debentures due for redemption during the next financial year must be invested or deposited in specified securities (government securities, bank deposits, etc.) on or before 30 April of that year. The investment earns interest but remains earmarked for redemption. Both mechanisms ensure that a company does not default on debenture holders by forcing it to accumulate cash‑backed resources from profits and to lock‑in liquid assets ahead of the redemption date. DRR is an internal appropriation; DRI is an external investment. They operate together: DRR builds the reserve over the life of the debenture, while DRI guarantees immediate liquidity for the upcoming redemption tranche.
steps: The one rule to remember: a company must set aside 25 % of the face value of every debenture issue as a profit‑based reserve (DRR) and, each year, invest 15 % of the next year’s redemption amount in safe assets (DRI) by…
Here is why: 1.
Legal mandate – Section 71 of the Companies Act 2013 makes DRR compulsory for all public companies issuing debentures; private companies are exempt unless their articles require it. 2.
Profit‑only source – DRR cannot be created from capital reserves or share premium; it must come from divisible profits, ensuring that owners’ equity is not eroded to pay creditors. 3.
Restricted utilisation – The reserve can be applied only towards debenture redemption; any other use is a violation. 4.
Liquidity guarantee – DRI forces the company to convert a portion of the reserve into marketable securities well before the redemption date, reducing default risk. 5.
remember: State the percentage of nominal value that must be transferred to Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) under the Companies Act 2013.
Explain why DRR must be created out of profits and not out of capital reserves.
