cards.title: This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the preparation and…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the preparation and presentation of final accounts of companies as mandated by the Companies Act 2013, specifically Schedule III Part I, and the relevant Accounting Standards. It establishes the structural framework for the Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss, including the mandatory notes to accounts that disclose accounting policies, contingent liabilities, and other explanatory information. The chapter links five critical sub‑topics: (1) the prescribed format of the Balance Sheet under Schedule III Part I with its classification of assets and liabilities into current and non‑current; (2) the treatment of proposed dividends under AS‑4 (Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date), which requires that a dividend proposed after the reporting period but before approval of financial statements be disclosed as a note rather than recognised as a liability; (3) the nomenclature amendments for Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) that align terminology with the revised Schedule III, affecting line items such as “Tangible Assets” and “Intangible Assets”; (4) the separate disclosure of current maturities of long‑term borrowings, which splits the portion of long‑term debt repayable within twelve months into current liabilities while the remainder stays non‑current; and (5) the disclosure requirements for Securities Premium, which must be shown under “Reserves and Surplus” with details of utilisation as per Section 52 of the Companies Act. Together, these elements ensure that a company’s financial statements present a true and fair view, comply with statutory format, and meet the disclosure expectations of regulators, investors, and auditors.
steps: The chapter teaches how to prepare a company’s final accounts in the format prescribed by Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013, incorporating key accounting standards and recent amendments.
Here is why: the statutory format ensures comparability across companies;
AS‑4 governs post‑balance‑sheet events like proposed dividends;

PPE nomenclature changes align the balance sheet with current terminology; separating current maturities of long‑term borrowings improves liquidity assessment; and securities premium disclosure protects shareholder…
Consider a hypothetical company, “Mohan Textiles Ltd.”, preparing its 31 March 2025 Balance Sheet.

First, the accountant lists all assets and liabilities under the Schedule III heads — Non‑current Assets (Property, Plant and Equipment, Intangible Assets), Current Assets (Inventories, Trade Receivables, Cash), Equity…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Schedule II”) reveals the misconception that the schedule for depreciation (Schedule II) also governs financial statement presentation, confusing asset depreciation rules with presentation format.
remember: Which Schedule of the Companies Act 2013 prescribes the format for a company’s Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss.
Explain why a proposed dividend declared after the reporting date but before the financial statements are approved is not recognised as a liability on the balance sheet date.
Evaluate the impact of the PPE nomenclature amendment on the comparability of financial statements across two consecutive years.

cards.title: The Balance Sheet per Schedule III Part I of the Companies Act 2013 prescribes…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Balance Sheet per Schedule III Part I of the Companies Act 2013 prescribes a uniform structure for all Indian companies. It divides the statement into Equity and Liabilities (share capital, reserves & surplus, non‑current liabilities, current liabilities) and Assets (non‑current assets, current assets). Each line item must be presented in the order and with the headings specified in the Schedule. Notes to Accounts form an integral part of the Balance Sheet; they disclose accounting policies, contingent liabilities, details of share capital, reserves, long‑term borrowings, provisions, and any other information required by accounting standards (e.g., AS‑1, AS‑4, AS‑10). The format ensures comparability across periods and companies, and the notes provide the qualitative detail that the face of the Balance Sheet cannot show. This node covers only the layout, classification, and note‑disclosure requirements; treatment of proposed dividend, PPE nomenclature changes, current maturities of long‑term borrowings, and securities‑premium disclosure are addressed in sibling nodes.
steps: The Balance Sheet must follow the exact sequence prescribed in Schedule III Part I; any deviation makes the statement non‑compliant.
Here is why: the Companies Act mandates a uniform presentation so that investors, regulators, and auditors can compare companies across industries and years.

First, the Equity and Liabilities side opens with Share Capital (authorised, issued, subscribed, paid‑up), followed by Reserves and Surplus (capital reserve, securities premium, general reserve, surplus).
Next come Non‑Current Liabilities – long‑term borrowings (debentures, term loans), deferred tax liabilities, other long‑term liabilities, and long‑term provisions.
Then Current Liabilities – short‑term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities, and short‑term provisions.

On the Assets side, Non‑Current Assets appear first: Property, Plant & Equipment (PPE), intangible assets, capital work‑in‑progress, non‑current investments, deferred tax assets, long‑term loans & advances, and other…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Reserves and Surplus, Share Capital, Non‑Current Liabilities”) reveals the misconception that alphabetical or logical grouping overrides the statutory sequence.
remember: List the first three major headings on the “Equity and Liabilities” side of a Schedule III Part I Balance Sheet.
A company shows “Securities Premium” under “Current Liabilities”. Identify the error and state the correct heading.
Evaluate whether “Deferred Tax Assets” can be shown as a Current Asset.

cards.title: Under Accounting Standard 4 (AS‑4) Contingencies and Events Occurring After the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Under Accounting Standard 4 (AS‑4) Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date, a proposed dividend is an event that occurs after the reporting period but before the financial statements are approved. At the balance‑sheet date the company has no present obligation to pay the dividend because the obligation arises only when shareholders approve it at the annual general meeting. Consequently, AS‑4 requires that no provision or liability be recognised for the proposed dividend. Instead, the amount must be disclosed in the Notes to Accounts (typically under “Contingent Liabilities and Commitments” or a separate “Proposed Dividend” note) stating the rate per share, the class of shares, and the total amount. This treatment differs from a declared dividend (approved by shareholders), which becomes a liability and is shown under “Current Liabilities” as “Dividend Payable”. The Companies Act 2013 and Schedule III (Division I) prescribe presentation of proposed dividend under “Current Liabilities” as a separate line item, but AS‑4, being the accounting standard, governs recognition and measurement; therefore, for ISC purposes the AS‑4 treatment — non‑recognition and note disclosure — is the conceptual basis. The relationship between the two frameworks is a frequent exam focus: students must explain why AS‑4 does not recognise a liability while Schedule III shows it, and how the note disclosure satisfies both.
steps: Under AS‑4, a proposed dividend is not a liability at the balance‑sheet date because the company has no present obligation to pay it until shareholders approve it. Here is why: first, the Conceptual Framework defines a…
A dividend proposed by the board after the year‑end is not a past event — it is a future decision pending shareholder approval.

Second, AS‑4 explicitly states that dividends proposed or declared after the balance‑sheet date but before approval of the financial statements are not recognised as liabilities; they are disclosed in the notes.
Third, the note disclosure must include the dividend rate per share, the class of shares (equity/preference), and the total amount, enabling users to assess the future cash outflow.

Fourth, if the same dividend were declared (approved by shareholders) before the financial statements are approved, it would become a present obligation and be shown under “Current Liabilities” as “Dividend Payable”.
Fifth, consider Tata Motors Ltd.: its board proposes ₹5 per equity share on 30 May 2025 for the year ended 31 March 2025.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “record it as a current liability called Proposed Dividend”) reveals the misconception that any board decision creates an immediate obligation, confusing board proposal with shareholder approval.
remember: What is the AS‑4 treatment for a dividend proposed by the board after the balance‑sheet date but before the financial statements are approved.
Why does AS‑4 prohibit recognition of a proposed dividend as a liability at the balance‑sheet date.
Evaluate the statement: “Schedule III shows proposed dividend under Current Liabilities, therefore AS‑4 is overridden and we must record a liability.”.

cards.title: The PPE nomenclature amendments refer to the changes introduced in Schedule III…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The PPE nomenclature amendments refer to the changes introduced in Schedule III (Part I) of the Companies Act, 2013, vide the Companies (Accounting Standards) Amendment Rules, 2016 and subsequent notifications. The key amendments are: 1. Renaming “Fixed Assets” to “Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE)” – aligning terminology with Ind AS 16 and international practice. 2. Separate disclosure of “Capital Work‑in‑Progress (CWIP)” – previously clubbed under Fixed Assets, now shown as a distinct line item under PPE. 3. Introduction of “Intangible Assets under Development” – a new line for intangible assets not yet ready for use, distinct from “Intangible Assets”. 4. Re‑classification of “Bearer Plants” – moved from “Biological Assets” to PPE when they meet the definition of PPE. 5. Enhanced note‑disclosure requirements – gross block, accumulated depreciation, impairment, and reconciliation of opening/closing balances for each class. These amendments affect the presentation of the Balance Sheet (Schedule III Part I) and the accompanying notes to accounts, but do not alter the recognition or measurement principles governed by Ind AS 16/Ind AS 38. The changes are mandatory for all companies preparing financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013, from the financial year beginning on or after 1 April 2017.
steps: The one thing to remember: Schedule III amendment replaces the single “Fixed Assets” heading with three distinct heads – Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE), Capital Work‑in‑Progress (CWIP), and Intangible Assets under…
Here is why: the old format hid assets under construction inside “Fixed Assets”, making it hard for users to separate ready‑to‑use assets from those still being built.
The amendment forces a clean split.

Consider a manufacturing company, Maharashtra Steel Ltd. Before amendment its Balance Sheet showed: - Fixed Assets (Net) ₹ 500 cr. After amendment the same data must be presented as: - Property, Plant and Equipment…
This granularity lets analysts compute ratios like “CWIP to PPE” – a key indicator of future capacity expansion.
An exam trap: students often forget to re‑classify “Bearer Plants” (e.g., tea bushes) from “Biological Assets” to PPE when they meet the PPE definition.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Tangible Assets”) reveals the misconception that the old term “Tangible Assets” is still used – confusing the pre‑amendment classification with the current mandatory heading.
remember: What is the new Schedule III heading that replaces “Fixed Assets” in the Balance Sheet of a company.
Explain why “Capital Work‑in‑Progress” is now shown as a separate line item under PPE instead of being merged within “Fixed Assets”.

cards.title: Current maturities of long‑term borrowings represent the portion of non‑current…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Current maturities of long‑term borrowings represent the portion of non‑current debt that is contractually payable within the next operating cycle (normally 12 months). Under Schedule III Part I of the Companies Act 2013, long‑term borrowings are split: the amount due after 12 months stays under Non‑Current Liabilities → Long‑Term Borrowings; the amount due within 12 months is re‑classified to Current Liabilities → Current Maturities of Long‑Term Borrowings. This re‑classification does not change the total debt; it only improves liquidity disclosure. The note to accounts must disclose the original loan amount, interest rate, repayment schedule, and security offered. The treatment aligns with Ind AS 1 (Presentation of Financial Statements) and the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, ensuring users can assess short‑term solvency. The concept links to Proposed dividend (node 003) because both affect current liabilities, and to Securities Premium (node 006) when premium is used to redeem debt.
steps: Current maturities of long‑term borrowings are the slice of a multi‑year loan that falls due within the next 12 months and must be shown as a current liability.

Here is why: the Companies Act 2013 Schedule III demands a clear distinction between obligations payable after one year and those payable within one year, because creditors and investors rely on the current‑liability…
Consider a company, Maharashtra Textiles Ltd., which borrowed ₹50 crore at 9 % p.a. repayable in 10 equal annual instalments of ₹5 crore each.
At 31 March 2025, the loan balance is ₹30 crore.
The next instalment of ₹5 crore is due on 30 June 2025 — within 12 months.
Therefore, ₹5 crore is re‑classified as Current Maturities of Long‑Term Borrowings under Current Liabilities, while the remaining ₹25 crore stays under Non‑Current Liabilities.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “keep the whole loan under Long‑Term Borrowings”) reveals the misconception that classification follows the original loan term rather than the remaining maturity.
remember: What is the correct balance‑sheet classification for the portion of a long‑term loan payable within the next 12 months.
A company has a ₹20 crore loan repayable in 4 equal yearly instalments. At year‑end, two instalments have been paid. How much appears as current maturity.
Evaluate the impact on the current ratio if a firm re‑classifies ₹8 crore from long‑term borrowings to current maturities, assuming current assets ₹40 crore and current….

cards.title: Securities premium is the amount received by a company over and above the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Securities premium is the amount received by a company over and above the nominal (face) value of its shares or other securities when they are issued at a premium. Under Schedule III Part I of the Companies Act 2013, the premium is credited to a distinct reserve titled “Securities Premium Reserve” (or “Securities Premium Account”) and disclosed under the head “Reserves and Surplus” in the equity section of the balance sheet. The disclosure requirements are: 1. Separate line item – It cannot be merged with share capital, general reserve or profit‑and‑loss balance. 2. Notes to accounts – The notes must state the source of the premium (e.g., fresh issue, rights issue, conversion of debentures, employee stock options) and any utilisation during the year (e.g., writing off preliminary expenses, buy‑back of shares, bonus issue). 3. Restrictions on use – Section 52 of the Companies Act 2013 permits utilisation only for specified purposes: issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, commission/discount on issue of shares/debentures, buy‑back of own shares, and redemption of preference shares/debentures. Any other use requires a special resolution and compliance with SEBI (LODR) Regulations. 4. Presentation – In the balance sheet, the reserve appears after “Capital Reserve” and before “General Reserve”. The note also reconciles opening balance, additions, deductions and closing balance. The concept links to share capital accounting (node) and current maturities of long‑term borrowings (node) because premium on conversion of debentures affects both equity and liability classification.
steps: Takeaway: Securities premium must be shown as a separate reserve under “Reserves and Surplus” with a detailed note disclosing its source, movement and statutory utilisation limits.

Here is why: the Companies Act 2013 treats premium as a capital receipt that strengthens the equity base but is not part of share capital; mixing it would obscure the true capital structure and mislead users.
First, when shares are issued at a premium, the journal entry debits Bank and credits Share Capital (face value) and Securities Premium Reserve (premium amount).
This reserve is then reported in the balance sheet after Capital Reserve.

Second, the notes to accounts must present a reconciliation: opening balance, additions (fresh issue, conversion of debentures, ESOP exercise), deductions (utilisation for bonus issue, buy‑back, writing off expenses)…
Each addition/deduction is cross‑referenced to the relevant board resolution or statutory provision.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Share Capital”) reveals the misconception that premium is part of share capital rather than a distinct capital reserve, confusing the classification of equity components.
remember: State the balance‑sheet head under which Securities Premium Reserve appears as per Schedule III Part I.
Explain why securities premium cannot be used for declaring dividends.

cards.title: The Statement of Profit and Loss as per Schedule III Part II of the Companies…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Statement of Profit and Loss as per Schedule III Part II of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes a uniform format for presenting a company’s financial performance for a reporting period. It replaces the earlier “Profit and Loss Account” format and aligns with Ind AS/Accounting Standards. The statement is divided into two main sections: Income (Revenue from Operations, Other Income) and Expenses (Cost of Materials Consumed, Purchases of Stock-in-Trade, Changes in Inventories of Finished Goods/Work-in-Progress/Stock-in-Trade, Employee Benefits Expense, Finance Costs, Depreciation and Amortisation Expense, Other Expenses). The difference yields Profit before Exceptional Items and Tax, adjusted for Exceptional Items to arrive at Profit before Tax. Tax Expense (Current Tax and Deferred Tax) is then deducted to give Profit for the Period. Other Comprehensive Income (items not reclassified to profit or loss) is presented separately, leading to Total Comprehensive Income. Finally, Earnings per Share (Basic and Diluted) is disclosed. Notes to accounts provide details on each line item, accounting policies, and contingent liabilities. This format ensures comparability across companies and compliance with statutory disclosure requirements under Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013.
steps: The Statement of Profit and Loss under Schedule III Part II is the statutory performance report that every Indian company must prepare, and its structure is fixed by law to ensure comparability.

Here is why: the format forces a clear separation between operating results (Revenue from Operations) and non-operating income (Other Income), and it isolates financing costs (Finance Costs) and non-cash charges…

Consider a manufacturing company, “Bharat Gears Ltd.” Its trial balance shows sales of ₹50 crore, raw material consumption ₹22 crore, wages ₹8 crore, interest on term loan ₹3 crore, depreciation ₹4 crore, and…
Following the prescribed order, we first present Revenue from Operations (₹50 crore), add Other Income (say ₹0.5 crore) to get Total Revenue (₹50.5 crore).

Then we list each expense head in the mandated sequence: Cost of Materials Consumed (₹22 crore), Changes in Inventories (assume nil), Employee Benefits Expense (₹8 crore), Finance Costs (₹3 crore), Depreciation &…
Total Expenses = ₹42 crore.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing Finance Costs after Other Expenses or omitting Exceptional Items) reveals the misconception that the order is flexible or that minor heads can be merged — the statute mandates the sequence for comparability.
remember: List the mandatory line items in the Statement of Profit and Loss as per Schedule III Part II in the correct order.
Why does Schedule III require Finance Costs and Depreciation & Amortisation to be disclosed as separate line items rather than included in Other Expenses.
A company incorrectly classifies a loss on sale of machinery (a non-recurring item) under Other Expenses instead of Exceptional….

cards.title: This node synthesises the five core sub‑topics of Chapter 08…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: This node synthesises the five core sub‑topics of Chapter 08 — Balance Sheet preparation per Schedule III Part I with notes to accounts, treatment of proposed dividend under AS‑4 (Contingencies and Events Occurring after the Balance Sheet Date), the revised nomenclature for Property, Plant & Equipment (PPE) as per the Companies (Accounting Standards) Amendment Rules, disclosure of current maturities of long‑term borrowings as a separate line item under current liabilities, and the presentation of Securities Premium under “Reserves & Surplus” with its utilisation restrictions. It connects each concept to the others: the Balance Sheet structure dictates where current maturities and securities premium appear; AS‑4 governs whether proposed dividend is a liability or a note; PPE nomenclature changes affect the fixed‑asset schedule and depreciation notes. The node’s purpose is to enable students to integrate these discrete rules into a complete, exam‑ready set of final accounts for a company, and to recognise the pattern of CISCE ISC questions that test such integration.

cards.title: Financial Statement Analysis is the systematic examination of a company’s…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Financial Statement Analysis is the systematic examination of a company’s Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss to assess its financial health, performance trends, and comparative position. The chapter introduces four core tools: 1. Comparative Statements – placing two or more periods (intra‑firm) or two firms (inter‑firm) side by side, showing absolute change (₹ difference) and percentage change (relative to the base period). 2. Common‑Size Statements – converting every line item of the Balance Sheet into a percentage of total assets (or total liabilities) and every line item of the Profit and Loss into a percentage of revenue from operations. This removes size bias and highlights structural shifts. 3. Absolute and Percentage Change Calculations – the arithmetic backbone that quantifies growth or decline in each account head. 4. Interpretation Framework – linking the computed changes to liquidity, solvency, profitability, and operational efficiency, enabling stakeholders (shareholders, creditors, management) to make informed decisions. These tools are inter‑dependent: comparative statements provide the raw movement; common‑size statements normalise that movement; absolute and percentage changes quantify it; together they form the analytical lens prescribed by the ISC syllabus for partnership and company accounts.
steps: The one thing to remember: Financial Statement Analysis converts raw accounting data into comparable, size‑neutral insights that reveal a firm’s true financial trajectory.

Here is why: accounting numbers alone are static; a ₹10 lakh profit means nothing unless we know whether it grew from ₹8 lakh or fell from ₹12 lakh, and whether the firm’s asset base doubled in the same period.
Comparative statements answer the “how much did it change?” question by placing two periods or two firms side by side, showing both the absolute rupee difference and the percentage shift.

Common‑size statements answer the “what share of the whole does each item occupy?” question by restating every figure as a percentage of a common base — total assets for the Balance Sheet, revenue from operations for…
This normalisation lets a ₹50 crore conglomerate and a ₹5 crore startup be compared on the same structural footing.
Absolute and percentage change calculations are the arithmetic engine behind both tools; they turn “sales rose” into “sales rose 12 % (₹6 crore)”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., selecting A) reveals the misconception that comparative statements are the only tool, ignoring the normalisation role of common‑size statements.

cards.title: Inter‑firm comparative statements are financial statements of two or more…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Inter‑firm comparative statements are financial statements of two or more independent entities prepared for the same accounting period and presented in adjacent columns. They enable horizontal analysis across firms by showing absolute figures, absolute differences, and percentage differences for each line item of the Balance Sheet and the Statement of Profit and Loss. The core sub‑concepts are: (1) Uniform accounting policies — both firms must follow the same recognition, measurement and disclosure standards (e.g., Ind AS 1/AS 1) so that figures are comparable; (2) Common classification — assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses are grouped under identical heads (e.g., “Current Assets – Inventories”, “Revenue from Operations”); (3) Absolute change — the arithmetic difference (Firm A − Firm B) for each item; (4) Percentage change — absolute change expressed as a percentage of the base firm’s figure (usually the larger or the industry benchmark); (5) Interpretation — analysing the differences to assess relative liquidity, solvency, profitability and operational efficiency. Unlike intra‑firm comparison (same firm across periods), inter‑firm comparison highlights competitive positioning, benchmarking against peers, and aids investors, creditors and regulators in decision‑making.
steps: Inter‑firm comparative statements are the primary tool for benchmarking one company against another in the same industry and period.
Here is why: they transform raw numbers into a side‑by‑side scorecard that reveals relative strengths and weaknesses instantly.
Consider two listed FMCG firms, Hindustan Unilever Ltd. (HUL) and ITC Ltd., both reporting for FY 2023‑24.
First, ensure both follow Ind AS 1 presentation — same line items, same order.
Next, extract each figure from their audited Balance Sheets and P&L statements.
Place HUL’s numbers in Column A, ITC’s in Column B. Compute Column C = A − B (absolute change) and Column D = (C ÷ B) × 100 (percentage change using ITC as base).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to track a single firm’s performance over several years”) reveals the misconception that comparative statements are only time‑series (intra‑firm) tools, confusing inter‑firm with intra‑firm analysis.

cards.title: Intra‑firm analysis (also called horizontal or time‑series analysis) examines…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Intra‑firm analysis (also called horizontal or time‑series analysis) examines the financial statements of a single enterprise over two or more consecutive accounting periods. The core tool is the comparative statement, where each line item — share capital, reserves, fixed assets, current assets, revenue from operations, expenses, profit before tax, etc. — is shown side‑by‑side for a base year and one or more current years. The analyst computes absolute change (current − base) and percentage change ((absolute ÷ base) × 100) to quantify growth or decline. This reveals patterns such as rising inventory, falling receivables, expanding reserves, or deteriorating profit margins. Unlike inter‑firm analysis (which benchmarks against peers), intra‑firm focuses solely on the entity’s own trajectory, making it essential for internal management, lenders assessing repayment capacity, and investors tracking consistency. The method assumes consistent accounting policies across periods; any change in policy must be disclosed and adjusted for comparability. Results feed directly into ratio analysis, cash‑flow forecasting, and strategic planning.
steps: Intra‑firm analysis compares a single company’s financial statements across two or more periods to reveal trends in performance and position.

Here is why: first, it isolates the entity’s own trajectory, removing peer‑group noise; second, by fixing a base year, every subsequent year becomes a benchmark for growth or decline; third, absolute changes show the…

Consider a Mumbai‑based textile firm, “Vastra Ltd.” Its 2022‑23 balance sheet shows share capital ₹5 cr, reserves ₹3 cr, fixed assets ₹12 cr, current assets ₹8 cr, current liabilities ₹4 cr. The 2023‑24 figures are…

Absolute changes: reserves +₹1 cr, fixed assets +₹2 cr, current assets +₹1 cr, current liabilities +₹1 cr. The analyst notes that reserves grew 33 % (next node), fixed assets expanded 17 %, while current liabilities…

The same layout applies to the statement of profit & loss: revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, operating expenses, profit before tax. By scanning the comparative columns, management spots that revenue grew 10 %…
This insight drives cost‑control measures.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “comparing two different companies’ balance sheets”) reveals the misconception that intra‑firm means inter‑firm — confusing “within the firm” with “between firms”.

cards.title: Absolute change and percentage change are the two quantitative lenses used in…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Absolute change and percentage change are the two quantitative lenses used in comparative financial statements (both intra‑firm and inter‑firm). Absolute change = Current‑period amount − Base‑period amount. It retains the original monetary unit (₹) and indicates the raw increase or decrease of each line item — revenue, expenses, assets, liabilities, or equity. Percentage change = (Absolute change ÷ Base‑period amount) × 100. It expresses the same movement as a proportion of the base, enabling comparison across items of different magnitudes (e.g., a ₹5 lakh rise in cash vs. a ₹5 crore rise in sales). Together they reveal trend direction, magnitude, and relative significance. In intra‑firm analysis they highlight a single entity’s growth or decline over years; in inter‑firm analysis they allow benchmarking of peers of unequal size. The two measures are complementary: absolute change answers “by how much?” while percentage change answers “how large relative to the starting point?”. Both are computed for every line item of the Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit & Loss before any common‑size or ratio analysis is undertaken.
steps: Takeaway: Absolute change gives the rupee difference between two periods; percentage change scales that difference to the base period, letting you compare items of vastly different sizes on a common footing.
Here is why: financial statements contain numbers that range from a few thousand (e.g., office supplies) to hundreds of crores (e.g., revenue).
A raw ₹10 lakh increase looks identical for both, but its impact is trivial for revenue and massive for supplies.
Percentage change normalises this by dividing the absolute change by the base amount.
Consider a hypothetical Indian manufacturer, Mahesh Steel Ltd. Its 2023 and 2024 figures (₹ in lakhs) are: | Item | 2023 (Base) | 2024 (Current) | Absolute Change | % Change |
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹−90,000) reveals the misconception that students subtract in the wrong order (Base − Current) or confuse “change” with “decrease” without checking sign.

cards.title: A common‑size financial statement expresses every line item as a percentage of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A common‑size financial statement expresses every line item as a percentage of a chosen base figure, enabling vertical analysis within a single period and horizontal comparison across periods or firms. For the balance sheet, the base is total assets (or total liabilities + equity); each asset, liability, and equity component is divided by total assets and multiplied by 100. For the statement of profit and loss, the base is revenue from operations (net sales); each revenue, expense, and profit item is divided by revenue from operations and multiplied by 100. This transformation removes the effect of scale, allowing an analyst to assess structural composition — such as the proportion of current assets to total assets, or the share of cost of goods sold in revenue — and to compare firms of differing sizes (inter‑firm) or the same firm over time (intra‑firm). The method builds directly on the absolute and percentage change techniques covered earlier, extending them from period‑to‑period variation to a static structural snapshot. Common‑size statements are a prerequisite for ratio analysis, trend analysis, and for meeting disclosure requirements under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (LODR) Regulations.
steps: The takeaway: a common‑size statement rewrites every rupee amount as a percentage of a single base, turning absolute numbers into a comparable structure that reveals the financial architecture of any enterprise.

Here is why: first, the base for the balance sheet is total assets (or total liabilities + equity), so each asset, liability, and equity item becomes a slice of the whole; second, the base for the profit‑and‑loss…

Consider a hypothetical Indian manufacturer, “Maharashtra Steel Ltd.” Its balance sheet shows total assets ₹500 crore, with property, plant & equipment ₹300 crore, current assets ₹150 crore, and intangible assets ₹50…
To prepare the common‑size balance sheet, divide each figure by ₹500 crore and multiply by 100: PPE = 60 %, current assets = 30 %, intangibles = 10 %.
The statement of profit and loss shows revenue from operations ₹800 crore, cost of goods sold ₹480 crore, employee benefits ₹80 crore, finance costs ₹40 crore, and profit before tax ₹200 crore.
Using revenue as base: COGS = 60 %, employee benefits = 10 %, finance costs = 5 %, PBT = 25 %.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “revenue from operations”) reveals the misconception that the same base is used for both the balance sheet and the profit‑and‑loss statement, confusing vertical analysis of financial position with that of performance.

cards.title: Trend Analysis is a horizontal financial statement analysis technique that…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Trend Analysis is a horizontal financial statement analysis technique that expresses each line item of a financial statement (Balance Sheet or Statement of Profit and Loss) as a percentage of a chosen base year. The base year is typically the earliest year in the series and is assigned 100%. Subsequent years are calculated as (Current Year Amount ÷ Base Year Amount) × 100. This reveals the direction, magnitude, and consistency of changes over time, enabling intra-firm performance evaluation and inter-firm comparison when base years align. It builds on comparative statements (absolute and percentage change) and common-size statements by adding a time-series dimension, helping users identify patterns such as steady growth, cyclical fluctuations, or deteriorating margins. The method assumes comparability of accounting policies across periods; any change in policy must be disclosed and adjusted for meaningful trends.
steps: Trend analysis converts raw rupee amounts into a comparable percentage series anchored to a base year, making multi-year patterns instantly visible.
Here is why: a ₹10 lakh increase in revenue means little without knowing whether it represents 2% or 20% growth over the base.
First, select a base year — usually the earliest year — and set every line item to 100%.
Next, for each subsequent year, divide the item’s amount by the base year amount and multiply by 100.
The resulting trend percentages show the relative size of each item over time.
For example, if a company’s revenue trend percentages are 100, 112, 125, 138, the revenue grew 38% over four years.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., using the previous year as denominator) reveals the misconception that trend analysis is a year‑on‑year change measure rather than a base‑year anchored series.
remember: What is the formula for calculating the trend percentage of a financial statement item for a given year.

cards.title: Ratio analysis is a quantitative technique that expresses relationships between…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Ratio analysis is a quantitative technique that expresses relationships between selected items of a company’s financial statements (Balance Sheet, Statement of Profit and Loss) as fractions, percentages, or proportions. It classifies ratios into four broad categories: liquidity ratios (e.g., Current Ratio, Quick Ratio) measure short‑term solvency; solvency/leverage ratios (e.g., Debt‑Equity Ratio, Proprietary Ratio) assess long‑term financial stability; activity/turnover ratios (e.g., Inventory Turnover, Receivables Turnover) gauge operational efficiency; and profitability ratios (e.g., Gross Profit Ratio, Net Profit Ratio, Return on Capital Employed) evaluate earning capacity. Each ratio uses data from the same accounting period, enabling intra‑firm comparison across years (trend analysis) and inter‑firm comparison across companies of different sizes. Ratios complement comparative statements (absolute/percentage change) and common‑size statements by providing standardized, dimensionless metrics that remove the effect of scale. They are derived from the same ledger balances used in earlier nodes (–005) but focus on relative rather than absolute changes.
steps: Ratio analysis converts absolute rupee figures into comparable metrics so that a ₹50 crore firm and a ₹5 crore firm can be judged on the same scale.
Here is why: absolute numbers hide efficiency; a large company may have huge profits but low margins, while a small one may be highly profitable per rupee of sales.
First, identify the decision context — creditors need liquidity ratios, investors need profitability ratios, management needs activity ratios.
Second, extract the required line items from the audited financial statements (e.g., Current Assets, Current Liabilities, Cost of Goods Sold, Revenue from Operations).
Third, apply the standard formulae: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities;
Quick Ratio = (Current Assets – Inventory – Prepaid Expenses) / Current Liabilities;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ratio analysis replaces the need for a Balance Sheet”) reveals the misconception that ratios are standalone statements rather than analytical tools derived from the statements.

cards.title: Financial Statement Analysis in the CISCE ISC curriculum integrates three core…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Financial Statement Analysis in the CISCE ISC curriculum integrates three core tools: comparative statements, common‑size statements, and absolute/percentage change calculations. Comparative statements place financial data of two or more periods (intra‑firm) or two or more entities (inter‑firm) in adjacent columns, enabling horizontal analysis. Absolute change is the simple difference (Current Year – Base Year); percentage change expresses that difference as a proportion of the base figure, revealing the magnitude of movement. Common‑size statements convert each line item into a percentage of a common base — total assets for the Balance Sheet, revenue from operations for the Statement of Profit and Loss — facilitating vertical analysis and cross‑size comparability. Together, these techniques allow users to spot trends, assess structural shifts (e.g., rising debt‑equity ratio), and benchmark performance across firms of different scales. The synthesis node emphasizes selecting the appropriate tool, interpreting combined outputs, and presenting findings in the format demanded by ISC examination questions (tabular presentation, concise commentary, and mark‑wise allocation).
steps: The single most important takeaway is that ISC examiners reward a structured three‑step workflow: (1) tabulate data in comparative or common‑size format, (2) compute absolute and percentage changes accurately, (3) write…
Here is why: ISC questions typically allocate 2 marks for the table, 2 marks for calculations, and 4–6 marks for interpretation; missing any step loses easy marks.

Consider a typical 10‑mark question: “From the following Balance Sheets of X Ltd. and Y Ltd., prepare a common‑size Balance Sheet and comment on the financial structure.” Step 1 — set up a column for each firm, a column…
Step 2 — compute each item’s percentage (Item ÷ Total Assets × 100) to two decimal places.
Step 3 — compare the percentages: if X Ltd. shows 45% share capital vs Y Ltd.’s 30%, note that X relies more on owners’ funds, implying lower financial risk.
An edge‑case trap: students often forget to express percentages to two decimals or omit the “%” sign, losing presentation marks.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., using current year as denominator) reveals the misconception that percentage change is always calculated on the latest figure, confusing base‑year anchoring with year‑on‑year growth rates.
remember: State the formula for percentage change used in comparative financial statements.

cards.title: A Cash Flow Statement (CFS) is a financial report prepared in accordance with…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A Cash Flow Statement (CFS) is a financial report prepared in accordance with Accounting Standard‑3 (Revised) that presents the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents of an enterprise during a specific period. It classifies cash movements into three activities: 1. Operating Activities – principal revenue‑generating activities (e.g., cash received from customers, cash paid to suppliers, employees, tax authorities). 2. Investing Activities – acquisition and disposal of long‑term assets and investments (e.g., purchase of machinery, sale of investments). 3. Financing Activities – changes in the size and composition of owners’ capital and borrowings (e.g., issue of shares, repayment of debentures, payment of dividend). Cash equivalents are short‑term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of value change (e.g., treasury bills, commercial paper). The statement reconciles the opening and closing cash balances, explaining the net change. It is mandatory for all companies under the Companies Act, 2013 and for listed entities under SEBI (LODR) Regulations. The indirect method, prescribed by AS‑3, starts from profit before tax and adjusts for non‑cash items, changes in working capital, and other items to arrive at cash generated from operations.
steps: The cash flow statement is the only financial statement that tracks actual cash movements, making it indispensable for assessing liquidity.
Here is why: profit figures can be inflated by credit sales and non‑cash expenses, but cash flow reveals whether a firm can pay its bills, service debt, and fund growth.

Consider a textile manufacturer in Surat that reports ₹50 lakh profit but has ₹40 lakh tied up in receivables; its cash flow statement will show a modest operating cash inflow, alerting the banker to the real repayment…

The statement’s three‑bucket structure mirrors the economic decisions managers make daily: running the core business (operating), expanding capacity (investing), and choosing the capital mix (financing).
AS‑3 (Revised) mandates this format for all companies, ensuring comparability across industries.
Cash equivalents such as 91‑day treasury bills are included because they are as good as cash for meeting short‑term obligations.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to show profit earned during the period”) reveals the misconception that the cash flow statement replaces the income statement, confusing accrual profit with cash generation.
remember: What is the primary objective of a cash flow statement according to AS‑3 (Revised).
Why are cash equivalents included along with cash in the cash flow statement.
Evaluate the statement: “A cash flow statement prepared under the indirect method starts with net profit after tax.”.

cards.title: The cash flow statement (CFS) is a mandatory financial statement under the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The cash flow statement (CFS) is a mandatory financial statement under the Companies Act 2013 and Ind AS 7 (aligned with AS‑3 Revised) that classifies all cash inflows and outflows during a period into operating, investing, and financing activities. Its importance lies in revealing the liquidity position that the profit‑and‑loss account and balance sheet conceal: profit may include non‑cash items (depreciation, accruals) while the CFS shows actual cash generated or consumed. Stakeholders — shareholders, lenders, creditors, tax authorities, and management — use it to assess solvency, evaluate dividend‑paying capacity, monitor capital‑expenditure funding, and verify compliance with debt covenants. It also enables intra‑period cash‑management decisions such as timing of vendor payments or short‑term borrowing. The statement bridges accrual accounting and cash reality, making it indispensable for financial analysis, valuation (DCF), and regulatory reporting in India.
steps: The cash flow statement is the single most reliable indicator of a company’s ability to generate cash, because profit figures can be inflated by accounting choices while cash flows cannot.

Here is why: first, it separates cash earned from core operations (e.g., cash received from customers of a Mumbai‑based textile exporter) from cash used to buy machinery or repay a term loan from State Bank of India…

Second, it exposes the timing mismatch between revenue recognition and cash collection — a firm may book ₹5 crore sales on credit but collect only ₹2 crore in the quarter, a gap the profit‑and‑loss hides.

Third, lenders rely on operating cash flow to compute debt‑service coverage ratios mandated by RBI’s Master Circular on Prudential Norms; a strong profit with weak operating cash flow signals higher default risk.

Fourth, dividend policy under Section 123 of the Companies Act 2013 requires “profits available for distribution” which are ultimately constrained by cash availability; the CFS shows whether the board’s proposed…

Fifth, investors use free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure) for DCF valuation — a metric impossible to derive without the CFS. Consider a Bengaluru SaaS startup reporting ₹50 lakh net profit…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the profit‑and‑loss account shows cash because it records sales”) reveals the misconception that revenue recognition equals cash receipt — confusing accrual revenue with cash collection.
remember: State one primary reason why the cash flow statement is considered more reliable than the profit‑and‑loss account for assessing a company’s liquidity.

cards.title: AS‑3 (Revised), issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: AS‑3 (Revised), issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) and mandated under the Companies Act, 2013, prescribes the presentation of a Cash Flow Statement for all companies except One Person Companies and small companies meeting specified thresholds. The standard requires cash flows to be classified into operating, investing, and financing activities, with a reconciliation of opening and closing cash and cash equivalents. It defines cash as cash on hand and demand deposits; cash equivalents are short‑term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known amounts of cash and subject to insignificant risk of value change (e.g., treasury bills, commercial paper). The indirect method — adjusting profit before tax for non‑cash items, changes in working capital, and tax paid — is the default for operating activities, though the direct method is permitted. AS‑3 also governs treatment of interest and dividends (received/paid), taxes on income, and extraordinary items, ensuring comparability across periods and entities.
steps: AS‑3 (Revised) is the single authoritative standard that dictates how every Indian company must structure its Cash Flow Statement so that users can compare cash‑generating ability across firms and periods.
Here is why: first, the standard forces a uniform three‑bucket classification — operating, investing, financing — which prevents companies from hiding cash outflows in the wrong category.
Second, it defines cash and cash equivalents narrowly, excluding short‑term investments that carry market risk, thereby ensuring the statement reflects truly liquid resources.

Third, it mandates the indirect method for operating activities, starting from profit before tax and adjusting for non‑cash expenses (depreciation, amortisation), gains/losses on asset sales, and changes in working…

Fourth, it prescribes consistent treatment of interest and dividends: interest paid is a financing outflow, interest received an investing inflow; dividends paid are financing outflows, dividends received are operating…
Fifth, it requires a reconciliation of opening and closing cash and cash equivalents, making the statement a complete bridge between two balance sheets.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., selecting A) reveals the misconception that any short‑term investment qualifies, ignoring the “insignificant risk” criterion.
remember: Which of the following is NOT classified as a cash equivalent under AS‑3….
