The third argument is technique selection: when the integrand contains a function and its derivative, substitution u=g(x) simplifies the integral; when the integrand is a product of two functions where one simplifies on…
The fourth argument is the constant of integration: indefinite integrals represent a family of curves differing by a vertical shift, so C must always be written.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3x^3+C or x^3 without +C) reveals the misconception that the constant factor remains unchanged or that the constant of integration can be omitted — both indicate a failure to apply the reverse power rule correctly and to recognise the…
remember: What is the indefinite integral of f(x)=3x^2 with respect to x.
Explain why _0^π x\,dx = 2 even though the graph of x lies partly below the x-axis on [π,2π].
Evaluate the claim: “Integration by parts can be used for any product of two functions.”.

cards.title: A definite integral of a function f(x) over a closed interval [a,b] is the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A definite integral of a function f(x) over a closed interval [a,b] is the limit of a Riemann sum as the partition norm tends to zero, denoted _a^b f(x)\,dx. It represents the net signed area between the curve y=f(x) and the x-axis from x=a to x=b. If F(x) is any antiderivative of f(x) (i.e., F'(x)=f(x)), the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states _a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b)-F(a). Properties include linearity _a^b [α f(x)+β g(x)]dx = α _a^b f(x)dx + β _a^b g(x)dx, additivity over intervals _a^b f(x)dx = _a^c f(x)dx + _c^b f(x)dx, and reversal _a^b f(x)dx = - _b^a f(x)dx. The average value of f on [a,b] is (1)/(b-a) _a^b f(x)dx. These concepts extend indefinite integration (node 003) to compute measurable quantities such as area, displacement, and total accumulated change.
steps: The definite integral converts a rate function into a total quantity by summing infinitely many infinitesimal contributions — this is the single idea that links area, displacement, and accumulated change.
Here is why: the Riemann sum approximates the area under y=f(x) with rectangles of width Δ x and height f(x_i^); as Δ x→0 the sum approaches the exact net signed area.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus then provides a practical shortcut: instead of limits, find any antiderivative F and compute F(b)-F(a).

Consider a car’s velocity v(t)=3t^2 m/s from t=0 to t=4 s. The distance travelled is _0^4 3t^2\,dt = [t^3]_0^4 = 64 m. If the velocity becomes negative (car reverses), the integral gives net displacement; to get total…
A common exam trap: forgetting to change limits when using substitution.
For _0^1 2x\,e^x^2\,dx, let u=x^2, then du=2x\,dx; when x=0, u=0; when x=1, u=1.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ _a^b f(x)\,dx = F(a)-F(b)”) reveals the misconception that the order of limits does not matter — confusing the subtraction direction and ignoring the sign change when limits are reversed.
remember: State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 2) in your own words and write the formula.
Explain why _-2^2 x^3\,dx = 0 without computing the antiderivative.
Evaluate _0^π/2 ^2 x\,dx and interpret the result geometrically.

cards.title: This node covers applications of definite integrals to find areas bounded by…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This node covers applications of definite integrals to find areas bounded by curves. The definite integral _a^b f(x)\,dx represents the signed area between the graph of y=f(x), the x‑axis, and the vertical lines x=a and x=b. When f(x)≥ 0 on [a,b], the integral equals the geometric area. For two continuous curves y=f(x) (upper) and y=g(x) (lower) on [a,b] with f(x)≥ g(x), the area between them is _a^b [f(x)-g(x)]\,dx. The concept extends the indefinite integration (antiderivatives) taught in the previous node by imposing limits and interpreting the result as a measurable quantity (area in square units). It connects to derivative applications because the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links the area function A(x)= _a^x f(t)\,dt to the derivative A'(x)=f(x). The node also introduces the idea of splitting the interval when curves intersect, ensuring the integrand remains non‑negative for area calculation.
steps: The definite integral _a^b f(x)\,dx gives the exact area between the curve y=f(x) and the x‑axis from x=a to x=b when f(x)≥ 0.
Here is why: the integral is defined as the limit of a Riemann sum Σ f(x_i^)Δ x, which adds the areas of infinitesimally thin rectangles under the curve.
First, identify the interval [a,b] and verify that f(x) does not change sign; if it does, split the interval at the zeros.
Second, find an antiderivative F(x) of f(x).
Third, apply the Fundamental Theorem: _a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b)-F(a).
For area between two curves y=f(x) (top) and y=g(x) (bottom), the height of each rectangle is f(x)-g(x), so the area is _a^b [f(x)-g(x)]\,dx.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it gives the slope of the curve”) reveals the misconception that integration only reverses differentiation without geometric meaning.
remember: What does the definite integral _a^b f(x)\,dx represent geometrically when f(x)≥ 0 on [a,b].
If f(x) is negative on the entire interval [a,b], what is the value of _a^b f(x)\,dx and how does it relate to the geometric area.
A student claims that the area between y=x^2 and y=x from x=0 to x=1 is _0^1 (x^2 - x)\,dx. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A first‑order first‑degree differential equation (DE) involves the derivative…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A first‑order first‑degree differential equation (DE) involves the derivative dy/dx and the variables x and y, with the derivative appearing only to the first power and not multiplied by itself. The general form is dy/dx = f(x, y). Three standard types are solved analytically: (1) Separable variables: f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) → ∫dy/h(y) = ∫g(x)dx + C. (2) Homogeneous: f(x, y) = F(y/x) → substitute y = vx to separate. (3) Linear: dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) → integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx) gives solution y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C. The solution is a family of curves (general solution) containing an arbitrary constant C; a particular solution is obtained by applying an initial condition y(x₀) = y₀. These DEs model growth/decay, cooling, mixing, and electrical circuits in applied mathematics.
steps: The one thing to remember: Every first‑order linear DE can be solved by multiplying both sides by an integrating factor that turns the left‑hand side into an exact derivative.
Here is why: (1) The integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx) is designed so that d/dx(y·IF) = IF·dy/dx + y·IF·P(x).
(2) Multiplying the standard form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) by IF makes the left side exactly d/dx(y·IF).
(3) Integrating both sides with respect to x yields y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C, which is the general solution.
(4) The constant C is fixed by an initial condition, giving a unique curve that models the physical situation.
Consider a typical ISC problem: “The rate of change of charge Q on a capacitor in an RC circuit is dQ/dt + (1/RC)Q = V/R, with Q(0)=0.” Identify P(t)=1/RC (constant), Q(t)=V/R (constant).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “IF = ∫P(x)dx”) reveals the misconception that the integrating factor is the integral itself rather than its exponential — confusing the antiderivative with the multiplicative factor that creates an exact derivative.
remember: State the standard form of a first‑order linear differential equation and define the integrating factor.
Given the DE dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy), explain why it is homogeneous and outline the substitution that separates variables.
Evaluate the claim: “The DE dy/dx + 2xy = x is not linear because the coefficient of y contains x.”.

cards.title: This node covers the application of definite integrals to compute the area…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This node covers the application of definite integrals to compute the area between two curves and the volume of solids generated by revolving a plane region about an axis. The area between curves y = f(x) (upper) and y = g(x) (lower) from x = a to x = b is A = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) – g(x)] dx, provided f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b]. For volumes, the disc method gives V = π ∫ₐᵇ [R(x)]² dx when the region is revolved about the x‑axis, where R(x) is the distance from the axis to the curve. The washer method extends this to V = π ∫ₐᵇ ([R_outer(x)]² – [R_inner(x)]²) dx for a hollow solid. These formulas rely on the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the concept of Riemann sums. The node also addresses setting up correct limits of integration, identifying top/bottom or outer/inner functions, and handling cases where curves intersect within the interval, requiring splitting the integral. Units: area in square units (e.g., m²), volume in cubic units (e.g., m³). The techniques are foundational for later work in differential equations, probability density functions, and commerce applications such as consumer surplus.
steps: The area between two curves and the volume of a solid of revolution are both obtained by slicing the region into infinitesimally thin strips, approximating each strip by a rectangle or disc, and summing the…

Here is why: the definite integral is the limit of a Riemann sum, and each geometric quantity (area, volume) can be expressed as such a sum when the slices are chosen perpendicular to the axis of integration.
Consider a region bounded above by y = f(x) and below by y = g(x) from x = a to x = b. A vertical strip of width Δx has height f(x) – g(x); its area is approximately [f(x) – g(x)] Δx.
Summing and taking the limit gives A = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) – g(x)] dx. For volume, revolve the same strip about the x‑axis: it generates a washer with outer radius f(x) and inner radius g(x).

The washer’s volume is π([f(x)]² – [g(x)]²) Δx, leading to V = π ∫ₐᵇ ([f(x)]² – [g(x)]²) dx. If the region touches the axis, g(x) = 0 and the formula reduces to the disc method V = π ∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx. A common exam trap…
For example, area between y = sin x and y = cos x from 0 to π/2 requires splitting at π/4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., A = ∫ₐᵇ [g(x) – f(x)] dx) reveals the misconception that the order of subtraction does not matter, ignoring that area must be non‑negative and the upper curve must be subtracted from the lower curve.
remember: State the formula for the area between two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) from x = a to x = b, assuming f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b].
Explain why the disc method formula V = π ∫ₐᵇ [R(x)]² dx gives the volume of a solid obtained by revolving y = R(x) about the x‑axis.
A student writes the volume of the solid formed by revolving the region between y = x² and y = x about the x‑axis from x = 0 to x = 1 as V = π ∫₀¹ (x² – x)² dx. Evaluate this….

cards.title: This node synthesises the applications of derivatives
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This node synthesises the applications of derivatives (rate of change, optimisation, tangents, normals, related rates) and integration (indefinite integrals, definite integrals, area under curves, differential equations) covered in nodes through. It establishes the structural links: the derivative of a function gives instantaneous rate; the integral accumulates that rate over an interval. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus binds them: if F'(x)=f(x), then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b)−F(a). In applied contexts, derivatives model marginal cost, velocity, slope of tangent; integrals model total cost, displacement, area, consumer surplus. The node also maps the typical ISC question patterns: (i) optimisation word problems, (ii) area between curves, (iii) solving first‑order differential equations, (iv) interpreting graphs of f, f′, f″. Mastery requires fluency in switching representations — algebraic, graphical, numerical — and in recognising which calculus tool the question demands.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that every ISC calculus problem reduces to recognising whether you need a rate (derivative) or an accumulation (integral) and then applying the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as…

Here is why: the exam consistently pairs a word problem with a hidden calculus core — “maximum profit” signals f′(x)=0, “total distance” signals ∫v(t)dt, “area between curves” signals ∫(top−bottom)dx.
Consider a typical 2023 ISC question: “A company’s marginal cost is C′(x)=3x²−12x+15; fixed cost is ₹200.
Find the cost of producing 10 units.” The keyword “marginal” tells you C′ is given; you must integrate to get C(x), add the constant from fixed cost, then evaluate at x=10.
The steps are: (1) identify the operation (integration), (2) perform ∫(3x²−12x+15)dx = x³−6x²+15x + K, (3) use C(0)=200 → K=200, (4) compute C(10)=1000−600+150+200=750.
Units: ₹.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “∫_a^b f(x)dx = F(b)−F(a)”) reveals confusion between Part 1 (derivative of an integral) and Part 2 (evaluation of a definite integral).
remember: State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part 1 in your own words.
A particle moves along a line with velocity v(t)=4t−3 m/s. Explain why the displacement from t=1 s to t=4 s is given by ∫_1^4 v(t) dt, not by v(4)−v(1).
Evaluate the claim: “If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)>0, then f has a local maximum at x=c.”.

cards.title: Probability quantifies the likelihood of an event occurring in a random…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Probability quantifies the likelihood of an event occurring in a random experiment. For a finite sample space S with equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event E ⊆ S is P(E) = (n(E))/(n(S)), where n(·) denotes the number of outcomes. The axioms of probability (non‑negativity, normalization, additivity for mutually exclusive events) extend this definition to infinite and non‑uniform spaces. A random variable X assigns a real number to each outcome; its probability distribution (discrete: probability mass function, continuous: probability density function) describes how probability mass is spread over the values of X. The expectation E(X) (or mean) is the long‑run average value of X, computed as Σ x\,P(X=x) for discrete variables or x\,f(x)\,dx for continuous ones. Variance and higher moments capture dispersion and shape. This chapter introduces these core ideas — sample spaces, events, random variables, common distributions (binomial, Poisson, normal, exponential), and expectation — and shows why they are indispensable for modelling uncertainty in fields such as finance, quality control, epidemiology, and data science.
steps: This chapter equips you with the language and tools to quantify uncertainty, model random phenomena, and make informed decisions using probability distributions and expectation.

First, probability axioms give a rigorous foundation: any probability lies between 0 and 1, the sure event has probability 1, and probabilities of mutually exclusive events add up. This structure lets us build models…
Second, random variables translate outcomes into numbers.

A discrete random variable (e.g., number of heads in 10 coin tosses) uses a probability mass function; a continuous one (e.g., time between customer arrivals at a Mumbai local train station) uses a density function.
Recognising which type fits a situation is crucial — using a continuous model for count data leads to nonsense.

Third, each named distribution captures a specific pattern: binomial for fixed trials with two outcomes, Poisson for rare events over time/space, normal for aggregated measurements, exponential for waiting times.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “P(E)=n(S)/n(E)”) reveals the misconception that probability is the inverse ratio, confusing the numerator and denominator.
remember: Define the probability of an event E in a finite sample space S with equally likely outcomes.
If two events A and B are mutually exclusive, what is P(A ∪ B)? Explain why.
A student claims that the probability of getting a head in a fair coin toss changes after five consecutive heads. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A random variable X assigns a real number to each outcome of a random…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A random variable X assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment. Its probability distribution describes how total probability 1 is allocated among the possible values of X. For a discrete random variable the distribution is given by a probability mass function (PMF) p(x)=P(X=x) satisfying 1. p(x)≥ 0 for all x, 2. Σ_x p(x)=1. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is F(x)=P(X≤ x)=Σ_t≤ xp(t). It is non‑decreasing, right‑continuous, with _x→-∞F(x)=0 and _x→∞F(x)=1. For a continuous random variable the distribution is described by a probability density function (PDF) f(x)≥0 with _-∞^∞f(x)\,dx=1. The CDF is F(x)= _-∞^xf(t)\,dt. Key relationships: the PMF/PDF uniquely determines the CDF and vice‑versa (by differencing or differentiation). Expectation, variance, and higher moments are derived from the distribution but are treated in the next node. Common named discrete distributions (binomial, Poisson, geometric) and continuous distributions (uniform, exponential, normal) are specific families whose PMF/PDF have closed forms; this node only establishes the general framework.
steps: The one thing to remember: a probability distribution is a complete, rule‑based allocation of total probability 1 to every possible value of a random variable, and the CDF is its running total.
Here is why: 1.
Random variable as a bridge – It converts outcomes (e.g., “die shows 4”) into numbers so we can do arithmetic. 2.

PMF/PDF as the allocation rule – For discrete variables the PMF gives the exact probability of each value; for continuous variables the PDF gives a density whose integral over an interval yields the probability.
Both must be non‑negative and sum/integrate to 1. 3.

CDF as the universal tool – Whether discrete or continuous, F(x)=P(X≤ x) works the same way. It turns “probability of exactly 3” into F(3)-F(2) for discrete, or “probability between 2 and 5” into F(5)-F(2) for…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “p(x)≤1 and Σ p(x)=0”) reveals the misconception that probabilities are bounded above by 1 individually but can sum to zero — confusing the upper bound with the normalization requirement.
remember: State the two necessary conditions for a function p(x) to be a valid probability mass function of a discrete random variable.
A student claims that for a continuous random variable the probability density function f(x) can be greater than 1. Is this claim correct? Justify.
Given the PMF p(0)=0.1, p(1)=0.3, p(2)=0.4, p(3)=0.2, evaluate the statement: “The cumulative distribution function F(1.5)=0.4.” State true or false with reasoning.

cards.title: For a discrete random variable X taking values x_1, x_2…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: For a discrete random variable X taking values x_1, x_2,, x_n with probabilities p_1, p_2,, p_n (where Σ p_i = 1), the mathematical expectation (or expected value) is defined as E(X) = Σ_i=1^n x_i\,p_i. For a continuous random variable with probability density function f(x) defined on an interval I, the expectation is E(X) = _I x\,f(x)\,dx. Expectation is a linear operator: for any constants a,b and random variables X,Y, E(aX + bY) = aE(X) + bE(Y). If g(X) is a function of X, then E[g(X)] = Σ g(x_i)p_i (discrete) or g(x)f(x)dx (continuous). The expectation of a constant c is c. Variance, covered later, uses E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2. This node focuses solely on computing and interpreting E(X) and E[g(X)] for standard distributions (uniform, binomial, Poisson, normal, exponential) introduced in the sibling node.
steps: The expectation of a random variable is the weighted average of its possible values, where the weights are the probabilities; it is the single number that best represents the long‑run centre of the distribution.
Here is why: (1) The formula E(X)=Σ x_i p_i directly mirrors the arithmetic mean of a large sample where each value x_i appears proportionally to p_i.
(2) Linearity E(aX+bY)=aE(X)+bE(Y) holds even when X and Y are dependent, making expectation uniquely tractable.
(3) For any function g, E[g(X)] is obtained by replacing x_i with g(x_i) in the sum (or x with g(x) in the integral) — no new distribution of g(X) is required.
(4) Standard distributions have closed‑form expectations: uniform on [a,b] gives (a+b)/2; binomial (n,p) gives np;
Poisson (λ) gives λ; normal (μ,σ^2) gives μ; exponential (λ) gives 1/λ.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., E(X)=(1)/(n)Σ x_i) reveals the misconception that expectation is a simple arithmetic mean ignoring probabilities — confusing a sample mean with the theoretical weighted average.
remember: State the formula for the expectation of a discrete random variable X with values x_i and probabilities p_i.
A random variable X has the following probability mass function: P(X=1)=0.2,\;P(X=2)=0.5,\;P(X=3)=0.3. Without calculating, explain whether E(X) will be closer to 2 or to 3.
Evaluate the statement: “For any random variable X, E(X^2) = [E(X)]^2.”.

cards.title: For a discrete random variable X with possible values x_i and corresponding…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: For a discrete random variable X with possible values x_i and corresponding probabilities p_i, the expectation (mean) is μ = E[X] = Σ x_i p_i. The variance of X, denoted Var(X) or σ^2, measures the average squared deviation of X from its mean: Var(X)=E\! [(X-μ)^2 ]=Σ (x_i-μ)^2 p_i. Variance is always non‑negative because each squared term is ≥ 0 and probabilities are non‑negative. If X is constant (all probability on a single value), the variance is zero. The standard deviation σ is the positive square‑root of variance, σ= Var(X), and restores the original units of X. Key properties (derived from the definition) include: 1. Var(aX+b)=a^2 Var(X) for constants a,b (shifting by b does not affect spread; scaling by a scales variance by a^2). 2. For independent random variables X and Y, Var(X+Y)= Var(X)+ Var(Y). 3. Variance equals the second central moment and can also be computed as Var(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2. These concepts build directly on expectation (node) and prepare for later topics such as covariance and higher‑order moments.
steps: The variance of a random variable quantifies the average squared deviation from its mean, and its square root gives the standard deviation, which measures spread in the same units as the variable.
Here is why: 1.
Connection to expectation – Variance is defined as the expectation of the squared deviation (X-μ)^2; thus it directly uses the expectation concept already mastered. 2.

Units and interpretability – Squaring removes sign issues, yielding a non‑negative measure; taking the square‑root returns the spread to the original unit, making standard deviation practical for reporting. 3.
Algebraic convenience – The alternative formula Var(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2 often simplifies calculations, especially when E[X] and E[X^2] are easy to obtain. 4.

Behaviour under transformations – Knowing how variance changes with scaling and shifting lets us solve real‑world problems (e.g., converting currency, adjusting scores) without recomputing the full distribution.
remember: Define variance of a discrete random variable and write its formula.
Explain why variance is always non‑negative.
A random variable X takes values 2, 4, 6 with equal probability. Compute its variance and state whether the variance can exceed the square of the mean.

cards.title: A binomial distribution models the number of successes X in n independent…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A binomial distribution models the number of successes X in n independent Bernoulli trials, each with constant success probability p. The trials are identical, independent, and have exactly two outcomes: success (probability p) and failure (probability q=1-p). The probability mass function is P(X=k)= nkp^k q^n-k for k=0,1,,n. The expectation is E(X)=np and variance is Var(X)=npq. This distribution generalises the Bernoulli distribution (which is the n=1 case) and connects to the Poisson distribution when n is large and p small. It also underpins the normal approximation for large n. The parameters n and p fully specify the distribution; n is a positive integer, p∈[0,1].
steps: The binomial distribution exactly describes the count of successes in a fixed number of independent, identical trials with two outcomes.
Here is why: first, the number of trials n is fixed in advance, not random.
Second, each trial is independent — the outcome of one does not affect another.
Third, the success probability p stays constant across trials.
Fourth, every trial yields only success or failure.
Consider a student guessing on a 10-question multiple-choice test with 4 options each.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only two outcomes and constant p”) reveals the misconception that independence and fixed n are optional — students often forget that without independence the binomial model fails, and without fixed n the distribution becomes negative…
remember: State the four necessary conditions for a random experiment to be modeled by a binomial distribution.
A student claims that drawing 5 cards from a standard deck without replacement and counting the number of aces can be modeled as a binomial distribution with n=5 and….
For X B(10,0.3), which is larger: P(X=3) or P(X=4)? Justify without full calculation.

cards.title: The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution that models the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution that models the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space when these events happen with a known constant mean rate λ and independently of the time since the last event. Its probability mass function is P(X = k) = (e^{-λ} λ^k) / k! for k = 0, 1, 2, …, where λ > 0 is the average number of occurrences per interval. The distribution has the unique property that its mean and variance are both equal to λ. It arises naturally as the limiting case of the binomial distribution when the number of trials n → ∞, the success probability p → 0, while the product np = λ remains constant. This makes it an excellent approximation for rare events in large populations. The Poisson process also possesses the memoryless property for inter-arrival times (exponential distribution), though that is beyond this node. Key assumptions: events occur singly, the average rate is constant, and occurrences in disjoint intervals are independent. Violations (e.g., clustering, time-varying rate) invalidate the model.
steps: The Poisson distribution models counts of rare, independent events occurring at a constant average rate λ, with both mean and variance equal to λ.
Here is why: it emerges when a binomial experiment has huge n and tiny p such that np = λ stays fixed; the binomial PMF then simplifies to the Poisson formula.
Consider a bookstore that sells rare books at an average of 4 per week.
The weekly sales count X follows Poisson(4).
To find P(X = 2), we substitute λ = 4, k = 2 into P(X = k) = e^{-λ} λ^k / k!.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., P(X = k) = λ^k e^{-λ} / k) reveals the misconception that the factorial denominator is optional or that the formula is symmetric in λ and k — confusing the roles of rate and count.
remember: Write the probability mass function of a Poisson distribution with parameter λ.
If X ~ Poisson(3), which is larger: P(X = 2) or P(X = 3)? Explain without full calculation.
A student claims that for a Poisson distribution, the variance is always less than the mean. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The exponential distribution is a continuous probability distribution that…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The exponential distribution is a continuous probability distribution that models the time between events in a Poisson process. It is characterised by a single rate parameter λ (lambda) > 0, which is the reciprocal of the mean waiting time. The probability density function (PDF) is f(x) = λ e^{-λ x} for x ≥ 0, and zero otherwise. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is F(x) = 1 - e^{-λ x}. The expectation (mean) is E[X] = 1/λ, and the variance is Var(X) = 1/λ². A defining property is memorylessness: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t) for all s, t ≥ 0. This means the distribution of remaining time does not depend on how much time has already elapsed. The exponential distribution is the continuous analogue of the geometric distribution and is a special case of the gamma distribution with shape parameter 1. It is widely used in reliability engineering, queuing theory, and survival analysis.
steps: The exponential distribution models waiting times where events occur continuously and independently at a constant average rate λ.
Here is why: its memoryless property makes it uniquely suited for processes where the past does not influence the future.
First, the PDF f(x) = λ e^{-λ x} integrates to 1 over [0, ∞), confirming it is a valid density.
Second, the CDF F(x) = 1 - e^{-λ x} gives direct access to probabilities like P(X ≤ x).
Third, expectation E[X] = ∫₀^∞ x λ e^{-λ x} dx = 1/λ, obtained via integration by parts (u = x, dv = λ e^{-λ x} dx).
Fourth, variance Var(X) = E[X²] - (E[X])², where E[X²] = 2/λ², yielding Var(X) = 1/λ².
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., f(x) = e^{-λ x} without λ, or support (-∞, ∞)) reveals the misconception that the rate parameter is optional or that the distribution is symmetric like the normal.
remember: State the probability density function of an exponential distribution with rate parameter λ and specify its support.
If X ~ Exp(λ), show that E[X] = 1/λ using integration by parts.
Evaluate the claim: "For an exponential random variable, the median is always less than the mean.".

cards.title: A probability distribution assigns a probability to each possible value of a…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A probability distribution assigns a probability to each possible value of a random variable. For a discrete random variable X, the probability mass function (pmf) p(x)=P(X=x) satisfies p(x)≥0 and Σ_x p(x)=1. For a continuous random variable, the probability density function (pdf) f(x)≥0 with _-∞^∞f(x)\,dx=1. The cumulative distribution function (cdf) F(x)=P(X≤ x) unifies both types. Expectation (mean) of X is E[X]=Σ_x x\,p(x) (discrete) or E[X]= _-∞^∞x\,f(x)\,dx (continuous). Variance measures spread: Var(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2. Key standard distributions include Bernoulli, Binomial (n,p), Poisson (λ), Uniform (a,b), and Normal (μ,σ^2). Their expectations and variances follow directly from the definitions: Binomial E[X]=np,\ Var(X)=npq; Poisson E[X]=λ,\ Var(X)=λ; Uniform E[X]=(a+b)/(2),\ Var(X)=((b-a)^2)/(12). Understanding how to identify the appropriate distribution, compute its parameters, and apply expectation/variance formulas is the core skill for ISC Applied Mathematics probability problems.
steps: Mastering the synthesis of probability distributions and expectation enables you to solve any ISC Applied Mathematics probability question by identifying the correct distribution, computing its parameters, and applying…
Here is why: first, every ISC problem begins with a description of a random experiment — you must decide whether the outcomes are countable (discrete) or measurable (continuous).

Second, once the type is fixed, you match the experiment to a standard distribution: coin tosses → Binomial; rare events over time → Poisson; equally likely outcomes on an interval → Uniform; measurement errors → Normal.
Third, the parameters (n, p, λ, a, b, μ, σ) are extracted from the wording (e.g., “10 trials, success probability 0.3” gives n=10, p=0.3).
Fourth, you write the pmf/pdf explicitly, then apply the expectation integral or sum. Fifth, variance follows from E[X^2]-(E[X])^2 or the known shortcut.
Consider a typical ISC question: “A factory produces bolts; 2% are defective.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., E[X]=Σ_x p(x)) reveals the misconception that expectation is just the sum of probabilities, confusing the definition of a probability distribution (which sums to 1) with the weighted average that defines expectation.
remember: State the formula for the expectation of a discrete random variable X with probability mass function p(x).
Explain why the expectation of a continuous uniform distribution on [a,b] is (a+b)/(2).
A student claims that for any random variable, Var(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Linear Programming (LP) is a branch of applied mathematics that deals with…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Linear Programming (LP) is a branch of applied mathematics that deals with optimising a linear objective function subject to a set of linear constraints. The objective function represents a quantity to be maximised (e.g., profit, output) or minimised (e.g., cost, time). The constraints are linear inequalities or equations that model resource limitations such as raw material availability, labour hours, budget caps, or production capacity. All variables are required to be non‑negative. The feasible region — the set of all points satisfying every constraint — is a convex polygon (in two variables) or a convex polyhedron (in higher dimensions). The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming states that if an optimal solution exists, it occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region. This chapter introduces two core sub‑topics: (1) Formulation — translating a word problem into decision variables, an objective function, and a system of linear constraints; (2) Graphical Solution — plotting the constraints on a Cartesian plane, identifying the feasible region, and evaluating the objective function at each vertex to locate the optimum. Later nodes will extend these ideas to the Simplex method, sensitivity analysis, and special cases such as unbounded or infeasible problems.
steps: The one thing you must remember: Linear Programming converts a resource‑allocation decision into a mathematical model where the best solution always sits at a corner of the feasible region.
Here is why: 1.

Real‑world decisions — how many units of each product to make, how to allocate a marketing budget, how to schedule staff — involve limited resources and a clear goal (maximise profit or minimise cost). 2.
By expressing the goal and the limits as linear equations/inequalities, we create a model that a computer (or a graph) can solve systematically. 3.
The feasible region is the set of all possible decisions that respect every limit; because all constraints are linear, this region is a convex polygon. 4.
A linear objective function increases (or decreases) uniformly in a fixed direction; therefore its extreme value over a convex polygon must occur at a vertex. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “objective function, constraints, and feasible region”) reveals the misconception that the feasible region is a model component rather than a geometric consequence of the constraints.
remember: What are the three essential components of a Linear Programming model.
Why must the optimal solution of a two‑variable linear program, if it exists, occur at a vertex of the feasible region.
A student claims that if a Linear Programming problem has multiple optimal solutions, they must all lie on a single edge of the feasible region. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is a mathematical model used to allocate…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is a mathematical model used to allocate scarce resources among competing activities in order to optimise a linear objective function. The formulation consists of three essential components: 1. Decision variables x_1, x_2,, x_n – quantities to be determined (e.g., number of units of each product). They are continuous and non‑negative: x_i ≥ 0. 2. Objective function Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 + + c_nx_n – a linear expression representing total profit, cost, time, etc., to be maximised or minimised. The coefficients c_i are the contribution per unit of x_i. 3. Constraints – a set of linear inequalities or equations that restrict the decision variables: a_11x_1 + a_12x_2 + + a_1nx_n \ (≤, =, ≥) \ b_1 \\ a_21x_1 + a_22x_2 + + a_2nx_n \ (≤, =, ≥) \ b_2 \\ \\ a_m1x_1 + a_m2x_2 + + a_mnx_n \ (≤, =, ≥) \ b_m where a_ij are resource‑usage coefficients and b_i are available amounts. The standard form of an LPP requires all constraints as equalities with slack/surplus variables added, all variables non‑negative, and the objective expressed as maximisation. The canonical form keeps inequalities (≤ for maximisation, ≥ for minimisation) and non‑negativity. Correct formulation translates a word problem into this precise algebraic structure, enabling subsequent solution by graphical or simplex methods.
steps: The formulation of an LPP is the bridge that converts a practical decision into a solvable mathematical model.

Here is why: every optimisation story — whether a farmer allocating land, a factory scheduling machines, or a student planning study hours — shares the same skeleton: limited resources, competing uses, and a single…
First, list all controllable quantities; these become decision variables x_1, x_2,.
In a small bakery producing butter cookies (x_1) and chocolate chip cookies (x_2), the variables are the daily dozens of each type.
Second, express the goal as a linear function of those variables.
If butter cookies earn ₹30 per dozen and chocolate chip ₹40, the profit to maximise is Z = 30x_1 + 40x_2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “objective function, constraints, and feasible region”) reveals the misconception that the feasible region is part of the formulation rather than a consequence of the constraints.
remember: What are the three essential components of a linear programming formulation.
Explain why slack variables are added when converting a “≤” constraint to standard form.
A student writes the constraint for a minimum production requirement of 50 units as x_1 + x_2 ≤ 50. Evaluate this formulation.

cards.title: Graphical solution of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) with two decision…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Graphical solution of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) with two decision variables is the geometric method of locating the feasible region defined by a system of linear inequalities (constraints) and then evaluating the linear objective function at each vertex (corner point) of that region. The feasible region is the intersection of half‑planes corresponding to each constraint, including non‑negativity restrictions x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. If the region is bounded, the optimal value (maximum or minimum) of the objective function Z = c₁x + c₂y occurs at one or more corner points; if unbounded, an optimum may not exist. When the objective line is parallel to a boundary segment, every point on that segment yields the same optimal value (multiple optimal solutions). Infeasibility arises when the half‑planes have empty intersection. The method relies on the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming: an optimal solution, if it exists, lies at a vertex of the feasible polygon.
steps: The graphical method turns an algebraic optimisation problem into a visual search: the feasible region is a convex polygon (or empty), and the objective function is a family of parallel lines whose intercept moves until…
Here is why: each linear inequality splits the plane into two half‑planes; the feasible side is found by testing the origin (or any point not on the line).
The intersection of all feasible half‑planes, together with x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, is the feasible region.
Because the objective function is linear, its value changes uniformly along any direction; the extreme values over a convex set must occur at extreme points — the vertices.
Consider a maximisation problem: Maximise Z = 5x + 7y subject to 30x + 20y ≤ 2000 (flour), 10x + 15y ≤ 1500 (oil), x ≤ 30, y ≤ 20, x, y ≥ 0.
Plot each line: 30x + 20y = 2000 → intercepts (66.7, 0) and (0, 100); 10x + 15y = 1500 → intercepts (150, 0) and (0, 100); x = 30 vertical; y = 20 horizontal.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the feasible region is the area under the objective function line”) reveals the misconception that the objective function determines feasibility, confusing optimisation with constraint satisfaction.
remember: What is the feasible region in a two‑variable linear programming problem.
Explain why the optimal value of a linear objective function over a bounded feasible polygon must occur at a vertex.
A student claims that if the feasible region is unbounded, the maximisation problem always has no finite maximum. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming problems (LPPs) with more than two decision variables. It requires the LPP to be expressed in standard form: the objective function is maximization (or minimization converted to maximization), all constraints are equations with non‑negative right‑hand sides, and all variables (including slack, surplus, and artificial variables) are non‑negative. A basic solution is obtained by setting n-m variables (non‑basic) to zero and solving the remaining m equations for the basic variables, where m is the number of constraints and n the total variables. If all basic variables are non‑negative, the solution is a basic feasible solution (BFS). Each BFS corresponds to a vertex of the feasible polyhedron. The simplex algorithm starts at an initial BFS (usually the origin after adding slack variables) and moves along edges to adjacent BFSs that improve the objective value. The optimality condition for a maximization problem is that all reduced costs (coefficients in the objective row of the tableau) are ≤ 0; for minimization they are ≥ 0. The pivot operation selects an entering variable (most positive reduced cost for max) and a leaving variable (minimum ratio test) to maintain feasibility. This node covers conversion to standard form, identification of initial BFS, and the structure of the simplex tableau; the iterative pivot steps are reserved for the next node.
steps: The simplex method solves linear programming problems with many variables by converting them into a standard form and iteratively moving between basic feasible solutions until optimality is reached.
Here is why: (1) Graphical method fails beyond two variables because we cannot visualize higher‑dimensional feasible regions.
(2) Standard form turns inequalities into equations using slack (for ≤), surplus (for ≥), and artificial (for =) variables, preserving the feasible set while enabling matrix algebra.
(3) A basic feasible solution corresponds to a corner of the feasible polyhedron; the simplex algorithm jumps from corner to corner along edges, guaranteeing improvement at each step.
(4) The tableau organizes coefficients so that pivot operations are simple row operations, making the method systematic and programmable.
(5) The optimality condition (all reduced costs ≤ 0 for max) tells us when no adjacent corner gives a better objective value.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “slack variable changes the objective function”) reveals the misconception that slack variables affect the optimization goal rather than merely accounting for surplus capacity.
remember: What is the purpose of adding a slack variable to a “≤” constraint when converting an LPP to standard form.
In a maximization LPP in standard form, the initial basic feasible solution is obtained by setting all original decision variables to….
Given the constraint 2x_1 + 3x_2 ≥ 12 in a maximization problem, describe how to convert it to standard form and identify the type of variable added.

cards.title: Duality in linear programming is a fundamental theoretical relationship that…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Duality in linear programming is a fundamental theoretical relationship that associates every linear programming problem (called the primal) with another linear programming problem (called the dual). For a primal in standard maximization form: Maximize Z = c^T x subject to Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0, the dual is a minimization problem: Minimize W = b^T y subject to A^T y ≥ c, y ≥ 0. The variables of the dual (y) correspond to the constraints of the primal, and the constraints of the dual correspond to the variables of the primal. Key theorems: Weak Duality — for any feasible primal x and feasible dual y, c^T x ≤ b^T y. Strong Duality — if the primal has an optimal solution, then the dual also has an optimal solution and their objective values are equal. Complementary Slackness — at optimality, for each primal constraint either the slack is zero or the corresponding dual variable is zero, and vice versa. Duality provides economic interpretation (shadow prices), enables sensitivity analysis, and offers computational advantages (solving the dual may be easier). The dual of the dual is the primal. This node covers formulation of the dual, the duality theorems, and their application in solving LPPs and interpreting shadow prices.
steps: The takeaway: Every linear programming problem has a mirror-image dual problem whose optimal value equals the primal's optimal value, and the dual variables represent the marginal worth (shadow prices) of the primal…
Here is why: (1) Duality transforms a maximization into a minimization, swapping constraints and variables, which often simplifies computation when the primal has many constraints but few variables.
(2) Weak duality guarantees that any feasible dual solution provides an upper bound on the primal objective, enabling bounds without full optimization.
(3) Strong duality ensures that if an optimal solution exists for one, it exists for the other with identical objective values, so solving the dual solves the primal.
(4) Complementary slackness gives a practical check: at optimality, a resource with slack (unused) has zero shadow price, and a resource fully used has a positive shadow price.
(5) Economic interpretation: dual variables tell a manager how much profit would increase per extra unit of a scarce resource — crucial for decision-making.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing the dual as a maximization or using ≤ in dual constraints) reveals the misconception that the dual has the same objective sense as the primal — confusing the symmetry rules.

cards.title: Sensitivity analysis (also called post‑optimality analysis) examines how the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Sensitivity analysis (also called post‑optimality analysis) examines how the optimal solution of a linear programming (LP) model changes when the parameters — objective‑function coefficients c_j or right‑hand‑side (RHS) values b_i — are varied within certain limits. The key outputs are shadow prices (dual variables) π_i, which measure the instantaneous rate of change of the optimal objective value Z^ with respect to a one‑unit increase in the i^th resource: π_i = (∂ Z^)/(∂ b_i) (units: ₹ per unit of resource). Related quantities are reduced costs c_j = c_j - Σ_i π_i a_ij, indicating how much the objective coefficient of a non‑basic variable must improve before it enters the basis. Allowable increase and allowable decrease give the range over which each π_i remains valid. All symbols are defined with SI‑compatible units: Z^ in rupees (₹), b_i in physical units (e.g., kg, hours), π_i in ₹/unit, c_j in ₹/unit of decision variable, and c_j in ₹/unit. Sensitivity analysis links the primal optimal tableau to the dual solution, providing economic interpretation without re‑solving the LP from scratch.
steps: Takeaway: The shadow price tells you exactly how much the optimal objective value will change for a one‑unit increase in a resource, provided the change stays within the allowable range.
Here is why: 1.
Link to duality: At optimality, the primal solution satisfies complementary slackness, which forces the simplex multipliers to equal the dual variables; these multipliers are the shadow prices. 2.
Economic interpretation: A shadow price of ₹ 5/unit for a machine hour means that renting an extra hour of that machine will raise profit by ₹ 5, as long as the current basis remains optimal. 3.

Allowable range concept: The basis (set of basic variables) does not change until a constraint’s RHS shifts enough to make another constraint tight; the allowable increase/decrease quantifies this safety margin. 4.

Reduced cost signal: For a non‑basic variable, a negative reduced cost (in a maximisation problem) indicates that improving its objective coefficient by that amount would make it profitable to produce. 5.

cards.title: Applications of Linear Programming refer to the translation of real‑world…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Applications of Linear Programming refer to the translation of real‑world optimisation situations into a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) – a mathematical model with a linear objective function (to be maximised or minimised) subject to a set of linear equality or inequality constraints – and then interpreting the optimal solution of that LPP in the original context. The process builds directly on the formulation node (where decision variables, objective, and constraints are identified) and the graphical solution node (where the feasible region and corner‑point solutions are visualised). In applications, the focus shifts from abstract solving to contextual modelling: e.g., diet problems (minimising cost while meeting nutrient requirements), transportation problems (minimising shipping cost from sources to destinations), assignment problems (minimising time or cost when assigning agents to tasks), and production‑mix problems (maximising profit given limited machine hours, labour, and raw materials). Each application retains the linear structure because the underlying relationships – cost per unit, resource consumption per unit, profit per unit – are proportional to the quantity decided. Thus, applications demonstrate how the theoretical tools of formulation and graphical (or algebraic) solution become decision‑making aids in economics, commerce, engineering, and public policy. cards.title: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical technique for optimising a linear…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical technique for optimising a linear objective function subject to a set of linear constraints. The formulation stage translates a real‑world decision problem into three precise components: (1) decision variables (e.g., x_1, x_2 representing quantities of products), (2) an objective function Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 to be maximised or minimised, and (3) a system of linear inequalities a_11x_1 + a_12x_2 ≤ b_1,\; a_21x_1 + a_22x_2 ≤ b_2,\; x_1,x_2 ≥ 0 that capture resource limits, demand caps, or policy rules. The graphical solution method, applicable only when there are two decision variables, plots each constraint as a half‑plane on the Cartesian plane; the intersection of all half‑planes is the feasible region. By the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming, if an optimal solution exists it occurs at a vertex (corner point) of this convex polygon. The corner‑point method evaluates Z at every vertex and selects the one giving the best value. Special cases — unbounded feasible region, infeasibility, and alternative optima — must be recognised because ISC examiners frequently test them. This node synthesises formulation and graphical solution, maps the typical ISC mark distribution (formulation 4 marks, graph 6 marks, interpretation 2 marks), and provides practice with past‑paper style questions.
steps: The one thing you must remember: In every ISC Linear Programming question, the optimal value — if it exists — is always found at a corner of the feasible region, so your graph must be accurate and every vertex evaluated.
Here is why: the objective function is a family of parallel straight lines; as you slide the line in the direction of improvement, the last point of contact with the feasible polygon is a vertex.
First, translate the word problem into symbols.
Identify the two decision variables (usually quantities of two products), write the profit or cost as Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2, then list each resource limit as a linear inequality.
Indian exam contexts often use hectares, litres, machine hours, or rupees — keep units consistent.
Second, draw the axes with a suitable scale (e.g., 1 cm = 10 units).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “objective function, feasible region, optimal solution”) reveals the misconception that solution‑stage concepts belong to the formulation stage, confusing the model with its graphical representation.

cards.title: Financial Mathematics II extends the time‑value‑of‑money framework to three…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Financial Mathematics II extends the time‑value‑of‑money framework to three core instruments. A perpetuity is an infinite stream of equal cash flows C occurring at regular intervals; its present value is PV = (C)/(i) where i is the periodic effective interest rate. Stocks (equity shares) represent ownership; valuation models such as the constant‑growth dividend discount model P_0 = (D_1)/(k-g) link expected dividends D_1, required return k and growth rate g. Bonds are debt contracts with a face value F, coupon rate c, maturity n and yield y; price is the present value of coupons plus redemption: P = Σ_t=1^n (cF)/((1+y)^t) + (F)/((1+y)^n). The chapter shows how these formulas derive from the same discounting principle, how market rates affect prices, and how to compare investment alternatives using yield measures (current yield, yield to maturity, holding‑period return). Relationships: perpetuity is a bond with infinite maturity and no redemption; stock valuation reduces to a perpetuity when growth is zero; bond pricing uses the same annuity factor that appears in loan amortisation (covered in Chapter 5).
steps: The one thing to remember: Every financial instrument in this chapter is valued by discounting its expected cash flows at an appropriate rate — perpetuities, stocks, and bonds differ only in the pattern and duration of…
Here is why: 1.
Common discounting engine – Chapter 5 taught that a rupee tomorrow is worth less than a rupee today.
The same factor v = (1)/(1+i) powers all three valuations. 2.
Perpetuity as the simplest pattern – Cash flows never stop, so the infinite geometric series collapses to C/i.
This is the limiting case of an annuity when n → ∞. 3.

cards.title: A perpetuity is a financial instrument that promises a constant (or growing)…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A perpetuity is a financial instrument that promises a constant (or growing) cash flow C at regular intervals (usually annually) for an infinite time horizon. The present value PV of a level perpetuity is derived by discounting each payment at the periodic interest rate r: PV = (C)/(r) For a growing perpetuity where payments increase at a constant rate g (g<r), the formula becomes: PV = (C)/(r-g) Key relationships: - C = periodic cash flow (coupon, dividend, rent) in ₹ per period. - r = discount rate (required rate of return) per period, expressed as a decimal. - g = constant growth rate of the cash flow per period, decimal. - The perpetuity is the limiting case of an annuity as the number of periods n → ∞. - Stocks with constant dividends and irredeemable bonds are practical examples. - The concept underpins valuation of preferred shares, consols, and real‑estate rent rolls.
steps: The present value of a perpetuity equals the periodic payment divided by the discount rate because an infinite stream of equal payments forms a convergent geometric series whose sum is C/r.
Here is why: consider a perpetuity paying ₹C at the end of each year forever.
The present value of the first payment is C/(1+r), the second is C/(1+r)^2, and so on. Summing this infinite series gives C × [1/(1+r) + 1/(1+r)^2 + ].
The bracket is a geometric series with first term 1/(1+r) and common ratio 1/(1+r); its sum is (1/(1+r))/(1-1/(1+r)) = 1/r.
Multiplying by C yields PV = C/r.
If payments grow at rate g, the k-th payment is C(1+g)^k-1.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., PV = C × r) reveals the misconception that present value grows with the interest rate, confusing future‑value logic with discounting.

cards.title: A stock (or equity share) represents a unit of ownership in a joint‑stock…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A stock (or equity share) represents a unit of ownership in a joint‑stock company. Each share has a nominal (face) value (e.g., ₹10) printed on the certificate, a market value that fluctuates on the stock exchange, and may carry a dividend declared by the board. The dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the current market price, expressed as a percentage. The rate of return on a stock combines dividend income and capital appreciation (or depreciation) over the holding period. Valuation models treat a stock as a stream of future dividends; the constant‑growth dividend discount model (Gordon model) values a share as P_0 = (D_1)/(r-g), where D_1 is the expected dividend next period, r the required rate of return, and g the constant growth rate of dividends. Stocks differ from perpetuities (previous node) because dividends are not guaranteed and may grow, while a perpetuity pays a fixed amount forever. They also differ from bonds (next node) which are debt instruments with fixed coupons and maturity. Key sub‑concepts: preference shares (fixed dividend, priority), equity shares (variable dividend, voting rights), bonus shares, rights issue, and stock splits. Understanding stocks requires present‑value techniques, growth‑rate estimation, and risk‑adjusted discount rates.
steps: The one thing to remember: A stock’s intrinsic value equals the present value of all expected future dividends, and for constant‑growth dividends this simplifies to P_0 = D_1/(r-g).
Here is why: 1.
Ownership claim – A share gives a proportional claim on the company’s residual earnings after all obligations. 2.
Dividend stream – The cash flow to the shareholder is the dividend; if dividends grow at a steady rate g, the stream is a growing perpetuity. 3.
Time value of money – Future dividends must be discounted at the investor’s required return r to reflect risk and opportunity cost. 4.
Gordon model derivation – Summing the discounted growing dividends yields the closed‑form formula P_0 = D_1/(r-g), provided r>g. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 8 % by using face value ₹10 instead of market price) reveals the misconception that dividend yield is based on nominal value rather than the current market price.

cards.title: A bond is a fixed‑income security representing a loan made by an investor to a…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A bond is a fixed‑income security representing a loan made by an investor to a borrower (typically a corporation or government). The borrower agrees to pay periodic coupon payments C (usually semi‑annual or annual) at a stated coupon rate r_c on the face value F (also called par value or principal) and to repay F at maturity after n periods. The market price P of a bond is the present value of all future cash flows discounted at the prevailing market yield y (yield to maturity). Key relationships: - Coupon payment C = F × r_c. - Current yield = (C)/(P). - Yield to maturity (YTM) y solves P = Σ_t=1^n (C)/((1+y)^t) + (F)/((1+y)^n). - If P > F the bond trades at a premium; if P < F at a discount; if P = F at par. Bonds differ from stocks (equity) because they confer no ownership, have a fixed maturity, and their cash flows are contractual. They also differ from perpetuities which have no maturity. Understanding bond pricing requires the time‑value‑of‑money concepts covered in the perpetuity and stock nodes.
steps: The one thing to remember: A bond’s market price is the present value of its promised coupon stream and principal repayment, discounted at the current market yield; when yields rise, prices fall, and vice‑versa.
Here is why: a bond is essentially a bundle of two cash‑flow streams — an annuity of coupon payments and a single lump‑sum principal at maturity.
The present‑value machinery you mastered for perpetuities and stocks applies directly.
Consider a 5‑year Government of India bond with face value ₹1,00,000, annual coupon 7 % (₹7,000 per year).
If the market demands a 6 % yield, each ₹7,000 coupon is discounted at 6 % and the ₹1,00,000 principal is also discounted at 6 % for 5 years.
Summing these present values gives a price above ₹1,00,000 — a premium bond — because the coupon rate exceeds the market yield.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “YTM is the coupon rate”) reveals the misconception that the stated coupon rate equals the investor’s actual return, ignoring price differences and reinvestment assumptions.

cards.title: Bond valuation determines the present value of a bond’s future cash flows…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Bond valuation determines the present value of a bond’s future cash flows — periodic coupon payments and the principal repayment at maturity — using the prevailing market yield as the discount rate. The key relationship is: Bond Price = PV(coupons) + PV(face value). When the coupon rate equals the market yield, the bond trades at par (price = face value). If the coupon rate exceeds the market yield, the bond trades at a premium (price > face value); if lower, at a discount. Yield measures include Current Yield (annual coupon ÷ market price) and Yield to Maturity (YTM), the internal rate of return equating the present value of all cash flows to the current price. Approximate YTM formulas provide quick estimates, while exact YTM requires iterative solving. This node extends the bond basics from node by quantifying price‑yield dynamics and introducing the computational tools used in ISC examinations.
steps: The fair price of a bond is the sum of the present values of its future coupons and its redemption amount, discounted at the market’s required yield.
Here is why: every rupee received later is worth less today because of the time value of money.
Consider a Government of India 7 % 2030 bond with face value ₹1,000, 5 years to maturity, and a market yield of 6 %.
The annual coupon is ₹70.
The present value of the coupons is ₹70 × [1 – (1.06)⁻⁵]/0.06 = ₹70 × 4.21236 = ₹294.87.
The present value of the face value is ₹1,000/(1.06)⁵ = ₹747.26.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., omitting the face‑value term or using simple interest) reveals the misconception that only coupons matter — ignoring principal repayment at maturity.

cards.title: An annuity is a finite series of equal cash flows (payments or receipts)…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: An annuity is a finite series of equal cash flows (payments or receipts) occurring at regular intervals. Let P denote the payment amount in Indian rupees (₹), r the interest rate per period expressed as a decimal (dimensionless), and n the total number of periods (dimensionless). For an ordinary annuity, payments occur at the end of each period; its present value (PV) is given by PV = P [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] / r, and its future value (FV) by FV = P [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1] / r. If payments occur at the beginning of each period (annuity due), each value is multiplied by (1 + r). A perpetuity is the limiting case of an ordinary annuity as n → ∞, yielding PV = P / r. Thus annuities bridge the gap between single‑sum cash flows and perpetual streams, and they underpin loan amortisation (EMIs), sinking funds, and regular investment plans such as SIPs.
steps: The present value of an ordinary annuity equals the payment multiplied by the factor [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] / r. Here is why: 1.
Each payment P made at the end of period k is discounted back to time zero by the factor (1 + r)⁻ᵏ. 2.
Summing these discounted values from k = 1 to n gives a finite geometric series with first term P (1 + r)⁻¹ and common ratio (1 + r)⁻¹. 3.
The sum of a geometric series a (1 − rⁿ) / (1 − r) yields PV = P [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] / r after algebraic simplification. 4.
Multiplying the ordinary‑annuity PV by (1 + r) shifts each payment one period earlier, giving the annuity‑due formula. 5.
As n grows large, (1 + r)⁻ⁿ → 0, so PV approaches P / r, the perpetuity value, showing the connection between the two concepts.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as PV = P × n × (1 + r)ⁿ reveals the misconception that payments compound forward rather than being discounted back; it confuses future value with present value and ignores the time value of money.
remember: State the formula for the present value of an ordinary annuity and define each symbol.

A student argues that increasing the number of periods n always increases the present value of an ordinary annuity. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Bond valuation determines the theoretical fair price of a bond by discounting…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Bond valuation determines the theoretical fair price of a bond by discounting its future cash flows — periodic coupon payments and the face value at maturity — at the prevailing market yield (yield to maturity, YTM). The bond price P is the sum of the present value of an annuity (coupons) and the present value of a lump sum (face value): P = C × 1 - (1+r)^-nr + F × (1+r)^-n, where C is the periodic coupon payment, r is the YTM per period, n is the number of periods, and F is the face value. The current yield is the annual coupon divided by the current price. Macaulay duration is the weighted average time to receive the bond’s cash flows, with weights proportional to the present value of each cash flow. Modified duration = (Macaulay duration)/(1+r) measures the percentage price change for a small change in yield. Convexity captures the curvature of the price-yield relationship, improving the duration approximation for larger yield changes. These concepts are interlinked: YTM is the internal rate of return equating price to discounted cash flows; duration and convexity quantify interest rate risk, which is crucial for portfolio management and risk assessment in Indian fixed-income markets.
steps: The fair price of a bond is the present value of its future cash flows discounted at the yield to maturity, and duration measures its sensitivity to interest rate changes.

Here is why: first, a bond’s cash flows are contractual and known — coupons and principal — so they can be valued like any annuity plus a lump sum. Second, the discount rate (YTM) reflects the market’s required return…
Third, duration condenses the entire cash flow pattern into a single number that approximates the percentage price change for a small yield shift, making risk comparison across bonds straightforward.
Fourth, convexity accounts for the fact that the price-yield curve is not linear, so duration alone underestimates price gains when yields fall and overestimates losses when yields rise.
Consider a 10-year ₹1,000 face value bond with an 8% annual coupon.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., P = C × n + F) reveals the misconception that future cash flows are not discounted — ignoring the time value of money entirely.

cards.title: Financial Mathematics II synthesises three core instruments: perpetuity…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Financial Mathematics II synthesises three core instruments: perpetuity, stocks, and bonds. A perpetuity is an infinite series of equal cash flows C occurring at regular intervals; its present value is PV = (C)/(r) where r is the periodic discount rate (per annum unless stated). Stocks (equity shares) represent ownership; the constant‑growth dividend discount model values a share as P_0 = (D_1)/(r-g) with D_1 the next dividend, r the required return, and g the perpetual growth rate (g<r). Bonds are debt securities paying periodic coupons C and repaying face value F at maturity n periods; price P = Σ_t=1^n(C)/((1+r)^t) + (F)/((1+r)^n). The chapter links these through the common discounting principle, the distinction between nominal and effective rates, and the treatment of semi‑annual coupons. Relationships: perpetuity is a bond with infinite maturity and no principal repayment; stock valuation reduces to perpetuity when g=0; bond pricing uses the same PV annuity factor that underpins perpetuity. All formulas assume discrete compounding unless continuous compounding is explicitly required (reserved for later modules).
steps: The single most important takeaway is that every ISC financial‑mathematics problem reduces to discounting cash flows at the correct periodic rate — master the rate conversion and the cash‑flow timeline, and the marks…

Here is why: the ISC paper repeatedly tests whether you can (a) spot the compounding frequency, (b) list each cash flow with its period, (c) apply the right formula, and (d) carry units through to the final answer.
Consider a typical 6‑mark question: “A 10 % semi‑annual coupon bond of face value ₹1 000 matures in 5 years.
The market yield is 12 % p.a. compounded semi‑annually.
Find the bond price.” Step 1 – Convert the annual nominal yield to a periodic rate: r = 12\%/2 = 6\% = 0.06 per half‑year.
Step 2 – Determine number of periods: n = 5 × 2 = 10.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., PV = C × r) reveals the misconception that multiplication by the rate gives present value, confusing the perpetuity factor with the interest‑amount formula.

cards.title: Index numbers are statistical measures that express the relative change in a…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Index numbers are statistical measures that express the relative change in a variable (price, quantity, or value) or a group of variables over time, geographic areas, or other characteristics, using a chosen base period as 100. They condense multidimensional data into a single comparable figure, enabling inflation tracking, cost‑of‑living adjustments, and policy formulation. Construction methods differ by the weighting scheme: Laspeyres uses base‑period quantities, Paasche uses current‑period quantities, and Fisher takes the geometric mean of the two to reduce bias. Moving averages are smoothing techniques applied to time‑series data; a simple moving average (SMA) of order k replaces each observation by the arithmetic mean of the current and the preceding k − 1 values, while a weighted moving average (WMA) assigns pre‑specified weights (often decreasing for older observations) to emphasise recent information. Both index numbers and moving averages transform raw series into interpretable signals — indices for cross‑sectional comparison, moving averages for trend extraction — and together they form the analytical backbone of economic and business forecasting in the ISC Applied Mathematics curriculum.
steps: The chapter equips you with two complementary lenses — index numbers for comparing aggregates across time or space, and moving averages for revealing the underlying trend in a noisy series.
First, index numbers answer “how much has the cost of living risen?” by collapsing a basket of prices into a single percentage relative to a base year.
The choice of weights (base‑year quantities vs. current‑year quantities) determines whether the index overstates (Laspeyres) or understates (Paasche) inflation;
Fisher’s geometric mean balances the two. Second, moving averages answer “what is the genuine direction of sales?” by averaging away short‑term jitter.

A 3‑month SMA on monthly sales replaces each month’s figure with the mean of that month and the two preceding months; a WMA might give weights 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 to the most recent three months, making the series more…
Third, both tools share a common workflow: define the purpose, select the base or window, choose the formula, compute, and interpret.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “an index number gives the absolute price level in rupees”) reveals the misconception that an index retains the original unit — confusing a relative measure with an absolute one.
