Thus the determinant measures whether the linear transformation represented by A collapses volume (zero determinant) or preserves a reversible scaling (non‑zero determinant). The inverse matrix reverses that transformation, allowing us to solve linear systems Ax=b by x=A^-1b.
steps: Takeaway: The inverse of a square matrix A exists exactly when its determinant |A| is non‑zero, and is computed as A^-1=(1)/(|A|) adj(A).
Here is why: 1.

Geometric meaning of the determinant: |A| equals the factor by which the unit n-dimensional cube’s volume is scaled under the transformation A. If |A|=0, the transformation flattens the cube into a lower‑dimensional…
Adjoint encodes the cofactors: The cofactor matrix C contains signed minors C_ij=(-1)^i+jM_ij.
Its transpose adj(A)=C^ T satisfies the identity A\, adj(A)= adj(A)\,A=|A|I_n.
This shows that scaling the adjoint by 1/|A| yields a matrix that, when multiplied by A, gives the identity. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., pmatrix0.8&-0.3\-0.6&0.4 pmatrix)** reveals the misconception that the adjoint is obtained without transposing the cofactor matrix, confusing the positions of the off‑diagonal elements.
remember: Find the inverse of the matrix A= pmatrix2&3\\1&4 pmatrix.
Find the inverse of the matrix B= pmatrix1&2&3\\0&1&4\\5&6&0 pmatrix.
Explain why a square matrix with zero determinant cannot possess an inverse.

cards.title: The adjoint (or adjugate) of a square matrix A of order n is the transpose of…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The adjoint (or adjugate) of a square matrix A of order n is the transpose of its cofactor matrix. If C_ij denotes the cofactor of element a_ij, then adj A = [C_ji]. For a non‑singular matrix (|A| ≠ 0), the inverse is given by A^-1 = (1)/(|A|) adj A. This relationship ties together three core ideas: (1) the determinant |A| as a scalar measure of volume scaling, (2) the cofactor matrix that encodes signed minors, and (3) the transpose operation that aligns cofactors for the reversal of linear transformations. A matrix is singular if |A| = 0; such matrices have no inverse. The adjoint satisfies A ( adj A) = ( adj A) A = |A| I_n. These properties are direct consequences of Laplace expansion and are used to solve linear systems AX = B by X = A^-1B, to analyse consistency, and to compute areas/volumes in coordinate geometry.
steps: The inverse of a non‑singular square matrix can be obtained by dividing its adjoint by its determinant.

Here is why: the adjoint packs all cofactors in a transposed arrangement so that when multiplied by the original matrix, each diagonal entry becomes the determinant (by Laplace expansion along a row) and every…
This yields A( adj A)=|A|I.
Dividing by the non‑zero scalar |A| gives the inverse.
Consider a shopkeeper in Jaipur who sells three items — pens, notebooks, and erasers.

The cost prices per unit form a matrix C, and the selling prices form another matrix S. If the total revenue vector R is known, the quantities sold Q satisfy S Q = R. Provided |S|≠0, the shopkeeper computes S^-1 via the…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “adjoint is the same as the inverse”) reveals the misconception that adjoint and inverse are identical, ignoring the scaling by 1/|A| and the fact that adjoint exists even for singular matrices.
remember: Define the adjoint of a square matrix A of order 3.
Explain why A( adj A) = |A|I holds for any 3×3 matrix A.
Without finding the full inverse, determine whether the matrix B = bmatrix1&2&3\\0&1&4\\5&6&0 bmatrix is invertible.

cards.title: A determinant is a scalar value associated with a square matrix that encodes…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A determinant is a scalar value associated with a square matrix that encodes key algebraic properties of the linear transformation represented by that matrix. For an n × n matrix A = [a_ij], the determinant (A) (or |A|) is defined recursively via cofactor expansion: (A) = Σ_j=1^n (-1)^i+j a_ij M_ij for any fixed row i, where M_ij is the minor obtained by deleting row i and column j. Core properties include: (1) (I)=1; (2) swapping two rows changes sign; (3) multiplying a row by scalar k multiplies the determinant by k; (4) adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the determinant unchanged; (5) (AB)= (A) (B). These properties allow simplification before expansion. Applications: solving linear systems via Cramer’s rule (x_i = ( (A_i))/( (A)) where A_i replaces column i with constants), testing matrix invertibility ( (A)≠0), and computing area/volume scaling factors. In the ISC syllabus, determinants up to order 3 are examined, with emphasis on property‑based simplification, evaluation of determinants containing variables, and solving simultaneous equations.
steps: The single most important takeaway: In ISC exams, never expand a 3×3 determinant directly if you can first create zeros using row/column operations — this saves time and reduces arithmetic errors.

Here is why: ISC papers frequently give determinants with parameters (e.g., a, b, c) or symmetric structures where a single operation (like C_1 ← C_1+C_2+C_3) produces a common factor or a zero column, turning a 9‑term…
Instead, apply R_1 ← R_1+R_2+R_3 to get a row of (a+b+c), factor it out, then use C_1 ← C_1-C_2, C_2 ← C_2-C_3 to create zeros and a 2×2 determinant that expands instantly.
This pattern — “sum of rows/columns → factor → difference of columns → evaluate” — appears in over 60% of ISC determinant proofs.
For solving equations, Cramer’s rule is the standard method when (A)≠0.
Compute (A) first; if zero, check consistency by comparing ranks (augmented matrix) — a step often missed.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the determinant becomes zero” or “the determinant remains unchanged”) reveals the misconception that row operations always preserve the determinant value, confusing the “add multiple of row” operation (which preserves the determinant)…
remember: State the effect on the determinant of a 3×3 matrix when two rows are interchanged.
Given (A)=5 for a 3×3 matrix A, find (2A) and explain the reasoning.
Evaluate whether the following statement is true or false: “If (A)=0 for a 3×3 coefficient matrix A, the system AX=B has no solution.” Justify.

cards.title: Differentiation is the process of determining the instantaneous rate of change…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Differentiation is the process of determining the instantaneous rate of change of a function y = f(x) with respect to its independent variable x. The derivative f'(x) or (dy)/(dx) quantifies how y changes for an infinitesimal change in x. This chapter extends the basic rules (sum, product, quotient, chain) to three advanced situations: 1. Composite differentiation – when a function is built by nesting one function inside another, e.g. y = (x^2). The chain rule (dy)/(dx) = (dy)/(du)·(du)/(dx) is applied repeatedly. 2. Implicit differentiation – when y is not isolated but defined implicitly by an equation F(x,y)=0 (e.g. x^2+y^2=25). Differentiating both sides with respect to x treats y as a function of x and uses (dy)/(dx) wherever y appears. 3. Logarithmic differentiation – when a function involves products, quotients, or powers of functions, taking natural logarithms first simplifies differentiation: y = f(x) then (1)/(y)(dy)/(dx) = (d)/(dx)[ f(x)]. These three techniques are interconnected: composite functions often appear inside implicit relations, and logarithmic differentiation frequently reduces a composite product to a sum of simpler derivatives. Together they equip students to differentiate any algebraic, trigonometric, exponential, or logarithmic expression encountered in the ISC Applied Mathematics syllabus.
steps: The one thing to remember: Every complicated derivative in this chapter is just the chain rule applied in a clever disguise.
Here is why: 1.
Composite functions hide one function inside another; the chain rule peels the layers one by one. 2.
Implicit relations hide y inside an equation; differentiating both sides forces the chain rule on every y term, producing (dy)/(dx) automatically. 3.
Logarithmic differentiation turns products and powers into sums and multiples, letting the chain rule work on simple logarithms instead of messy originals.
Consider a typical ISC problem: “Find (dy)/(dx) if y = (x^2+1)^ x.” Direct differentiation looks impossible.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “product rule”) reveals the misconception that each technique has its own independent rule rather than being a strategic use of the chain rule.
remember: What is the primary rule that underlies composite, implicit, and logarithmic differentiation.
Explain why implicit differentiation does not require solving for y explicitly before differentiating.
Evaluate the statement: “Logarithmic differentiation is only useful for functions with variable exponents.”.

cards.title: Composite differentiation, governed by the chain rule…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Composite differentiation, governed by the chain rule, computes the derivative of a function formed by composing two or more functions. If y = f(u) and u = g(x), then the derivative of y with respect to x is (dy)/(dx) = (dy)/(du) · (du)/(dx). This extends to longer chains: for y = f(g(h(x))), (dy)/(dx) = f'(g(h(x))) · g'(h(x)) · h'(x). The rule applies to algebraic, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions, and underpins implicit and logarithmic differentiation (covered in sibling nodes and). The chain rule is essential whenever a function’s argument is itself a function of the independent variable.
steps: The chain rule states that the derivative of a composite function is the product of the derivative of the outer function evaluated at the inner function and the derivative of the inner function.
Here is why: a change in x first alters the inner function u = g(x); that change then propagates through the outer function y = f(u).
The total rate is the product of these two successive rates.
Consider the function y = (x^2).
The outer function is u with derivative u; the inner function is u = x^2 with derivative 2x.
Multiplying gives (dy)/(dx) = (x^2) · 2x = 2x (x^2).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., - (3x) ) reveals the misconception that the chain rule only requires differentiating the outer function and ignoring the inner function’s derivative.
remember: What is the derivative of y = (3x) with respect to x.
If y = (2x^3 + 5)^4, a student writes (dy)/(dx) = 4(2x^3 + 5)^3. Explain why this is incomplete.
Evaluate the derivative of y = ( x) at x = (π)/(4).

cards.title: Implicit differentiation is a technique to compute the derivative (dy)/(dx)…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Implicit differentiation is a technique to compute the derivative (dy)/(dx) when y is defined implicitly as a function of x by an equation F(x, y) = 0, rather than explicitly as y = f(x). The method applies the chain rule to every term containing y, treating y as a differentiable function of x. Differentiating both sides of F(x, y) = 0 with respect to x yields an expression involving (dy)/(dx), which is then solved algebraically. The result is often written as (dy)/(dx) = -(∂ F/∂ x)/(∂ F/∂ y), provided ∂ F/∂ y ≠ 0. This process extends naturally to higher‑order derivatives (e.g., (d^2y)/(dx^2) ) by differentiating the first‑derivative equation again. Implicit differentiation is essential for curves that are not graphs of functions (circles, ellipses, lemniscates) and for related‑rates problems where variables are linked by a constraint. It builds directly on the chain rule for composite functions (covered in) and prepares the ground for logarithmic differentiation, where taking logs converts products/quotients into sums before implicit differentiation.
steps: Implicit differentiation lets you find (dy)/(dx) directly from an equation linking x and y without solving for y first.

Here is why: many real‑world relationships — like the shape of a satellite dish (parabola) or the pressure‑volume curve of a gas — are naturally given by equations such as x^2 + y^2 = r^2 or PV = nRT. Solving for y…
The chain rule handles this: every time you differentiate a term containing y, you multiply by (dy)/(dx) because y is a function of x. Consider the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25.
Differentiate term‑by‑term: (d)/(dx)(x^2) = 2x;
(d)/(dx)(y^2) = 2y (dy)/(dx) (chain rule);
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ y is just a variable, so differentiate normally”) reveals the misconception that implicit relations are the same as explicit functions y = f(x), ignoring the dependency of y on x.
remember: What is the derivative (dy)/(dx) for the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25 obtained by implicit differentiation.
Explain why the chain rule must be applied to every term containing y when differentiating implicitly.
Evaluate the statement: “Implicit differentiation always gives (dy)/(dx) as a function of x only.”.

cards.title: Logarithmic differentiation is a technique for finding the derivative of…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Logarithmic differentiation is a technique for finding the derivative of functions that are products, quotients, or powers where the variable appears both in the base and the exponent. For a differentiable function y = f(x) > 0, we take natural logarithms on both sides: y = f(x). Differentiating implicitly with respect to x gives (1)/(y)(dy)/(dx) = (f'(x))/(f(x)). Hence (dy)/(dx) = y · (f'(x))/(f(x)). For a function of the form y = u(x)^v(x) (with u(x) > 0), we write y = v(x) u(x) and differentiate: (1)/(y)(dy)/(dx) = v'(x) u(x) + v(x)(u'(x))/(u(x)). The method reduces algebraic complexity by converting products into sums and powers into products, leveraging the chain rule and properties of logarithms. It is applicable only where the function is positive (or we work with absolute values) and differentiable.
steps: Logarithmic differentiation turns multiplicative complexity into additive simplicity — take ln, differentiate, multiply back.
Here is why: the derivative of a product of many factors or a power with variable exponent becomes a sum of simpler derivatives after applying.
Consider the function y = x^x.
Direct differentiation is not covered by elementary rules because the exponent is not constant.
Taking natural logs gives y = x x. Differentiating implicitly: (1)/(y)(dy)/(dx) = x + x·(1)/(x) = x + 1.
Multiplying by y = x^x yields (dy)/(dx) = x^x( x + 1).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “differentiate directly using the product rule”) reveals the misconception that logarithmic differentiation is just another name for the product rule, ignoring the logarithmic transformation that simplifies the algebra.
remember: State the first step in logarithmic differentiation for a function y = f(x) where f(x) > 0.
Explain why we multiply by the original function y after differentiating y implicitly.
A student differentiates y = (2x+1)^3x and writes (dy)/(dx) = (2x+1)^3x (3 (2x+1) + (6x)/(2x+1) ). Evaluate the correctness.

cards.title: The derivatives of the six inverse trigonometric functions — arcsin x…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The derivatives of the six inverse trigonometric functions — arcsin x, arccos x, arctan x, arccot x, arcsec x, arccsc x — are algebraic expressions that give the instantaneous rate of change of the angle (in radians) with respect to its trigonometric ratio. For a differentiable function u(x), the chain rule extends these formulas: d/dx[arcsin u] = u′/√(1−u²), d/dx[arccos u] = −u′/√(1−u²), d/dx[arctan u] = u′/(1+u²), d/dx[arccot u] = −u′/(1+u²), d/dx[arcsec u] = u′/(|u|√(u²−1)), d/dx[arccsc u] = −u′/(|u|√(u²−1)). Each formula is valid only on the principal domain of the corresponding inverse function (e.g., arcsin u requires |u|≤1). These derivatives arise from implicit differentiation of the defining relations (e.g., y = arcsin x ⇔ x = sin y) and are essential for solving problems involving angles of elevation, related rates, and optimisation in applied mathematics and physics.
steps: The derivative of an inverse trigonometric function converts a rate of change of a ratio into a rate of change of an angle.

Here is why: each inverse function is defined by restricting a trigonometric function to a principal interval where it is one‑to‑one; differentiating the identity (e.g., sin(arcsin x)=x) implicitly yields the derivative…
Consider the three supporting arguments: (1) The principal domains guarantee the square‑root expressions are real and non‑negative.
(2) The chain rule extends the basic formulas to any differentiable inner function u(x).
(3) The absolute value in arcsec and arccsc derivatives preserves the sign of the derivative on the respective domains.
Now follow the narrative steps: Start with y = arcsin x. By definition, x = sin y with y ∈ [−π/2, π/2].
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., dy/dx = 1/√(x²−1)) reveals the misconception that the square‑root sign can be ignored or that the domain is |x|>1, confusing arcsin with arcsec.
remember: State the derivative of y = arcsin x and its domain of validity.
Explain why the derivative of arccos x carries a negative sign while arcsin x does not.
Evaluate the claim: “The derivative of arctan x is 1/(1+x²) for all real x, so the function is always increasing.”.

cards.title: Differentiation of inverse trigonometric functions concerns finding the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Differentiation of inverse trigonometric functions concerns finding the derivative of expressions such as y = sin⁻¹(u), y = cos⁻¹(u), y = tan⁻¹(u) etc., where u is a differentiable function of x. The process relies on the chain rule and the implicit relationship that defines each inverse function (e.g., sin y = u for y = sin⁻¹ u). By differentiating both sides of the defining equation and solving for dy/dx, we obtain algebraic formulas that involve only u and du/dx. These results connect directly to the earlier concepts of composite differentiation (chain rule) and implicit differentiation, because each inverse trigonometric function is a composite of the basic trigonometric function and its inverse, and its derivative is most naturally derived via implicit differentiation. The derivatives are: - d/dx[sin⁻¹ u] = (1/√(1‑u²))·du/dx, |u| < 1 - d/dx[cos⁻¹ u] = ‑(1/√(1‑u²))·du/dx, |u| < 1 - d/dx[tan⁻¹ u] = (1/(1+u²))·du/dx, all real u - d/dx[cot⁻¹ u] = ‑(1/(1+u²))·du/dx, all real u - d/dx[sec⁻¹ u] = (1/(|u|√(u²‑1)))·du/dx, |u| > 1 - d/dx[csc⁻¹ u] = ‑(1/(|u|√(u²‑1)))·du/dx, |u| > 1 Understanding these formulas enables students to differentiate complex expressions that appear in physics (angles of vectors, pendulum motion) and engineering (signal phase, robotics).
steps: The derivative of an inverse trigonometric function is obtained by differentiating its defining implicit relation and then solving for dy/dx, which invariably introduces the chain rule for the inner function.

Here is why: each inverse trigonometric function answers the question “what angle gives this trigonometric ratio?” For example, y = sin⁻¹ x means sin y = x. Differentiating both sides with respect to x produces cos…

The same pattern holds for the other five functions, with the only changes being the sign and the expression under the radical, reflecting the different defining equations (cos y = x, tan y = x, etc.).
Consider a right‑triangle diagram: label the angle θ, the opposite side x, and the hypotenuse 1 for the sine case.
The sine of θ is opposite/hypotenuse = x/1, so θ = sin⁻¹ x. If x changes, the triangle’s shape changes and θ changes.
The rate dθ/dx is exactly the derivative we just derived.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., dy/dx = 1/(1‑x²)) reveals the misconception that the derivative of an inverse function is simply the reciprocal of the derivative of the original function, forgetting to apply the Pythagorean identity that arises from the implicit…
remember: What is the derivative of y = sin⁻¹ x with respect to x.
Explain why d/dx[cos⁻¹ x] = ‑d/dx[sin⁻¹ x].
Given y = tan⁻¹(2x), find dy/dx at x = ½.

cards.title: Higher‑order derivatives extend the concept of differentiation by repeatedly…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Higher‑order derivatives extend the concept of differentiation by repeatedly applying the derivative operator. If y = f(x) is a differentiable function, its first derivative f'(x) = (dy)/(dx) gives the instantaneous rate of change. The second derivative f''(x) = (d^2y)/(dx^2) = (d)/(dx) ((dy)/(dx) ) measures how the rate of change itself varies — concavity, acceleration, or curvature. The nth derivative f^(n)(x) = (d^n y)/(dx^n) is defined recursively as the derivative of the (n-1)th derivative, provided each predecessor exists. In applied contexts, the second derivative often represents acceleration (when x is time), the third derivative jerk, and the fourth derivative snap. Notation includes Leibniz (d^n y)/(dx^n), Lagrange f^(n)(x), and Newton y, y for time‑dependent variables. Existence of higher‑order derivatives requires the function to be sufficiently smooth (continuously differentiable up to that order). Relationships with earlier subtopics: composite, implicit and logarithmic differentiation rules apply unchanged when differentiating repeatedly; parametric and inverse‑trigonometric functions (covered in preceding nodes) also yield higher‑order derivatives by successive application of the chain rule.
steps: Higher‑order derivatives are obtained by differentiating a function repeatedly, each step using the same rules mastered earlier.

Here is why: the first derivative gives slope; the second derivative tells how that slope changes — whether the graph curves upward (concave up) or downward (concave down); the third derivative describes the rate of…
Consider a car moving along a straight road: position s(t), velocity v(t)=s'(t), acceleration a(t)=v'(t)=s''(t), jerk j(t)=a'(t)=s'''(t).
The constant jerk means acceleration increases uniformly.
For a composite function y= (x^2), first derivative y'=2x (x^2) by chain rule.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 12x^2-6x) reveals the misconception that the constant term +2 in f'(x) differentiates to -6x instead of 0 — forgetting that the derivative of a constant is zero.
remember: What is the second derivative of f(x)=x^4-3x^2+2x.
If y= ( x), find y'' and state its sign for x∈(0,π).
Evaluate the claim: “The third derivative of any polynomial of degree 2 is zero.”.

cards.title: Composite differentiation applies the chain rule to nested functions…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Composite differentiation applies the chain rule to nested functions: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f'(g(x))·g'(x). This extends to multiple layers, e.g., y = sin(e^{x^2}) requires successive differentiation of outer to inner functions. Implicit differentiation handles equations where y is not isolated, such as x^2 + y^2 = a^2. Differentiating both sides with respect to x treats y as a function of x, yielding 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = -x/y. Logarithmic differentiation simplifies functions of the form y = u(x)^{v(x)} or products/quotients of many factors by taking natural logarithms: ln y = v(x) ln u(x), then differentiating implicitly gives (1/y) dy/dx = v'(x) ln u(x) + v(x) u'(x)/u(x). The three techniques are interconnected: composite functions often appear inside implicit relations (e.g., sin(xy) = x), and logarithmic differentiation converts exponentiation into multiplication, after which the chain rule and product rule (both composite techniques) complete the derivative. In ISC examinations, questions frequently combine these methods — for instance, differentiating y = (sin x)^{cos x} uses logarithmic differentiation followed by the chain rule and product rule. Mastery requires recognizing the algebraic structure of a function and selecting the most efficient technique, while maintaining rigorous notation (dy/dx, d/dx) and simplifying final expressions.
steps: Mastering the interplay of composite, implicit, and logarithmic differentiation lets you tackle any ISC differentiation problem by choosing the most efficient technique.

First, composite functions model real-world nested dependencies such as the compound interest formula A = P(1 + r/n)^{nt} where the exponent itself contains a product; the chain rule peels each layer systematically.
Second, implicit differentiation handles curves defined by relations like x^3 + y^3 = 3axy (the folium of Descartes) without solving for y, a common ISC question on tangents and normals.

Third, logarithmic differentiation converts variable exponents and large products into sums, turning y = (x^2+1)^{sin x} into ln y = sin x ln(x^2+1), after which the product rule and chain rule finish the job. Fourth…
Fifth, recognizing the algebraic structure — nested functions, implicit relations, or variable exponents — saves time and reduces algebraic errors under exam pressure.
Here is why: consider the ISC 2023 question "If y = (tan x)^{cot x}, find dy/dx." The function has a variable base and exponent, so logarithmic differentiation is the natural first step.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., dy/dx = cos(x^2) only) reveals the misconception that the derivative of the inner function can be omitted — confusing the chain rule with simple substitution.
remember: State the chain rule for differentiating a composite function y = f(g(x)).
Explain why implicit differentiation is necessary for the equation x^2 + y^2 = 25.
Evaluate the claim: "Logarithmic differentiation can only be used for functions with variable exponents.".

cards.title: Integration is the inverse process of differentiation.
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Integration is the inverse process of differentiation. A standard integral (or indefinite integral) of a function f(x) is a family of functions F(x) such that F′(x)=f(x), written ∫f(x)dx = F(x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant. A definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx evaluates the net signed area between the curve y=f(x) and the x‑axis from x=a to x=b; it yields a specific number, not a family. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links the two: if F is an antiderivative of f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b)−F(a). This chapter introduces the table of standard integrals (powers, trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic) and the properties of definite integrals (linearity, additivity, reversal of limits). Mastery of these tools enables computation of areas, volumes, work, and accumulated quantities in physics, economics, and engineering.
steps: This chapter equips you with the toolkit to compute areas, accumulated quantities, and solve real‑world rate problems using both standard and definite integrals.
First, standard integrals give you a ready reference: every basic function you differentiated in Class 11 now has a known antiderivative, so you can write ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C instantly.

Second, definite integrals turn those antiderivatives into numbers by applying limits, letting you measure the exact area under a curve between two points — think of the distance a car travels when its velocity varies.
Third, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is the bridge: it tells you that evaluating F(b)−F(a) is exactly the same as summing infinitely many rectangles under the curve.
Fourth, properties like linearity (∫[af+bg]=a∫f+b∫g) and additivity (∫ₐᶜ = ∫ₐᵇ+∫ᵇᶜ) let you break complex problems into simpler pieces.

Finally, you will see Indian‑context examples: calculating the total water stored in a tank with a varying inflow rate, or the total revenue from a marginal revenue function — both modelled by definite integrals.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only definite integrals”) reveals the misconception that integration always yields a numeric value, ignoring the role of the constant of integration in indefinite integrals.
remember: What are the two main types of integrals introduced in this chapter.
Explain why a definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx can be interpreted as the net area between the curve y=f(x) and the x‑axis.
Assess the statement: “Knowing the table of standard integrals is sufficient to solve any integration problem in this chapter.”.

cards.title: Standard integrals (also called elementary antiderivatives) are a finite set of…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Standard integrals (also called elementary antiderivatives) are a finite set of integration formulas that are derived directly from the fundamental differentiation rules and are accepted without proof in the ISC Applied Mathematics syllabus. Each formula expresses the indefinite integral f(x)\,dx = F(x)+C where F'(x)=f(x) and C is an arbitrary constant of integration. The core list includes: Power rule: x^n\,dx = x^n+1n+1+C for n≠ -1. Reciprocal: (1)/(x)\,dx = |x|+C. Exponential: e^x\,dx = e^x+C; a^x\,dx = (a^x)/( a)+C (a>0, a≠1). Logarithmic: x\,dx = x x - x + C. Trigonometric: x\,dx = - x+C; x\,dx = x+C; ^2 x\,dx = x+C; ^2 x\,dx = - x+C; x x\,dx = x+C; x x\,dx = - x+C. Inverse trigonometric: (1)/(1+x^2)\,dx = ^-1x+C; (1)/(√(1-x^2))\,dx = ^-1x+C; (1)/(x√(x^2-1))\,dx = ^-1|x|+C. These formulas are inter‑related: the trigonometric integrals follow from the derivatives of,, etc.; the inverse‑trigonometric integrals follow from the derivatives of ^-1, ^-1, ^-1. Mastery of this set allows a student to integrate any linear combination of the above functions by applying linearity [af(x)+bg(x)]\,dx = a f(x)\,dx + b g(x)\,dx and the constant‑multiple rule. The node does not cover integration by substitution, parts, or partial fractions — those belong to later concept nodes.
steps: The one thing you must remember: Every standard integral is the exact reverse of a basic derivative you already know; if you can differentiate it, you can integrate it by reading the derivative table backwards.
Here is why: differentiation rules are deterministic — each elementary function has a unique derivative.
Integration is the inverse operation, so the antiderivative of a function is simply the function whose derivative gives the original.
The ISC syllabus codifies the most frequent derivatives into a ready‑reference list so that you do not have to re‑derive them in the exam.
Consider the power rule.
You know (d)/(dx)x^n+1 = (n+1)x^n.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ^2 x\,dx = x + C) reveals the misconception that the integral of a squared trigonometric function follows the same pattern as x x\,dx = x + C, confusing the derivative of x with that of x.
remember: Write the standard integral formula for ^2 x\,dx.
Explain why (1)/(x)\,dx = |x|+C includes an absolute value, whereas e^x\,dx = e^x+C does not.
Evaluate the claim: “ (dx)/(1+x^2) = ^-1x + C is valid for all real x without any domain restriction.”.

cards.title: A definite integral of a function f(x) over a closed interval [a…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A definite integral of a function f(x) over a closed interval [a, b] is the limit of a Riemann sum as the partition norm approaches zero, denoted ∫_a^b f(x) dx. It represents the net signed area between the curve y = f(x) and the x‑axis from x = a to x = b. If F(x) is any antiderivative of f(x) (i.e., F′(x) = f(x)), the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). The integral inherits linearity: ∫_a^b [α f(x) + β g(x)] dx = α ∫_a^b f(x) dx + β ∫_a^b g(x) dx. Additivity over intervals gives ∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∫_a^c f(x) dx + ∫_c^b f(x) dx for a ≤ c ≤ b. Reversing limits changes sign: ∫_a^b f(x) dx = −∫_b^a f(x) dx. The integrand f(x) must be integrable (e.g., continuous or piecewise continuous) on [a, b]. The result is a real number, not a function, and carries the product of the units of f(x) and x.
steps: The definite integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx gives a single number — the net signed area between the curve y = f(x) and the x‑axis from x = a to x = b — and is computed by finding any antiderivative F(x) of f(x) and subtracting…

Here is why: the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus bridges the two central ideas of calculus — accumulation (integration) and rate of change (differentiation) — so that the labor of summing infinitely many rectangles…
Consider a velocity‑time graph for a scooter travelling on a Delhi road: the area under the v‑t curve from t = 0 s to t = 10 s equals the total displacement.
If the scooter reverses direction, the graph dips below the time axis; the definite integral automatically subtracts that backward distance, yielding net displacement.
To evaluate ∫_1^3 (2x + 3) dx, first find an antiderivative: F(x) = x² + 3x.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(a) − F(b)”) reveals the misconception that the order of subtraction does not matter, confusing the net signed area with a symmetric difference and ignoring the orientation of the interval.
remember: State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for a continuous function f on [a, b] and its antiderivative F.
Explain why ∫_a^b f(x) dx = −∫_b^a f(x) dx using the definition of the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums.
Evaluate the claim: “If f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b], then ∫_a^b f(x) dx gives the exact area between the curve and the x‑axis.” Is the claim always true? Justify.

cards.title: Integration by substitution reverses the chain rule…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Integration by substitution reverses the chain rule: if an integrand is a composite function f(g(x)) multiplied by the derivative of the inner function g′(x), we set u = g(x) so that du = g′(x)dx and the integral becomes ∫ f(u) du. Integration by parts reverses the product rule: for ∫ u dv, we choose parts u and dv such that du and v are easier to handle, giving ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Both techniques extend the repertoire of standard integrals (learned in node) and enable evaluation of definite integrals (node) when the antiderivative is not immediately recognizable. They are algebraic tools that preserve the value of the integral while simplifying its form, and they apply to algebraic, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic expressions commonly encountered in ISC Applied Mathematics.
steps: Takeaway: To integrate a product or a composite function, we reverse the product or chain rule by choosing a suitable substitution or parts, thereby transforming the integral into a standard form.
Here is why: differentiation rules are reversible; integration seeks the original function whose derivative matches the integrand. 1.
Chain‑rule reversal (substitution).
If the integrand contains f(g(x)) and g′(x) as a factor, setting u = g(x) turns ∫ f(g(x))g′(x)dx into ∫ f(u)du, which is often a standard integral. 2.
Product‑rule reversal (parts).

When the integrand is a product u·v′ (or u dv), we let U = u and dV = v′dx so that dU = u′dx and V = v; the formula ∫ U dV = UV − ∫ V dU splits the problem into a known term and a usually simpler integral. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “let u = e^{x²}”) reveals the misconception that the exponential part must be substituted, ignoring that its derivative 2x e^{x²} does not appear as a factor; this leads to an incorrect expression ∫ du/u which does not match the original…
remember: State the substitution u = g(x) that simplifies ∫ 2x e^{x²}dx.
Explain why, in integration by parts, the choice u = ln x, dv = dx is preferable to u = dx, dv = ln x for ∫ ln x dx.
Evaluate ∫₀^{π} sin x dx using the substitution u = cos x. State whether the result is positive, negative, or zero and justify.

cards.title: The definite integral of a continuous function f(x) over [a,b] represents the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The definite integral of a continuous function f(x) over [a,b] represents the signed area between the curve y=f(x) and the x-axis. When f(x)≥ 0 on [a,b], the area A is exactly _a^b f(x)\,dx (square metres if x is in metres). For two curves y=f(x) and y=g(x) with f(x)≥ g(x) on [a,b], the area between them is _a^b [f(x)-g(x)]\,dx. If the region is revolved about the x-axis, the volume generated by the disk method is V=π _a^b [f(x)]^2\,dx (cubic metres). When a hollow solid is formed between f(x) and g(x) (f(x)≥ g(x)≥ 0), the washer method gives V=π _a^b ([f(x)]^2-[g(x)]^2 )\,dx. These applications rely on the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the additive property of integrals, linking the antiderivative to geometric measurement. The variable x is the independent variable (length), f(x),g(x) are dependent variables (length), a,b are limits (length), and the results carry units of area (m^2) or volume (m^3).
steps: The definite integral is a geometric accumulator: it adds up infinitely many infinitesimal rectangles to give exact area or volume.
Here is why: (1) The Riemann sum Σ f(x_i^)Δ x approximates area by rectangles; the limit as Δ x→0 is the definite integral.
(2) When the function is non‑negative, the limit equals the actual area.
(3) For two curves, subtracting the lower from the upper gives the strip height, so the integral of the difference yields the enclosed area.
(4) Rotating a vertical strip about the x-axis produces a disk of radius f(x) and thickness dx; its volume is π f(x)^2 dx. Summing these disks gives the disk formula.
(5) If a hole exists, the washer cross‑section has outer radius f(x) and inner radius g(x); the volume element is π(f(x)^2-g(x)^2)dx.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “The integral always gives area regardless of sign”) reveals the misconception that the definite integral automatically yields positive area, ignoring that negative function values produce negative signed area.
remember: State the formula for the area bounded by the curve y = f(x), the x-axis, and the lines x = a and x = b when f(x) ≥ 0 on [a,b].
If f(x) = x^2 on [0,2], explain why _0^2 x^2\,dx gives the area under the curve.
A student writes Area = _0^π x\,dx = 0. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Integration techniques extend the repertoire of standard integrals by…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Integration techniques extend the repertoire of standard integrals by transforming complicated integrands into known forms. Integration by substitution (also called change of variable) uses the chain rule in reverse: if u = g(x) is a differentiable function, then f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = f(u)\,du. This reduces the integral to a standard form in u. Integration by parts derives from the product rule for differentiation: u\,dv = uv - v\,du. Here u and dv are chosen so that du and v are simpler than the original integrand. Both methods apply to indefinite and definite integrals; for definite integrals the limits transform accordingly: _a^b f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = _g(a)^g(b) f(u)\,du and _a^b u\,dv = [uv ]_a^b - _a^b v\,du. Mastery requires recognizing patterns — composite functions suggest substitution; products of algebraic, exponential, trigonometric, or logarithmic functions suggest parts. The node also covers the LIATE heuristic (Logarithmic, Inverse trigonometric, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential) for choosing u in parts, and the back-substitution step to return to the original variable.
steps: The one thing to remember: every integral that is not a direct standard form can be attacked by either substituting a new variable to simplify the inner function or by splitting a product into two factors using…
Here is why: the chain rule and product rule are the only differentiation rules that create composite or product structures; their inverses are substitution and parts.
When you see f(g(x))g'(x), the derivative of the inner function g'(x) is already present — substitute u=g(x).
When you see a product u· v' where neither factor is the derivative of the other, assign u to the factor that simplifies on differentiation (LIATE) and dv to the rest.
Consider the integral x e^x^2\,dx.
The exponent x^2 has derivative 2x; the integrand contains x but not 2x.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “choose u as the exponential because it stays the same”) reveals the misconception that the function which does not change on differentiation should be u — actually we want du to be simpler than u.
remember: State the integration by parts formula and name the rule used to choose u.
For the integral x x\,dx, which factor should be u and which dv? Explain using LIATE.
A student writes (3x)\,dx = - (3x) + C. Identify the error and give the correct result.

cards.title: Trigonometric integrals involve integrands that are products or powers of the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Trigonometric integrals involve integrands that are products or powers of the six basic trigonometric functions (sin x, cos x, tan x, cot x, sec x, csc x). The core strategy is to reduce the power or convert the product into a sum using Pythagorean identities (sin²x+cos²x=1, 1+tan²x=sec²x, 1+cot²x=csc²x) and double‑angle formulas (sin²x=(1‑cos2x)/2, cos²x=(1+cos2x)/2). For integrals containing √(a²‑x²), √(a²+x²) or √(x²‑a²), trigonometric substitution (x = a sinθ, a tanθ, a secθ respectively) transforms the algebraic radical into a trigonometric expression that simplifies via the same identities. Reduction formulas, derived by integration by parts, give recursive relations such as ∫sinⁿx dx = –(1/n)sinⁿ⁻¹x cosx + (n‑1)/n ∫sinⁿ⁻²x dx, allowing any integer power to be lowered step by step until a basic integral remains. This node builds on standard integrals, definite integrals, substitution, integration by parts and partial fractions (‑006) and prepares for the synthesis node.
steps: The one essential takeaway: every trigonometric integral can be reduced to a polynomial in sine and cosine (or tangent and secant) by repeatedly applying sin²x+cos²x=1 and the double‑angle formulas, after which a simple…

Any power sinⁿx cosᵐx can be handled by peeling off one factor of the odd‑powered function, converting the remaining even powers using sin²x=1‑cos²x or cos²x=1‑sin²x, and substituting u = cos x or u = sin x. If both…

For radicals √(a²‑x²), the substitution x = a sinθ converts the square root into a cosθ, and dx = a cosθ dθ, yielding an integral purely in θ that is solved by the power‑reduction techniques just described.
The same logic applies to √(a²+x²) with x = a tanθ and √(x²‑a²) with x = a secθ.
Consider ∫sin³x cos²x dx. Since the power of sine is odd, write sin³x = sin²x·sinx = (1‑cos²x)sinx.
Let u = cosx, du = –sinx dx. The integral becomes –∫(1‑u²)u² du = –∫(u²‑u⁴)du = –(u³/3‑u⁵/5)+C = –(cos³x/3‑cos⁵x/5)+C.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing the minus sign or writing (n+1)/n) reveals the misconception that integration by parts always adds the integral term instead of subtracting it, confusing the sign convention.
remember: State the reduction formula for ∫sinⁿx dx (n ≥ 2) and identify each term.
Explain why the substitution u = cosx is effective for ∫sin³x cos²x dx but u = sinx would not simplify it as directly.
Evaluate the two methods for ∫tan²x dx: (a) using tan²x = sec²x‑1, (b) writing tan²x = sin²x/cos²x and substituting u = cosx. Which is more efficient and why.

cards.title: This node synthesises the two core sub‑topics of Chapter 13…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This node synthesises the two core sub‑topics of Chapter 13: standard integrals and definite integrals. Standard integrals are the antiderivative formulas for elementary functions — algebraic (∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C, n≠−1), trigonometric (∫sin x dx = −cos x + C, ∫cos x dx = sin x + C), exponential (∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C), and logarithmic (∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C). Definite integrals extend these by evaluating the antiderivative at upper and lower limits: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F′(x)=f(x). The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links the two: differentiation and integration are inverse processes. Key properties of definite integrals — linearity (∫(af+bg)=a∫f+b∫g), additivity over intervals (∫ₐᵇ+∫ᵇᶜ=∫ₐᶜ), reversal (∫ₐᵇ = −∫ᵇₐ), and symmetry (∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a−x) dx) — are repeatedly tested in ISC papers. Exam patterns emphasise: (i) direct evaluation using standard forms, (ii) manipulation using properties before integrating, (iii) application to area, average value, and simple differential equations, and (iv) “show that” proofs requiring algebraic manipulation of the integral expression. Mastery means recognising which property or substitution simplifies a given integral, executing the algebra without sign errors, and presenting the final answer with correct limits and constant handling.
steps: Mastering ISC Integral questions requires recognising standard forms, applying the Fundamental Theorem correctly, and using properties to simplify before integrating.
Here is why: the ISC paper rarely asks for a bare ∫xⁿ dx; it embeds the integral in a definite form, combines functions, or asks for a proof using symmetry.
First, build a mental “formula deck” of the 12 most common standard integrals (power, exponential, log, sin, cos, sec², cosec², sec tan, cosec cot, 1/√(a²−x²), 1/(a²+x²), 1/(x√(x²−a²))).
When you see ∫₀¹ (2x+3)e^{x²+3x} dx, spot the derivative of the exponent inside — substitution u = x²+3x turns it into ∫ eᵘ du, a standard form.
Second, always check limits after substitution: if u = x²+3x, then u(0)=0, u(1)=4, so the definite integral becomes ∫₀⁴ eᵘ du = e⁴−1.
Forgetting to change limits is a classic trap that costs 1–2 marks.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) without the constant C, or ∫ sin x dx = cos x + C) reveals the misconception that the constant of integration is optional or that the derivative of cos x is sin x instead of −sin x.
remember: List the standard integral formulas for ∫ xⁿ dx (n≠−1), ∫ eˣ dx, ∫ sin x dx, and ∫ 1/x dx.
Explain why ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ᵇₐ f(x) dx using the definition of the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums.
A student evaluates ∫₀² (x² + 3) dx as [x³/3 + 3x]₀² = (8/3 + 6) − (0 + 0) = 26/3. Is this correct? If not, identify the error.

cards.title: This chapter introduces the mathematical modelling of commercial activities…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This chapter introduces the mathematical modelling of commercial activities using functions of a single variable, usually the quantity produced or sold x. The cost function C(x) represents total expenditure (fixed + variable) to produce x units; its derivative C'(x) is the marginal cost. The revenue function R(x)=p(x)· x gives total income from selling x units at price p(x); its derivative R'(x) is the marginal revenue. The profit function P(x)=R(x)-C(x) measures net gain; maximising profit requires solving P'(x)=0 i.e. R'(x)=C'(x) and verifying the second‑derivative condition P''(x)<0. Marginal analysis interprets these derivatives as the instantaneous rate of change of cost, revenue, or profit per additional unit. Maximisation problems apply the first‑ and second‑derivative tests to find optimal production levels, break‑even points, and price‑output decisions. All functions are assumed continuous and differentiable on the relevant domain, and quantities are measured in units (e.g., items) while monetary values are in Indian Rupees (₹).
steps: The chapter shows how calculus turns everyday business questions into optimisation problems: given cost and revenue structures, find the output that maximises profit.

Here is why: every commercial decision — how many units to produce, what price to set, whether to expand — hinges on comparing the extra benefit of one more unit (marginal revenue) with its extra cost (marginal cost).

First, we define the total cost function C(x) comprising fixed costs (rent, salaries) that do not vary with output and variable costs (raw materials) that do. Next, the revenue function R(x) captures income, often as…
Profit is simply the difference P(x)=R(x)-C(x).
Marginal analysis then introduces the derivatives C'(x), R'(x), P'(x) as the instantaneous change per additional unit.
The profit‑maximising condition P'(x)=0 reduces to R'(x)=C'(x); the second‑derivative test P''(x)<0 confirms a maximum.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Integration, Differential equations, Probability”) reveals the misconception that this chapter repeats earlier calculus topics instead of applying them to commerce.
remember: List the five sub‑topics covered in Chapter 14 of ISC Applied Mathematics.
Explain why the condition R'(x)=C'(x) is necessary for profit maximisation.
A student claims that if marginal revenue is positive, profit must be increasing. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: In commerce calculus, the cost function C(x) expresses the total monetary…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: In commerce calculus, the cost function C(x) expresses the total monetary outlay required to produce x units of a good or service. It is the sum of fixed cost F (costs that do not vary with output, e.g., rent, salaries) and variable cost V(x) (costs that change proportionally with output, e.g., raw materials, direct labour). For linear variable costs, V(x)=v\,x where v is the constant variable cost per unit (₹/unit). Thus C(x)=F+v\,x. From C(x) we derive two key marginal concepts: - Marginal Cost (MC) = (dC)/(dx)=v (the instantaneous cost of producing one additional unit). - Average Cost (AC) = (C(x))/(x)= (F)/(x)+v (cost per unit at output x). The relationship between MC and AC determines cost behaviour: when MC < AC, AC falls; when MC > AC, AC rises; MC = AC at the minimum point of AC. These functions are the foundation for revenue, profit, and optimisation analyses covered in subsequent nodes.
steps: The total cost of production is a linear function of output when variable cost per unit is constant.
Here is why: fixed costs remain unchanged regardless of how many units are produced, while variable costs increase proportionally.
Consider a textbook publisher: the press setup cost ₹2,00,000 is fixed; each book printed adds ₹150 for paper and ink. If x books are printed, total cost C(x)=2,00,000+150x.
The marginal cost is the derivative C'(x)=150, meaning every extra book costs exactly ₹150.
The average cost is AC(x)=(2,00,000)/(x)+150; as x grows, the fixed‑cost component (2,00,000)/(x) shrinks, so AC falls until the marginal cost equals average cost.
Setting MC=AC gives 150=(2,00,000)/(x)+150 → (2,00,000)/(x)=0, which has no finite solution; thus AC approaches ₹150 asymptotically but never reaches a minimum at a finite output.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing C(x)=F+v without the variable x) reveals the misconception that variable cost is a lump sum rather than a per‑unit rate.
remember: State the general form of a linear total cost function and define each symbol with its SI unit.
Explain why marginal cost equals the slope of the total cost curve for a linear cost function.
A firm’s total cost function is C(x)=5000+20x. Evaluate whether the average cost is decreasing, constant, or increasing at x=100 and justify using the MC‑AC relationship.

cards.title: In commerce mathematics, revenue (often denoted R) is the monetary value…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: In commerce mathematics, revenue (often denoted R) is the monetary value obtained from selling x units of a product at a price p(x) that may depend on the quantity sold. The total revenue function is R(x)=p(x)· x. When the price is constant (perfectly elastic demand), p(x)=p_0 and R(x)=p_0x is linear. In realistic markets the demand curve slopes downward, so p(x) decreases with x and R(x) becomes a concave quadratic or higher‑order polynomial. Average revenue (AR) equals R(x)/x = p(x); it is simply the price per unit. Marginal revenue (MR) is the derivative MR = (dR)/(dx) and measures the extra revenue from selling one more unit. For a linear demand p(x)=a-bx, R(x)=ax-bx^2 and MR = a-2bx. Revenue links directly to cost (previous node) and profit (next node) through π(x)=R(x)-C(x). Understanding the shape of R(x) and its marginal counterpart is essential for optimisation problems later in the chapter.
steps: Takeaway: Revenue is the product of price and quantity sold, and its marginal value tells you how much extra money each additional unit brings — a key input for any profit‑maximisation decision.
Here is why: 1.
Revenue starts with the demand curve.
In a market the price a firm can charge usually falls as it tries to sell more.
That relationship p(x) is the demand function.
Multiplying price by quantity gives the total revenue function R(x)=p(x)\,x. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as R(x)=p_0+x reveals the misconception that revenue adds price and quantity instead of multiplying them — confusing addition with the correct product operation.
remember: State the formula for total revenue R(x) when the price per unit is a constant p_0.
Explain why average revenue (AR) is always equal to the price function p(x) for any demand curve.
A firm faces the demand function p(x)=200-0.5x (₹ per unit, x in units). Evaluate whether the statement “Marginal revenue is always positive for this firm” is true or false.

cards.title: A profit function P(x) gives the total profit (in rupees) earned when a firm…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A profit function P(x) gives the total profit (in rupees) earned when a firm produces and sells x units of a product. It is defined algebraically as the difference between the revenue function R(x) and the cost function C(x): P(x)=R(x)-C(x) - x – quantity produced and sold (unit: number of items, dimensionless). - R(x) – total revenue (unit: ₹). - C(x) – total cost (unit: ₹). - P(x) – total profit (unit: ₹). The profit function inherits the domains of R(x) and C(x); typically x≥0. Marginal profit, the instantaneous rate of change of profit with respect to quantity, is the derivative P'(x)=R'(x)-C'(x). Thus marginal profit equals marginal revenue minus marginal cost. Understanding P(x) allows us to locate the output level where profit is greatest by analysing where P'(x)=0 and P''(x)<0.
steps: Takeaway: Profit is maximised when marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Why this is true: 1.
Profit is defined as the difference between revenue and cost, so any change in profit comes from changes in revenue and cost. 2.
Differentiating the profit function gives P'(x)=R'(x)-C'(x); the terms R'(x) and C'(x) are marginal revenue and marginal cost respectively. 3.
Setting P'(x)=0 yields R'(x)=C'(x); at this point profit is neither increasing nor decreasing with output. 4.
If the profit curve is concave down (P''(x)<0), the stationary point is a maximum. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “P(x)=R(x)+C(x)”) reveals the misconception that profit adds cost to revenue, confusing the idea that cost reduces earnings.
remember: State the profit function in terms of revenue and cost functions.
If R(x)=15x-0.01x^2 and C(x)=200+3x, find the profit function and simplify.
Explain why a firm cannot maximise profit by simply maximising revenue.

cards.title: Marginal analysis in commerce applies the concept of the derivative to cost…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Marginal analysis in commerce applies the concept of the derivative to cost, revenue, and profit functions to study the effect of producing and selling one additional unit. Let C(x) denote the total cost (in rupees) of producing x units, R(x) the total revenue (in rupees) from selling x units, and P(x)=R(x)−C(x) the profit (in rupees). The marginal cost (MC) is the instantaneous rate of change of total cost with respect to quantity, defined as MC = dC/dx, measured in rupees per unit. Similarly, marginal revenue (MR) = dR/dx (rupees per unit) and marginal profit (MP) = dP/dx = MR − MC (rupees per unit). These quantities approximate the change in total cost, revenue, or profit when x increases by a small amount Δx, because MC·Δx ≈ ΔC for sufficiently small Δx. In decision‑making, a firm should increase output as long as MR > MC, because each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, raising profit. When MR = MC, profit is stationary; if the second derivative of profit is negative, this point yields maximum profit. Conversely, if MR < MC, producing additional units reduces profit. Marginal analysis thus links the mathematical tool of differentiation to practical business choices such as optimal production level, pricing, and acceptance of special orders. It builds directly on the earlier nodes that defined cost, revenue, and profit functions, and it prepares the learner for the subsequent node on maximisation problems where the condition MR = MC is used to locate the optimum.
steps: The marginal cost (or revenue) of producing one more unit equals the instantaneous rate of change of the total cost (or revenue) function, found by differentiation.
Here is why: First, the derivative dC/dx gives the slope of the tangent to the cost curve at a point, representing how cost changes for an infinitesimally small increase in output.

Second, for a small but finite change Δx, the linear approximation ΔC ≈ (dC/dx)·Δx holds; setting Δx = 1 unit shows that the marginal cost approximates the actual extra cost of producing one additional unit when the…
Third, marginal revenue works analogously, providing the extra revenue from selling one more unit, and comparing MR with MC tells whether profit will rise, fall, or stay unchanged.

Fourth, when MR exceeds MC, expanding output increases total profit; when MR is less than MC, output should be reduced; the profit‑maximising level occurs where MR = MC, provided the profit curve is concave down…
Consider a small workshop that manufactures leather wallets.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "Marginal cost is the total cost divided by quantity") reveals the misconception of confusing marginal with average cost.
remember: State the definition of marginal cost and write its mathematical expression in terms of the total cost function C(x).
Explain why the marginal cost at a production level x₀ can be approximated by the cost difference for producing one extra unit when Δx = 1, and discuss the limitation of this….
Given the total cost function C(x)=0.02x^3−0.6x^2+5x+150 (rupees), determine whether the marginal cost is increasing or decreasing at x=10 units. Show your working.

cards.title: Maximisation problems in commerce apply differential calculus to determine the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Maximisation problems in commerce apply differential calculus to determine the output level that yields the greatest profit, revenue, or minimum cost. Given a cost function C(x) and a revenue function R(x) where x is the quantity produced and sold (units), the profit function is π(x) = R(x) – C(x). The first‑order condition for an interior maximum is π′(x) = 0 ⇔ R′(x) = C′(x), i.e., marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC). The second‑order condition requires π″(x) < 0 ⇔ R″(x) < C″(x) to confirm a maximum rather than a minimum. If the domain is restricted (e.g., capacity limits), endpoints are also evaluated. The method extends to revenue maximisation (R′(x)=0, R″(x)<0) and cost minimisation (C′(x)=0, C″(x)>0). All functions are assumed continuous and differentiable on the relevant interval. The solution provides the optimal production quantity x and the corresponding maximum profit π(x), maximum revenue R(x), or minimum cost C(x). Units: x in units, C,R,π in ₹ (Indian rupees), marginal values in ₹/unit.
steps: The optimal production level is found where marginal revenue equals marginal cost and the profit curve is concave down.
Here is why: profit changes with each extra unit; when the extra revenue from one more unit exactly matches its extra cost, profit stops rising and begins to fall if we go further.
Consider a bakery that sells cakes.
Its total cost is C(x) = 2000 + 50x + 0.5x² (₹) and it sells each cake at a price that yields revenue R(x) = 200x – 0.2x² (₹).
Step 2: Differentiate: π′(x) = 150 – 1.4x.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “set total revenue equal to total cost”) reveals the misconception that maximising profit means breaking even, confusing the profit‑maximising condition with the break‑even point.
remember: State the first‑order condition for profit maximisation in terms of marginal revenue and marginal cost.
A firm’s profit function is π(x) = –2x² + 80x – 500. Explain why the second derivative test is necessary after solving π′(x)=0.
Evaluate the claim: “If marginal revenue is constant, profit is maximised at the highest possible output.”.

cards.title: Elasticity of demand (Ed) quantifies the responsiveness of quantity demanded…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Elasticity of demand (Ed) quantifies the responsiveness of quantity demanded (Q) to a change in price (P). For a differentiable demand function Q = f(P), the point price elasticity of demand is defined as Ed = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q). Since dQ/dP is negative for normal goods, Ed is negative; economists often use its absolute value |Ed|. If |Ed| > 1, demand is elastic (revenue rises when price falls); if |Ed| < 1, demand is inelastic (revenue falls when price falls); if |Ed| = 1, demand is unit‑elastic (revenue unchanged). A key relationship links marginal revenue (MR) to elasticity: MR = P (1 + 1/Ed). This formula shows that MR is positive only when demand is elastic (|Ed| > 1), zero at unit elasticity, and negative when inelastic. The concept extends to income elasticity and cross‑price elasticity, but this node focuses on price elasticity as a tool for revenue optimisation, building directly on the marginal analysis and maximisation techniques covered in earlier nodes.
steps: The takeaway: Elasticity of demand turns the abstract derivative dQ/dP into a decision‑making metric that tells a firm exactly whether a price cut will raise or lower total revenue.
Here is why: 1.
Derivative alone is not enough — dQ/dP depends on units (e.g., cups per rupee vs. thousands of units per rupee).
Elasticity removes units by multiplying by P/Q, giving a pure number comparable across products. 2.
Revenue change sign hinges on elasticity — Total revenue R = P·Q.
Differentiating: dR/dP = Q + P·dQ/dP = Q(1 + Ed).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Ed = ΔQ/ΔP”) reveals the misconception that elasticity is a simple slope rather than a unit‑free ratio of percentage changes.
remember: Define point price elasticity of demand and state its formula for a demand function Q = f(P).
If the demand function is Q = 1000 – 50P, calculate the elasticity at P = ₹10 and interpret whether demand is elastic, inelastic, or unit‑elastic.
A firm faces demand P = 200 – 0.2Q.….

cards.title: In commerce mathematics, let x denote the quantity of goods produced and sold.
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: In commerce mathematics, let x denote the quantity of goods produced and sold. The cost function C(x) gives total expenditure (₹) to produce x units; its derivative MC = dC/dx is the marginal cost (₹ per unit), the instantaneous cost of one additional unit. The revenue function R(x) gives total income (₹) from selling x units; its derivative MR = dR/dx is the marginal revenue (₹ per unit), the extra income from one more unit. The profit function P(x) = R(x) − C(x) represents net gain (₹). Its derivative MP = dP/dx = MR − MC is the marginal profit. Profit is maximised when MP = 0 ⇔ MR = MC, provided the profit curve is concave down at that point, i.e. d²P/dx² < 0. If the second derivative is positive, the stationary point is a minimum; if zero, further investigation is needed. These relationships link cost, revenue, profit and their marginal counterparts, forming the basis for optimisation problems in business.
steps: The profit‑maximising output level is found where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, provided the profit function is concave down at that point.
Here is why: First, profit is defined as the difference between revenue and cost, P(x)=R(x)−C(x).
Differentiating gives the marginal profit MP= dP/dx = dR/dx − dC/dx = MR−MC.
Second, a necessary condition for an extremum (maximum or minimum) of a differentiable function is that its first derivative equals zero; thus MP=0 leads to MR=MC.
Third, to distinguish a maximum from a minimum we examine the second derivative: d²P/dx² = dMR/dx − dMC/dx.
If this value is negative, the profit curve bends downward and the stationary point is a maximum; if positive, it is a minimum.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Marginal cost is total cost divided by output”) reveals the misconception of confusing marginal with average cost, ignoring that marginal concerns the change from one extra unit, not the spread over all units.
remember: Define marginal cost and state its symbol and SI unit.
Explain why setting the derivative of the profit function to zero is necessary (but not sufficient) for locating a maximum profit.
Given profit function P(x)=−2x²+40x−150, determine whether the critical point gives maximum or minimum profit and find the profit value.

cards.title: A differential equation is an equation that relates a function with its…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A differential equation is an equation that relates a function with its derivatives. In this chapter we focus on first‑order, first‑degree ordinary differential equations (ODEs) of the form (dy)/(dx) = f(x, y). The chapter covers two fundamental solution techniques: (1) Variable separable equations, where the equation can be rewritten as g(y)\,dy = h(x)\,dx and integrated directly; (2) Linear equations of the form (dy)/(dx) + P(x)y = Q(x), solved using an integrating factor μ(x) = e^ P(x)\,dx. Both methods rely on the fundamental theorem of calculus and the concept of antiderivatives studied in earlier calculus chapters. The chapter also introduces the idea of a general solution (containing an arbitrary constant) and a particular solution obtained by applying an initial condition. These techniques form the backbone for modelling dynamic systems in physics, biology, economics and engineering, and they are explicitly required in the ISC Applied Mathematics syllabus for the 2025‑26 examination.
steps: The chapter equips you with two universal recipes — variable separable and linear — to solve any first‑order, first‑degree ODE that appears in the ISC Applied Mathematics paper.

Here is why: every dynamic model (population, cooling, investment growth) reduces to a rate equation (dy)/(dx)=f(x,y); if the right‑hand side splits into a product of a function of x and a function of y, the equation is…
If the equation can be arranged as (dy)/(dx)+P(x)y=Q(x), it is linear and the integrating factor μ(x)=e^ P(x)dx turns the left side into an exact derivative, allowing direct integration.

Consider a typical ISC problem: “The rate of change of a bacterial culture is proportional to its size.” This translates to (dN)/(dt)=kN, a variable separable equation; separating gives (dN)/(N)=k\,dt and integrating…

For a linear example, “A loan of ₹1,00,000 accrues interest at 8% per annum while ₹10,000 is repaid yearly” leads to (dA)/(dt)=0.08A-10000, a linear ODE with P(t)=-0.08 and Q(t)=-10000; the integrating factor e^-0.08t…
A common exam trap is forgetting the constant of integration after the first integration step — always write “+ C” immediately.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ (dy)/(dx)=P(x)y+Q(x) solved by separation of variables”) reveals the misconception that any first‑order ODE can be separated; linear equations require the integrating factor method unless Q(x)=0, in which case they become separable.
remember: State the general form of a first‑order linear differential equation and name the function used to solve it.
Given the differential equation (dy)/(dx) = (x^2)/(y), explain why it is variable separable and write the separated form.
Evaluate the claim: “Every variable separable differential equation can also be solved as a linear equation.” Provide a justification.

cards.title: A first‑order differential equation is called variable separable if it can be…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A first‑order differential equation is called variable separable if it can be expressed in the form dy/dx = g(x) · h(y) where g(x) is a function of x alone and h(y) is a function of y alone. By algebraic manipulation we rewrite it as (1/h(y)) dy = g(x) dx provided h(y) ≠ 0. Both sides are then integrated independently: ∫ (1/h(y)) dy = ∫ g(x) dx + C, where C is an arbitrary constant. The process yields an implicit relation between y and x; if an initial condition y(x₀)=y₀ is given, C is determined to obtain a particular solution. This method relies entirely on the ability to separate the differentials dy and dx, which is possible only when the right‑hand side factorises into a product of a pure‑x function and a pure‑y function. It is the simplest analytical technique for solving first‑order ODEs and serves as a foundation for more advanced methods such as linear equations (next node) and exact equations. The key sub‑concepts are: (i) recognition of separable structure, (ii) algebraic separation of variables, (iii) integration of standard forms, and (iv) application of initial conditions to fix the constant of integration.
steps: The variable separable method solves any first‑order differential equation that can be written as dy/dx = g(x)h(y) by isolating all y‑terms with dy and all x‑terms with dx, then integrating each side independently.
Here is why: (1) The equation’s right‑hand side factorises into a product of a function of x and a function of y, which is the defining property.
(2) Dividing by h(y) and multiplying by dx yields a purely y‑dependent differential on the left and a purely x‑dependent differential on the right.
(3) Integration of each side is a direct application of the antiderivative skills mastered in Class 11.
(4) The constant of integration appears only once because the two indefinite integrals differ by a constant.
(5) An initial condition pins down that constant, giving a unique particular solution.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “any equation with dy/dx can be separated”) reveals the misconception that separation is always possible — confusing algebraic manipulation with structural factorisation.
remember: State the condition for a first‑order differential equation to be variable separable.
Given dy/dx = (x²+1)/(y²+1), explain why it is separable and write the separated form.
A student writes the separated form of dy/dx = x·y as dy/y = x dx. Is this correct? Justify.

cards.title: A first‑order linear differential equation in the dependent variable y and…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A first‑order linear differential equation in the dependent variable y and independent variable x has the standard form (dy)/(dx) + P(x)\,y = Q(x) where P(x) and Q(x) are continuous functions of x on an interval I. The equation is linear because the unknown function y and its derivative (dy)/(dx) appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together. The integrating factor (IF) is defined as μ(x) = \! ( P(x)\,dx ) Multiplying the whole equation by μ(x) converts the left‑hand side into the exact derivative of the product μ(x)y: (d)/(dx) [μ(x)\,y ] = μ(x)\,Q(x) Integrating both sides with respect to x yields the general solution y(x) = (1)/(μ(x)) ( μ(x)\,Q(x)\,dx + C ) where C is an arbitrary constant determined by an initial condition y(x_0)=y_0. Relationship to variable‑separable equations (covered in node): a separable equation can be written as (dy)/(dx)=g(x)h(y). If h(y)=y the equation becomes linear with P(x)=-g(x) and Q(x)=0. Thus linear equations generalise the separable case where the dependent variable appears linearly. Key quantities and symbols - x – independent variable (often time t in applications) - y – dependent variable (e.g., displacement, concentration, charge) - P(x) – coefficient function (units: reciprocal of x’s unit) - Q(x) – forcing function (units: same as (dy)/(dx)) - μ(x) – integrating factor (dimensionless) - C – constant of integration (units: same as y)
steps: The one thing to remember: any first‑order linear ODE can be solved by multiplying with an integrating factor that turns the left side into a perfect derivative, after which a single integration gives the solution.
Here is why: the equation (dy)/(dx)+P(x)y=Q(x) is not directly integrable because the derivative of y is mixed with y itself.
If we find a function μ(x) such that μ(dy)/(dx)+μ P y = (d)/(dx)(μ y), then the left side becomes the derivative of a product.
The condition for μ is (dμ)/(dx) = μ P, whose solution is μ = e^ P dx. This μ is the integrating factor.
Consider a practical Indian example: a mixing tank in a dairy plant.
Fresh milk (pure fat‑free) enters at 5\ L/min while a well‑stirred mixture leaves at the same rate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (dy)/(dx) + 3x^2 y = x) reveals the misconception that the sign of P(x) does not change when moving terms across the equality — students forget to subtract 3x^2 y from both sides.
remember: Write the standard form of the linear differential equation (dy)/(dx) = 3x^2 y + x.
For the ODE (dy)/(dx) + (2)/(x)y = x^2, find the integrating factor μ(x).
Evaluate whether the function y = e^-x^2 _0^x e^t^2dt satisfies the linear ODE (dy)/(dx) + 2xy = 1.

cards.title: A first‑order differential equation is called homogeneous if it can be…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A first‑order differential equation is called homogeneous if it can be expressed in the form dy/dx = f(y/x) or, equivalently, as M(x,y)dx + N(x,y)dy = 0 where M and N are homogeneous functions of the same degree n. A function F(x,y) is homogeneous of degree n if F(tx,ty) = tⁿF(x,y) for all t > 0. In the ratio form, the right‑hand side depends solely on the quotient y/x, which means the slope at any point (x,y) is determined by the direction from the origin. This property allows the substitution y = vx (or x = vy), transforming the equation into a variable‑separable form in v and x. The method builds directly on the variable‑separable technique (node) and the algebraic manipulation of homogeneous functions studied in Class 11. Unlike linear equations (node) which require an integrating factor, homogeneous equations exploit symmetry under scaling. The solution yields an implicit or explicit relation between x and y, often involving logarithmic or inverse trigonometric functions. The concept is restricted to first‑order, first‑degree equations; higher‑order homogeneous equations belong to a later chapter.
steps: The takeaway: Every homogeneous first‑order DE can be solved by the substitution y = vx, which converts it into a variable‑separable equation in v and x. Here is why: (1) Homogeneity means the DE’s structure is…
(2) This scale invariance forces the derivative dy/dx to depend only on the ratio y/x.
(3) Setting y = vx makes that ratio the new variable v, and the chain rule gives dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
(4) Substituting back yields an equation where v and x separate, allowing direct integration.
(5) The final step replaces v with y/x to obtain the solution in original variables.
Consider the DE dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “M and N must be polynomials of the same degree”) reveals the misconception that only polynomials can be homogeneous — but functions like sin(y/x) or e^(y/x) are also homogeneous of degree 0.
remember: State the necessary and sufficient condition for a first‑order differential equation M(x,y)dx + N(x,y)dy = 0 to be homogeneous.
Given dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy), show that it is homogeneous and state its degree.
A student claims that any equation of the form dy/dx = f(y/x) is homogeneous. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: An exact differential equation is a first‑order equation that can be written in…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: An exact differential equation is a first‑order equation that can be written in the form M(x,y)\,dx + N(x,y)\,dy = 0 where there exists a function φ(x,y) (called a potential function) such that dφ = (∂φ)/(∂ x)dx + (∂φ)/(∂ y)dy = M\,dx + N\,dy. Consequently, (∂φ)/(∂ x)=M and (∂φ)/(∂ y)=N. For such a φ to exist, the mixed partial derivatives must be equal: (∂ M)/(∂ y) = (∂ N)/(∂ x). This condition is necessary; in a simply‑connected domain it is also sufficient (Poincaré lemma). When the condition holds, one can recover φ by integrating M with respect to x (treating y as constant) or N with respect to y, then determining the unknown function of the other variable by comparison. The general solution is given implicitly by φ(x,y)=C. Variable separable and linear equations are special cases: a separable equation g(y)dy=f(x)dx is exact with φ=G(y)-F(x); a linear equation dy/dx+P(x)y=Q(x) becomes exact after multiplication by an integrating factor, which is itself derived from the exactness condition. Thus exactness provides a unifying viewpoint that encompasses the earlier sub‑topics and extends to a broader class of first‑order equations.
steps: An exact first‑order differential equation M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0 can be solved by finding a potential function φ(x,y) whose total differential equals the left‑hand side.
Here is why: 1.
The equality of mixed partials ∂ M/∂ y = ∂ N/∂ x guarantees that the vector field (M,N) is conservative, so a scalar potential φ exists. 2.
Integrating M with respect to x (holding y fixed) gives φ = M\,dx + g(y), where g(y) is an unknown function of y. 3.
Differentiating this expression with respect to y and setting it equal to N determines g'(y), hence g(y) up to an additive constant. 4.
Substituting g(y) back yields φ(x,y); the solution is the level curve φ(x,y)=C. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “∂ M/∂ x = ∂ N/∂ y”) reveals the misconception of swapping the variables in the partial derivatives, confusing which function is differentiated with respect to which variable.
remember: State the condition for exactness of a differential equation written as M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0.
Given M=2xy and N=x^2+y^2, test whether Mdx+Ndy=0 is exact.
Determine whether (y x- y)dx+( x-x y)dy=0 is exact, and if so find its general solution.

cards.title: An exact differential equation is a first‑order equation that can be written in…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: An exact differential equation is a first‑order equation that can be written in the form M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0 where M and N are functions of the two independent variables x and y. The equation is exact if there exists a function (x,y) (called a potential function) such that (∂ )/(∂ x)=M(x,y) (∂ )/(∂ y)=N(x,y). A necessary and sufficient condition for exactness on a simply‑connected domain is (∂ M)/(∂ y)=(∂ N)/(∂ x). When this condition holds, the differential form Mdx+Ndy is the total differential d; integrating d =0 gives (x,y)=C, which is the implicit solution. Exact equations generalise variable‑separable forms (where M depends only on x and N only on y) and linear equations (which become exact after multiplying by an integrating factor). Thus, exactness sits between the simplest separable cases and the broader class solvable by integrating factors.
steps: Takeaway: An exact differential equation can be solved by finding a single potential function whose total differential reproduces the given Mdx+Ndy.
Here is why: 1.
Condition check – Equality of the mixed partial derivatives guarantees the existence of a potential function (Poincaré lemma). 2.
Integration of M – Integrate M(x,y) with respect to x while treating y as constant; this yields plus an unknown function of y. 3.
Determine the unknown – Differentiate the result with respect to y and set it equal to N(x,y); solve for the unknown function. 4.
