Assemble solution – Combine the parts to obtain (x,y)=C.
remember: State the condition that must be satisfied for M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0 to be an exact differential equation.
Explain why solving an exact differential equation reduces to finding a potential function (x,y) such that d =Mdx+Ndy.
Given M(x,y)=2xy and N(x,y)=x^2+3y^2, test exactness and solve the differential equation.

cards.title: An exact differential equation is a first‑order first‑degree equation that can…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: An exact differential equation is a first‑order first‑degree equation that can be written in the form M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0 where M and N are functions of the independent variable x and dependent variable y. The equation is exact if there exists a potential function (x,y) such that (∂ )/(∂ x)=M(x,y) (∂ )/(∂ y)=N(x,y). Equivalently, exactness is tested by the equality of mixed partial derivatives (∂ M)/(∂ y)=(∂ N)/(∂ x). When this condition holds, the solution is given implicitly by (x,y)=C, where C is an arbitrary constant. Exact equations generalise variable‑separable and linear equations: a separable equation g(y)dy=f(x)dx is exact with M=-f(x), N=g(y); a linear equation dy/dx+P(x)y=Q(x) becomes exact after multiplying by its integrating factor. Thus exactness provides a unified test for integrability and a systematic method to construct the solution via the potential function.
steps: Takeaway: An exact differential equation can be solved by finding a single potential function whose total differential reproduces the given Mdx+Ndy.
Why this works: 1.
The condition ∂ M/∂ y=∂ N/∂ x guarantees that the mixed partial derivatives of a candidate are equal, a necessary condition for the existence of a smooth (Poincaré lemma). 2.
Integrating M with respect to x yields up to an unknown function of y; differentiating this result and equating to N determines that unknown function. 3.
The resulting (x,y)=C implicitly satisfies the original equation because d =Mdx+Ndy=0. 4.
If the equation is not exact, an integrating factor (often a function of x or y alone) can sometimes restore exactness, extending the method’s reach. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as “∂ M/∂ x=∂ N/∂ y” reveals the misconception of confusing the variables with respect to which the partial derivatives are taken, indicating a lack of understanding of the symmetry required for exactness.
remember: State the exactness condition for a differential equation M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0.
Explain why the condition ∂ M/∂ y=∂ N/∂ x guarantees the existence of a potential function.
Test whether (2xy+y^3)dx+(x^2+3xy^2)dy=0 is exact. If exact, find its solution.

cards.title: Synthesis of differential equations in this chapter means recognising whether a…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Synthesis of differential equations in this chapter means recognising whether a given first‑order equation can be solved by separating variables or by using an integrating factor. A variable‑separable equation has the form (dy)/(dx) = g(x)h(y) and is solved by rewriting as (1)/(h(y))dy = g(x)dx and integrating both sides. A linear first‑order equation has the standard form (dy)/(dx) + P(x)y = Q(x); its solution uses the integrating factor μ(x) = e^ P(x)dx to obtain yμ = Qμ\,dx + C. The synthesis step requires the student to (i) identify the type, (ii) apply the correct method, (iii) handle initial conditions to find the particular constant, and (iv) interpret the solution in applied contexts such as population growth, cooling, or electrical circuits. The relationship between the two methods is that both reduce the problem to integration, but the algebraic manipulation differs: separation isolates y and x on opposite sides, while the linear method multiplies the whole equation by a function of x to make the left side an exact derivative. Mastery includes recognising equations that can be transformed into one of these forms (e.g., homogeneous equations reducible to separable, or Bernoulli equations reducible to linear) and selecting the most efficient route under exam time pressure.
steps: The single most important takeaway is: In the ISC exam, always first rewrite the equation in standard form to decide between separation and integrating factor; never jump to integration without this classification.
Here is why: ISC papers frequently present equations that look messy but become either separable or linear after simple algebra.
For example, (dy)/(dx) = (x+y)/(x-y) is homogeneous and can be turned separable by substituting y = vx;
(dy)/(dx) + y x = x is already linear.
Recognising the form saves time and avoids the common trap of attempting separation on a linear equation (or vice‑versa) and getting stuck.
Supporting argument 1: Standard‑form checklist.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is linear because it has y in denominator”) reveals the misconception that any equation with y in denominator is linear; linearity requires the dependent variable and its derivative to appear only to the first power and not in…
remember: Identify the type of the differential equation (dy)/(dx) = (x^2 + y^2)/(xy).
Explain why the integrating factor for (dy)/(dx) + 2xy = x is e^x^2 and not e^2x.
Evaluate the claim: “Every first‑order differential equation that can be written as (dy)/(dx) = f(x)g(y) is also linear.”.

cards.title: This chapter introduces the core probabilistic framework for decision‑making…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This chapter introduces the core probabilistic framework for decision‑making under uncertainty. Conditional probability P(A|B) quantifies the likelihood of event A given that B has occurred, forming the basis for updating beliefs. Bayes theorem P(A|B)=(P(B|A)P(A))/(P(B)) reverses the conditioning, allowing inference from observed evidence to hidden causes. A random variable X assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment; its probability distribution lists all possible values with associated probabilities. The mean μ = E[X] = Σ x_i p_i (or integral for continuous) measures central tendency, while the variance σ^2 = E[(X-μ)^2] = Σ (x_i-μ)^2 p_i measures spread. These concepts are interlinked: conditional probabilities feed Bayes updates; random variables model outcomes whose distributions are often derived using conditional reasoning; mean and variance summarise those distributions for risk assessment and prediction.
steps: This chapter equips you with a complete toolkit for modelling uncertainty: updating probabilities with new information, reversing cause‑effect reasoning, quantifying random outcomes, and summarising their behaviour with…
Here is why: real‑world decisions — from medical diagnosis to stock‑market risk — rarely deal with fixed probabilities; they require updating as evidence arrives.
Conditional probability formalises that update.
Bayes theorem then lets you start from observed data (a positive test) and infer the hidden reality (disease presence).
Random variables translate qualitative outcomes (win/lose, defective/working) into numbers so that calculus and algebra can be applied.
Mean and variance compress an entire distribution into two actionable figures: expected value and risk.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “probability distributions, hypothesis testing, regression, correlation”) reveals the misconception that this chapter covers inferential statistics rather than foundational probability tools.
remember: List the four main sub‑topics covered in this chapter.
Explain why conditional probability is a prerequisite for understanding Bayes theorem.
Evaluate the statement: “The mean of a random variable always equals its most likely value.”.

cards.title: Conditional probability quantifies the likelihood of an event A occurring given…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Conditional probability quantifies the likelihood of an event A occurring given that another event B has already occurred, denoted P(A|B). It is defined as P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B), provided P(B) > 0. Here P(A∩B) is the joint probability that both A and B happen, and P(B) is the marginal probability of B. This definition leads directly to the multiplication rule: P(A∩B) = P(A|B)·P(B) = P(B|A)·P(A). Two events are independent iff P(A|B) = P(A) (or equivalently P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B)). Conditional probability satisfies the axioms of probability on the reduced sample space B: P(A|B) ≥ 0, P(B|B) = 1, and for mutually exclusive events A₁, A₂, …, P(∪Aᵢ|B) = ΣP(Aᵢ|B). It also obeys the complement rule: P(A'|B) = 1 – P(A|B). The concept extends to chains of conditioning: P(A∩B∩C) = P(A)·P(B|A)·P(C|A∩B). Understanding conditional probability is essential for Bayes’ theorem, random variables, and stochastic processes later in the chapter.
steps: Conditional probability updates the chance of an event when we learn that another event has occurred.
Here is why: the sample space shrinks to the given event B, and we renormalise probabilities inside B. Consider a standard deck of 52 cards.
Let A = “draw a king” and B = “draw a face card (J, Q, K)”.
P(A∩B) = 4/52 = 1/13 because every king is a face card.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “P(A|B) = P(A)P(B)”) reveals the misconception that conditional probability equals the product of marginal probabilities, confusing it with the multiplication rule for independent events.
remember: Define conditional probability P(A|B) and state the condition required for its existence.
If P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, and P(A∩B)=0.2, compute P(A|B) and P(B|A). Are A and B independent? Justify.
Evaluate the statement: “If P(A|B)=P(A), then A and B are mutually exclusive.” State true or false with reasoning.

cards.title: Bayes’ theorem provides a rule for reversing conditional probabilities.
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Bayes’ theorem provides a rule for reversing conditional probabilities. Let A_1, A_2,, A_n be a partition of the sample space S (mutually exclusive and exhaustive events) with prior probabilities P(A_i) > 0. For any event B with P(B) > 0, the posterior probability of A_i given B is P(A_i B) = P(B A_i)\,P(A_i)Σ_j=1^n P(B A_j)\,P(A_j). The denominator is the total probability of B obtained via the law of total probability. The theorem connects three concepts: prior probability P(A_i) (belief before evidence), likelihood P(B A_i) (probability of evidence under each hypothesis), and posterior probability P(A_i B) (updated belief). It is a direct consequence of the definition of conditional probability P(A_i B) = (P(A_i ∩ B))/(P(B)) and the symmetry P(A_i ∩ B) = P(B A_i)P(A_i). In applied contexts — medical testing, spam filtering, quality control — Bayes’ theorem quantifies how new data should modify initial assessments.
steps: Bayes’ theorem lets us turn “probability of evidence given hypothesis” into “probability of hypothesis given evidence”.
Here is why: the theorem is algebraically derived from the definition of conditional probability and the law of total probability, so it always holds for any partition of the sample space.
First, recognise the structure: a set of mutually exclusive causes A_1,,A_n (e.g., “machine 1 produced the item”, “machine 2 produced the item”) and an observed effect B (e.g., “item is defective”).
The prior P(A_i) reflects production shares; the likelihood P(B A_i) reflects each machine’s defect rate.
Second, compute the total probability of the effect: P(B)=Σ_i P(B A_i)P(A_i).
This step aggregates all ways the defect could arise.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing P(A_i B)=P(B A_i)P(A_i) without the denominator) reveals the misconception that the denominator is optional — confusing the joint probability with the conditional probability.
remember: State Bayes’ theorem for a partition A_1, A_2, A_3 and an event B.
A disease affects 1 % of a population. A test has sensitivity 95 % and specificity 90 %. Explain why the posterior probability of disease given a positive test is not 95 %.
Evaluate the claim: “If a test’s sensitivity and specificity are both 99 %, then a positive result means you have the disease with 99 % probability.”.

cards.title: A random variable (RV) is a function X…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A random variable (RV) is a function X: Ω → R that maps every outcome ω in the sample space Ω of a random experiment to a real number. Random variables are classified as discrete (taking a countable set of values {x_1,x_2, }) or continuous (taking values in an interval of R). For a discrete RV the probability mass function (PMF) is p_X(x_i)=P(X=x_i) with Σ_i p_X(x_i)=1. For a continuous RV the probability density function (PDF) f_X(x) satisfies f_X(x)≥ 0 and _-∞^∞ f_X(x)\,dx =1; probabilities are obtained as P(a≤ X≤ b)= _a^b f_X(x)\,dx. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) F_X(x)=P(X≤ x) unifies both types: for discrete F_X(x)=Σ_x_i≤ xp_X(x_i), for continuous F_X(x)= _-∞^x f_X(t)\,dt. Two RVs X,Y are independent iff P(X≤ x, Y≤ y)=F_X(x)F_Y(y) for all x,y. This node introduces the concept, notation, and classification; computation of mean and variance is covered in the next node.
steps: A random variable is a numerical summary of a random experiment; it turns outcomes like “head” or “tail” into numbers such as 1 and 0 so that we can calculate with them.
Here is why: every probabilistic model eventually needs numbers to compute averages, risks, or probabilities of ranges.
Consider a simple experiment: drawing a card from a well‑shuffled 52‑card deck and noting its rank (Ace=1,…,King=13).
The sample space has 52 equally likely outcomes.
Define X = rank of the drawn card.
X is a discrete random variable taking values {1,2,,13} with PMF p_X(k)=4/52=1/13 for each k. The CDF is F_X(x)=0 for x<1, F_X(x)= x /13 for 1≤ x<13, and F_X(x)=1 for x≥13.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the PMF must integrate to 1”) reveals the misconception that discrete and continuous RVs share the same normalisation rule — confusing summation with integration.
remember: State the definition of a discrete random variable and give the condition that its probability mass function must satisfy.
Explain why the value of a probability density function f_X(x) at a point x is not a probability.
A student claims: “If X and Y are independent random variables, then P(X≤ 2, Y≤ 3)=P(X≤ 2)+P(Y≤ 3).” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: For a random variable X, the mean (expected value) E[X] is the…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: For a random variable X, the mean (expected value) E[X] is the probability‑weighted average of all possible values. For a discrete variable with probability mass function p(x), E[X]=Σ x\,p(x); for a continuous variable with density f(x), E[X]= x\,f(x)\,dx. The variance Var(X) measures the average squared deviation from the mean: Var(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2. The standard deviation σ_X= Var(X) restores the original units. Key properties: linearity of expectation E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b; variance scaling Var(aX+b)=a^2 Var(X); independence gives Var(X+Y)= Var(X)+ Var(Y). These concepts link the probability model (pmf/pdf) to summary measures used in inference, risk assessment, and decision‑making.
steps: The mean and variance completely summarise the centre and spread of a random variable, and they obey simple algebraic rules that make calculations fast.
Here is why: (1) Expectation is a linear operator, so E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b — no need to re‑derive the distribution.
(2) Variance scales with the square of the multiplier, Var(aX+b)=a^2 Var(X), because adding a constant does not change spread.
(3) For independent variables, variances add, which is the foundation of portfolio risk and error propagation.
(4) The standard deviation returns the original units, enabling direct comparison with the mean.
(5) These formulas hold for both discrete and continuous cases, differing only in summation versus integration.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Σ (x-μ)p(x) without squaring) reveals the misconception that variance is the average deviation rather than the average squared deviation — confusing mean absolute deviation with variance.
remember: State the formula for the variance of a discrete random variable X in terms of its probability mass function p(x).
A random variable Y has mean 8 and variance 9. What are the mean and variance of Z = 3Y - 4.
Evaluate the claim: “If two random variables have the same mean, they must have the same variance.”.

cards.title: A binomial distribution models the number of successes X in a fixed number n of…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A binomial distribution models the number of successes X in a fixed number n of independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same success probability p (and failure probability q=1-p). The random variable X takes integer values 0,1,…,n. Its probability mass function (PMF) is P(X = k)= nkp^kq^\,n-k, k=0,1,…,n, where nk= (n!)/(k!(n-k)!) is the binomial coefficient. The distribution is completely described by the two parameters (n,p); hence we write X (n,p). Key derived quantities are the mean (expected value) μ =E[X]=np and the variance σ^2=Var[X]=npq. Both are dimensionless because they are averages of counts. The binomial distribution connects to earlier concepts: it is a specific type of random variable (discrete), its mean and variance are applications of the general formulas taught in the previous node, and it relies on the idea of independent trials, which stems from basic probability and conditional probability.
steps: Takeaway: The binomial distribution gives the exact probability of obtaining any specific number of successes in a fixed number of independent yes/no trials with constant success probability.
Here is why: 1.
Each trial is a Bernoulli experiment with two outcomes (success/failure) and probability p of success, independent of other trials. 2.
The number of ways to arrange k successes among n trials is nk; multiplying by the probability of any particular arrangement p^kq^n-k yields the PMF. 3.
Summing k· P(X=k) over all k simplifies to np using properties of the binomial theorem, giving the mean. 4.
A similar summation for E[X^2] leads to Var[X]=npq.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., P(X=k)=np^k(1-p)^n-k) reveals the misconception that the binomial coefficient is unnecessary, confusing the PMF with a simple product of probabilities and ignoring the count of distinct arrangements.
remember: State the formula for the probability mass function of a binomial random variable X (n,p).
If a fair coin is tossed 10 times, what is the probability of obtaining exactly 6 heads.
Explain why the variance of a binomial distribution is npq and not np.

cards.title: A continuous random variable X can take any real value in an interval.
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A continuous random variable X can take any real value in an interval. Its behaviour is described by a probability density function (PDF) f(x) ≥ 0 such that P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫_a^b f(x) dx. The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the most important continuous distribution, characterised by two parameters: mean μ (location) and variance σ² (spread). Its PDF is f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) exp[-(x-μ)²/(2σ²)]. The standard normal distribution has μ = 0, σ = 1; any normal variable X can be standardised via Z = (X-μ)/σ. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z) gives probabilities. The normal distribution is symmetric about μ, with inflection points at μ±σ. The empirical rule states: ~68% of data lies within μ±σ, ~95% within μ±2σ, ~99.7% within μ±3σ. This node builds on discrete distributions (Binomial, Poisson) from the previous slice and prepares for hypothesis testing and confidence intervals in the synthesis node.
steps: The normal distribution is the backbone of statistical inference because many natural and social measurements — heights, test scores, measurement errors — follow this bell curve.
Takeaway: Any normal problem reduces to finding areas under the standard normal curve after standardising.
Here is why: the normal PDF has no elementary antiderivative, so we rely on pre‑computed tables of Φ(z) for the standard normal.
By converting X ~ N(μ, σ²) to Z = (X-μ)/σ ~ N(0,1), we reuse a single table for all normal problems.
Supporting argument 1: The PDF f(x) is symmetric about μ, so P(X < μ) = 0.5.
This symmetry simplifies tail probabilities: P(X > μ + kσ) = P(X < μ - kσ).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 0.0228) reveals the misconception that the table gives the upper tail directly — students often read Φ(z) as P(Z > z) instead of P(Z ≤ z).
remember: A continuous random variable X follows N(100, 25). What is P(X < 110).
If Z ~ N(0,1), which of the following equals P(-1.5 < Z < 1.5)? A) 0.8664 B) 0.9332 C) 0.0668 D) 0.1336.
The lifetimes of LED bulbs from a Delhi factory are normally distributed with mean 5000 hours and standard deviation 400….

cards.title: This node synthesizes four core concepts of Chapter 16…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This node synthesizes four core concepts of Chapter 16: conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem, random variables, and their mean and variance. Conditional probability P(A|B) = (P(A ∩ B))/(P(B)) quantifies the likelihood of event A given that B has occurred. Bayes’ theorem P(A|B) = (P(B|A)P(A))/(P(B)) reverses the conditioning, enabling posterior probability updates from prior knowledge and new evidence. A random variable X maps each outcome of a random experiment to a real number; its probability distribution lists values x_i with probabilities p_i. The mean (expected value) E(X) = Σ x_i p_i measures central tendency, while the variance Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 measures dispersion. These ideas interlink: conditional probabilities often define the distribution of a random variable (e.g., number of successes in Bernoulli trials), and Bayes’ theorem updates the parameter probabilities of that distribution. Mastery requires fluently moving between these representations to model real-world uncertainty and solve ISC examination problems.
steps: The key takeaway: ISC probability questions test your ability to chain conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem, and random variable expectations in a single coherent solution.
Here is why: First, examiners often embed a Bayes’ theorem step inside a larger problem where you must first compute a conditional probability from a given table or tree diagram.
Second, the posterior probabilities from Bayes become the probability mass function of a random variable whose mean and variance are then asked.
Third, ISC marking allocates separate marks for stating the correct formula, substituting values, and interpreting the result — missing any step loses marks.
Consider a typical 2023 ISC question: “A factory has two machines M1 and M2 producing 60% and 40% of output.
Defect rates are 2% and 5%.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., P(A|B) = P(A)P(B)) reveals the misconception that conditional probability equals the product of marginal probabilities, confusing independence with conditioning.
remember: Write the formula for conditional probability P(A|B) and state the condition required for it to be defined.
Explain why P(A|B) is generally not equal to P(B|A). Give a concrete example with numbers.
A student claims: “If two events are independent, then P(A|B) = P(A).” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique used to find…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique used to find the best outcome (maximum profit, minimum cost, maximum output, etc.) in a model whose requirements are represented by linear relationships. An LP model consists of three core components: 1. Decision variables – quantities to be determined (e.g., number of units of product A and B). 2. Objective function – a linear expression in the decision variables that is to be maximised or minimised (e.g., total profit = 5x + 8y). 3. Constraints – a system of linear inequalities or equations that restrict the decision variables (e.g., resource limits: 2x + 3y ≤ 100; non‑negativity: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0). The feasible region is the set of all points satisfying every constraint; it is a convex polygon (or polyhedron in higher dimensions). The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming states that if an optimal solution exists, it occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region. Solution methods include the graphical method (for two variables) and the simplex algorithm (for many variables). LP is widely applied in production planning, transportation, diet formulation, finance, and scheduling.
steps: Linear programming turns a “best mix” decision into a precise mathematical model whose optimum is guaranteed to sit at a corner of the feasible region.

Here is why: the objective function is a family of parallel straight lines; as we slide this line in the direction of improvement, the last point of contact with the convex feasible polygon is always a vertex.
Consider a small bakery that makes butter cookies (₹12 profit each) and chocolate chip cookies (₹15 profit each).
Flour limits production to 4x + 3y ≤ 240 kg, oven time to 2x + 5y ≤ 200 minutes, and both x, y ≥ 0.
The feasible region is the polygon bounded by these lines and the axes.
By evaluating the profit function 12x + 15y at each vertex — (0,0), (60,0), (0,40), and the intersection of the two resource lines — we find the maximum profit without testing every interior point.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “objective function, constraints, and feasible region”) reveals the misconception that the feasible region is an input rather than a derived set of points satisfying the constraints.
remember: What are the three mandatory components of a linear programming model.
Explain why the optimal solution of a linear programming problem, if it exists, must occur at a vertex of the feasible region.
A student claims that any real‑world optimisation problem can be solved by linear programming. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Linear Programming (LP) formulation is the process of converting a real‑world…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Linear Programming (LP) formulation is the process of converting a real‑world optimisation problem into a precise mathematical model. The model consists of three essential components: (1) Decision variables (e.g., x_1, x_2, ) representing quantities to be determined, such as units of products to produce; (2) an Objective function Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 + which is a linear expression to be maximised (profit, revenue) or minimised (cost, time); (3) a set of Linear constraints Σ a_ijx_j \ (≤, =, ≥) \ b_i that capture resource limitations, demand requirements, or technological restrictions. Additionally, Non‑negativity restrictions x_j ≥ 0 are imposed because negative quantities are physically meaningless. The formulation step precedes any solution method (graphical, simplex) and determines the feasible region — the set of all variable values satisfying all constraints. A well‑posed formulation ensures that every feasible solution corresponds to a viable real‑world plan and that the optimal solution of the model yields the true optimum of the original problem. Sub‑concepts include standard form (all constraints as ≤ with slack variables), canonical form, and the distinction between binding and non‑binding constraints at optimality.
steps: The takeaway: A correct LP formulation captures every real‑world limitation and the exact goal in linear algebraic form, turning a messy decision into a structured model ready for solution.
Here is why: (1) Decision variables are the levers you control — they must be defined unambiguously with units.
(2) The objective function quantifies the goal (profit, cost) as a linear combination of those variables.
(3) Constraints translate scarce resources, contracts, or physical laws into linear inequalities/equalities.
(4) Non‑negativity is not optional; it reflects reality.
(5) Standardising the model (adding slack/surplus) prepares it for any solution technique.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “objective function, constraints, and feasible region”) reveals the misconception that the feasible region is part of the formulation rather than a consequence of it.
remember: What are the three essential components of a linear programming formulation.
A student writes the machine‑hour constraint as 2x + 3y ≥ 100 when the machine has at most 100 hours available. Identify the error and give the correct constraint.
Evaluate whether non‑negativity constraints x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 are necessary in every LP formulation.

cards.title: Graphical solution of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is the method of…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Graphical solution of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is the method of finding the optimal value of a linear objective function Z = c_1x + c_2y subject to a set of linear inequality constraints a_i1x + a_i2y ≤ (≥) b_i and non‑negativity x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 by plotting each constraint as a half‑plane on the Cartesian plane. The intersection of all half‑planes forms the feasible region, a convex polygon (possibly unbounded). By the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming, if an optimum exists it occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region. The algorithm: (1) convert each inequality to an equation, (2) draw the line, (3) shade the correct side using a test point (usually the origin), (4) identify the feasible polygon, (5) list its vertices, (6) evaluate Z at each vertex, (7) select the maximum (or minimum) value. If the feasible region is unbounded, a finite optimum may still exist; otherwise the problem is infeasible (empty region) or unbounded (objective can increase indefinitely). This graphical method is limited to two decision variables; higher dimensions require the simplex method (covered later).
steps: The one thing to remember: In a two‑variable LPP the optimal value of the objective function always occurs at a vertex of the feasible region, so you only need to test the corner points.

Here is why: the objective function is a family of parallel lines; moving the line in the direction of improvement slides it across the convex feasible polygon until it last touches the polygon — that contact point is a…
Consider the tiffin example: constraints x ≤ 30 (idli limit), y ≤ 20 (dosa limit), 2x + 3y ≤ 100 (batter limit), x, y ≥ 0.
Step 1: Draw each line — x=30 vertical, y=20 horizontal, 2x+3y=100 intercepts (50,0) and (0,33.33).
Step 2: Shade the side satisfying each inequality (test origin).
Step 3: The overlapping polygon has vertices (0,0), (30,0), (30,13.33), (20,20), (0,20).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the area under the objective function line”) reveals the misconception that the objective function shapes the feasible region, confusing the role of constraints with the objective.
remember: What is the feasible region in a graphical LPP.
Why does the optimal solution of a two‑variable LPP always lie at a vertex of the feasible region.
A student graphs the constraints x + y ≤ 10, x ≥ 2, y ≥ 3 and claims the feasible region is a triangle with vertices (2,3), (2,8), (7,3). Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming problems (LPPs) that are too large for graphical solution. It operates on the standard form of an LPP: Maximize Z = c^T x subject to Ax ≤ b,\; x ≥ 0. Each inequality constraint Σ a_ijx_j ≤ b_i is converted to an equality by adding a slack variable s_i ≥ 0, yielding Σ a_ijx_j + s_i = b_i. The vector (x, s) now has n+m variables. A basic feasible solution (BFS) selects m basic variables (initially the slacks) and sets the remaining n non‑basic variables to zero. The simplex tableau organizes coefficients, the objective row, and the right‑hand side. An entering variable is chosen by the most negative reduced cost (for maximization); a leaving variable is determined by the minimum ratio test to maintain feasibility. Pivoting updates the tableau. The process repeats until no negative reduced costs remain, indicating optimality. The method exploits the fact that an optimal solution, if it exists, occurs at a vertex (extreme point) of the feasible polyhedron, and it moves systematically from vertex to adjacent vertex improving the objective.
steps: The simplex method solves LPPs by moving from one basic feasible solution to an adjacent one that improves the objective, guaranteeing optimality in finite steps.

Here is why: each BFS corresponds to a vertex of the feasible region; the algorithm checks the reduced costs to see if any non‑basic variable can increase the objective, and if so, it pivots to a neighboring vertex.
Consider the tiffin service: you have constraints on flour (≤ 100 kg), oil (≤ 50 L), and time (≤ 8 hours).
After formulation, you get: Maximize Z = 30x_1 + 40x_2 subject to 2x_1 + 3x_2 ≤ 100, x_1 + 2x_2 ≤ 50, 0.5x_1 + 0.25x_2 ≤ 8, x_1,x_2 ≥ 0.
Step 1 – Standard form: Add slack variables s_1,s_2,s_3 ≥ 0: 2x_1 + 3x_2 + s_1 = 100 x_1 + 2x_2 + s_2 = 50 0.5x_1 + 0.25x_2 + s_3 = 8 Objective: Z - 30x_1 - 40x_2 = 0.
Step 2 – Initial tableau: Write coefficients in a matrix with rows for constraints and objective, columns for x_1,x_2,s_1,s_2,s_3, RHS. Basic variables are s_1,s_2,s_3 with identity columns.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “slack variables are the decision variables we want to maximize”) reveals the misconception that slack variables are part of the original objective rather than auxiliary variables that measure surplus capacity.
remember: What is the purpose of adding slack variables when converting a ≤ constraint to standard form in the simplex method.
Why must all variables (including slacks) be non‑negative in the standard form of a maximization LPP.
A student claims: “The initial basic feasible solution of any LPP in standard form always corresponds to the origin in the original decision‑variable space.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming problems (LPPs) with any number of decision variables and constraints. It operates on the standard form of an LPP: maximise Z = c^Tx subject to Ax = b,\; x ≥ 0, where slack/surplus variables convert inequalities to equalities. The method starts at a basic feasible solution (BFS) — typically the origin where all original variables are zero and slack variables equal the right‑hand side constants. An initial simplex tableau organises the coefficients of the objective function and constraints. At each iteration, an entering variable (most negative reduced cost in a maximisation problem) and a leaving variable (determined by the minimum ratio test) are selected. A pivot operation updates the tableau, moving to an adjacent BFS with a higher (or equal) objective value. The process terminates when all reduced costs are non‑negative (optimality) or when no leaving variable exists (unboundedness). The final tableau yields the optimal values of decision variables, slack/surplus variables, and the maximum Z. The simplex method guarantees finite termination for non‑degenerate problems and provides the basis for sensitivity analysis and duality.
steps: The simplex method is a systematic tabular procedure that moves from one basic feasible solution to an adjacent one with a better objective value until no improvement is possible.
Here is why: the feasible region of an LPP is a convex polyhedron; the optimal solution always lies at a vertex (basic feasible solution).
The simplex algorithm walks along edges of this polyhedron, each pivot corresponding to moving to a neighbouring vertex.
Consider a tiffin service that now offers three boxes: Veg (₹50 profit), Non‑veg (₹70 profit), Snack (₹30 profit).
Resources: 100 kg rice, 80 kg dal, 60 kg vegetables, 40 hours labour.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing x_2 because -3 is “less negative”) reveals the misconception that any negative reduced cost can enter — but the simplex rule picks the most negative to guarantee the steepest ascent per iteration.
remember: In the initial simplex tableau for a maximisation problem, the reduced cost row shows values -5, -3, 0, 0 for variables x_1, x_2, s_1, s_2. Which variable should enter the basis.
During a simplex iteration, the entering column has coefficients 2, -1, 0, 4 in the constraint rows, and the RHS values are 20, 15, 10, 30. Which row leaves the basis.
A student claims: “If the minimum ratio test yields a tie between two rows, the simplex method will cycle indefinitely.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The simplex method is an algebraic algorithm for solving linear programming problems (LPP) with any number of decision variables. It requires the LPP to be expressed in standard form: maximize Z = c^Tx subject to Ax = b,\; x ≥ 0. Inequality constraints are converted to equalities by adding slack variables (for ≤ constraints), surplus variables (for ≥ constraints), and artificial variables (for ≥ or = constraints when an initial basic feasible solution is not obvious). All variables, including slacks and surpluses, are non‑negative. A basic feasible solution (BFS) corresponds to setting non‑basic variables to zero and solving for basic variables; the initial BFS uses slack/artificial variables as the basis. The simplex tableau organizes the coefficients of the constraints and the objective function (written as Z - c^Tx = 0) into a matrix. Each iteration selects an entering variable (most negative reduced cost c_j - z_j in a maximization problem) and a leaving variable (minimum ratio test b_ia_ij for positive a_ij) to pivot, moving to an adjacent BFS with a higher objective value. This node covers only the conversion to standard form and the construction of the initial tableau; subsequent iterations, optimality conditions, and special cases are reserved for later nodes.
steps: The simplex method solves linear programming problems of any size by systematically moving from one basic feasible solution to an adjacent one with a better objective value, using a tableau that encodes the constraints…
Here is why: (1) Standard form converts all inequalities into equalities with non‑negative variables, making the problem amenable to matrix algebra.
(2) Slack, surplus, and artificial variables supply an obvious initial basic feasible solution — the slack variables become the initial basis for ≤ constraints.
(3) The tableau arranges coefficients so that elementary row operations (pivots) correspond to moving between basic feasible solutions.
(4) For maximization, the most negative coefficient in the objective row indicates the variable that will increase Z fastest per unit increase.
(5) The minimum ratio test guarantees the new solution stays feasible by preventing any basic variable from becoming negative.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “slack variables are added to ≥ constraints”) reveals the misconception that slack and surplus are interchangeable — confusing the direction of the inequality.
remember: What is the purpose of adding a slack variable to a ≤ constraint when converting an LPP to standard form.
In a maximization problem, why is the variable with the most negative coefficient in the objective row chosen as the entering variable.
A student claims that the initial basic feasible solution obtained by setting all decision variables to zero is always optimal. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The Simplex method is an algebraic procedure for solving Linear Programming…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: The Simplex method is an algebraic procedure for solving Linear Programming Problems (LPP) that have more than two decision variables, where the graphical method fails. It starts by converting every ≤ constraint into an equality by adding a slack variable (representing unused resources) and, if needed, surplus or artificial variables for ≥ or = constraints. The problem is then expressed in standard form: maximize Z = c^Tx subject to Ax = b,\; x ≥ 0. A basic feasible solution (BFS) corresponds to a corner point of the feasible region; the method moves from one BFS to an adjacent one by pivoting—exchanging a non‑basic variable (entering) with a basic variable (leaving)—while always improving (or maintaining) the objective value. The optimality condition for a maximization problem is that all reduced costs Δ_j = c_j - z_j ≤ 0; if any Δ_j > 0, increasing that variable raises Z. The method terminates when this condition holds, yielding the optimal BFS, or detects unboundedness/infeasibility. Thus, the Simplex method links formulation (constraints → standard form), graphical intuition (corner‑point search), and algebraic iteration (tableau pivots) to solve LPP efficiently.
steps: The Simplex method systematically moves from one feasible corner point to another, improving the objective value until no further improvement is possible.
Here is why: 1.
Standard form conversion transforms inequalities into equalities, exposing the slack variables that measure unused resources and allowing the problem to be handled with matrix algebra. 2.
Tableau representation stores the coefficients of constraints, the objective function, and the current basic variables in a compact array, making the pivot operation a simple row‑operation. 3.
Optimality test uses reduced costs Δ_j = c_j - z_j; if all are non‑positive for a maximization, any increase in a non‑basic variable cannot raise Z, so the current BFS is optimal. 4.
Pivot selection chooses the entering variable with the largest positive Δ_j (steepest ascent) and the leaving variable via the minimum ratio test to preserve feasibility. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Slack variables increase the objective function value”) reveals the misconception that slack variables contribute to profit, whereas they only account for unused capacity and have zero coefficient in the objective.
remember: What is the primary role of slack variables in a Linear Programming Problem.
Why does the Simplex method stop when all reduced costs Δ_j = c_j - z_j are ≤ 0 for a maximization problem.
In a maximization tableau, if Δ_x₃ = +4 and Δ_x₅ = +2, which variable should enter the basis and why.

cards.title: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique used to…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique used to maximise or minimise a linear objective function subject to a set of linear inequality or equality constraints. The decision variables (e.g., quantities of products) are continuous and non‑negative. The feasible region defined by the constraints is a convex polygon (in two variables) or a convex polyhedron (in higher dimensions). The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming states that if an optimal solution exists, it occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region. The graphical method solves two‑variable LP problems by plotting each constraint as a half‑plane, identifying the intersection (feasible region), and evaluating the objective function at each vertex. The simplex method extends this to n‑variables using tableau iterations. In the CISCE ISC syllabus, only formulation of real‑world problems into LP models and the graphical solution for two variables are examined; sensitivity analysis, duality, and integer programming are reserved for higher studies.
steps: The single most important takeaway for the ISC exam is that every linear programming question, no matter how wordy, reduces to three mechanical steps: formulate, graph, evaluate vertices — and the optimal answer is…

Here is why: the objective function is a family of parallel lines; moving this line in the direction of optimisation (increase for maximisation, decrease for minimisation) stops exactly when it last touches the feasible…

Consider a typical ISC problem: a factory makes two types of pens, A and B. Each pen A needs 2 g plastic and 1 g ink; pen B needs 1 g plastic and 2 g ink. Daily supplies are 100 g plastic and 80 g ink. Profit per pen A…
Step 1 — formulate: let x = number of pen A, y = number of pen B. Maximise Z = 5x + 4y subject to 2x + y ≤ 100, x + 2y ≤ 80, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
Step 2 — graph: plot the two lines 2x + y = 100 and x + 2y = 80 on the same axes, shade the region satisfying both inequalities and the axes.
The feasible region is a quadrilateral with vertices (0,0), (50,0), (40,20), (0,40).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., using “≥” for resource constraints) reveals the misconception that “at most” translates to “greater than or equal to”, confusing the direction of inequality.
remember: Write the linear programming formulation for: “A farmer has 200 kg of wheat and 150 kg of….
For the LP: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, 2x + y ≤ 5, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, list all corner points of the feasible region.
Evaluate whether the LP: Maximise Z = 4x + 3y subject to x + 2y ≤ 8, 3x + y ≤ 9, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 has multiple optimal solutions.

cards.title: Chapter 18 of ISC Applied Mathematics introduces three core…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Chapter 18 of ISC Applied Mathematics introduces three core financial‑mathematics tools used in personal finance, corporate planning and banking. 1. Perpetuity – a stream of equal cash flows that continues indefinitely. Its present value (PV) is the amount that, invested today at a given interest rate, would generate those endless payments. The key relationship is PV = C / i, where C is the periodic payment and i the effective interest rate per period. 2. Sinking Fund – a fund built by making regular equal deposits so that a known future sum (the target amount) is accumulated at a specified date. The deposit amount (R) is derived from the future‑value‑of‑annuity formula: R = FV · i / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1], where n is the number of periods. 3. EMI (Equated Monthly Instalment) – the fixed monthly repayment on a loan that covers both principal and interest. For a loan principal P, monthly interest rate r and tenure of N months, EMI = P · r · (1 + r)ᴺ / [(1 + r)ᴺ − 1]. The three concepts share the same mathematical foundation: the time value of money expressed through geometric series. Perpetuity is the limiting case of an annuity as n → ∞; sinking fund is the inverse problem of finding the periodic contribution for a given future value; EMI is the loan‑amortisation counterpart where the present value of all instalments equals the loan amount. Mastery of these formulas enables students to evaluate investment schemes, plan capital replacements and compare loan offers — skills directly tested in ISC board papers and useful for real‑life financial decisions.
steps: The one thing to remember: All three tools — perpetuity, sinking fund, EMI — are special cases of the same annuity mathematics, differing only in whether the cash‑flow stream is infinite, finite with a target future…
Here is why: the time value of money tells us that a rupee today is worth more than a rupee tomorrow.
An ordinary annuity values a finite series of equal payments; letting the number of periods go to infinity collapses the denominator to the interest rate, giving the perpetuity formula PV = C/i.
A sinking fund asks the reverse question: what equal deposit R will grow to a desired future sum FV?
Solving the future‑value‑of‑annuity equation for R yields the sinking‑fund deposit formula.

An EMI problem gives the present value (the loan principal) and asks for the level payment that makes the present value of all payments equal to that principal — the standard loan‑amortisation formula.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹80 000) reveals the misconception that the student multiplied C by i instead of dividing, confusing the present‑value of a perpetuity with the interest earned in one period.
remember: What is the present value of a perpetuity that pays ₹10 000 at the end of each year if the effective annual interest rate is 8 %.
A company wants to accumulate ₹20 lakh in 8 years by making equal annual deposits into a sinking fund earning 6 % p.a. compounded….
Evaluate the statement: “For a given loan amount and tenure, a higher interest rate always leads to a proportionally higher EMI.”.

cards.title: A perpetuity is a series of equal cash flows C paid at regular intervals…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A perpetuity is a series of equal cash flows C paid at regular intervals (usually annually) that continues forever. The present value (PV) of an ordinary perpetuity (first payment at the end of the first period) is given by PV = (C)/(i) where i is the effective interest rate per period expressed as a decimal. If the first payment occurs immediately (perpetuity due), the present value is PV_due = C + (C)/(i) = C (1+(1)/(i) ). A growing perpetuity has payments that increase at a constant rate g per period (g < i). Its present value is PV_growing = (C)/(i-g). Key relationships: - The perpetuity formula is the limiting case of the present value of an annuity as the number of periods n → ∞. - The interest rate i must be greater than the growth rate g for a growing perpetuity to have a finite value. - Perpetuities are used to value consols, preferred shares, and certain real‑estate income streams. All quantities are expressed in monetary units (INR) for cash flows, and the interest rate is dimensionless (per period). Time is measured in periods (years, half‑years, quarters) consistent with the payment frequency.
steps: The present value of a perpetuity equals the periodic payment divided by the interest rate per period.
Here is why: a perpetuity is an infinite stream of equal payments C. Discounting each payment back to today gives the series C/(1+i) + C/(1+i)^2 + C/(1+i)^3 +.
This is an infinite geometric series with first term a = C/(1+i) and common ratio r = 1/(1+i).
Since |r|<1 for any positive i, the sum to infinity is a/(1-r) = (C/(1+i))/(1-1/(1+i)) = (C)/(i).
Consider a concrete Indian example: a government consol pays ₹1,000 every year forever.
If the market yield is 8 % per annum (i=0.08), the price you should pay today is PV = 1000/0.08 = ₹12,500.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹125,000) reveals the misconception that the formula is C × i instead of C / i — confusing multiplication with division of the rate.
remember: What is the present value of an ordinary perpetuity that pays ₹2,500 per year if the effective annual interest rate is 5 %.
A perpetuity due pays ₹3,000 at the beginning of each….
Evaluate the statement: “A growing perpetuity with a growth rate equal to the interest rate has a finite present value.”.

cards.title: A sinking fund is a financial arrangement in which a series of equal periodic…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A sinking fund is a financial arrangement in which a series of equal periodic payments (deposits) are made into an account that earns compound interest, so that the accumulated amount equals a predetermined future liability or replacement cost. The fund is “sunk” because the money is set aside and not available for other uses until the target date. Let the future amount required be S (₹), the periodic deposit be R (₹ per period), the interest rate per period be i (decimal, e.g., 0.08 for 8 %), and the number of periods be n. The future value of an ordinary annuity gives the relationship S = R ((1+i)^n - 1)/(i) Solving for the periodic deposit yields the sinking‑fund factor R = S (i)/((1+i)^n - 1) If the fund is used to repay a loan, the borrower pays interest on the loan separately and simultaneously builds the sinking fund to retire the principal at maturity. The total periodic outlay is therefore the loan interest plus the sinking‑fund deposit. Key sub‑concepts: - Ordinary annuity future value – the mathematical engine behind the sinking fund. - Sinking‑fund factor – the multiplier that converts a future sum into the required periodic deposit. - Loan‑sinking‑fund method – a debt‑repayment technique where the principal is repaid only at maturity, while a parallel fund accumulates the principal. All quantities are expressed in Indian rupees (₹) for monetary values; i and n are dimensionless.
steps: A sinking fund is a systematic savings plan where equal periodic deposits accumulate with compound interest to meet a known future liability.
Here is why: 1.
Purpose clarity – Whether a company must repay a ₹50 lakh debenture in 5 years or a household wants ₹10 lakh for a roof replacement, the future amount S is fixed. 2.
Annuity engine – Each deposit R earns interest for the remaining periods; the sum of all compounded deposits is exactly the future‑value‑of‑ordinary‑annuity formula. 3.
Sinking‑fund factor – Rearranging the annuity formula isolates R, giving a direct multiplier i/[(1+i)^n-1] that converts S into the required deposit. 4.

Loan‑sinking‑fund method – The borrower pays interest on the original principal each period (e.g., 9 % on ₹15 lakh = ₹1,35,000 per year) and simultaneously deposits R into the fund earning a possibly different rate…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., R = S ((1+i)^n-1)/(i)) reveals the misconception that the sinking‑fund factor is the same as the future‑value annuity factor, confusing the multiplier for R with the multiplier for S.
remember: Define a sinking fund and write the formula for the periodic deposit R required to accumulate a future sum S in n periods at interest rate i per period.
Explain why the sinking‑fund factor (i)/((1+i)^n-1) is the reciprocal of the future‑value‑of‑annuity factor ((1+i)^n-1)/(i).
A firm must repay a ₹10 lakh loan in 4 years. It sets up a sinking fund earning 8 % p.a. compounded annually. Evaluate whether an annual deposit of ₹2,00,000 is sufficient.

cards.title: Equated Monthly Instalment (EMI) is the constant periodic payment made by a…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Equated Monthly Instalment (EMI) is the constant periodic payment made by a borrower to repay a loan with interest over a fixed tenure. Let the principal be P (currency units), the annual nominal interest rate be i (decimal), compounded monthly, and the loan tenure be N months. The monthly interest rate is r = i/12. The EMI, denoted E, is derived from the present value of an ordinary annuity: P = E [ 1 - (1+r)^-Nr ] E = P\,r\,(1+r)^N(1+r)^N - 1. Each EMI consists of an interest component I_k = outstanding principal_k-1× r and a principal repayment component P_k = E - I_k. The outstanding principal after the k^th EMI is P_k = P_k-1 - P_k. The loan amortisation schedule lists I_k, P_k and the remaining balance for every month. This node covers the derivation of the EMI formula, construction of amortisation tables, and the effect of prepayment or change in interest rate on the schedule. It does not cover sinking‑fund calculations (node) or perpetuity valuation (node).
steps: The EMI is the single fixed payment that exactly clears a loan when made every month for the agreed tenure.
Here is why: the loan amount equals the present value of all future EMIs discounted at the monthly rate.
First, convert the annual nominal rate to a monthly rate r = i/12.
Second, recognise that the series of N equal payments E forms an ordinary annuity whose present value is E 1-(1+r)^-Nr.
Equating this to the principal P and solving for E yields the EMI formula.
Third, each EMI splits into interest on the opening balance and principal repayment; the interest portion falls while the principal portion rises over time.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., E = P r N) reveals the misconception that EMI is simple interest multiplied by tenure, ignoring compounding and the time‑value‑of‑money principle.
remember: State the formula for EMI E in terms of principal P, monthly interest rate r, and number of months N.
A loan of ₹5 lakh at 12 % p.a. compounded monthly is to be repaid in 36 equal monthly….
Evaluate the statement: “Prepaying a lump sum always reduces the total interest paid, regardless of whether the bank reduces the EMI or the tenure.”.

cards.title: A growing perpetuity is a series of infinite cash flows where each payment…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A growing perpetuity is a series of infinite cash flows where each payment increases at a constant rate g per period. The first payment C occurs at the end of the first period, the second payment is C(1+g), the third C(1+g)^2, and so on. The present value (PV) of this infinite stream, discounted at an interest rate r per period (with r > g), is given by PV = C / (r - g). This formula is derived from the sum of an infinite geometric series. The concept extends the level perpetuity (where g = 0) to account for inflation, dividend growth, or rental escalations. It is crucial for valuing stocks with constant dividend growth (Gordon Growth Model), real estate with escalating leases, and endowment funds with inflation-indexed payouts. The relationship between the variables is inverse: higher growth g increases PV, while higher discount rate r decreases PV. The condition r > g is necessary for convergence; if g ≥ r, the present value is infinite, implying the asset is overvalued or the assumptions are unsustainable.
steps: The present value of a growing perpetuity is PV = C/(r-g), provided r > g, because the infinite sum of discounted growing cash flows forms a convergent geometric series.
Here is why: each cash flow grows by factor (1+g) while being discounted by factor (1+r), so the ratio of successive terms is (1+g)/(1+r) < 1, ensuring convergence.
Consider a company that just paid a dividend of ₹100 and is expected to grow dividends at 4% per year forever.
If investors require a 10% return, the stock's intrinsic value is ₹100(1.04)/(0.10-0.04) = ₹1733.33.
Notice we use the next dividend C = 100(1.04) because the formula assumes the first payment occurs one period from now. If the dividend was just paid, we must compound it forward one period.
A common exam trap: using the current dividend instead of the next dividend.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹6,250 from using C = 500 and r = 0.08 only, ignoring growth) reveals the misconception that growing perpetuity can be valued as a level perpetuity by ignoring the growth rate, which underestimates the value when g > 0.
remember: What is the present value of a growing perpetuity that pays ₹500 at the end of the first year, with payments growing at 3% per year, discounted at 8% per year.
A student argues that if the growth rate g equals the discount rate r, the present value formula gives division by zero, so the present value is zero. Evaluate this claim.
A stock is expected to pay a dividend of ₹20 next year, growing at 5%….

cards.title: A growing perpetuity is a series of cash flows that continue indefinitely…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A growing perpetuity is a series of cash flows that continue indefinitely, with each payment increasing at a constant growth rate g per period. The first payment C occurs at the end of period 1. The present value PV is derived by discounting each growing cash flow at the periodic interest rate r (with r > g for convergence). The closed‑form formula is PV = C / (r – g). This extends the level perpetuity (PV = C / r) by incorporating growth. The relationship between sub‑concepts: level perpetuity is the special case g = 0; deferred perpetuity delays the first payment; growing perpetuity adds a constant growth factor. All three share the discounting principle but differ in cash‑flow pattern. The formula assumes payments are made at regular intervals (usually annually), growth is compounded each period, and the discount rate exceeds the growth rate to ensure a finite present value.
steps: The present value of a growing perpetuity is PV = C/(r–g), provided the discount rate r exceeds the growth rate g. Here is why: each cash flow grows geometrically, so the infinite series of discounted payments forms a…
If the market discount rate is 9%, the property’s value today is ₹1,00,000/(0.09–0.04) = ₹20,00,000.
The derivation starts with PV = C/(1+r) + C(1+g)/(1+r)² + C(1+g)²/(1+r)³ + ….
Factor C/(1+r) and recognise the common ratio (1+g)/(1+r).
Summing the infinite geometric series gives PV = [C/(1+r)] / [1 – (1+g)/(1+r)] = C/(r–g).
A common exam trap: forgetting to check r > g; if g ≥ r, the denominator is zero or negative, making the formula invalid — the series diverges.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “infinite PV means infinite wealth”) reveals the misconception that mathematical divergence equates to economic infinite worth, ignoring that no rational investor would pay an infinite price for a finite real income stream.
remember: State the formula for the present value of a growing perpetuity and the condition for its validity.
A student argues that if the growth rate equals the discount rate, the present value becomes infinite, so the investment is infinitely valuable. Evaluate this claim.
Given a growing perpetuity with first payment ₹5,000, growth rate 6%, and discount rate 10%, a student calculates PV = 5,000/(0.06–0.10) =….

cards.title: A sinking fund is a fund into which periodic deposits are made to accumulate a…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: A sinking fund is a fund into which periodic deposits are made to accumulate a specified future amount, often to replace an asset or repay a debt. When the deposits increase by a constant amount G each period (forming an arithmetic progression), the fund is called an arithmetic‑gradient sinking fund. Let the first deposit be A (in ₹), the interest rate per period be i (dimensionless, expressed as a decimal), and the number of periods be n. The future value FV (in ₹) after n periods is the sum of two components: 1. The future value of an ordinary annuity of amount A each period: FV_A=A\; (1+i)^n-1i 2. The future value of the gradient series, which can be viewed as a series of delayed unit payments of G: FV_G=G\; (1+i)^n-i\,n-1i^2 Hence, the total future value is FV = A\; (1+i)^n-1i\;+\;G\; (1+i)^n-i\,n-1i^2 When G=0 the expression reduces to the ordinary sinking‑fund formula, showing that the arithmetic‑gradient fund generalises the equal‑deposit case. If the fund were to continue forever (n→∞) and the gradient were zero, the present value would approach that of a perpetuity; thus the gradient sinking fund bridges ordinary annuities, perpetuities, and more complex cash‑flow patterns.
steps: Takeaway: The future value of a sinking fund that receives deposits increasing by a fixed amount each period equals the sum of the future value of an equal‑deposit annuity and the future value of an arithmetic‑gradient…
Here is why: 1.

Any cash‑flow pattern can be decomposed into simpler, well‑understood streams; the gradient fund splits naturally into a constant annuity (amount A each period) and a gradient that starts at zero and grows by G each…
The constant annuity’s future value is the standard compound‑interest formula A\,s_n|i where s_n|i=((1+i)^n-1)/i. 3.

The gradient series can be written as G times the sum of delayed unit payments: one unit at the end of period 2, two units at the end of period 3, …, (n-1) units at the end of period n. Summing this weighted series and…
Setting G=0 collapses the gradient term to zero, leaving only the annuity component, which confirms consistency with the ordinary sinking‑fund result already studied. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., FV = A (1+i)^n-1i + G (1+i)^n-1i) reveals the misconception that the gradient term uses the same denominator as the annuity term, ignoring the extra i in the denominator that arises from summing the weighted delayed payments.
remember: State the formula for the future value of an arithmetic‑gradient sinking fund and identify each symbol.
Explain why the gradient term contains i^2 in its denominator, using the concept of delayed unit payments.
A student asserts that doubling the gradient G will always double the future value of the sinking fund, regardless of the values of A, i, and n. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Perpetuity, sinking fund and EMI are three applications of the time value of…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Perpetuity, sinking fund and EMI are three applications of the time value of money. A perpetuity is an infinite series of equal cash flows A occurring at regular intervals; its present value (PV) is PV = (A)/(i), where i is the effective interest rate per period (dimensionless, expressed as a decimal). A sinking fund is a series of equal deposits R made to accumulate a specified future sum FV; the deposit needed is R = (FV\,i)/((1+i)^n-1), with n the number of periods. An EMI (equal monthly instalment) is the fixed payment E that amortises a loan principal P over n periods at rate i: E = (P\,i\,(1+i)^n)/((1+i)^n-1). All three formulas share the compound factor (1+i)^n; perpetuity is the limiting case of an annuity as n→∞, sinking fund solves for the payment given a future value, and EMI solves for the payment given a present value. Quantities are measured in rupees (₹); time in years (or months) and interest rate as a decimal per compounding period.
steps: Takeaway: In financial planning, perpetuity, sinking fund and EMI are inter‑related tools that convert between present and future values using the same compound interest factor.

Here is why: each formula originates from the sum of a geometric series; the factor ((1+i)^n-1)/(i) appears as the future value of an ordinary annuity, its reciprocal (i)/((1+i)^n-1) gives the sinking fund payment, and…
Consider a college that wishes to fund a perpetual scholarship of ₹20 000 per year.
The scholarship’s present value is a perpetuity calculation: PV = (20 000)/(0.08)=₹2 50 000 at 8 % p.a.
To create this corpus, the college plans a sinking fund over 10 years.
Using the sinking‑fund formula with FV=2 50 000, i=0.08, n=10 gives the annual deposit R = 2 50 000×0.08(1.08)^10-1≈₹17 255.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., PV = A× i) reveals the misconception that the present value grows with the interest rate, confusing the inverse relationship between rate and value.
remember: State the formula for the present value of a perpetuity and define each symbol.
Explain why the sinking fund payment formula can be obtained by solving the future value of an ordinary annuity for the payment.
Determine whether the following statement is true or false: “If the interest rate is doubled, the present value of a perpetuity is halved.”.

cards.title: This chapter introduces the financial instruments — equity shares…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: This chapter introduces the financial instruments — equity shares, preference shares, debentures, and bonds — that constitute the capital market. It defines the key quantities: face value (nominal value), market price, dividend (for shares) or coupon interest (for bonds), and the various yield measures such as dividend yield, earnings yield, current yield, and yield to maturity. The relationship between these quantities is established: the return an investor earns is the cash flow (dividend or interest) relative to the price paid, while valuation is the process of estimating a fair market price from expected future cash flows discounted at an appropriate rate. The chapter also distinguishes between primary and secondary markets, explains the role of stock exchanges (BSE, NSE) and the concept of market capitalization. It sets the stage for the subsequent nodes by outlining the logical flow: first, terminology and classification; second, simple return calculations; third, present‑value based valuation models for bonds and shares; fourth, risk‑adjusted performance measures. All concepts are grounded in the Indian regulatory framework (SEBI guidelines, Companies Act provisions) and use rupee‑denominated examples.
steps: This chapter equips you with the framework to evaluate any stock, share, or bond by linking its market price to the cash flows it generates, so you can compare investments on a common basis.
Here is why: first, every security is a promise of future cash — dividends for shares, coupons and principal for bonds — and the price you pay today must reflect the value of those promises.
Second, the market price fluctuates with demand, interest rates, and company performance, while face value remains fixed; understanding this gap is the core of valuation.

Third, return measures such as dividend yield (annual dividend ÷ market price) and current yield (annual coupon ÷ market price) give a quick snapshot, but they ignore capital gains and time value of money, which later…
Fourth, the chapter arranges topics in a logical ladder: terminology → simple returns → present‑value valuation → risk‑adjusted comparison, mirroring how a portfolio analyst builds a decision model.
Consider an Indian investor, Priya, who has ₹50,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “face value is the price you pay to buy the share”) reveals the misconception that face value equals purchase price, confusing a static accounting number with a dynamic market valuation.
remember: What is the face value of a share, and how does it differ from its market price.
Explain why the dividend yield of a share can be misleading if used alone to judge investment attractiveness.
Evaluate the statement: “A bond trading at a premium always offers a lower current yield than its coupon rate.”.

cards.title: Valuation and returns form the core of analysing equity shares and bonds.
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Valuation and returns form the core of analysing equity shares and bonds. Face Value (FV) is the nominal value printed on the security. Market Value (MV) is the current trading price. For shares, Dividend per Share (D) = (Dividend Rate % × FV) / 100. Dividend Yield (DY) = (D / MV) × 100, showing the annual dividend income as a percentage of the market price. Capital Gain = Selling Price – Purchase Price (adjusted for brokerage). Total Return = Dividends Received + Capital Gain – Brokerage Paid. Return on Investment (ROI) = (Total Return / Total Investment) × 100, where Total Investment includes purchase cost plus brokerage. For bonds, Coupon Payment (C) = (Coupon Rate % × FV) / 100 per period. Bond Price (P) = Σ_{t=1}^{n} [C / (1+r)^t] + FV / (1+r)^n, where r is the periodic required yield and n is the number of periods to maturity. Valuation links expected cash flows (dividends or coupons) to a present price using the investor’s required rate of return. Returns quantify the profitability of the investment over the holding period. The two concepts are intertwined: a higher required return lowers the fair valuation, while actual returns depend on realised dividends, price changes, and transaction costs.
steps: The fair price of any income‑generating asset equals the present value of its expected future cash flows discounted at the investor’s required return.
Here is why: every rupee received tomorrow is worth less than a rupee today because money can earn interest; discounting translates future dividends or coupons into today’s equivalent.

First, identify the cash flow stream: for a share it is the series of dividends (often assumed constant or growing) and the expected resale price; for a bond it is the fixed coupon payments plus the face value at…
Second, choose an appropriate discount rate — the dividend yield for shares or the yield to maturity for bonds.
Third, apply the present value formula: for a perpetual constant dividend, Price = D / r; for a finite horizon bond, sum the discounted coupons and the discounted face value.
Fourth, compute returns by comparing total cash inflows (dividends, coupons, sale proceeds) with total cash outflows (purchase price, brokerage).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Dividend Yield = (Dividend per Share / Face Value) × 100) reveals the misconception that yield is based on face value rather than the actual price paid, confusing nominal return with market‑based return.
remember: What is the formula for dividend yield of a share.
A share with face value ₹100 pays a 12% dividend. Its market price is ₹150. Calculate the dividend yield.
Evaluate the statement: “A bond trading at a premium always gives a lower return than its coupon rate.”.

cards.title: Bond valuation determines the fair market price of a fixed‑income security by…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Bond valuation determines the fair market price of a fixed‑income security by discounting its promised future cash flows — periodic coupon payments and the principal repayment at maturity — to the present using an appropriate discount rate. The discount rate reflects the market’s required rate of return for bonds of similar risk and maturity, often called the yield to maturity (YTM). The present value (PV) of each cash flow is calculated as CFₜ/(1+y)ᵗ, where CFₜ is the cash flow at time t, y is the periodic yield (expressed as a decimal), and t is the number of periods. Summing these PVs gives the theoretical bond price. If the coupon rate equals the market yield, the bond trades at par (price = face value). If the coupon rate exceeds the market yield, the bond trades at a premium (price > face value); if lower, at a discount. Current yield is a simpler measure: annual coupon payment divided by current market price, ignoring capital gains or losses. YTM, by contrast, is the internal rate of return that equates the present value of all future cash flows to the current price, assuming all coupons are reinvested at the same rate. Bond prices and yields move inversely: when market yields rise, existing bond prices fall, and vice versa. This node focuses on the mechanics of pricing plain‑vanilla bonds, computing YTM (both exact via iteration and approximate formula), and interpreting premium/discount status. It builds on the dividend‑yield and capital‑gain concepts from node and prepares for advanced topics such as bond duration, convexity, and yield‑curve analysis in later nodes.
steps: The fair price of a bond equals the present value of its future coupon payments and principal repayment, discounted at the market’s required yield.
Here is why: (1) A bond’s cash flows are contractual and known in advance, making them a stream of certain payments.
(2) Money today is worth more than the same amount tomorrow, so each future rupee must be discounted by the opportunity cost of capital — the market yield.
(3) The discount rate that equates the sum of discounted cash flows to the current market price is the yield to maturity, the bond’s internal rate of return.
(4) Because the coupon rate is fixed, any change in market yield forces the bond price to adjust inversely to keep the YTM aligned with the market.
Consider a 10 % annual coupon bond with face value ₹1,000, 5 years to maturity, when the prevailing market yield for similar risk is 12 %.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 8 %) reveals the misconception that current yield equals the coupon rate, ignoring the effect of market price deviating from face value.

cards.title: Valuation of fixed‑income and equity securities rests on the time value of…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Valuation of fixed‑income and equity securities rests on the time value of money: a rupee received tomorrow is worth less than a rupee today. For a bond, the price (P) equals the present value of all future cash flows — periodic coupon payments (C) and the face value (F) at maturity — discounted at the market‑required yield (y). The current yield (CY) measures annual income relative to the current market price: CY = C / P. The yield to maturity (YTM) is the internal rate of return that equates the present value of cash flows to the bond’s price; an approximation is YTM ≈ [C + (F – P)/n] / [(F + P)/2], where n is years to maturity. For equity, the Gordon Growth Model values a share as P₀ = D₁ / (r – g), where D₁ is next year’s expected dividend, r the required return, and g the constant dividend growth rate. Key relationships: bond price and yield move inversely; higher coupon or lower yield raises price; for shares, higher growth or lower required return raises valuation. These concepts link cash‑flow timing, discount rates, and risk‑adjusted returns — the core of investment analysis in Applied Mathematics.
steps: The price of any financial asset equals the present value of its expected future cash flows discounted at a risk‑adjusted rate.
Here is why: 1.
Cash‑flow certainty — Bonds promise fixed coupons and principal, so their valuation uses a single discount rate (YTM). 2.
Discounting mechanics — Each coupon is an annuity payment; the face value is a lump sum. The present‑value formula PV = C × [1 – (1+y)⁻ⁿ]/y + F/(1+y)ⁿ captures both. 3.
Yield measures — Current yield gives a quick income snapshot;
YTM incorporates capital gain/loss if the bond is held to maturity.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., CY = C / F) reveals the misconception that yield is based on face value rather than the price actually paid — confusing nominal return with realised return.

cards.title: Valuation of debentures and bonds determines the present value of all future…
cards.subject: Applied Mathematics
cards.definition: Valuation of debentures and bonds determines the present value of all future cash flows — periodic coupon payments and the principal repayment at maturity — discounted at the prevailing market yield (required rate of return). The key variables are face value (F), coupon rate (c), coupon payment (C = c×F), years to maturity (n), and market yield (y). The bond price (P) equals the sum of discounted coupons plus discounted face value: P = Σ_{t=1}^{n} C/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^n. When the coupon rate equals the market yield, the bond trades at par (P = F). If coupon rate > yield, the bond trades at a premium (P > F); if coupon rate < yield, it trades at a discount (P < F). Yield to Maturity (YTM) is the internal rate of return that equates the present value of cash flows to the current market price. Current Yield = Annual Coupon / Current Market Price. Bond pricing theorems state: (1) prices move inversely to yields; (2) longer maturity bonds are more price-sensitive to yield changes; (3) lower coupon bonds have higher price volatility. These relationships are quantified by duration and convexity, which measure interest rate risk. This node focuses on the mechanics of pricing, YTM computation, and the interpretation of premium/discount status, building on the time-value-of-money concepts from earlier nodes.
