remember: What is the primary type of repetitive DNA sequence analysed in modern STR‑based DNA fingerprinting.
Explain why the product rule is used to calculate the random match probability of a multi‑locus STR profile.
A forensic sample yields a partial profile with only 8 of 13 loci. Evaluate the evidential value of this partial profile.

cards.title: A centrifuge is an instrument that uses centrifugal force…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A centrifuge is an instrument that uses centrifugal force — the apparent outward force experienced by a mass moving in a circular path — to separate particles suspended in a liquid according to their size, shape, density and viscosity of the medium. The rotor holds tubes or bottles at a fixed radius r and rotates at angular velocity ω (rad s⁻¹). The relative centrifugal field (RCF) expressed as multiples of g (9.81 m s⁻²) is RCF = (ω² r)/g = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × N² × r (where N is revolutions per minute and r is in centimetres). Key sub‑concepts: - Rotor types – fixed‑angle (tubes at ~45°) for pelleting; swinging‑bucket (tubes swing horizontal) for density‑gradient separations. - Speed ranges – low‑speed (≤ 5 000 rpm) for cell pellets; high‑speed (15 000–25 000 rpm) for organelles; ultracentrifuge (> 50 000 rpm) for macromolecules (DNA, viruses). - Temperature control – refrigerated models (4 °C) prevent heat‑induced denaturation during long runs. - Safety – imbalance detection, lid‑lock, rotor‑life logging. The centrifuge links directly to downstream nodes: LAF hood (aseptic handling of separated fractions), CO₂ incubator (culture of pelleted cells), bioreactor (scale‑up of clarified broth), and cell‑counting/viability assays that require a clean cell suspension.
steps: The centrifuge separates mixtures by spinning them so that denser particles move outward faster than lighter ones, producing a pellet at the tube bottom and a supernatant above.
Here is why: centrifugal force scales with the square of angular speed and linearly with radius, so a modest increase in rpm dramatically raises the effective g‑force.
First, the rotor geometry decides the separation mode.
Fixed‑angle rotors hold tubes at a constant angle; particles travel a short distance to the tube wall and slide down, ideal for quick pelleting of bacteria or mammalian cells.
Swinging‑bucket rotors let tubes swing horizontal at speed, creating a long, uniform path — perfect for density‑gradient centrifugation of organelles or viruses.
Second, speed selection follows the target particle’s sedimentation coefficient (Svedberg unit).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., RCF = N × r) reveals the misconception that centrifugal force is linear in speed rather than quadratic, ignoring the ω² dependence.
remember: What is the formula to convert revolutions per minute (rpm) to relative centrifugal field (RCF) for a rotor of radius r (cm).
A protocol requires 12 000 × g for 15 min using a fixed‑angle rotor of maximum radius 8 cm. Calculate the required rpm (nearest whole number).
Compare fixed‑angle and swinging‑bucket rotors for separating a mitochondrial fraction from a liver homogenate. Which rotor gives better resolution and why.

cards.title: A Laminar Air Flow (LAF) hood is a primary containment device that provides an…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A Laminar Air Flow (LAF) hood is a primary containment device that provides an ISO Class 5 (Class 100) aseptic workspace by directing HEPA‑filtered air in a unidirectional, laminar stream across the work surface. Two main configurations exist: horizontal flow, where air moves from the back of the hood toward the operator, and vertical flow, where air descends from the top onto the work surface and exits through the front grille. The HEPA filter (High‑Efficiency Particulate Air) removes ≥99.97 % of particles ≥0.3 µm, ensuring that the work zone remains essentially particle‑free. Proper operation requires a certified airflow velocity (typically 0.3–0.5 m s⁻¹), regular validation (smoke pattern test, particle count, filter integrity test), and strict work practices — such as keeping materials at least 15 cm inside the sash, avoiding rapid movements, and decontaminating surfaces with 70 % ethanol before and after use. LAF hoods are indispensable for animal cell culture, plant tissue culture, and microbial manipulations where contamination would compromise experimental integrity or product safety.
steps: The LAF hood is the single most critical piece of equipment that guarantees a contamination‑free environment for every cell culture manipulation in this chapter.

Here is why: the hood creates a unidirectional stream of HEPA‑filtered air that sweeps particles away from the work zone, maintaining ISO Class 5 cleanliness; the two airflow patterns — horizontal and vertical — each…

Consider a typical animal cell culture session: the researcher first wipes the hood interior with 70 % ethanol, allows the airflow to stabilize for 15 minutes, then places sterile flasks, pipettes, and media inside the…
Because the air moves uniformly at 0.4 m s⁻¹, any airborne microbes introduced by the operator’s hands are instantly carried toward the exhaust grille, never settling on the open flask.

In a plant tissue culture lab, a vertical flow hood is preferred when handling hormone‑supplemented media that may generate aerosols; the downward flow pushes any droplets away from the operator’s face.
An edge‑case trap in exams: students often confuse a biosafety cabinet (which protects the user, product, and environment) with a LAF hood (which protects only the product).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “99.9 %”) reveals the misconception that HEPA filters are only required to meet a generic “high efficiency” label rather than the precise 99.97 % threshold mandated for laminar flow hoods.
remember: What is the minimum particle removal efficiency of a HEPA filter used in a LAF hood for particles of 0.3 µm diameter.
Why is a vertical flow LAF hood preferred over a horizontal flow hood when working with volatile organic solvents in plant tissue culture.
Evaluate the statement: “A LAF hood can be used as a substitute for a Class II biosafety cabinet when handling pathogenic bacteria.”.

cards.title: A stirred‑tank bioreactor (STR) is a cylindrical vessel equipped with a…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A stirred‑tank bioreactor (STR) is a cylindrical vessel equipped with a centrally mounted impeller (usually Rushton turbine or pitched‑blade) that provides mechanical agitation. The vessel is jacketed for temperature control, fitted with spargers for gas (air/O₂/CO₂) introduction, and instrumented with probes for pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), temperature, and sometimes redox potential. Sterile ports allow inoculation, sampling, and addition of feeds or bases/acids. The impeller creates a homogeneous suspension, enhances mass transfer (kLa), and prevents cell settling. STRs operate in batch, fed‑batch, or continuous modes and are the workhorse for large‑scale mammalian cell culture (e.g., CHO cells for monoclonal antibodies) and microbial fermentation. Scale‑up follows constant power‑per‑volume (P/V), tip speed, or kLa criteria. The STR’s design balances shear sensitivity of animal cells (low shear impellers, baffles) with the need for adequate oxygen transfer. It integrates with upstream (seed train) and downstream (harvest) processes, and its control system (PLC/SCADA) maintains set‑points via PID loops for pH (CO₂/NaOH), DO (air/O₂ blend), and temperature (jacket water).
steps: The stirred‑tank bioreactor is the central “factory floor” where living cells are cultivated at scale under tightly controlled conditions.
Here is why: it combines mechanical agitation, gas sparging, and real‑time feedback to keep temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen within narrow windows that mammalian cells demand.
Consider a 10 L laboratory STR used to expand a CHO cell line producing a therapeutic antibody.

The vessel is a stainless‑steel cylinder with a 1:2 height‑to‑diameter ratio, four vertical baffles to break vortex formation, and a Rushton turbine impeller positioned one‑third of the liquid height from the bottom.
The jacket circulates water at 37 °C; a PID controller adjusts jacket temperature within ±0.1 °C.

A ring sparger at the base releases fine bubbles of air/oxygen; the DO probe (polarographic or optical) feeds a cascade that enriches inlet gas with pure O₂ when DO falls below 30 % air saturation. pH is held at 7.0 ±…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “baffles increase the impeller speed”) reveals the misconception that baffles affect motor performance rather than flow pattern.
remember: What is the primary purpose of baffles in a stirred‑tank bioreactor.
Why is a Rushton turbine commonly used in microbial fermentations but often replaced by a pitched‑blade impeller in mammalian cell culture.
Evaluate the statement: “Maintaining constant tip speed during scale‑up guarantees identical shear environment for the cells.”.

cards.title: A sparged bioreactor (also called an air‑lift or bubble‑column reactor)…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A sparged bioreactor (also called an air‑lift or bubble‑column reactor) supplies dissolved oxygen and removes carbon dioxide by sparging sterile gas (usually air or oxygen‑enriched air) through a porous sparger at the base of a vertical vessel. The rising bubbles create a circulation loop: an up‑flow riser where gas‑liquid mixture rises, and a down‑flow downcomer where liquid descends, establishing mixing without mechanical impellers. Key parameters include gas hold‑up (ε_g), volumetric mass‑transfer coefficient (k_La), bubble size distribution, and superficial gas velocity (U_g). Sparged reactors are preferred for shear‑sensitive cultures (animal cells, plant cell suspensions) because they generate lower shear stress than stirred‑tank reactors. They also have simpler construction, lower capital cost, and easier scale‑up based on constant k_La or constant power‑per‑volume criteria. However, they offer less precise control of mixing intensity and can suffer from foaming, requiring antifoam agents or mechanical foam breakers. Applications include large‑scale production of monoclonal antibodies (hybridoma technology), recombinant proteins, and secondary metabolites from plant cell cultures.
steps: The takeaway: Sparged bioreactors use rising gas bubbles to simultaneously oxygenate and mix cultures, making them ideal for shear‑sensitive animal and plant cells.

Here is why: First, the sparger at the vessel base releases fine bubbles; as they rise, buoyancy creates a density difference between the gas‑rich riser and the gas‑poor downcomer, establishing a continuous circulation…
Second, the large interfacial area of small bubbles yields a high volumetric mass‑transfer coefficient (k_La), ensuring sufficient dissolved oxygen for high‑density cultures.
Third, because there is no impeller, the shear stress experienced by cells is an order of magnitude lower than in stirred tanks, preserving viability of fragile hybridoma or plant suspension cells.
Fourth, scale‑up is guided by maintaining constant k_La or constant superficial gas velocity (U_g = Q_g / A), which is simpler than matching impeller tip speed.

Fifth, Indian biotech firms such as Serum Institute of India use air‑lift reactors for bulk vaccine antigen production, while Biocon employs bubble columns for recombinant insulin precursor fermentation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the impeller pushes the liquid around”) reveals the misconception that sparged reactors rely on mechanical stirring, confusing them with stirred‑tank bioreactors.
remember: What is the primary driving force for liquid circulation in a sparged (air‑lift) bioreactor.
Why are sparged bioreactors preferred over stirred‑tank reactors for culturing hybridoma cells producing monoclonal antibodies.
Evaluate the statement: “Increasing the gas flow rate in a sparged bioreactor always improves oxygen transfer without any drawbacks.”.

cards.title: A CO₂ incubator is a sealed, temperature‑controlled chamber used for animal…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A CO₂ incubator is a sealed, temperature‑controlled chamber used for animal cell culture that maintains a constant 5 % CO₂ (v/v), 37 °C temperature, and ≥95 % relative humidity. The CO₂ dissolves in the culture medium to form carbonic acid, which together with the bicarbonate buffer (HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃) stabilises the pH around 7.4, a critical condition for enzyme activity and cell metabolism. Temperature controls the rate of cellular processes; excessive heat denatures proteins, while low temperature slows growth. Humidity prevents evaporation of water from the medium, which would otherwise increase osmolarity and stress cells. The incubator also incorporates HEPA‑filtered air inflow to minimise microbial contamination and alarms for CO₂, temperature, or humidity deviations. It works in tandem with vessels such as T‑flasks, multi‑well plates, or bioreactor culture bags, providing the macro‑environment while the vessels supply the micro‑environment (media, cells). Understanding the CO₂ incubator links directly to media preparation (e.g., DMEM, RPMI) that rely on bicarbonate buffering, and to downstream techniques like hybridoma technology or tissue engineering where stable pH is essential for product viability.
steps: A CO₂ incubator maintains a stable 5 % CO₂, 37 °C, and high humidity environment essential for animal cell culture because it stabilises the pH of bicarbonate‑buffered media, thereby supporting cell growth and viability.
Here is why: 1.
CO₂ and pH balance – When CO₂ dissolves in medium, it forms carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which dissociates to bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) and protons (H⁺).
The Henderson‑Hasselbalch equation shows that a constant 5 % CO₂ fixes the [H₂CO₃]/[HCO₃⁻] ratio, keeping pH near 7.4 despite cellular metabolism producing acidic or basic metabolites. 2.

Temperature control – Enzyme kinetics follow the Q₁₀ rule; a 10 °C rise roughly doubles reaction rates. 37 °C mimics mammalian physiological temperature, ensuring optimal metabolic activity without causing heat‑shock…
Humidity importance – Open culture vessels lose water to the incubator atmosphere.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “10 % CO₂”) reveals the misconception that higher CO₂ always improves growth, ignoring that excess CO₂ drives pH below 7.0, causing acidosis and cell death.
remember: What is the standard CO₂ percentage (v/v) maintained in a CO₂ incubator for mammalian cell culture.
Explain why a 5 % CO₂ atmosphere is necessary when using DMEM as culture medium.
If the humidity inside a CO₂ incubator falls to 70 %, what is the most likely immediate effect on adherent cells cultured in open dishes.

cards.title: A T‑flask (tissue‑culture flask) is a sterile…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A T‑flask (tissue‑culture flask) is a sterile, single‑use or reusable polystyrene vessel designed for adherent animal cell culture. It provides a defined growth surface (e.g., 25 cm², 75 cm², 175 cm², 225 cm²) on which anchorage‑dependent cells attach, spread, and proliferate in a thin film of culture medium (typically 5–10 mL per 25 cm²). The flask’s canted neck allows easy pipette access while minimising contamination risk; caps are either solid (for sealed incubation) or vented with a 0.2 µm hydrophobic filter to permit gas exchange (O₂/CO₂) without microbial entry. T‑flasks are used inside a CO₂ incubator (5 % CO₂, 37 °C, >95 % humidity) to maintain physiological pH via the bicarbonate buffer system. They are handled exclusively in a laminar‑air‑flow (LAF) hood to preserve sterility. Scaling up from a T‑25 to a T‑175 or to multi‑layer flasks (e.g., CellSTACK) follows the same surface‑area‑to‑volume principle, enabling stepwise expansion before transfer to stirred‑tank or sparged bioreactors. Surface treatments (tissue‑culture‑treated, collagen‑coated, poly‑L‑lysine) modify hydrophilicity and charge to enhance attachment of fastidious lines. The flask’s optical clarity permits routine phase‑contrast microscopy without opening the vessel, supporting confluence assessment and contamination checks.
steps: The T‑flask is the workhorse vessel that translates a few millilitres of cell suspension into a confluent monolayer by providing a defined, sterile growth surface and controlled gas exchange.

Here is why: the flat, tissue‑culture‑treated polystyrene base maximises the area‑to‑volume ratio, allowing nutrients and gases to diffuse rapidly across the thin medium layer while giving anchorage‑dependent cells…
First, the researcher selects a flask whose surface area matches the desired cell yield — for example, a T‑75 (75 cm²) seeded at 1 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻² will yield ~7.5 × 10⁵ cells at confluence.
Second, the vented cap with a 0.2 µm filter lets the 5 % CO₂ atmosphere equilibrate with the bicarbonate‑buffered medium, stabilising pH at 7.2–7.4 without opening the flask.

Third, all manipulations — thawing cells, seeding, medium changes, passaging — occur inside a Class II LAF hood where HEPA‑filtered laminar flow sweeps particles away from the open neck, preventing microbial ingress.
Fourth, the flask sits in a humidified CO₂ incubator at 37 °C; the high humidity (≥95 %) prevents medium evaporation, which would otherwise increase osmolarity and stress cells.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it filters the culture medium”) reveals the misconception that the cap filter processes liquid — confusing gas‑exchange filtration with media sterilisation, which is done separately using a 0.2 µm syringe filter before adding medium to…
remember: What is the primary function of the 0.2 µm hydrophobic filter in a vented T‑flask cap.
Why must T‑flasks be handled inside a laminar‑air‑flow hood rather than on an open bench.
A researcher seeds 2 × 10⁵ cells into a T‑75 flask (75 cm²) containing 15 mL….

cards.title: Sterilization techniques are validated procedures that eliminate all viable…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Sterilization techniques are validated procedures that eliminate all viable microorganisms — including bacterial endospores — from instruments, media, surfaces, and gases used in cell culture. The principal methods are moist heat (autoclaving at 121 °C, 15 psi for 15–20 min), dry heat (160–180 °C for 2 h), filtration (0.22 µm membrane for heat‑labile solutions), chemical agents (70 % ethanol, 0.1 % mercuric chloride for plant explants), and radiation (UV‑C 254 nm for surfaces, γ‑irradiation for disposable plastics). Each technique is chosen based on material compatibility, throughput, and the sterility assurance level (SAL) required. Autoclaving is the gold standard for glassware, metal instruments, and aqueous media; filtration preserves thermolabile components such as growth factors; UV exposure is limited to surface decontamination inside laminar airflow hoods; chemical sterilants are used for plant tissue explants where heat would damage tissue. Validation involves biological indicators (Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores) and routine monitoring of temperature, pressure, and exposure time. Proper sterilization prevents contamination that would compromise experimental reproducibility, cell line integrity, and downstream applications such as hybridoma production or tissue engineering.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that sterilization method must match the thermal and chemical stability of the item being sterilized, otherwise the material is damaged or sterility is not achieved.

Here is why: moist heat autoclaving denatures proteins and nucleic acids of all microbes, including spores, but it will degrade heat‑labile vitamins and growth factors; therefore, media containing such components are…

Dry heat at 160–180 °C is reserved for glassware and metal instruments that can withstand prolonged exposure without corrosion, while UV‑C light at 254 nm is only effective on exposed surfaces because it cannot…

Chemical sterilants like 70 % ethanol act by protein denaturation and lipid dissolution, suitable for wiping surfaces and brief explant treatment, whereas mercuric chloride (0.1 %) is used for surface sterilization of…

Validation is non‑negotiable: each autoclave run must include a biological indicator strip containing Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores; after incubation, absence of growth confirms a sterility assurance level of…

In practice, a student preparing DMEM for animal cell culture would filter‑sterilize the complete medium, autoclave the empty T‑flasks and pipettes, wipe the LAF hood with 70 % ethanol, and UV‑irradiate the hood for 15…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “autoclave at 121 °C for 15 min”) reveals the misconception that all culture components can withstand moist heat, ignoring the thermal sensitivity of biologics.
remember: Which sterilization method is most appropriate for a heat‑labile protein supplement (e.g., recombinant insulin) added to cell culture medium.
Why is UV‑C irradiation not used to sterilize liquid culture media.
A student autoclaves a batch of DMEM containing 10 % fetal bovine serum at 121 °C for 20 min. Evaluate the outcome.

cards.title: Cryopreservation is the process of preserving viable cells, tissues…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Cryopreservation is the process of preserving viable cells, tissues, or organisms at ultra‑low temperatures (typically –196 °C in liquid nitrogen) by arresting all metabolic activity while maintaining structural integrity. The core principle is controlled cooling (≈ –1 °C min⁻¹) in the presence of a cryoprotective agent (CPA) — commonly dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or glycerol — which replaces intracellular water, depresses the freezing point, and reduces ice‑crystal formation that would otherwise rupture membranes. After equilibration with CPA, samples are loaded into cryovials, placed in a programmable rate freezer or an isopropanol‑based “Mr. Frosty” container for passive cooling, then transferred to liquid‑nitrogen storage. Viability post‑thaw is assessed by trypan blue exclusion, Evan’s blue, or flow cytometry. Critical parameters include CPA concentration (usually 5–10 % v/v), cooling rate, storage temperature stability, and rapid thawing (37 °C water bath) followed by stepwise CPA removal to avoid osmotic shock. Cryopreservation underpins biobanking, hybridoma line maintenance, stem‑cell repositories, and the global exchange of genetically engineered cell lines.
steps: Cryopreservation succeeds only when ice formation is controlled so that cells survive the freeze‑thaw cycle.
Here is why: uncontrolled freezing creates large extracellular ice crystals that mechanically shear membranes and concentrate solutes to toxic levels, killing the cells.
Consider a typical mammalian cell line (e.g., CHO‑K1) grown to 80 % confluence in a T‑75 flask.
First, the spent medium is removed and cells are detached with trypsin‑EDTA, then resuspended in complete medium at 1 × 10⁶ cells mL⁻¹.
A cryoprotectant — usually 10 % (v/v) DMSO — is added dropwise while gently swirling;
DMSO penetrates the membrane, replaces intracellular water, and lowers the freezing point, limiting intracellular ice nucleation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “50 % DMSO”) reveals the misconception that higher CPA always gives better protection, ignoring DMSO’s cytotoxicity at room temperature and the osmotic stress during thawing.
remember: What is the typical final concentration of DMSO used as a cryoprotectant for mammalian cell lines.
Why is a controlled cooling rate of approximately –1 °C min⁻¹ critical during cryopreservation.
Evaluate the statement: “Cells can be stored indefinitely at –80 °C without loss of viability.”.

cards.title: Cell counting is the quantitative determination of the number of cells in a…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Cell counting is the quantitative determination of the number of cells in a defined volume of suspension. It underpins every downstream application — seeding density for culture, dosing for transfection, calculating growth rates, and quality control of bioprocesses. The classical method uses a hemocytometer (Improved Neubauer chamber) where a known chamber depth (0.1 mm) and grid area (1 mm² per large square) give a calibrated volume of 0.1 µL per large square. The formula cells mL^-1 = average count per large square × dilution factor × 10^41 derives from the chamber volume (0.1 µL = 10⁻⁴ mL). Modern labs also employ automated image‑based counters (e.g., Countess, TC20) that capture bright‑field or fluorescence images and apply software algorithms to distinguish cells from debris, and impedance‑based Coulter counters that measure voltage pulses as cells pass through an aperture. All methods require a representative, well‑mixed sample, appropriate dilution (typically 1:10–1:100) to keep counts within the optimal range (50–250 cells per large square for hemocytometer), and exclusion of non‑cellular particles (via trypan blue or fluorescent viability dyes, covered in the next node). Accuracy depends on chamber cleanliness, correct coverslip placement (Newton’s rings), and statistical counting of at least 4–8 large squares. The result feeds directly into seeding calculations: V_seed = N_desiredC_measured where N_desired is the target cell number and C_measured the concentration obtained.
steps: Cell counting converts a microscopic snapshot into a precise concentration that drives every culture decision.
Here is why: the number of cells you seed determines growth kinetics, product yield, and reproducibility — an error of 20 % at seeding propagates exponentially.
Consider a typical ISC practical: you have a T‑75 flask of HEK‑293 cells at ~80 % confluence.
You detach them with trypsin, resuspend in 10 mL complete DMEM, and need to seed a 6‑well plate at 2 × 10⁵ cells well⁻¹.
First, you mix 100 µL of suspension with 100 µL trypan blue (1:2 dilution) and load 10 µL onto a cleaned hemocytometer.
You count the four corner large squares (each 1 mm²) and the centre square, obtaining 45, 52, 48, 50, and 51 cells respectively.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “1 µL”) reveals the misconception that the depth is 1 mm instead of the standardized 0.1 mm, leading to a ten‑fold concentration error.
remember: What is the calibrated volume of one large square (1 mm²) of an Improved Neubauer hemocytometer chamber.
A student counts an average of 60 cells per large square using a 1:20 dilution. What is the cell concentration in cells mL⁻¹.
Why must at least four large squares be counted on a hemocytometer.

cards.title: Evan’s blue (EB) is an azo dye that selectively penetrates cells with…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Evan’s blue (EB) is an azo dye that selectively penetrates cells with compromised plasma membranes, staining them blue while viable cells exclude the dye due to intact membrane integrity. The assay relies on the principle of membrane impermeability: live cells maintain selective permeability, preventing EB entry; dead or damaged cells lose this barrier, allowing EB to bind intracellular proteins and nucleic acids. After incubation (typically 2–5 min at room temperature), the cell suspension is examined under a light microscope or counted using a hemocytometer (linking to the prerequisite node Cell counting). Viability (%) = (Number of unstained cells ÷ Total cells counted) × 100. The method is rapid, inexpensive, and compatible with both adherent and suspension cultures, but it does not distinguish early apoptotic cells (which may still exclude EB) from truly viable ones. Results are often cross‑validated with metabolic assays (e.g., MTT) or flow cytometry (FACS, sibling node sorting (FACS)). EB staining is also used in plant protoplast viability and microbial culture checks, making it a versatile tool across the chapter’s subtopics.
steps: Evan’s blue reports cell viability by staining only membrane‑compromised cells blue, letting a simple count give a health percentage.
Here is why: the plasma membrane of a living cell is a selective barrier; its lipid bilayer and associated proteins prevent large, charged molecules like EB from entering.

When a cell dies — through necrosis, mechanical damage, or severe toxicity — the membrane ruptures or becomes leaky, allowing EB to diffuse in and bind intracellular components, turning the cell blue.
Consider a typical ISC practical: you harvest a 1 mL suspension of CHO cells, mix 100 µL with 100 µL of 0.4 % EB, wait 3 minutes, then load 10 µL onto a hemocytometer.
Under 10× objective you count 200 total cells in the four corner squares, of which 180 are clear and 20 are blue.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “EB enters live cells because they are metabolically active”) reveals the misconception that metabolic activity drives dye uptake, confusing metabolic assays (MTT) with membrane‑exclusion assays.
remember: What is the fundamental principle that allows Evan’s blue to differentiate live from dead cells.
A student prepares a 1:1 mixture of cell suspension and 0.4 % Evan’s blue, counts 250 total cells and 30 blue cells. What is the viability percentage.
Why might Evan’s blue give a falsely high viability reading in a culture undergoing early apoptosis.

cards.title: Fluorescence‑Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) is a specialized flow‑cytometry…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Fluorescence‑Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) is a specialized flow‑cytometry technique that physically separates heterogeneous cell populations into defined sub‑populations based on their light‑scattering and fluorescence characteristics. Cells are first labelled with fluorochrome‑conjugated antibodies or dyes that bind to specific surface markers, intracellular proteins, or nucleic acids. The labelled suspension is hydrodynamically focused into a single‑cell stream that intersects a laser beam. Each cell scatters light (forward scatter ≈ size, side scatter ≈ granularity) and emits fluorescence at characteristic wavelengths. Detectors convert these optical signals into electronic pulses. A real‑time decision circuit applies user‑defined gates; cells meeting the criteria are given an electrostatic charge (+/−) as the stream breaks into droplets. Charged droplets are deflected by an electric field into collection tubes, while uncharged droplets go to waste. FACS thus links quantitative optical analysis (measurement) with physical separation (sorting), enabling downstream applications such as cloning, transcriptomics, or adoptive cell therapy. Key sub‑concepts include: (1) hydrodynamic focusing for single‑cell interrogation, (2) fluorochrome selection and spectral overlap compensation, (3) gating hierarchy (live → singlet → lineage → functional marker), (4) sort modes (purity, yield, single‑cell), and (5) post‑sort validation (re‑analysis, viability). The instrument integrates fluidics, optics, electronics, and software; each component influences resolution, speed, and sterility.
steps: FACS converts optical signatures of individual cells into physical separation, making it the workhorse for isolating rare populations such as haematopoietic stem cells or tumour‑infiltrating lymphocytes.

Here is why: the instrument first aligns cells in a single file using hydrodynamic focusing, then interrogates each cell with one or more lasers, and finally charges and deflects droplets containing cells of interest.

Consider a typical experiment: peripheral blood mononuclear cells are stained with anti‑CD4‑FITC and anti‑CD8‑PE, plus a viability dye. The sample runs at 20 µL/min through a 100 µm nozzle at 20 psi. Forward and side…
A viability gate removes dead cells.
A CD4⁺CD8⁻ gate defines helper T cells.
The sort decision is set to “Purity” mode, charging only droplets that contain a single CD4⁺ event.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “FACS separates cells by size using a centrifuge”) reveals the misconception that FACS is a bulk separation method like centrifugation, confusing physical sedimentation with single‑cell optical interrogation.
remember: What does the acronym FACS stand for, and what is its fundamental operating principle.
Why is hydrodynamic focusing essential for accurate FACS analysis and sorting.
A researcher claims that FACS can sort cells based on size alone without any fluorescent label. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: LB medium is a chemically defined…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: LB medium is a chemically defined, rich bacterial growth medium originally formulated by Giuseppe Bertani in 1951 for Escherichia coli and other enteric bacteria. It exists in two common formulations: Lennox (L‑LB) — 10 g L⁻¹ tryptone, 5 g L⁻¹ yeast extract, 5 g L⁻¹ NaCl — and Miller (M‑LB) — 10 g L⁻¹ tryptone, 5 g L⁻¹ yeast extract, 10 g L⁻¹ NaCl. The higher salt in Miller mimics intestinal osmolarity and improves plasmid stability. LB agar adds 15 g L⁻¹ bacteriological agar for solid surfaces. Because tryptone provides peptides and amino acids while yeast extract supplies B‑vitamins and nucleotides, LB supports rapid logarithmic growth (doubling ~20 min at 37 °C) without requiring defined supplements. It is the default medium for routine cloning, library propagation, and recombinant protein expression in E. coli and is referenced in the ISC Biotechnology syllabus under “Media types: LB”.
steps: LB medium is the universal “starter soup” for E. coli because its two standard recipes (Lennox and Miller) give predictable, fast growth and reliable plasmid maintenance.

Here is why: first, tryptone (pancreatic digest of casein) supplies a broad peptide pool that E. coli can import via oligopeptide transporters, eliminating the need for amino‑acid biosynthesis during early log phase.
Second, yeast extract contributes nucleotides, B‑vitamins, and trace metals that act as cofactors for DNA replication and transcription.

Third, the NaCl concentration sets the osmotic environment: 5 g L⁻¹ (Lennox) reduces ionic stress for sensitive strains, while 10 g L⁻¹ (Miller) stabilises high‑copy plasmids by lowering the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio…
Consider a typical ISC practical: you need 250 mL Miller LB agar for blue‑white screening.

You weigh 2.5 g tryptone, 1.25 g yeast extract, 2.5 g NaCl, and 3.75 g agar, dissolve in 200 mL distilled water, adjust volume to 250 mL, autoclave, cool to ~50 °C, add antibiotic (e.g., 100 µg mL⁻¹ ampicillin), pour…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “10 g L⁻¹ NaCl”) reveals the misconception that Lennox and Miller have identical salt levels — confusing the two standard recipes.
remember: State the exact composition (g L⁻¹) of Lennox LB broth.
Why does Miller LB contain twice the NaCl of Lennox LB.
Evaluate the claim: “LB agar can be prepared by simply adding agar to LB broth after autoclaving.”.

cards.title: White’s medium, formulated by Philip R. White in 1963, is a fully defined…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: White’s medium, formulated by Philip R. White in 1963, is a fully defined, low‑salt plant tissue culture medium. It contains macronutrients (nitrate, phosphate, sulfate, calcium, magnesium, potassium), micronutrients (iron‑EDTA, boron, manganese, zinc, copper, molybdenum, iodine, cobalt), a vitamin suite (thiamine‑HCl, pyridoxine‑HCl, nicotinic acid, glycine), myo‑inositol, and a carbon source (typically 20 g L⁻¹ sucrose). Its low total ionic strength (≈ 20 mM) reduces osmotic stress, making it especially suitable for root cultures, callus induction, and haploid/triploid production via anther or ovary culture. Unlike Murashige‑Skoog (MS) medium, which is high in ammonium and nitrate, White’s medium favours organogenesis over rapid callus proliferation. It is routinely used in Indian university labs for micropropagation of banana, sugarcane, and medicinal plants, and serves as a baseline for testing hormone supplements (auxins, cytokinins). The medium is sterilised by autoclaving (121 °C, 15 psi, 20 min) after pH adjustment to 5.7‑5.8. Its defined nature allows reproducible experiments in somatic hybridisation, embryo rescue, and synthetic seed encapsulation, linking directly to the totipotency concept covered earlier.
steps: White’s medium is a defined, low‑salt plant tissue culture medium that reliably supports root and callus growth, making it a standard for studying organogenesis in vitro.
Here is why: first, its low ionic strength (≈ 20 mM) mimics the natural soil solution around roots, preventing osmotic shock that can inhibit delicate meristematic cells.
Second, the nitrate‑to‑ammonium ratio (≈ 20:1) favours organised organ formation rather than unorganised callus, which is critical for haploid and triploid production via anther culture.

Third, the vitamin profile (thiamine, pyridoxine, nicotinic acid, glycine) matches the metabolic needs of many dicotyledonous species, including economically important Indian crops like banana (Musa spp.) and turmeric…

Fourth, the medium’s defined nature allows precise manipulation of hormone supplements — for example, adding 2,4‑D for callus induction or NAA for root elongation — without unknown interactions from undefined components.
Consider a typical Class 12 lab: students prepare 1 L of White’s medium, adjust pH to 5.8, autoclave, then inoculate 0.5 cm carrot root explants.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the ratio is 1:1 like in MS medium”) reveals the misconception that all plant media share the same nitrogen balance — confusing the high‑ammonium MS formulation with the low‑ammonium White’s formulation.
remember: What is the typical nitrate‑to‑ammonium molar ratio in White’s medium, and why is this ratio significant for plant organogenesis.
A student prepares White’s medium but forgets to add iron‑EDTA. Predict the visible symptoms in carrot root cultures after two weeks and explain the physiological basis.
Evaluate the suitability of White’s medium for large‑scale micropropagation of banana (Musa spp.) in a commercial bioreactor, considering both advantages and limitations.

cards.title: RPMI (Roswell Park Memorial Institute) medium is a chemically defined…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: RPMI (Roswell Park Memorial Institute) medium is a chemically defined, bicarbonate‑buffered culture medium originally formulated for the growth of human lymphoid cells. Its basal formulation includes 21 essential and non‑essential amino acids (e.g., L‑glutamine, L‑arginine), 11 vitamins (notably biotin, folic acid, B₁₂), inorganic salts (NaCl, KCl, CaCl₂, MgSO₄, NaH₂PO₄), D‑glucose (2 g L⁻¹), phenol red as a pH indicator, and 2 g L⁻¹ NaHCO₃ for CO₂‑dependent buffering. The medium is supplied as a powder or liquid concentrate; final preparation requires dissolution in sterile water, pH adjustment to 7.2–7.4 with sterile 1 M NaOH or HCl, and filtration through a 0.22 µm membrane. RPMI is typically supplemented with 10 % heat‑inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS) to provide growth factors, lipids and attachment proteins. It is the medium of choice for suspension cultures of hematopoietic cells (T‑cells, B‑cells, NK cells), hybridoma lines for monoclonal antibody production, and many primary lymphocyte assays. Compared with DMEM (high glucose, pyruvate, higher vitamin content) and White’s medium (plant‑tissue oriented), RPMI has lower calcium and phosphate, making it less prone to precipitation in CO₂ incubators. Its osmolarity (~300 mOsm kg⁻¹) matches human plasma, reducing osmotic stress. The medium’s composition directly influences cell viability, proliferation rate, and functional read‑outs such as cytokine secretion, linking it to downstream applications in immunology, vaccine development and tissue engineering.
steps: The one thing to remember: RPMI is a bicarbonate‑buffered, low‑calcium, physiologic‑osmolarity medium specifically designed for human lymphoid and hybridoma cells, and its performance hinges on correct CO₂‑dependent pH…
Here is why: 1.

Origin and purpose – Developed at Roswell Park in the 1960s for leukemia cell lines, RPMI’s formulation mirrors human plasma osmolarity and provides the nutrients that rapidly dividing lymphocytes demand. 2.
Buffer system – The 2 g L⁻¹ NaHCO₃ works only inside a 5 % CO₂ incubator; the dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, establishing a pH ≈ 7.2.
Without the incubator the medium alkalinises, phenol red turns magenta, and cells experience stress. 3.

Low calcium & phosphate – Compared with DMEM, RPMI contains ~0.4 mM Ca²⁺ and ~0.8 mM phosphate, minimising precipitation of calcium‑phosphate crystals that would cloud the medium and damage delicate suspension cells. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “HEPES buffers RPMI”) reveals the misconception that all cell‑culture media use zwitterionic buffers — confusing RPMI’s CO₂‑dependent system with HEPES‑supplemented media used for open‑system work.
remember: What is the primary buffering system in RPMI medium and what incubator condition is required for it to function.
Why is RPMI preferred over DMEM for culturing human T‑lymphocytes in suspension.
Evaluate the statement: “Adding 10 % FBS to RPMI is optional because the basal medium already contains all essential nutrients.”.

cards.title: Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) is a chemically defined…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) is a chemically defined, serum‑free basal medium widely used for mammalian cell culture. It is derived from Eagle’s Minimum Essential Medium (MEM) but contains a four‑fold higher concentration of glucose (4.5 g L⁻¹) and increased levels of amino acids, vitamins and inorganic salts. The high glucose supports rapid proliferation of transformed or high‑metabolic‑rate cell lines (e.g., HeLa, HEK‑293). DMEM uses a sodium bicarbonate (3.7 g L⁻¹) buffer system that requires a 5 % CO₂ atmosphere in a CO₂ incubator to maintain physiological pH 7.2‑7.4. It lacks proteins, lipids and growth factors; therefore, researchers supplement it with 5‑10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) or defined serum‑free additives. Variants exist: low‑glucose DMEM (1 g L⁻¹), DMEM/F‑12 (1:1 mix with Ham’s F‑12), and phenol‑red‑free versions for fluorescence assays. The medium is sterilised by 0.22 µm filtration, stored at 2‑8 °C, and warmed to 37 °C before use. Its composition is standardized (e.g., CaCl₂ 200 mg L⁻¹, MgSO₄ 97.7 mg L⁻¹, KCl 400 mg L⁻¹, NaCl 6.4 g L⁻¹, NaHCO₃ 3.7 g L⁻¹, glucose 4.5 g L⁻¹, essential and non‑essential amino acids, vitamins such as choline chloride, folic acid, nicotinamide, pyridoxine HCl, riboflavin, thiamine HCl). DMEM’s high nutrient density makes it the default choice for routine maintenance, transfection, and viral production in animal cell culture laboratories.
steps: DMEM is the workhorse medium for most mammalian cell lines because its high glucose and enriched amino‑acid/vitamin profile meet the energetic and biosynthetic demands of rapidly dividing cells.

Here is why: the four‑fold glucose increase over MEM fuels glycolysis and provides carbon skeletons for nucleotide and lipid synthesis; the elevated amino‑acid pool prevents limitation during protein production; the…
Consider a typical ISC laboratory: you receive a bottle of DMEM powder (≈13.4 g L⁻¹).

You dissolve it in 900 mL ultrapure water, add 3.7 g NaHCO₃, adjust pH to 7.2 with sterile 1 M NaOH while bubbling 5 % CO₂, bring volume to 1 L, filter through a 0.22 µm membrane into sterile bottles, and store at 4 °C.
Before seeding cells, you warm 500 mL to 37 °C, supplement with 10 % heat‑inactivated FBS, 1 % penicillin‑streptomycin, and optionally 2 mM L‑glutamine.

The cells (e.g., HEK‑293) attach within hours and double every 24 h. If you mistakenly use low‑glucose DMEM for these cells, growth slows because glycolytic flux cannot meet ATP demand — a common exam trap.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “2 g L⁻¹”) reveals the misconception that DMEM and RPMI have similar glucose levels — confusing the two media’s formulations.
remember: What is the glucose concentration in standard high‑glucose DMEM.
Why does DMEM require a 5 % CO₂ incubator for pH stability.
Evaluate the suitability of high‑glucose DMEM for primary rat hippocampal neurons cultured for 14 days.

cards.title: Microbial fermentation is the controlled cultivation of microorganisms…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Microbial fermentation is the controlled cultivation of microorganisms (bacteria, yeast, fungi) in a nutrient medium to produce biomass, primary metabolites (ethanol, lactic acid, amino acids) or secondary metabolites (antibiotics, enzymes, vitamins). The process occurs in a bioreactor (stirred‑tank or sparged) where parameters — pH, temperature, dissolved oxygen, agitation, and substrate feed — are monitored and regulated. Fermentation modes include batch (all nutrients added at start), fed‑batch (substrate fed incrementally to avoid inhibition), and continuous (chemostat or turbidostat, where fresh medium enters and culture exits at equal rates). Key concepts: inoculum development, sterilization of medium and vessel (see sibling nodes on sterilization techniques and bioreactors), growth kinetics (lag, exponential, stationary, death phases), product formation kinetics (growth‑associated, non‑growth‑associated, mixed), and downstream processing (cell separation, product purification). Media such as LB (for E. coli), White’s (plant cells), RPMI/DMEM (animal cells) are selected per organism; however, microbial fermentation typically uses defined or complex media optimized for yield. The node links to growth kinetics and continuous culture devices (turbidostat, chemostat) for deeper quantitative treatment.
steps: Takeaway: Fermentation is the scalable, controlled use of microbial metabolism to convert substrates into valuable products, and its efficiency hinges on choosing the right mode, bioreactor, and process control strategy.
Here is why: 1.
Mode determines productivity and control.
Batch fermentation is simple — all nutrients loaded, culture runs to completion — ideal for small‑scale antibiotic production (e.g., penicillin).
Fed‑batch adds substrate gradually, preventing overflow metabolism (e.g., acetate formation in E. coli recombinant protein runs) and extending exponential phase, boosting yield.
Continuous modes (chemostat, turbidostat) maintain cells in steady‑state exponential growth, giving constant product output — used for single‑cell protein or ethanol. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “batch for ethanol, continuous for penicillin”) reveals the misconception that product value alone dictates mode, ignoring growth‑associated vs. non‑growth‑associated kinetics and economic scale.
remember: Name the three main fermentation modes and give one industrial product typically made by each mode.
Explain why dissolved oxygen (DO) control is critical in aerobic stirred‑tank fermentation and describe two engineering methods to increase oxygen transfer rate (OTR).
Evaluate the statement: “Fed‑batch fermentation is always superior to batch because it gives higher final cell density.” Provide a reasoned judgment.

cards.title: Growth kinetics quantifies the rate at which microbial populations increase…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Growth kinetics quantifies the rate at which microbial populations increase under defined conditions. It links the specific growth rate (μ, h⁻¹) to substrate concentration (S, g L⁻¹) through the Monod equation μ = μₘₐₓ·S/(Kₛ+S), where μₘₐₓ is the maximum specific growth rate and Kₛ the half‑saturation constant. Batch cultures display lag, exponential, stationary and death phases; fed‑batch and continuous (chemostat, turbidostat) modes maintain cells in exponential growth by controlling substrate feed or dilution rate (D, h⁻¹). Yield coefficients (Yₓ/ₛ, g cells g⁻¹ substrate) and maintenance coefficients (mₛ, g substrate g⁻¹ cells h⁻¹) describe conversion efficiency. These parameters are essential for designing bioprocesses, scaling up from shake flasks to industrial bioreactors, and predicting product formation kinetics.
steps: Growth kinetics is the quantitative backbone of every microbial bioprocess — it tells you how fast cells multiply, how much substrate they need, and when they will stop.
Here is why: the specific growth rate μ links cell division to substrate availability through the Monod relationship, which mirrors enzyme‑substrate saturation.
First, in a batch culture cells pass through lag, exponential, stationary and death phases; μ is constant only during exponential growth, allowing calculation of doubling time t_d = ln 2/μ.
Second, the Monod equation μ = μₘₐₓ·S/(Kₛ+S) shows that at low S growth is substrate‑limited (first‑order), while at high S it approaches μₘₐₓ (zero‑order).
Third, yield coefficient Yₓ/ₛ converts substrate consumed into biomass formed, and maintenance coefficient mₛ accounts for substrate used for non‑growth energy.
Fourth, continuous culture (chemostat) operates at steady state where dilution rate D equals μ; if D > μₘₐₓ washout occurs.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “μ is the change in cell number per hour”) reveals the misconception that μ is an absolute rate rather than a specific (per‑biomass) rate.
remember: Define specific growth rate (μ) and state its unit.
Explain why the Monod equation reduces to first‑order kinetics at low substrate concentrations.
A chemostat is operated at D = 0.8 h⁻¹ with μₘₐₓ = 0.6 h⁻¹. Predict the outcome and justify.

cards.title: A turbidostat is a continuous‑culture device that maintains a fixed microbial…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A turbidostat is a continuous‑culture device that maintains a fixed microbial cell concentration by regulating the medium inflow rate in response to real‑time optical density (OD) readings. A photometric sensor (usually at 600 nm) monitors culture turbidity; when OD exceeds a preset set‑point, a controller increases the pump speed, diluting the culture, and when OD falls below the set‑point the pump slows. Unlike a chemostat, where the dilution rate is fixed and the steady‑state cell density varies with the growth rate, a turbidostat keeps cell density constant while the dilution rate fluctuates to match the instantaneous specific growth rate (µ). This makes it ideal for studying organisms with variable µ, for selecting mutants with altered growth kinetics, and for maintaining high‑density cultures for product formation. The system comprises a sterile growth vessel, a peristaltic pump, an inline OD probe, a feedback controller (often PID), and an effluent line. Key relationships: OD ∝ cell dry weight (within linear range); dilution rate D = F/V (F = flow rate, V = working volume); at steady state in a turbidostat, D = µ because the controller forces the culture to the OD set‑point. The turbidostat therefore directly links the measurable optical signal to the physiological parameter µ, enabling dynamic experiments such as nutrient‑shift studies or adaptive laboratory evolution.
steps: A turbidostat maintains a constant cell density by continuously adjusting the dilution rate based on real‑time optical density measurements.
Here is why: the culture’s turbidity, measured at 600 nm, is directly proportional to biomass concentration within the linear range of the spectrophotometer.

When the OD rises above the user‑defined set‑point, the controller commands the peristaltic pump to increase fresh medium inflow, instantly diluting the culture and lowering OD; when OD falls below the set‑point, the…

This negative‑feedback loop forces the system to a dynamic steady state where the dilution rate D equals the instantaneous specific growth rate µ, because any deviation in µ immediately changes OD, which the controller…
The inline probe records OD every few seconds; a PID algorithm computes the required pump speed to minimise the error between measured OD and set‑point.
Second, as the culture grows, µ may change due to nutrient limitation, product inhibition, or genetic mutation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “pH”) reveals the misconception that turbidostats control chemical parameters rather than biomass; pH is typically monitored in a separate pH‑stat, not used for dilution control.
remember: What physical quantity does a turbidostat measure continuously to regulate culture density.
Explain why the dilution rate in a turbidostat is not constant, unlike in a chemostat.
A researcher sets a turbidostat target OD = 0.6 for Saccharomyces cerevisiae in a 1 L….

cards.title: Bioinformatics is the interdisciplinary field that develops and applies…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Bioinformatics is the interdisciplinary field that develops and applies computational methods to acquire, store, organise, analyse, and interpret biological data, especially nucleic‑acid and protein sequences. Its need arises from the exponential growth of sequence data generated by high‑throughput sequencing technologies; without algorithms, databases, and statistical models, the raw data would remain an unsearchable flood. The field integrates concepts from molecular biology (genes, genomes, expression), computer science (data structures, algorithms, machine learning), and statistics (probability models, hypothesis testing). Core sub‑concepts include primary databases (EMBL, GenBank, DDBJ) that archive raw sequences; secondary databases (SWISS‑PROT) that provide curated protein annotations; retrieval systems (Entrez, Taxonomy Browser) that enable querying; and analytical tools (BLAST, FASTA) for sequence alignment and homology inference. Genomics (structural and functional) uses these resources to map genomes, identify cDNA, ESTs, and STSs, while proteomics extends the analysis to protein structure, function, and expression profiles. The Human Genome Project exemplified the necessity of bioinformatics by coordinating international data sharing and annotation pipelines. DNA microarrays and SNP discovery further rely on bioinformatics for experimental design, data normalisation, and association studies. Thus, bioinformatics is the essential bridge that transforms raw molecular data into biological knowledge and biotechnological applications.
steps: Bioinformatics is the computational backbone that makes modern molecular biology possible because the volume of sequence data far exceeds human capacity to read it manually.
Here is why: first, high‑throughput sequencers now produce terabases of data per run, creating a data deluge that only automated pipelines can store and index.

Second, biological meaning resides in patterns — conserved motifs, open reading frames, regulatory elements — that require algorithmic detection such as dynamic‑programming alignment (Needleman‑Wunsch, Smith‑Waterman)…

Third, comparative genomics across species demands rapid retrieval of orthologous sequences, a task served by integrated systems like Entrez that link nucleotide, protein, taxonomy, and literature databases.
Fourth, functional annotation transfers knowledge from model organisms to humans; curated databases like SWISS‑PROT provide experimentally verified protein functions that propagate through homology.

Fifth, clinical applications — diagnosing genetic disorders, tracking pathogen evolution, designing vaccines — rely on real‑time variant calling and SNP annotation pipelines built on these foundations.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “both are equally curated”) reveals the misconception that all biological databases undergo the same level of expert validation; in reality, primary archives prioritise completeness and speed, whereas secondary databases prioritise…
remember: What is the primary reason bioinformatics became essential after the advent of high‑throughput sequencing.
Explain how a primary nucleotide database differs from a protein‑sequence annotation database in terms of content and curation level.
Evaluate the statement: “BLAST and FASTA are interchangeable because both perform sequence alignment.”.

cards.title: The European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) Nucleotide Sequence Database…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: The European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) Nucleotide Sequence Database, now operated by the European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL‑EBI) as part of the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA), is a primary, open‑access repository for DNA and RNA sequences. Together with GenBank (USA) and the DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ), it forms the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC). The three partners exchange data daily, ensuring that each accession number refers to the same sequence worldwide. An EMBL entry follows a structured flat‑file format containing mandatory fields: ID (entry identifier), AC (accession number with version), DE (description), KW (keywords), OS (organism species), OC (taxonomic classification), FH (feature table header), FT (feature table with coding regions, exons, etc.), and SQ (sequence data). Submissions are made via the Webin portal; each receives a unique accession (e.g., AB123456) and a version suffix (e.g.,.1) that increments on updates. EMBL provides retrieval through the EB‑eye search engine, programmatic APIs (REST, SOAP), and bulk FTP downloads. Because it is a primary database, it stores raw experimental sequences without curation, unlike secondary databases such as SWISS‑PROT that add functional annotation. The INSDC synchronization guarantees that a sequence deposited in EMBL appears in GenBank and DDBJ within 24 hours, enabling global reproducibility.
steps: EMBL (European Molecular Biology Laboratory) Nucleotide Sequence Database is a primary, comprehensive, freely accessible repository of DNA and RNA sequences that forms one‑third of the International Nucleotide Sequence…

Here is why this matters: first, the INSDC daily synchronization ensures that a sequence deposited in any partner receives the same accession number and version across all three, eliminating duplication and confusion.
Second, the structured flat‑file format — ID, AC, DE, KW, OS, OC, FH, FT, SQ — provides a machine‑readable standard that bioinformatics pipelines worldwide can parse reliably.
Third, the Webin submission portal enforces mandatory metadata (sample source, sequencing method, assembly level) so that downstream users can assess data quality.

Fourth, retrieval tools such as EB‑eye (web search), RESTful APIs (e.g., `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/api/fasta/AB123456`), and bulk FTP (`ftp://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/ena/sequence/`) give researchers…
Fifth, versioning (e.g., AB123456.1 → AB123456.2) tracks corrections without breaking existing references; superseded entries remain archived for provenance.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “EMBL stands for European Molecular Biology Library and belongs to the UN”) reveals the misconception that EMBL is a generic library rather than a specific laboratory‑run database, and confuses INSDC with unrelated international bodies.
remember: What does EMBL stand for and which international collaboration does it belong to.
Why is daily data exchange among EMBL, GenBank, and DDBJ essential for global bioinformatics research.
A student claims that EMBL stores protein sequences with functional annotations. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) is a division of the…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) is a division of the United States National Library of Medicine (NLM) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Established in 1988, it creates and maintains a suite of integrated databases — most notably GenBank (nucleotide sequences), PubMed (biomedical literature), Protein, Gene, Genome, Taxonomy, and dbSNP (single nucleotide polymorphisms). NCBI provides the Entrez retrieval system, which cross‑links these databases so a query on a gene name returns its sequence, literature, 3‑D structure, pathways, and taxonomic lineage in one view. It also hosts the BLAST family of local‑alignment tools for rapid sequence similarity searching. NCBI collaborates with the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA/EMBL‑EBI) and the DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ) as the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC), ensuring daily synchronization of submissions. For a Class 12 biotechnology student, NCBI is the primary portal to retrieve raw sequence data, annotate genes, explore variation, and perform comparative genomics — all essential for projects on gene cloning, phylogeny, or disease‑associated SNPs.
steps: NCBI is the central, freely accessible hub where every experimentally determined DNA, RNA, or protein sequence is deposited, curated, and linked to literature, taxonomy, and variation data.

Here is why: first, the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) guarantees that a sequence submitted to GenBank appears in EMBL‑EBI and DDBJ within 24 hours, so researchers worldwide see…

Second, NCBI’s Entrez system ties each sequence record to PubMed abstracts, Gene summaries, Protein 3‑D structures (via MMDB), and the Taxonomy Browser, turning a raw string of A/T/G/C into a biological story.
Third, the BLAST suite lets a student in Mumbai compare a 500‑bp PCR product against the entire non‑redundant database in seconds, returning hits ranked by statistical significance (E‑value).

Fourth, RefSeq provides a non‑redundant, curated reference set — each gene has a single, stable accession (e.g., NM_000518 for human HBB) — which is the gold standard for annotation and clinical reporting.
Fifth, dbSNP catalogs millions of human variants with allele frequencies from 1000 Genomes and gnomAD, enabling association studies.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “GenBank is a curated, non‑redundant reference set like RefSeq”) reveals the misconception that archival and reference databases are the same — confusing submitter‑supplied records with expert‑curated standards.
remember: What is the primary purpose of the NCBI GenBank database within the INSDC framework.
Why does NCBI maintain both GenBank and RefSeq, and how do their accession prefixes differ.
A student runs BLASTn on a 600‑bp query and obtains a hit with E‑value 2e‑45, 98 % identity over 580 bp. Evaluate whether this hit is biologically significant.

cards.title: The DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ) is one of the three primary members of the…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: The DNA Data Bank of Japan (DDBJ) is one of the three primary members of the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC), alongside EMBL‑EBI (Europe) and NCBI GenBank (USA). DDBJ receives, validates, archives, and distributes nucleotide sequence submissions (DNA, RNA, and associated metadata) from researchers globally. Each entry receives a unique accession number (e.g., “AB123456”) and is synchronised daily with its INSDC partners, ensuring identical content across all three mirrors. DDBJ also provides retrieval tools (ARSA, getentry) and links to protein databases such as UniProt/SWISS‑PROT. Its role is essential for comparative genomics, phylogenetic analysis, and functional annotation because it guarantees open, standardised, and version‑controlled access to raw sequence data.
steps: DDBJ is the Japanese pillar of the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration, guaranteeing that every DNA sequence deposited anywhere appears identically in all three partner banks.

Here is why: first, INSDC was created to avoid fragmentation — without a shared standard, a gene sequenced in Tokyo might carry a different identifier than the same gene deposited in Boston, breaking comparative studies.
Second, DDBJ assigns a stable accession number at submission, runs automated quality checks (vector contamination, format compliance), and then releases the record to the public domain.
Third, daily data exchange ensures that a researcher in Delhi querying GenBank sees the exact same sequence version as a colleague in Osaka querying DDBJ.
Fourth, DDBJ’s retrieval interfaces (ARSA for keyword search, getentry for direct accession fetch) mirror NCBI’s Entrez and EMBL’s Sequence Retrieval System, so learning one transfers to the others.
Fifth, cross‑references to UniProt/SWISS‑PROT let a student move from a nucleotide entry to its protein product in a single click, illustrating the central dogma flow from gene to protein.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “INSDC includes SWISS‑PROT”) reveals the misconception that protein databases are part of the nucleotide collaboration — SWISS‑PROT is a curated protein sequence resource, not a primary nucleotide archive.
remember: What is the full form of INSDC and which three databases constitute it.
Explain why a researcher in India would obtain the same nucleotide sequence whether they query DDBJ or NCBI GenBank.
A student claims that DDBJ accession numbers always start with “AB”. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: SWISSPROT (Swiss‑Prot Protein Knowledgebase) is a curated…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: SWISSPROT (Swiss‑Prot Protein Knowledgebase) is a curated, non‑redundant protein sequence database maintained by the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB) and the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI). Each entry contains a single, experimentally validated protein sequence with extensive annotation: protein name, gene name, organism, function, catalytic activity, pathway membership, post‑translational modifications, subcellular location, domain structure, and cross‑references to nucleotide databases (EMBL/GenBank/DDBJ), literature (PubMed), and structural databases (PDB). SWISSPROT is manually reviewed, ensuring high reliability; it is complemented by TrEMBL, an automatically annotated, larger supplement. The database uses a flat‑file format with standardized line codes (ID, AC, DE, GN, OS, OX, GN, DR, CC, SQ) enabling programmatic parsing. SWISSPROT serves as the primary reference for protein identification in proteomics, functional genomics, and comparative studies, and its accession numbers (e.g., P12345) are stable identifiers used worldwide.
steps: SWISSPROT is the gold‑standard, manually curated protein sequence database that provides a single, non‑redundant, experimentally validated entry per protein.

Here is why: manual curation removes errors and redundancy, giving researchers a trustworthy reference for functional annotation, unlike automatically generated databases that may contain fragments or mis‑annotations.

First, each protein sequence submitted to SWISSPROT is checked by expert biocurators who verify the amino‑acid chain against experimental evidence (e.g., Edman degradation, mass spectrometry) and literature.

Second, the entry is enriched with standardized annotation — function, catalytic activity, pathway, subcellular location, domains, and post‑translational modifications — using controlled vocabularies (Gene Ontology…
Third, stable accession numbers (e.g., P04637 for human p53) allow unambiguous citation across publications and databases.
Fourth, cross‑references (DR lines) link to nucleotide entries in EMBL/GenBank/DDBJ, structural data in PDB, and literature in PubMed, creating an integrated knowledge network.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “TrEMBL has more accurate sequences because it is larger”) reveals the misconception that database size equals quality — confusing quantity of entries with reliability of annotation.
remember: What is the primary distinguishing feature of SWISSPROT compared with TrEMBL.
Why are stable accession numbers (e.g., P12345) important in SWISSPROT.
Evaluate the statement: “Because SWISSPROT is smaller than TrEMBL, it is less useful for proteomics studies.”.

cards.title: GenBank is the primary nucleotide sequence database maintained by the National…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: GenBank is the primary nucleotide sequence database maintained by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) in the United States. It forms part of the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) together with EMBL‑EBI (Europe) and DDBJ (Japan); the three repositories exchange data daily so that each holds an identical, comprehensive collection. Each entry in GenBank receives a unique accession number (e.g., NM_001234) and contains the raw nucleotide sequence, annotated features (coding regions, promoters, introns), bibliographic references, and taxonomic lineage. The database supports flat‑file, FASTA, and ASN.1 formats and is searchable via Entrez, BLAST, and programmatic APIs (E‑utilities). GenBank is the foundation for downstream analyses such as gene prediction, phylogenetic reconstruction, primer design, and comparative genomics. Its curated subset, RefSeq, provides non‑redundant, standards‑based reference sequences for model organisms and human genes.
steps: GenBank is the central, publicly accessible nucleotide archive that synchronises daily with EMBL‑EBI and DDBJ to form a single global sequence pool.
Here is why: the INSDC agreement ensures that a sequence deposited in any one of the three databases appears in the others within 24 hours, giving researchers worldwide identical data.
First, every submission receives a permanent accession number that never changes, while version numbers track updates; this guarantees reproducibility in publications.

Second, the flat‑file format organises information hierarchically — LOCUS gives sequence length and molecule type, DEFINITION provides a concise description, FEATURES annotates genes, CDS, regulatory elements, and…
Third, Entrez integrates GenBank with PubMed, Taxonomy, and Protein databases, allowing a single query to pull nucleotide, protein, and literature links.
Fourth, BLAST uses GenBank as its default target database, so a student in Mumbai can paste a PCR product sequence and instantly see homologous genes from rice, human, or Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the accession number indicates the organism’s taxonomic ID”) reveals the misconception that accession numbers encode biological metadata rather than serving as stable database keys.
remember: What is the primary purpose of the accession number assigned to each GenBank entry.
Why does the INSDC daily data exchange between GenBank, EMBL‑EBI, and DDBJ matter for a researcher in India.
A student claims that the FEATURES table in a GenBank flat‑file contains only the coding sequence (CDS) coordinates. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Entrez is the integrated, text‑based search and retrieval system developed and…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Entrez is the integrated, text‑based search and retrieval system developed and maintained by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). It provides a single query interface that simultaneously accesses over 30 interlinked databases — including Nucleotide (GenBank, EMBL, DDBJ), Protein (UniProt/Swiss‑Prot, RefSeq), Gene, Genome, PubMed, Taxonomy, Structure, and others. Each database record carries a unique identifier (UID) and a set of standardized fields (accession, version, GI, organism, molecule type, feature table). Entrez uses a Boolean query language (AND, OR, NOT, field tags such as [Organism], [Gene Name], [Accession]) and supports history servers that store recent result sets for combination queries. The system returns results in multiple formats (FASTA, GenBank, XML, ASN.1) and offers programmatic access via the Entrez Programming Utilities (E‑utilities: ESearch, EFetch, ESummary, ELink, EInfo, EGQuery, ESpell). Entrez also powers the “LinkOut” service that connects a record to external resources (e.g., Ensembl, PDB, KEGG). In the ISC curriculum, Entrez is the primary retrieval tool taught for obtaining nucleotide and protein sequences, gene annotations, taxonomic lineages, and bibliographic references needed for downstream analyses such as BLAST, phylogeny, or primer design.
steps: Entrez is the single gateway that lets a biologist move from a gene name to its DNA, RNA, protein, and literature records without leaving the NCBI site.
Here is why: the system unifies over thirty databases through stable UIDs and pre‑computed links, so a query in one database instantly surfaces related entries in all others.

First, understand the query language — field tags such as `[Gene Name]`, `[Organism]`, `[Accession]`, and Boolean operators let you narrow a search from “insulin” (thousands of hits) to “human insulin mRNA RefSeq” (a…
Second, the History server assigns a `WebEnv` and `query_key` to every search; you can then run a second search and combine the two sets with `OR` or `AND` without re‑downloading data.

Third, each record can be fetched in FASTA for alignment, GenBank for annotation, or XML for programmatic parsing — choose the format that matches your downstream tool (BLAST, Clustal, primer design).

Fourth, E‑utilities expose the same functionality to scripts: `esearch` returns a `query_key`; `efetch` with that key streams the records; `elink` discovers neighbour records (e.g., from a nucleotide UID to its protein…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It caches the full FASTA files for faster download”) reveals the misconception that the History server holds sequence data rather than only lightweight query identifiers.
remember: What is the primary purpose of the Entrez History server in a multi‑step retrieval workflow.
A student writes the Entrez query `insulin[Gene Name] AND human[Organism]` in the Protein database and obtains zero hits. Explain why this happens and give the corrected query.
Compare the result formats FASTA, GenBank, and XML for a nucleotide record retrieved via….

cards.title: The NCBI Taxonomy Browser is a web‑based tool that presents the hierarchical…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: The NCBI Taxonomy Browser is a web‑based tool that presents the hierarchical classification of organisms stored in the NCBI Taxonomy database. Each taxon (species, genus, family, etc.) is assigned a stable, numeric Taxonomy Identifier (taxid). The browser displays the full lineage — from cellular organisms down to the requested rank — and provides direct hyperlinks to all sequence entries (Nucleotide, Protein, Gene, Genome, etc.) associated with that taxid. It integrates with ENTREZ: a taxonomy search in ENTREZ returns the taxid, which the Browser then uses to filter sequence databases, enabling cross‑database retrieval without ambiguous common names. The tool also supports downloading lineage tables, viewing taxonomic ranks, and navigating to sibling or child taxa. Because the taxonomy is curated by NCBI staff using phylogenetic evidence, it serves as the authoritative reference for organism‑centric queries in genomics, transcriptomics and proteomics pipelines.
steps: The Taxonomy Browser is the NCBI tool that lets you explore the hierarchical classification of organisms and directly link to all sequence data associated with any taxon.
Here is why: first, every organism in NCBI receives a permanent taxid, eliminating confusion from synonyms or common names.
Second, the browser shows the complete lineage — kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species — so you can see evolutionary context at a glance.
Third, each taxon page contains “Links” that launch pre‑filtered ENTREZ queries for Nucleotide, Protein, Gene, Genome, PubMed, etc., giving instant access to all molecular records for that taxon.
Fourth, you can download the lineage as a tab‑delimited file, which is essential for building custom reference databases or annotating metagenomic bins.
Consider a Class 12 project on “Comparative mitochondrial genomes of big cats”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It aligns sequences from different species”) reveals the misconception that the Taxonomy Browser performs sequence analysis — it only organizes and links taxonomic information.
remember: What is the primary purpose of the NCBI Taxonomy Browser.
Why is a stable Taxonomy ID (taxid) essential for retrieving sequence data across NCBI databases.
Assess the limitation of using common names instead of taxids in the Taxonomy Browser.

cards.title: Structural genomics is the systematic determination of the complete DNA…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Structural genomics is the systematic determination of the complete DNA sequence of an organism’s genome, including the assembly of chromosomes, identification of genes, regulatory elements, and repetitive regions. It produces a physical map — a linear order of nucleotides — and annotates features such as open reading frames, promoters, and non‑coding RNAs. Functional genomics builds on this scaffold to investigate how the genome operates: it measures gene expression (transcriptomics), studies protein‑DNA interactions, and links genotype to phenotype through techniques like DNA microarrays, RNA‑seq, and CRISPR screens. The two are interdependent; a high‑quality structural assembly is prerequisite for accurate expression quantification, while functional data refine structural annotation by confirming exon‑intron boundaries and revealing alternative splicing. Together they enable comparative genomics, evolutionary studies, and the identification of disease‑associated variants such as SNPs.
steps: The takeaway: Structural genomics provides the static blueprint of an organism’s DNA, while functional genomics reveals how that blueprint is dynamically read in different contexts.
Here is why: First, a genome must be sequenced and assembled into contiguous chromosomes; this is the structural foundation.
Second, annotation pipelines predict genes, regulatory motifs, and non‑coding elements on that scaffold.
Third, functional genomics interrogates the annotated genome by measuring which genes are transcribed, when, and at what level — using microarrays or RNA‑seq.
Fourth, integration of structural and functional data enables systems‑level insights such as pathway reconstruction or biomarker discovery.
Fifth, the Human Genome Project exemplifies this pipeline: a reference assembly (structural) followed by ENCODE and GTEx projects (functional) that mapped regulatory landscapes across tissues.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “structural genomics studies protein structures”) reveals the misconception that “structural” refers to protein 3D structure rather than genome architecture.
remember: Define structural genomics and functional genomics in one sentence each.
Why is a high‑quality structural genome assembly a prerequisite for reliable functional genomics analyses such as RNA‑seq.
Assess the limitation of using only ESTs for functional annotation of a newly sequenced genome.

cards.title: Complementary DNA (cDNA) is a double‑stranded DNA molecule synthesized in vitro…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Complementary DNA (cDNA) is a double‑stranded DNA molecule synthesized in vitro from a single‑stranded mRNA template by the action of reverse transcriptase. The first strand is generated using an oligo‑dT primer (or random hexamers) that anneals to the poly‑A tail of eukaryotic mRNA; reverse transcriptase then extends the primer, producing an RNA‑DNA hybrid. RNase H degrades the RNA strand, and DNA polymerase I (or a similar activity) synthesises the second DNA strand, yielding a double‑stranded cDNA that lacks introns, promoter sequences, and other non‑coding regions present in the original genomic DNA. cDNA therefore represents only the expressed portion of the genome (the transcriptome) at the time of extraction.
