First law – The mass m of a substance produced at an electrode is directly proportional to the total charge Q that passes: m = Z\,Q where Z (electrochemical equivalent) is the mass deposited per coulomb (kg C⁻¹). Since Q = I\,t (current I in amperes, time t in seconds), the law can be written m = Z\,I\,t. Second law – When the same quantity of charge passes through different electrolytes, the masses of substances liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights E (mass per mole of electrons, kg equiv⁻¹). Combining with the first law gives m = (E)/(F)\,Q where F = 96 485 C mol⁻¹ (Faraday constant) is the charge carried by one mole of electrons. Thus Z = E/F. The laws link three measurable quantities — current, time, and mass — to the stoichiometry of the redox half‑reaction (via E). They apply to any electrolytic cell, whether aqueous (e.g., CuSO₄) or molten (e.g., NaCl), and form the basis for calculating electroplating yields, battery capacities, and industrial chlorine‑alkali production.
steps: Faraday’s laws let you calculate exactly how much substance is produced or consumed at an electrode from the total electric charge passed.
Here is why: 1.
Charge‑mass proportionality – The first law states a linear link: double the charge, double the deposit.
This follows because each electron reduces one ion (or oxidises one species) in a fixed stoichiometric ratio. 2.
Universal constant – The Faraday constant F (96 485 C mol⁻¹) converts moles of electrons into coulombs, making the law independent of the electrolyte. 3.
Equivalent weight bridges chemistry and electricity – E (kg equiv⁻¹) translates the chemical stoichiometry (e.g., Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu, E = 63.5 g / 2 = 31.75 g equiv⁻¹) into an electrical quantity. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “mass is proportional to current only”) reveals the misconception that time is irrelevant, confusing instantaneous current with total charge.
remember: State Faraday’s first law of electrolysis and define each symbol with its SI unit.
Explain why Faraday’s second law uses equivalent weight rather than molar mass.
A student passes 1.2 A through a CuSO₄ solution for 15 min and obtains 0.38 g of copper. The theoretical mass from Faraday’s laws is 0.37 g. Evaluate the result.

cards.title: A battery is an assembly of one or more electrochemical cells that convert…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A battery is an assembly of one or more electrochemical cells that convert stored chemical energy directly into electrical energy through spontaneous redox reactions. In a primary cell the overall reaction is irreversible under normal conditions; the reactants are consumed and the cell cannot be recharged economically (e.g., Leclanché dry cell, zinc‑carbon, alkaline MnO₂, mercury oxide, silver oxide). In a secondary cell (rechargeable battery) the redox reaction is reversible: passing an external current in the opposite direction restores the original reactants (e.g., lead‑acid, nickel‑cadmium, nickel‑metal‑hydride, lithium‑ion). Key parameters: cell voltage (E_cell) = E°_cathode – E°_anode (V), capacity (C) = I × t (ampere‑hour, Ah), energy (W·h) = E_cell × C, energy density (Wh kg⁻¹ or Wh L⁻¹), power density (W kg⁻¹), cycle life (number of charge‑discharge cycles before capacity falls to 80 %). Internal resistance (r) causes voltage drop under load: V_terminal = E_cell – I·r. The electrochemical series (node 005) predicts feasible redox couples; the Nernst equation (node 006) gives voltage dependence on concentration; Faraday’s laws (node 008) relate charge passed to mass of active material transformed. Primary cells are chosen for long shelf‑life, low self‑discharge, and low cost; secondary cells for high energy density, high power, and many cycles. Environmental considerations (heavy‑metal toxicity, recycling) influence modern selection.
steps: Takeaway: A battery is a practical galvanic cell (or stack of cells) whose chemistry decides whether it is single‑use (primary) or rechargeable (secondary); the choice hinges on voltage, capacity, energy density, cycle…
Here is why: 1.
Primary cells rely on irreversible redox couples.

The common zinc‑carbon dry cell uses Zn(s) → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anode and 2MnO₂(s) + 2NH₄⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mn₂O₃(s) + 2NH₃ + H₂O at the cathode, giving ~1.5 V. Once MnO₂ is reduced, the reaction cannot be driven backward without…
Alkaline cells replace NH₄Cl with KOH, reducing internal resistance and raising capacity.
Mercury and silver‑oxide cells give very flat discharge curves (1.35 V, 1.55 V) used in hearing aids and cameras. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “primary cells have lower voltage”) reveals the misconception that voltage defines the category rather than reaction reversibility.
remember: State the fundamental chemical difference between a primary cell and a secondary cell.
A zinc‑carbon dry cell delivers a steady current of 0.15 A for 20 h before its voltage drops below the usable….
Evaluate the claim: “Lithium‑ion batteries are always superior to lead‑acid batteries for every application.”.

cards.title: Corrosion is the spontaneous, electro‑chemical deterioration of a metal caused…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Corrosion is the spontaneous, electro‑chemical deterioration of a metal caused by its reaction with the environment, most commonly oxygen and moisture. In aqueous media the metal surface behaves as a mixed galvanic cell: anodic sites where metal M → Mⁿ⁺ + n e⁻ (oxidation) and cathodic sites where O₂ + 2 H₂O + 4 e⁻ → 4 OH⁻ (reduction in neutral/alkaline) or 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → H₂ (in acidic). The overall reaction forms metal oxides/hydroxides (e.g., Fe₂O₃·xH₂O). The driving force is the difference in electrode potentials between the metal and the reduction couple, quantified by the Nernst equation. Corrosion rate can be expressed as mass loss per unit area per time or as corrosion current density (i_corr) using Faraday’s law: m = (I t M)/(n F). Prevention strategies interrupt the electrochemical circuit: (1) barrier protection — paints, varnishes, polymer coatings, metal plating (Sn, Cr, Zn) that physically separate metal from electrolyte; (2) sacrificial anode (cathodic protection) — attaching a more active metal (Mg, Zn, Al) that corrodes preferentially, supplying electrons to the protected structure; (3) impressed‑current cathodic protection — an external DC source forces the structure to be the cathode; (4) corrosion inhibitors — chemicals (phosphates, chromates, organic amines) that adsorb on the surface and raise the activation barrier for both anodic and cathodic reactions; (5) material selection — using alloys (stainless steel, Cu‑Ni) with passivating oxide films. The choice depends on environment (marine, industrial, soil), cost, and service life.
steps: Corrosion is an uncontrolled galvanic cell on a metal surface; the one thing to remember is that prevention always means breaking the electron flow between anodic and cathodic sites.
Here is why: the metal itself provides the conductive path for electrons, while water with dissolved ions supplies the electrolyte.
At anodic patches the metal oxidises, releasing electrons that travel through the bulk metal to cathodic patches where oxygen (or H⁺) is reduced.
The resulting metal ions combine with OH⁻ to form porous rust that offers no protection.
First, recognise the two half‑reactions.
For iron in neutral water: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2 e⁻ (E° = –0.44 V) and O₂ + 2 H₂O + 4 e⁻ → 4 OH⁻ (E° = +0.40 V).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ directly) reveals the misconception that corrosion is a simple direct combination, ignoring the electrochemical electron‑transfer steps that define the galvanic cell on the metal surface.
remember: Write the balanced overall corrosion reaction for iron in neutral aqueous solution, identifying the anodic and cathodic half‑reactions.
Explain why zinc protects iron when used as a galvanised coating, even if the coating is scratched.
A student claims that “cathodic protection always requires an external power source.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: The rate of a chemical reaction quantifies the speed at which reactants are…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The rate of a chemical reaction quantifies the speed at which reactants are consumed or products are formed. For a general reaction aA + bB → cC + dD, the rate r is defined as r = -(1)/(a)(d[A])/(dt) = -(1)/(b)(d[B])/(dt) = (1)/(c)(d[C])/(dt) = (1)/(d)(d[D])/(dt) where [X] denotes molar concentration (mol L⁻¹) of species X and t is time (s). The negative signs for reactants ensure a positive rate value. Two representations are used: Average rate over a finite interval Δ t: r_avg = -(1)/(a)(Δ[A])/(Δ t). Instantaneous rate at a specific time: the derivative r = -(1)/(a)(d[A])/(dt), obtained graphically as the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve. The SI unit of rate is mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. This definition links stoichiometry to measurable concentration changes and provides the foundation for rate laws, order, and molecularity discussed in later nodes.
steps: The rate of reaction is the speedometer of chemistry — it tells how fast concentrations change per unit time.
Here is why: (1) Reactions occur by collisions; the frequency of effective collisions per second appears as a concentration change.
(2) Stoichiometry forces a fixed ratio between the disappearance of reactants and appearance of products, so a single rate value describes the whole reaction.
(3) Average rate gives an overall picture over a period, while instantaneous rate captures the exact speed at a moment, just as a speedometer shows instantaneous velocity.
(4) Graphically, concentration–time curves let us read both rates: the secant slope for average, the tangent slope for instantaneous.
(5) The sign convention (negative for reactants) guarantees a positive rate, avoiding confusion.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., r = -(d[N_2])/(dt) = -(d[H_2])/(dt) = (d[NH_3])/(dt) ) reveals the misconception that stoichiometric coefficients are ignored, treating all species as changing at the same molar rate.
remember: Define the rate of reaction for the reaction N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) → 2NH_3(g) in terms of concentration changes of each species.
Explain why the rate of reaction is expressed as a positive quantity even though reactant concentrations decrease with time.
A student plots concentration of reactant A versus time for a reaction and draws a secant line between t=0 and t=100 s, then a tangent at t=50 s. Which slope corresponds to the….

cards.title: The law of mass action states that for an elementary reaction the rate is…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The law of mass action states that for an elementary reaction the rate is directly proportional to the product of the molar concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced elementary equation. For a generic elementary step ν_A A + ν_B B → products the instantaneous rate r is r = k [A]^ν_A[B]^ν_B where k is the rate constant (temperature‑dependent but concentration‑independent), [A] and [B] are molar concentrations (mol L⁻¹), and ν_A,ν_B are the stoichiometric numbers (dimensionless). The law applies strictly to elementary reactions — single‑step processes whose molecularity equals the sum of the stoichiometric coefficients. For overall (multi‑step) reactions the observed rate law may have different orders; the law of mass action then serves only as a starting point for proposing a mechanism. The relationship between the law and the rate expression is foundational: the rate expression (or rate law) is the mathematical form derived from the law of mass action for a given elementary step. Units of k follow from the overall order n = Σ ν_i: [k] = mol^1-n\,L^n-1\,s^-1. This node connects the qualitative idea that “more reactant → faster reaction” to a quantitative rate law used in subsequent nodes (effect of concentration, order and molecularity, integrated rate equations).
steps: The law of mass action gives a direct, quantitative link between reactant concentrations and the instantaneous rate of an elementary reaction.

Here is why: the rate of an elementary step is proportional to the frequency of effective collisions, and collision frequency is proportional to the product of the reactant concentrations raised to their stoichiometric…
First, consider an elementary bimolecular reaction A + B → products.
In a 1 L vessel at 298 K, if [A]=0.10\ mol L^-1 and [B]=0.20\ mol L^-1, the collision frequency (and thus the rate) is proportional to (0.10)(0.20)=0.020.

Doubling [A] to 0.20 mol L⁻¹ doubles the product to 0.040, so the rate doubles — a direct consequence of the law. Second, for a termolecular elementary step 2A + B → products the rate law becomes r = k[A]^2[B].
The exponent 2 reflects the need for two A molecules to collide simultaneously with one B molecule; the probability of such a three‑body encounter scales with [A]^2[B].
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “rate = k[A][B] for any reaction”) reveals the misconception that stoichiometric coefficients always equal reaction orders, ignoring the elementary‑step requirement.
remember: State the law of mass action for an elementary reaction ν_A A + ν_B B → products.
Explain why the law of mass action cannot be applied directly to the overall reaction 2NO_2 + F_2 → 2NO_2F to obtain its rate law.
Evaluate the statement: “For a first‑order elementary decomposition A → products, the rate constant k has units of mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.”.

cards.title: The effect of concentration on reaction rate is quantified by the rate law
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The effect of concentration on reaction rate is quantified by the rate law (or rate equation). For a reaction aA + bB → products, the instantaneous rate r is expressed as r = k [A]^x [B]^y where [A] and [B] are molar concentrations (mol L⁻¹), x and y are the orders with respect to A and B (determined experimentally, not necessarily equal to stoichiometric coefficients), and k is the rate constant at a given temperature. The overall order is n = x + y. The rate law shows that rate is directly proportional to each reactant concentration raised to its order. If x = 1, doubling [A] doubles the rate; if x = 2, doubling [A] quadruples the rate. The units of k depend on overall order: for order n, k has units mol^1-n\,L^n-1\,s^-1. This node connects the qualitative law of mass action (rate ∝ product of active masses) to the quantitative rate law used for kinetic calculations.
steps: The rate of a chemical reaction changes with reactant concentrations according to the rate law, where each concentration is raised to a power equal to its order.

Here is why: the law of mass action states that rate is proportional to the product of active masses; the rate law makes this proportionality exact by introducing a constant k and experimentally determined exponents.
First, write the generic rate law r = k[A]^x[B]^y.
Second, recognise that the orders x, y are found by measuring initial rates while varying one reactant at a time — a method called the initial rates method.
Third, determine the units of k by substituting the units of rate (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹) and concentration (mol L⁻¹) into the rate law; for overall order n, k carries units mol^1-n\,L^n-1\,s^-1.
Fourth, apply the law: for a first‑order dependence on A, halving [A] halves the rate; for a second‑order dependence, halving [A] reduces the rate to one‑quarter.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., r = k[A]^a[B]^b using stoichiometric coefficients) reveals the misconception that reaction order equals stoichiometry — orders are experimental, not theoretical.
remember: State the general form of the rate law for a reaction involving reactants A and B, defining each symbol.
For a reaction that is first order in A and zero order in B, how does the rate change if [A] is tripled and [B] is halved.
Evaluate the statement: “If a reaction is second order overall, its rate constant k has units of L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.”.

cards.title: A rate expression (or rate law) is a mathematical equation that relates the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A rate expression (or rate law) is a mathematical equation that relates the instantaneous rate of a chemical reaction to the molar concentrations of the reactants, each raised to a power called the order with respect to that reactant. For a general reaction aA + bB → products the differential rate law is written as rate = -(1)/(a)(d[A])/(dt) = -(1)/(b)(d[B])/(dt) = k[A]^m[B]^n where - k is the rate constant (temperature‑dependent, units vary with overall order), - m and n are the orders with respect to A and B (determined experimentally, not necessarily equal to stoichiometric coefficients), - the overall order is m+n. The rate expression follows from the law of mass action (node) and the observed effect of concentration (node). It is a differential equation; its integrated forms (zero‑, first‑, second‑order) are treated in later nodes. The rate constant k carries the temperature dependence described by the Arrhenius equation (node). Units of k are derived so that the rate always has SI units of mol L^-1s^-1.
steps: The rate expression is the quantitative bridge that turns the qualitative observation “rate increases with concentration” into a precise predictive tool.
Supporting argument 1 – From proportionality to power law: The law of mass action states that rate is proportional to the product of reactant concentrations.
Experiments show the proportionality is not always linear; each concentration may be raised to an empirical power (order).
Supporting argument 2 – Rate constant encapsulates temperature: All temperature effects are collected into k; at a fixed temperature k is constant, allowing concentration‑only studies.
Supporting argument 3 – Orders are experimental: Stoichiometric coefficients do not dictate orders; they must be found by the method of initial rates or other kinetic techniques.
Supporting argument 4 – Units of k reveal overall order: By demanding that rate has units mol L^-1s^-1, the units of k adjust (e.g., s^-1 for first order, L mol^-1s^-1 for second order).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ m and n are the stoichiometric coefficients”) reveals the misconception that the balanced equation dictates the rate law, confusing stoichiometry with kinetics.
remember: Define the term “rate law” and state the physical meaning of each symbol in the expression rate = k[A]^m[B]^n.
For the reaction A + 2B → C, the rate law is found to be rate =….
Two students propose rate laws for the same reaction: Student X writes rate =….

cards.title: Order of reaction is the sum of the powers to which the concentration terms are…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Order of reaction is the sum of the powers to which the concentration terms are raised in the experimentally determined rate law. For a reaction aA + bB → products with rate law rate=k[A]^m[B]^n, the overall order is m+n. The individual orders m and n are obtained from concentration‑rate data and need not equal the stoichiometric coefficients a and b. Order can be zero, fractional, or negative and is an empirical quantity. Molecularity applies only to an elementary (single‑step) reaction and is defined as the number of reactant molecules (or ions, atoms) that simultaneously collide to form products. It is always a positive integer (1, 2, or rarely 3). For an elementary step, molecularity equals the order of that step, but for a complex (multi‑step) reaction the overall order is the sum of orders of the rate‑determining step and any preceding equilibria, and it generally differs from the molecularities of the individual steps. Key relationships: - Rate law → order (experimental). - Elementary step → molecularity = order of that step. - Complex mechanism → overall order ≠ sum of molecularities; only the rate‑determining step’s molecularity directly influences the observed rate law. SI units: rate constant k has units mol^1-(m+n)L^m+n-1s^-1 so that rate (mol L^-1s^-1) is dimensionally consistent.
steps: Takeaway: Order is an experimentally determined exponent sum in the rate law, while molecularity is the integer count of reactant particles in a single elementary collision; they coincide only for elementary reactions.
Here is why: In the previous node you learned to write a rate expression rate=k[A]^m[B]^n.
The exponents m and n are found by varying concentrations and measuring initial rates — this is the method of initial rates.
Adding them gives the overall order.
Because these exponents come from data, they can be fractions (e.g., ½ order in H_2 for the H_2+Br_2 reaction) or even negative (inhibition).
Now consider a reaction that occurs in one step: NO + O_3 → NO_2 + O_2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “order equals the stoichiometric coefficients in the balanced equation”) reveals the misconception that the balanced equation directly gives the rate law, confusing stoichiometry with kinetics.
remember: Define the term “order of reaction” and state how it is obtained experimentally.
A reaction has the rate law rate=k[A]^1/2[B]^2. What is its overall order? Can this reaction be elementary? Justify.
For the elementary reaction 2NO + O_2 → 2NO_2, write the rate law and state its molecularity and order.

cards.title: The integrated rate equation is the mathematical expression obtained by…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The integrated rate equation is the mathematical expression obtained by integrating the differential rate law, giving concentration of a reactant as an explicit function of time. For a zero‑order reaction the rate is independent of concentration: rate = k₀, so integration yields [A]_t = [A]_0 - k_0 t. For a first‑order reaction the rate is proportional to the reactant concentration: rate = k₁[A]; integration gives ([A]_0/[A]_t) = k_1 t or [A]_t = [A]_0 e^-k_1 t. In both cases k is the rate constant with units that make the equation dimensionally consistent (M s⁻¹ for zero order, s⁻¹ for first order). These equations connect the experimentally measurable concentration‑time data to the kinetic parameters (order, rate constant) and provide the basis for half‑life calculations (next node). They also enable graphical tests: a plot of [A] vs t is linear for zero order, while [A] vs t is linear for first order.
steps: The integrated rate equations for zero‑ and first‑order reactions let us calculate concentration at any time directly from the rate constant and initial concentration.
Here is why: the differential rate law tells us how fast concentration changes at an instant, but experiments give us concentration after a finite time.
Integration bridges that gap. Consider a zero‑order decomposition of ammonia on a hot platinum surface.
The rate law is -d[NH_3]/dt = k_0.
Integrating from t=0 (where [NH_3]=[NH_3]_0) to a generic time t gives [NH_3]_t = [NH_3]_0 - k_0 t. The concentration falls linearly; when it reaches zero the reaction stops.
The slope of a [NH_3] vs t plot is -k_0 and the intercept is [NH_3]_0.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “k_0 has units s⁻¹”) reveals the misconception that all rate constants share the same unit, confusing zero‑order with first‑order kinetics.
remember: Write the integrated rate equation for a zero‑order reaction and state the units of its rate constant.
A reaction follows first‑order kinetics with k = 2.5 × 10^-3\,s^-1. If the initial concentration is 0.80 M, what is the concentration after 200 s.
Given the following concentration‑time data for a reaction, decide whether it is zero‑ or first‑order and justify your choice. | t (s) | [A] (M) | |------|--------| | 0 | 0.100 |….

cards.title: Half‑life (t½) is the time required for the concentration (or amount) of a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Half‑life (t½) is the time required for the concentration (or amount) of a reactant to decrease to one‑half of its initial value. For a zero‑order reaction, t½ = [A]₀ / (2k) and depends on the initial concentration [A]₀. For a first‑order reaction, t½ = ln 2 / k, which is independent of [A]₀. The concept links directly to the integrated rate equations: the zero‑order integrated law [A] = [A]₀ – kt and the first‑order integrated law ln([A]₀/[A]) = kt. Half‑life provides a convenient experimental handle to determine the rate constant k and to classify reaction order. It is expressed in seconds (s) or minutes (min) in SI units.
steps: The half‑life of a first‑order reaction is constant, whereas for a zero‑order reaction it varies with the initial concentration.
Here is why: starting from the integrated rate law for a first‑order process, ln([A]₀/[A]) = kt, set [A] = [A]₀/2 to obtain ln 2 = k t½, giving t½ = ln 2/k.
Because ln 2 and k are constants, t½ does not contain [A]₀.
For a zero‑order reaction the integrated law is [A] = [A]₀ – kt; substituting [A] = [A]₀/2 yields [A]₀/2 = [A]₀ – k t½, so t½ = [A]₀/(2k).
Thus t½ is directly proportional to the starting concentration.
Consider a laboratory experiment where 0.10 M of a reactant decays to 0.05 M in 200 s. If the same reaction is repeated with 0.20 M and the half‑life remains 200 s, the reaction is first‑order.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., t½ = [A]₀/(2k) with unit mol L⁻¹ s) reveals the misconception of confusing zero‑order and first‑order half‑life formulas.
remember: State the half‑life expression for a first‑order reaction and its SI unit.
Explain why the half‑life of a zero‑order reaction depends on the initial concentration while that of a first‑order reaction does not.
A reaction shows half‑lives of 50 s, 100 s, and 200 s when started with initial concentrations 0.10 M, 0.20 M, and 0.40 M respectively. Determine the reaction order.

cards.title: The effect of temperature on reaction rate is quantified by the temperature…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The effect of temperature on reaction rate is quantified by the temperature dependence of the rate constant k. According to collision theory, only molecules with kinetic energy ≥ activation energy Eₐ can react. As temperature rises, the Maxwell‑Boltzmann distribution shifts: a larger fraction of molecules possess energy ≥ Eₐ, increasing the frequency of effective collisions. This exponential relationship is described by the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(–Eₐ/RT), where A is the pre‑exponential factor (frequency of collisions with proper orientation), R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. The temperature coefficient (often Q₁₀) expresses how many times the rate increases for a 10 °C rise; for many reactions Q₁₀ ≈ 2–3. Temperature also influences A slightly, but the dominant effect is through the exponential term. Understanding this links the qualitative observation “heat speeds up reactions” to the quantitative framework used in the next node (Arrhenius equation).
steps: Increasing temperature increases the rate constant because a larger fraction of molecules possess energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
Here is why: at a given temperature, molecular speeds follow a Maxwell‑Boltzmann distribution.
Only molecules with kinetic energy ≥ Eₐ can react upon collision.
Raising T broadens the distribution and shifts its peak to higher energies, dramatically increasing the high‑energy tail.
Consider a typical Indian kitchen: dough ferments faster in summer (≈30 °C) than in winter (≈15 °C) because yeast enzymes work more rapidly at higher temperatures — until they denature.
The quantitative link is the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(–Eₐ/RT).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “temperature has no effect on k”) reveals the misconception that rate constant is independent of temperature — confusing rate constant with rate law concentration terms.
remember: State the effect of increasing temperature on the rate constant of a reaction.
Explain why a 10 °C rise in temperature roughly doubles the rate of many reactions.
A student claims that all reactions proceed faster at higher temperature. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The Arrhenius equation quantitatively describes the temperature dependence of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The Arrhenius equation quantitatively describes the temperature dependence of the rate constant k for a chemical reaction. It is expressed as k = A exp(–Eₐ / (R T)) where A (pre‑exponential factor) reflects the frequency of collisions with proper orientation, Eₐ (activation energy) is the minimum energy required for a successful reaction, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the universal gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature in kelvin. Taking natural logarithms gives the linear form ln k = ln A – Eₐ / (R T) which allows determination of Eₐ and A from a plot of ln k versus 1/T. The equation connects the macroscopic observable k to molecular‑level energy barriers and collision statistics, and it underpins the temperature‑effect concepts introduced in the previous node (Effect of temperature).
steps: The Arrhenius equation is the quantitative bridge that turns the qualitative statement “rate increases with temperature” into a precise mathematical relationship.
Here is why: the rate constant k grows exponentially as the thermal energy RT becomes comparable to the activation barrier Eₐ.
First, consider a simple gas‑phase reaction A → B. Molecules must collide with at least Eₐ joules per mole to react.
Only a fraction f = exp(–Eₐ/(RT)) of collisions possess this energy (Boltzmann distribution).
Multiplying the total collision frequency Z by f and a steric factor p gives k = pZ exp(–Eₐ/(RT)).
The product pZ is the pre‑exponential factor A. Second, taking natural logs yields ln k = ln A – Eₐ/(R)·(1/T).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving Eₐ in kJ mol⁻¹ without conversion) reveals the misconception that units can be mixed in the exponent; the exponent must be dimensionless, so Eₐ and R T must share the same energy unit.
remember: Write the Arrhenius equation in its exponential form and list each symbol with its SI unit.
A reaction has k = 2.5 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 300 K and k = 1.2 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ at 320 K. Calculate the activation energy Eₐ in kJ mol⁻¹.
Given the Arrhenius plot (ln k vs 1/T) for a reaction yields a straight line of slope –1.25 × 10⁴ K and intercept 23.0. Determine Eₐ (kJ mol⁻¹) and A (s⁻¹).

cards.title: Transition elements (d‑block elements) are those in which the (n‑1)d subshell…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Transition elements (d‑block elements) are those in which the (n‑1)d subshell is progressively filled across a period while the ns subshell contains one or two electrons. The general electronic configuration is (n‑1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻². For the first transition series (n = 4) this reads 3d¹⁻¹⁰ 4s⁰⁻². Two notable exceptions arise from the extra stability of half‑filled and fully‑filled d subshells: chromium (Cr) adopts [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ instead of 3d⁴ 4s², and copper (Cu) adopts [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ instead of 3d⁹ 4s². Similar anomalies occur in the second (4d) and third (5d) series (e.g., Mo, Ag, Au). The (n‑1)d electrons are less effectively shielded than ns electrons, so the effective nuclear charge felt by d electrons increases across the series, causing a gradual contraction in atomic radii (the “d‑block contraction”). This configuration underpins the variable oxidation states (from +2 to the group number), formation of coloured ions (d‑d transitions), paramagnetism (unpaired d electrons), and catalytic activity (ability to adopt multiple oxidation states). The node does not cover magnetic moment calculations, compound structures, or lanthanoid/actinoid chemistry — those belong to sibling nodes.
steps: The one thing to remember: In transition elements the (n‑1)d orbitals are close enough in energy to the ns orbital that electrons occupy them before the ns orbital is completely filled, producing the characteristic…
Here is why: 1.
Energy ordering – For n = 4, the 3d and 4s orbitals are nearly degenerate.
The 4s orbital fills first (K, Ca) because it is slightly lower in energy when empty.
Once 4s has two electrons, the increasing nuclear charge pulls the 3d orbital down, so subsequent electrons enter 3d. 2.
Exchange energy and symmetry – A half‑filled d⁵ or fully‑filled d¹⁰ subshell gains extra stability from maximum exchange energy and symmetrical electron distribution.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s¹) reveals the misconception that the half‑filled d subshell always forces a 4s¹ configuration, ignoring that Mn already has a half‑filled d⁵ with a filled 4s², which is lower in energy.
remember: Write the ground‑state electronic configuration of a neutral manganese (Mn) atom (Z = 25) using noble‑gas core notation.
Explain why chromium (Cr, Z = 24) adopts the configuration [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ instead of the expected [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
Evaluate the statement: “All first‑row transition metal ions lose their 4s electrons before any 3d electrons.” Provide a counter‑example if the statement is false.

cards.title: Transition elements are d‑block elements (Groups 3–12) whose atoms or common…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Transition elements are d‑block elements (Groups 3–12) whose atoms or common ions have an incomplete d‑subshell (d¹–d⁹). Their general electronic configuration is (n‑1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻². Key properties arise from the partially filled d‑orbitals: 1. Variable oxidation states – electrons can be lost from both ns and (n‑1)d orbitals, giving multiple stable oxidation numbers (e.g., Mn: +2, +3, +4, +6, +7). 2. Formation of coloured ions/compounds – d‑d transitions absorb visible light; the colour observed is the complementary colour of the absorbed wavelength. 3. Paramagnetism – unpaired d‑electrons give a magnetic moment μ = √[n(n+2)] BM (Bohr magnetons), where n = number of unpaired electrons. 4. Catalytic activity – ability to adopt multiple oxidation states and provide vacant d‑orbitals for substrate adsorption (e.g., Fe in Haber process, V₂O₅ in Contact process). 5. Complex formation – small size, high charge density and vacant d‑orbitals allow coordination with ligands, giving octahedral, tetrahedral or square‑planar geometries. 6. High melting/boiling points and metallic bonding – strong metallic bonds due to delocalised d‑electrons. These properties are inter‑linked: the same incomplete d‑subshell that permits variable oxidation states also enables d‑d transitions, paramagnetism and ligand coordination.
steps: The one thing to remember: All characteristic properties of transition elements — variable oxidation states, colour, paramagnetism, catalysis and complex formation — stem directly from their incomplete d‑subshell.
Here is why: 1.
Electron availability – Because (n‑1)d and ns orbitals are close in energy, electrons can be removed from either, giving multiple oxidation states.

For example, manganese loses 2 e⁻ from 4s² to give Mn²⁺ (d⁵), then further d‑electrons to reach Mn⁷⁺ in MnO₄⁻. 2. d‑d transitions – In an octahedral field the five d‑orbitals split into t₂g (lower) and e_g (higher).
An electron can jump from t₂g to e_g by absorbing a photon of visible light; the complementary colour is observed.
Cu²⁺ (d⁹) absorbs orange‑red, so its solutions appear blue. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “copper is not a transition element because it has a full d‑subshell in Cu⁺”) reveals the misconception that the elemental ground state alone decides the classification, ignoring the cationic configurations that define transition…
remember: State the general electronic configuration of transition elements and identify which d‑block element in the first series does not qualify as a transition element according to the….
Explain why aqueous Cu²⁺ solutions are blue while Zn²⁺ solutions are colourless, using the concept of d‑d transitions.
Evaluate the statement: “All transition‑metal ions are paramagnetic.” Provide a counter‑example and the reasoning.

cards.title: Potassium permanganate is an ionic compound with formula KMnO₄…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Potassium permanganate is an ionic compound with formula KMnO₄, composed of monovalent potassium cations (K⁺) and tetrahedral permanganate anions (MnO₄⁻). In the permanganate ion, manganese attains a formal oxidation state of +7, giving it a d⁰ electron configuration (3d⁰4s⁰). The Mn–O bonds are best described as covalent with significant π‑bonding arising from overlap of filled O 2p orbitals with empty Mn 3d orbitals, resulting in four equivalent Mn–O bond lengths of approximately 1.63 Å. The ion adopts a regular tetrahedral geometry (point group T_d) with O–Mn–O angles of 109.5°. In the solid state, KMnO₄ crystallises in an orthorhombic lattice (space group Pnma) where each K⁺ is coordinated by eight oxygen atoms from surrounding MnO₄⁻ tetrahedra. The compound is diamagnetic because the Mn(VII) centre has no unpaired electrons. Its intense purple colour originates from a ligand‑to‑metal charge‑transfer (LMCT) transition (O 2p → Mn 3d) rather than d‑d transitions, which are absent in a d⁰ system. The structure underpins its strong oxidising ability: the high oxidation state and the stability of the tetrahedral MnO₄⁻ ion make electron gain (reduction to MnO₂, Mn²⁺, etc.) thermodynamically favourable.
steps: The structure of potassium permanganate is defined by a tetrahedral permanganate ion (MnO₄⁻) paired with potassium cations in an orthorhombic lattice.

Here is why: the manganese atom in KMnO₄ is in the +7 oxidation state, leaving a d⁰ configuration; with no d‑electrons, the ion cannot undergo d‑d transitions, so its intense purple colour must arise from a…
Consider the oxidation‑state calculation: let x be the oxidation number of Mn; the overall charge of MnO₄⁻ is –1, each oxygen is –2, so x + 4(–2) = –1 → x = +7.
This +7 state is the highest known for manganese and forces the four Mn–O bonds to be equivalent, giving a regular tetrahedron (VSEPR: four bonding pairs, zero lone pairs).
The Mn–O distance (~1.63 Å) is shorter than a typical Mn–O single bond because of π‑bonding from filled O 2p orbitals into empty Mn 3d orbitals.
In the solid, each K⁺ is eight‑coordinate, surrounded by oxygen atoms from eight different MnO₄⁻ tetrahedra, forming an orthorhombic Pnma lattice.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., +6) reveals the misconception that the permanganate ion carries a –2 charge like chromate (CrO₄²⁻), ignoring that KMnO₄ contains MnO₄⁻, not MnO₄²⁻.
remember: What is the oxidation state of manganese in potassium permanganate (KMnO₄).
Explain why the permanganate ion (MnO₄⁻) is diamagnetic.
Evaluate the statement: “The purple colour of KMnO₄ is due to d‑d transitions in the Mn(VII) centre.”.

cards.title: The permanganate ion (MnO₄⁻) adopts a tetrahedral molecular geometry.
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The permanganate ion (MnO₄⁻) adopts a tetrahedral molecular geometry. Manganese is in the +7 oxidation state (d⁰ configuration) and forms four σ‑bonds with four oxygen atoms, with no lone pairs on the central metal. According to VSEPR theory, four bonding domains (steric number = 4) arrange themselves to minimise repulsion, giving a tetrahedral electron‑domain geometry and a tetrahedral molecular shape. The hybridisation of manganese is sp³, producing four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals that overlap with oxygen p‑orbitals. All O–Mn–O bond angles are 109.5°, and the ion possesses Td symmetry. This geometry is isostructural with other tetrahedral oxoanions such as chromate (CrO₄²⁻) and sulfate (SO₄²⁻). The tetrahedral shape influences the ion’s reactivity, colour, and crystal packing in solid KMnO₄.
steps: The permanganate ion is tetrahedral because manganese(vii) has four bonding pairs and zero lone pairs, giving a steric number of four.
Here is why: first, the d⁰ configuration of Mn(VII) means no d‑electrons occupy the valence shell, so only the four Mn–O σ‑bonds determine geometry.
Second, VSEPR predicts that four electron domains adopt a tetrahedral arrangement to minimise repulsion.
Third, sp³ hybridisation of the manganese atom creates four equivalent orbitals directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron.
Fourth, experimental evidence (X‑ray diffraction, IR/Raman spectra) confirms equal Mn–O bond lengths and 109.5° angles.
Fifth, this geometry is shared by other d⁰ tetraoxoanions, reinforcing the predictive power of the model.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “square planar”) reveals the misconception that transition‑metal centres always adopt square planar geometry due to d‑orbital involvement, ignoring the d⁰ configuration and VSEPR rules.
remember: What is the molecular geometry of the permanganate ion (MnO₄⁻).
Using VSEPR theory, explain why MnO₄⁻ adopts a tetrahedral shape rather than a square planar shape.
A student claims that the permanganate ion has a square planar geometry because manganese is a transition metal. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The “uses” of potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) and potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇)…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The “uses” of potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) and potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇) refer to their practical applications as strong oxidising agents, derived from their high oxidation states (Mn⁺⁷, Cr⁺⁶) and characteristic tetrahedral or dimeric tetrahedral structures. In acidic medium, MnO₄⁻ gains five electrons to become colourless Mn²⁺, while Cr₂O₇²⁻ gains six electrons to form green Cr³⁺. These predictable electron‑transfer stoichiometries make them ideal for redox titrations, where the colour of the permanganate ion itself serves as a self‑indicator. Beyond analysis, KMnO₄ oxidises organic compounds (e.g., alcohols, alkenes) and is employed as a disinfectant in water treatment and wound care because it destroys microbes by oxidising cellular components. K₂Cr₂O₇ is central to the leather‑tanning industry, where Cr⁶⁺ is reduced to Cr³⁺, cross‑linking collagen fibres; it also oxidises primary alcohols to aldehydes and carboxylic acids (Jones reagent) and is used in the manufacture of pigments and corrosion inhibitors. The uses therefore stem directly from the oxidising power imparted by their electronic structures and are limited only by side reactions (e.g., chloride oxidation by permanganate) or toxicity (chromate(VI) carcinogenicity).
steps: The primary use of potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate in the laboratory is as reliable oxidising agents in redox titrations because their intense colours provide a clear, self‑indicating endpoint and their…
Here is why: 1.
Oxidising strength: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ has E° = +1.51 V and Cr₂O₇²⁻/Cr³⁺ has E° = +1.33 V, both high enough to oxidise common analytes like Fe²⁺, H₂O₂, and oxalic acid. 2.
Self‑indication: The deep purple of MnO₄⁻ disappears upon reduction to colourless Mn²⁺; the orange of Cr₂O₇²⁻ fades to green Cr³⁺.
No external indicator is needed, reducing error. 3.
Predictable electron change: Each permanganate ion accepts exactly five electrons; each dichromate ion accepts six electrons.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Mn is +4”) reveals the misconception that the oxidation state follows the oxide MnO₂, ignoring the overall charge balance of the permanganate ion.
remember: State the oxidation state of manganese in KMnO₄ and chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇.
Explain why potassium permanganate acts as a self‑indicator in redox titrations.
A student claims that potassium dichromate can be used to test for reducing sugars in urine because it turns green on reduction. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇, is an ionic compound composed of two potassium…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇, is an ionic compound composed of two potassium cations (K⁺) and one dichromate anion (Cr₂O₇²⁻). The dichromate anion contains two chromium(VI) centres, each in a d⁰ electronic configuration (Cr: [Ar] 3d⁰ 4s⁰). Each Cr(VI) is tetrahedrally coordinated by four oxygen atoms: three terminal Cr=O bonds (bond order ≈2, length ≈1.66 Å) and one bridging Cr–O–Cr bond (bond order ≈1, length ≈1.79 Å). The two CrO₄ tetrahedra share a single μ‑oxo oxygen, giving a Cr–O–Cr angle of approximately 126°. The overall charge of the anion is –2, balanced by the two K⁺ ions in the crystal lattice. In the solid state, K₂Cr₂O₇ adopts a triclinic lattice (space group P‑1) with each K⁺ surrounded by eight oxygen atoms from neighbouring dichromate ions. The compound is a powerful oxidising agent in acidic medium, being reduced to Cr³⁺ (green) while the dichromate ion (orange) is consumed. Its structure directly explains its redox behaviour: the high oxidation state (+6) of Cr and the relatively weak Cr–O–Cr bridge facilitate electron transfer.
steps: The dichromate ion Cr₂O₇²⁻ is built from two tetrahedral CrO₄ units that share one corner oxygen, giving a Cr–O–Cr bridge with a ~126° angle.
Here is why: each Cr(VI) centre is d⁰ and prefers tetrahedral coordination with four oxygens; sharing one oxygen satisfies the valence of both Cr atoms while keeping the overall charge –2.

Consider the Lewis structure: each terminal oxygen forms a double bond to Cr (formal charge 0 on O, +2 on Cr), while the bridging oxygen forms single bonds to both Cr atoms (formal charge –1 on O, +1 on each Cr).
The resonance‑averaged structure shows bond orders of ~2 for terminal Cr=O and ~1 for the bridge, explaining the observed bond‑length difference (1.66 Å vs 1.79 Å).
In the solid, K⁺ ions occupy interstitial sites, each coordinated by eight O atoms from surrounding dichromate anions, forming a stable ionic lattice.

An Indian laboratory example: when you add dilute H₂SO₄ to solid K₂Cr₂O₇, the orange solution turns green as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺; the colour change directly reflects the breaking of the Cr–O–Cr bridge and…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., CrO₄²⁻) reveals the misconception that dichromate is simply a monomeric chromate ion, confusing it with the chromate anion which has a different structure and charge.
remember: What is the chemical formula of the dichromate anion.
Explain why the dichromate ion contains a Cr–O–Cr bridge rather than a direct Cr–Cr bond.
A student claims that the dichromate ion contains a Cr–Cr single bond. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The dichromate ion (Cr₂O₇²⁻) consists of two CrO₄ tetrahedra that share a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The dichromate ion (Cr₂O₇²⁻) consists of two CrO₄ tetrahedra that share a single corner oxygen atom. Each chromium(VI) centre is surrounded by four oxygen atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement, corresponding to sp³ hybridisation. The terminal Cr–O bonds are shorter (≈1.66 Å) than the bridging Cr–O bonds (≈1.79 Å) because the bridging oxygen carries a formal negative charge and participates in two Cr–O bonds. The Cr–O–Cr angle is approximately 126°, significantly larger than the typical bent angle of water (104.5°) due to repulsion between the two bulky tetrahedral units and the absence of lone‑pair–lone‑pair repulsion on the bridging oxygen (which has two lone pairs but is constrained by the rigid CrO₄ frameworks). The ion possesses a C₂ axis passing through the bridging oxygen and the midpoint of the Cr–Cr vector, making it non‑planar and chiral in a static sense (though rapid inversion occurs in solution). This three‑dimensional shape dictates the ion’s oxidising power, crystal packing in K₂Cr₂O₇, and its reactivity in redox titrations. The geometry is a direct consequence of VSEPR theory applied to each Cr centre (four electron domains) and the bridging oxygen (two bonding domains, two lone pairs), modified by the steric demand of the two tetrahedra.
steps: The dichromate ion is built from two tetrahedral CrO₄ units that share one oxygen atom, giving a bent Cr–O–Cr bridge with an angle of about 126°.

Here is why: each Cr(VI) has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so VSEPR predicts a perfect tetrahedron (109.5°) around Cr. The bridging oxygen, however, has two bonding pairs (to the two Cr atoms) and two lone…
This steric repulsion is the key exam trap — students often quote the water angle without considering the bulk of the CrO₄ groups.
Consider the ion as two identical pyramids (tetrahedra) glued at their tips.
The Cr–Cr distance can be found by treating the two Cr–O(bridging) bonds as sides of an isosceles triangle with included angle 126°.
Using the law of cosines, D = √[2d²(1 − cosθ)], where d = 1.79 Å and θ = 126°.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “octahedral” or “square planar”) reveals the misconception that high oxidation‑state transition metals always adopt six‑coordinate geometries, ignoring the d⁰ electron count of Cr(VI) which favours four‑coordinate tetrahedral structures.
remember: What is the molecular geometry around each chromium atom in the dichromate ion (Cr₂O₇²⁻).
Why is the Cr–O–Cr bond angle in dichromate (≈126°) larger than the H–O–H angle in water (≈104.5°).
A student states that the dichromate ion is planar because it contains a Cr–O–Cr bridge. Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: The “uses” of d‑ and f‑block elements refer to the practical applications that…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The “uses” of d‑ and f‑block elements refer to the practical applications that arise from their characteristic chemical behaviours: variable oxidation states, formation of stable complex ions, catalytic activity, and distinctive colours. Transition metals such as Fe, Cu, Zn, and Mn are employed in structural alloys, electrical conductors, and as catalysts in industrial processes (e.g., Haber‑Bosch, Ostwald). Their oxo‑anions, permanganate (MnO₄⁻) and dichromate (Cr₂O₇²⁻), serve as powerful oxidising agents in quantitative analysis, water treatment, and organic synthesis because Mn(VII) and Cr(VI) are readily reduced to Mn(II) and Cr(III) with visible colour changes. Lanthanoids exhibit sharp f‑f transitions that make them valuable as phosphors in lighting and display technologies, while their magnetic moments enable high‑performance permanent magnets (e.g., Nd₂Fe₁₄B). Actinoids, principally uranium and plutonium, are exploited as nuclear fuels due to their ability to undergo fission, releasing large amounts of energy. Thus, the uses are directly linked to electronic structure (accessible d‑ or f‑electrons), redox flexibility, and the resulting physicochemical properties.
steps: The practical uses of d‑ and f‑block elements stem from their variable oxidation states, ability to form coloured complexes, and catalytic activity.
Here is why: 1.

Redox versatility – Transition metals can readily gain or lose electrons, making their oxo‑anions strong oxidants (MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺, Cr₂O₇²⁻ → Cr³⁺) that decolourise upon reduction, a basis for titrations and disinfection.…

Complex formation and colour – Partially filled d‑orbitals absorb visible light, giving intensely coloured compounds used as pigments, indicators, and in analytical tests (e.g., the brown ring test for nitrate). 3.

Catalytic competence – Adsorption of reactants on metal surfaces and facile interconversion between oxidation states lower activation energies in processes such as hydrogenation (Ni, Pt) and oxidation (V₂O₅ in contact…
Lanthanoid luminescence – Shielded 4f electrons give sharp emission lines;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is used as a reducing agent in bleaching”) reveals the misconception that permanganate’s role is to donate electrons, confusing its strong oxidising nature with that of reductants like Na₂SO₃.

cards.title: Lanthanoids are the 14 elements from cerium (Z=58) to lutetium (Z=71) in which…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Lanthanoids are the 14 elements from cerium (Z=58) to lutetium (Z=71) in which the 4f subshell is progressively filled. Their general ground‑state electron configuration is [Xe] 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s². The most stable oxidation state is +3, arising from loss of the two 6s electrons and one 5d/4f electron. Across the series the ionic radius of Ln³⁺ decreases steadily — the lanthanide contraction — because the 4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) experienced by the outer electrons increases. This contraction influences the chemistry of the subsequent transition series (e.g., Zr/Hf, Nb/Ta). Lanthanoids are typically paramagnetic due to unpaired 4f electrons; their magnetic moments are well described by the spin‑only formula μ_so = √[n(n+2)] BM, where n is the number of unpaired f‑electrons. They find use in catalysts (CeO₂), phosphors (Eu³⁺, Tb³⁺), and high‑strength alloys (misch metal). Actinoids comprise the 14 elements from thorium (Z=90) to lawrencium (Z=103) with progressive filling of the 5f subshell. Their general configuration is [Rn] 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s². Unlike lanthanoids, the 5f orbitals are more radially extended, allowing greater participation in bonding. Consequently actinoids exhibit a wider range of oxidation states (+3 to +7 for early members) and all are radioactive; only thorium‑232 and uranium‑238 have half‑lives long enough to be found in macroscopic quantities. Actinide contraction parallels lanthanide contraction but is less regular due to variable 5f occupancy. Applications centre on nuclear energy (U, Pu), neutron sources (Am‑Be), and smoke detectors (Am‑241). The two series are grouped together as f‑block elements because their differentiating electrons enter an inner f subshell, giving them distinct chemical behaviour from the d‑block transition elements covered in earlier nodes.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that lanthanoids and actinoids are defined by the filling of inner 4f and 5f orbitals, which makes their chemistry dominated by a stable +3 oxidation state for lanthanoids and a…

Here is why: first, the differentiating electrons enter an (n‑2)f subshell that lies radially inside the valence s and d orbitals; this poor shielding causes a steady increase in effective nuclear charge, shrinking the…

Second, because the 4f orbitals are core‑like, they do not participate significantly in bonding, so lanthanoids almost exclusively show the +3 state; the 5f orbitals of early actinoids (Th–Pu) are more diffuse, allowing…

Third, all actinoids are radioactive; the longest‑lived isotopes (Th‑232, U‑238) are primordial, while the heavier members are synthetic and decay rapidly — a key point for nuclear‑chemistry questions.

Fourth, magnetic properties arise solely from unpaired f‑electrons; the spin‑only formula works well because orbital angular momentum is largely quenched in the solid state, giving moments that match experimental values…
Fifth, practical uses stem from these electronic features: CeO₂ exploits the Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺ redox couple for catalytic converters;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s²) reveals the misconception that the 5d subshell fills completely before the 4f, confusing the lanthanoids with the transition‑metal filling order.

Evaluate the statement: “All actinoids are radioactive and have no stable isotopes.”.

cards.title: A ligand (from Latin ligare, “to bind”) is an ion or molecule that donates at…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A ligand (from Latin ligare, “to bind”) is an ion or molecule that donates at least one pair of electrons to a central metal atom/ion to form a coordinate (dative) covalent bond, thereby creating a coordination entity. Ligands are classified by denticity — the number of donor atoms they use to bind the metal: monodentate (one donor atom, e.g., NH₃, Cl⁻, H₂O), bidentate (two donor atoms, e.g., ethylenediamine “en”, oxalate C₂O₄²⁻), tridentate, tetradentate, pentadentate, hexadentate (e.g., EDTA⁴⁻). Ligands may be neutral (NH₃, H₂O, CO) or anionic (Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻, C₂O₄²⁻). The charge a ligand contributes to the overall complex equals its own ionic charge (zero for neutral ligands). Chelating ligands are polydentate ligands that form a ring (chelate) with the metal, increasing stability (chelate effect). Ambidentate ligands possess two possible donor atoms but bind through only one at a time (e.g., SCN⁻ can bind via S or N). The coordination sphere comprises the central metal ion plus all directly attached ligands; it is written inside square brackets. The coordination number (next node) equals the total number of donor atoms bound to the metal. Ligand field strength (spectrochemical series) influences d‑orbital splitting but is covered in VBT/CFT (node 05_006).
steps: Takeaway: A ligand is any species that donates one or more electron pairs to a metal centre, and its denticity and charge dictate the composition and charge of the resulting coordination sphere.
Supporting argument 1 – Electron‑pair donation: Coordinate bonds form when a ligand’s lone pair overlaps an empty orbital on the metal.
This is the same dative bonding seen in NH₄⁺ (NH₃ → H⁺) but extended to transition metals with vacant d‑orbitals.
Supporting argument 2 – Denticity determines geometry: A monodentate ligand occupies one coordination site; a bidentate ligand occupies two adjacent sites, forcing a chelate ring.
The number of donor atoms (denticity) directly adds to the coordination number.
Supporting argument 3 – Charge bookkeeping: The overall charge of the coordination sphere = oxidation state of metal + Σ(charges of ligands).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing NH₃) reveals the misconception that any ligand with a lone pair is automatically bidentate, confusing the presence of a lone pair with the number of donor atoms available for coordination.
remember: Which of the following ligands is bidentate? (a) NH₃ (b) Cl⁻ (c) ethylenediamine (en) (d) H₂O.
A student writes the coordination sphere of a complex containing Fe³⁺, two oxalate ions (C₂O₄²⁻) and two water molecules as….
Evaluate the statement: “All polydentate ligands are chelating ligands.”.

cards.title: The coordination number (CN) of a central metal atom/ion in a coordination…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The coordination number (CN) of a central metal atom/ion in a coordination entity is the total number of donor atoms from ligands that are directly bonded to it through coordinate (dative) bonds. It counts each donor atom separately, so a bidentate ligand such as ethylenediamine (en) contributes 2 to the CN, while a monodentate ligand such as Cl⁻ contributes 1. The CN determines the geometry of the complex (e.g., CN = 4 → tetrahedral or square‑planar; CN = 6 → octahedral). It is an integer, typically 2, 4, or 6 for common ISC complexes, but can range from 2 to 12 in known chemistry. The CN is distinct from the oxidation state (which counts electron loss/gain) and from the charge of the complex ion. In the IUPAC name, the CN is not written explicitly but is implicit in the ligand prefixes (di‑, tri‑, tetra‑, etc.) and the geometry term (e.g., “octahedral”). Relationship to sub‑concepts: - Ligand denticity (covered in node) directly adds to CN. - Coordination sphere (node) encloses the metal and its CN‑defining donor atoms. - Nomenclature (node) uses CN‑derived prefixes. - Werner’s theory (node) introduced primary (CN) and secondary valences. - VBT/CFT (node) uses CN to predict hybridisation and d‑orbital splitting.
steps: The coordination number is the total count of donor atoms directly attached to the central metal ion, and it dictates the complex’s geometry.
Here is why: each ligand donates one or more lone pairs; the metal accepts them into vacant orbitals, forming coordinate bonds.
The number of such bonds equals the CN. 1.
Identify ligands and their denticity – From the formula, list every ligand and note whether it is monodentate (e.g., H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻), bidentate (en, oxalate), or polydentate (EDTA⁴⁻). 2.
Multiply ligand count by denticity – For [Co(en)₃]³⁺, three en ligands × 2 donor atoms each = CN = 6. 3.
Sum contributions – In [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], two NH₃ (1 each) + two Cl⁻ (1 each) = CN = 4. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “4 because the charge is 4‑”) reveals the misconception that overall charge determines CN, confusing oxidation state with donor‑atom count.
remember: What is the coordination number of the central metal ion in the complex ion [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻.
Explain why the coordination number of [Co(en)₃]³⁺ is 6 even though only three ligand molecules are present.

cards.title: The coordination sphere (or inner sphere) of a complex is the central metal…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The coordination sphere (or inner sphere) of a complex is the central metal atom/ion together with all ligands directly attached to it through coordinate bonds. It is represented inside square brackets, e.g. [Co(NH_3)_6]^3+. The coordination number equals the number of donor atoms in this sphere. The outer sphere (ionization sphere) consists of counter‑ions that balance the overall charge of the complex but are not coordinated to the metal; they are written outside the brackets, e.g. [Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3. The inner sphere behaves as a single chemical entity in reactions such as substitution, while outer‑sphere ions dissociate freely in solution. The distinction is crucial for naming, isomerism, and predicting conductivity: only outer‑sphere ions contribute to molar conductivity in dilute solution. The concept links directly to Werner’s primary and secondary valences and underpins the classification of coordination compounds into ionisation, hydrate, and coordination isomers.
steps: The coordination sphere is the chemically bonded core of a complex; everything inside the square brackets moves and reacts as one unit.
Here is why: the metal–ligand coordinate bonds are strong enough to survive dissolution, whereas outer‑sphere ions are only electrostatically held and separate instantly in water.
Consider the classic example [Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3.
The six ammonia molecules are directly bound to cobalt(III) — they form the inner sphere.
The three chloride ions sit outside the brackets; they are the outer sphere.
When this solid dissolves, it yields one [Co(NH_3)_6]^3+ cation and three free Cl^- anions, giving a 1:3 electrolyte.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the counter‑ions are inside the brackets”) reveals the misconception that the brackets merely group the whole formula rather than distinguish bonded ligands from free ions.
remember: What is written inside the square brackets of a coordination compound formula.
Explain why [Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3 conducts electricity more strongly than [Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2 at the same concentration.
A student writes the formula of a complex as [Ni(CN)_4]K_2. Evaluate whether this correctly represents the inner and outer spheres for a nickel(II) cyanide complex.

cards.title: Nomenclature of coordination compounds follows IUPAC rules…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Nomenclature of coordination compounds follows IUPAC rules: the cation is named before the anion; within the coordination sphere, ligands are listed alphabetically ignoring multiplicative prefixes (di‑, tri‑, tetra‑). Anionic ligands end in “‑o” (chloro, cyano), neutral ligands retain their common names (aqua, ammine, carbonyl), and cationic ligands end in “‑ium” (hydrazinium). The metal name uses its elemental name for neutral or cationic complexes; for anionic complexes the metal takes the “‑ate” suffix (e.g., ferrate). Oxidation state of the metal is indicated in Roman numerals in parentheses. Coordination number equals the number of donor atoms bound to the metal. Isomerism arises from different spatial arrangements (geometrical: cis‑/trans‑, fac‑/mer‑; optical: enantiomers) or different connectivity (linkage, ionisation, coordination, hydrate). Structural isomerism changes the bonding pattern; stereoisomerism retains connectivity but differs in 3‑D orientation. The coordination sphere (inner sphere) includes the metal and directly bound ligands; counter‑ions lie outside (outer sphere).
steps: The one rule to remember: “Name the cation first, then the anion; inside the sphere list ligands alphabetically, indicate metal oxidation state, and use ‘‑ate’ for anionic complexes.” Here is why: the IUPAC system was…
First, identify the coordination sphere from the formula — everything inside square brackets.
In [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ the inner sphere is Co(NH₃)₅Cl²⁺; the two chloride ions outside are counter‑ions.
Second, list ligands alphabetically by their name (ignoring di‑, tri‑).
For the example: ammine (NH₃) comes before chloro (Cl⁻).
Because there are five ammine ligands, use “pentaammine”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “dichlorotetraaquachromium(III) chloride”) reveals the misconception that multiplicative prefixes determine alphabetical order — they are ignored; only the ligand root name matters.
remember: Write the IUPAC name of [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl.

Evaluate the statement: “All octahedral complexes of the type MA₂B₂C₂ are optically active.”.

cards.title: Werner’s coordination theory (1893) postulates that a metal atom/ion in a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Werner’s coordination theory (1893) postulates that a metal atom/ion in a complex exhibits two distinct valences: 1. Primary valence (oxidation state) – the number of charges the metal must balance with anionic ligands or counter‑ions; it is satisfied by ions outside the coordination sphere and is ionisable. 2. Secondary valence (coordination number) – the fixed number of ligand donor atoms directly attached to the metal in a definite spatial arrangement (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar, etc.). These ligands constitute the inner coordination sphere (written inside square brackets). The coordination sphere (inner sphere) is non‑ionisable; the ionisation sphere (outer sphere) contains counter‑ions that balance the primary valence and dissociate in solution. Werner’s theory explains: - Why complexes such as [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ give three chloride ions on dissolution (primary valence = 3, secondary valence = 6). - The existence of geometrical and optical isomerism arising from the fixed geometry of the secondary valence. - The distinction between ligands (neutral or anionic donor atoms) and counter‑ions. Key relationships: coordination number = number of donor atoms in inner sphere; oxidation state = charge on metal after assigning ligand charges; total charge of complex = oxidation state + sum of ligand charges. The theory laid the groundwork for later Valence Bond Theory (VBT) and Crystal Field Theory (CFT).
steps: Takeaway: Werner’s theory separates a metal’s oxidation state (primary valence) from its fixed coordination geometry (secondary valence), and this split explains both the ionisation behaviour and the stereochemistry of…
Here is why: 1.

Two valences, two spheres – The metal uses its primary valence to bind counter‑ions ionically (outer sphere) and its secondary valence to bind ligands covalently/coordinate‑covalently in a rigid polyhedron (inner…
Fixed coordination number – For a given metal in a given oxidation state, the secondary valence is constant (e.g., Co³⁺ almost always 6).
This fixes the shape (octahedral for 6) and makes isomerism possible. 3.
Ionisation test – When a complex dissolves, only outer‑sphere ions dissociate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “primary valence = coordination number”) reveals the misconception that oxidation state and coordination number are identical, confusing charge balance with spatial arrangement.
remember: State the two valences proposed by Werner and indicate which one corresponds to the coordination number.
A complex [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl is dissolved in water. How many ions will be produced per formula unit? Explain using Werner’s theory.
Evaluate the statement: “Werner’s secondary valence is always equal to the number of ligands attached to the metal.”.

cards.title: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) describes coordination bonds as overlap between metal…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) describes coordination bonds as overlap between metal hybrid orbitals and ligand donor orbitals. The metal ion undergoes hybridisation (sp³, dsp², d²sp³, sp³d², etc.) to create a set of equivalent orbitals directed toward the ligands, giving a predictable geometry (tetrahedral, square planar, octahedral). Crystal Field Theory (CFT) treats ligands as point charges that generate an electrostatic field around the metal centre. This field lifts the degeneracy of the five d‑orbitals: in an octahedral field the d‑orbitals split into lower‑energy t₂g (dxy, dyz, dzx) and higher‑energy eg (dz², dx²‑y²) sets, with a splitting energy Δ₀. In tetrahedral fields the splitting is inverted and smaller (Δₜ ≈ 4/9 Δ₀). The magnitude of Δ depends on the metal oxidation state, nature of the ligand (spectrochemical series), and geometry. Electron filling of the split d‑orbitals follows Hund’s rule and Pauli principle, determining the number of unpaired electrons and thus magnetic moment (μ = √[n(n+2)] BM). The same d‑d transitions that arise from Δ give rise to colour. VBT explains geometry and bond formation; CFT explains magnetic and spectral properties. Together they provide a comprehensive, though approximate, picture of coordination compounds.
steps: Valence Bond Theory and Crystal Field Theory together explain the bonding, geometry, magnetism, and colour of coordination compounds by describing how metal orbitals interact with ligand fields.
First, VBT assigns a hybridisation to the metal centre based on the number of ligand donor atoms and the availability of inner (n‑1)d or outer nd orbitals.
For example, [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ uses dsp² hybridisation (square planar) because Ni²⁺ (d⁸) can pair its electrons in the lower‑energy d‑orbitals and use one 3d, one 4s, and two 4p orbitals for σ‑bonding.
Second, CFT treats ligands as negative point charges that repel the metal d‑orbitals differently depending on their spatial orientation.
In an octahedral field the eg orbitals point directly at ligands and are raised in energy, while t₂g orbitals lie between ligands and are lowered.
The energy gap Δ₀ determines whether electrons pair (low‑spin) or occupy all five orbitals singly before pairing (high‑spin).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “dsp² hybridisation, square planar”) reveals the misconception that all Ni²⁺ complexes are square planar, ignoring ligand field strength and the fact that dsp² requires a strong‑field ligand to pair electrons in the 3d orbitals.
remember: State the hybridisation and geometry predicted by VBT for the complex [NiCl₄]²⁻.
Explain why [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is diamagnetic while [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is paramagnetic, using CFT.
A student measures the absorption maximum of an octahedral complex at 550 nm. Calculate Δ₀ in cm⁻¹ and kJ….

cards.title: Applications of coordination compounds refer to their practical utilisation in…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Applications of coordination compounds refer to their practical utilisation in fields such as catalysis, medicine, analytical chemistry, and materials science, where measurable quantities evaluate performance. Key quantities include: turnover frequency (TOF, s⁻¹), which measures how many substrate molecules a catalyst converts per active site per second; stability constant (K, dimensionless), expressing the equilibrium ratio of complex to free metal and ligand; molar absorptivity (ε, L·mol⁻¹·cm⁻¹), governing the intensity of colour in spectrophotometric assays; and drug dosage (mg·kg⁻¹), indicating the amount of a metallodrug administered per body mass. These symbols and SI units allow scientists to compare, optimise, and scale up the use of coordination compounds from laboratory bench to industrial plant or clinic. The effectiveness of an application depends on how ligands tune the metal’s electronic environment, thereby altering reactivity, selectivity, and spectroscopic properties.
steps: Coordination compounds are indispensable in real‑world technologies because their tunable metal–ligand interactions enable precise control over reactivity, selectivity, and stability.
Here is why: 1.
Ligand field strength and chelate effect dictate how tightly a metal binds ligands, which directly influences catalytic turnover and complex stability in biological systems. 2.
The electronic transitions of d‑electrons give rise to characteristic colours, allowing these compounds to serve as dyes, pigments, or spectroscopic indicators. 3.
Redox‑active metal centres can switch oxidation states under mild conditions, making them effective catalysts for electron‑transfer reactions such as hydrogenation or oxidation. 4.
The ability to form soluble or insoluble complexes with specific ions is exploited in water‑softening, metal‑recovery, and drug delivery.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 6) reveals the misconception that platinum must always adopt an octahedral geometry, ignoring that d⁸ Pt(II) commonly prefers a square‑planar arrangement with coordination number 4.
remember: What is the coordination number of the platinum atom in cisplatin, [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].
Explain why ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA) forms more stable complexes with Ca²⁺ than with Na⁺.
A student claims that increasing the ligand field splitting (Δ) always increases the colour intensity of a coordination compound. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) are saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons in which one…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) are saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons in which one or more hydrogen atoms are substituted by halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I). Haloarenes (aryl halides) are aromatic hydrocarbons where a hydrogen on the benzene ring is replaced by a halogen. Classification depends on the carbon bearing the halogen: primary (1°), secondary (2°), tertiary (3°) for haloalkanes; and on the ring substitution pattern (ortho, meta, para) for dihaloarenes. Nomenclature follows IUPAC rules: the halogen is treated as a substituent (fluoro‑, chloro‑, bromo‑, iodo‑) with locants indicating its position on the longest carbon chain or on the aromatic ring. Preparation methods include free‑radical halogenation of alkanes, addition of HX to alkenes, replacement of –OH by halogen using PX₃, PX₅, SOCl₂, and electrophilic aromatic substitution for haloarenes. Physical properties (boiling point, density, solubility) trend with molecular mass and polarity. Chemical reactivity is dominated by nucleophilic substitution (SN1, SN2) and elimination (E1, E2) for haloalkanes; haloarenes undergo nucleophilic aromatic substitution only under strong conditions (e.g., NaNH₂, high temperature) or via addition‑elimination (benzyne mechanism). The chapter also covers uses: chloroform as anaesthetic (historical), carbon tetrachloride as solvent, DDT as insecticide, and freons as refrigerants, linking structure to environmental impact.
steps: The chapter equips you to recognise, name, and predict the behaviour of every halogen‑substituted organic molecule you will meet in ISC chemistry.
Here is why: (1) Halogen substitution dramatically alters polarity, boiling point, and reactivity, turning inert alkanes into versatile synthetic intermediates.

(2) The carbon‑halogen bond strength and the stability of the resulting carbocation or transition state decide whether a reaction follows SN1 (unimolecular, carbocation intermediate, favoured by 3° substrates, polar…

(3) Aromatic halides resist SN1/SN2 because the C–X bond has partial double‑bond character; they react only via addition‑elimination (benzyne) or under harsh nucleophilic aromatic substitution conditions.
(4) Industrial relevance — chloroform, carbon tetrachloride, DDT, freons — illustrates how structure dictates utility and environmental persistence.

Consider a typical ISC question: “Write the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)CH₃ and predict its major substitution mechanism with aqueous NaOH.” You first number the chain (butan‑2‑yl chloride), note the secondary carbon, and…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “bromopropane” without locant) reveals the misconception that locants are optional for terminal substituents — IUPAC requires explicit numbering even when unambiguous.

cards.title: Haloalkanes are aliphatic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of an…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Haloalkanes are aliphatic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I). They are classified by the hybridisation and substitution pattern of the carbon bearing the halogen: primary (1°) – carbon attached to one other carbon; secondary (2°) – attached to two carbons; tertiary (3°) – attached to three carbons. Additional categories include allylic (halogen on sp³ carbon adjacent to a C=C), benzylic (halogen on sp³ carbon adjacent to an aromatic ring), vinylic (halogen directly on sp² carbon of a C=C), and aryl (halogen directly on sp² carbon of an aromatic ring). Haloarenes are aromatic compounds where a halogen is directly attached to an sp² carbon of a benzene ring. Nomenclature follows IUPAC: the parent chain is the longest continuous carbon chain containing the halogen; numbering gives the halogen the lowest possible locant; halogen prefixes (fluoro‑, chloro‑, bromo‑, iodo‑) are treated alphabetically with other substituents. For haloarenes, the ring is the parent (benzene) and the halogen is indicated by prefix with locants (e.g., 1,2‑dichlorobenzene). Common names (e.g., benzyl chloride, allyl bromide) are still used but systematic names are preferred in examinations. Classification determines reactivity trends: 3° haloalkanes favour SN1, 1° favour SN2, while aryl and vinylic halides are unreactive under both mechanisms due to partial double‑bond character of the C–X bond.
steps: The key to mastering haloalkane and haloarene nomenclature is to first classify the compound by the carbon–halogen bond environment, then apply systematic IUPAC rules to name it unambiguously.
Here is why: (1) Classification depends on the hybridisation and substitution pattern of the carbon bearing the halogen, which directly predicts reactivity trends.
(2) Primary, secondary, and tertiary labels describe the number of carbon neighbours on that carbon.
(3) Allylic and benzylic positions are activated by resonance, while vinylic and aryl halides have a partial double‑bond character that makes them inert to SN1/SN2.
(4) IUPAC naming uses the longest carbon chain (or benzene ring) as parent, assigns the lowest possible locant to the halogen, and lists substituents alphabetically.
(5) Common names like “benzyl chloride” persist in textbooks and exam questions, so recognising them is essential.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “bromopropane” without a locant) reveals the misconception that locants are optional for terminal…
