cards.title: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) and haloarenes (aryl halides) are organic compounds…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) and haloarenes (aryl halides) are organic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane or aromatic ring are replaced by halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I). Their preparation relies on introducing halogen via substitution, addition, or diazonium routes, while their physical and chemical properties stem from the polarity of the C–X bond and the size/polarizability of the halogen. In terms of classification, haloalkanes are primary, secondary, or tertiary depending on the carbon bearing the halogen; haloarenes retain the aromatic system and are named as aryl halides. Nomenclature follows IUPAC rules: the halogen is indicated by a prefix (fluoro‑, chloro‑, bromo‑, iodo‑) with locants, and the parent chain or ring is numbered to give the lowest set of locants. Preparation methods include: (i) free‑radical halogenation of alkanes (Cl₂, Br₂ under UV), (ii) addition of HX to alkenes (Markovnikov or anti‑Markovnikov with peroxides), (iii) substitution of alcohols using SOCl₂, PBr₃, or the Lucas reagent (HCl/ZnCl₂), (iv) Finkelstein exchange (NaI in acetone) for iodides, (v) Sandmeyer reaction (diazonium salt + CuX) for aryl halides, and (vi) Balz‑Schiemann for fluorides. Physical properties show a steady increase in boiling point and density with increasing atomic mass of the halogen due to greater London forces; haloalkanes are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Chemically, they undergo nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2), elimination (E1/E2), reactions with metals (Grignard formation), and, for haloarenes, electrophilic aromatic substitution is deactivated but still possible under harsh conditions. Understanding these preparation routes and property trends links directly to the classification and nomenclature discussed earlier and provides the foundation for mechanistic study in the next node.
steps: The preparation of haloalkanes and haloarenes hinges on selecting a method that converts a suitable precursor into the desired C–X bond while controlling regioselectivity and yield, and their observable properties…

First, different precursors (alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, diazonium salts) require distinct reagents because the C–H, C=C, C–O, or Ar–N₂⁺ bonds have varying bond energies and susceptibilities to halogen attack; for…

Second, regioselectivity is governed by rules such as Markovnikov addition for HX, anti‑Markovnikov in peroxide‑mediated reactions, and preferential substitution at benzylic or allylic positions via free‑radical…

Fourth, chemical reactivity trends (SN1 vs SN2 favorability, elimination ease) are anticipated from the stability of carbocations or the steric hindrance around the carbon bearing the halogen, which in turn informs…

cards.title: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) and haloarenes (aryl halides) undergo…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) and haloarenes (aryl halides) undergo characteristic reactions dictated by the carbon–halogen bond polarity and the hybridisation of the carbon bearing the halogen. In haloalkanes, the sp³ carbon allows both nucleophilic substitution (SN1 for tertiary, SN2 for primary) and β‑elimination (E1/E2) to give alcohols, nitriles, ethers, alkenes, or organometallic reagents (Grignard). Haloarenes, with an sp² carbon bonded to the halogen, resist SN1/SN2 under normal conditions because the C–X bond acquires partial double‑bond character via resonance; they require harsh conditions (high temperature, pressure, strong nucleophiles, or activating groups such as –NO₂ ortho/para) for nucleophilic aromatic substitution. Both classes participate in metal‑mediated couplings: the Wurtz reaction (Na, dry ether) yields symmetrical alkanes from haloalkanes, while the Grignard reaction (Mg, dry ether) forms versatile nucleophiles for C–C bond formation. Reduction (Zn/HCl, LiAlH₄) converts them to alkanes. Industrially, haloalkanes serve as solvents (CH₂Cl₂, CCl₄), refrigerants (CFCs, now phased out), and intermediates in polymer synthesis; haloarenes such as chlorobenzene are precursors for phenol (Dow process), aniline, and agrochemicals. The reactivity trends — primary > secondary > tertiary for SN2, reverse for SN1, and aryl halides inert unless activated — unify the prediction of products across these transformations.

Bond polarity and carbon hybridisation control the pathway – sp³ C–X bonds in haloalkanes are polar and accessible to backside attack (SN2) or can ionise to carbocations (SN1), whereas sp² C–X bonds in haloarenes are…

Substrate structure decides SN1 vs SN2 – tertiary halides favour SN1/E1 via stable carbocations; primary halides favour SN2/E2 with strong nucleophiles/bases; secondary halides show mixed behaviour. 3.

Activation enables aryl substitution – electron‑withdrawing groups (–NO₂, –CN) ortho/para to the halogen stabilise the Meisenheimer complex, allowing nucleophilic aromatic substitution under milder conditions. 4.
Metals convert halides into nucleophiles – Mg in dry ether forms Grignard reagents (R‑MgX) that attack carbonyls;

cards.title: Polyhalogen compounds are organic molecules in which two or more halogen atoms…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Polyhalogen compounds are organic molecules in which two or more halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I) are bonded to the same or different carbon atoms of an alkyl or aryl group. Key representatives in the ISC syllabus include trichloromethane (chloroform, CHCl₃), tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄), triiodomethane (iodoform, CHI₃), and dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT, C₁₄H₉Cl₅). Their preparation often involves halogenation of methane or ethanol (for chloroform/iodoform) and Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of chlorobenzene with chloral (for DDT). Physical properties: higher molecular masses give higher boiling points and densities than monohalo analogues; they are generally non‑polar, immiscible with water, and good solvents for non‑polar substances. Chemical reactivity: the C–X bonds are strengthened by electron‑withdrawing halogens, making nucleophilic substitution slower; however, α‑halogenated carbonyls (chloroform, iodoform) undergo base‑induced cleavage (haloform reaction). Uses: chloroform as anaesthetic (historical) and solvent; CCl₄ as fire‑extinguisher fluid and NMR solvent; iodoform as antiseptic; DDT as insecticide (now banned/restricted). Environmental impact: persistence, bioaccumulation, ozone depletion (CCl₄), and toxicity drive regulatory phase‑outs under the Stockholm Convention.
steps: Polyhalogen compounds are defined by the presence of two or more halogen atoms on a carbon skeleton, which dramatically alters their physical and chemical behaviour compared to monohalo analogues.

Here is why: the electron‑withdrawing inductive effect of each halogen increases the electron deficiency of the carbon bearing the halogens, but simultaneously the bulky halogen atoms create steric shielding that…

Consider chloroform (CHCl₃): it is prepared in the lab by heating ethanol or acetone with bleaching powder (CaOCl₂), which supplies chlorine and calcium hydroxide; the reaction proceeds via chlorination of the methyl…
Carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) is obtained by exhaustive chlorination of methane or carbon disulfide, but its use as a solvent has declined because it depletes stratospheric ozone and is hepatotoxic.
Iodoform (CHI₃) forms when a methyl ketone (or ethanol) is treated with iodine and base — the haloform reaction — giving a yellow precipitate that serves as a diagnostic test for CH₃CO– groups.

DDT is synthesised by the Friedel‑Crafts condensation of chlorobenzene with chloral (CCl₃CHO) in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄; its insecticidal action stems from disruption of sodium channels in nerve membranes…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ethanol + PCl₅”) reveals the misconception that phosphorus halides are used for polyhalogenation — they only replace –OH with a single halogen.

cards.title: Polyhalogen compounds are organic molecules in which two or more halogen atoms…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Polyhalogen compounds are organic molecules in which two or more halogen atoms (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine) are covalently bonded to a carbon skeleton. They are classified as trihalomethanes (CHX₃), tetrahalomethanes (CX₄), polyhalogenated alkenes, and polyhalogenated aromatics (e.g., DDT, BHC). The presence of multiple electron‑withdrawing halogens increases the polarity of each C–X bond, enhances the acidity of any remaining α‑hydrogen, and imparts high thermal and chemical stability. Key representatives include chloroform (CHCl₃), carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄), iodoform (CHI₃), freons (CFCs), p,p′‑DDT (C₁₄H₉Cl₅), and benzene hexachloride (BHC, C₆H₆Cl₆). Their preparation often extends reactions studied for monohalo compounds: haloform reaction (methyl ketones + X₂/NaOH → CHX₃), exhaustive chlorination of methane (CH₄ + 4Cl₂ → CCl₄ + 4HCl), and electrophilic aromatic substitution (chloral + chlorobenzene → DDT). Reactions include hydrolysis (slow for CCl₄, faster for CHCl₃ giving formates), reduction (Zn/HCl gives CH₂Cl₂ from CHCl₃), and dehydrohalogenation. Environmentally, their persistence leads to bioaccumulation, ozone depletion (CFCs), and endocrine disruption (DDT), prompting international bans under the Stockholm Convention. This node connects the mechanistic foundation of SN1/SN2 and aromatic substitution (nodes 004, 006) to real‑world chemical behaviour and regulatory chemistry.
steps: Polyhalogen compounds exhibit enhanced stability and unique reactivity due to multiple halogen substituents, leading to significant industrial applications but also persistent environmental hazards.

Here is why: first, each additional halogen withdraws electron density inductively, making the carbon centre more electrophilic and any remaining C–H bonds more acidic; this underpins the haloform reaction where a…

Second, exhaustive halogenation of alkanes (e.g., methane to CCl₄) proceeds via free‑radical chain substitution, with each step becoming progressively slower because the C–H bond strength increases as halogens replace…

Third, in aromatic systems, multiple chlorinations give isomers like p,p′‑DDT, whose synthesis uses the Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of chlorobenzene with chloral (CCl₃CHO) under concentrated H₂SO₄ — a direct application…

Fourth, the high C–Cl bond dissociation energy (~339 kJ mol⁻¹) and steric crowding in CCl₄ render it resistant to nucleophilic attack, explaining its former use as an inert solvent; however, under UV light it undergoes…
Fifth, DDT’s lipophilicity (log P ≈ 6) causes bioaccumulation in food chains, leading to eggshell thinning in birds — a classic case study in environmental chemistry.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “dichloromethane”) reveals the misconception that only one halogen replaces the methyl group — confusing partial halogenation with the exhaustive haloform process.

Evaluate the statement: “DDT is an ideal insecticide because it is highly toxic to insects but harmless to humans.”.

cards.title: Synthesis of haloalkanes and haloarenes refers to the planned construction of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Synthesis of haloalkanes and haloarenes refers to the planned construction of carbon‑halogen bonds from simpler precursors by applying knowledge of classification, nomenclature, preparation, reaction mechanisms and uses. It requires the student to retrograde‑analyse a target molecule, identify the bond to be formed, and select a precursor and reaction condition that favour the desired pathway (SN1, SN2, electrophilic aromatic substitution, free‑radical halogenation, etc.) while minimising side‑reactions such as elimination or rearrangement. The concept integrates the classification nodes (primary, secondary, tertiary, aryl, allyl, benzylic) with nomenclature rules that allow unambiguous communication of structures, the preparation nodes that list laboratory and industrial methods (e.g., free‑radical chlorination of alkanes, Sandmeyer reaction for aryl halides, hydrohalogenation of alkenes), the properties node that highlights physical trends (boiling points, polarity, solubility) influencing reaction choice, the SN1/SN2 mechanisms node that explains how substrate structure, nucleophile strength, solvent polarity and temperature dictate the pathway, and the reactions‑and‑uses node that outlines typical transformations (substitution, elimination, coupling, Grignard formation) and their applications in pharmaceuticals, agro‑chemicals and polymers. In the CISCE ISC examination, synthesis questions appear as multi‑step problems that test the ability to write balanced equations, calculate yields, predict stereochemistry and suggest reagents; they also assess familiarity with the marking scheme, time management and common traps such as rearrangements, competing eliminations and solvent effects. Practice through past papers and targeted numerical problems consolidates these skills, enabling the student to move from recall of facts to application and evaluation in unfamiliar contexts.
steps: Effective synthesis of haloalkanes and haloarenes relies on a backward‑retrosynthetic approach that matches the target functional group with a suitable precursor and reaction condition, guided by mechanistic preferences…

First, retrosynthetic analysis identifies the bond that must be formed and selects a precursor that avoids carbocation rearrangements and competing elimination; for example, to synthesize tert‑butyl chloride one…

Second, the choice between SN1 and SN2 pathways depends on substrate structure (primary, secondary, tertiary, allyl, benzylic) and solvent/nucleophile characteristics; a primary halide with a strong nucleophile in a…

Third, CISCE exam patterns allocate marks for balanced equations (1 mark), correct reagents and conditions (1 mark), yield calculations (2 marks) and discussion of side‑products or stereochemistry (1 mark); awareness of…

Fourth, repeated practice with past papers reveals common traps such as solvent‑induced elimination (e.g., ethanolic KOH giving alkenes instead of substitution), rearrangements in secondary carbocations during SN1, and…
Consider the synthesis of 2‑chloro‑2‑methylbutane from 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol.

cards.title: Alcohols are organic compounds in which a hydroxyl (‑OH) group is attached to a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Alcohols are organic compounds in which a hydroxyl (‑OH) group is attached to a saturated carbon atom; they are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary based on the number of carbon atoms bonded to the carbon bearing the ‑OH. Phenols consist of a hydroxyl group directly bonded to an aromatic ring, which delocalises the oxygen lone pair into the ring and makes the O–H bond significantly more acidic than in aliphatic alcohols. Ethers contain an oxygen atom linked to two alkyl or aryl groups (R–O–R′); the oxygen is sp³ hybridised and the C–O–C angle is about 111°. The chapter connects three core ideas: (1) preparation routes — hydration of alkenes, reduction of carbonyls, and Grignard reactions for alcohols; electrophilic aromatic substitution for phenols; Williamson synthesis and dehydration of alcohols for ethers. (2) Physical properties — hydrogen‑bonding in alcohols and phenols gives higher boiling points than ethers of comparable molar mass; phenols show appreciable water solubility due to the –OH group. (3) Chemical reactivity — alcohols undergo oxidation, esterification and substitution; phenols undergo electrophilic substitution at ortho/para positions and form phenoxide ions with bases; ethers are relatively inert but cleave with strong acids (HI, HBr) and undergo peroxide formation on standing. Understanding these relationships lets you predict reaction outcomes and design synthetic sequences.
steps: The one big idea: alcohols, phenols and ethers share an oxygen atom but differ dramatically in acidity, reactivity and utility because of the carbon framework attached to that oxygen.

Here is why: first, the carbon bearing the –OH in alcohols is sp³ hybridised, so the O–H bond is only weakly polarised; in phenols the oxygen is attached to an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring, allowing the negative…

Second, ethers lack an O–H bond entirely, so they cannot hydrogen‑bond to themselves; their boiling points are close to those of alkanes of similar mass, yet the lone pairs on oxygen make them good solvents for polar…

Third, preparation routes exploit these electronic differences: alkenes add water (Markovnikov) to give alcohols; carbonyl compounds are reduced (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄) or attacked by Grignard reagents; phenols arise from…

Consider a real‑world Indian context: the ethanol blended in petrol (E10) comes from fermentation of sugarcane molasses — a primary alcohol; the antiseptic “Dettol” contains chloroxylenol, a phenolic derivative; and the…

As you move to the next nodes, you will see how each family’s unique electronic structure dictates its reaction map — oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes, electrophilic substitution on phenols, and acid‑catalysed…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “all three have the same –OH group”) reveals the misconception that the presence of oxygen alone defines the functional group, ignoring the carbon hybridisation and connectivity that distinguish alcohols, phenols and ethers.
remember: Name the functional group present in ethanol, phenol and diethyl ether respectively.
Explain why phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol.

cards.title: Alcohols are organic compounds containing a hydroxyl (‑OH) group attached to a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Alcohols are organic compounds containing a hydroxyl (‑OH) group attached to a saturated carbon atom. They are classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°), or tertiary (3°) based on the number of carbon atoms bonded to the carbon bearing the –OH group. Preparation routes include: (i) acid‑catalysed hydration of alkenes (Markovnikov addition), (ii) fermentation of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂) using yeast, (iii) reduction of aldehydes, ketones, or esters with NaBH₄/LiAlH₄, and (iv) reaction of Grignard reagents with carbonyl compounds followed by hydrolysis. Physical properties are dominated by hydrogen bonding: higher boiling points, solubility in water for low‑molecular‑weight alcohols, and neutral pH. Chemical properties: (a) reaction with active metals (Na, K) liberating H₂; (b) oxidation — 1° alcohols give aldehydes (with PCC) or carboxylic acids (with K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄), 2° alcohols give ketones, 3° alcohols resist oxidation; (c) dehydration with conc. H₂SO₄ (170 °C → alkenes, 140 °C → ethers); (d) esterification with carboxylic acids (Fischer esterification); (e) Lucas test (ZnCl₂/HCl) distinguishes 1°, 2°, 3° alcohols by rate of alkyl chloride formation. These reactions interlink — oxidation state changes, carbocation stability, and nucleophilic substitution — forming the core of alcohol chemistry in the ISC syllabus.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that the –OH group dictates both the physical behaviour (hydrogen bonding) and the chemical reactivity (oxidation, dehydration, substitution) of alcohols, and the carbon skeleton…
Here is why: 1.
Hydrogen bonding makes alcohols higher‑boiling and water‑miscible up to C₄; this explains why ethanol mixes with water in sanitiser while hexane does not. 2.
Oxidation proceeds via loss of α‑hydrogen; primary alcohols have two α‑H and can be oxidised twice (aldehyde → acid), secondary have one α‑H (ketone), tertiary have none (no reaction). 3.
Dehydration follows E1 mechanism; carbocation stability (3° > 2° > 1°) controls rate and product distribution (Zaitsev alkene). 4.
Lucas test exploits the same carbocation stability: 3° alcohols react instantly, 2° within 5‑10 min, 1° hardly at all. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “diethyl ether”) reveals the misconception that the same reagent always gives ether — confusing the 140 °C condition (ether formation) with the 170 °C condition (alkene formation).
remember: Name the gaseous product formed when ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170 °C.
Explain why tertiary butyl alcohol reacts instantly with Lucas reagent while n‑butanol shows no visible reaction at room temperature.
Evaluate the statement: “All alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids using acidified K₂Cr₂O₇.”.

cards.title: Phenols are aromatic compounds in which a hydroxyl (–OH) group is directly…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Phenols are aromatic compounds in which a hydroxyl (–OH) group is directly bonded to an sp²‑hybridised carbon of a benzene ring. The acidity of phenols (pKₐ ≈ 10) arises because the phenoxide ion formed after deprotonation is stabilised by resonance delocalisation of the negative charge over the ortho and para positions of the ring. Electron‑withdrawing substituents (–NO₂, –CN, –COOH) increase acidity by further stabilising the anion, while electron‑donating groups (–CH₃, –OH, –OR) decrease it. Phenols undergo characteristic reactions: (1) acid‑base reaction with NaOH/Na₂CO₃ to give phenoxides; (2) reaction with Na metal liberating H₂; (3) electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) at ortho/para positions — nitration (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ gives o‑ and p‑nitrophenol), halogenation (Br₂/CS₂ gives 2,4,6‑tribromophenol), sulfonation (conc. H₂SO₄ gives o‑ and p‑phenolsulfonic acid); (4) Kolbe’s reaction (phenoxide + CO₂ under pressure → salicylate); (5) Reimer‑Tiemann reaction (phenol + CHCl₃/NaOH → o‑hydroxybenzaldehyde); (6) oxidation (Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ or Fremy’s salt) to p‑benzoquinone. These reactions exploit the activated ring and the phenoxide nucleophilicity. The chapter’s sibling node covers aliphatic alcohol preparation/properties; this node focuses exclusively on phenol acidity and its reaction repertoire.
steps: The single most important takeaway: Phenol’s acidity and reactivity are governed by the resonance‑stabilised phenoxide ion, which makes the –OH proton unusually labile and the ring highly activated toward electrophilic…
Here is why: 1.
Resonance delocalisation – After losing H⁺, the negative charge on oxygen is shared by the ortho and para carbons of the benzene ring.
Draw the three canonical forms; each places the charge on a carbon, lowering the energy of the conjugate base relative to alkoxides where no such delocalisation exists. 2.
Substituent effects – Electron‑withdrawing groups (–NO₂ at para) pull electron density through both –I and –M, further stabilising the anion and lowering pKₐ (p‑nitrophenol pKₐ ≈ 7.1).
Electron‑donating groups (–CH₃) push electron density, raising pKₐ (p‑cresol ≈ 10.2).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “phenol is more acidic because the benzene ring is electron‑withdrawing”) reveals the misconception that the ring exerts a net –I effect; actually the ring donates electron density by resonance, but the key is delocalisation of the…
remember: State the approximate pKₐ value of phenol and explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
Predict the major product(s) when phenol is treated with bromine water at room temperature. Justify your answer.
Evaluate the statement: “Phenol reacts with sodium carbonate to evolve CO₂, just like carboxylic acids.” Provide a reasoned verdict.

cards.title: Ethers are a class of organic compounds with the general formula R–O–R′ where R…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Ethers are a class of organic compounds with the general formula R–O–R′ where R and R′ are alkyl or aryl groups. The oxygen atom is sp³ hybridised, bearing two lone pairs, which makes ethers Lewis bases and moderately polar but unable to hydrogen‑bond with themselves. Preparation methods include: (1) Williamson ether synthesis — nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkoxide ion (RO⁻) with a primary alkyl halide (R′X) to give R–O–R′; (2) Acid‑catalysed dehydration of two alcohol molecules (intermolecular) at 140 °C using conc. H₂SO₄, suitable for symmetrical ethers; (3) Alkoxymercuration‑demercuration of alkenes using an alcohol as nucleophile, giving Markovnikov addition of –OR across the double bond; (4) Reaction of diazomethane with alcohols (specialised). Key properties: ethers have lower boiling points than isomeric alcohols due to absence of intermolecular H‑bonding; they are soluble in water up to 3‑4 carbons because oxygen can accept H‑bonds from water. Chemically, ethers are relatively inert but undergo cleavage with concentrated HI or HBr (SN2 for primary, SN1 for tertiary alkyl groups) to give alkyl halides and alcohols. They also form peroxides on prolonged exposure to air/light — a safety hazard. Ethers react with PCl₅ to give alkyl chlorides, and with strong oxidising agents (e.g., KMnO₄) only under forcing conditions. The C–O bond is strong, so ethers resist nucleophilic attack unless activated by strong acids.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that ether synthesis revolves around forming a C–O bond via nucleophilic attack of an alkoxide on an alkyl halide (Williamson) or via acid‑catalysed condensation of two alcohol…

Here is why: (1) The alkoxide is a strong nucleophile and a strong base; its reaction with a primary alkyl halide proceeds cleanly by SN2, but with secondary/tertiary halides elimination competes — this is the classic…
(2) Acid‑catalysed dehydration requires two alcohol molecules; at 140 °C the equilibrium favours ether, but at 180 °C elimination to alkene dominates — a temperature‑control nuance often tested.

(3) Alkoxymercuration‑demercuration adds –OR across an alkene with Markovnikov orientation without carbocation rearrangements, because the mercurinium ion intermediate is bridged; this connects to alkene hydration…

(4) Cleavage by HI/HBr: the protonated ether oxygen becomes a good leaving group; primary alkyl groups undergo SN2 attack by iodide, while tertiary groups form stable carbocations leading to SN1 — students must…

(5) Peroxide formation: ethers with α‑hydrogen atoms slowly react with O₂ to give hydroperoxides, which can explode on distillation; adding a few crystals of FeSO₄ or storing over Na wire prevents this — a practical…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “heat ethanol with Na metal”) reveals the misconception that sodium metal produces ethers — sodium actually generates sodium ethoxide, which would need an alkyl halide for Williamson synthesis, not another ethanol molecule.
remember: Name the reagent and condition used to prepare diethyl ether from ethanol in the laboratory.
Explain why Williamson ether synthesis fails when a tertiary alkyl halide is used with sodium ethoxide.
Evaluate the statement: “Ethers are completely inert to all acids and bases under normal conditions.”.

cards.title: This concept node integrates the reactivity patterns of alcohols, phenols…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: This concept node integrates the reactivity patterns of alcohols, phenols, and ethers to predict and design interconversion pathways. It builds on the individual preparation and properties covered in nodes (alcohols), (phenols), and (ethers). Key relationships include: (1) Acidity trend — phenols (pKa ≈ 10) > alcohols (pKa ≈ 16–18) > ethers (no acidic proton); (2) Nucleophilic substitution — alcohols undergo SN1/SN2 after protonation; phenols do not undergo SN1/SN2 at the aromatic carbon but their phenoxide ions are strong nucleophiles for Williamson ether synthesis; ethers undergo acid-catalysed cleavage (SN2 for primary alkyl, SN1 for tertiary/aryl). (3) Electrophilic aromatic substitution — phenols and aryl ethers (anisole) activate the ring (ortho/para directing), with phenol more activated due to –OH vs –OR. (4) Oxidation — primary/secondary alcohols oxidise to carbonyls; phenols oxidise to quinones; ethers are generally inert to mild oxidants. (5) Interconversion reactions: alcohol → ether (Williamson, dehydration), phenol → ether (Williamson), ether → alcohol/phenol (acidic cleavage), alcohol → carbonyl (oxidation), carbonyl → alcohol (reduction). Understanding these links enables multi-step synthesis planning, a core ISC skill.
steps: The central takeaway: Alcohols, phenols, and ethers form an interconnected reactivity triangle where acidity, nucleophilicity, and susceptibility to oxidation/cleavage dictate feasible interconversions.
Here is why: each class shares an oxygen atom but differs in hybridisation and resonance, leading to distinct chemical behaviours that can be exploited synthetically.

Consider the acidity ladder: phenol (pKa ~10) loses a proton to form phenoxide, a resonance-stabilised anion; ethanol (pKa ~16) gives ethoxide, a stronger base but no resonance; diethyl ether has no acidic proton.
This means phenoxide is a better nucleophile for SN2 on alkyl halides (Williamson) than ethoxide, yet ethoxide can also perform Williamson.
However, phenoxide’s resonance delocalisation makes it less basic, reducing elimination side reactions — a classic exam trap where students wrongly predict elimination with bulky halides.

Next, ether cleavage: anisole (methyl phenyl ether) with hot HI yields phenol + CH3I (SN2 at methyl) because the aryl–O bond is strong; but tert-butyl methyl ether gives tert-butanol + CH3I (SN1 at tert-butyl).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ethanol > phenol) reveals the misconception that alkyl groups increase acidity by inductive effect, ignoring resonance stabilisation in phenoxide.
remember: Which of the following correctly orders the acidity of phenol, ethanol, and diethyl ether.
Explain why sodium phenoxide reacts with methyl iodide to give anisole in high yield, whereas sodium ethoxide with tert-butyl bromide gives mainly elimination product.
Evaluate the claim: “Anisole undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution faster than phenol because the methoxy group is a stronger electron donor than hydroxyl.”.

cards.title: Acid‑catalyzed cleavage of ethers is a nucleophilic substitution reaction in…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Acid‑catalyzed cleavage of ethers is a nucleophilic substitution reaction in which an ether (R–O–R′) reacts with a strong acid (usually HX, X = Cl, Br, I) under heating to give an alcohol and an alkyl halide. The ether oxygen is first protonated, making it a good leaving group; the conjugate base X⁻ then attacks the more substituted carbon (if the ether is unsymmetrical) in an SN1‑like pathway, or the less hindered carbon in an SN2 pathway depending on structure and conditions. This reaction links the preparation topic (ethers from Williamson synthesis) to the properties topic (reactivity of ethers) and shows how functional‑group interconversion converts an ether back to alcohols and halides, which are covered in the alcohol and haloalkane sections. The process is kinetically controlled; the rate law is first order in ether and first order in proton concentration, reflecting the bimolecular nature of the rate‑determining step. Acid‑catalyzed cleavage of ethers is a nucleophilic substitution reaction in which an ether (R–O–R′) reacts with a strong acid (usually HX, X = Cl, Br, I) under heating to give an alcohol and an alkyl halide. The ether oxygen is first protonated, making it a good leaving group; the conjugate base X⁻ then attacks the more substituted carbon (if the ether is unsymmetrical) in an SN1‑like pathway, or the less hindered carbon in an SN2 pathway depending on structure and conditions. This reaction links the preparation topic (ethers from Williamson synthesis) to the properties topic (reactivity of ethers) and shows how functional‑group interconversion converts an ether back to alcohols and halides, which are covered in the alcohol and haloalkane sections. The process is kinetically controlled; the rate law is first order in ether and first order in proton concentration, reflecting the bimolecular nature of the rate‑determining step.
steps: The rate of acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage depends linearly on both ether concentration and proton concentration.
Here is why: 1.
Protonation of the ether oxygen is a rapid pre‑equilibrium step; the concentration of the protonated ether is proportional to [ether][H⁺]. 2.
The subsequent nucleophilic attack by halide (X⁻) on the protonated ether is the rate‑determining step; its rate is proportional to the concentration of the protonated ether and [X⁻]. 3.
Because [X⁻] is essentially constant when the acid is in large excess, the overall rate simplifies to k′[ether][H⁺].
Consider a round‑bottom flask containing diethyl ether (CH₃CH₂–O–CH₂CH₃) and concentrated HCl. The ether oxygen is protonated to give CH₃CH₂–O⁺H–CH₂CH₃, weakening the C–O bond.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “rate = k[ether]²”) reveals the misconception that two ether molecules collide in the rate‑determining step, ignoring the essential role of proton activation.... through 6 The rate law is rate = k[ether][H⁺]. Step‑by‑step…
remember: State the rate law for acid‑catalyzed cleavage of an ether and explain why it is first order in ether and first order in….
Explain why cleavage of tert‑butyl methyl ether with HBr gives tert‑butyl bromide as the major product, whereas cleavage of ethyl methyl ether gives bromoethane as the major….
A student claims that increasing the concentration of NaCl in the reaction mixture will speed up the acid‑catalyzed cleavage of diethyl ether with HCl. Evaluate this….

cards.title: The quantitative acidity of phenols is expressed by the acid dissociation…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The quantitative acidity of phenols is expressed by the acid dissociation constant Ka and its negative logarithm pKa = –log₁₀Ka. For phenol (C₆H₅OH), Ka ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ (pKa ≈ 10.0) at 298 K. Electron‑withdrawing substituents (–NO₂, –CN, –COOH) stabilize the phenoxide anion through –I and –R effects, lowering pKa; electron‑donating groups (–CH₃, –OH, –OR) raise pKa. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log₁₀([phenoxide]/[phenol]), relates the buffer pH to the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid. This equation is valid when the concentrations of phenol and phenoxide are much larger than the [H⁺] from water auto‑ionisation and when the acid is not too strong (pKa > 2). Buffer capacity is maximum when [phenoxide] = [phenol] (pH = pKa) and falls sharply when the ratio exceeds 10:1 or 1:10. These concepts extend the qualitative acidity trends introduced in the phenol node into a quantitative framework required for buffer design and titration calculations in the ISC examination.
steps: The acidity of phenols can be quantified using pKa values, which are lowered by electron‑withdrawing substituents, and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation allows precise buffer calculations.
First, pKa = –log₁₀Ka provides a direct measure of acid strength: a phenol with pKa 7.2 (p‑nitrophenol) is about 10³ times more acidic than phenol (pKa 10.0).
This difference arises because the nitro group withdraws electron density through both –I and –R effects, delocalising the negative charge of the phenoxide ion over the ring and the nitro group.
In contrast, a methyl group donates electrons (+I), raising pKa to ~10.2 for p‑cresol.
Second, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is derived from Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] by taking –log₁₀: pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]).
For a phenol buffer, HA = phenol, A⁻ = phenoxide.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “pKa = log Ka”) reveals the misconception that the logarithm is positive — confusing pKa with log Ka and missing the sign convention that makes stronger acids have smaller pKa values.
remember: Define pKa and state its mathematical relationship with Ka.
Explain why p‑nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 7.2) is a stronger acid than phenol (pKa ≈ 10.0).
A student claims that a buffer made from equal concentrations of phenol (pKa = 10.0) and sodium phenoxide has pH = 7. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: This synthesis node consolidates the three concept nodes
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: This synthesis node consolidates the three concept nodes (preparation & properties of alcohols; phenols – acidity & reactions; ethers – preparation & properties) into an exam‑focused toolkit. It maps each sub‑topic to the typical ISC question patterns: 1‑mark recall (name the reagent), 2‑mark reasoning (explain why phenol is more acidic), 3‑mark mechanism (show the SN2 step in Williamson ether synthesis), 5‑mark multi‑part (design a synthesis from a given alkene to a target ether). The node provides worked numericals (e.g., yield calculations, stoichiometry of neutralisation), diagnostic questions graded from recall to past‑paper style, and competency items that test interpretation of experimental observations. It does not re‑teach mechanisms or properties — those belong to the concept nodes — but shows how to select, combine and present that knowledge under exam conditions.
steps: The single most important takeaway is: ISC Chemistry rewards structured, mark‑aware answers — know the pattern, then fill in the chemistry.
Here is why: the board repeats a small set of question templates each year; recognising the template lets you deploy the right depth (definition, mechanism, calculation) without wasting time.
First, classify every question by its command word: “Name” → 1 mark recall;
“Explain” → 2 marks reasoning;
“Write the mechanism” → 3 marks stepwise arrows;
“Design a synthesis” → 5 marks multi‑step with reagents and conditions.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “PCl₅”) reveals the misconception that any chlorinating agent works — but PCl₅ gives a mixture and is not the standard lab reagent taught in ISC.
remember: Name the reagent used to convert ethanol to ethyl chloride in the laboratory.
Explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
Evaluate the statement: “Williamson ether synthesis proceeds via an SN1 mechanism when a tertiary alkyl halide is used.”.

cards.title: Aldehydes (R‑CHO), ketones (R‑CO‑R′) and carboxylic acids (R‑COOH) share the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Aldehydes (R‑CHO), ketones (R‑CO‑R′) and carboxylic acids (R‑COOH) share the carbonyl functional group (C=O) but differ in the substituents attached to the carbonyl carbon. In aldehydes the carbonyl carbon bears at least one hydrogen; in ketones it is bonded to two carbon groups; in carboxylic acids it is bonded to a hydroxyl group. The chapter covers three interconnected themes: (1) Preparation and properties – oxidation of primary/secondary alcohols, ozonolysis of alkenes, Friedel‑Crafts acylation, and physical properties such as boiling points governed by dipole‑dipole interactions. (2) Nucleophilic addition reactions – the carbonyl carbon’s electrophilicity invites attack by nucleophiles (HCN, Grignard reagents, NaBH₄, LiAlH₄, alcohols, amines) leading to cyanohydrins, alcohols, acetals, imines and more; the mechanism proceeds via a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. (3) Carboxylic acids: acidity and reactions – the –COOH group donates a proton (Ka ≈ 10⁻⁵) because the conjugate base is resonance‑stabilised; reactions include esterification (Fischer), decarboxylation, reduction to primary alcohols, and formation of acid derivatives (acyl chlorides, anhydrides, amides). Together these topics explain the reactivity pattern of the carbonyl group across synthetic organic chemistry and biological systems.
steps: The carbonyl group (C=O) is the central reactive motif that unifies aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids; mastering its behaviour unlocks the whole chapter.

Here is why: the carbonyl carbon is electron‑deficient because the electronegative oxygen pulls electron density, making it a target for nucleophiles; the nature of the substituents (H, alkyl, OH) modulates this…

First, consider preparation: primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes (PCC, DMP) and further to acids (KMnO₄); secondary alcohols give ketones; ozonolysis of alkenes cleaves the double bond to carbonyl fragments;
Friedel‑Crafts acylation installs an acyl group on an aromatic ring.
These routes are the synthetic entry points you will use in later nodes.
Second, nucleophilic addition: a nucleophile (Nu⁻) attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide; protonation yields the addition product.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the common group is –OH and carbon is sp³”) reveals the misconception that the hydroxyl group defines these families, confusing alcohols with carbonyl compounds.
remember: Name the functional group common to aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids and state the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon.
Explain why aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones toward nucleophilic addition.
Evaluate the statement: “Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols because the carboxylate anion has two equivalent resonance structures while phenoxide has only one.”.

cards.title: Aldehydes (R‑CHO) and ketones (R‑CO‑R′) are carbonyl compounds where the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Aldehydes (R‑CHO) and ketones (R‑CO‑R′) are carbonyl compounds where the carbonyl carbon is sp²‑hybridised and bears a polar C=O bond. In aldehydes the carbonyl carbon is attached to at least one hydrogen; in ketones it is bonded to two carbon groups. This structural difference governs their preparation and reactivity. Key laboratory preparations: 1. Oxidation of alcohols – Primary alcohols give aldehydes with mild oxidants (PCC, DMP, Swern); secondary alcohols give ketones with the same reagents or with Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄). Over‑oxidation to carboxylic acids is avoided by using stoichiometric mild oxidants. 2. Hydration of alkynes (Kucherov reaction) – Terminal alkynes yield methyl ketones (Markovnikov addition of water followed by enol‑keto tautomerisation); internal alkynes give symmetrical or mixed ketones. Acetylene exceptionally gives acetaldehyde. 3. Rosenmund reduction – Acid chlorides are hydrogenated over Pd/BaSO₄ poisoned with quinoline or sulfur to stop at the aldehyde; aliphatic acid chlorides often undergo side reactions. 4. Friedel‑Crafts acylation – Aromatic ketones are obtained by acylating benzene with an acid chloride/AlCl₃; the resulting aryl ketone can be reduced to alkylbenzene (Clemmensen/Wolff‑Kishner) if needed. 5. Other routes – Ozonolysis of alkenes, Sommelet reaction (benzyl halides to aldehydes), and hydroformylation of alkenes (oxo process). Physical properties: Lower members are gases or volatile liquids; boiling points rise with molecular mass due to dipole‑dipole interactions. They are soluble in organic solvents; small aldehydes/ketones (up to 4 carbons) are miscible with water because the carbonyl oxygen hydrogen‑bonds with water. Chemical properties centre on nucleophilic addition at the carbonyl carbon. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because (i) the carbonyl carbon is less sterically hindered and (ii) alkyl groups donate electron density, reducing electrophilicity. Typical reactions: addition of HCN, NaHSO₃, Grignard reagents, alcohols (acetal formation), ammonia derivatives (imines, oximes), and oxidation (aldehydes → carboxylic acids with Tollens’, Fehling’s, Benedict’s reagents). Ketones resist mild oxidation but undergo cleavage with strong oxidants (e.g., hot KMnO₄). Both undergo reduction to alcohols (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄) and condensation (aldol, Cannizzaro for non‑α‑hydrogen aldehydes). These preparations and properties set the stage for the detailed mechanistic study of nucleophilic addition in the next concept node.
steps: Aldehydes and ketones are versatile carbonyl compounds prepared mainly by controlled oxidation of alcohols or hydration of alkynes, and their reactivity stems from the polar C=O bond which undergoes nucleophilic…

First, the oxidation route: a primary alcohol like ethanol can be stopped at acetaldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in dichloromethane at 0 °C; if we used hot acidified KMnO₄ we would overshoot to acetic…
This mirrors the kitchen trick of simmering wine just long enough to get a tangy aldehyde note without turning it into vinegar.
Secondary alcohols such as propan‑2‑ol give acetone under the same mild conditions.
Second, the Kucherov hydration: passing propyne through dilute H₂SO₄ with HgSO₄ catalyst adds water across the triple bond.
The initial enol (CH₃‑C(OH)=CH₂) instantly tautomerises to acetone.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “acidified KMnO₄”) reveals the misconception that any strong oxidant can be controlled to stop at the aldehyde; in reality, strong oxidants in aqueous medium continue to the carboxylic acid.
remember: Name the reagent commonly used to oxidise a primary alcohol to an aldehyde without over‑oxidation to the carboxylic acid.
Why does the hydration of propyne (CH≡C‑CH₃) give acetone, whereas hydration of 1‑butyne (CH≡C‑CH₂‑CH₃) gives butan‑2‑one.
A student claims that Rosenmund reduction of benzoyl chloride with Pd/BaSO₄ yields benzoic acid. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Nucleophilic addition reactions involve the attack of a nucleophile
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Nucleophilic addition reactions involve the attack of a nucleophile (a species with a lone pair or negative charge) on the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of aldehydes or ketones. The carbonyl carbon is sp²‑hybridised, trigonal planar, and bears a partial positive charge because of the electronegative oxygen. The nucleophile donates its electron pair to form a new σ‑bond, converting the carbonyl to a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. Protonation of this intermediate (by solvent or added acid) yields the final addition product, commonly an alcohol, cyanohydrin, bisulfite adduct, or imine depending on the nucleophile. The reaction rate is governed by two main factors: (i) the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon, which increases with electron‑withdrawing substituents and decreases with electron‑donating alkyl groups, and (ii) steric hindrance around the carbonyl, which is lower in aldehydes (one alkyl group) than in ketones (two alkyl groups). Acid catalysis enhances electrophilicity by protonating the carbonyl oxygen; base catalysis can increase nucleophile strength. These reactions connect to the preparation node (where aldehydes/ketones are made) and lead forward to the carboxylic acids node, where further oxidation of aldehydes yields acids.
steps: The rate of nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones depends primarily on the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and the steric hindrance around it. Here is why: 1.
Electronic effect: Alkyl groups donate electrons through hyperconjugation, reducing the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.
Aldehydes have only one such group, ketones have two, making aldehydes more electrophilic. 2.
Steric effect: Approach of a nucleophile is hindered by bulky substituents.
Aldehydes present a smaller steric profile, allowing easier nucleophilic attack. 3.
Catalysis: Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen by an acid increases the carbon’s electrophilicity; deprotonation of the nucleophile (e.g., generating CN⁻ from HCN) raises its nucleophilicity. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “sp³”) reveals the misconception that the carbon is already tetrahedral, confusing the starting material with the addition product.
remember: What is the hybridisation state of the carbonyl carbon in aldehydes and ketones before nucleophilic addition.
Explain why aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.
A student claims that treating acetaldehyde with NaCN followed by hydrolysis yields acetic acid. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Carboxylic acids (R‑COOH) are organic compounds containing a carbonyl carbon…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Carboxylic acids (R‑COOH) are organic compounds containing a carbonyl carbon double‑bonded to oxygen and single‑bonded to a hydroxyl group. Their acidity arises from the equilibrium R‑COOH ⇌ R‑COO⁻ + H⁺ with acid‑dissociation constant Ka = [R‑COO⁻][H⁺] / [R‑COOH] and pKa = –log₁₀ Ka. The conjugate base (carboxylate) is resonance‑stabilised: the negative charge delocalises over the two oxygens, lowering the energy of the anion and favouring dissociation. Electron‑withdrawing substituents (–Cl, –NO₂, –CF₃) increase acidity by stabilising the anion inductively; electron‑donating groups (–CH₃, –OCH₃) decrease it. Typical pKa values: formic acid 3.75, acetic acid 4.76, benzoic acid 4.20, chloroacetic acid 2.86. Key reactions of carboxylic acids (all proceed via the carbonyl carbon): 1. Esterification (Fischer): R‑COOH + R'‑OH ⇌ R‑COOR' + H₂O (acid‑catalysed, equilibrium). 2. Acid chloride formation: R‑COOH + SOCl₂ → R‑COCl + SO₂ + HCl. 3. Reduction: LiAlH₄ reduces –COOH to primary alcohol (R‑CH₂OH). 4. Decarboxylation (β‑keto acids, Kolbe’s electrolysis): R‑COOH → RH + CO₂. 5. Salt formation with bases (NaOH, NaHCO₃) giving water‑soluble carboxylates. 6. Hell‑Volhard‑Zelinsky (HVZ) α‑halogenation using Br₂/PBr₃. The acidity constant links structure to reactivity: stronger acids (lower pKa) give more reactive carboxylates in nucleophilic acyl substitution.
steps: Carboxylic acids are the most acidic common organic functional group because their conjugate base is resonance‑stabilised over two electronegative oxygens.

Here is why: the –COOH group can lose a proton to give a carboxylate anion where the negative charge is delocalised equally between the two oxygens, lowering the anion’s energy and shifting the equilibrium toward…
Consider acetic acid (CH₃COOH) in water: Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵, pKa = 4.76.
If we replace a hydrogen on the α‑carbon with chlorine, the –I effect pulls electron density away from the carboxylate, further stabilising it; chloroacetic acid’s Ka rises to 1.38 × 10⁻³ (pKa 2.86).
This inductive trend is predictable: more electronegative substituents → stronger acid.
In reactions, the carbonyl carbon remains electrophilic.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Ka = [R‑COOH] / ([R‑COO⁻][H⁺])) reveals the misconception that the equilibrium constant is written with reactants over products, confusing Ka with the reciprocal expression for the association constant.
remember: State the expression for the acid‑dissociation constant (Ka) of a generic carboxylic acid R‑COOH and define each term.
Explain why chloroacetic acid (ClCH₂COOH) is a stronger acid than acetic acid (CH₃COOH) using inductive effects.
Evaluate the claim: “Phenol is a stronger acid than benzoic acid because the phenoxide ion is resonance‑stabilised over the aromatic ring.”.

cards.title: Carboxylic acid derivatives are organic compounds in which the hydroxyl (‑OH)…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Carboxylic acid derivatives are organic compounds in which the hydroxyl (‑OH) group of a carboxylic acid (‑COOH) is replaced by another substituent X, giving the general structure R‑CO‑X. Common X groups include chloride (‑COCl, acyl chloride), acyloxy (‑CO‑OCOR, anhydride), alkoxy (‑CO‑OR, ester) and amino (‑CO‑NR₂, amide). The carbonyl carbon remains electrophilic, but now a leaving group (X) is attached, allowing nucleophilic acyl substitution: a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate, which then expels X⁻ to regenerate the carbonyl. Reactivity follows the order acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide, dictated by the leaving‑group ability of X (Cl⁻ is a weak base, good leaving group; ‑NH₂ is a strong base, poor leaving group) and the extent of resonance donation to the carbonyl (amide > ester > anhydride > acyl chloride). Preparation methods include: acyl chlorides from carboxylic acids with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) or phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅); anhydrides by dehydration of two acid molecules (e.g., acetic anhydride from acetyl chloride + acetate); esters via Fischer esterification (acid + alcohol, H⁺ catalyst) or from acyl chlorides/anhydrides + alcohol; amides from acyl chlorides/anhydrides + ammonia or amines, or from acids + amines with coupling agents. These reactions are the logical extension of the nucleophilic addition reactions studied for aldehydes/ketones, but differ because a leaving group permits substitution rather than addition. Understanding this hierarchy enables prediction of product outcomes in synthetic sequences involving acid derivatives.
steps: The reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophiles follows the order acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide due to the combined effects of leaving‑group ability and resonance stabilization.
Here is why: 1.
Leaving‑group ability determines how readily the X group departs after nucleophilic attack.
Chloride ion is a weak base (pKa of HCl ≈ –7) and thus an excellent leaving group, whereas amide nitrogen is a strong base (pKa of conjugate acid ≈ 10‑11) and a poor leaving group. 2.
Resonance donation from X into the carbonyl reduces electrophilicity.
In amides, the lone pair on nitrogen delocalises strongly onto the carbonyl carbon, giving significant double‑bond character to the C‑N bond and decreasing the carbonyl’s susceptibility to attack.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., R‑CHO) reveals the misconception that acyl chlorides are aldehydes, confusing the substituent (‑Cl) with a hydrogen atom and overlooking the retention of the carbonyl group bonded to chlorine.
remember: State the general molecular formula for an acyl chloride derived from a monocarboxylic acid R‑COOH.
Explain why acyl chlorides react more rapidly with nucleophiles than esters, using electronic and leaving‑group arguments.
A student asserts that amides hydrolyse as easily as esters under acidic conditions. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The Cannizzaro reaction is a base‑catalysed disproportionation of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The Cannizzaro reaction is a base‑catalysed disproportionation of non‑α‑hydrogen aldehydes (i.e., aldehydes with no α‑hydrogen atoms) into a primary alcohol and a carboxylate salt. Hydroxide ion adds to the carbonyl carbon of one aldehyde molecule forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. This intermediate transfers a hydride ion to a second aldehyde molecule, generating an alkoxide of the alcohol and a carboxylate anion. The reaction is overall: 2 RCHO + OH⁻ → RCH₂OH + RCOO⁻. It proceeds only for aldehydes lacking α‑hydrogens (e.g., formaldehyde, benzaldehyde, p‑nitrobenzaldehyde) because α‑hydrogen containing aldehydes prefer aldol condensation via enolate formation. Crossed Cannizzaro reactions use two different non‑α‑hydrogen aldehydes; the more electrophilic aldehyde (usually formaldehyde) is oxidised, while the other is reduced. Intramolecular Cannizzaro occurs with dialdehydes like glyoxal. The reaction is important industrially for producing polyols such as pentaerythritol (from formaldehyde and acetaldehyde via crossed Cannizzaro followed by aldol). This node builds on nucleophilic addition of hydroxide to carbonyls (node) and the concept of α‑hydrogen acidity (node).
steps: The Cannizzaro reaction is a base‑catalysed disproportionation where two molecules of a non‑α‑hydrogen aldehyde convert into one molecule of a primary alcohol and one molecule of a carboxylate salt.

Here is why: the absence of α‑hydrogen prevents enolate formation, so the aldehyde cannot undergo aldol condensation; instead, hydroxide adds to the carbonyl, and the resulting alkoxide donates a hydride to a second…
Consider the mechanism: (1) OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon of aldehyde A giving a tetrahedral alkoxide.
(2) This alkoxide transfers a hydride ion to the carbonyl carbon of aldehyde B, producing an alkoxide of the alcohol (from B) and a carboxylate (from A).
(3) Proton transfers from water yield the final alcohol and carboxylic acid salt.
For example, formaldehyde (HCHO) with concentrated NaOH gives methanol (CH₃OH) and sodium formate (HCOONa).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "any aldehyde with a carbonyl group undergoes Cannizzaro") reveals the misconception that the reaction is general for all aldehydes, ignoring the crucial role of α‑hydrogen in directing the pathway toward aldol condensation.
remember: Define the Cannizzaro reaction and state the structural requirement for an aldehyde to undergo it.
Explain why formaldehyde undergoes Cannizzaro reaction but acetaldehyde does not.
Compare the Cannizzaro reaction and the aldol condensation in terms of α‑hydrogen requirement, products, and catalyst.

cards.title: The haloform reaction is a base‑catalysed halogenation and cleavage of methyl…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The haloform reaction is a base‑catalysed halogenation and cleavage of methyl ketones (R‑CO‑CH₃) and acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) using halogen (Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) in aqueous alkali. The overall transformation converts the methyl carbonyl compound into a carboxylate anion (R‑COO⁻) and a haloform (CHX₃, where X = Cl, Br, I). The reaction proceeds via three successive α‑halogenations of the methyl group to give the trihalomethyl ketone (R‑CO‑CX₃), which is then attacked by hydroxide at the carbonyl carbon, cleaving the C‑C bond to yield the carboxylate and the trihalomethyl anion (CX₃⁻). The latter rapidly abstracts a proton from water to form the haloform (CHX₃). For iodine, the product iodoform (CHI₃) is a pale‑yellow crystalline solid with a characteristic antiseptic odour, making the iodoform test a standard qualitative tool for detecting the CH₃CO– moiety. The stoichiometry requires three equivalents of halogen and four equivalents of hydroxide per mole of methyl ketone. The reaction is irreversible under the conditions used and does not occur with ketones lacking α‑hydrogens on a methyl group (e.g., benzophenone) or with carboxylic acids/esters under the same conditions. The iodoform test is also positive for ethanol and secondary alcohols that oxidise to methyl ketones under the reaction conditions (e.g., isopropanol → acetone).
steps: The haloform reaction uniquely identifies the CH₃CO– group by converting it into a yellow precipitate of iodoform and a carboxylate.
Here is why: the reaction combines three α‑halogenations with a nucleophilic acyl substitution that cleaves a C‑C bond, a sequence that only occurs when a methyl group is attached to the carbonyl.
Consider acetone (CH₃COCH₃) treated with I₂/NaOH.
First, hydroxide abstracts an α‑hydrogen to form an enolate, which attacks I₂ to give CH₃COCH₂I.
This repeats twice more to yield CH₃COCI₃.
The electron‑withdrawing CI₃ group makes the carbonyl carbon highly electrophilic; hydroxide adds to give a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses, expelling the trihalomethyl anion (CI₃⁻).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the product is the carboxylate") reveals the misconception that the anion remains as an ion — confusing the fate of the two fragments after C‑C bond cleavage.
remember: What is the immediate organic product formed when the trihalomethyl anion (CX₃⁻) abstracts a proton from water in the haloform reaction.
Why does benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO) not give a positive iodoform test, while acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) does.
A student claims that the iodoform test can distinguish between propanone (acetone) and butan‑2‑one (methyl ethyl ketone). Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: This node consolidates the synthetic toolkit for aldehydes, ketones…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: This node consolidates the synthetic toolkit for aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids covered in nodes 002‑007 and translates it into the patterns that appear in CISCE ISC Class 12 Chemistry papers. It defines the reagent‑product map for key transformations: oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes (PCC, DMP) and to acids (KMnO₄, CrO₃/H₂SO₄), oxidation of secondary alcohols to ketones (PCC, PDC), reduction of carbonyls (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄), nucleophilic addition of Grignard reagents, cyanide, and bisulfite, and the interconversion of acids, esters, and acid chlorides. It also specifies the typical ISC question archetypes — short‑answer reagent identification, mechanism drawing with arrow‑pushing, numerical yield calculations (theoretical, actual, percentage), and multi‑step synthesis design — and the marking scheme (1 mark per correct reagent, 2 marks for a complete mechanism, 3 marks for a balanced yield calculation with units). The node links each synthetic decision to the underlying electronic and steric factors taught earlier, and it emphasizes the exam‑level precision required: SI units (mol, g, dm³), significant figures (minimum three), and correct structural representation (condensed or skeletal). It does not re‑teach mechanisms or acidity trends; those remain in their respective concept nodes.
steps: Mastering ISC aldehyde‑ketone‑acid synthesis means recognizing the reagent‑product map, spotting the question archetype, and executing yield calculations with correct significant figures.

First, the reagent‑product map is a mental lookup table: PCC/DMP stop at aldehydes, KMnO₄/H₂SO₄ push to acids, NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes/ketones but not esters, LiAlH₄ reduces acids/esters to alcohols, Grignard adds to…
Second, ISC papers recycle four question archetypes — reagent identification (1 mark), mechanism drawing (2 marks), numerical yield (3 marks), and multi‑step synthesis (4‑5 marks).

Third, yield calculations follow a fixed stoichiometric pathway: write balanced equation, convert given mass to moles (molar mass in g mol⁻¹), use mole ratio to find theoretical moles of product, convert to grams, then…
Fourth, common traps include using KMnO₄ for a sensitive aldehyde (over‑oxidation), forgetting aqueous work‑up after Grignard addition, and reporting yield without units.
Fifth, time management: allocate ~1 min per mark; a 3‑mark yield problem deserves ~3 minutes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “KMnO₄ in acidic medium”) reveals the misconception that all strong oxidising agents can be tuned to stop at the aldehyde; in reality, KMnO₄ under aqueous conditions continues to the acid.
remember: Name the reagent that selectively oxidises a primary alcohol to an aldehyde without further oxidation to the carboxylic acid.
Explain why sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) reduces aldehydes and ketones but does not reduce esters under normal conditions.
A student proposes using hot, concentrated KMnO₄ to oxidise a secondary alcohol to a ketone. Evaluate the suitability of this reagent for that transformation.

cards.title: Chapter 9 of the ISC Class 12 Physical Chemistry syllabus covers organic…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Chapter 9 of the ISC Class 12 Physical Chemistry syllabus covers organic compounds that contain nitrogen as a functional group. The major sub‑topics are: (1) Amines – classification into primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary based on the number of carbon‑bound substituents on nitrogen; their preparation via reduction of nitro compounds, ammonolysis of alkyl halides, Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, and Hofmann rearrangement; and their basicity trends governed by inductive, resonance, and solvation effects. (2) Diazonium salts – formation from aromatic primary amines by diazotisation (NaNO₂/HCl, 0‑5 °C), stability differences between aliphatic and aromatic diazonium ions, and their synthetic utility in Sandmeyer, Gattermann, and coupling reactions to introduce –Cl, –Br, –CN, –OH, –NO₂, and azo dyes. (3) Cyanides and isocyanides – nomenclature, preparation (dehydration of formamides for isocyanides, nucleophilic substitution for cyanides), and characteristic reactions (hydrolysis to acids/amides, reduction to amines, addition to carbonyls). The chapter emphasises structure‑property relationships, reaction mechanisms, and the strategic importance of nitrogen functionalities in synthesis, drug design, and the dye industry.
steps: The chapter is a toolbox of nitrogen‑based functional groups that lets you build medicines, dyes, and polymers by mastering three pillars: amine classification and basicity, diazonium salt chemistry, and…
Here is why: nitrogen’s lone pair makes it a versatile nucleophile and base, but its behaviour changes dramatically with hybridisation and substituents.
First, amines are sorted by how many carbons attach to nitrogen — primary (one), secondary (two), tertiary (three), quaternary (four, positively charged).

This classification predicts basicity: aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because alkyl groups donate electron density inductively, while aromatic amines are weaker because the lone pair delocalises into…

Second, aromatic primary amines undergo diazotisation with nitrous acid at 0‑5 °C to give diazonium salts, which are stable enough to be isolated but reactive enough to undergo Sandmeyer (CuX), Gattermann (Cu/HX), and…

Third, cyanides (R‑CN) and isocyanides (R‑NC) differ only in the point of attachment of the carbon/nitrogen triple bond; this small change flips their reactivity — cyanides act as nucleophiles at carbon, isocyanides at…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary based on hydrogen count”) reveals the misconception that classification depends on hydrogen atoms rather than carbon groups — the defining criterion is the number of alkyl/aryl groups bonded…
remember: Name the four classes of amines based on the number of carbon substituents attached to nitrogen.
Explain why aniline is a weaker base than cyclohexylamine, referring to electronic effects.
Evaluate the statement: “Aliphatic diazonium salts are stable enough to be isolated and used in synthesis like aromatic diazonium salts.”.

cards.title: An amine is an organic derivative of ammonia (NH₃) in which one or more…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: An amine is an organic derivative of ammonia (NH₃) in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. Classification depends on the number of carbon‑containing substituents attached to the nitrogen atom. A primary (1°) amine has one alkyl/aryl group (R‑NH₂); a secondary (2°) amine has two (R₂NH); a tertiary (3°) amine has three (R₃N). When nitrogen forms four σ‑bonds to carbon groups, it bears a formal positive charge and exists as a quaternary ammonium cation (R₄N⁺) paired with an anion (e.g., Cl⁻). The nitrogen in amines is sp³ hybridised with a lone pair, giving a pyramidal geometry (≈107° bond angle). Nomenclature follows IUPAC: the parent alkane name receives the suffix “‑amine” with a locant for the carbon bearing the –NH₂ group (e.g., propan‑1‑amine). For secondary and tertiary amines, the largest alkyl group is chosen as the parent and the smaller groups are named as N‑substituents (e.g., N‑methylethanamine). Aromatic amines (anilines) are named as derivatives of aniline (aminobenzene). Classification influences physical properties (boiling point, solubility) and chemical reactivity (basicity, nucleophilicity, acylation). This node covers only the structural classification and naming; preparation methods, basicity trends, diazonium chemistry, and cyanide/isocyanide chemistry are treated in subsequent nodes.
steps: The class of an amine is defined solely by how many carbon groups are bonded to the nitrogen atom, and this count dictates its name, shape, and chemical behaviour.
First, counting substituents on nitrogen directly yields the class: one carbon group → primary (R‑NH₂), two → secondary (R₂NH), three → tertiary (R₃N), four → quaternary ammonium (R₄N⁺).

Second, IUPAC naming rules diverge with class: primary amines use the “‑amine” suffix on the parent chain (propan‑1‑amine); secondary and tertiary amines treat the largest alkyl group as the parent and prefix the…
Third, hybridisation remains sp³ for 1°–3° amines, giving a pyramidal geometry, but quaternary nitrogen becomes tetrahedral with no lone pair.

Fourth, physical properties follow the substitution pattern: boiling points rise with increasing alkyl bulk due to stronger van der Waals forces, yet hydrogen‑bonding ability drops from primary (two N‑H bonds) to…
Fifth, gas‑phase basicity increases with electron‑donating alkyl groups (3° > 2° > 1°), while aqueous basicity is modulated by solvation, often giving 2° > 1° > 3°.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing (b)) reveals the misconception that two alkyl groups already make a tertiary amine, confusing secondary with tertiary classification.
remember: Which of the following is a tertiary amine? (a) CH₃NH₂ (b) (CH₃)₂NH (c) (CH₃)₃N (d) CH₃CH₂NH₂.
Explain why N‑methylethanamine is classified as a secondary amine even though its carbon skeleton contains two carbon atoms in the ethyl group.
A student claims that quaternary ammonium salts are amines. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Preparation of nitrogen‑containing organic compounds in this chapter covers…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Preparation of nitrogen‑containing organic compounds in this chapter covers four families: amines (aliphatic and aromatic), diazonium salts, cyanides, and isocyanides. Amines are accessed mainly by reduction of nitro compounds (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, catalytic H₂), nucleophilic substitution of alkyl halides with ammonia (ammonolysis), Gabriel phthalimide synthesis (phthalimide anion + alkyl halide → primary amine after hydrolysis), Hofmann bromamide degradation (amide + Br₂/NaOH → primary amine with one fewer carbon), reductive amination (aldehyde/ketone + NH₃ + H₂/Ni), and reduction of nitriles (LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni). Diazonium salts are prepared by diazotization: a primary aromatic amine reacts with NaNO₂/HCl at 0‑5 °C to give the diazonium chloride. Alkyl cyanides (nitriles) are obtained via SN2 displacement of halogen in alkyl halides by KCN, by dehydration of primary amides (P₂O₅ or POCl₃), or from cyanohydrins of aldehydes. Isocyanides (isonitriles) are synthesized by the carbylamine reaction: a primary amine + chloroform + base (KOH) → isocyanide + 3KCl + 3H₂O. Each method exploits a core transformation — reduction, nucleophilic substitution, or diazotization — and the choice depends on the target amine class (primary, secondary, tertiary) and carbon skeleton.
steps: The preparation of nitrogen‑containing organic compounds relies on a few core transformations — reduction, nucleophilic substitution, and diazotization — that convert readily available precursors into amines, diazonium…

First, reduction of nitro groups is the classic route to aromatic amines: nitrobenzene + Sn/HCl (or Fe/HCl, or H₂/Pd) gives aniline; the same reagents reduce aliphatic nitro compounds to aliphatic amines.

Second, nucleophilic substitution of alkyl halides with ammonia (ammonolysis) yields a mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and quaternary ammonium salts; using excess ammonia favours the primary amine.

Third, the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis circumvents over‑alkylation: potassium phthalimide undergoes SN2 with an alkyl halide, and subsequent hydrazinolysis or alkaline hydrolysis releases the primary amine cleanly.

Fourth, Hofmann bromamide degradation shortens the carbon chain by one: a primary amide treated with Br₂/NaOH loses the carbonyl carbon as CO₂, giving a primary amine with one fewer carbon — a key exam trap because the…
Fifth, reductive amination of aldehydes/ketones with ammonia and H₂/Ni (or NaBH₃CN) installs an amino group directly onto a carbonyl carbon, preserving the carbon skeleton.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “LiAlH₄”) reveals the misconception that any strong reducing agent works — LiAlH₄ does reduce nitro groups but is not the conventional lab method for aromatic nitro reduction and can give side products.
remember: Name the reagent combination used in the laboratory to reduce nitrobenzene to aniline.
Why does Gabriel phthalimide synthesis yield only primary amines.
Compare the suitability of reduction of nitriles versus reductive amination for preparing a primary amine with one extra carbon.

cards.title: Basicity of an amine is its tendency to accept a proton from water…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Basicity of an amine is its tendency to accept a proton from water, forming its conjugate acid and hydroxide ion. Quantitatively, it is expressed by the base‑dissociation constant K_b = ([BH^+][OH^-])/([B]), where [B] is the concentration of the free amine, [BH^+] that of its protonated form, and [OH^-] the hydroxide concentration; K_b is dimensionless. The negative logarithm, pK_b = - K_b, provides a convenient scale (lower pK_b = stronger base). Basicity is inversely related to the acidity of the conjugate acid: pK_a(BH^+) + pK_b(B) = pK_w = 14.00 at 25 °C (ionic product of water). Structural factors modulate basicity: electron‑donating alkyl groups increase electron density on nitrogen, raising K_b; electron‑withdrawing groups (e.g., –NO₂, –COOH) decrease it. Aromatic amines are far less basic than aliphatic ones because the lone pair delocalises into the benzene ring, reducing its availability for protonation. Steric hindrance around nitrogen also lowers basicity by impeding solvation of the conjugate acid. Solvation in water stabilises BH^+ and OH^-, enhancing observed basicity.
steps: The basicity of an amine is determined by the availability of its lone pair for protonation, which is modulated by electronic, steric, and solvation effects.
Here is why: 1.

Electronic effect – Alkyl groups donate electron density through +I effect, increasing the electron density on nitrogen and making the lone pair more basic; aryl groups withdraw via resonance, decreasing basicity. 2.
Steric effect – Bulky substituents hinder approach of a proton and destabilise the solvated conjugate acid, lowering observed basicity. 3.
Solvation effect – Water stabilises the ions BH^+ and OH^-; amines that form better‑solvated conjugate acids show higher basicity.
Consider a simple equilibrium set‑up: a known concentration of amine (e.g., 0.10 mol L⁻¹ ethylamine) is mixed with distilled water at 25 °C.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “K_b has units of mol L⁻¹”) reveals the misconception that equilibrium constants retain the units of concentration, ignoring that they are ratios of activities (or concentrations) and thus unitless.
remember: Define the base‑dissociation constant K_b for an amine and state its units.
Explain why aniline is a weaker base than cyclohexylamine, using electronic and resonance arguments.
A student claims that increasing the number of alkyl groups on nitrogen always increases basicity. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Diazonium salts are aromatic compounds bearing the –N₂⁺X⁻ functional group
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Diazonium salts are aromatic compounds bearing the –N₂⁺X⁻ functional group (X⁻ = Cl⁻, Br⁻, BF₄⁻, etc.), formed by the diazotization of primary aromatic amines (ArNH₂) with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO₂ and a strong acid) at 0–5 °C. The reaction proceeds via nitrosation of the amine to an N‑nitrosoamine, followed by protonation and loss of water to give the diazonium cation. The counter‑ion influences stability: chloride and bromide salts are moderately stable as solids at low temperature; tetrafluoroborate and hexafluorophosphate salts are more stable and can be isolated. Diazonium salts undergo two major reaction classes: (1) nucleophilic substitution (Sandmeyer, Gattermann, and related reactions) where the –N₂⁺ group is replaced by Cl, Br, CN, OH, etc., with loss of N₂; (2) electrophilic aromatic substitution (coupling) with activated arenes (phenols, anilines) to form azo dyes. The –N₂⁺ group is a powerful electron‑withdrawing group, making the aromatic ring highly susceptible to electrophilic attack at the para/ortho positions. Temperature control is critical because diazonium cations decompose via SN1 or radical pathways to give phenols, aryl cations, or biaryls. Understanding diazonium chemistry links amine basicity (node 09_004) to synthetic routes for halides, cyanides, phenols, and azo compounds (node 09_006).
steps: Diazonium salts are the key versatile intermediates that allow direct replacement of the amino group on an aromatic ring with a variety of substituents under mild conditions.

Here is why: the –NH₂ group is a strong ortho/para director but cannot be directly displaced; diazotization converts it into a superb leaving group (N₂) that departs spontaneously, generating an aryl cation or radical…
First, the amine is dissolved in excess mineral acid (usually HCl) and cooled to 0–5 °C.
Sodium nitrite is added slowly; the nitrous acid formed nitrosates the amine, and after protonation and dehydration the diazonium chloride precipitates or stays in solution.
The low temperature suppresses decomposition to phenol (via water attack) or biaryl (via radical coupling).

Second, the choice of counter‑ion matters: chloride is convenient for Sandmeyer reactions with CuCl/CuBr/CuCN; tetrafluoroborate gives a crystalline, shelf‑stable salt that can be filtered and stored briefly at –20 °C.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “NaNO₃ + H₂SO₄”) reveals the misconception that any nitrite/nitrate salt with acid works; nitrate does not generate nitrous acid under these conditions.
remember: What reagent combination generates nitrous acid in situ for the diazotization of aniline.
Why is the diazotization of aniline performed at 0–5 °C rather than at room temperature.
Compare the stability and handling of benzenediazonium chloride versus benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate.

cards.title: Cyanides (nitriles) are organic compounds containing the –C≡N functional group…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Cyanides (nitriles) are organic compounds containing the –C≡N functional group where the carbon of the triple bond is bonded to an alkyl or aryl group (R‑C≡N). Isocyanides (isonitriles) are structural isomers with the –N≡C group bonded through nitrogen (R‑N≡C). Both are derived from the same molecular formula (R‑CN) but differ in connectivity, giving distinct physical and chemical properties. Cyanides are prepared mainly by nucleophilic substitution of alkyl halides with KCN (SN2) or by dehydration of primary amides (P₂O₅, SOCl₂). Isocyanides arise from the reaction of primary amines with chloroform and base (carbylamine reaction) or from alkyl halides with AgCN (the “silver cyanide” route, which favours the isocyanide due to the softer Ag⁺ ion). Hydrolysis of cyanides under acidic or basic conditions yields carboxylic acids (or their salts) and ammonia; reduction (LiAlH₄, H₂/Ni) gives primary amines. Isocyanides hydrolyse to give primary amines and formic acid derivatives, and they undergo addition reactions at the carbon of the –N≡C group (e.g., with Grignard reagents). A key diagnostic test: the carbylamine reaction (primary amine + CHCl₃ + KOH → foul‑smelling isocyanide) confirms primary amines; cyanides do not give this test. Infrared spectroscopy shows a sharp C≡N stretch near 2250 cm⁻¹ for cyanides and a broader N≡C stretch near 2150 cm⁻¹ for isocyanides.
steps: The key takeaway is that cyanides and isocyanides are constitutional isomers differing only in the atom (C vs N) attached to the carbon chain, and this single connectivity change flips their reactivity, odour and…

First, the connectivity dictates the site of nucleophilic attack: in nitriles the electrophilic carbon of the C≡N bond is attacked, leading to hydrolysis to acids or reduction to amines; in isocyanides the carbon of the…

Second, the choice of cyanide source controls the product: KCN (hard K⁺) favours carbon attack giving nitriles, while AgCN (soft Ag⁺) favours nitrogen attack giving isocyanides – a classic illustration of HSAB theory.
