cards.title: In Java, a statement is the smallest executable unit that performs an action.
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In Java, a statement is the smallest executable unit that performs an action. Statements terminate with a semicolon (`;`) and can be grouped into blocks using braces (`{ }`). Major categories include expression statements (assignments, method calls, increment/decrement), declaration statements (introducing variables with optional initialization), control‑flow statements (`if`, `switch`, `for`, `while`, `do‑while`, `break`, `continue`, `return`), and the empty statement (`;`). A block is itself a statement that defines a new scope for variables. Statements execute sequentially unless redirected by control‑flow constructs. They differ from expressions, which produce values, because statements produce side‑effects (state change, I/O, control transfer). The Java Language Specification defines the grammar for each statement type, and the compiler checks for reachability and definite assignment. Understanding statements is prerequisite for mastering method bodies, constructors, and the scope rules covered in the next node.
steps: A statement is a complete command to the Java runtime, always ending with a semicolon or a brace‑enclosed block.
Here is why: every executable line in a method body must be a statement; without it the compiler cannot generate bytecode.
First, expression statements evaluate an expression for its side‑effect — assignment (`x = 5;`), method call (`System.out.println("Hello");`), or increment (`i++;`).
Second, declaration statements introduce variables (`int count = 0;`) and optionally initialise them; they also end with a semicolon.
Third, control‑flow statements direct execution: `if (mark >= 40) pass = true;` chooses a path, `for (int i=0;i<5;i++) sum+=i;` repeats a block, `return result;` exits a method.
Fourth, a block (`{ int tmp = a; a = b; b = tmp; }`) groups statements and creates a local scope.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing only B) reveals the misconception that only declarations need semicolons, ignoring that every expression statement must end with `;`.
remember: Which of the following is a valid Java statement? A) `int x = 10` B) `int x = 10;` C) `x = 10` D) `x = 10;`.
Explain why the following code fragment causes a compile‑time error: ```java if (a > b) int temp = a; a = b; b = temp; ```.

cards.title: In Java, scope defines the region of source code where a variable name is…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In Java, scope defines the region of source code where a variable name is visible and can be referenced. The language distinguishes four principal scopes: block scope, method (local) scope, class (instance) scope, and class (static) scope. A variable declared inside a pair of braces `{ … }` — such as in an `if`, `for`, `while`, or a standalone block — has block scope and ceases to exist when the block ends. A variable declared as a formal parameter or inside a method body but not inside a nested block has method scope; it is accessible throughout the method after its declaration. Instance variables (non‑static fields) belong to each object and are accessible from any non‑static method of the class, while static variables belong to the class itself and are shared across all instances. Shadowing occurs when a variable in an inner scope has the same name as one in an outer scope; the inner variable hides the outer one for the duration of the inner scope. Lifetime — the period during which storage exists — is tied to scope for local variables (created on entry, destroyed on exit) but differs for fields (instance variables live as long as the object lives; static variables live for the program’s duration). Understanding scope prevents accidental reuse of names, avoids “variable not found” compile errors, and underpins encapsulation.
steps: In Java, a variable’s scope determines exactly where in the program the variable can be accessed, and it is fixed at compile time.
Here is why: the compiler enforces scope rules to guarantee that every name resolves to a unique declaration, preventing ambiguous references.
Consider a typical class `StudentRecord` with an instance field `int rollNo;` (instance scope) and a static field `static String schoolName = "KV";` (static scope).
Inside a method `void printDetails()`, a local variable `String localName = "Anita";` has method scope.
If the method contains a `for` loop `for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String temp = "temp" + i;
System.out.println(temp); }`, the variable `i` and `temp` have block scope limited to the loop body; they vanish after the closing brace.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “`k` is visible throughout the method”) reveals the misconception that loop headers behave like method‑level declarations, confusing block scope with method scope.

cards.title: A method in Java is a named block of code that performs a specific task and…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A method in Java is a named block of code that performs a specific task and optionally returns a value. It is defined by a signature comprising an access modifier (public, private, protected), optional specifiers (static, final, abstract), a return type (primitive, reference, or void), a method name, and a parameter list enclosed in parentheses. The method body, enclosed in braces, contains statements that execute when the method is invoked. Methods enable modularity, reuse, and abstraction: a caller supplies arguments matching the parameter types, the method executes within its own stack frame, and control returns to the caller with a value if the return type is not void. Overloading allows multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists; the compiler resolves the call at compile time based on argument types. Instance methods operate on an object's state and can access instance variables and the implicit `this` reference; static methods belong to the class, cannot use `this`, and are invoked via the class name. Method calls create a new activation record on the call stack, preserving local variables and the return address. Access modifiers control visibility across classes and packages, while the `final` specifier prevents overriding. The `return` statement terminates execution and optionally supplies a value compatible with the declared return type. Understanding method signatures, parameter passing (by value for primitives, by reference for objects), and the distinction between static and instance contexts is essential for designing clear, maintainable Java programs.
steps: A method is a reusable code block that accepts inputs, performs work, and optionally produces an output.
Here is why: methods turn repeated logic into a single definition, reducing errors and making programs easier to read.
First, the signature tells the compiler what the method expects and what it gives back; the parameter list defines the types and order of values the caller must supply.
Second, the body executes in its own stack frame, so local variables are isolated from the caller — this is why changes to primitive parameters do not affect the caller’s variables.

Third, overloading lets you provide several ways to do a similar task, such as `area(int side)` for a square and `area(int length, int breadth)` for a rectangle; the compiler picks the matching overload at compile time.
Fourth, static methods belong to the class and are called with `ClassName.method()`, while instance methods need an object and can use `this` to refer to the current object.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `public void add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`) reveals the misconception that a `void` method can return a value — `void` methods cannot use `return` with an expression.

cards.title: A static member in Java is a field, method, block…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A static member in Java is a field, method, block, or nested class declared with the `static` keyword. It is associated with the class itself rather than with any instance. Consequently, static fields (class variables) exist as a single copy in memory, shared by all instances. Static methods can be invoked without creating an object and can only access static members directly; they cannot use `this` or `super`. Static initialization blocks execute once when the class is loaded, before any objects are created. Static nested classes behave like top‑level classes but reside inside another class’s namespace. Static members enable utility functions, constants, counters, and shared state across objects. They interact with instance members: instance methods may access static members freely, but static methods cannot access instance members without an object reference. The `static` modifier also applies to imports (`import static`) allowing direct use of static members without class qualification. Understanding static members is essential for designing singletons, factories, and memory‑efficient APIs.
steps: Static members belong to the class, not to any object, so they are created once when the class loads and shared by all instances.
Here is why: the JVM allocates a single memory slot for each static field in the method area, whereas each object gets its own copy of instance fields in the heap.
First, consider a counter that tracks how many `Student` objects exist.
Declaring `static int count = 0;` inside `Student` and incrementing it in the constructor ensures every new object sees the same updated value.
Second, utility methods like `Math.sqrt` are static because they perform calculations without needing object state; they can be called as `Math.sqrt(25)` without a `Math` instance.
Third, static initialization blocks (`static { … }`) run once during class loading, ideal for one‑time setup such as loading a native library or initializing a complex constant.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 11) reveals the misconception that each object gets its own copy of a static field, confusing static with instance variables.

cards.title: The this keyword in Java is a reference variable that always points to the…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: The this keyword in Java is a reference variable that always points to the current instance of the class whose method or constructor is being executed. It is implicitly available inside every non‑static method and constructor. Its primary uses are: (1) disambiguating instance variables from parameters or local variables that share the same name; (2) invoking another constructor of the same class (constructor chaining) via `this(...)` as the first statement; (3) returning the current object from a method to enable method chaining; (4) passing the current object as an argument to another method or constructor. Because static members belong to the class rather than any instance, this cannot be used in a static context. The reference is final — it cannot be reassigned. Understanding this is essential for writing clear, maintainable object‑oriented code and for correctly implementing patterns such as builders, fluent interfaces, and observer registration.
steps: The this keyword is the built‑in reference that every object holds to itself, allowing the object to refer to its own fields and methods without ambiguity.

Here is why: when a method parameter shares a name with an instance variable, the parameter shadows the field; prefixing the field with `this.` tells the compiler “use the object’s own field.” Consider a `Student` class…
Inside the setter, `this.name = name;` assigns the parameter to the instance field.
Next, constructor chaining: a class may have multiple constructors.
The no‑argument constructor can call `this("Unknown", 0);` to delegate to the parameterised constructor, avoiding code duplication.
This call must be the first statement.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it refers to the class itself”) reveals the misconception that this is a class‑level reference like `ClassName.class`, confusing instance context with static context.

cards.title: An array in Java is a fixed‑size…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: An array in Java is a fixed‑size, homogeneous data structure that stores elements of a single type in contiguous memory locations. A single‑dimensional array is a linear sequence accessed by one zero‑based index, e.g. `int[] scores = new int[10];` creates ten `int` cells initialised to `0`. A multi‑dimensional array is implemented as an array of arrays; `int[][] matrix = new int[3][4];` yields three row‑arrays each of length four. The `length` field gives the size of the first dimension (`matrix.length == 3`) and each row’s length (`matrix[0].length == 4`). Elements are accessed as `matrix[row][col]`. Arrays are objects, so assignment copies the reference, not the contents. The memory layout is row‑major by default, meaning rows are stored consecutively; this underpins the address‑calculation concepts covered in the next nodes. Basic operations — declaration, instantiation, initialization, traversal with loops, and reading `length` — form the foundation for sorting, searching, and recursion algorithms later in the chapter.
steps: Arrays in Java are fixed‑size containers that store elements of the same type in contiguous memory, accessed by zero‑based indices.
First, a single‑dimensional array maps directly to a linear sequence of cells; the statement `int[] marks = new int[5];` allocates five `int` slots initialised to `0`.

Second, a multi‑dimensional array is an array of arrays; `int[][] timetable = new int[5][6];` creates five row‑arrays each of length six, so `timetable[2][3]` refers to the fourth period of the third day. Third, the…
Fourth, array literals (`int[] primes = {2,3,5,7};`) combine declaration and initialization in one line.
Fifth, because arrays are objects, `int[] copy = original;` makes both variables point to the same heap object — changes through `copy` affect `original`.
Consider a practical example: storing marks of 30 students for 5 subjects.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “garbage values” or “null”) reveals the misconception that Java behaves like C/C++ where uninitialised memory contains indeterminate data; in Java, array creation guarantees zero‑initialisation for primitives.

cards.title: Row‑major address calculation determines the linear memory address of an…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Row‑major address calculation determines the linear memory address of an element `A[i][j]` in a two‑dimensional array declared as `A[rows][cols]`. The base address `BA` is the address of `A[0][0]`. Each element occupies `W` bytes (size of the data type). In row‑major layout the elements of row 0 occupy the first `cols` positions, row 1 the next `cols`, etc. Therefore the offset of `A[i][j]` from the base is `(i cols + j) W`. The absolute address is `BA + (i cols + j) W`. This formula extends to higher dimensions by nesting the same logic: for a 3‑D array `A[d1][d2][d3]` the offset becomes `((i d2 + j) d3 + k) W`. Row‑major is the default layout in Java, C, and C++; column‑major (covered in the next node) stores columns contiguously. Understanding the relationship between logical indices and physical offsets is essential for pointer arithmetic, memory‑efficient algorithms, and interfacing with low‑level APIs.
steps: The one thing to remember: In row‑major order the address of `A[i][j]` equals the base address plus `(i number_of_columns + j) element_size`.
Here is why: memory is a one‑dimensional sequence of bytes.

When a 2‑D array is allocated, the compiler linearises it by placing all columns of row 0, then all columns of row 1, and so on. Consider `int marks[3][4];` – three rows, four columns, each `int` occupies 4 bytes.
The base address `BA` points to `marks[0][0]`.
Row 0 occupies bytes `BA` to `BA + 44 - 1`.
Row 1 starts at `BA + 44`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `BA + (i + j) W`) reveals the misconception that rows and columns contribute additively rather than multiplicatively, ignoring that each row spans `C` elements.
remember: What is the row‑major address formula for a 2‑D array `A[R][C]` with base address `BA` and element size `W`.
Given `int matrix[4][6];` with base address 2000, what is the address of `matrix[2][3]`? (Assume `int` = 4 bytes.).
A student writes the address of `A[i][j][k]` in a 3‑D array `A[D1][D2][D3]` as `BA + (iD2D3 + jD3 + k)`. Is this correct? Explain.

cards.title: Column‑major order is a linearisation scheme for multi‑dimensional arrays where…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Column‑major order is a linearisation scheme for multi‑dimensional arrays where the leftmost index (column) varies slowest and the rightmost index (row) varies fastest. For a two‑dimensional array `A[rows][cols]` with base address `B`, element size `w` bytes, and zero‑based indices `i` (row) and `j` (column), the address of `A[i][j]` is `B + w (j rows + i)`. This contrasts with row‑major order (covered in node) where the row index varies slowest. Column‑major is the native layout in languages such as Fortran and in mathematical libraries (e.g., BLAS), and it influences cache performance when algorithms traverse arrays column‑wise. Understanding the formula enables correct address calculation for pointer arithmetic, memory‑mapped I/O, and interfacing with external libraries that expect column‑major layout.
steps: The key takeaway is that in column‑major order the column index multiplies the number of rows, so the address grows by whole columns before moving to the next row. Here is why: memory is a one‑dimensional sequence of…

In column‑major the first column occupies the first `rows` slots, the second column the next `rows` slots, and so on. Consider a 3 × 4 integer array (`rows=3`, `cols=4`, `w=4` bytes) with base address 1000.
The element `A[0][0]` is at 1000. `A[1][0]` follows at 1004, `A[2][0]` at 1008.
The next column starts at `A[0][1]` = 1012, which equals `1000 + 4 (13 + 0)`.
The pattern continues: each new column adds `rows w` bytes.
A common exam trap is forgetting that the row count, not the column count, multiplies the column index.

cards.title: Bubble sort is a simple comparison‑based sorting algorithm that repeatedly…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Bubble sort is a simple comparison‑based sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through an array, compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. The pass‑through is repeated until no swaps are needed, which means the array is sorted. Each complete pass places the next largest element at its final position at the end of the unsorted portion, so the inner loop can shrink by one each iteration. The algorithm has a worst‑case and average time complexity of O(n²) and a best‑case of O(n) when the array is already sorted and an optimisation flag stops early. It is stable (equal elements keep their relative order) and in‑place (requires only O(1) extra space). Bubble sort is primarily taught for its conceptual clarity and as a baseline to understand more efficient sorts such as selection sort and insertion sort, which are covered in the next nodes.
steps: Bubble sort works by repeatedly bubbling the largest unsorted element to its correct position at the end of the array.
Here is why: each pass compares adjacent pairs and swaps them when the left element is greater, so the largest element “bubbles” rightwards until it settles at the last unsorted index.
Consider an array `int[] a = {5, 1, 4, 2, 8}`.
Pass 1: compare 5 and 1 → swap → {1,5,4,2,8}; compare 5 and 4 → swap → {1,4,5,2,8}; compare 5 and 2 → swap → {1,4,2,5,8}; compare 5 and 8 → no swap.
Largest element 8 is now at index 4.
Pass 2 ignores index 4: compare 1 and 4 → no swap; compare 4 and 2 → swap → {1,2,4,5,8}; compare 4 and 5 → no swap.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `if (a[j] < a[j+1])`) reveals the misconception that the algorithm moves smaller elements rightwards instead of larger elements leftwards, confusing the direction of bubbling.
remember: What is the primary condition used to decide a swap in bubble sort when sorting in ascending order.
Explain why bubble sort is considered a stable sorting algorithm.
Evaluate the claim: “Bubble sort always performs exactly n‑1 passes regardless of input.”.

cards.title: Selection sort is an in‑place comparison sorting algorithm that divides the…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Selection sort is an in‑place comparison sorting algorithm that divides the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix. At each pass i (0 ≤ i < n‑1) it scans the unsorted suffix A[i…n‑1] to locate the index minIdx of the minimum element, then swaps A[i] with A[minIdx]. After the swap the element at position i is in its final sorted position and the sorted prefix grows by one. The algorithm performs exactly n‑1 passes, each requiring a linear scan of the remaining unsorted part, yielding a time complexity of Θ(n²) comparisons and at most n‑1 swaps. Space complexity is O(1) auxiliary. Unlike bubble sort, selection sort minimizes data movement, making it useful when writes are costly. It is not stable because equal elements may change relative order during swaps. The algorithm works on any mutable indexed collection (arrays, ArrayList) and is a classic example of the “select‑and‑place” paradigm, contrasting with insertion sort’s “insert‑into‑place” approach.
steps: Selection sort builds the sorted array one position at a time by repeatedly selecting the smallest remaining element and swapping it into place.
Here is why: the algorithm maintains the invariant that the subarray A[0…i‑1] is sorted and contains the i smallest elements in their final positions, while A[i…n‑1] holds the unsorted remainder.
Consider an array of six integers representing the marks of six students: [72, 45, 58, 91, 33, 67].
Pass 0 scans indices 0‑5, finds the minimum 33 at index 4, swaps A[0] and A[4] → [33, 45, 58, 91, 72, 67].
Pass 1 scans indices 1‑5, minimum is 45 already at index 1, swap with itself → no change.
Pass 2 scans indices 2‑5, minimum 58 at index 2 → no change.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “n² comparisons”) reveals the misconception that the inner loop always runs n times, ignoring the shrinking unsorted suffix.
remember: What is the number of comparisons performed by selection sort on an array of size n.
Explain why selection sort is not a stable sorting algorithm.

cards.title: Insertion sort is a simple, stable, in‑place comparison‑based sorting algorithm.
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Insertion sort is a simple, stable, in‑place comparison‑based sorting algorithm. It maintains a sorted sub‑array `arr[0…i‑1]` and iteratively inserts `arr[i]` into this sub‑array by shifting all greater elements one position rightwards. The algorithm runs two nested loops: the outer loop index `i` runs from `1` to `n‑1`; the inner loop moves backwards from `i‑1` while `arr[j] > key`. After the inner loop terminates, `key` is placed at `arr[j+1]`. Time complexity is `O(n²)` in worst and average cases, `O(n)` when the input is already sorted (best case). Space complexity is `O(1)` auxiliary. Because it only swaps adjacent elements when necessary, it is stable — equal elements retain their original relative order. Insertion sort is preferred for small or nearly sorted data sets and serves as the basis for more advanced algorithms such as Shell sort and Timsort.
steps: Takeaway: Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by repeatedly inserting the next unsorted element into its correct position among the already sorted elements.
Here is why: the algorithm mimics the way we manually sort a hand of cards.
Consider an array `a = [5, 2, 9, 1, 5]`.
Initially the sorted part contains only `a[0] = 5`.
Compare `key` with `a[0] = 5`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the whole array is sorted”) reveals the misconception that insertion sort finishes early — confusing the invariant with the final post‑condition.

Explain why insertion sort is stable, referencing the comparison condition in the inner loop.
Given the array `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]`, after the third outer iteration (`i = 3`) what is the array content? Show the steps.

cards.title: The `java.lang.String` class represents an immutable sequence of Unicode…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: The `java.lang.String` class represents an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. Immutability means every operation that appears to modify a String — concatenation, substring, replace — actually creates a new String object, leaving the original unchanged. This guarantees thread safety and allows String literals to be interned in the constant pool, saving memory when identical literals appear. The `java.lang.StringBuffer` class provides a mutable sequence of characters with synchronized methods, making it safe for concurrent access. It maintains an internal character array that expands automatically (capacity doubles plus two) when the appended data exceeds current capacity. Both classes implement `CharSequence` and share many methods (`length()`, `charAt(int)`, `substring(int,int)`, `indexOf(String)`), but StringBuffer adds mutators such as `append()`, `insert()`, `delete()`, `reverse()`, and `setCharAt(int,char)`. StringBuilder, introduced in Java 5, offers the same API without synchronization for single‑threaded performance; it is not part of the ISC syllabus but worth noting. Understanding the memory implications — String creates many short‑lived objects during heavy concatenation, while StringBuffer reuses its buffer — is essential for writing efficient ISC programs, especially in recursion or file‑processing tasks where large texts are built incrementally.
steps: The one thing to remember: String is immutable and creates new objects on every modification, while StringBuffer is mutable, thread‑safe, and expands its internal buffer automatically.
Here is why: Java stores String literals in a special constant pool so identical literals share the same object; this saves heap space but forces every edit to allocate a fresh String.
StringBuffer avoids that allocation storm by keeping a resizable `char[]` buffer.
Consider a program that reads a 10 MB log file line by line and builds a single report string.
Using `String report = ""; report += line;` inside the loop creates a new String of increasing size each iteration — millions of temporary objects, heavy GC pressure, and O(n²) time.
Switching to `StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer(); sb.append(line);` reuses the same buffer, growing it geometrically (capacity = old2+2), yielding near O(n) time and far fewer objects.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `Exam2024 Exam2024`) reveals the misconception that `concat` mutates the original String — confusing String’s immutability with StringBuffer’s mutability.

cards.title: Recursion is a programming technique where a method calls itself to solve a…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Recursion is a programming technique where a method calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. For the factorial function, the mathematical definition is n! = n × (n‑1)! for n > 0, with the base case 0! = 1. In Java, a recursive factorial method receives an integer n, checks if n == 0 (base case) and returns 1; otherwise it returns n factorial(n‑1). The call stack stores each pending multiplication until the base case is reached, then unwinds, multiplying the returned values. Key sub‑concepts: base case (termination condition), recursive case (self‑call with reduced argument), call stack (memory for pending calls), and stack overflow risk if the base case is missing or recursion depth exceeds JVM limits. Recursion mirrors mathematical induction and is contrasted with iterative loops that use explicit state variables.
steps: The one thing to remember: a recursive factorial works only when a clear base case stops the self‑calls and each recursive step moves the argument toward that base case.
Here is why: the factorial of n is defined as n multiplied by the factorial of n‑1, so the problem naturally shrinks by one each call.
Consider the call factorial(3).
The method checks n == 0?
No, so it returns 3 factorial(2).
That call again checks n == 0?

cards.title: Binary search is a divide‑and‑conquer algorithm that locates a target value…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Binary search is a divide‑and‑conquer algorithm that locates a target value within a sorted array by repeatedly comparing the target with the middle element of the current search interval. If the target equals the middle element, the search succeeds; if the target is smaller, the algorithm recurses on the left sub‑array; if larger, it recurses on the right sub‑array. The recursive formulation requires three parameters: the array, the low index, and the high index. The base case occurs when low exceeds high, indicating the target is absent. The mid index is computed as `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` to avoid integer overflow. Each recursive call reduces the problem size by roughly half, yielding a time complexity of O(log n) and a space complexity of O(log n) due to the call stack. The algorithm assumes the array is sorted in ascending order; it does not work on unsorted data. Binary search is a classic example of recursion where the problem is broken into a smaller instance of the same problem, mirroring the factorial recursion pattern but with a branching factor of one (only one recursive call per invocation). Understanding the invariant — that the target, if present, always lies within the current low‑high bounds — is essential for correct implementation and for proving correctness.
steps: The key takeaway is that recursive binary search solves the search problem by halving the search interval at each step, guaranteeing logarithmic time.
Here is why: first, the array must be sorted; otherwise the halving logic fails.
Second, the recursive function receives the current bounds low and high; if low > high the key is not present — this is the base case.
Third, the mid index is computed safely to avoid overflow, then the key is compared with arr[mid].
Fourth, depending on the comparison, the function calls itself with either the left half (low, mid‑1) or the right half (mid+1, high).
Fifth, each call reduces the interval size by about half, so the maximum depth of recursion is ⌈log₂ n⌉.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “low == high”) reveals the misconception that the search stops when only one element remains, ignoring that the final comparison at that single element still requires a recursive call that will then set low > high.

cards.title: Base conversion is the process of representing a non‑negative integer in a…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Base conversion is the process of representing a non‑negative integer in a different radix (base). The most common algorithm taught in ISC Class 12 is the repeated‑division method: repeatedly divide the number by the target base, record each remainder as a digit (0‑9, A‑F for bases >10), and read the remainders in reverse order to obtain the converted representation. Recursion implements this naturally: the base case occurs when the quotient becomes zero; each recursive call processes the quotient and appends the current remainder after the deeper call returns, automatically producing the correct digit order. The concept links to earlier recursion nodes (factorial, binary search) by illustrating a divide‑and‑conquer pattern where the problem size shrinks by a factor of the base each call. It also connects to the String/StringBuffer node because the resulting digits are often accumulated in a string builder. Understanding base conversion is essential for low‑level programming, memory addressing, and interpreting machine‑level data, and it prepares students for the Tower of Hanoi recursion that follows.
steps: The one thing to remember: recursive base conversion builds the answer backwards by letting the deepest call return first, so each remainder is appended after the recursive call returns.
Here is why: the repeated‑division algorithm produces least‑significant digits first.
A loop would store them in an array and reverse at the end; recursion uses the call stack as that implicit storage.

cards.title: The Tower of Hanoi is a classic recursive problem defined by three pegs…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: The Tower of Hanoi is a classic recursive problem defined by three pegs (source, auxiliary, destination) and n disks of distinct sizes. The objective is to transfer the entire stack from the source peg to the destination peg obeying two rules: only one disk may be moved at a time, and a larger disk may never rest on a smaller disk. The optimal solution follows a simple recurrence: to move n disks, first move n‑1 disks from source to auxiliary using destination as spare, then move the largest disk from source to destination, finally move the n‑1 disks from auxiliary to destination using source as spare. This yields the recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n‑1) + 1 with base case T(1) = 1, whose closed form is 2ⁿ − 1 moves. The algorithm demonstrates divide‑and‑conquer recursion, stack‑frame management, and exponential time complexity, linking directly to the recursion concepts covered in factorial, binary search, and base conversion nodes.
steps: The optimal solution for Tower of Hanoi always requires exactly 2ⁿ − 1 moves, and the recursive algorithm achieves this by solving two identical sub‑problems of size n‑1 around a single move of the largest disk.

Here is why: the largest disk cannot be moved until all smaller disks are cleared off it, which forces the first sub‑problem; after the largest disk reaches the destination, the smaller stack must be reassembled on top…

For n = 3 the recursive calls unfold as: move 2 disks from A to B (using C), move disk 3 from A to C, move 2 disks from B to C (using A).
Each “move 2 disks” again splits into moving 1 disk, moving the second, moving the first.
The call stack depth equals n, and each level prints one move for the current largest disk.

cards.title: Inheritance in Java is a mechanism where a new class (derived or subclass)…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Inheritance in Java is a mechanism where a new class (derived or subclass) acquires the fields and methods of an existing class (superclass or base class) using the `extends` keyword. The subclass automatically receives all non‑private members of the superclass, enabling code reuse and establishing an “is‑a” relationship. The superclass defines generic behaviour; the subclass can inherit that behaviour unchanged, override specific methods to provide specialised implementations, or add new members. Constructors are not inherited, but a subclass constructor must invoke a superclass constructor (explicitly via `super(...)` or implicitly via the no‑argument constructor) to initialise the inherited state. The `Object` class is the ultimate superclass of every Java class, supplying fundamental methods such as `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()`. Access modifiers control visibility: `public` and `protected` members are accessible in subclasses, while `private` members are not. The `protected` modifier grants access to subclasses even in different packages, a key concept for designing extensible libraries. Abstract classes may declare abstract methods that force subclasses to provide concrete implementations, enforcing a contract. This node focuses on the core idea of super and derived classes; member access details, method redefinition, abstract classes, `Object` class, `protected` visibility, polymorphism, and interfaces are covered in subsequent sibling nodes.
steps: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend the behaviour of a superclass without copying code.

Here is why: the `extends` keyword creates an “is‑a” link, so every subclass object contains a complete superclass object inside it. First, the superclass defines common state and behaviour — for example, a `Vehicle`…
Second, a subclass `Car extends Vehicle` automatically gets `speed` and `start()`; it can add `numberOfDoors` and override `start()` to include a fuel‑check.
Third, when a `Car` object is created, its constructor must call `super()` (or `super(args)`) to initialise the `Vehicle` part before initialising `Car`‑specific fields.
Fourth, if the subclass does not override a method, the superclass version runs — this is the default inheritance behaviour.

Fifth, the `Object` class sits at the top of every hierarchy, so even a class that does not explicitly extend another still inherits `toString()`, `equals()`, etc. Consider a real‑world Indian example: a `BankAccount`…

cards.title: Member access in inheritance controls the visibility of fields, methods…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Member access in inheritance controls the visibility of fields, methods, and constructors of a superclass to its subclasses. Java provides four access levels: public (visible everywhere), protected (visible within the same package and to subclasses even in different packages), default/package‑private (visible only within the same package), and private (visible only inside the declaring class). A subclass inherits all non‑private members of its superclass; private members are not inherited but can be reached indirectly through public or protected accessor/mutator methods. The keyword super allows a subclass to explicitly invoke a superclass’s constructor or access a hidden superclass member (e.g., `super.method()`). Access rules also apply when a subclass declares a member with the same name — this is redefinition (covered in the next node). Understanding these rules is essential for encapsulation, secure design, and correct polymorphic behaviour.

Here is why: the access modifier on a member determines its visibility contract.

cards.title: Redefinition in Java inheritance occurs when a subclass declares a field or…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Redefinition in Java inheritance occurs when a subclass declares a field or method that has the same identifier (and, for methods, the same signature) as a member of its superclass. Variable redefinition (also called field hiding): the subclass introduces a new field with the same name. The two fields coexist in memory; which one is accessed depends on the static type of the reference. A `Super` reference sees the superclass field, a `Sub` reference sees the subclass field. No polymorphism is involved — the hidden field is not overridden. Method redefinition (method overriding): the subclass provides a new implementation with the same name, return type (or covariant return), and parameter list. The `@Override` annotation signals intent and lets the compiler check correctness. At runtime, the JVM uses dynamic binding: the actual object’s class determines which method body executes, regardless of the reference type. Overriding respects the Liskov Substitution Principle — the subclass method must accept at least the same arguments and return a type compatible with the superclass contract. Key relationships: - Overriding requires inheritance and non‑private, non‑final, non‑static methods. - Field hiding works for any non‑private field, even `static`. - `super.field` / `super.method()` explicitly accesses the hidden/overridden superclass member. - `protected` visibility (covered in node 06_006) allows subclasses in other packages to override/hide. - Abstract methods (node 06_004) must be overridden in concrete subclasses. - The `Object` class (node 06_005) supplies default `toString`, `equals`, `hashCode` that are commonly overridden. Understanding the distinction between static binding (field access, static methods) and dynamic binding (instance method calls) is essential for predicting program behaviour.

Here is why: the language separates compile‑time knowledge (the declared type of a variable) from run‑time reality (the concrete object created with `new`).
When you write `Super s = new Sub();`, the compiler only knows `s` as `Super`.
Accessing `s.field` therefore resolves to `Super.field` because fields are resolved statically.
Calling `s.method()` however triggers a virtual‑method lookup at run time, so `Sub.method()` executes.

cards.title: An abstract class in Java is a class declared with the `abstract` keyword that…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition:
An abstract class in Java is a class declared with the `abstract` keyword that cannot be instantiated directly. It serves as a partial implementation and a contract for its subclasses. An abstract class may contain:
- Abstract methods — declared with `abstract` and no body; every concrete subclass must override them.
- Concrete methods — fully implemented methods that subclasses inherit as‑is or may override.
- Fields, constructors, and initializers — constructors are invoked during subclass instantiation (via `super()`), allowing common initialization logic.
- Access modifiers — members can be `public`, `protected`, `private`, or package‑private; `protected` members are visible to subclasses (see node protected visibility). Relationship to other sub‑concepts:
- Inheritance (node super and derived classes): an abstract class is a superclass; concrete subclasses extend it.
- Redefinition (node redefinition of variables and methods): subclasses must redefine (implement) each abstract method; they may also override concrete methods.
- Polymorphism (node subclass polymorphism and dynamic binding): a reference of the abstract type can point to any concrete subclass object, enabling dynamic method dispatch.
- Interfaces (node interfaces: implementing through classes): abstract classes differ from interfaces by allowing state (fields) and constructors, and by supporting single inheritance only. The abstract class thus captures “what must be done” (abstract methods) while optionally providing “how some things are done” (concrete methods), enforcing a design contract without dictating full implementation.
steps: An abstract class in Java defines a common template that can contain both implemented and unimplemented methods, and it cannot be instantiated directly.
Here is why: an abstract class represents an incomplete type — it declares what operations must exist (abstract methods) while optionally supplying how some operations work (concrete methods).
This mirrors a blueprint for a house: the blueprint specifies that every house must have a `buildRoof()` step, but the exact roof design is left to each builder (subclass).

cards.title: `java.lang.Object` is the root class of the Java class hierarchy.
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: `java.lang.Object` is the root class of the Java class hierarchy. Every class, whether user‑defined or from the standard library, implicitly extends `Object` unless it explicitly extends another class. Consequently, all objects inherit a set of fundamental methods: `toString()` for a textual representation, `equals(Object)` for logical equality, `hashCode()` for hash‑based collections, `getClass()` for runtime type information, `clone()` for shallow copying (protected), `finalize()` (deprecated) for cleanup, and the monitor methods `wait()`, `notify()`, `notifyAll()` for thread synchronization. These methods provide a baseline contract that any object can fulfil or override. Overriding `toString()`, `equals()`, and `hashCode()` is a common practice to give domain‑specific meaning. The `protected` visibility of `clone()` and `finalize()` restricts direct access to subclasses, reinforcing encapsulation. Understanding `Object` is essential for polymorphism, collection frameworks, and writing robust `equals`/`hashCode` contracts.
steps: Every Java class ultimately inherits from `java.lang.Object`, giving all objects a shared toolkit of essential methods.
Here is why: the language designers made `Object` the universal superclass so that any reference can be treated uniformly, enabling collections, reflection, and polymorphism.

First, the default `toString()` returns the class name followed by `@` and the hexadecimal hash code; overriding it lets a `Student` object print `"Student{name='Asha', roll=12}"` instead of `Student@3f2a1c`.
Second, `equals(Object)` by default checks reference identity (`==`); a proper override compares relevant fields and must be symmetric, transitive, and consistent with `hashCode()`.
Third, `hashCode()` must produce the same integer for equal objects; a common recipe combines field hash codes using a prime multiplier.
Fourth, `getClass()` returns the runtime `Class` object, useful for type‑safe casting.

cards.title: Protected visibility is an access modifier in Java that sits between `private`…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Protected visibility is an access modifier in Java that sits between `private` and `public`. A member (field, method, or constructor) declared `protected` is accessible within its own package (package‑private access) and by any subclass, regardless of the package in which that subclass resides. This dual‑scope rule enables controlled inheritance: the superclass exposes implementation details to its direct and indirect descendants while still hiding them from unrelated code. The modifier does not apply to top‑level classes or interfaces — only to members. When a subclass overrides a `protected` method, the overriding method may keep `protected` or widen to `public`, but it cannot narrow to `default` or `private`. Similarly, a `protected` field can be read or written by subclass code directly, supporting the “template method” pattern where the superclass defines algorithm structure and subclasses fill in `protected` hooks. Understanding `protected` is essential for designing extensible class hierarchies without leaking internal state to the whole application.
steps: The key takeaway: A `protected` member is visible to its own package and to every subclass, even across packages, but invisible to unrelated classes in other packages.
Here is why: Java’s access control is designed to support encapsulation while still allowing inheritance‑based extension.
First, package‑private (default) access already grants visibility to all classes in the same package. `protected` adds a second dimension — subclass access — which crosses package boundaries.

Second, this rule lets a superclass expose helper methods or state that subclasses need to customise behaviour without making those helpers part of the public API. Third, the compiler enforces that an overriding method…
Fourth, constructors can be `protected`, preventing direct instantiation by outsiders while allowing subclass constructors to invoke `super(...)`.

Fifth, a common exam trap: a subclass in a different package can access a `protected` field only through inheritance (i.e., `this.field` or `super.field`), not by creating an instance of the superclass and dereferencing…

cards.title: Subclass polymorphism allows a variable of a superclass type to refer to an…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Subclass polymorphism allows a variable of a superclass type to refer to an object of any subclass. When a method is invoked through that reference, Java uses dynamic binding (late binding) to determine the actual method implementation at runtime based on the object's true class, not the reference type. This requires method overriding: the subclass provides a new implementation of a non‑static, non‑final, non‑private method with the same signature. The superclass may be concrete or abstract; abstract methods force subclasses to override. Dynamic binding enables extensible designs — new subclasses can be added without changing code that uses the superclass type. It differs from static binding (used for static, final, private methods) where the method is resolved at compile time. Polymorphism works with inheritance hierarchies and also with interfaces (covered later). Key relationships: inheritance provides the type hierarchy; method overriding supplies multiple implementations; dynamic binding selects the correct one at runtime. Protected visibility (previous node) allows subclasses to access superclass members, facilitating overriding. The Object class is the ultimate superclass, so every object can be treated polymorphically as Object.
steps: Polymorphism lets a single superclass reference invoke different subclass implementations at runtime.
Here is why: the JVM resolves the method call based on the actual object type, not the reference type; this is dynamic binding.
Overriding provides multiple implementations; the superclass defines the contract.
Consider a payment system: a superclass Payment with method process().
Subclasses CreditCardPayment, UPIPayment, NetBankingPayment each override process().
A Payment variable can hold any subclass object.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "static binding") reveals the misconception that method resolution always happens at compile time, confusing method overloading (static) with overriding (dynamic).

cards.title: In Java, an interface is a reference type that declares a set of abstract…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In Java, an interface is a reference type that declares a set of abstract method signatures (and, from Java 8 onward, default and static methods) without providing implementation bodies. A class implements an interface by using the `implements` keyword and supplying concrete definitions for every abstract method declared in the interface. This establishes a “is‑a” relationship between the class and the interface type, enabling polymorphic substitution: a variable of the interface type can refer to any object of a class that implements it. Multiple interfaces can be implemented by a single class, giving Java a form of multiple inheritance of type. Interfaces may also contain constant fields (implicitly `public static final`). The implementing class must be non‑abstract unless it declares itself abstract and leaves some methods unimplemented. Interface implementation is the primary mechanism for achieving contract‑based design and loose coupling in object‑oriented programs.
steps: An interface defines a contract that any implementing class must fulfil, enabling polymorphic use of unrelated classes.
First, an interface lists method signatures without bodies, so every class that implements it guarantees those behaviours.
Second, a class can implement several interfaces, gaining multiple types without inheriting implementation — this is Java’s answer to multiple inheritance.
Third, interface references allow code to depend on abstractions rather than concrete classes, reducing coupling.
Fourth, default methods let interfaces evolve without breaking existing implementors.
Fifth, constants in interfaces provide shared configuration values.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “extends”) reveals the misconception that interfaces are inherited like classes — confusing class inheritance with interface implementation.

cards.title: User‑defined behaviour in Java refers to the ability of a programmer to supply…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: User‑defined behaviour in Java refers to the ability of a programmer to supply concrete implementations for the abstract methods declared in an interface. An interface specifies a contract — method signatures without bodies — and any class that implements the interface must provide method bodies that define exactly how those operations behave. Because the Java runtime uses dynamic binding, a reference of the interface type can point to any implementing object, and the actual method executed is the one defined in that object’s class. This mechanism enables polymorphism: the same interface call can produce different results depending on the concrete class instantiated. The relationship builds on earlier concepts: inheritance (the class inherits the interface’s type), method redefinition (the class overrides the abstract methods), and protected/package‑private visibility rules that control access to the implemented methods. Unlike abstract classes, interfaces cannot hold state (no instance fields) and a class may implement multiple interfaces, allowing a single object to exhibit several distinct user‑defined behaviours simultaneously.
steps: The one thing to remember: An interface only declares what must be done; the class that implements it decides how it is done, and at runtime the JVM selects the class’s version.
Here is why: an interface is a pure contract — it lists method signatures but supplies no code.
When a class writes `implements MyInterface`, it promises to furnish a body for every abstract method.
The compiler checks this promise; if any method is missing, compilation fails.
At runtime, a variable of type `MyInterface` can refer to any object of a class that fulfilled the promise.
When a method is invoked on that variable, the JVM looks at the actual object’s class and executes that class’s version — this is dynamic binding.

cards.title: A Stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last‑In‑First‑Out (LIFO)…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A Stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last‑In‑First‑Out (LIFO) principle. It supports two primary operations: push (insert an element at the top) and pop (remove and return the top element). An auxiliary operation peek (or top) returns the top element without removing it. The stack can be implemented using an array (fixed capacity) or a singly linked list (dynamic capacity). In the array implementation a variable `top` stores the index of the current top element; initially `top = -1` denotes an empty stack. In the linked‑list implementation the head node always represents the top. Stacks are fundamental for recursion management, expression evaluation (infix‑to‑postfix conversion), backtracking algorithms, and memory management in runtime environments. The abstract data type (ADT) defines the contract: `push(item)`, `pop()`, `peek()`, `isEmpty()`, `isFull()` (for bounded stacks). All other chapter nodes (queue, circular queue, dequeue, linked list, trees) build on the understanding of linear ordering and pointer manipulation first introduced here.
steps: A stack is a LIFO container — the last element pushed is the first popped.
Here is why: the only accessible position is the top, so insertion and deletion happen at the same end, enforcing reverse order.
Consider a stack of plates at a wedding buffet in Delhi: you add clean plates on top, guests always take the top plate; the plate placed earliest ends up at the bottom and is used last.
Supporting argument 1 – Array implementation.

This gives O(1) time for all operations but fixed capacity.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `top = 2`) reveals the misconception that `pop` does not decrement `top` or that `push` increments twice.

cards.title: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First‑In‑First‑Out (FIFO)…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First‑In‑First‑Out (FIFO) principle. It supports two primary operations: enqueue (insert at the rear) and dequeue (remove from the front). Additional operations include peek (view front element without removal), isEmpty, and isFull (for bounded implementations). A queue can be implemented using an array (with front and rear indices) or a singly linked list (with front and rear pointers). In an array implementation, the rear index moves forward on each enqueue; the front index moves forward on each dequeue. When the rear reaches the array end, further enqueues are blocked unless a circular technique (covered in the next node) is used. In a linked‑list implementation, new nodes are attached after the rear node and the rear pointer is updated; removal adjusts the front pointer. Queues are used in breadth‑first traversal of trees, job scheduling, buffering streams, and simulation of waiting lines. The abstract data type (ADT) defines the behaviour; concrete classes (e.g., `ArrayQueue`, `LinkedQueue`) implement the ADT, often via a common `Queue` interface.
steps: The essential takeaway: a queue processes elements in the exact order they arrive, making it the natural structure for any “first‑come‑first‑served” scenario.

Here is why: (1) The FIFO rule guarantees fairness — no element can jump ahead of an earlier one. (2) Two pointers (front, rear) are sufficient to track the logical start and end, whether stored in an array or linked…
(3) Array implementation is simple but suffers from “false full” when rear hits the last index; this motivates the circular queue taught next.
(4) Linked implementation avoids fixed capacity but incurs node‑allocation overhead.
(5) Both implementations share the same ADT, so client code can swap them without change.
Consider a print spooler: jobs arrive from multiple applications.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 15) reveals the misconception that dequeue does not advance the front pointer, or that peek returns the most recently added element instead of the front.
remember: What is the output of the following sequence on an empty array‑based queue of capacity 5? enqueue(5); enqueue(10); dequeue(); enqueue(15); enqueue(20); dequeue(); dequeue()….

cards.title: A circular queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A circular queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO (First‑In‑First‑Out) discipline but stores elements in a fixed‑size array where the logical end connects to the logical start. Two pointers, `front` and `rear`, track the positions of the first and last valid elements. On each enqueue, `rear` advances by one using modulo arithmetic: `rear = (rear + 1) % capacity`. On each dequeue, `front` advances similarly. The queue is empty when `front == rear` and no elements are present; it is full when `(rear + 1) % capacity == front` (one slot is sacrificed to distinguish full from empty) or when a separate `count` variable equals `capacity`. This wrap‑around eliminates the need to shift elements after each dequeue, giving O(1) time for both insertion and removal. Compared with a linear queue (node), a circular queue reuses freed slots, making it ideal for bounded buffers such as keyboard input handling or network packet queues. The concept extends to double‑ended queues (dequeue, node) where insertion and deletion can occur at both ends, but the circular queue restricts operations to the rear and front only.
steps: A circular queue eliminates the wasted space of a linear queue by wrapping the rear pointer to the front using modulo arithmetic, enabling O(1) enqueue and dequeue on a fixed‑size array.
Here is why: in a linear queue, after several dequeues the front moves right and the empty slots at the beginning can never be reused unless all elements are shifted, an O(n) operation.
By treating the array as a ring, the next position after the last index is index 0, so freed slots become available again.
Consider a ticket‑booking counter at a railway station with a display that can show only 5 pending requests.
The display is a circular queue of capacity 5.
Initially `front = rear = 0`, `count = 0`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., `rear == front`) reveals the misconception that the same condition indicates both empty and full, ignoring the need to distinguish them.

cards.title: A deque (double‑ended queue) is an abstract data type that supports insertion…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A deque (double‑ended queue) is an abstract data type that supports insertion and deletion at both the front and the rear. Core operations are `insertFront(x)`, `insertRear(x)`, `deleteFront()`, `deleteRear()`, `peekFront()`, `peekRear()`, `isEmpty()`, and `size()`. Unlike a plain queue (which allows only rear‑insert and front‑delete) or a stack (front‑insert and front‑delete), a deque generalises both. In Java, a deque can be realised either by a custom class (using a fixed‑size array treated as a circular buffer or a linked list) or by implementing the standard `java.util.Deque<E>` interface, which provides ready‑made implementations such as `ArrayDeque` and `LinkedList`. The array‑based version achieves O(1) time for all operations by maintaining `front` and `rear` indices that wrap around via modulo arithmetic, while the linked‑list version uses nodes with `next` and `prev` pointers, also giving O(1) operations without size limits (except memory). Understanding deque builds directly on the circular queue concept (node) because the array implementation re‑uses its circular‑buffer technique, and it prepares students for later algorithmic applications such as infix‑to‑postfix conversion (node) where operators may need to be accessed from both ends.
steps: A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends, and in Java it can be realised either by a custom class using an array or by implementing the `java.util.Deque` interface with a linked list.

Here is why: the array version re‑uses the circular‑buffer technique from circular queues, giving constant‑time operations by wrapping indices; the linked‑list version avoids size limits by allocating nodes on demand.
Consider an array‑based deque of capacity 5.
We keep two indices, `front` and `rear`, initially both set to 0, and a `count` of elements.
To insert at the rear we place the element at `rear`, then update `rear = (rear + 1) % capacity` and increment `count`.
To delete from the front we retrieve the element at `front`, then set `front = (front + 1) % capacity` and decrement `count`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., O(n) because we must shift elements) reveals the misconception that array insertions always require shifting, ignoring the circular‑buffer technique that lets us add at the front without moving existing items.

cards.title: Infix, prefix, and postfix are three notations for writing arithmetic…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Infix, prefix, and postfix are three notations for writing arithmetic expressions. Infix places each binary operator between its two operands (e.g., A + B). Prefix (Polish notation) writes the operator before its operands (+ A B). Postfix (Reverse Polish notation) writes the operator after its operands (A B +). Conversion from infix to prefix or postfix is a classic stack‑based algorithm because the stack naturally handles operator precedence and parentheses. The Shunting‑yard algorithm scans the infix string left‑to‑right, using a stack to hold operators and left parentheses. When an operand is read it is appended to the output. When an operator is read, operators of higher or equal precedence (respecting associativity) are popped from the stack to the output before the new operator is pushed. A left parenthesis is pushed onto the stack; a right parenthesis triggers popping until the matching left parenthesis is discarded. After the scan, any remaining operators are popped to the output. For prefix conversion the infix string is first reversed, parentheses are swapped, the same algorithm produces postfix of the reversed expression, and the result is reversed again. The process relies on a clear precedence table (^,, /, +, -) and associativity rules (^ right‑associative, others left‑associative). Mastery of this conversion underpins expression evaluation, compiler design, and stack‑machine architectures.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that a stack lets us reorder operators from infix to postfix/prefix by delaying each operator until its operands are ready, respecting precedence and parentheses.
Here is why: 1.
Infix notation is human‑readable but ambiguous without precedence rules; postfix/prefix are unambiguous and stack‑evaluable. 2.
The stack stores operators whose right operand has not yet been seen; when a higher‑precedence operator arrives, the lower one must wait. 3.
Parentheses override precedence by acting as explicit grouping markers; the algorithm treats '(' as a sentinel that stops popping. 4.
Right‑associative exponentiation (^) requires a special case: we pop only operators of strictly higher precedence, not equal. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., A B + C ) reveals the misconception that operators are output in the order they appear, ignoring precedence; the student treats the expression as strictly left‑to‑right without using the stack to delay lower‑precedence operators.

cards.title: A singly linked list is a linear data structure composed of nodes…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A singly linked list is a linear data structure composed of nodes, each containing a data field and a reference (next) to the subsequent node. The list is accessed via a head reference pointing to the first node; the last node’s next reference is null. Insertion creates a new node and adjusts next references so the new node becomes part of the chain. There are four canonical insertion scenarios: (1) at the head — new node’s next becomes the current head, then head points to the new node; (2) at the tail — traverse to the last node, set its next to the new node; (3) after a given node — new node’s next becomes the given node’s next, then the given node’s next points to the new node; (4) at a specified position (1‑based) — traverse to the node at position‑1, then perform the after‑given‑node steps. All operations run in O(1) for head insertion and O(n) for tail or position‑based insertion because traversal may be required. The node class typically encapsulates an integer (or generic) data field and a Node next reference. Proper ordering of reference assignments is critical; assigning the previous node’s next before saving the original next loses the remainder of the list. This concept underpins later operations such as deletion, reversal, and extraction, and it contrasts with array‑based lists where insertion requires shifting elements.
steps: Insertion in a singly linked list is performed by creating a new node and adjusting the next references of the surrounding nodes so that the new node becomes part of the chain.
Here is why: the list is a chain of references; breaking the chain at the wrong point loses access to the remaining nodes.

The list itself is represented by a `Node head` field, initially null.

cards.title: Deletion in a singly linked list is the operation of removing a node that…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Deletion in a singly linked list is the operation of removing a node that matches a given key or position while preserving the list’s sequential integrity. The list is defined by a `Node` class holding `data` and a `next` reference, and a `head` reference pointing to the first node. Deletion requires locating the target node and its immediate predecessor because a singly linked list only permits forward traversal. Three primary cases arise: deleting the head node (update `head` to `head.next`), deleting a middle node (set `prev.next = curr.next`), and deleting the tail node (set `prev.next = null`). If the list is empty or the key is not found, the method typically returns a boolean `false` or throws an exception. The actual unlinking is an O(1) pointer change, but the search for the node is O(n) in the worst case. Java’s automatic garbage collection reclaims the unreferenced node, so explicit `free` is unnecessary. This operation builds on the insertion concepts from the previous node and prepares for reversal where pointer manipulation is extended. Correct handling of the `head` reference and the `prev` pointer is critical; a common exam trap is forgetting to update `head` when the first node is removed, leading to a memory leak or logical error.
steps: Deleting a node from a singly linked list requires locating the node and its predecessor, then rewiring the predecessor's next reference to bypass the target node, after which the unreferenced node is automatically…
Here is why: the singly linked structure only allows forward movement, so we must keep a trailing pointer (`prev`) while scanning with a leading pointer (`curr`).
Three distinct cases dictate the rewiring logic.
First, if the list is empty (`head == null`), deletion simply returns `false`.
Second, if the head node holds the key, we move `head` to `head.next`; the old head becomes unreachable and is garbage‑collected.
Third, for a middle or tail node, we advance `prev` and `curr` until `curr.data == key` or `curr == null`.

cards.title: Reversal of a singly linked list is the operation that transforms the list so…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Reversal of a singly linked list is the operation that transforms the list so that the original head becomes the tail and the original tail becomes the head, while preserving the relative order of the remaining nodes in reverse. In a singly linked list each node stores a reference to its successor only; therefore reversal must be performed by re‑assigning the `next` pointers. The standard iterative algorithm uses three pointers — `prev` (initially `null`), `curr` (initially `head`), and `next` (temporary) — and walks once through the list, at each step storing `curr.next` in `next`, pointing `curr.next` to `prev`, then advancing `prev` and `curr`. When `curr` becomes `null`, `prev` references the new head. A recursive version achieves the same effect by recursing to the end of the list and then rewiring pointers on the unwind. Both approaches run in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space (iterative) or O(n) call‑stack space (recursive). Reversal is a fundamental building block for algorithms such as palindrome checking, list folding, and certain queue implementations.
steps: The one thing to remember: reversing a singly linked list is achieved by redirecting each node’s `next` pointer to its predecessor while walking once through the list.
Here is why: a singly linked node only knows its successor, so we must remember the predecessor before we overwrite the link.
The three‑pointer technique (`prev`, `curr`, `next`) does exactly that.
Consider a list `10 → 20 → 30 → null`.
Initially `prev = null`, `curr = 10`.
Step 1: store `next = 20`; set `10.next = null`; move `prev = 10`, `curr = 20`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., O(n²)) reveals the misconception that pointer reassignment requires nested traversals — confusing reversal with algorithms that repeatedly search for the tail.

cards.title: Extraction in a singly linked list is the operation that removes a node at a…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Extraction in a singly linked list is the operation that removes a node at a given position (or the first node matching a key) and returns a reference to that removed node. The algorithm first locates the target node and its predecessor by traversing from the head. Once found, the predecessor’s `next` pointer is redirected to the target’s `next`, effectively bypassing the target. The target’s `next` is then set to `null` to isolate it, and the target reference is returned to the caller. If the position is 0 (head), the head pointer itself is updated to the second node. Extraction differs from deletion in that the removed node is preserved for further use rather than being discarded. It requires O(n) time in the worst case because the list may need to be scanned to the desired index, and O(1) auxiliary space. The operation maintains list integrity: size decreases by one, and no memory leaks occur if the language’s garbage collector reclaims unreferenced nodes. Extraction is a building block for higher‑level structures such as stacks, queues, and polynomial representations where elements must be taken out without destroying their data.
steps: Extraction removes a node from a singly linked list and hands the node back to the caller while keeping the remaining list intact.
Here is why: the operation must locate the node, rewire the predecessor’s `next` pointer, and isolate the removed node without losing any other elements.

cards.title: In a binary tree, the root is the unique topmost node that has no parent.
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In a binary tree, the root is the unique topmost node that has no parent. It serves as the entry point for all operations on the tree: traversal, insertion, deletion, and search. Every other node in the tree is reachable by following a unique path of left-child or right-child references starting from the root. The root’s degree (number of children) can be 0, 1, or 2; if the root has degree 0, the tree consists of only the root node and is called a trivial tree. The root defines the tree’s height (the longest downward path to a leaf) and level numbering (root at level 0). All subtrees are rooted at the root’s children; thus the root partitions the entire tree into a left subtree and a right subtree, each of which is itself a binary tree. In Java implementations, the root is typically stored as a reference variable of type Node in the BinaryTree class, and all public methods (e.g., insert, delete, traverse) begin by checking if root is null. The root’s value holds the data for the top element, and its left and right fields point to the roots of the left and right subtrees respectively. Understanding the root is foundational because concepts like depth, level, height, size, and balancing are all defined relative to the root.
steps: The root is the single node in a binary tree that has no parent, making it the mandatory starting point for every tree operation.
Here is why: without a root reference, the tree cannot be accessed, and all recursive algorithms rely on passing the root (or subtree roots) as the initial argument.
Consider a binary tree representing a company hierarchy: the CEO is the root, with two direct reports as left and right children.
Every employee traces their reporting line back to the CEO. In Java, the BinaryTree class holds a private Node root; when the tree is empty, root is null.
Insertion begins at root: if root is null, the new node becomes root; otherwise, we traverse left/right from root to find the insertion point.
Traversals (pre-order, in-order, post-order) are initiated by calling a helper method with root.

cards.title: A binary tree node is the fundamental building block of a binary tree data…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A binary tree node is the fundamental building block of a binary tree data structure. In Java it is typically represented as a class containing three fields: a data field that stores the value associated with the node (e.g., an integer, string, or object), a left reference of the same node type that points to the left child, and a right reference that points to the right child. Both references may be null, indicating the absence of a child. The node’s left and right references together define the node’s degree (0, 1, or 2) and establish the hierarchical relationships: the node becomes the parent of any non‑null child, those children become siblings of each other, and each child roots its own subtree. The collection of all nodes reachable from a given node forms its subtree; the entire tree is the subtree rooted at the root node. Concepts such as height, depth, level, size, and balance are derived from the arrangement of these nodes, but the node itself only encapsulates data and the two child links. Understanding the node’s structure is prerequisite for implementing insertion, deletion, traversal, and any algorithm that manipulates the tree.
steps: A binary tree node is simply a container that holds a value and two pointers to other nodes of the same type.
Here is why: the node’s data field stores the information the tree organizes; the left and right references create the branching structure; null references mark the termination of a branch.

The `data` field can be any type; `left` and `right` are references that either point to another `Node` object or are `null`.

cards.title: The height of a binary tree is the number of edges on the longest downward path…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: The height of a binary tree is the number of edges on the longest downward path from the root node to any leaf node. Formally, for a node n, height(n) = 0 if n is a leaf; otherwise height(n) = 1 + max(height(n.left), height(n.right)). The height of the whole tree is height(root). Height is distinct from depth (distance from root to a given node) and level (depth + 1). It determines the worst‑case time complexity of tree operations such as search, insertion, and deletion in unbalanced trees (O(height)). Height also relates to size (total nodes) and degree (maximum children per node). A perfectly balanced tree of N nodes has height ⌊log₂ N⌋, while a degenerate (skewed) tree has height N‑1. Understanding height is essential for analysing algorithmic performance and for implementing self‑balancing trees later.
steps: The height of a binary tree is the length of the longest root‑to‑leaf path measured in edges.
Here is why: every recursive step moves one edge deeper, so the maximum number of such steps from root to any leaf equals the tree’s height.
Consider a tree with root A, left child B, right child C, and B has a left leaf D. The paths are A‑B‑D (2 edges) and A‑C (1 edge); the longest has 2 edges, so height = 2.
First, identify the base case: a null node contributes ‑1 edge, a leaf contributes 0.
Second, apply the recursive formula height(node) = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right)).
Third, trace the recursion on the example: height(D)=0, height(B)=1+max(0,‑1)=1, height(C)=0, height(A)=1+max(1,0)=2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 1) reveals the misconception that height counts nodes instead of edges.
