cards.title: In a binary tree, the depth of a node is defined as the number of edges on the…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In a binary tree, the depth of a node is defined as the number of edges on the unique path from the root node to that node. By convention, the root has depth 0 because the path contains zero edges. For any other node, depth = depth(parent) + 1. Depth is closely related to other tree metrics: the level of a node is depth + 1 (so level starts at 1 for the root), the height of the tree is the maximum depth among all its nodes, and the size of a subtree rooted at a node depends on how deep its descendants can go. While height measures the “tallest” branch, depth measures the position of a specific node within those branches. Understanding depth enables precise discussion of tree traversals, balancing criteria, and algorithms that depend on node‑to‑root distance (e.g., computing the lowest common ancestor). This concept builds directly on the earlier node “height” and leads naturally to the next node “level”.
steps: The depth of a node in a binary tree equals the number of edges on the unique path from the root to that node.
Here is why: 1.
Root baseline – The root has no parent, so the path contains zero edges; thus depth(root)=0 establishes the reference point. 2.
Incremental rule – Moving from a node to any of its children adds exactly one edge to the path, therefore each child’s depth is one more than its parent’s depth. 3.

Connection to level and height – Level is simply depth + 1 (shifting the count to start at 1 for the root), and the tree’s height is the maximum depth observed among all nodes, linking local position to global shape.
Consider a binary tree used to store a family’s generational data: the root represents the grandparent (depth 0).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “1”) reveals the misconception that depth counts nodes instead of edges, confusing the inclusion of the starting node in the count.

cards.title: In a binary tree, the level of a node is defined as the number of edges on the…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In a binary tree, the level of a node is defined as the number of edges on the unique path from the root to that node. By convention the root node has level 0. If a node N has parent P, then `level(N) = level(P) + 1`. Level is a non‑negative integer that increases by one for each downward step. It is closely related to depth (often used synonymously) and to height (the maximum level among all nodes). Level helps in describing the shape of the tree, in algorithms that process nodes level‑by‑level (breadth‑first traversal), and in defining properties such as a complete binary tree where all levels except possibly the last are completely filled.
steps: The level of a node in a binary tree is its distance in edges from the root, with the root at level 0.
Here is why: the root has no parent, so the path length from root to itself is zero edges; every child adds exactly one edge to the path, so its level is one more than its parent’s level.
Consider a small tree where root A has left child B and right child C;
B has left child D. Using the rule, `level(A)=0`, `level(B)=level(A)+1=1`, `level(C)=1`, `level(D)=level(B)+1=2`.
This matches the intuitive “generation” count.
A common exam trap is confusing level with height: height of the tree is the maximum level among all nodes (here height = 2), while level is a property of each individual node.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “level 1”) reveals the misconception that counting starts at 1 like floor numbers, confusing 1‑based indexing with the 0‑based edge‑count definition used in computer science.

cards.title: In a binary tree, size (also called node count) is the total number of nodes…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In a binary tree, size (also called node count) is the total number of nodes present in the tree, including the root, all internal nodes, and all leaves. Formally, for any node N, `size(N) = 1 + size(N.left) + size(N.right)`, with the base case `size(null) = 0`. The size of the entire tree is `size(root)`. Size is a fundamental metric because many algorithms — such as checking completeness, balancing, or estimating memory consumption — depend on knowing how many nodes exist. It relates directly to other structural properties: a tree of height h can have at most `2^(h+1) - 1` nodes (perfect tree) and at least `h+1` nodes (skewed tree). Size also determines the maximum possible number of siblings, subtrees, and the degree distribution across the tree. In Java implementations, size is often maintained as an instance variable updated on every insertion or deletion to allow O(1) retrieval, or computed recursively when needed.
steps: The size of a binary tree is the total count of nodes, obtained by adding one for the current node to the sizes of its left and right subtrees.
Here is why: every node contributes exactly one to the total, and the subtrees partition the remaining nodes without overlap.
Consider a small tree drawn on a notebook: root A has left child B and right child C;
B has left child D. To find size, start at A — count 1, then recursively count B’s subtree (B, D → 2) and C’s subtree (C → 1).
This matches the recursive formula `size(node) = 1 + size(node.left) + size(node.right)`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “1 because the root exists”) reveals the misconception that a tree always has at least a root node, confusing the concept of a tree reference with an actual node object.

cards.title: In a binary tree, the degree of a node is the count of its immediate children…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In a binary tree, the degree of a node is the count of its immediate children (left and/or right). Because a binary node can have at most two children, the degree of any node is an integer in the set {0, 1, 2}. A leaf node has degree 0, a node with only a left or only a right child has degree 1, and a node with both children has degree 2. The degree of the tree (sometimes called the maximum degree) is the maximum degree among all nodes in that tree. This concept links directly to the size of the tree (total number of nodes) because the sum of degrees over all nodes equals the number of edges, which is size − 1. It also connects to height, depth, and level: nodes of degree 2 tend to increase branching factor, potentially reducing height for a given size. Understanding degree is essential before studying siblings (nodes sharing a parent) and subtrees (the tree rooted at a given node), because sibling relationships exist only when the parent’s degree is at least 2, and a subtree’s root inherits the degree of that node.
steps: The degree of a node is simply the number of children it has, and in a binary tree this number can only be 0, 1, or 2.
Here is why: a binary tree restricts each node to at most two pointers — left and right — so counting non‑null pointers gives the degree.
Consider a small binary tree with root A, left child B, right child C, and B having a left child D. Node A has two children → degree 2.
Node B has one child (D) → degree 1.
Node C has none → degree 0.
Node D has none → degree 0.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “1 because the node exists”) reveals the misconception that existence of the node itself contributes to degree, confusing node presence with child count.

cards.title: In a binary tree, siblings are two distinct nodes that share the same immediate…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: In a binary tree, siblings are two distinct nodes that share the same immediate parent. Formally, for nodes u and v (u ≠ v), they are siblings iff `parent(u) == parent(v)`. This relationship is symmetric and irreflexive. Siblings are always at the same depth (level) because they are one edge below their common parent. The concept links directly to degree (a parent of two children has degree 2) and to subtrees (each sibling roots its own subtree). Understanding siblings helps in algorithms that need to traverse or modify nodes level‑by‑level, such as breadth‑first search or heap operations where the left and right children of a node are processed together.
steps: Takeaway: Two nodes are siblings exactly when they share the same parent, which forces them to sit on the same level of the tree.
Here is why: a binary tree is built by linking each node to at most two children.
When a parent creates two children, those children are created in the same step and therefore have identical distance from the root — they are one edge deeper than the parent.
This makes their depth equal, and because depth defines level, they also share the same level.
Consider a binary tree representing a small Indian family business: the root is “Founder”.
The Founder has two children, “Elder Son” and “Younger Daughter”.

cards.title: A subtree of a binary tree is a tree consisting of a node in the original tree…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: A subtree of a binary tree is a tree consisting of a node in the original tree and all of its descendants. The node becomes the root of the subtree, and the edges connecting it to its children, grandchildren, and so on are retained. Every node in a binary tree is the root of a subtree; the whole tree itself is the subtree rooted at the original root. A subtree inherits the binary‑tree property: each node has at most two children. The size of a subtree is the number of nodes it contains; its height is the length of the longest downward path from its root to a leaf. Subtrees are recursive structures — the left and right children of the subtree root are themselves roots of subtrees. This recursive nature underpins many tree algorithms (traversal, search, insertion). The concept of a subtree is distinct from a subgraph: a subgraph may omit some descendants, whereas a subtree must include every descendant of its root. Siblings (nodes with the same parent) are roots of disjoint subtrees that together form the subtrees of their parent. Understanding subtrees is essential for defining tree traversals, for calculating tree properties recursively, and for operations such as copying or comparing trees.
steps: A subtree is any node together with all its descendants, forming a complete binary tree in its own right.

Here is why: first, the recursive definition of a binary tree states that a tree is either empty or consists of a root node with a left subtree and a right subtree; this directly makes every node the root of a subtree.
Second, the properties of the original tree — such as the binary‑node limit — are preserved in every subtree, so algorithms that work on the whole tree also work on any subtree.
Third, subtrees partition the tree: the left and right subtrees of a node are disjoint and together with the node itself constitute the subtree rooted at that node.
Consider a family tree drawn as a binary tree where each person has at most two children.

The subtree rooted at your father includes your father, you, your siblings, your children, and so on — everyone descended from him. If you pick a leaf (a person with no children), that leaf alone is a subtree of size 1…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “a subtree is any connected subset of nodes”) reveals the misconception that a subtree need not be closed under descendants — confusing subgraph with subtree.

cards.title: Input size is the quantitative measure of the data a program or algorithm…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Input size is the quantitative measure of the data a program or algorithm receives before it starts executing. In algorithmic analysis it is denoted by n and can represent the number of elements in an array, the length of a string, the number of vertices in a graph, or any parameter that grows with the problem instance. The choice of n must reflect the dominant factor that determines how many primitive operations (comparisons, assignments, arithmetic) the algorithm performs. For example, linear search on an array of length n examines each element once, so its running time is proportional to n. In contrast, binary search on a sorted array of length n halves the search space each step, giving a logarithmic relationship. Understanding input size is the foundation for estimating complexity, identifying the dominant term, and classifying best, average, and worst‑case behaviours, which are later expressed using Big O notation.

cards.title: Estimating complexity is the process of determining how the running time or…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Estimating complexity is the process of determining how the running time or resource usage of an algorithm scales with the size of its input, denoted n. It involves identifying the basic operations (comparisons, assignments, arithmetic, method calls) that dominate execution and expressing their count as a function f(n). The estimate ignores constant factors and lower‑order terms because they become insignificant for large n. The result is a high‑level classification such as O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), etc. This node focuses on the mechanics of counting: analysing loops, nested loops, recursive calls, and conditional branches to build f(n). It connects the concrete input size (node 001) to the abstract dominant term (node 003) and prepares the ground for best/average/worst‑case distinctions (nodes 004‑006) and full Big‑O analysis of standard algorithms (node 007).
steps: The one thing to remember: To estimate complexity, count how many times the most expensive basic operation runs as a function of the input size n, then keep only the fastest‑growing term.
Here is why: asymptotic analysis cares about growth for large n; constants and smaller terms never change the classification.

cards.title: The dominant term of a time‑complexity function T(n) is the single term that…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: The dominant term of a time‑complexity function T(n) is the single term that exhibits the highest asymptotic growth rate as the input size n approaches infinity. When a complexity expression is written as a sum of terms — such as polynomial terms (nᵏ), logarithmic terms (log n), linearithmic terms (n log n), or exponential terms (cⁿ) — the term with the greatest order in the standard hierarchy (constant < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < … < cⁿ) is the dominant term. All lower‑order terms and constant multipliers become insignificant in the limit and are discarded when expressing the complexity in Big‑O notation. Identifying the dominant term therefore directly yields the Big‑O class: if the dominant term is a·nᵏ, the algorithm is O(nᵏ); if it is a·cⁿ, the class is O(cⁿ). This concept links the concrete step‑counting skill from the previous node (estimating complexity) to the case‑analysis nodes (best, average, worst) and to the final Big‑O analysis of searching and sorting algorithms, because every case reduces to finding the fastest‑growing term of its respective T(n).
steps: The dominant term of a complexity function is the single term that grows fastest as the input size n becomes large, and it alone decides the algorithm’s Big‑O class.
Here is why: (1) As n increases, lower‑order terms such as 5n or 10 become negligible compared with n².
(2) Constant multipliers like 3 in 3n² do not change the growth rate; they only scale the curve.
(3) Big‑O notation formally captures this by keeping only the highest‑order term.
Consider a typical ISC problem: an algorithm runs in T(n) = 4n² + 7n log n + 20 steps.
For n = 10, the terms are 400, 70·log10≈70, and 20; the n² term already contributes most.

cards.title: Best case complexity describes the minimum amount of time (or space) an…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Best case complexity describes the minimum amount of time (or space) an algorithm requires for any input of size n, occurring when the input is arranged in the most favourable way. It is expressed using Big O notation after identifying the dominant term from the exact operation count under that optimal input. While the best case gives a lower bound on performance, it does not represent typical behaviour; average and worst‑case analyses are needed for a full picture. The concept builds on earlier ideas: input size determines the variable n, estimating complexity counts operations, and the dominant term isolates the growth rate that matters for large n. Understanding best case helps students recognise when an algorithm can be exceptionally fast (e.g., finding a key at the first position) and why such scenarios are useful for establishing lower bounds, even though they are rare in practice.
steps: The best case time complexity of an algorithm describes the minimum number of operations it performs for any input of size n, occurring when the input is arranged most favourably.
First, best case is found by examining the algorithm’s steps under the most advantageous input configuration.
Second, the exact operation count is simplified by keeping only the dominant term, which determines the Big O bound for the best case.
Third, while the best case reveals a lower bound, it does not reflect typical behaviour; average and worst‑case analyses are needed for realistic performance expectations.

Fourth, different algorithms exhibit distinct best‑case behaviours: linear search finishes in constant time when the target is first, binary search does the same when the target is the middle element, and an optimized…

cards.title: Average‑case complexity quantifies the expected resource consumption
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Average‑case complexity quantifies the expected resource consumption (time or space) of an algorithm when the input follows a specified probability distribution, usually the uniform distribution over all possible inputs of a given size n. It is expressed as a function A(n) = Σ p(i)·T(i) where p(i) is the probability of the i‑th input instance and T(i) its running time. In algorithm analysis we often assume each permutation of the input is equally likely, so the average case becomes the arithmetic mean of the running times over all permutations. This measure sits between best‑case (minimum over inputs) and worst‑case (maximum over inputs) and is crucial for algorithms whose performance varies widely with input arrangement, such as quicksort, linear search, or hash‑table operations. The dominant term of A(n) determines its Big‑O class; for example, linear search has average‑case Θ(n) because the expected position of the target is (n+1)/2. Understanding average case requires knowledge of input size, probability models, and the dominant‑term simplification taught in earlier nodes.
steps: Average‑case complexity tells us the typical effort an algorithm needs when inputs are randomly ordered.
Here is why: it bridges the gap between optimistic best‑case and pessimistic worst‑case, giving a realistic performance estimate for everyday data.
First, we define a probability model — usually every permutation of n distinct elements is equally likely.
Second, we compute the expected running time by summing the product of each input’s probability and its cost.
Third, we simplify the resulting expression by keeping only the dominant term, which yields the Big‑O class.
Consider linear search on an array of size n: the target can be at any position 1…n with probability 1/n, and if absent we check all n positions.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “n/2”) reveals the misconception that the sum of first n integers is n²/2 instead of n(n+1)/2, ignoring the +1 term that matters for exact counts.
remember: What is the average‑case number of comparisons for linear search on an array of size n when the target is guaranteed to be present and each position is equally likely.
Explain why quicksort’s average‑case time complexity is Θ(n log n) while its worst case is Θ(n²).
A student claims that for any algorithm, average‑case complexity is always asymptotically between best‑case and worst‑case complexities. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Worst‑case time complexity of an algorithm is a function T_worst(n) that gives…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Worst‑case time complexity of an algorithm is a function T_worst(n) that gives the maximum number of elementary operations (comparisons, assignments, arithmetic) the algorithm performs over all possible inputs of size n. It is expressed using Big‑O notation as O(f(n)) where f(n) is the dominant term of the upper bound. Unlike best‑case (minimum steps) or average‑case (expected steps under a probability distribution), worst‑case provides a guaranteed performance ceiling, making it essential for real‑time systems and competitive programming where latency spikes are unacceptable. The worst‑case analysis assumes an adversarial input that forces the algorithm down its most expensive path — e.g., a sorted array for quick‑sort with a naïve pivot, or a key absent from a linear search. It is related to the dominant‑term concept because lower‑order terms and constants are dropped, leaving only the growth rate that matters for large n. Understanding worst‑case also underpins the analysis of searching and sorting algorithms in the next node.
steps: The worst‑case complexity is the maximum number of steps an algorithm can take for any input of size n, giving a guaranteed upper bound.
Here is why: it protects system designers from unexpected slowdowns by assuming the most hostile input arrangement.

Consider a linear search on an array of length n. The algorithm checks each element sequentially until it finds the target or reaches the end. The worst case occurs when the target is absent or placed at the last…
This yields T_worst(n)=n → O(n).
For binary search on a sorted array, the worst case happens when the target is not present, requiring _2 n + 1 comparisons → O( n).
In sorting, bubble sort always performs (n(n-1))/(2) comparisons regardless of input order, so its worst case is O(n^2).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., O(1) or O( n)) reveals the misconception that the algorithm might “get lucky” or that the search halves the search space, confusing linear search with binary search.
remember: What is the worst‑case time complexity of linear search on an unsorted array of size n.
Explain why the worst‑case complexity of binary search on a sorted array of size n is O( n) and not O(n).
A student claims that quick‑sort always runs in O(n n) time. Using worst‑case analysis, evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Big O notation describes the asymptotic upper bound of an algorithm’s running…
cards.subject: Computer Science
cards.definition: Big O notation describes the asymptotic upper bound of an algorithm’s running time as a function of the input size n. It captures the dominant term of the exact cost function after discarding lower‑order terms and constant factors. For searching algorithms, linear search examines every element once, giving a worst‑case cost of n comparisons → O(n). Binary search repeatedly halves the search interval, yielding a recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+O(1) whose solution is O(log n). For sorting, quadratic algorithms such as bubble sort, selection sort, and insertion sort perform roughly n²/2 comparisons in the worst case → O(n²). Divide‑and‑conquer sorts like merge sort and quicksort (average case) follow T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) → O(n log n). The best, average, and worst cases differ: insertion sort achieves O(n) on already sorted data, while quicksort degrades to O(n²) when partitions are highly unbalanced. Big O analysis therefore lets us compare algorithms by their growth rates, independent of hardware or implementation constants, and guides the choice of algorithm for a given problem size.
steps: Big O notation captures the dominant growth rate of an algorithm’s running time as the input size increases, allowing you to compare searching and sorting methods without measuring actual seconds.

Here is why: first, the input size n defines the problem scale; every algorithm’s cost can be expressed as a function of n. Second, counting basic operations (comparisons, swaps) yields an exact cost function; the term…
Third, best, average, and worst cases arise from different input arrangements; for example, insertion sort runs in O(n) on sorted data but O(n²) on reverse‑sorted data.
Fourth, searching algorithms illustrate the contrast: linear search always scans all n elements in the worst case → O(n), while binary search halves the search space each step → O(log n).

Fifth, sorting algorithms split into quadratic (bubble, selection, insertion) and divide‑and‑conquer (merge, quicksort) families; the former have O(n²) worst case, the latter O(n log n) average case, with quicksort’s…
Consider a classroom roll‑call list of 500 names.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., O(1)) reveals the misconception that search always finishes in constant time, confusing best‑case (element found at first position) with worst‑case analysis.
remember: What is the worst‑case time complexity of linear search in Big O notation.
Explain why binary search has O(log n) worst‑case complexity.
A student claims that bubble sort’s best‑case complexity is O(n²). Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: In microeconomic theory, demand refers to the quantity of a good or service…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: In microeconomic theory, demand refers to the quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at various possible prices during a specific period, ceteris paribus. It is an effective desire backed by purchasing power, distinguishing it from mere wants or needs. The relationship between price and quantity demanded is inverse (law of demand) and is represented by a demand schedule (tabular) and a demand curve (graphical, downward sloping). Demand is a flow concept measured per unit of time (e.g., units per month). It depends on the good’s own price, consumer income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes, expectations, and number of buyers. The demand function mathematically expresses this dependence: Qd = f(Px, Y, Pr, T, E, N). A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along the demand curve; changes in any other determinant cause a shift of the demand curve. Understanding demand is foundational for analyzing consumer equilibrium, market equilibrium, elasticity, and welfare economics.
steps: Demand is the effective desire backed by purchasing power and willingness to pay at a given price.
Here is why: without any one of the three pillars — desire, ability, willingness — no transaction occurs, and the concept of demand collapses to a mere wish.
First, consider a Class 12 student who wants a premium smartphone priced at ₹70,000.
The desire exists, but if the student’s pocket money is ₹5,000, ability to pay is absent; demand is zero.
Second, even with ability, willingness matters: a wealthy collector may afford the phone but refuses to buy because he prefers a different brand; again demand is zero.
Third, when all three align — desire for the phone, ₹70,000 in the bank, and willingness to part with that amount — the student becomes a demander at that price.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “demand is just what people want”) reveals the misconception that desire alone constitutes demand, ignoring the necessity of purchasing power and willingness.
remember: Define demand and list the three essential conditions that must be satisfied for a want to become demand.
A student says, “If the price of mangoes falls, the demand for mangoes will increase.” Identify the error and restate the statement correctly using proper terminology.
Evaluate whether the following scenario represents a change in demand or a change in quantity demanded: “Due to a successful advertising campaign, more teenagers start buying….

cards.title: Demand for a commodity is the quantity consumers are willing and able to…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Demand for a commodity is the quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase at various prices, ceteris paribus. The factors (determinants) of demand are variables that, when they change, cause the entire demand curve to shift rightward (increase in demand) or leftward (decrease in demand). The principal factors are: 1. Price of the good itself – causes a movement along the curve, not a shift (covered in node 005). 2. Consumer income – for normal goods, higher income shifts demand right; for inferior goods, it shifts left. 3. Prices of related goods – a rise in the price of a substitute (e.g., tea vs. coffee) shifts demand for the good right; a rise in the price of a complement (e.g., petrol for cars) shifts demand left. 4. Tastes and preferences – advertising, health reports, or cultural trends can shift demand. 5. Expectations of future prices or income – anticipated price hikes raise current demand; expected income loss lowers it. 6. Number of buyers – population growth or market entry of new consumers shifts demand right. These factors operate simultaneously; the net shift is the vector sum of their individual effects. Understanding them is essential before writing the demand function (node 003) and deriving the law of demand (node 004).
steps: Demand for a good changes not only because of its own price but also due to income, prices of related goods, tastes, expectations, and the number of buyers, each causing a shift of the entire demand curve.
Here is why: 1.
Income effect – When a middle‑class family in Bengaluru gets a Diwali bonus, they buy more branded sneakers (normal good) at every price, shifting the sneaker demand curve right.
If the same bonus makes them switch from coarse rice to basmati, coarse‑rice demand shifts left because it is an inferior good. 2.
Prices of related goods – A sudden spike in petrol prices (complement to cars) makes families postpone car purchases, shifting the car demand curve left.
Conversely, if the price of tea rises, coffee demand shifts right as consumers substitute. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “price of the good itself”) reveals the misconception that any price change shifts the curve, confusing movement along the curve with a shift of the curve.
remember: List the six non‑price determinants of demand that cause a shift of the demand curve.
Explain how an increase in consumer income shifts the demand curve for a normal good and for an inferior good, using an Indian example for each.
Evaluate the statement: “A rise in the price of petrol will increase the demand for cars because people will want to travel more.” Identify the error and correct it.

cards.title: A demand function expresses the quantitative relationship between the quantity…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: A demand function expresses the quantitative relationship between the quantity demanded of a good (Qd) and its determinants. In the CISCE ISC syllabus the standard specification is: Qd = f(P, Y, Pr, T, E, N) where - P = own price of the good (₹ per unit) - Y = consumer’s disposable income (₹ per period) - Pr = price of related goods — substitutes (e.g., Yippee) and complements (e.g., Maggi masala) - T = tastes and preferences (captured by a shift parameter) - E = expectations about future prices or income - N = number of buyers in the market The function is usually linearised for classroom analysis: Qd = a – bP + cY + dPr + eT + fE + gN, with a, b, c, d, e, f, g > 0 (except b > 0 ensures the law of demand). The coefficients show the sensitivity (elasticity) of demand to each factor. This node focuses on constructing, interpreting, and using the demand function; derivation of the law of demand, movements vs shifts, and exceptions are covered in sibling nodes.
steps: The demand function is a compact algebraic statement that tells exactly how many units consumers will buy at any combination of price, income, related‑goods prices, tastes, expectations, and market size.
Here is why: it turns the qualitative list of factors from the previous node into a quantitative tool that can be used for forecasting, policy simulation, and equilibrium analysis.

First, each determinant enters with a theoretically predicted sign: own price (negative), income (positive for normal goods), substitute price (positive), complement price (negative), favourable taste shift (positive)…

Second, the linear form Qd = a – bP + cY + dPr + eT + fE + gN lets us plug in real numbers — for instance, a = 500, b = 2, c = 0.01, d = 1.5, e = 10, f = 5, g = 0.2 — and instantly compute Qd for any scenario.

Third, because only P appears with a negative sign on the right‑hand side, a change in P moves us along a fixed curve; any change in Y, Pr, T, E, or N alters the intercept (a + cY + dPr + eT + fE + gN) and therefore…

Fourth, the coefficients are the building blocks for price elasticity (–b·P/Qd), income elasticity (c·Y/Qd), and cross‑elasticity (d·Pr/Qd), linking this node forward to elasticity concepts in later chapters.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “income has a negative sign for all goods”) reveals the misconception that higher income always reduces demand — confusing inferior goods with the normal‑good assumption used in the basic linear model.
remember: List the six standard determinants of demand that appear in the CISCE ISC demand function Qd = f(P, Y, Pr, T, E, N) and state the expected sign of each coefficient in a linearised….
Given the linear demand function Qd = 500 – 2P + 0.01Y + 1.5Pr + 10T + 5E + 0.2N, explain why a rise in consumer income from ₹30,000 to ₹35,000 shifts the demand curve rather than….
Evaluate the statement: “In the demand function Qd = a – bP + cY, the coefficient b measures the income elasticity of demand.”.

cards.title: The Law of Demand states that, ceteris paribus…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The Law of Demand states that, ceteris paribus, there is an inverse relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded by a rational consumer. Its derivation rests on utility maximisation: a consumer allocates income so that the marginal utility per rupee spent is equal across all goods (MUₓ/Pₓ = MUᵧ/Pᵧ = λ). When the price of good X falls, MUₓ/Pₓ rises above λ, prompting the consumer to buy more X until MUₓ falls (by diminishing marginal utility) and equality is restored. The resulting price‑quantity pairs trace the individual demand curve. Aggregating across consumers yields the market demand curve. The derivation links three core concepts: (1) diminishing marginal utility (MU falls as consumption rises), (2) the equimarginal principle (equalising MU per rupee), and (3) the budget constraint (PₓQₓ + PᵧQᵧ = M). Changes in income, tastes, or prices of related goods shift the curve; only own‑price changes cause movement along it.
steps: The law of demand emerges because a rational consumer equalises marginal utility per rupee across all goods; when a good’s price falls, its MU‑per‑rupee rises, so the consumer buys more until diminishing MU restores…
Here is why: start with a consumer who spends a fixed income M on two goods, X and Y. The utility‑maximisation condition is MUₓ/Pₓ = MUᵧ/Pᵧ = λ (the marginal utility of money).
Suppose Pₓ drops from ₹20 to ₹15 while MUₓ at the current bundle is 30 utils.
Initially MUₓ/Pₓ = 30/20 = 1.5; after the fall it becomes 30/15 = 2.0, which exceeds λ.
The consumer now gains more satisfaction per rupee from X, so she reallocates spending toward X. As she buys more X, MUₓ falls (law of diminishing marginal utility) until MUₓ/Pₓ again equals λ.
The new equilibrium quantity of X is higher — this price‑quantity pair is a point on the demand curve.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “MUₓ = MUᵧ”) reveals the misconception that equal marginal utilities, not equal marginal utilities per rupee, drive optimal choice — ignoring price differences.
remember: State the utility‑maximisation condition that underlies the derivation of the law of demand for a two‑good case.
Explain why a fall in the price of good X leads to an increase in its quantity demanded, using the concept of diminishing marginal utility.
Evaluate the statement: “The law of demand can be derived without assuming diminishing marginal utility.”.

cards.title: Movement along a demand curve occurs when only the own price of the good…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Movement along a demand curve occurs when only the own price of the good changes, causing quantity demanded to change while all other determinants (income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations) stay constant. A shift of the demand curve happens when any non‑price determinant changes — such as a rise in consumer income, a change in preferences, a price change of a substitute or complement, or altered expectations — so that at every price a different quantity is demanded. The demand function Q_d = f(P, Y, P_s, P_c, T, E) makes this explicit: a change in P produces a movement; a change in Y, P_s, P_c, T, or E produces a shift. Graphically, a movement is a slide from one point to another on the same curve; a shift draws a new curve leftward (decrease in demand) or rightward (increase in demand). Understanding this distinction is essential for analysing market equilibrium, price elasticity, and policy impacts.
steps: The key takeaway: a change in the good’s own price moves you along the demand curve; any other change draws a new demand curve.
Here is why: the demand curve is drawn ceteris paribus — all non‑price factors are held fixed.
When only price varies, the quantity demanded responds according to the law of demand, tracing points on the existing curve.
When income rises, consumers can afford more at every price, so the whole curve shifts rightward.
A change in taste, say a celebrity endorsing a brand, also shifts the curve rightward because willingness to pay increases at each price.
If the price of a substitute (e.g., tea) falls, demand for the original good (coffee) shifts leftward as consumers switch.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the demand curve shifts right”) reveals the misconception that any increase in quantity demanded means a shift, confusing “change in quantity demanded” with “change in demand”.
remember: What happens on a demand diagram when the price of the good itself falls, all else equal.
If consumers’ incomes rise and the good is normal, how does the demand curve respond.
A news report says the price of petrol has fallen. Explain the effect on the demand curve for cars.

cards.title: Exceptions to the law of demand are goods for which the quantity demanded rises…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Exceptions to the law of demand are goods for which the quantity demanded rises as price rises, violating the usual inverse price‑quantity relationship. The main categories are: 1. Giffen goods – inferior staples (e.g., coarse rice in low‑income households) where the negative income effect of a price rise outweighs the substitution effect, so consumers buy more despite the higher price. 2. Veblen goods – conspicuous‑consumption luxuries (e.g., designer handbags, high‑end cars) where a higher price enhances perceived status, increasing demand. 3. Necessities with no close substitutes – essential medicines or salt; demand is nearly perfectly inelastic, so a price rise barely reduces quantity demanded, and in extreme cases (e.g., panic buying) quantity may even rise. 4. Speculative assets – shares, cryptocurrency, or real estate where buyers expect future price gains; a current price rise signals further appreciation, prompting more purchases. 5. Quality‑price inference goods – products where consumers use price as a quality signal (e.g., premium branded spices); a price cut may be interpreted as quality deterioration, reducing demand. Each exception hinges on the relative strength of income, substitution, psychological, or expectation effects, which are explored later in cardinal and ordinal utility analysis.
steps: The key takeaway is that the law of demand holds for most goods, but specific income, psychological, or expectation mechanisms can reverse the price‑quantity link.
First, consider Giffen goods: a poor household spends most of its income on a staple like coarse wheat.
When the price of wheat rises, the household’s real income falls sharply; it cannot afford superior cereals, so it cuts back on them and buys even more wheat to survive.
The income effect dominates the substitution effect, producing an upward‑sloping demand segment.
Second, Veblen goods operate through social signalling.
A luxury SUV priced at ₹1.2 crore may sell fewer units than the same model at ₹1.5 crore because the higher price amplifies its status value among affluent buyers in metros like Mumbai or Delhi.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “normal goods like wheat”) reveals the misconception that any staple is a Giffen good, ignoring the requirement that the income effect must outweigh the substitution effect.
remember: Name any three exceptions to the law of demand and give a one‑sentence Indian example for each.
Explain why a Giffen good’s demand curve slopes upward, referring explicitly to income and substitution effects.
Evaluate the statement: “All luxury goods are Veblen goods.” Provide a reasoned judgment.

cards.title: Cardinal utility assumes satisfaction can be measured in absolute units (utils).
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Cardinal utility assumes satisfaction can be measured in absolute units (utils). Total Utility (TU) is the sum of utilities derived from all units consumed: TU = Σ MUᵢ. Marginal Utility (MU) is the change in TU from consuming one additional unit: MU = ΔTU/ΔQ. The TU‑MU relationship is deterministic: as long as MU > 0, TU rises; when MU = 0, TU reaches its peak; when MU < 0, TU declines. This relationship underpins the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility (next node) and the derivation of the demand curve through consumer equilibrium. The concepts are expressed in discrete units (utils) and are assumed additive and independent across goods.
steps: The TU‑MU relationship is the arithmetic backbone of cardinal utility: TU is the cumulative sum of MU, and MU is the discrete derivative of TU. Here is why: TU increases as long as each extra unit adds positive utility…
Consider a student buying cups of chai at a campus canteen.
The first cup yields 10 utils, the second 7, the third 3, the fourth 0, the fifth –2.
TU after each cup: 10, 17, 20, 20, 18.
MU sequence: 10, 7, 3, 0, –2.

Plotting TU gives a concave curve peaking at the fourth cup; plotting MU gives a downward‑sloping line crossing the horizontal axis at the fourth cup. This visual link lets us locate the saturation point without…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “MU is the average utility per unit”) reveals the misconception that MU equals TU/Q, confusing marginal with average.
remember: Define Total Utility and Marginal Utility and state the mathematical relationship between them.
A consumer’s TU schedule for good X is: Q=1 TU=12, Q=2 TU=20, Q=3 TU=25, Q=4 TU=27, Q=5 TU=26. Calculate MU for each unit and identify the quantity where TU is maximum.
Explain why the MU curve must intersect the horizontal axis at the quantity where TU is at its maximum.

cards.title: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that, ceteris paribus…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that, ceteris paribus, as a consumer consumes successive units of a homogeneous good within a given time period, the marginal utility (additional satisfaction) derived from each extra unit declines. Total Utility (TU) continues to rise as long as Marginal Utility (MU) is positive, but at a decreasing rate; TU reaches its maximum when MU becomes zero and falls if MU turns negative. This law underpins the downward‑sloping demand curve because a rational consumer will buy more only at a lower price when MU falls. It assumes cardinal measurability of utility, constant marginal utility of money, rationality, and no change in tastes, income, or prices of related goods. The relationship with the TU‑MU schedule (covered in the previous node) is direct: MU is the slope of the TU curve, and diminishing MU means the TU curve becomes progressively flatter.
steps: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility asserts that each additional unit of a good yields less extra satisfaction than the previous one, provided all other factors stay constant.
Here is why: first, human wants are satiable — after a point the intensity of desire falls.

Second, goods are not perfect substitutes for each other; the first unit satisfies the most urgent want, the next unit a less urgent one. Third, the marginal utility of money is assumed constant, so the consumer’s…
Fourth, consumption occurs in a continuous, short period so that tastes and income remain unchanged.
Consider a student buying cups of chai from a campus canteen: the first cup (₹10) gives 20 utils, the second 15 utils, the third 8 utils, the fourth 2 utils, and the fifth 0 utils.
Plotting TU (cumulative) gives 20, 35, 43, 45, 45 — rising but flattening.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Total utility falls with each extra unit”) reveals the misconception that total utility and marginal utility move together — confusing the level of satisfaction with its incremental change.
remember: State the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility in one sentence.
Explain why the assumption of constant marginal utility of money is necessary for the law to hold.
Evaluate the statement: “If marginal utility becomes negative, total utility must also be negative.”.

cards.title: Consumer’s equilibrium under cardinal utility refers to the combination of…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Consumer’s equilibrium under cardinal utility refers to the combination of goods that maximises a consumer’s total utility given a fixed income and market prices. For a single commodity, equilibrium occurs when the marginal utility (MU) derived from the last unit consumed equals its price (P), assuming the marginal utility of money (MUm) is constant and equal to one util per rupee. In a multi‑commodity setting, the condition extends to the equimarginal principle: MUₓ/Pₓ = MUᵧ/Pᵧ = … = MUm. This node focuses on the single‑good case, deriving the equilibrium condition from the law of diminishing marginal utility (covered in node) and the TU‑MU relationship (node). Graphically, equilibrium is the quantity where the MU curve intersects the horizontal price line. The concept links directly to the Law of Equimarginal Utility (node), which generalises the condition to several goods.
steps: Consumer equilibrium is the quantity where the marginal utility of the last unit consumed exactly equals its price, because only then does the consumer have no incentive to buy more or less.
Here is why: (1) The law of diminishing marginal utility ensures MU falls as consumption rises.
(2) Price is constant for a price‑taking consumer.
(3) If MU > P, the consumer gains net utility by buying another unit; if MU < P, the consumer loses utility on the last unit and should reduce consumption.
(4) Therefore, the optimal quantity is where MU = P. (5) This condition also equals the marginal utility of money when MUm = 1 util/₹.
Consider Riya, who loves mangoes at ₹40/kg.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “TU = P”) reveals confusion between total and marginal utility — total utility is the sum of all marginal utilities, not the decision variable for the next unit.
remember: State the condition for consumer equilibrium in the single‑commodity cardinal utility framework.
If the marginal utility of the 4th unit of a good is 25 utils and its price is ₹20, should the consumer buy the 4th unit? Explain.
Given MU schedule: Q=1→50, Q=2→40, Q=3→30, Q=4→20, Q=5→10 utils. Price = ₹25. Determine equilibrium quantity and justify.

cards.title: The Law of Equimarginal Utility states that a rational consumer maximises total…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The Law of Equimarginal Utility states that a rational consumer maximises total utility by allocating income across goods such that the marginal utility per unit of money spent is equal for all goods consumed. Formally, for goods X and Y with prices Px and Py, equilibrium requires MUx/Px = MUy/Py = MUm, where MUm is the marginal utility of money. The law extends the single‑good consumer equilibrium (MU = P·MUm) to multiple goods, assuming cardinal measurability of utility, constant marginal utility of money, and diminishing marginal utility for each good. It links the cardinal utility framework (TU‑MU relationship, Law of Diminishing MU) to the consumer’s optimal basket and provides the foundation for deriving the demand curve from utility maximisation. The condition also implies that if MUx/Px > MUy/Py, the consumer should shift expenditure from Y to X until equality is restored.
steps: The Law of Equimarginal Utility tells us that a consumer reaches maximum satisfaction when the last rupee spent on each good yields the same marginal utility.
Here is why: (1) Utility is cardinal and measurable in utils;
(2) Marginal utility of each good diminishes as more is consumed;
(3) Marginal utility of money remains constant for small income changes;
(4) Rational consumers compare MU per rupee across goods and reallocate until equality holds;
(5) This equality generates the consumer’s demand schedule for each good.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “MUx = MUy”) reveals the misconception that absolute marginal utilities must be equal, ignoring price differences.
remember: State the equimarginal condition for a consumer buying two goods X and Y with prices Px and Py.
Explain why a consumer will reallocate spending if MUx/Px > MUy/Py.
Evaluate the statement: “The Law of Equimarginal Utility assumes that marginal utility of money changes with income.”.

cards.title: Ordinal utility theory ranks bundles of goods without measuring utility in…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Ordinal utility theory ranks bundles of goods without measuring utility in absolute units. An indifference curve (IC) is the locus of all combinations of two goods (say, X and Y) that yield the same level of satisfaction to a rational consumer. Key properties: (1) ICs slope downward — more of one good requires less of the other to keep utility constant. (2) ICs are convex to the origin — the marginal rate of substitution (MRS = –ΔY/ΔX) diminishes as X increases, reflecting diminishing marginal willingness to substitute. (3) Higher ICs represent higher utility levels; they never intersect because that would imply inconsistent preferences. An indifference map is a family of ICs showing the consumer’s complete preference ordering. The analysis assumes completeness, transitivity, non‑satiation, and continuity of preferences. Unlike cardinal utility, no numerical utility values are assigned; only the ranking matters. The MRS at any point equals the slope of the tangent to the IC and also equals the ratio of marginal utilities (MUx/MUy) when a differentiable utility function exists. This node covers the meaning, shape, properties, and the concept of MRS; budget line and consumer equilibrium are treated in subsequent nodes.
steps: The one thing to remember: an indifference curve maps all bundles that give a consumer equal satisfaction, and its convex shape captures the idea that the more you have of a good, the less you are willing to give up of…
Here is why: (1) Preferences are ordinal — we only need to know which bundle is preferred, not by how much.
(2) Non‑satiation means more is better, so curves further from the origin represent higher utility.

(3) Diminishing MRS follows from the convexity assumption: as you consume more samosas, each additional samosa adds less extra satisfaction, so you surrender fewer chai for it. (4) ICs cannot cross because crossing…
(5) The slope of the IC at any point is the MRS, which equals the ratio of marginal utilities when a utility function exists, linking ordinal and cardinal frameworks.
Consider Riya, a Class 12 student in Mumbai, who spends her pocket money on vada pav (X) and cold coffee (Y).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it shows the maximum utility a consumer can achieve”) reveals the misconception that an IC indicates an optimum rather than a constant‑utility locus.
remember: What does an indifference curve represent in ordinal utility analysis.
Why are indifference curves convex to the origin for normal goods.
Evaluate the statement: “Two indifference curves can intersect if the consumer’s preferences change over time.”.

cards.title: The budget line (or budget constraint) represents all combinations of two goods…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The budget line (or budget constraint) represents all combinations of two goods that a consumer can purchase given a fixed money income and the prevailing market prices. Formally, for goods X and Y with prices P_X and P_Y and money income M, the budget line is the set of points (X,Y) satisfying P_X X + P_Y Y = M. Its intercepts are M/P_X on the X‑axis and M/P_Y on the Y‑axis. The slope equals -P_X/P_Y, reflecting the market rate of substitution: the amount of Y that must be forgone to obtain one more unit of X. A change in income shifts the line parallel (outward for a rise, inward for a fall) while a change in the price of one good rotates the line about the intercept of the other good. The budget line is the foundation for ordinal utility analysis; consumer equilibrium under indifference‑curve analysis occurs where the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the budget line, i.e., where the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio.
steps: The budget line is the consumer’s feasible set: every point on or below the line can be afforded, every point above cannot.
Here is why: the line translates the abstract idea of “limited money” into a concrete geometric boundary that can be combined with indifference curves to find the optimal bundle.
First, write the identity P_X X + P_Y Y = M. For example, if a student in Mumbai has ₹500, the price of a vada pav is ₹25 and a cutting chai is ₹10, the equation is 25X + 10Y = 500.
The X‑intercept (maximum vada pavs) is 500/25 = 20; the Y‑intercept (maximum chai) is 500/10 = 50.
The slope -25/10 = -2.5 means each extra vada pav costs 2.5 cups of chai.
Second, an increase in pocket money to ₹600 shifts the line outward parallelly: new intercepts 24 and 60, slope unchanged.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 40X + 20Y = 400) reveals the misconception that income is halved when writing the equation — confusing the budget constraint with the intercept calculation.

cards.title: Consumer’s equilibrium under ordinal utility occurs when a rational consumer…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition:
Consumer’s equilibrium under ordinal utility occurs when a rational consumer allocates a fixed money income across two goods such that the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) between the goods equals their price ratio, and the chosen bundle lies on the budget line. Formally, for goods X and Y with prices P_X and P_Y and income M, equilibrium satisfies:
1. Tangency condition: MRS_XY = (MU_X)/(MU_Y) = (P_X)/(P_Y).
2. Budget constraint: P_X X + P_Y Y = M.
3. Convexity: Indifference curves are convex to the origin (diminishing MRS), ensuring the tangency is a maximum, not a minimum.
If the tangency condition cannot be met (e.g., perfect substitutes or perfect complements), equilibrium occurs at a corner solution where the consumer spends all income on one good or consumes goods in fixed proportions. This node builds on the indifference curve and budget line concepts; it does not re‑derive their properties.
steps: The consumer reaches equilibrium where the highest attainable indifference curve just touches the budget line, so the slope of the indifference curve (MRS) equals the slope of the budget line (price ratio).
Here is why: the budget line shows all bundles the consumer can afford; indifference curves rank bundles by preference.
Moving along the budget line, the consumer gains utility until the marginal gain from swapping one good for another exactly matches the market trade‑off (price ratio).
At that point, any further swap would reduce total satisfaction.
First, write the utility function (e.g., U = X^0.5Y^0.5) and compute marginal utilities MU_X = 0.5X^-0.5Y^0.5, MU_Y = 0.5X^0.5Y^-0.5.
Their ratio gives MRS_XY = Y/X.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “total utility is maximised when marginal utilities are equal”) reveals the misconception that cardinal equality of marginal utilities is required, confusing cardinal with ordinal analysis.
remember: State the two necessary conditions for a consumer’s equilibrium in the ordinal utility framework.
Explain why the tangency condition MRS_XY=P_X/P_Y is sufficient for a maximum only when indifference curves are convex to the origin.
A consumer has utility U = X + 2Y, prices P_X=10, P_Y=20, income M=200. Determine the equilibrium bundle and justify whether it is interior or corner.

cards.title: Elasticity of demand quantifies the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Elasticity of demand quantifies the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in one of its determinants — primarily price, but also income, price of related goods, and expectations. The core concept is the price elasticity of demand (PED), defined as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, holding other factors constant. A PED greater than 1 (in absolute value) indicates elastic demand: consumers react strongly to price changes. A PED less than 1 indicates inelastic demand: quantity demanded is relatively unresponsive. Unitary elasticity (PED = 1) means proportional changes. The concept extends to income elasticity of demand (YED) — responsiveness to income changes — and cross elasticity of demand (XED) — responsiveness to price changes of substitutes or complements. Degrees of elasticity (perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic, relatively elastic, relatively inelastic, unitary) classify the magnitude of responsiveness. Measurement methods — percentage (point) method, total expenditure (outlay) method, and geometric (arc) method — provide alternative computational routes. Understanding the meaning of elasticity is foundational; subsequent nodes (types, degrees, measurement techniques, cross and income elasticity) build on this core definition.
steps: Elasticity of demand is the measure of how much quantity demanded stretches or shrinks when a determinant such as price, income, or the price of a related good changes.
Here is why: the law of demand tells us that price and quantity move in opposite directions, but it does not tell us how much quantity moves.

Elasticity fills that gap by giving a pure number — a ratio of percentage changes — that is independent of units, allowing comparison across goods (e.g., petrol vs. mangoes) and across markets (e.g., rural vs. urban…
Consider a street vendor selling samosas at ₹10 each.
If he raises the price to ₹12 and sales fall from 200 to 150 pieces a day, the percentage price rise is 20 % and the percentage quantity fall is 25 %.
The price elasticity of demand is 25 %/20 % = 1.25 (elastic).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it measures the change in total revenue when price changes”) reveals the misconception that elasticity is about revenue rather than quantity responsiveness — confusing the outcome (revenue) with the definition (quantity‑price…

cards.title: Elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in a determinant. The three principal types are: 1. Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) – the percentage change in quantity demanded of a good divided by the percentage change in its own price, holding all else constant. It captures the law of demand’s intensity. 2. Income Elasticity of Demand (YED) – the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in consumer income, with prices unchanged. It classifies goods as normal (YED > 0), inferior (YED < 0), necessities (0 < YED < 1) or luxuries (YED > 1). 3. Cross Elasticity of Demand (XED) – the percentage change in quantity demanded of good A divided by the percentage change in price of good B. Positive XED indicates substitutes (e.g., tea and coffee); negative XED indicates complements (e.g., petrol and cars); zero XED means unrelated goods. These three types are mutually exclusive lenses: PED isolates own‑price effects, YED isolates income effects, XED isolates inter‑good price effects. Together they form the analytical toolkit for demand analysis in microeconomics.
steps: Takeaway: There are exactly three distinct types of demand elasticity — price, income, and cross — each answering a different “what‑if” question about demand.
Here is why: 1.
Price elasticity answers “What happens to quantity demanded if the good’s own price changes?” It is the most frequently used because firms set prices. 2.
Income elasticity answers “What happens if consumers’ purchasing power changes?” It helps policymakers and firms anticipate demand shifts during economic cycles. 3.
Cross elasticity answers “What happens if the price of a related good changes?” It reveals competitive or complementary relationships, vital for product‑line decisions.
Consider a Delhi‑based startup selling electric scooters.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Price Elasticity of Demand”) reveals the misconception that any elasticity involving a percentage change must be price‑related, ignoring the distinct role of income as a demand determinant.
remember: Which type of elasticity measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the consumer’s income, holding prices constant.

cards.title: The degree of price elasticity of demand (PED) classifies the responsiveness of…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The degree of price elasticity of demand (PED) classifies the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price into five distinct categories based on the numerical value of the elasticity coefficient (Ed = %ΔQd / %ΔP). 1. Perfectly Elastic (Ed = ∞) – An infinitesimal price increase causes quantity demanded to fall to zero; the demand curve is horizontal. 2. Perfectly Inelastic (Ed = 0) – Quantity demanded does not change regardless of price; the demand curve is vertical. 3. Unitary Elastic (Ed = 1) – Percentage change in quantity demanded equals percentage change in price; total revenue remains constant. 4. Relatively Elastic (Ed > 1) – Quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price; total revenue moves opposite to price. 5. Relatively Inelastic (0 < Ed < 1) – Quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price; total revenue moves in the same direction as price. These degrees are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive for any linear or non‑linear demand schedule. They provide the foundation for revenue‑maximisation decisions, tax incidence analysis, and pricing strategies used by Indian firms such as Amul (relatively inelastic for milk) or low‑cost airlines (relatively elastic for leisure travel). The classification also links directly to the expenditure method (node 005) and geometric method (node 006) for measuring elasticity at a point or over an arc.
steps: The degree of elasticity is a simple numeric label that instantly tells you whether a price change will raise or lower total revenue.
Here is why: the elasticity coefficient (Ed) compares the proportional change in quantity demanded to the proportional change in price.
When Ed > 1, quantity reacts more than price, so a price cut expands revenue (relatively elastic).
When Ed < 1, quantity reacts less, so a price hike expands revenue (relatively inelastic).
At Ed = 1, revenue stays unchanged (unitary).

The two extremes — Ed = 0 (vertical curve) and Ed = ∞ (horizontal curve) — are theoretical benchmarks: perfectly inelastic goods (e.g., life‑saving insulin) see no quantity response, while perfectly elastic goods (e.g.…

cards.title: The percentage method (also called the proportionate or flux method) measures…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The percentage method (also called the proportionate or flux method) measures price elasticity of demand (Ed) as the ratio of the percentage change in quantity demanded to the percentage change in price, both computed from the original (base) values. Formally, E_d = (\% Δ Q_d)/(\% Δ P) = ((Δ Q)/(Q)× 100)/((Δ P)/(P)× 100) = (Δ Q)/(Δ P)×(P)/(Q) where Q and P are the initial quantity demanded and price, and Δ Q, Δ P are the absolute changes. The coefficient is unit‑free. If |E_d|>1 demand is elastic; |E_d|=1 unitary elastic; |E_d|<1 inelastic. The sign is conventionally negative (law of demand), but the absolute value is used for classification. This method links directly to the degrees of elasticity covered earlier (perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic, relatively elastic, relatively inelastic, unitary) by providing a numerical threshold for each degree. It is the simplest computational approach and serves as the foundation for the expenditure and geometric methods that follow.
steps: The percentage method gives a single number that tells you exactly how responsive quantity demanded is to a price change.
Here is why: it converts absolute changes into relative (percentage) terms, making the measure independent of units — whether price is in rupees or dollars, quantity in kilograms or pieces.
First, identify the initial price (P) and quantity (Q).
Second, find the new price and quantity after the change.
Third, compute \% Δ P = P_new-PP×100 and \% Δ Q = Q_new-QQ×100.
Fourth, divide \% Δ Q by \% Δ P to obtain E_d.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., E_d = (Δ Q)/(Δ P) without percentages) reveals the misconception that elasticity is a simple slope, ignoring the need for a unit‑free measure.
remember: What is the formula for price elasticity of demand using the percentage method.
If the price of a good rises from ₹50 to ₹60 and quantity demanded falls from 100 units to 80 units, calculate the price elasticity of demand using the percentage method and state….
Evaluate the statement: "The percentage method always gives the same elasticity coefficient regardless of whether price rises or falls.".

cards.title: The expenditure method (also called the total outlay method) measures price…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The expenditure method (also called the total outlay method) measures price elasticity of demand by observing the direction of change in total expenditure (TE = Price × Quantity) when price changes. If a price increase leads to an increase in TE, the percentage fall in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage rise in price, implying elasticity less than one (inelastic demand). Conversely, if a price increase causes TE to fall, quantity demanded falls proportionately more than price rises, indicating elasticity greater than one (elastic demand). When TE remains unchanged despite a price change, the percentage changes in price and quantity are equal, yielding unitary elasticity (Ed = 1). This method avoids explicit percentage calculations by using the inverse relationship between price and total expenditure along a demand curve. It is particularly useful when only price and total revenue data are available, as in many Indian retail and wholesale settings where firms track monthly sales turnover. The method links directly to the total revenue test used by businesses for pricing decisions under GST regimes.
steps: The expenditure method tells you the elasticity category by simply watching whether total spending on a good rises, falls, or stays constant when its price changes.
Here is why: total expenditure (TE) equals price (P) multiplied by quantity demanded (Q).
When price rises, two opposing forces act on TE — the higher price per unit pushes TE up, while the lower quantity demanded pulls TE down.
If the price effect dominates, TE rises and demand is inelastic (Ed < 1).
If the quantity effect dominates, TE falls and demand is elastic (Ed > 1).
If they exactly offset, TE is unchanged and demand is unitary elastic (Ed = 1).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It calculates the exact elasticity coefficient using percentages”) reveals the misconception that the expenditure method yields a precise numerical value like the percentage method, confusing classification with computation.
remember: What does the expenditure method of measuring price elasticity of demand observe to classify elasticity.
If the price of a commodity increases and the total expenditure on it decreases, what is the price elasticity of demand.
A student claims that when total expenditure remains constant after a price change, demand is perfectly inelastic. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The geometric method measures elasticity of demand at a specific point on a…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: The geometric method measures elasticity of demand at a specific point on a demand curve by using the ratio of two segments of the curve: the lower segment (distance from the point to the Y‑axis along the demand curve) and the upper segment (distance from the point to the X‑axis along the demand curve). For a straight‑line demand curve, elasticity (E_d) = lower segment ÷ upper segment. If the demand curve is non‑linear, a tangent is drawn at the point of interest and the same ratio is applied to the tangent line. This method yields point elasticity, which can be compared with arc elasticity (percentage method) and total expenditure method. While the percentage method uses proportional changes in price and quantity, and the expenditure method looks at total revenue changes, the geometric method provides a visual, instantaneous measure that is especially useful when the demand curve is linear or when a tangent approximates curvature. It links to the concept of degrees of elasticity: if the lower segment exceeds the upper segment, E_d > 1 (elastic); if equal, E_d = 1 (unitary); if lower segment is smaller, E_d < 1 (inelastic). The geometric method therefore translates the slope of the demand curve into a dimensionless responsiveness measure, bridging graphical intuition with numerical elasticity values.
steps: The geometric method provides an instantaneous, point‑specific measure of elasticity by comparing the lengths of the lower and upper segments of a demand curve (or its tangent).

Here is why: First, for a linear demand curve the ratio of the lower segment to the upper segment is mathematically identical to the algebraic expression E_d = (dQ/dP)·(P/Q), as shown by similar triangles formed with…

Second, when the demand curve is curved, a tangent at the point of interest linearizes the curve locally; the tangent’s lower‑to‑upper‑segment ratio therefore gives the elasticity at that exact point, preserving the…

Third, the ratio is dimensionless because both segments are measured in the same unit (e.g., centimetres on graph paper), so the elasticity value is independent of the scale chosen for the axes, making the method robust…

Fourth, the method directly visualises the relationship between slope and responsiveness: a steeper curve (larger lower segment relative to upper segment) yields higher elasticity, while a flatter curve yields lower…
Consider a linear demand curve for onions in a Mumbai market that intercepts the quantity axis at 120 kg (when price is zero) and the price axis at ₹60 /kg (when quantity is zero).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "elasticity = upper segment ÷ lower segment") reveals the misconception that the ratio is reversed, confusing which segment corresponds to the price axis and which to the quantity axis, leading to an inverted elasticity value and…
remember: State the formula for elasticity of demand using the geometric method on a straight‑line demand curve.
Explain why the geometric method yields the same elasticity value as the percentage method for a linear demand curve.

cards.title: Cross elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of the quantity demanded…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Cross elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of the quantity demanded of good X to a change in the price of good Y. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded of X divided by the percentage change in price of Y (Exy = %ΔQx / %ΔPy). A positive value indicates substitutes (e.g., tea and coffee), a negative value indicates complements (e.g., petrol and cars), and zero means unrelated goods. Income elasticity of demand measures how quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in consumer income (Ey = %ΔQ / %ΔY). Positive income elasticity denotes normal goods; if Ey > 1 the good is a luxury (e.g., branded smartphones), if 0 < Ey < 1 it is a necessity (e.g., wheat). Negative income elasticity characterises inferior goods (e.g., coarse cereals). Both elasticities are dimensionless, allowing comparison across products and markets. They extend the price‑elasticity framework covered in earlier nodes (percentage, expenditure, geometric methods) by shifting the causal variable from own‑price to related‑price or income.
steps: Cross and income elasticity extend the demand‑sensitivity toolkit by asking “what happens to demand for X when Y’s price or consumer income changes?” — the one thing to remember is that sign and magnitude of these…
First, cross elasticity (Exy) uses the same percentage‑change logic as price elasticity but replaces own‑price with the price of a related good.
A positive Exy means X and Y are substitutes: when tea becomes costlier, coffee demand rises — think of Tata Tea vs. Nescafé in Indian kirana stores.
A negative Exy signals complements: a rise in petrol price reduces car demand, as seen with Maruti Suzuki sales during fuel‑price hikes.
Zero Exy implies no relationship (e.g., salt and smartphones).
Second, income elasticity (Ey) swaps the causal variable for consumer income.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Exy = %ΔPy / %ΔQx”) reveals the misconception that the numerator and denominator can be swapped — confusing cause (price of Y) with effect (quantity of X).
remember: Define cross elasticity of demand and state the formula using percentage changes.

cards.title: Stock refers to the total quantity of a good that a producer possesses at a…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Stock refers to the total quantity of a good that a producer possesses at a given point in time, irrespective of price. It is a static concept measured in physical units (e.g., tonnes of steel in a plant’s yard). Supply, by contrast, is the quantity of that good a producer is willing and able to offer for sale at various prices during a specific period. Supply is a flow concept, expressed as a schedule or curve showing the price‑quantity relationship. The key distinction: stock is the reservoir; supply is the tap. A change in price moves the producer along the supply curve (quantity supplied changes) but does not alter the stock unless production or purchases occur. Determinants such as technology, input prices, and expectations shift the entire supply curve, while stock changes only when actual output or inventory adjustments happen. Understanding this separation is essential before analysing the law of supply, movements versus shifts, and elasticity of supply.
steps: The one thing to remember: stock is the total amount a firm owns right now; supply is the amount it chooses to sell at each possible price.
Here is why: a firm’s warehouse may hold 10,000 units of a product (stock).
At a market price of ₹50, the firm may offer 2,000 units; at ₹70, it may offer 4,000 units.
The warehouse content (stock) stays 10,000 unless the firm produces more or buys inventory.
The supply schedule shows the relationship between price and quantity offered, not the warehouse level.
Consider a Mumbai‑based auto‑components maker: its stock of brake pads includes finished goods, work‑in‑progress, and raw materials.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “stock is measured in rupees”) reveals the misconception that stock is a value concept rather than a physical quantity.
remember: Define stock and supply in your own words and state the unit of measurement for each.
Explain why a rise in market price leads to an increase in quantity supplied but does not directly change the firm’s stock.
A textile mill in Surat holds 50,000 metres of fabric in its….

cards.title: Determinants of supply are the non‑price factors that shift the entire supply…
cards.subject: Economics
cards.definition: Determinants of supply are the non‑price factors that shift the entire supply curve of a good or service. In the CISCE ISC Microeconomic Theory syllabus they are: (1) Price of inputs (raw materials, labour, energy) – higher input costs raise marginal cost, reducing supply at every price; (2) Technology – improvements lower per‑unit cost, shifting supply rightward; (3) Prices of related goods in production (joint supply, competitive supply) – a rise in the price of a substitute in production (e.g., wheat vs. barley) pulls resources away, decreasing supply of the original good; (4) Government policy – taxes (GST, excise) increase cost, subsidies lower it; (5) Expectations of future prices – if producers expect higher prices later, they withhold current supply; (6) Number of sellers – more firms enter the market, increasing market supply; (7) Natural conditions – weather, climate, natural disasters affect agricultural and extractive supply. Each determinant operates ceteris paribus; a change in any one moves the supply curve, while a change in the good’s own price causes a movement along the curve (covered in node). The supply function can be written as Qs = f(P, Pi, T, G, E, N, W) where Pi = input prices, T = technology, G = government policy, E = expectations, N = number of sellers, W = natural factors.
steps: The supply curve shifts only when a non‑price determinant changes; the good’s own price merely moves us along a fixed curve.
Here is why: each determinant alters the cost or profitability of producing every unit, so producers revise the quantity they are willing to offer at all prices.
Consider a textile mill in Surat.

If the price of cotton (an input) rises 15 %, the mill’s marginal cost curve shifts upward; at the prevailing market price of cloth, the profit‑maximising output falls, and the mill supplies less at every price — the…
Conversely, adoption of automated looms (technology) cuts labour cost per metre, shifting the supply curve right.
A GST hike on steel from 12 % to 18 % raises input cost for automobile makers in Pune, shifting car supply left.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “consumer income” or “price of the good itself”) reveals the misconception that demand‑side factors or own‑price changes shift supply — confusing movement along the curve with a shift.
remember: List the seven non‑price determinants of supply as per the ISC syllabus.
Explain why a rise in the price of an input shifts the supply curve leftward, using marginal cost reasoning.

cards.title: The Law of Supply states that, ceteris paribus…
cards.subject: Economics
