cards.title: Stanza‑wise paraphrase (part 1) covers the opening eight lines (the octave) of…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Stanza‑wise paraphrase (part 1) covers the opening eight lines (the octave) of Donne’s Holy Sonnet X, “Death be not Proud.” The poem is a single 14‑line Petrarchan sonnet; the first two quatrains (lines 1‑8) form the argument that Death is neither mighty nor dreadful. A paraphrase restates each quatrain in plain prose, preserving the logical flow: 1. Quatrain 1 (lines 1‑4) – The speaker addresses Death directly, denying its pride and power. He claims Death is not “mighty” nor “dreadful” because those it “overthrows” do not truly die; they merely sleep. 2. Quatrain 2 (lines 5‑8) – The speaker expands the metaphor: Death is a slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men. It dwells with poison, war, and sickness — lowly companions — and its “stroke” is no more than a short sleep induced by poppy or charms. The paraphrase must keep the speaker’s defiant tone, the personification of Death, and the theological premise that Christian resurrection renders Death temporary. Relationships between sub‑concepts: personification ↔ argumentative strategy; metaphysical conceit (Death as sleep) ↔ Christian eschatology; rhetorical questions ↔ persuasive structure.
steps: The octave of “Death be not Proud” is a single, sustained argument that Death’s apparent power is an illusion.
Here is why: Donne opens with a direct address — “Death be not proud” — instantly personifying Death as a boastful figure.
He then denies the two attributes Death claims: might and dread.
The evidence?
Those Death “overthrows” do not die; they merely “sleep.” This sleep metaphor is the core conceit: just as a night’s rest ends in waking, the Christian believes bodily death ends in resurrection.
In the second quatrain, the speaker demotes Death to a servant — “slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men” — and lists its squalid companions: poison, war, sickness.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Death is powerful because it kills everyone”) reveals the misconception that the speaker accepts Death’s surface power instead of seeing the theological counter‑argument.
remember: What is the speaker’s main claim about Death in the first quatrain (lines 1‑4).
Explain how the “sleep” metaphor functions in lines 3‑4.
Evaluate the effectiveness of personifying Death as a “slave” in lines 5‑6.

cards.title: Stanza‑wise paraphrase (part 2) covers the third quatrain (lines 9‑12) and the…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Stanza‑wise paraphrase (part 2) covers the third quatrain (lines 9‑12) and the concluding couplet (lines 13‑14) of Donne’s Holy Sonnet 10. In the third quatrain the speaker strips death of autonomy, calling it a “slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men” and noting that it dwells with “poison, war, and sickness.” The comparison of death’s stroke to the sleep induced by “poppy or charms” further reduces its terror. The couplet then delivers the theological climax: “One short sleep past, we wake eternally / And death shall be no more; Death, thou shalt die.” The paraphrase must restate these ideas in clear prose, preserving the logical progression from death’s subservience to its ultimate abolition. It links the earlier portrayal of death as proud (part 1) to its final defeat, showing how each metaphor builds the argument that death is powerless before Christian resurrection.
steps: The takeaway: the poem’s final six lines turn death from a proud tyrant into a powerless servant and finally into a defeated enemy that will itself die. Here is why: first, Donne redefines death’s agency by listing its…
Second, he places death in the company of poison, war, and sickness, reducing it to a mere symptom of human misery.

Third, the simile “poppy or charms can make us sleep as well / And better than thy stroke” equates death’s feared blow with a harmless, drug‑induced nap. Fourth, the couplet shifts from metaphor to doctrine: the “short…
Fifth, the closing declaration “Death, thou shalt die” personifies death as a mortal being, sealing the argument.

Consider a student in Mumbai who fears the monsoon floods; the poet’s logic is like telling the flood, “You are only water obeying gravity, you cannot drown the city forever — after the rain the sun returns and the…

Walk through each line: line 9 names the masters; line 10 lists the grim companions; line 11 introduces the poppy comparison; line 12 asks why death swells with pride; line 13 reframes death as a brief sleep; line 14…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “lines 5‑8”) reveals the misconception that the quatrains are grouped by theme rather than by the fixed sonnet structure.
remember: Which lines form the third quatrain of “Death be not Proud”.
Why does the speaker call death a “slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men”.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the simile “poppy or charms can make us sleep as well / And better than thy stroke” in diminishing death’s power.

cards.title: Imagery in “Death be not Proud” consists of the concrete pictures Donne paints…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Imagery in “Death be not Proud” consists of the concrete pictures Donne paints to make the abstract idea of death tangible: the “rest and sleep” that death mimics, the “poppy or charms” that induce a deeper slumber, and the final “eternal wake” where death itself dies. Figurative language includes personification (Death addressed as a proud person), metaphor (death as a short sleep), simile (“as rest and sleep”), paradox (“Death, thou shalt die”), and apostrophe (direct address to an abstract force). These devices work together: personification gives Death a voice to be argued with; metaphor and simile reduce its terror to a familiar, harmless experience; paradox flips the power dynamic; apostrophe makes the argument intimate. The relationship among them is hierarchical — personification sets the stage, metaphor and simile supply the comparative logic, paradox delivers the theological punch, and apostrophe sustains the persuasive tone throughout the sonnet.
steps: The poem’s central claim is that Death is powerless because it is merely a brief sleep before eternal life, and Donne proves this by stacking sleep‑related images and figures of speech that systematically dismantle…

Here is why: first, the opening apostrophe “Death, be not proud” personifies Death as an arrogant listener, allowing the speaker to argue directly with it. Second, the simile “as rest and sleep” and the metaphor “thou…

Third, the catalogue of sleep‑inducing agents — “poppy or charms” — extends the metaphor, suggesting that if drugs can mimic death, death itself is no more mysterious than a drugged nap. Fourth, the paradox “Death, thou…
Fifth, the final image of “eternal wake” replaces the temporary sleep of death with a permanent, joyful awakening, completing the metaphorical arc from fear to triumph.

Consider how each device builds on the previous: personification creates a dialogue; simile and metaphor supply the comparative logic; the extended catalogue deepens the comparison; paradox delivers the theological…
An exam trap is to treat each figure in isolation — ISC markers reward showing how the cluster works as a single persuasive engine.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is a metaphor because Death is compared to a proud man”) reveals the misconception that any comparison is a metaphor, ignoring that apostrophe is a direct address to an absent or abstract entity and personification gives it human…
remember: Identify the figure of speech in the opening address “Death, be not proud” and state its immediate effect on the reader.
Explain how the simile “as rest and sleep” functions within the poem’s argument.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the extended catalogue “poppy or charms” in strengthening the poem’s central metaphor.

cards.title: Form, sound, and rhythm in Donne’s “Death be not Proud” refer to the structural…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Form, sound, and rhythm in Donne’s “Death be not Proud” refer to the structural and auditory architecture that shapes the poem’s persuasive force. The form is a Petrarchan sonnet: an octave (ABBAABBA) presenting the problem — death’s false pride — followed by a sestet (CDDCEE) delivering the resolution — death’s ultimate defeat. The meter is predominantly iambic pentameter (five iambs per line), giving a conversational yet elevated pulse; occasional trochaic substitutions and feminine endings create subtle tension. Rhyme binds the argument: the octave’s enclosed rhymes mirror death’s self‑contained arrogance, while the sestet’s looser pattern reflects the speaker’s expanding freedom. Sound devices — alliteration (“Mighty and dreadful”), assonance (“thou think’st thou dost”), and consonance (“slave to fate”) — reinforce key words and control pacing. Enjambment and caesura manipulate breath: lines 1‑4 flow with minimal pause, then a strong caesura at “for thou art not so” forces a rhetorical stop. Together, these elements make the poem’s logic audible; the disciplined form mirrors the speaker’s intellectual control, while rhythmic variations underscore the emotional climax at the volta.
steps: The poem is a Petrarchan sonnet in iambic pentameter whose disciplined form and controlled sound patterns reinforce the argument that death is powerless.
Here is why: first, the octave’s enclosed ABBAABBA rhyme traps death’s boast in a tight sonic cage, mirroring the speaker’s logical containment of death’s claims.

Second, the steady iambic pulse creates a calm, reasoned voice; when a trochaic inversion opens line 9 (“Thou art slave…”), the rhythm stumbles, signalling the volta and the speaker’s shift from description to…

Third, sound devices such as the repeated “th” in “though some have called thee” and the assonant “ou” in “thou think’st thou dost” bind the octave’s accusations, while the sestet’s softer “s” and “l” sounds (“slave”…

Fourth, enjambment between lines 3‑4 (“overthrow / Die not”) drags the reader forward, mimicking death’s futile grasp, whereas the strong caesura after “so” in line 2 forces a rhetorical pause that isolates the rebuttal.
Fifth, the sestet’s rhyme relaxation (CDDCEE) mirrors the expanding freedom of the soul after “one short sleep”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ABAB CDCD”) reveals the misconception that the poem uses a Shakespearean alternating rhyme rather than the Petrarchan envelope form.
remember: What is the rhyme scheme of the octave in Donne’s “Death be not Proud”.
How does the volta at line 9 affect the poem’s argumentative movement.
Evaluate whether the consistent iambic pentameter strengthens or weakens the speaker’s defiance of death.

cards.title: Tone is the author’s implied attitude toward the subject…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Tone is the author’s implied attitude toward the subject, conveyed through diction, syntax, and rhetorical stance; mood is the emotional atmosphere evoked in the reader. In “Death be not Proud,” the tone shifts from confrontational mockery in the opening quatrain (“Death, be not proud”) to calm triumph in the sestet (“Death, thou shalt die”). The mood moves from solemn awe at death’s apparent power to reassuring relief as the speaker reveals death’s impotence. Tone and mood are interdependent: the speaker’s defiant tone creates a mood of empowerment, while the underlying Christian certainty steadies the mood into quiet victory. Recognising both requires tracking word‑choice (e.g., “mighty,” “dreadful,” “slave”), sentence structure (imperatives, rhetorical questions), and the poem’s metaphysical argument that death is merely a short sleep before eternal waking.
steps: The one thing to remember: Donne’s speaker adopts a deliberately arrogant tone to strip Death of its terror, turning the poem’s mood from dread into quiet victory.

Here is why: first, the opening apostrophe “Death, be not proud” uses an imperative to address Death as a person, establishing a confrontational tone that immediately reduces Death from a cosmic force to a listener.
Second, the speaker calls Death “mighty and dreadful” only to undercut those adjectives with “for thou art not so,” a syntactic reversal that mocks Death’s reputation.

Third, the extended metaphor of sleep (“rest and sleep, which but thy pictures be”) reframes death as a brief, harmless nap, shifting the mood from fear to familiarity — like a student realising a scary exam is just a…

Fourth, the volta at line 9 (“Thou art slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men”) introduces a logical argument: Death serves lower powers, so its pride is absurd; this rational tone steadies the mood into…
Finally, the closing couplet (“Death, thou shalt die”) delivers a paradoxical triumph — the speaker’s tone becomes prophetic, and the mood settles into serene assurance that eternal life follows.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “reverent awe”) reveals the misconception that apostrophe always signals respect — here it signals challenge.
remember: What is the primary tone of the opening quatrain (lines 1‑4) in “Death be not Proud”.
How does the metaphor of sleep in lines 5‑8 contribute to the poem’s mood.
Evaluate whether the speaker’s tone in the sestet (lines 9‑14) is more rational or emotional.

cards.title: The central idea of “Death be not Proud” is the Christian assertion that death…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: The central idea of “Death be not Proud” is the Christian assertion that death is not a terrifying sovereign but a powerless transition into everlasting life. The poem dismantles death’s pride by exposing its dependence on chance, kings, and desperate men, and by redefining it as a brief sleep preceding resurrection. Three major themes intertwine: (1) Mortality vs. Immortality – physical death is temporary, while the soul’s life is permanent; (2) Divine Triumph – God’s power renders death a servant, not a master; (3) Human Courage – the speaker’s defiant tone encourages believers to face death without fear. The title, taken from the opening apostrophe, functions as a thematic thesis: it commands death to abandon its false pride, signalling the poem’s argument that death’s apparent might is an illusion. Understanding these elements requires recognizing how metaphysical wit, paradox, and theological conviction work together to transform a universal fear into a confident declaration of victory.
steps: The poem’s central claim is that death is a powerless illusion because Christian resurrection guarantees eternal life.

Here is why: first, Donne personifies death and directly addresses it, stripping away its mystique by calling it “poor death” and a “slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men.” Second, he reframes death as a short…
Third, the final couplet declares “Death, thou shalt die,” a paradox that seals the argument: death itself perishes when the soul enters immortality.
Consider the metaphor of sleep: just as a student in Mumbai might fear a night‑time power cut but knows electricity returns at dawn, the speaker knows death’s darkness is temporary.

The title “Death be not Proud” acts as a battle cry; it is both a command and a summary, telling death to abandon its false arrogance because the speaker’s faith has already won. An exam trap: students often confuse the…
Remember, the argument rests on the certainty of resurrection, not on human will alone.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “The poem says death is scary but we should be brave”) reveals the misconception that the speaker relies on human courage alone, ignoring the theological basis of resurrection.
remember: What is the central idea of “Death be not Proud” in one sentence.
How does Donne use the metaphor of sleep to undermine death’s power.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the poem’s argument that death is not mighty.

cards.title: Key quotations with explanation involves selecting the most significant lines…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Key quotations with explanation involves selecting the most significant lines from Donne’s Holy Sonnet 10, identifying their literal meaning, the metaphysical conceits they employ, and their contribution to the poem’s argument that death is powerless. Each quotation is examined for (1) speaker and addressee (the poet addressing personified Death), (2) imagery (sleep, poppy, slave, eternal waking), (3) rhetorical devices (apostrophe, paradox, irony), and (4) thematic function (undermining death’s pride, asserting Christian resurrection). The explanations link the quotations to the poem’s structure — octave presenting death’s false majesty, sestet refuting it — and to the broader metaphysical tradition of using startling comparisons to reveal spiritual truth. This node does not re‑teach stanza‑wise paraphrase, form, or tone; it deepens understanding by showing how individual lines carry the poem’s central argument.

Here is why: 1.

The opening apostrophe “Death, be not proud, though some have called thee / Mighty and dreadful, for thou art not so” immediately strips death of grandeur by addressing it as a person who can be commanded. 2.

The conceit “Thou art slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men” reduces death to a servant of external forces, using the metaphysical strategy of turning a feared abstraction into a lowly subordinate. 3.
The comparison “poppy or charms can make us sleep as well / And better than thy stroke” equates death’s stroke with a harmless drug, suggesting death is no more fearsome than a sedative. 4.
The climactic couplet “One short sleep past, we wake eternally / And death shall be no more;

cards.title: This node equips students with the exact question patterns…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: This node equips students with the exact question patterns, marking expectations, and answer structures that the CISCE ISC English (801) paper uses for John Donne’s “Death be not Proud”. It maps each syllabus‑aligned skill — reference‑to‑context identification, thematic analysis, language and imagery commentary, comparative evaluation, and personal response — to concrete practice items. steps: The single most important takeaway is that ISC examiners reward answers that move from precise textual anchoring to thematic synthesis within a fixed mark framework.

Here is why: every question, whether a 2‑mark reference‑to‑context or a 15‑mark essay, follows a predictable rubric — identification (1 mark), explanation (1‑2 marks), analysis of technique (2‑3 marks), and personal or…

cards.title: Format & structure of this skill defines the mandatory layout elements for…
cards.subject: English
cards.definition: Format & structure of this skill defines the mandatory layout elements for every ISC Class 12 composition and directed‑writing task. A composition (essay, article, story) requires a centred title, an introductory paragraph that states the thesis, 3‑5 body paragraphs each with a topic sentence, supporting details and a linking sentence, and a concluding paragraph that restates the thesis and offers a final thought. Directed writing (formal letter, report, speech, notice, email) follows a prescribed template: sender’s address, date, receiver’s address (for letters), subject line, salutation, body organised in clear paragraphs (opening, details, action/closure), complimentary close, signature and designation. The relationship between sub‑concepts is hierarchical — the macro‑structure (title, paragraphs) governs the micro‑structure (sentence variety, cohesion devices). Correct format carries dedicated marks (usually 2‑3 out of 20) and signals organisational competence before language quality is assessed.
steps: The single most important rule is that every ISC writing task must begin with its prescribed format skeleton before a single word of content is written.

Here is why: examiners award format marks instantly; a missing subject line or misplaced signature loses those marks regardless of how eloquent the body is. Consider the formal letter — start with the sender’s address…
Next line: date in “15 March 2026” format.
Leave a blank line, then the receiver’s address on the left, same punctuation.
Subject line follows, centred, prefixed by “Subject:” and a concise phrase (e.g., “Request for Leave”).
Salutation (“Respected Sir/Madam,”) on the left, then a blank line.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing the subject before the date) reveals the misconception that the subject line is part of the heading block rather than a separate line after the receiver’s address.
