A student sets up the area between y = x^2 and y = x from x = 0 to x = 2 as _0^2 (x^2 - x) \, dx. Evaluate whether this setup is correct.

cards.title: The area of a plane region bounded by curves expressed as functions of y
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The area of a plane region bounded by curves expressed as functions of y (i.e., x = f(y) and x = g(y)) and the horizontal lines y = c and y = d (with c < d) is given by the definite integral of the difference between the rightmost and leftmost x‑coordinates with respect to y. If the region is bounded on the left by the y‑axis (x = 0) and on the right by x = f(y), the area simplifies to ∫_c^d f(y) dy. This technique extends the vertical‑strip method (∫ (top − bottom) dx) taught in the previous nodes ( and) by swapping the roles of x and y. It is essential when curves are not single‑valued functions of x (e.g., x = y^2) or when the region’s boundaries are naturally described by horizontal lines. The integral computes the limit of the sum of areas of infinitesimally thin rectangles of width Δy and length (x_right(y) − x_left(y)). The result is a positive scalar quantity measured in square units (e.g., m², cm²). The method requires identifying the correct y‑limits (intersection points of the curves solved for y) and ensuring x_right(y) ≥ x_left(y) throughout the interval.
steps: The area of a region bounded by curves given as x = f(y) is found by integrating the horizontal length (x_right − x_left) with respect to y, because each infinitesimal strip runs horizontally.

Here is why: when curves are easier to express as functions of y, vertical strips would require splitting the region into multiple parts, while horizontal strips capture the whole region in a single integral.
Consider the region bounded by the parabola x = y^2 and the line x = y + 2.
First, find intersection points by solving y^2 = y + 2 → y^2 − y − 2 = 0 → (y−2)(y+1)=0 → y = 2, y = −1.
These are the limits c = −1, d = 2.
For each y in [−1, 2], the right boundary is the line x = y + 2 and the left boundary is the parabola x = y^2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “yes, it’s the same area”) reveals the misconception that the variable of integration does not matter — confusing the geometric orientation of strips with the algebraic form of the integral.
remember: A student writes the area between x = y^2 and x = 4 as ∫_{0}^{4} (√x − (−√x)) dx. Is this correct for horizontal strips? Explain.
Why must the limits of integration for horizontal strips be the y‑coordinates of intersection points, not the x‑coordinates.
Evaluate the claim: “For any region, the area computed by horizontal strips equals the area computed by vertical strips, so the method choice is irrelevant.”.

cards.title: The area of a region bounded by two curves expressed as functions of y…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The area of a region bounded by two curves expressed as functions of y, x = f(y) (right boundary) and x = g(y) (left boundary), between horizontal lines y = c and y = d (with c < d), is given by the definite integral A = _c^d [ f(y) - g(y) ] \, dy, provided f(y) ≥ g(y) for all y ∈ [c, d]. This method, called horizontal strip integration, is used when the curves are more naturally described as x in terms of y (e.g., x = y^2, x = √(y)) or when vertical strips would require splitting the region into multiple sub‑regions. The concept extends the vertical‑strip formula A = _a^b [y_top(x) - y_bottom(x)] \, dx by swapping the roles of x and y. It relies on the ability to invert functions or to work directly with equations given in the form x = h(y). The limits c and d are the y-coordinates of the intersection points of the two curves, found by solving f(y) = g(y). The integrand f(y) - g(y) represents the horizontal length of a typical strip at height y. The result is a positive scalar measured in square units (e.g., m^2 if coordinates are in metres). This technique is essential for regions where vertical integration is cumbersome or impossible without partitioning.
steps: The one thing to remember: When curves are easier to express as x in terms of y, integrate horizontally — the area is _c^d [x_right(y) - x_left(y)] \, dy. Here is why: In the previous nodes you learned to slice a region…
But many curves — like the parabola x = y^2 or the circle x = √(a^2 - y^2) — are not single‑valued functions of x; they would require splitting the region into two or more parts.
By switching the independent variable to y, each curve becomes a single function x = h(y), and a single integral suffices.
Consider the region bounded by the parabola x = y^2 and the line x = y + 2.
If you try vertical strips, the top and bottom boundaries change at x = 1 (where the parabola meets the line), forcing two integrals.
With horizontal strips, the right boundary is always the line x = y + 2 and the left boundary is always the parabola x = y^2 for y from -1 to 2 (the y-coordinates of intersection).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., A = _c^d [g(y) - f(y)] \, dy) reveals the misconception that the order of subtraction does not matter — it does, because area must be positive and f(y) ≥ g(y) on [c,d].
remember: Write the formula for the area of a region bounded by x = f(y) (right) and x = g(y) (left) between y = c and y = d.
A region is bounded by y = x^2 and y = 2x. Explain why horizontal strip integration might be simpler than vertical strip integration for this region.
Given the curves x = y^2 and x = 4 - y^2, decide whether the area between them from y = -1 to y = 1 is correctly given by _-1^1 [(4 - y^2) - y^2] \, dy. Justify.

cards.title: The area of a region bounded by curves expressed as functions of y
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The area of a region bounded by curves expressed as functions of y (i.e., x = g₁(y) and x = g₂(y)) and horizontal lines y = c and y = d (with c < d) is computed by integrating the horizontal strip width with respect to y. If the right boundary is x = g_R(y) and the left boundary is x = g_L(y) over [c, d], the area A = ∫_{c}^{d} [g_R(y) − g_L(y)] dy. This method is essential when curves are more naturally described as x in terms of y (e.g., parabolas opening left/right, circles, or inverse functions) or when vertical strips would require splitting the region into multiple sub‑regions. The concept extends the vertical‑strip formula A = ∫_{a}^{b} [f_U(x) − f_L(x)] dx by swapping the roles of x and y. It relies on the same Riemann‑sum principle: partition the y‑interval, approximate each strip by a rectangle of width Δy and length g_R(y_i) − g_L(y_i), and take the limit as Δy → 0. The formula holds provided g_R and g_L are continuous on [c, d] and g_R(y) ≥ g_L(y) for all y in the interval. If the curves intersect within [c, d], the interval must be split at intersection points so that the right/left ordering remains consistent on each sub‑interval.
steps: The area of a region bounded by curves expressed as x = g(y) is found by integrating the horizontal strip width (right curve minus left curve) with respect to y. Here is why: vertical strips (dx) work well when…
Consider the region bounded by the parabola x = y² and the line x = 4.
The curves intersect when y² = 4 → y = −2, 2.
For each y in [−2, 2], the right boundary is x = 4 and the left boundary is x = y².
The horizontal strip width is 4 − y².
Integrating from y = −2 to 2 gives A = ∫_{−2}^{2} (4 − y²) dy = [4y − y³/3]_{−2}^{2} = (8 − 8/3) − (−8 + 8/3) = 32/3 square units.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., A = ∫_{c}^{d} [g_L(y) − g_R(y)] dy) reveals the misconception that the order of subtraction does not matter — it does, because area must be positive and the right curve has larger x‑values.
remember: State the formula for the area of a region bounded by x = g_R(y) (right), x = g_L(y) (left), y = c, y = d (c < d) using horizontal strips.
Explain why the horizontal‑strip method is preferred over vertical strips for the region bounded by x = y² and x = 4.
Evaluate the claim: "If the curves intersect at y = −1 and y = 2, the area between x = y² and x = y + 2 is ∫_{−1}^{2} (y² − (y + 2)) dy.".

cards.title: The area of a region bounded by two curves expressed as functions of y…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The area of a region bounded by two curves expressed as functions of y, x = f(y) (right boundary) and x = g(y) (left boundary), between the horizontal lines y = c and y = d (where c < d and f(y) ≥ g(y) for all y in [c, d]), is given by the definite integral ∫_c^d [f(y) - g(y)] dy. This method, called integration with respect to y or using horizontal strips, is the counterpart to the vertical-strip method (∫_a^b [f(x) - g(x)] dx) taught earlier. The two approaches are related by the inverse relationship between x and y: if a curve is given as y = h(x), its inverse x = h⁻¹(y) (when it exists) allows horizontal slicing. The limits c and d are the y-coordinates of the intersection points of the curves, found by solving f(y) = g(y). This technique is essential when the region is not vertically simple (i.e., a vertical line intersects the region in more than one segment) or when the curves are naturally defined as x = f(y), such as parabolas opening left/right (x = y²) or lines (x = y + 2). The area computed is a positive scalar quantity measured in square units (e.g., m²). The method extends directly to regions bounded by more than two curves by partitioning the y-interval where the right/left functions change.
steps: The area between two curves can be found by integrating with respect to y using horizontal strips when the curves are more naturally described as functions of y. This approach mirrors the vertical-strip method but swaps…
Second, find the y-coordinates of intersection by solving f(y) = g(y); these become the limits c and d. Third, set up the integral ∫_c^d [f(y) - g(y)] dy. Fourth, evaluate.
Consider the region bounded by the parabola x = y² and the line x = y + 2.
Solving y² = y + 2 gives y = -1 and y = 2.
An Indian analogy: imagine a rectangular plot of land bounded on the left by a curved river (x = y²) and on the right by a straight road (x = y+2).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ∫_c^d [g(y) - f(y)] dy) reveals the misconception that the order of subtraction does not matter, ignoring that area must be positive and the right curve minus the left curve gives a positive integrand.
remember: State the formula for the area between two curves x = f(y) and x = g(y) from y = c to y = d, where f(y) ≥ g(y).
Why might we choose to integrate with respect to y instead of x when finding the area between two curves.
A student sets up the integral for the area between x = y² and x = y + 2 using vertical strips (with respect to x). Evaluate whether this approach is correct and explain.

cards.title: Applications of integrals in this chapter focus on computing planar areas…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Applications of integrals in this chapter focus on computing planar areas bounded by curves defined by functions y = f(x) and y = g(x) over a closed interval [a,b]. The area under a single curve y = f(x) above the x-axis from x=a to x=b is given by the definite integral _a^b f(x)\,dx, provided f(x)≥ 0 on [a,b]. If the curve dips below the axis, the integral yields signed area; the geometric area is obtained by splitting the interval at the zeros of f and taking absolute values. The area between two curves y = f(x) (upper) and y = g(x) (lower) on [a,b] where f(x)≥ g(x) is _a^b [f(x)-g(x)]\,dx. The limits a,b are the x-coordinates of intersection points obtained by solving f(x)=g(x). When curves intersect multiple times, the interval is partitioned at each intersection and the appropriate upper‑lower order is used on each sub‑interval. This synthesis node consolidates the two concepts, highlights typical ISC question patterns (area bounded by parabola and line, area between two parabolas, area involving trigonometric functions, and area with absolute value functions), and provides practice in setting up integrals, choosing correct limits, and interpreting signed versus geometric area.
steps: The one thing to remember: Every area problem reduces to writing a definite integral of (upper − lower) with limits at the intersection points, then evaluating it correctly.
Here is why: the definite integral is the limit of a Riemann sum of vertical strips; each strip’s height is the vertical distance between the two bounding curves.
First, sketch the curves (even a rough mental picture) to see which function lies above the other on each sub‑interval.
Second, find all intersection points by solving f(x)=g(x); these x-values become the limits of integration.
Third, if the upper‑lower order changes at an intersection, split the integral at that point and write separate integrals with the correct order.
Fourth, watch for curves crossing the x-axis: the integral of a single curve below the axis gives negative signed area, so take absolute value or split at the zero.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it gives the perimeter of the curve”) reveals the misconception that integration measures length rather than area, confusing the integral of a function with the arc‑length formula.
remember: What is the geometric interpretation of the definite integral _a^b f(x)\,dx when f(x)≥ 0 on [a,b].
Given two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) that intersect at x = a and x = b with f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a,b], write the integral expression for the area between them.
A student computes the area between y = x^2 and y = x from x=0 to x=1 as _0^1 (x^2 - x)\,dx = -(1)/(6) and reports the area as -(1)/(6) square units. Evaluate this response.

cards.title: A differential equation is an equation that relates an unknown function y(x) to…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A differential equation is an equation that relates an unknown function y(x) to its derivatives (dy)/(dx), (d^2y)/(dx^2),. The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative that appears; the degree is the exponent of that highest‑order derivative after the equation has been made polynomial in derivatives (i.e., cleared of fractions and radicals). The chapter covers four core ideas: 1. Order and degree – classification tool that decides which solution method applies. 2. Variable separable equations – equations that can be written as g(y)\,dy = f(x)\,dx; integration on each side yields the general solution. 3. Homogeneous equations – first‑order equations of the form (dy)/(dx)=F\! ((y)/(x) ) where F is a homogeneous function of degree zero; the substitution y=vx reduces them to variable‑separable form. 4. Linear differential equations – first‑order equations (dy)/(dx)+P(x)y=Q(x); the integrating factor e^ P(x)\,dx converts the left side into an exact derivative, giving the solution y· IF = Q(x)· IF\,dx + C. These sub‑concepts build on each other: identifying order/degree tells you whether the equation is first‑order (eligible for the three solution techniques) or higher‑order (treated later). Variable‑separable and homogeneous methods are special cases of the broader linear framework when P(x) or Q(x) take particular forms. Together they form the toolkit for solving most first‑order problems encountered in ISC examinations and in modelling physical systems such as population growth, radioactive decay, and RC circuits.
steps: The one thing to remember: every first‑order differential equation in this chapter falls into one of three solvable patterns — variable separable, homogeneous, or linear — and recognising the pattern is the key to…
If you can classify the equation correctly, the rest is routine calculus.
Consider the equation (dy)/(dx) = (x^2+y^2)/(xy).
At first glance it looks messy, but notice that the right‑hand side is a function of (y)/(x) alone: (x^2+y^2)/(xy) = (1+(y/x)^2)/(y/x).
This is the hallmark of a homogeneous equation.
The substitution y=vx (so (dy)/(dx)=v+x(dv)/(dx)) turns it into v+x(dv)/(dx) = (1+v^2)/(v), which separates to (v)/(1+v^2)\,dv = (dx)/(x).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “order 2, degree 1”) reveals the misconception that degree is the power of the first derivative or that the coefficient 3 reduces the degree.
remember: What is the order and degree of the differential equation ((d^2y)/(dx^2) )^2 + 3(dy)/(dx) = 5y.
Which of the following first‑order equations is variable separable? (a) (dy)/(dx) = (x+y)/(x-y) (b) (dy)/(dx) = (y)/(x) (c) (dy)/(dx) + y = e^x.
A student claims that the differential equation (dy)/(dx) = (x^2+y^2)/(xy) is linear because it can be written as (dy)/(dx) - (x)/(y) = (y)/(x). Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: In a differential equation involving an unknown function y(x) and its…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In a differential equation involving an unknown function y(x) and its derivatives, the order is the order of the highest derivative that appears. If the highest derivative is (d^n y)/(dx^n), the order is n. The degree is defined only when the equation can be expressed as a polynomial in its derivatives (i.e., no radicals, fractions, or transcendental functions of derivatives). After clearing fractions and radicals, the degree is the exponent of the highest‑order derivative term. For instance, in ((d^2y)/(dx^2) )^3 + ((dy)/(dx) )^2 = 0 the order is 2 and the degree is 3. If the equation contains ((dy)/(dx) ) or √((d^2y)/(dx^2)), the degree is not defined because the equation is not a polynomial in the derivatives. Order is always a positive integer; degree is a positive integer when defined. These two numbers classify differential equations before any solution method is chosen.
steps: The order of a differential equation is the highest derivative present, and its degree is the power of that highest derivative once the equation is a polynomial in derivatives.
Here is why: order tells us how many initial conditions are needed for a unique solution; degree tells us the algebraic complexity of the highest derivative term.
Consider the equation ((d^2y)/(dx^2) )^2 + 3(dy)/(dx) = x. The highest derivative is (d^2y)/(dx^2), so the order is 2.
The equation is already a polynomial in (d^2y)/(dx^2) and (dy)/(dx); the exponent of (d^2y)/(dx^2) is 2, hence the degree is 2.
Now examine √((d^2y)/(dx^2)) + (dy)/(dx) = 0.
The highest derivative is still (d^2y)/(dx^2) (order 2), but the square‑root prevents the equation from being a polynomial in that derivative.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “order 3, degree 2”) reveals the misconception that the exponent of the highest derivative determines the order, confusing order with degree.
remember: State the order and degree of the differential equation ((d^2y)/(dx^2) )^3 + ((dy)/(dx) )^2 = 0.
Explain why the degree of the differential equation ((dy)/(dx) ) = x is not defined.
A student writes the degree of ((d^3y)/(dx^3) )^2 + ((d^2y)/(dx^2) ) = 5 as 2. Is this correct? Justify.

cards.title: A first‑order differential equation is called variable separable if it can be…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A first‑order differential equation is called variable separable if it can be written in the form (dy)/(dx) = g(x) \, h(y) or equivalently (1)/(h(y)) \, dy = g(x) \, dx. Here g(x) is a function of the independent variable x only, and h(y) is a function of the dependent variable y only. The method consists of algebraically separating the differentials dy and dx so that all y -terms (including dy ) lie on one side and all x -terms (including dx ) on the other. Both sides are then integrated with respect to their own variable, yielding an implicit general solution (1)/(h(y)) \, dy = g(x) \, dx + C, where C is an arbitrary constant. If an initial condition y(x_0)=y_0 is given, the constant is determined to obtain a particular solution. The concept builds directly on the order‑and‑degree classification (node) and on indefinite integration techniques from Class 11. It does not cover homogeneous or linear equations, which are treated in later nodes.
steps: The one thing to remember: If a first‑order ODE can be rearranged so that every y and dy sit on one side and every x and dx on the other, you solve it by integrating each side independently.

Here is why: the derivative dy/dx is a ratio of differentials; when the right‑hand side factorises into a product of a pure‑x function and a pure‑y function, the differentials can be “cross‑multiplied” without changing…
This is legitimate because we treat dy and dx as infinitesimals that obey the same algebraic rules as finite quantities — a standard heuristic in ISC calculus.
Supporting argument 1 – Identification.
Write the equation as dy/dx = f(x,y).
Check whether f(x,y) can be expressed as g(x)h(y).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “f(x,y) must be a sum of a function of x and a function of y”) reveals the misconception that separability means additive separation rather than multiplicative factorisation.
remember: State the condition that a first‑order differential equation (dy)/(dx)=f(x,y) must satisfy to be classified as variable separable.
Given (dy)/(dx) = (x^2+1)/(y^2-4), explain why this ODE is separable and write the separated form before integration.
Evaluate the statement: “When solving a separable ODE, the constant of integration can be placed on either side of the equation without affecting the final solution.”.

cards.title: A first‑order differential equation is called homogeneous when it can be…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A first‑order differential equation is called homogeneous when it can be written in the form (dy)/(dx)=f\! ((y)/(x) ) or equivalently as M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0 where M and N are homogeneous functions of the same degree n; i.e. M(tx,ty)=t^nM(x,y) and N(tx,ty)=t^nN(x,y) for any non‑zero scalar t. The key property is that the right‑hand side depends only on the ratio y/x (or x/y). This allows the substitution y=vx (or x=vy), which transforms the equation into a variable‑separable form in the variables v and x. After separation, integration yields an implicit relation between v and x; back‑substituting v=y/x gives the general solution. The concept links directly to the variable‑separable method (node) and prepares the ground for linear differential equations (node) where the integrating factor technique is used.
steps: The one essential takeaway: any first‑order differential equation where every term is a homogeneous function of the same degree can be solved by the substitution y=vx, which reduces it to a variable‑separable equation.
Here is why: a homogeneous function satisfies f(tx,ty)=t^nf(x,y); therefore the ratio y/x (or x/y) captures the entire dependence of the derivative on the variables.
By setting y=vx, we have dy/dx=v+x\,dv/dx.
Substituting into (dy)/(dx)=f(y/x) gives v+x(dv)/(dx)=f(v), which rearranges to (dv)/(f(v)-v)=(dx)/(x) — a separable form.
Consider the equation (x^2+y^2)dx-2xy\,dy=0.
Both M=x^2+y^2 and N=-2xy are homogeneous of degree 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “M and N must be polynomials of the same degree”) reveals the misconception that homogeneity is only about polynomial degree, ignoring non‑polynomial homogeneous functions like (y/x) or e^y/x.
remember: State the condition for a first‑order differential equation M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0 to be homogeneous.
Given (dy)/(dx)= x^2+3y^22xy, explain why the substitution y=vx is appropriate and write the resulting separable equation in v and x.
Evaluate the statement: “Every separable differential equation is homogeneous.” Provide a counterexample if false.

cards.title: A first‑order linear differential equation in the dependent variable y and…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A first‑order linear differential equation in the dependent variable y and independent variable x has the standard form (dy)/(dx) + P(x)\,y = Q(x), where P(x) and Q(x) are continuous functions of x on an interval. The equation is linear because y and its derivative appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together. The order is one (the highest derivative is (dy)/(dx)) and the degree is one (the derivative is not raised to any power). To solve it we use an integrating factor (IF) μ(x) = e^ P(x)\,dx. Multiplying the whole equation by μ(x) makes the left‑hand side an exact derivative: (d)/(dx) (μ(x)\,y ) = μ(x)\,Q(x). Integrating both sides with respect to x gives the general solution y\,μ(x) = μ(x)\,Q(x)\,dx + C, where C is an arbitrary constant. This concept builds on the earlier nodes: order and degree identify the equation’s type; variable separable and homogeneous equations are special cases where Q(x)=0 or the equation can be rearranged into separable form. Linear equations are more general because they allow a non‑zero Q(x) that is not a function of y.
steps: The one thing to remember: Every first‑order linear differential equation can be solved by multiplying with an integrating factor that turns the left side into a perfect derivative.
Here is why: 1.
The standard form isolates the derivative term and expresses the equation as a linear combination of y and (dy)/(dx). 2.
The integrating factor μ(x)=e^ P(x)dx is chosen precisely so that (d)/(dx)(μ y)=μ(dy)/(dx)+μ P y. 3.
After multiplication, the equation becomes (d)/(dx)(μ y)=μ Q, which is directly integrable. 4.
The constant of integration C captures the family of all solutions; an initial condition pins down a unique particular solution.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (dy)/(dx)=P(x)y+Q(x)) reveals the misconception that the derivative term must be alone on the left; the standard form requires the derivative plus the P(x)y term on the left and Q(x) on the right.
remember: What is the standard form of a first‑order linear differential equation.
Explain why the integrating factor μ(x)=e^ P(x)dx works for solving (dy)/(dx)+P(x)y=Q(x).
A student writes the solution of (dy)/(dx)+3y=6 as y=2+Ce^3x. Evaluate this solution.

cards.title: A first‑order differential equation written in the differential form M(x,y)dx +…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A first‑order differential equation written in the differential form M(x,y)dx + N(x,y)dy = 0 is called exact if there exists a differentiable function F(x,y) such that dF = M dx + N dy. This is equivalent to the condition that the mixed partial derivatives of M and N are equal: ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x, provided M, N, ∂M/∂y, ∂N/∂x are continuous in a simply connected region. When the condition holds, the general solution is given implicitly by F(x,y) = C, where F is obtained by integrating M with respect to x (treating y as constant) and then determining the arbitrary function of y by comparing ∂F/∂y with N. The method generalises the idea of a total derivative and applies to equations that are neither separable nor linear. It connects to the earlier nodes: variable‑separable and homogeneous equations are special cases where the exactness condition is trivially satisfied, while linear equations require an integrating factor to become exact. This node focuses solely on recognising exactness and constructing F; integrating factors for non‑exact equations are reserved for the next node.
steps: The one thing to remember: An exact differential equation can be solved directly by finding a potential function whose total differential matches the given equation, provided the condition ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x holds.
Here is why: 1.
The exactness condition guarantees the existence of a function F(x,y) with dF = M dx + N dy. 2.
Once F is found, the solution is simply F(x,y) = constant — no further manipulation needed. 3.
The method works for many DEs that are not separable or linear, expanding the toolkit. 4.
Checking exactness is a quick algebraic test before attempting more involved techniques. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “∂M/∂x = ∂N/∂y”) reveals the misconception that the partial derivatives must be taken with respect to the same variable, confusing the roles of M and N.
remember: State the condition for a differential equation M(x,y)dx + N(x,y)dy = 0 to be exact.
Given M = 3x²y + 2y and N = x³ + 2x, determine whether the DE M dx + N dy = 0 is exact.
A student claims that if a differential equation is exact, then it must also be variable separable. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A Bernoulli differential equation is a first‑order ordinary differential…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A Bernoulli differential equation is a first‑order ordinary differential equation of the form (dy)/(dx)+P(x)\,y = Q(x)\,y^\,n, where P(x) and Q(x) are known functions of the independent variable x, n is a real constant with n≠0,1, and y=y(x) is the unknown dependent variable. When n=0 or n=1 the equation reduces to a linear first‑order ODE, which is already covered in the node on linear differential equations. For other values of n the equation is non‑linear, but the substitution v = y^\,1-n transforms it into a linear equation in v: (dv)/(dx)+(1-n)P(x)\,v = (1-n)Q(x). Thus the Bernoulli equation bridges the gap between purely linear equations (treated earlier) and more complex non‑linear forms. It shares the same order (first) as the equations studied in nodes 002‑005, but its degree becomes apparent only after the substitution, linking the concepts of order and degree (node 002) with the method of integrating factors used for linear equations (node 005).
steps: Takeaway: A Bernoulli differential equation can always be transformed into a linear first‑order ODE by the substitution v = y^1-n.

Here is why: The non‑linear term y^n prevents direct integration, but raising both sides to the power 1-n converts the product y· y^n into a single power of y. Differentiating v=y^1-n yields (dv)/(dx)=(1-n)y^-n(dy)/(dx).
Substituting (dy)/(dx) from the original equation eliminates the non‑linearity, leaving a linear expression in v. Supporting arguments: 1.
The substitution is motivated by the chain rule; it mirrors the technique used to homogenise a non‑linear term. 2.
After substitution, the integrating factor method (already learnt for linear equations) applies unchanged. 3.
The method works for any real n≠0,1, showing the broad applicability of the approach.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “n can be any real number”) reveals the misconception that the linear cases n=0 or n=1 are excluded, ignoring that they are already covered by the linear differential equation node and would make the substitution unnecessary.
remember: State the general form of a Bernoulli differential equation and specify the condition on the exponent n.
Explain why the substitution v=y^1-n linearises a Bernoulli equation.
Determine whether the equation (dy)/(dx)+2xy = 4x^3y^2 is Bernoulli. If yes, identify n.

cards.title: Differential equations relate a function to its derivatives.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Differential equations relate a function to its derivatives. The order is the highest derivative present; the degree is the power of that highest derivative after the equation is made polynomial in derivatives. Variable separable equations can be written as f(y)\,dy = g(x)\,dx allowing direct integration. Homogeneous equations have the form (dy)/(dx)=F\! ((y)/(x) ) and are solved by the substitution y=vx. Linear first‑order equations are (dy)/(dx)+P(x)y=Q(x); their solution uses the integrating factor μ(x)=e^ P(x)dx. This node synthesises these four types, shows how to recognise each in ISC papers, and practises the typical multi‑step problems that combine identification, substitution, integration, and application of initial conditions.
steps: The single most important takeaway is: every ISC differential‑equation question begins with identifying the type — order, degree, and whether it is separable, homogeneous, or linear — because the solution method is…
Here is why: the ISC marking scheme awards the first 1–2 marks solely for correct identification; a wrong classification leads to an entirely incorrect solution path and zero further credit.

Consider a typical 2023 ISC paper question: “Solve (x^2+y^2)dx-2xy\,dy=0 given y(1)=2.” The equation is not obviously separable; rewriting as (dy)/(dx)=(x^2+y^2)/(2xy) reveals it is homogeneous of degree 0.

The substitution y=vx converts it to a separable equation in v and x. After integration we obtain |x|+(1)/(2) |1+v^2|=C, back‑substitute v=y/x, apply the initial condition, and simplify to x^2+y^2=5x.
Now examine a linear‑type trap: “Solve (dy)/(dx)+y x= x.” The integrating factor is μ=e^ x\,dx=e^- | x|= x. Multiplying through gives (d)/(dx)(y x)= ^2 x; integrating yields y x= x+C.
A common exam error is forgetting the absolute value in | x| and dropping the constant of integration before applying the initial condition.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “order 3, degree 2”) reveals the misconception that the exponent on the highest derivative determines the order, confusing the roles of order and degree.
remember: State the order and degree of the differential equation ((d^2y)/(dx^2) )^3+2(dy)/(dx)-5y=0.
Explain why the differential equation (dy)/(dx)=(x^2+y^2)/(xy) is homogeneous and outline the substitution that solves it.
Evaluate the claim: “Every first‑order linear differential equation can be solved by the variable separable method.” Provide a counterexample if false.

cards.title: A scalar is a physical quantity completely described by a single real number…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A scalar is a physical quantity completely described by a single real number (its magnitude) and an appropriate unit, e.g., mass (kg), temperature (K), time (s). A vector is a physical quantity that requires both magnitude and a specific direction for complete description, and it obeys the triangle (or parallelogram) law of addition, e.g., displacement (m), velocity (m s⁻¹), force (N). Vectors are represented by directed line segments; the length denotes magnitude, the arrowhead denotes direction. Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of their initial points. The zero vector has zero magnitude and arbitrary direction. A unit vector has magnitude one and indicates direction. Position vectors, components, scalar (dot) product, vector (cross) product, and applications such as work done and projections are built upon this fundamental distinction and are treated in subsequent nodes.
steps: A vector is a quantity that possesses both magnitude and direction, whereas a scalar has only magnitude.
Here is why: first, physical phenomena like force and velocity cannot be fully described by a number alone; the direction of action changes the effect.
Second, vectors obey the triangle law of addition — placing the tail of one vector at the head of another yields a resultant that is independent of the order, a property scalars do not share.
Third, the mathematical representation of a vector as v=v_xi+v_yj+v_zk explicitly encodes direction through the unit vectors i,j,k along the coordinate axes.
Consider a cricket ball bowled at 140 km/h towards the batsman; the speed (140 km/h) is a scalar, but the velocity (140 km/h towards the batsman) is a vector.
If the same ball is bowled at the same speed but towards the slips, the velocity vector changes though the scalar speed remains unchanged.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing force because it “feels strong”) reveals the misconception that any quantity with a “size” is a scalar, confusing magnitude-only with magnitude-plus-direction.
remember: Which of the following is a scalar quantity? (a) Force (b) Velocity (c) Temperature (d) Displacement.
Explain why electric current is considered a scalar despite having a direction in a circuit.
A student says “Any quantity with direction is a vector.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: A vector is a quantity that possesses both magnitude and direction…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A vector is a quantity that possesses both magnitude and direction, unlike a scalar which has only magnitude. The magnitude (or modulus) of a vector a=a_1i+a_2j+a_3k is the non‑negative scalar |a|=√(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2). It represents the “size” of the vector and carries the same SI unit as the physical quantity the vector describes (metre for displacement, newton for force, metre per second for velocity). The direction of a vector in three‑dimensional space is uniquely specified by its direction cosines l,m,n, where l= α=(a_1)/(|a|),\; m= β=(a_2)/(|a|),\; n= γ=(a_3)/(|a|). Here α,β,γ are the angles the vector makes with the positive x, y, and z axes respectively. The direction cosines satisfy l^2+m^2+n^2=1 and are dimensionless. An equivalent description uses direction ratios a_1,a_2,a_3 (the components themselves), which are proportional to the direction cosines. Magnitude and direction together determine a vector completely: two vectors are equal iff they have the same magnitude and the same direction (i.e., identical direction cosines). This concept links directly to the earlier node on scalars and vectors and prepares the ground for position vectors, where the magnitude becomes the distance of a point from the origin and the direction cosines give the line’s orientation.
steps: The magnitude and direction of a vector are the two inseparable attributes that make a vector a vector; without either, the description collapses to a scalar or an incomplete entity.
Here is why: magnitude quantifies “how much” while direction cosines quantify “which way”.
Together they allow us to move from a geometric arrow to an algebraic triplet (a_1,a_2,a_3) and back.
First, recall the Pythagorean theorem in three dimensions: the distance from the origin to the point (a_1,a_2,a_3) is √(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2).

This distance is exactly the magnitude of the position vector OP. The same formula works for any vector because a vector can be translated to start at the origin without changing its length or orientation.
Second, direction cosines are simply the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the coordinate axes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “magnitude is a_1+a_2+a_3”) reveals the misconception that magnitude is a simple algebraic sum of components, confusing vector addition with scalar addition.
remember: Define the magnitude of a vector a=a_1i+a_2j+a_3k and state its SI unit when a represents a displacement.
Calculate the magnitude of the vector v=5i-12j. Give the answer with correct unit if v represents a velocity in m/s.
Two vectors a and b have the same magnitude 10 but different direction cosines. Can a and b be equal? Justify.

cards.title: A position vector of a point P(x,y,z) in three‑dimensional space is the vector…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A position vector of a point P(x,y,z) in three‑dimensional space is the vector r=x\,i+y\,j+z\,k that joins the origin O(0,0,0) to P. Its components x,y,z are the Cartesian coordinates of P measured in metres (SI unit). The magnitude |r|= x^2+y^2+z^2 gives the straight‑line distance OP. The direction cosines ℓ=(x)/(|r|), m=(y)/(|r|), n=(z)/(|r|) satisfy ℓ^2+m^2+n^2=1 and describe the orientation of r relative to the coordinate axes. Position vectors are bound vectors — they are fixed to the origin — unlike free vectors which can be translated. They provide the bridge between coordinate geometry and vector algebra: any geometric problem about points, distances, or directions can be recast in terms of position vectors, enabling the use of dot and cross products in later nodes.
steps: The position vector is the unique arrow from the origin to a point, encoding both distance and direction in a single algebraic object.
Here is why: it turns geometric location into numbers that can be manipulated with vector algebra.
First, any point P(x,y,z) corresponds to OP=xi+yj+zk; the coefficients are exactly the coordinates.
Second, the length of this arrow is |OP|= x^2+y^2+z^2, a direct application of the Pythagorean theorem in three dimensions.
Third, the direction cosines ℓ,m,n are the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the positive x, y, z axes; they are obtained by dividing each component by the magnitude.

Fourth, because the tail is fixed at the origin, two points have the same position vector only if they coincide — this bound nature distinguishes position vectors from free vectors like force or velocity, which can…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the vector from P to the origin”) reveals the misconception that the direction of a position vector can be reversed — it is always directed from the origin to the point.
remember: Define the position vector of a point P(x,y,z) in three‑dimensional space.
If the position vector of point A is a=3i+4j, find its magnitude and direction cosines.
Evaluate the statement: “The position vector of a point does not depend on the choice of origin.”.

cards.title: A vector component is the projection of a vector onto a chosen coordinate axis.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A vector component is the projection of a vector onto a chosen coordinate axis. In three‑dimensional Cartesian space we fix an orthonormal basis {i, j, k} along the x, y, z axes. Any vector a can be uniquely expressed as a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k, where a₁, a₂, a₃ are real numbers called the scalar components (or simply components) of a. The vector components are a₁i, a₂j, a₃k. The magnitude |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²). The direction cosines are l = a₁/|a|, m = a₂/|a|, n = a₃/|a|, satisfying l² + m² + n² = 1. The direction ratios are any triple proportional to (a₁, a₂, a₃). Components connect directly to the position vector of a point P(x, y, z): OP = xi + yj + zk. They also underpin the dot and cross products, which are treated in later nodes.
steps: The component form of a vector is its unique address in a Cartesian coordinate system, and every vector operation reduces to arithmetic on these components.
Here is why: once we fix an orthonormal basis {i, j, k}, any vector a is completely determined by the three numbers (a₁, a₂, a₃) that tell how far a reaches along each axis.
These numbers are obtained by dropping perpendiculars from the tip of a onto the axes — the lengths of those perpendiculars (with sign) are the scalar components.
Because the basis vectors are mutually perpendicular and of unit length, the Pythagorean theorem gives the magnitude directly as √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²).
Direction cosines are simply the components divided by the magnitude, so they are the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the positive axes.
Consider a force F = 6i – 8j + 10k newtons acting on a particle.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “components are 5, 3, 2” ignoring the minus sign) reveals the misconception that components are always positive magnitudes — forgetting that components carry sign indicating direction along the axis.
remember: Write the vector v = 5i – 3j + 2k in component form and state its scalar components.
A vector a has magnitude 13 and direction ratios 2, 3, 6. Find its scalar components.
Evaluate the statement: “If a vector’s direction cosines are (1/√3, 1/√3, 1/√3), then its components must be equal.”.

cards.title: The scalar (dot) product of two vectors a and b, denoted a·b…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The scalar (dot) product of two vectors a and b, denoted a·b, is a real number defined in two equivalent ways. Geometrically, a·b = |a||b|cosθ, where |a| and |b| are the magnitudes (lengths) of the vectors and θ is the angle between them (0 ≤ θ ≤ π). Algebraically, if a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k and b = b₁i + b₂j + b₃k in a rectangular Cartesian system, then a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. The result is a scalar, not a vector; it carries the unit of the product of the units of the component vectors (e.g., if components are in metres, the dot product is in m²). The dot product is commutative (a·b = b·a), distributive over addition (a·(b+c) = a·b + a·c), and compatible with scalar multiplication ((λa)·b = λ(a·b)). Two non‑zero vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) iff their dot product is zero. The dot product also gives the projection of one vector onto another: the scalar projection of a on b is a·b/|b|, and the vector projection is (a·b/|b|²) b. This concept links directly to the earlier nodes on components and magnitude/direction, and it underpins the applications of work done and projections.
steps: The scalar product turns two vectors into a single number that captures how much they point in the same direction.
Here is why: the geometric definition a·b = |a||b|cosθ shows that only the component of a along b (or vice versa) contributes; the perpendicular component is multiplied by cos 90° = 0 and vanishes.
This matches the everyday idea of “effective push”.
First, recall from node 10_004 that any vector can be split into rectangular components a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k.
Multiplying the two component forms and using i·i = j·j = k·k = 1, i·j = j·k = k·i = 0 yields the algebraic formula a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.
This equivalence is the bridge between geometry and computation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing a·b = |a||b|sinθ) reveals the misconception that the dot product uses sine like the cross product — confusing the two products.
remember: State the geometric definition of the scalar (dot) product of two vectors a and b, including the meaning of each symbol.
Given a = 3i – 4j and b = –2i + j, compute a·b using the algebraic formula and state whether the angle between them is acute, right, or obtuse.
Evaluate the statement: “If a·b = 0, then either a = 0 or b = 0.” Justify your answer.

cards.title: The vector (cross) product of two vectors a and b, denoted a × b…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The vector (cross) product of two vectors a and b, denoted a × b, is a vector c whose magnitude is |a||b| sin θ, where θ is the angle between a and b (0° ≤ θ ≤ 180°). The direction of c is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b, determined by the right‑hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand from a to b; the extended thumb points along c. In component form, if a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k and b = b₁i + b₂j + b₃k, then a × b = (a₂b₃ – a₃b₂)i + (a₃b₁ – a₁b₃)j + (a₁b₂ – a₂b₁)k, which can be written as the determinant of a 3×3 matrix with unit vectors i, j, k in the first row. The cross product is anti‑commutative (a × b = –b × a), distributive over addition, and not associative. Geometrically, |a × b| equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b. If a and b are parallel (θ = 0° or 180°), the cross product is the zero vector. The cross product is defined only in three‑dimensional space (and seven‑dimensional space, but the latter is beyond ISC scope). It relates to the scalar (dot) product through the identity |a × b|² + (a·b)² = |a|²|b|².
steps: The cross product of two vectors yields a third vector perpendicular to both, with magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram they span.
Here is why: (1) The magnitude |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ directly measures the “spread” between the vectors; when they are parallel the area is zero, when perpendicular it is maximal.
(2) The right‑hand rule gives a unique orientation, making the cross product a true vector (not a scalar).
(3) The component formula using a 3×3 determinant provides a systematic computational method that works for any pair of 3‑D vectors.
(4) Anti‑commutativity (a × b = –b × a) reflects the reversal of orientation when the order is swapped.
(5) The cross product is essential for physical quantities like torque (τ = r × F) and angular momentum (L = r × p).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., |a × b| = |a||b| cos θ) reveals the misconception that the cross product uses cosine like the dot product, confusing the two products.
remember: State the formula for the magnitude of the cross product of two vectors a and b in terms of their magnitudes and the angle between them.
If a × b = 0, what can you conclude about the vectors a and b? Explain your reasoning.
A student claims that the cross product is commutative, i.e., a × b = b × a. Evaluate this claim with a counter‑example.

cards.title: Work done by a constant force is defined as the scalar (dot) product of the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Work done by a constant force is defined as the scalar (dot) product of the force vector F and the displacement vector d of the point of application: W = F =|F||d| θ, where θ is the angle between F and d. Work is a scalar quantity; its SI unit is the joule (J), equivalent to one newton‑metre (N·m). The sign of W indicates energy transfer: positive when the force has a component along the displacement (force does work on the object), negative when the force opposes the motion (work is done against the force), and zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement (no energy transfer in that direction). This definition builds directly on the scalar product concept (node) and uses position vectors and components (nodes‑) to express F and d in coordinate form.
steps: Work done by a constant force equals the dot product of the force vector and the displacement vector.

Here is why: the dot product extracts the component of one vector along the direction of the other and multiplies it by the magnitude of the second vector, which is precisely the physical meaning of work – only the part…
Consider a constant force F acting on a particle that moves from point A to point B along a straight line.
The displacement vector d = AB is known.
If we resolve F into a component parallel to d (F_ =|F| θ) and a component perpendicular to d, the perpendicular component does no displacement in its direction, so it contributes zero work.
The parallel component moves the particle through distance |d|, giving work W = F_ |d| = |F||d| θ.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., W = |F|+|d|) reveals the misconception that work is a simple addition of magnitudes, ignoring the directional nature of force and displacement.
remember: State the formula for work done by a constant force in terms of the force vector F, displacement vector d, and the angle θ between them.
Explain why the work done by a force is zero when the force acts perpendicular to the displacement of the object.
A 10 N force acts on a block that moves 5 m east. If the force is directed 60° north of east, calculate the work done by the force.

cards.title: The projection of a vector a onto another non‑zero vector b quantifies the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The projection of a vector a onto another non‑zero vector b quantifies the component of a that lies in the direction of b. There are two related quantities: the scalar projection (also called the component) and the vector projection. The scalar projection, denoted comp_ b a, is a signed magnitude given by ( a· b)/(\| b\|). It equals \| a\| θ, where θ is the angle between a and b; a positive value indicates that a has a component along b, a negative value indicates opposition, and zero means orthogonality. The vector projection, denoted proj_ b a, is the vector that represents this component: proj_ b a = (( a· b)/(\| b\|^2) ) b. It is always parallel (or anti‑parallel) to b and has magnitude | comp_ b a|. Projection is directly derived from the dot product, which itself connects magnitude, direction, and the cosine of the included angle. Consequently, projection links the concepts of scalar (dot) product, magnitude, components, and work done (where work = force · displacement = magnitude of force × projection of displacement onto force direction). Understanding projection enables decomposition of any vector into orthogonal parts relative to a chosen direction, a tool used repeatedly in physics and engineering.
steps: The projection of a vector onto another vector gives the component of the first vector that lies along the direction of the second vector.
Here is why: 1.
The dot product a· b = \| a\|\| b\| θ isolates the cosine of the angle between the vectors. 2.
Dividing by \| b\| yields \| a\| θ, which is precisely the length of the shadow of a on the line of b when a light source is perpendicular to b. 3.
Multiplying this signed length by the unit vector b/\| b\| reconstructs the actual vector component parallel to b. 4.
Consequently, the scalar projection tells us how much of a points along b (positive if same sense, negative if opposite), while the vector projection gives that amount as a true vector. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as “ a· b” reveals the misconception that the dot product itself equals the projection, ignoring the need to divide by the magnitude of b to obtain a component rather than a raw product of magnitudes.
remember: State the formula for the scalar projection of vector a onto vector b.
Explain why the vector projection of a onto b is the zero vector when a is perpendicular to b.
A student claims that the magnitude of the vector projection of a onto b is always less than or equal to the magnitude of a. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Three‑Dimensional Geometry extends the two‑dimensional coordinate system by…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Three‑Dimensional Geometry extends the two‑dimensional coordinate system by adding a third axis (z‑axis) perpendicular to the xy‑plane. A point in space is represented by an ordered triple (x, y, z). Direction ratios of a line are any three numbers proportional to the direction cosines, which are the cosines of the angles that the line makes with the positive x, y, and z axes. If a line has direction cosines l, m, n, then l² + m² + n² = 1. The vector equation of a line passing through a point with position vector a and parallel to a vector b is r = a + λb, λ ∈ ℝ. The Cartesian form is (x−x₁)/a = (y−y₁)/b = (z−z₁)/c where (a, b, c) are direction ratios. The angle θ between two lines with direction cosines (l₁,m₁,n₁) and (l₂,m₂,n₂) is given by cos θ = l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₁n₂. The shortest distance between two skew lines r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂ is d = |(a₂−a₁)·(b₁×b₂)| / |b₁×b₂|. These concepts interlink: direction cosines define orientation, line equations locate the line, angles measure inclination, and the shortest distance quantifies separation of non‑intersecting lines.
steps: The chapter equips you with a complete toolkit to describe and analyse any straight line in three‑dimensional space.

Here is why: direction cosines give a unique orientation signature for a line; the line equation translates that orientation and a fixed point into a locus of all points on the line; the angle formula lets you compare…

Consider a railway track running from Howrah to New Delhi: its direction cosines tell you the compass bearing and gradient, the line equation lets you locate any point along the track, the angle with another track tells…
Start by recalling that a vector b = ai + bj + ck has direction ratios (a, b, c).
Normalize to get direction cosines l = a/√(a²+b²+c²), etc. Then write the vector equation r = a + λb.
Convert to Cartesian by equating components.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “direction cosines are the same as direction ratios”) reveals the misconception that scaling does not affect orientation — confusing proportionality with equality.
remember: What is the fundamental relationship between direction ratios (a, b, c) and direction cosines (l, m, n) of a line in space.
Given a line passing through (2, −1, 3) with direction ratios (4, 5, −2), write its vector equation.
Two lines have direction cosines (1/√3, 1/√3, 1/√3) and (1/√2, 0, −1/√2). Find the angle between them.

cards.title: Direction cosines of a line in three‑dimensional space are the cosines of the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Direction cosines of a line in three‑dimensional space are the cosines of the angles α, β, γ that the line makes with the positive x‑, y‑, and z‑axes respectively. They are denoted by l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ and satisfy the fundamental relation l² + m² + n² = 1 because they are the components of a unit vector along the line. Direction ratios (a, b, c) are any three real numbers proportional to the direction cosines: a: b: c = l: m: n. If a, b, c are given, the direction cosines are obtained by normalising: l = a/√(a²+b²+c²), m = b/√(a²+b²+c²), n = c/√(a²+b²+c²). The sign of each cosine indicates whether the line points toward the positive or negative side of the corresponding axis. Two lines are parallel iff their direction ratios are proportional; they are perpendicular iff the dot product of their direction‑cosine vectors is zero (l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₁n₂ = 0). These concepts form the algebraic backbone for writing the equation of a line, finding angles between lines, and computing shortest distances later in the chapter.
steps: The one thing to remember: direction cosines are the components of a unit vector along the line, and any set of direction ratios can be turned into direction cosines by dividing by the magnitude of the ratio vector.
Here is why: a line in space has an orientation but no fixed position.
The angles α, β, γ it makes with the axes completely describe that orientation.

Cosines of these angles give a unit vector (l, m, n) because the sum of squares of the components of any unit vector equals one. Any three numbers (a, b, c) that keep the same proportion as (l, m, n) are called…
To move from ratios to cosines we simply normalise: compute the magnitude √(a²+b²+c²) and divide each ratio by it. Consider a line passing through the origin and the point (2, − 3, 6).
The vector from the origin to the point is 2i − 3j + 6k, so its direction ratios are (2, − 3, 6).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., l + m + n = 1) reveals the misconception that cosines add linearly rather than quadratically, confusing vector magnitude with scalar sum.
remember: What is the fundamental relation satisfied by the direction cosines l, m, n of any line in space.
A line has direction ratios (3, 4, 0). Explain why its direction cosines are (3/5, 4/5, 0) and not (3, 4, 0).
Evaluate the statement: “If two lines have direction ratios (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6), they are perpendicular.”.

cards.title: The equation of a line in space describes the set of all points whose position…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The equation of a line in space describes the set of all points whose position vectors satisfy a linear relation with a given point and a direction. If a line passes through point A with position vector a and is parallel to a non‑zero vector b, its vector equation is r = a + λ b, where λ ∈ R is a scalar parameter. In Cartesian coordinates, if A(x_1,y_1,z_1) and direction ratios of b are l,m,n (not all zero), the symmetric (Cartesian) form is (x-x_1)/(l) = (y-y_1)/(m) = (z-z_1)/(n). When any direction ratio is zero, the corresponding numerator is set equal to zero (e.g., l=0 ⇒ x=x_1). Direction cosines l,m,n are the cosines of angles the line makes with the positive axes; they satisfy l^2+m^2+n^2=1. The vector form is unique up to the choice of a and scaling of b; the symmetric form is unique up to a common non‑zero factor multiplying l,m,n. This node covers only the derivation and use of these forms; angle between lines and shortest distance are treated in later nodes.
steps: The one thing to remember: a line in space is completely determined by a point on it and a direction vector; every point on the line corresponds to a unique real parameter λ in r=a+.

Here is why: (1) The vector form directly encodes the geometric idea of starting at a and moving along b. (2) The parameter λ measures signed distance in units of |b|; when b is a unit vector, λ equals the actual…
(3) The symmetric form eliminates λ and gives a quick test for collinearity of three points.
(4) Zero direction ratios are handled by setting the corresponding coordinate constant, avoiding division by zero.
(5) Converting between forms is a routine algebraic manipulation that appears in every ISC paper.

cards.title: The angle between two lines in space is defined as the acute angle…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The angle between two lines in space is defined as the acute angle (0° ≤ θ ≤ 90°) between their direction vectors. If the lines have direction ratios (a₁, b₁, c₁) and (a₂, b₂, c₂), the cosine of the angle is given by cos θ = |a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂| / (√(a₁²+b₁²+c₁²) · √(a₂²+b₂²+c₂²)). When direction cosines (l₁, m₁, n₁) and (l₂, m₂, n₂) are used, the formula simplifies to cos θ = |l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₁n₂| because each set satisfies l²+m²+n²=1. The absolute value ensures the angle is acute regardless of the orientation of the direction vectors. Two lines are parallel if their direction ratios are proportional (θ=0°), and perpendicular if the dot product of their direction ratios is zero (θ=90°). This concept directly uses the direction cosines/ratios introduced in the previous node and the line equations from the node before that.
steps: The angle between two lines in space is always taken as the acute angle between their direction vectors, obtained by the absolute value of the dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes.

Here is why: the dot product gives the cosine of the angle between the directed vectors, but lines have no direction; reversing one vector changes the sign of the cosine, so we use the absolute value to get a unique…
First, identify the direction ratios of each line from its equation.
In symmetric form (x−x₁)/a = (y−y₁)/b = (z−z₁)/c, the denominators (a,b,c) are the direction ratios.
In vector form r = a + λb, the vector b provides the ratios.
Second, compute the dot product a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂.

cards.title: The shortest distance between two lines in three‑dimensional space is the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The shortest distance between two lines in three‑dimensional space is the minimum Euclidean distance between any point on the first line and any point on the second line. For two lines given in vector form r = a_1 + λ b_1 and r = a_2 + μ b_2, where a_1, a_2 are position vectors of points on the lines and b_1, b_2 are their direction vectors, the shortest distance d is - Skew lines (non‑parallel, non‑intersecting): d = |(a_2 - a_1) · (b_1 × b_2)||b_1 × b_2|. The numerator is the absolute scalar triple product of the joining vector and the two direction vectors; the denominator is the magnitude of the cross product, which gives a vector perpendicular to both lines. - Parallel lines (b_1 b_2): d = |(a_2 - a_1) × b_1||b_1|. Here the cross product of the joining vector with the common direction yields a vector whose magnitude equals the perpendicular distance times |b_1|. If the lines intersect, the scalar triple product (or the cross‑product magnitude for parallel case) becomes zero, giving d = 0. The formula relies on the properties of the scalar triple product [u\,v\,w] = u · (v × w) and the fact that b_1 × b_2 is orthogonal to both direction vectors.
steps: The shortest distance between two lines in space is the length of the common perpendicular segment that joins them.

Here is why: any two non‑parallel lines in 3‑D either intersect (distance zero) or are skew; for skew lines there is exactly one line segment perpendicular to both, and its length is the minimum distance.
Consider two lines r = a_1 + λ b_1 and r = a_2 + μ b_2.
The vector joining a point on the first line to a point on the second is a_2 - a_1 + μ b_2 - λ b_1.
The component of this joining vector along the direction perpendicular to both lines is obtained by projecting onto b_1 × b_2.
Because b_1 × b_2 is orthogonal to both b_1 and b_2, the scalar projection of the joining vector onto this perpendicular direction is ((a_2 - a_1) · (b_1 × b_2))/(|b_1 × b_2|).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., d = ((a_2 - a_1) · (b_1 × b_2))/(|b_1 × b_2|) without absolute value) reveals the misconception that distance can be negative, confusing signed projection with actual length.

cards.title: A plane in three‑dimensional space is a two‑dimensional flat surface that…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A plane in three‑dimensional space is a two‑dimensional flat surface that extends infinitely. It is uniquely determined by a point A(x_1,y_1,z_1) on the plane and a non‑zero vector n=ai+bj+ck perpendicular to the plane (the normal vector). The vector equation is r =d where r=xi+yj+zk is the position vector of any point on the plane and d=a with a the position vector of the known point. In Cartesian form this becomes a(x-x_1)+b(y-y_1)+c(z-z_1)=0 or ax+by+cz=d. If three non‑collinear points A,B,C are given, the normal can be obtained as n=(b-a)×(c-a) and the same equation follows. The direction ratios of the normal are (a,b,c); direction cosines are (a)/(√(a^2+b^2+c^2)),(b)/(√(a^2+b^2+c^2)),(c)/(√(a^2+b^2+c^2)). A point (x_0,y_0,z_0) lies on the plane iff its coordinates satisfy the Cartesian equation.
steps: A plane in space is uniquely determined by a point on it and a vector perpendicular to it, giving the equation r =d.

Here is why: the dot product r measures the projection of the position vector onto the normal; for all points on the plane this projection is constant, equal to the projection of the known point’s position vector.

cards.title: The angle between two intersecting planes is defined as the acute angle between…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The angle between two intersecting planes is defined as the acute angle between their normal vectors. If the planes are given in vector form as r · n_1 = d_1 and r · n_2 = d_2, their normals are n_1 and n_2. The cosine of the angle θ between the planes is θ = (|n_1 · n_2|)/(|n_1|\,|n_2|). In Cartesian form, planes a_1x + b_1y + c_1z + d_1 = 0 and a_2x + b_2y + c_2z + d_2 = 0 have normals (a_1,b_1,c_1) and (a_2,b_2,c_2), giving θ = (|a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2|)/(√(a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2)\,√(a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2)). Two planes are parallel iff their normals are parallel (n_1 n_2), i.e., (a_1)/(a_2)=(b_1)/(b_2)=(c_1)/(c_2); the angle is 0°. They are perpendicular iff n_1 · n_2 = 0, i.e., a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0; the angle is 90°. This concept builds directly on direction cosines/ratios, equation of a line, and the equation of a plane, using the dot product to transfer the idea of angle from lines to planes.
steps: The angle between two planes is the acute angle between their normal vectors, found using the dot product formula θ = |n_1 _2|/(|n_1||n_2|).
Here is why: two intersecting planes meet along a line; the angle between the planes is measured in a plane perpendicular to that line, which is exactly the angle between the normals.
Normals capture the orientation of a plane uniquely, just as direction vectors capture a line's orientation.
The dot product gives the cosine of the angle between the normals; taking the absolute value selects the acute angle (or 90° if perpendicular).
This works for both vector form r =d and Cartesian form ax+by+cz+d=0 because the coefficients (a,b,c) are the normal's direction ratios.
Special cases: if normals are parallel, θ=1 and θ=0° (parallel planes); if normals are perpendicular, θ=0 and θ=90°.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., θ = (n_1 · n_2)/(|n_1|\,|n_2|) without absolute value) reveals the misconception that the angle between planes can be obtuse, confusing it with the angle between vectors which can be >90°.

cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node synthesises the four core subtopics of Chapter 11: direction cosines and ratios, equation of a line in space, angle between two lines, and shortest distance between two lines. Direction cosines (l, m, n) are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the positive x, y, z axes; they satisfy l²+m²+n²=1 and are derived from direction ratios (a, b, c) by normalising. The equation of a line can be expressed in vector form r = a + λb, parametric form, or symmetric (Cartesian) form (x−x₁)/a = (y−y₁)/b = (z−z₁)/c, where a is a point on the line and b gives its direction. The angle θ between two lines with direction vectors b₁, b₂ is given by cos θ = |b₁·b₂|/(|b₁||b₂|). The shortest distance between two skew lines r = a₁+λb₁ and r = a₂+μb₂ is d = |(a₂−a₁)·(b₁×b₂)| / |b₁×b₂|; for parallel lines the formula reduces to the perpendicular distance from a point on one line to the other. These concepts interlink: direction ratios feed into line equations, which supply direction vectors for angle and distance calculations. Mastery requires moving fluently among vector, parametric, and Cartesian representations and recognising when lines are parallel, intersecting, or skew.

cards.title: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique used to…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique used to determine the maximum or minimum value of a linear objective function subject to a set of linear inequality or equality constraints. The objective function represents the quantity to be optimised — such as profit, cost, or time — expressed as a linear combination of decision variables. Constraints are linear relations that model resource limitations, capacity bounds, or policy rules; they restrict the feasible values of the decision variables. The collection of all points satisfying every constraint forms the feasible region, a convex polygon (or polyhedron in higher dimensions) in the coordinate space of the variables. The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming states that if an optimal solution exists, it occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region. The graphical method solves two‑variable LP problems by plotting each constraint as a half‑plane, shading the feasible region, and then sliding a family of parallel objective‑function lines until the last line touching the region identifies the optimum. This chapter introduces the three core ideas — formulation of constraints and objective function, identification of the feasible region, and the graphical solution procedure — and explains why LP is a cornerstone of operations research, economics, engineering design, and management science in the Indian context and worldwide.
steps: The one essential takeaway is that linear programming converts a real‑world “best decision” problem into a geometric search for a corner point of a polygon.

Here is why: first, every LP problem has three building blocks — decision variables that we control, a linear objective we want to maximise or minimise, and linear constraints that limit the variables.
Second, because all relations are linear, the set of all allowed variable pairs (the feasible region) is a convex polygon whose edges are pieces of the constraint lines.
Third, the Fundamental Theorem guarantees that the optimal value of the objective, if it exists, is attained at one of the polygon’s vertices; we never need to check interior points.

Fourth, the graphical method exploits this by drawing each constraint, shading the feasible side, and then moving a ruler‑parallel line representing the objective until it just leaves the polygon — the last contact…
Fifth, this visual approach works only for two variables, but it builds the intuition that underpins the algebraic simplex algorithm used for larger problems.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only an objective function and constraints”) reveals the misconception that variables are implicit — students often forget that variables must be explicitly defined before writing the objective or constraints.

cards.title: A Linear Programming Problem (LPP) consists of three essential components…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A Linear Programming Problem (LPP) consists of three essential components: decision variables, an objective function, and a set of constraints. Decision variables (usually x_1, x_2,, x_n) represent the quantities to be determined, such as the number of units of each product. The objective function is a linear expression Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 + + c_nx_n that quantifies the goal — maximise profit or minimise cost — where each coefficient c_j is the contribution per unit of variable x_j. Constraints are linear inequalities (or equations) that restrict the variables to reflect limited resources, technological requirements, or policy limits. They take the form a_i1x_1 + a_i2x_2 + + a_inx_n ≤ b_i (or ≥, =) for i = 1,,m, where a_ij is the amount of resource i consumed per unit of x_j and b_i is the total available amount of resource i. Additionally, non‑negativity constraints x_j ≥ 0 are imposed because negative production is meaningless. Together, the objective function and constraints define the feasible region (the set of all variable vectors satisfying every constraint). The optimal solution is a point in this region that gives the best value of Z. This node focuses solely on formulating the objective function and constraints; graphical identification of the feasible region and the solution method are covered in subsequent nodes.
steps: The objective function and constraints together capture the entire optimisation problem in algebraic form.
First, every LPP begins by naming the decision variables that represent controllable quantities.
Second, the objective function aggregates the contribution of each variable using per‑unit coefficients (profit, cost, time).
Third, each limited resource or requirement becomes a linear inequality linking the variables to the available amount.
Fourth, non‑negativity constraints are added because physical quantities cannot be negative.
Consider a small factory producing chairs (C) and tables (T).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “constraints can be equalities only”) reveals the misconception that standard form forbids inequalities — confusing standard form with canonical form used in some textbooks.

cards.title: In a Linear Programming Problem (LPP)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In a Linear Programming Problem (LPP), the feasible region is the set of all points (x, y) in the Cartesian plane that satisfy every constraint simultaneously, including the non‑negativity restrictions x ≥ 0,\; y ≥ 0. Each linear constraint a_i x + b_i y ≤ c_i (or ≥, =) divides the plane into two half‑planes; the feasible side is the half‑plane that contains points satisfying the inequality. The feasible region is the intersection of all these half‑planes. Geometrically it is a convex polygon (possibly unbounded) whose vertices are the intersection points of the boundary lines. If the intersection is empty, the LPP has no feasible solution. The feasible region is the domain over which the objective function Z = px + qy is optimised; by the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming, an optimal value (if it exists) occurs at a vertex of this region.
steps: The feasible region is the common overlap of all half‑planes defined by the constraints, and any optimal solution of the LPP must lie at one of its vertices.
Here is why: each inequality restricts the decision variables to one side of its boundary line; the feasible region is exactly the intersection of these restricted sides.

Because the objective function is linear, its level lines are parallel straight lines; moving a level line in the direction of improvement will eventually touch the feasible region at a corner point — if the region is…

cards.title: The graphical solution of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) with two decision…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The graphical solution of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) with two decision variables is a geometric technique that identifies the optimal value of a linear objective function subject to a set of linear inequality constraints. The constraints, each representing a limitation such as resource availability or production capacity, are plotted as half‑planes on the Cartesian plane. Their intersection forms the feasible region — a convex polygon (possibly unbounded) containing all points that satisfy every constraint simultaneously. According to the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming, if an optimal solution exists, it must occur at a vertex (corner point) of this feasible region. The solution procedure therefore consists of: (1) writing the objective function Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 (maximise or minimise); (2) graphing each constraint as a line and shading the admissible side; (3) determining the feasible region; (4) locating all corner points either by inspection or by solving the intersecting lines algebraically; (5) evaluating the objective function at each corner point; (6) selecting the point that gives the maximum (or minimum) value of Z. Two equivalent visual approaches are the corner‑point evaluation method and the iso‑profit (iso‑cost) line method, where a line representing a constant value of Z is moved parallel to itself until it just leaves the feasible region. Special cases — infeasible region (no common area), unbounded solution (objective can increase indefinitely), and multiple optimal solutions (entire edge yields same optimum) — are identified during this process. The method is limited to two variables because higher dimensions cannot be visualised on a plane; for more variables the simplex algorithm is used.
steps: The graphical solution of a two‑variable LPP finds the optimum by locating the feasible region’s corner points and evaluating the objective function there.
Here is why: (1) The feasible region is a convex polygon formed by intersecting half‑planes, so any line segment joining two feasible points stays inside.
(2) A linear objective function increases (or decreases) uniformly in a fixed direction; its maximum over a convex polygon must occur at a vertex.
(3) The iso‑profit line method visualises this by sliding a line of constant profit parallel to itself until it just touches the feasible region — the last contact point is optimal.
(4) Special cases appear when the feasible region is empty, unbounded in the direction of optimisation, or when an entire edge is parallel to the iso‑profit line.
Consider a farmer near Nashik who has 10 hectares of land, 1200 kg of fertiliser, and 800 hours of labour.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the feasible region is the area under the objective function line”) reveals the misconception that the objective function defines feasibility, confusing optimisation with constraint satisfaction.
