cards.title: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is the systematic process of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is the systematic process of converting a real‑world decision situation into a mathematical model consisting of three core components. First, decision variables (usually denoted x_1, x_2,, x_n) represent the quantities to be determined — for example, the number of idlis (x_1) and dosas (x_2) to produce. Second, the objective function is a linear expression Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 + + c_nx_n that must be maximized (profit, output) or minimized (cost, time); the coefficients c_i are the unit contributions of each variable. Third, constraints are a set of linear inequalities or equations a_i1x_1 + a_i2x_2 + + a_inx_n \ (≤, =, ≥) \ b_i that capture limited resources (flour, oil, labour hours), technological requirements, or market limits. All variables are also subject to non‑negativity restrictions x_i ≥ 0. This node builds directly on the concepts of constraints and objective function (node), the feasible region (node), and the graphical solution method (node) — formulation supplies the model that those nodes analyse and solve.
steps: Formulating a linear programming problem requires translating a real‑world decision scenario into decision variables, a linear objective function, and a set of linear constraints with non‑negativity conditions.

Here is why: every optimisation story — whether a factory scheduling production, a hospital allocating beds, or a student planning study hours — shares the same mathematical skeleton: choose quantities (variables) to…
First, identify the decision variables by asking “What quantities can I control?” In the tiffin example, the controllable quantities are the number of idlis and dosas; denote them x_1 and x_2.
Second, write the objective function by expressing the goal (maximise profit) as a linear combination of the variables: each idli yields ₹8 profit, each dosa ₹12, so Z = 8x_1 + 12x_2.

Third, list all resource limits as linear inequalities: rice flour 2 kg per idli and 3 kg per dosa, total 10 kg → 2x_1 + 3x_2 ≤ 10; oil 0.1 L per idli, 0.2 L per dosa, total 5 L → 0.1x_1 + 0.2x_2 ≤ 5; time 10 min per…
Fourth, ensure every expression is linear (no products, powers, or absolute values) and add non‑negativity x_1, x_2 ≥ 0.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “objective function, feasible region, optimal solution”) reveals the misconception that the feasible region and optimal solution are part of the formulation stage — they are actually analysis steps that come after the model is built.

cards.title: In linear programming, a special case occurs when the graphical solution of a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In linear programming, a special case occurs when the graphical solution of a linear programming problem (LPP) does not yield a unique, bounded optimum at a single corner point of the feasible region. There are three distinct types: 1. Infeasible LPP – The set of constraints is contradictory; no point satisfies all inequalities simultaneously, so the feasible region is empty (∅). Consequently, no value of the objective function can be attained. 2. Unbounded LPP – The feasible region is open and extends infinitely in the direction that improves the objective function (maximisation or minimisation). As a result, the objective function can increase (or decrease) without limit, yielding no finite optimal solution. 3. Multiple optimal solutions – The objective function line is parallel to a boundary edge of the feasible region. Every point on that edge segment gives the same optimal value, producing infinitely many optimal solutions (though the extreme points of the segment are the usual corner‑point candidates). These cases are directly linked to the shape and position of the feasible region derived from the constraints, and to the orientation of the objective‑function vector relative to the constraint boundaries. Recognising them prevents misinterpretation of graphical outputs and guides corrective modelling (e.g., tightening or relaxing constraints).

Finally, when the slope of the objective line equals the slope of a constraint that forms part of the region’s boundary, sliding the objective line outward touches the whole edge, giving equal optimal values at every…
Consider a mela stall again.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “infeasibility occurs when the objective function value is negative”) reveals the misconception that feasibility depends on the objective value rather than on the constraint intersection.
remember: State the necessary and sufficient condition for a linear programming problem to be infeasible when solved graphically.
Given the constraints x + 2y ≤ 8, 3x + y ≤ 9, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, determine whether the feasible region is bounded or unbounded. Justify your answer.
Evaluate the statement: “If the objective function line is parallel to a constraint that forms part of the feasible region’s boundary, the LPP must have multiple optimal….

cards.title: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is the process of translating…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem (LPP) is the process of translating a real‑world decision situation into a precise mathematical model consisting of three components: (1) Decision variables — usually denoted x_1, x_2,, x_n — representing the quantities to be determined (e.g., number of units of each product). (2) Objective function — a linear expression Z = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 + + c_nx_n to be maximised (profit, output) or minimised (cost, time). The coefficients c_i are the contribution per unit of each variable. (3) Constraints — a set of linear inequalities (or equations) a_11x_1 + a_12x_2 + + a_1nx_n ≤ (≥, =) b_1, …, a_m1x_1 + + a_mnx_n ≤ (≥, =) b_m that capture resource limits, demand requirements, or technical restrictions. Additionally, non‑negativity restrictions x_i ≥ 0 for all i are imposed because physical quantities cannot be negative. The feasible region of the LPP is the set of all points satisfying every constraint and non‑negativity condition. An optimal solution, if it exists, occurs at a corner point of this feasible region (Corner Point Theorem). The formulation step is independent of the solution method; it only requires that all relationships be linear. In the ISC syllabus, formulation is tested through word problems involving production planning, diet optimisation, transportation, and investment allocation.
steps: The one thing to remember: every LPP formulation follows the same three‑step recipe — variables → objective → constraints — and skipping any step makes the model incomplete.
Here is why: a word problem hides the mathematics inside a narrative.
The first task is to decide what we can control; these become the decision variables.
In a factory making chairs (x) and tables (y), we control how many of each to produce.
Next, we express what we want to achieve — usually maximum profit or minimum cost — as a linear combination of those variables.
If a chair gives ₹200 profit and a table ₹300, the objective is Maximise Z = 200x + 300y.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the second constraint should be x + y ≤ 50”) reveals the misconception that “at least 50 units” means a maximum limit, confusing “≥” with “≤”.
remember: List the three essential components of a Linear Programming Problem formulation in the correct order.
A student formulates the following LPP for a problem: “Maximise Z = 10x + 15y subject to 2x + 3y ≤ 100, x + y ≥ 50, x, y ≥ 0.” The original problem states: “A company makes two….
Evaluate the following two formulations for the same scenario: “A farmer has 10 hectares of….

cards.title: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique where a linear…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Linear Programming (LP) is a mathematical optimisation technique where a linear objective function — typically profit, cost, or time — is maximised or minimised subject to a set of linear inequality constraints that represent limited resources such as raw materials, labour hours, budget, or machine capacity. The decision variables (e.g., x_1, x_2) denote quantities to be determined. All constraints are expressed as a_i1x_1 + a_i2x_2 ≤ b_i (or ≥, =) with non‑negativity x_j ≥ 0. The collection of all points satisfying every constraint forms the feasible region, a convex polygon (or polyhedron in higher dimensions). By the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming, if an optimal solution exists it occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region. The graphical method solves two‑variable LPPs by plotting each constraint line, shading the feasible side, identifying the polygon, evaluating the objective function at every vertex, and selecting the best value. For more than two variables the simplex or interior‑point algorithms are used, but the ISC syllabus restricts to the graphical approach. Sensitivity analysis (shadow prices, range of optimality) is not required at this level.
steps: The single most important takeaway: In a two‑variable LPP the optimum always lies at a corner of the feasible polygon, so you only need to test those vertices.

Here is why: the objective function is a family of parallel lines; moving the line in the direction of improvement slides it across the feasible region until it last touches the region — that contact point is a vertex.
Consider a manufacturer producing two models of school bags, A and B. Model A needs 2 m fabric and 1 h labour;
Model B needs 1 m fabric and 3 h labour.
Weekly limits: 100 m fabric, 90 h labour.
Profit: ₹200 per A, ₹300 per B. Let x = units of A, y = units of B. Constraints: 2x + y ≤ 100 (fabric), x + 3y ≤ 90 (labour), x, y ≥ 0.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the optimum can be anywhere inside the feasible region”) reveals the misconception that the objective function can attain its extreme in the interior — confusing linear with non‑linear optimisation where interior critical points exist.
remember: State the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming for a two‑variable problem.
A student writes the constraint for “at most 50 kg of sugar” as x + y ≥ 50 where x and y are kilograms of two….
Evaluate the claim: “If the feasible region is unbounded, the LPP has no maximum.” Provide a counter‑example or justification.

cards.title: Probability quantifies the likelihood of an event occurring…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Probability quantifies the likelihood of an event occurring, expressed as a number between 0 and 1 inclusive. In this chapter the concept is extended through four interconnected sub‑topics. Conditional probability, denoted P(A|B), measures the chance of event A given that event B has already occurred; it is defined as P(A∩B)/P(B) provided P(B)>0. Bayes’ theorem reverses this conditioning, allowing us to compute P(B|A) from known values of P(A|B), P(B) and P(A) via the formula P(B|A)=P(A|B)P(B)/P(A). A random variable X assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment; its probability distribution lists all possible values x_i together with their probabilities P(X=x_i). For a discrete random variable the mean (expected value) is μ=E(X)=∑ x_i P(X=x_i) and the variance is σ²=Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]=∑ (x_i−μ)² P(X=x_i). For a continuous random variable the sums become integrals with the probability density function f(x). These four ideas form a logical chain: conditional probability provides the tool to update beliefs, Bayes’ theorem applies that tool to infer causes from observed effects, random variables translate outcomes into numerical quantities, and mean/variance summarise the central tendency and dispersion of those quantities. Mastery of this chain enables modelling of real‑world uncertainty such as medical test reliability, quality‑control sampling, and financial risk assessment.
steps: Takeaway: The chapter builds a single coherent framework — conditional probability updates beliefs, Bayes’ theorem inverts that update, random variables turn outcomes into numbers, and mean/variance summarise those…
Here is why: First, conditional probability formalises the everyday act of revising a prediction when new data arrives, such as a doctor updating disease likelihood after a test result.
Second, Bayes’ theorem provides the algebraic rule to reverse the direction of inference, turning “probability of test given disease” into “probability of disease given test”.
Third, a random variable assigns a numeric value to each outcome (e.g., number of defective items in a batch), and its probability distribution lists all possible values with their chances.
Fourth, the mean (expected value) gives the long‑run average outcome, while the variance measures how far actual outcomes typically deviate from that average.

Together these tools let a student analyse scenarios like: “A factory produces 2% defective bulbs; a quality check picks 5 bulbs — what is the expected number of defectives and how variable is that number?” The chapter…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., P(A|B) = P(A) P(B)) reveals the misconception that conditioning is the same as multiplying independent probabilities, confusing independence with conditioning.
remember: What is the formula for conditional probability P(A|B) in terms of P(A∩B) and P(B).
If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A|B) = 0.6, compute P(B|A) using Bayes’ theorem.
Evaluate the statement: “The mean of a random variable is always one of its possible values.” Provide a counterexample if false.

cards.title: Conditional probability quantifies the likelihood of an event A occurring under…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Conditional probability quantifies the likelihood of an event A occurring under the condition that another event B has already occurred, provided P(B)>0. It is denoted P(A B) and defined as P(A B)=(P(A∩ B))/(P(B)). Here P(A∩ B) is the joint probability that both A and B happen, and P(B) is the marginal probability of B. The definition implies the multiplication rule P(A∩ B)=P(A B)P(B)=P(B A)P(A). Conditional probability satisfies the axioms of probability on the reduced sample space B; thus 0≤ P(A B)≤1 and P(B B)=1. If A and B are independent, P(A B)=P(A). The concept extends to a finite or countable partition {B_i} of the sample space, leading to the law of total probability P(A)=Σ_i P(A B_i)P(B_i), which is the foundation for Bayes’ theorem (covered in the next node). All probabilities are dimensionless numbers between 0 and 1.
steps: Conditional probability re‑weights the sample space to the known event, so every calculation must use the reduced denominator P(B).
Here is why: when we learn that B has occurred, outcomes outside B become impossible; the new universe is B itself, and probabilities must sum to 1 over this universe.
Consider a standard deck of 52 cards.
Let A = “draw a king” and B = “draw a face card (J, Q, K)”.
There are 12 face cards, 4 of which are kings.
The unconditional P(A)=4/52=1/13.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “P(A B)=P(A)P(B)”) reveals the misconception that conditional probability equals the product of marginals — confusing it with the multiplication rule for independent events.
remember: State the formula for conditional probability P(A B) and the condition required for it to be defined.
In a class of 40 students, 25 study Mathematics, 20 study Physics, and 12 study….
Evaluate the statement: “If P(A B)=P(A), then events A and B are mutually exclusive.”.

cards.title: Bayes’ theorem provides a rule for reversing conditional probabilities.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Bayes’ theorem provides a rule for reversing conditional probabilities. Let {A_1, A_2,, A_n} be a partition of the sample space S (mutually exclusive and exhaustive events) with prior probabilities P(A_i) > 0. For any observed event B with P(B) > 0, the posterior probability of A_i given B is P(A_i B) = P(B A_i)\,P(A_i)Σ_j=1^n P(B A_j)\,P(A_j). The numerator is the product of the likelihood P(B A_i) and the prior P(A_i). The denominator is the total probability of the evidence B obtained via the law of total probability. The theorem connects three concepts: prior probability (belief before evidence), likelihood (probability of evidence under each hypothesis), and posterior probability (updated belief). It is the formal basis for statistical inference, diagnostic testing, and machine‑learning classification.
steps: Takeaway: Bayes’ theorem turns “probability of evidence given hypothesis” into “probability of hypothesis given evidence” by weighting each hypothesis with its prior and normalising by the total probability of the…
Supporting arguments: 1.
The theorem is a direct algebraic rearrangement of the definition of conditional probability applied to a partition. 2.
The denominator ensures the posterior probabilities sum to one, because the evidence B must have occurred through exactly one of the mutually exclusive hypotheses. 3.
In real‑world diagnostics, the prior reflects disease prevalence; the likelihood reflects test sensitivity/specificity; the posterior is the positive‑predictive value doctors need. 4.
Ignoring a hypothesis (e.g., forgetting a third machine in a factory) makes the denominator too small and inflates the remaining posteriors — a common exam trap.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing denominator as P(B) without expansion) reveals the misconception that the total probability of evidence is given directly, ignoring the need to sum over all hypotheses — a frequent error when students skip the law of total…
remember: State Bayes’ theorem for a partition {A_1, A_2,, A_n} and an event B with P(B)>0.
Given P(A)=0.3, P(B A)=0.7, P(B A^c)=0.2, compute P(A B).
A student argues: “If P(A B) > P(A), then event B causes event A.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A random variable X is a function that assigns a real number to every outcome…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A random variable X is a function that assigns a real number to every outcome in a sample space S of a random experiment. If X takes at most countably many distinct values, it is discrete; otherwise it is continuous. For a discrete random variable, the probability mass function (pmf) p(x)=P(X=x) gives the probability that X equals a specific value x. The pmf must satisfy: 1. p(x) ≥ 0 for all x, 2. Σ_x p(x) = 1. For a continuous random variable, the probability density function (pdf) f(x) describes relative likelihood; the probability that X lies in an interval [a,b] is _a^b f(x)\,dx. The pdf must satisfy: 1. f(x) ≥ 0 for all x, 2. _-∞^∞ f(x)\,dx = 1. The cumulative distribution function (cdf) F(x)=P(X≤ x) is defined for both types: for discrete F(x)=Σ_t≤ xp(t); for continuous F(x)= _-∞^x f(t)\,dt. The cdf is non‑decreasing, right‑continuous, with _x→-∞F(x)=0 and _x→∞F(x)=1. Random variables transform qualitative outcomes into numerical quantities, enabling algebraic manipulation of probabilities. This node builds on conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem (nodes and) by providing the framework to describe the full probabilistic behaviour of numerical outcomes, which is then used in the next node to compute mean and variance.
steps: A random variable converts every outcome of a random experiment into a real number, and its probability distribution tells exactly how the total probability 1 is spread over those numbers.
Here is why: 1.
Numerical representation – Without numbers we cannot calculate averages or spreads; a random variable provides that bridge. 2.
Two flavours – Discrete variables (e.g., number of heads in three coin tosses) take isolated values; continuous variables (e.g., waiting time for a local train) take any value in an interval. 3.

Probability mass vs. density – For discrete variables the pmf gives exact probabilities at each point; for continuous variables the pdf gives a density, and probabilities come from areas under the curve. 4.
Cumulative view – The cdf F(x)=P(X≤ x) works for both types and is the tool for finding percentiles and median. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “pmf can be negative for some values”) reveals the misconception that probability mass can be negative, confusing it with a density that can take negative values in signed measures — but probabilities are never negative.
remember: Define a discrete random variable and state the two conditions its probability mass function must satisfy.
Given a function f(x)=kx for x=1,2,3 and 0 otherwise, find k such that f(x) is a valid pmf.
A student claims that the function f(x)=2x for 0≤ x≤ 1 is a valid probability density function. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: For a discrete random variable X that can take values x_1, x_2…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: For a discrete random variable X that can take values x_1, x_2,, x_n with corresponding probabilities p(x_i) (where Σ p(x_i)=1), the mean (also called expected value) is μ = E(X)=Σ_i=1^n x_i\,p(x_i). It represents the long‑run average outcome if the experiment is repeated infinitely. The variance measures the average squared deviation from the mean: σ^2 = Var(X)=E\! [(X-μ)^2 ]=Σ_i=1^n (x_i-μ)^2\,p(x_i). An equivalent computational formula is Var(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2. The mean has the same unit as X; the variance has the unit of X squared (e.g., if X is metres, variance is metres²). These concepts build directly on the probability distribution introduced in the previous node (random variables and probability distributions) and are essential for later topics such as Bernoulli trials and binomial distribution.
steps: The mean of a random variable tells you the centre of its distribution, while the variance tells you how tightly the values cluster around that centre.
Here is why: consider a game where you draw a card from a well‑shuffled deck of 52 cards and win ₹10 for a heart, ₹5 for a face card that is not a heart, and ₹0 otherwise.
Let X be the amount won. The probabilities are: P(heart)=13/52=0.25 → win ₹10;
P(face non‑heart)=9/52≈0.1731 → win ₹5;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “μ = Σ x_i”) reveals the misconception that probabilities are ignored, treating all outcomes as equally likely.
remember: State the formula for the mean of a discrete random variable X and define each symbol.
If a random variable Y takes values -2,0,3 with probabilities 0.2,0.5,0.3 respectively, compute E(Y).
Explain why variance is always non‑negative.

cards.title: The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number n of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number n of independent Bernoulli trials, each with identical probability of success p and failure q = 1-p. A random variable X follows a binomial distribution, denoted X B(n,p), if its probability mass function is P(X = r) = nr p^r q^n-r for r = 0,1,,n. The mean is μ = np and the variance is σ^2 = npq. This distribution connects directly to the earlier concepts: conditional probability underpins the independence assumption, Bayes’ theorem can update p given data, and the mean/variance formulas extend the general definitions for discrete random variables. The binomial coefficient nr counts the distinct sequences yielding exactly r successes, linking combinatorics to probability.
steps: The binomial distribution gives the exact probability of a specific number of successes in a fixed set of independent, identical trials.

Here is why: each trial is a Bernoulli experiment with success probability p; the number of ways to arrange r successes among n trials is nr; multiplying by p^r q^n-r yields the probability of any one such sequence, and…
Consider a student answering 20 multiple‑choice questions, each with four options, by random guessing.
The number of correct answers X follows B(20, 0.25).
To find the chance of exactly 5 correct answers, compute 205(0.25)^5(0.75)^15.
For “at most 5 correct”, sum P(X=r) for r=0 to 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “three conditions: fixed trials, two outcomes, constant probability”) reveals the misconception that independence is optional — students often overlook independence because many textbook examples implicitly assume it.
remember: State the four conditions that define a binomial experiment.
A die is rolled 12 times. Let X be the number of times a ‘6’ appears. Write the distribution of X and compute P(X = 3).
Evaluate the claim: “If the mean of a binomial distribution is 8 and the variance is 4, then n=16 and p=0.5.”.

cards.title: A binomial experiment consists of n independent Bernoulli trials…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A binomial experiment consists of n independent Bernoulli trials, each with two outcomes: success (probability p) and failure (probability q = 1 − p). The random variable X counting the number of successes follows a binomial distribution, denoted X ~ B(n, p). Its probability mass function is P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, …, n. The mean (expected value) of X is μ = E(X) = np. The variance is σ² = Var(X) = npq, and the standard deviation is σ = √(npq). These formulas are derived from the linearity of expectation and the independence of trials: E(X) = Σ E(Xᵢ) = np, and Var(X) = Σ Var(Xᵢ) = npq because covariances are zero. This node connects the general definitions of mean and variance (covered in node) to the specific binomial case, and uses the binomial pmf (from node) to solve application problems such as finding the most likely number of successes, probabilities of ranges, and parameter estimation from given mean and variance.
steps: The mean and variance of a binomial distribution are np and npq respectively — these two numbers completely summarise the centre and spread of the distribution.
Here is why: each trial is a Bernoulli variable Xᵢ with E(Xᵢ)=p and Var(Xᵢ)=pq.

Because trials are independent, the total successes X = Σ Xᵢ has expectation Σ E(Xᵢ) = np and variance Σ Var(Xᵢ) = npq. Consider a student answering 50 multiple‑choice questions (4 options each) by random guessing.
Here n=50, p=0.25, so expected correct answers = 12.5 and variance = 50×0.25×0.75 = 9.375.
The standard deviation ≈ 3.06.
An ISC trap: they may ask “find the most probable number of successes”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., μ = n/p) reveals the misconception that mean scales inversely with probability, confusing the geometric distribution’s mean with the binomial’s.
remember: State the formula for the mean of a binomial distribution B(n, p) and explain what each symbol represents.
A binomial distribution has mean 12 and variance 3. Find n and p. Show all steps.
Evaluate the claim: “For a binomial distribution, the variance is always less than or equal to the mean.” Provide a mathematical justification.

cards.title: This node synthesizes the four core sub‑topics of Chapter 13…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: This node synthesizes the four core sub‑topics of Chapter 13: conditional probability P(A|B)=(P(A∩ B))/(P(B)), Bayes’ theorem P(B_i|A)=(P(A|B_i)P(B_i))/(Σ_j P(A|B_j)P(B_j)), discrete random variables with probability mass functions P(X=x_i), and their mean μ=E(X)=Σ x_iP(X=x_i) and variance σ^2=Var(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2. It shows how these concepts interlock: total probability feeds Bayes; a random variable’s distribution is built from conditional probabilities; mean and variance summarise that distribution. The node focuses on recognising ISC question patterns — multi‑stage experiments, “find the distribution then compute mean/variance”, “reverse conditional using Bayes” — and on selecting the right formula chain without re‑deriving basics.
steps: The one thing to remember: every ISC probability question is a chain — start by drawing the experiment’s stages, then pick the formula that links the known to the unknown.
Here is why: ISC papers rarely ask a single‑step recall; they combine a two‑stage experiment (e.g., machine → defect) with a “find the distribution of X” follow‑up.
First, sketch a tree diagram (describe in words: first branch = machine choice with probabilities 0.6/0.4; second branch = defect/no‑defect with conditional probabilities 0.02/0.98 and 0.05/0.95).
This visual maps directly to total probability P(D)=P(D|M_1)P(M_1)+P(D|M_2)P(M_2).
Second, if the question asks “given defective, which machine?”, flip the tree using Bayes: P(M_1|D)=(P(D|M_1)P(M_1))/(P(D)).

Third, when a random variable X is defined (e.g., number of defectives in two draws), list all outcomes (0,1,2) and compute their probabilities using the tree — this is the PMF. Fourth, apply the mean/variance formulas…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., P(A|B)=P(A)P(B)) reveals the misconception that conditioning is multiplication — confusing independence with the general definition.
remember: State the formula for conditional probability P(A|B).
If P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, P(A∩ B)=0.2, find P(A|B) and explain whether A and B are independent.
A student claims that Bayes’ theorem can only be applied when events are mutually exclusive. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter that exists in two types…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter that exists in two types, positive and negative, measured in coulombs (C). Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force F between two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by a distance r in vacuum is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. In vector form, F₁₂ = (1/4πϵ₀) (q₁ q₂ / r²) r̂₁₂, where r̂₁₂ is the unit vector from q₁ to q₂, ϵ₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻² is the permittivity of free space, and the constant k = 1/(4πϵ₀) ≈ 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². The force is attractive for opposite signs and repulsive for like signs, acting along the line joining the charges. The principle of superposition applies: the net force on a charge due to several other charges is the vector sum of the individual Coulomb forces. This law underpins the concepts of electric field (force per unit test charge), field lines (visualising field direction and strength), electric dipole (pair of equal and opposite charges), Gauss's theorem (relating flux through a closed surface to enclosed charge), electrostatic potential (work per unit charge), and the behaviour of conductors, insulators, dielectrics, and capacitors introduced in later nodes.
steps: Coulomb's law quantifies the electrostatic force between two point charges as directly proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation, acting along the line…
Here is why: the force depends only on the magnitudes of the charges and their distance, not on any medium (in vacuum).
The inverse‑square nature means doubling the distance reduces the force to one‑quarter, a pattern also seen in gravity and light intensity.
The vector form adds direction: like charges repel, opposite charges attract, so the force vector points away from or toward the other charge along the line connecting them.
Superposition allows us to treat each pair independently and then add the force vectors, which is essential for any multi‑charge problem.
Consider two small spheres, one charged +3 µC and the other –2 µC, placed 0.15 m apart on a smooth table.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing F = k q₁ q₂ / r without the square or omitting the unit vector) reveals the misconception that the force varies linearly with distance or that direction is irrelevant — confusing scalar magnitude with vector nature.
remember: State the mathematical expression for Coulomb's law in vector form and name each symbol with its SI unit.
Two identical point charges q are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. A third charge –q is placed at the remaining….
Evaluate the statement: “Coulomb's law holds for all charge distributions, including extended bodies, without any modification.”.

cards.title: Electric field lines are a pictorial representation of the electric field…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electric field lines are a pictorial representation of the electric field vector E in space. They are drawn such that the tangent to a line at any point gives the direction of E at that point. The number of lines crossing a unit area perpendicular to the lines is proportional to the magnitude of E (field line density ∝ |E|). By convention, lines originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges; for an isolated positive charge they extend to infinity, and for an isolated negative charge they come from infinity. The total number of lines leaving or entering a charge is proportional to the magnitude of that charge (N ∝ |q|). Field lines never intersect, because that would imply two directions for E at the same point. In a uniform field the lines are parallel and equally spaced. For an electric dipole the lines leave the positive charge and enter the negative charge, forming a characteristic pattern. Field lines are a conceptual tool; they have no physical existence and carry no SI unit. They provide a qualitative and semi‑quantitative link to Coulomb’s law (node) and Gauss’s theorem (node), where the flux through a surface equals the number of lines crossing it.
steps: The takeaway: electric field lines are a visual language that translates the invisible vector field E into intuitive curves whose density and direction encode the field’s magnitude and direction.
Here is why: first, the tangent rule makes the direction of force on a positive test charge immediately readable from the diagram.
Second, the density rule turns a qualitative picture into a semi‑quantitative one — where lines crowd, the field is strong; where they spread, it is weak.

Third, the source/sink rule (lines start on +q, end on –q) reflects the fact that electric flux originates and terminates on charges, foreshadowing Gauss’s law. Fourth, the non‑intersection rule follows from the…
Fifth, the proportionality between total lines and charge magnitude gives a simple scaling tool for comparing different charge configurations.
Consider a single +5 µC charge.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “field lines show the path a charge will follow”) reveals the misconception that field lines are trajectories — they indicate instantaneous direction only, not the actual path which depends on initial velocity.
remember: State two fundamental properties of electric field lines.
Why can electric field lines never intersect each other.
A student draws field lines for a positive point charge that are closer together near the charge and farther apart away from it. Evaluate whether this correctly represents the….

cards.title: An electric dipole consists of two point charges +q and –q separated by a small…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: An electric dipole consists of two point charges +q and –q separated by a small distance d. The dipole moment p is a vector defined as p = q d, directed from –q to +q; its SI unit is coulomb‑metre (C·m). In a uniform electric field E, the dipole experiences a torque τ = p × E (N·m) that tends to align p with E. The potential energy of the dipole in the field is U = –p·E (joule), minimum when p is parallel to E. The electric field of a dipole at a point on its axial line (distance r ≫ d) is E_axial = (1/4πϵ₀)(2p/r³) directed along p; on the equatorial line it is E_eq = (1/4πϵ₀)(p/r³) directed opposite to p. In a non‑uniform field the dipole also feels a net force F = (p·∇)E. These relations connect to polarization in dielectrics (later node) where molecular dipoles align with an external field, and to Gauss’s theorem applications for continuous charge distributions.
steps: An electric dipole is completely described by its dipole moment vector p = qd, and all its interactions with electric fields follow from this single vector.
Here is why: first, the dipole moment captures both the magnitude of charge separation and its direction, so torque τ = p × E and energy U = –p·E become simple vector operations.
Second, the far‑field of a dipole falls as 1/r³, with a factor of 2 on the axial line and 1 on the equatorial line, a result that appears repeatedly in ISC numerical problems.
Third, in a non‑uniform field the dipole experiences a net force F = (p·∇)E, which explains phenomena like dielectrophoresis.
Fourth, the sign convention for potential energy (minimum at θ = 0) is a common exam trap; students often write U = +pE cosθ and lose marks.
Fifth, the vector nature of p means that reversing the charge order flips the direction of p, changing the sign of torque and energy.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “unit is newton‑metre” or “vector points from +q to –q”) reveals the misconception that dipole moment is a torque or that its direction follows the field rather than the charge geometry.
remember: State the SI unit of electric dipole moment and write its vector definition.
A dipole of moment 4 × 10⁻⁸ C·m is placed in a uniform electric field of 5 × 10⁴ N/C at an angle of 60°. Calculate the torque acting on the dipole.
Evaluate the statement: “The potential energy of a dipole in a uniform electric field is zero when the dipole is perpendicular to the field.”.

cards.title: Gauss’s theorem (Gauss’s law) states that the electric flux through any closed…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Gauss’s theorem (Gauss’s law) states that the electric flux through any closed surface S is proportional to the total charge Qₑₙc enclosed by that surface: _S E· dA = Q_enc _0 where E is the electric field vector, dA is the outward‑pointing area element, and ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻² is the permittivity of free space. The theorem follows from Coulomb’s inverse‑square law and the superposition principle. It is most powerful when the charge distribution possesses high symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, or planar). By choosing a Gaussian surface that matches the symmetry, E becomes constant in magnitude over the surface and either parallel or perpendicular to dA, turning the surface integral into a simple algebraic equation. Applications include: Infinite line charge (λ C m⁻¹) → cylindrical Gaussian surface → E = λ2π _0r. Infinite plane sheet (σ C m⁻²) → pillbox Gaussian surface → E = σ2 _0 (independent of distance). Uniformly charged thin spherical shell → spherical Gaussian surface → outside: E = Q4π _0r^2; inside: E = 0. Uniform solid sphere → inside field grows linearly with r: E = Q r4π _0R^3. The theorem also underpins the concept of electric flux density D = ε₀E and leads directly to the differential form = ρ/ _0, which is a cornerstone of Maxwell’s equations (treated in higher studies).
steps: Gauss’s theorem lets you find electric fields of highly symmetric charge distributions by relating the total flux through a closed surface to the enclosed charge.
Here is why: the inverse‑square nature of Coulomb’s force makes the number of field lines crossing a closed surface depend only on how many charges are inside, not on their exact positions.

Consider a point charge q at the centre of a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r. The field magnitude is E = q/(4π _0r^2) everywhere on the sphere, and it points radially outward, parallel to dA. The flux integral…
Now extend this reasoning to three standard symmetries. 1.
Infinite line charge with linear density λ.
Choose a coaxial cylinder of radius r and length L. By symmetry, E is radial and constant on the curved surface; the flat ends contribute zero flux because E is parallel to them.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing ε₀ in F m⁻¹ without the C² N⁻¹ m⁻² equivalence) reveals confusion between permittivity and capacitance units.
remember: State the integral form of Gauss’s theorem and name each symbol with its SI unit.
Why does the electric field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell equal zero? Explain using Gauss’s law.
A student claims that for an infinite plane sheet of charge the electric field decreases with distance because the field lines spread out. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Electrostatic potential at a point is the work done per unit positive test…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electrostatic potential at a point is the work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to that point without acceleration. It is a scalar quantity denoted by V with SI unit volt (V), where 1\ V=1\ J/C. For a point charge Q, the potential at distance r is V = (1)/(4π _0)(Q)/(r). The potential due to a system of charges is the algebraic sum of individual potentials (superposition). Electrostatic potential energy U of a system of two charges q_1 and q_2 separated by r is the work required to assemble them: U = (1)/(4π _0)(q_1 q_2)/(r). For a test charge q placed in an external potential V, its potential energy is U = qV. The electric field E is the negative gradient of the potential: E = - V, and the potential difference between points A and B is V_B - V_A = - _A^B E· dl. Equipotential surfaces are loci of constant potential; no work is done moving a charge along them. These relations connect the field concept (from Gauss’s theorem) to energy methods used in conductors, dielectrics, and capacitors.
steps: The electrostatic potential at a point is the work per unit charge needed to bring a test charge from infinity to that point; it is a scalar field that completely determines the electric field through E = - V. Here is…
(2) The potential difference between two points equals the negative line integral of the field, making work calculations path‑independent for electrostatic fields.
(3) Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines, providing a visual tool for field geometry.
(4) Potential energy of a charge assembly follows directly from pairwise potentials, enabling energy‑based solutions for equilibrium and stability.
(5) Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium the field is zero, so the potential is constant — a key result used in the next node on conductors.
Consider a point charge Q = 5\ at the origin.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “potential is the force per unit charge”) reveals the misconception that potential and electric field are the same quantity, confusing a scalar energy‑per‑charge with a vector force‑per‑charge.
remember: Define electrostatic potential at a point due to a point charge and give its SI unit.
Why is electrostatic potential a scalar while electric field is a vector.
A student claims: “The potential energy of a system of two like charges is always positive.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: A conductor is a material that contains a large number of mobile charge…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A conductor is a material that contains a large number of mobile charge carriers (free electrons in metals, ions in electrolytes) which can move under the influence of an electric field. In electrostatic equilibrium the following properties hold simultaneously: 1. Electric field inside the bulk is zero ( E=0 ). Any internal field would exert a force on free charges, causing them to move until the field cancels. 2. All excess charge resides on the outer surface. Gauss’s law applied to a Gaussian surface just inside the conductor gives E· dA=Q_enc/ _0; with E=0 the enclosed charge must be zero, so any net charge must be on the surface. 3. The conductor is an equipotential volume. Since E=- V and E=0 inside, the potential V is constant throughout the conductor and on its surface. 4. Surface electric field is normal to the surface with magnitude E = σ/ _0, where σ is the local surface charge density. The tangential component would otherwise drive surface currents, contradicting equilibrium. 5. Charge distributes itself to make the surface an equipotential; on a sphere the distribution is uniform, on irregular shapes it concentrates at regions of high curvature (sharp points). These statements are direct consequences of Coulomb’s law, Gauss’s theorem, and the definition of electrostatic potential covered in earlier nodes. Conductors contrast with insulators (node) where charges are bound, and with dielectrics (node) where bound charges polarise but do not move freely.
steps: In electrostatic equilibrium a conductor has zero internal electric field, all excess charge on its outer surface, and a constant potential throughout its volume.
Here is why: 1.
Free charges respond instantly to any internal field.
If a field existed inside, the mobile electrons would experience a force F=qE and drift, constituting a current.
Electrostatic equilibrium by definition means no net current, so the field must vanish. 2.
Gauss’s law forces excess charge to the surface.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the charge density is uniform inside”) reveals the misconception that excess charge distributes through the bulk rather than residing on the surface.
remember: State the condition for electrostatic equilibrium inside a conductor and name the physical quantity that becomes uniform throughout its volume.
A solid conducting sphere of radius R carries a total charge Q. Using Gauss’s law, derive the expression for the electric field just outside the surface and explain why the field….
Evaluate the statement: “A hollow conducting shell with a point charge +q placed at its centre produces zero electric field in the cavity.”.

cards.title: An insulator is a material that offers extremely high opposition to the flow of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: An insulator is a material that offers extremely high opposition to the flow of electric charge, characterised by a resistivity typically greater than 10⁸ Ω·m and a wide forbidden energy band gap (usually >5 eV). In the band‑theory picture, the valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is empty at ordinary temperatures, so there are virtually no free electrons or holes to carry current. Unlike conductors, where charge carriers move freely, insulators support electrostatic fields without allowing a sustained current; the electric field inside a homogeneous insulator in static equilibrium is the same as the applied field because no free charges redistribute to cancel it. However, when an external electric field is applied, the bound electrons in the atoms or molecules shift slightly, creating induced dipoles — a phenomenon called dielectric polarisation. The polarisation vector P describes the dipole moment per unit volume, and the electric displacement D = ε₀E + P relates the macroscopic field to the free‑charge sources. All insulators are dielectrics, but not all dielectrics are perfect insulators; some (e.g., distilled water) exhibit a small but measurable conductivity. In electrostatics, insulators are essential for confining fields, forming capacitor dielectrics, and providing mechanical support for live conductors (e.g., porcelain discs on overhead lines). The key distinction from conductors is the absence of mobile charge carriers, while the link to dielectrics is the ability to become polarised.
steps: Insulators are materials that block the flow of electric charge because they lack mobile charge carriers, yet they can still be polarised by an external field.

Here is why: first, the band structure of an insulator shows a large energy gap between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band; thermal energy at room temperature (≈0.025 eV) is far too small to promote…

Second, because there are no free carriers, an applied static electric field cannot cause a drift current; the field penetrates the material unchanged, unlike in a conductor where free electrons rearrange to make the…
Third, the bound electrons in each atom or molecule are displaced slightly relative to their nuclei, creating microscopic dipoles that align with the field — this is dielectric polarisation.

Fourth, the macroscopic effect of these aligned dipoles is described by the polarisation vector P, which adds to ε₀E to give the electric displacement D; this relation is crucial when the insulator fills a capacitor…

Fifth, in practical Indian contexts, porcelain discs on 11 kV distribution lines and PVC sheathing on household wiring are everyday examples of insulators that both support conductors mechanically and prevent leakage…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “resistivity around 10⁴ Ω·m and band gap ≈1 eV”) reveals the misconception that insulators are merely poor conductors like semiconductors, confusing the orders of magnitude that separate the two classes.
remember: State the typical resistivity range of an insulator and the approximate band‑gap magnitude that explains this behaviour.
Explain why a plastic ruler rubbed with wool attracts small paper bits but does not allow a steady current to flow when connected across a battery.
A student claims that all dielectrics are perfect insulators. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A dielectric is an insulating material that becomes polarized when placed in an…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A dielectric is an insulating material that becomes polarized when placed in an electric field. Polarization P (C m⁻²) is the dipole moment per unit volume induced in the material. For linear, isotropic dielectrics P = ε₀ χₑ E, where χₑ (dimensionless) is the electric susceptibility and E (V m⁻¹) the macroscopic field. The electric displacement D = ε₀ E + P = ε E defines the permittivity ε = ε₀ εᵣ with relative permittivity εᵣ = 1 + χₑ. Bound charges appear: surface density σ_b = P·n̂ and volume density ρ_b = –∇·P. In a parallel‑plate capacitor, inserting a dielectric of thickness equal to plate separation multiplies capacitance by εᵣ (C = εᵣ C₀). The energy density in a dielectric is u = ½ D·E = ½ ε E². These relations connect microscopic dipole alignment to macroscopic circuit behaviour.
steps: The key takeaway: A dielectric reduces the effective electric field inside it by developing bound charges that oppose the applied field, and this reduction is quantified by the relative permittivity εᵣ.
Here is why: 1.
Molecular response – In an external field, bound charges in atoms or molecules shift, creating induced dipoles.
The collective dipole moment per unit volume is P. 2.
Bound charges – Non‑uniform P produces volume bound charge ρ_b = –∇·P; a discontinuity of P at surfaces yields σ_b = P·n̂.
These bound charges generate an opposing field. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “P is the total dipole moment of the sample”) reveals the misconception that polarization is an extensive quantity rather than an intensive density.
remember: Define electric polarization P and state its SI unit.
Explain why the electric field inside a uniformly polarized infinite slab is reduced compared with the applied field.
A student claims that the relative permittivity εᵣ of a dielectric can be less than 1. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A capacitor is a two‑terminal passive device that stores electrostatic energy…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A capacitor is a two‑terminal passive device that stores electrostatic energy by accumulating equal and opposite charges on two conductors separated by a dielectric. The capacitance C quantifies the charge Q stored per unit potential difference V between the conductors: C = Q/V. The SI unit is the farad (F), where 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹. For a parallel‑plate capacitor with plate area A and separation d in vacuum, C_0 = _0 A/d; inserting a dielectric of relative permittivity raises the capacitance to C = C_0. The energy stored is U = 12 C V^2 = 12 QV = Q^2/(2C). Capacitors in series share the same charge, while in parallel they share the same voltage; the equivalent capacitance follows 1/C_eq = Σ 1/C_i (series) and C_eq = Σ C_i (parallel). This node covers the definition, the parallel‑plate formula, the effect of dielectrics, energy storage, and the basic series/parallel rules; detailed network analysis and transient RC behaviour belong to later nodes.
steps: The capacitance of a capacitor is the ratio of the magnitude of charge on either conductor to the potential difference between them, and it depends only on geometry and the dielectric material.
Here is why: the electric field between two large parallel plates is uniform, E = σ/ where σ = Q/A and = _0.
The potential difference is V = Ed = Qd/( _0 A).
Rearranging gives C = Q/V = _0 A/d.
This derivation shows that capacitance grows with plate area and dielectric constant, and shrinks with plate separation.
Consider a parallel‑plate capacitor of area 2.0×10^-2\,m^2 and separation 1.0\,mm filled with mica ( = 5.4).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “farad = coulomb × volt”) reveals the misconception that capacitance multiplies charge and voltage instead of dividing them, confusing the definition C = Q/V with the energy formula U = 12 QV.
remember: State the SI unit of capacitance and write its definition in terms of base SI units.
A parallel‑plate capacitor has plate area A and separation d. If the plate area is doubled and the separation is halved while the dielectric remains air, by what factor does the….
A 10 µF capacitor is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the….

cards.title: A capacitor stores charge Q at a potential difference V…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A capacitor stores charge Q at a potential difference V; its capacitance is C = Q/V (SI unit farad, F). When several capacitors are combined, the equivalent capacitance C_eq depends on the connection. Series combination: The same charge Q resides on each capacitor because the inner plates are isolated. The total voltage is the sum of individual voltages V = Σ V_i. Using V_i = Q/C_i gives 1C_eq = Σ (1)/(C_i). The equivalent capacitance is always smaller than the smallest individual capacitor. Parallel combination: All capacitors share the same voltage V because their plates are directly connected. The total charge is the sum Q = Σ Q_i = Σ C_i V. Hence C_eq = Σ C_i. The equivalent capacitance is larger than any single capacitor. These rules follow directly from charge conservation and the definition of capacitance. They are used to simplify complex networks into a single equivalent capacitor for analysis of energy storage (U = 12 C_eq V^2) and transient response in RC circuits.
steps: The equivalent capacitance of a network is found by repeatedly replacing series or parallel groups with a single capacitor until one remains.

Here is why: In series the same charge flows through each capacitor, so the voltages add; in parallel the voltage is common, so the charges add. Consider three capacitors C_1 = 2\,, C_2 = 3\,, C_3 = 6\,.
First, C_2 and C_3 are in parallel: C_23=C_2+C_3 = 9\,.
This parallel block is then in series with C_1: 1C_eq = (1)/(2) + (1)/(9) = (11)/(18) → C_eq = (18)/(11)\, ≈ 1.64\,.
The equivalent is smaller than the smallest (2 µF) because series dominates.
If a 12 V battery is connected across the whole network, the total charge Q = C_eqV ≈ 19.6\,.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., C_eq = C_1+C_2+C_3) reveals the misconception that series addition works like parallel addition, confusing charge‑sharing with voltage‑sharing.
remember: State the formula for the equivalent capacitance of three capacitors C_1, C_2, C_3 connected in series.
Two identical capacitors of 4\, each are connected in parallel across a 10 V battery. What is the total charge drawn from the battery.
A student claims that in a series combination the voltage across each capacitor is the same. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Electric current (I) is the rate of flow of electric charge across a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electric current (I) is the rate of flow of electric charge across a cross‑section of a conductor. Quantitatively, I = (Q)/(t) for a constant flow, or I = (dQ)/(dt) for a time‑varying flow, where Q is the net charge passing the section in time t. The SI unit is the ampere (A), defined as one coulomb of charge passing per second (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). By convention, the direction of current is taken as the direction of flow of positive charge, opposite to the actual drift of electrons in metallic conductors. Current is a scalar quantity (it has magnitude and a sign indicating direction relative to a chosen reference) but obeys the principle of superposition in circuits. It is the fundamental quantity that links charge motion to observable effects such as heating (Joule’s law), magnetic fields (Ampère’s law), and chemical changes (electrolysis). In a circuit, a steady current requires a closed conducting path and a source of electromotive force (cell or battery) that maintains a potential difference. The relationship between current, drift velocity (v_d), number density of charge carriers (n), cross‑sectional area (A), and charge per carrier (e) is I = n A e v_d, which will be developed in the drift‑velocity node.
steps: Electric current is the rate at which charge crosses a chosen surface in a conductor.

Here is why: a steady current exists only when a continuous push (emf) maintains a net drift of charge carriers around a closed loop, and the magnitude of that drift per unit time is what we measure as amperes.
First, recall from Class 11 that charge is quantised and conserved; a current of 1 A means 1 C of charge passes each second, equivalent to roughly 6.24 × 10^18 electrons.

Second, the conventional direction — from positive to negative terminal outside the source — was fixed before the discovery of the electron; inside a metal the actual carriers are electrons moving opposite to this…
Third, a current can be constant (DC) or vary with time (AC); the instantaneous current is the derivative dQ/dt, which reduces to Q/t when the flow is uniform.
Fourth, without a closed conducting path the charge would accumulate, creating an opposing field that stops the flow — this is why a broken wire or an open switch yields zero current.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “volt” or “coulomb”) reveals the misconception that current is the same as potential difference or total charge, confusing the rate of flow with the quantity itself.
remember: State the SI unit of electric current and write the defining equation for average current.
A student says, “In a metal wire the current flows from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of the battery.” Evaluate this statement.
If a steady current of 2.5 A flows through a conductor for 4 minutes, calculate the total charge that passes a cross‑section.

cards.title: Drift velocity (v_d) is the average net velocity attained by charge carriers…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Drift velocity (v_d) is the average net velocity attained by charge carriers (usually electrons) in a conductor when an electric field is applied. It is directed opposite to the field for electrons and along the field for holes. The macroscopic electric current I is related to drift velocity by I = n A e v_d, where n is the number density of charge carriers (m⁻³), A is the cross‑sectional area of the conductor (m²), and e is the elementary charge (1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C). Equivalently, current density J = I/A = n e v_d. Typical drift velocities in household wiring are of order 10⁻⁴ m/s, many orders of magnitude smaller than the thermal speed of electrons (~10⁵ m/s). Despite this slowness, the electric field propagates at near the speed of light, establishing current almost instantly throughout the circuit. Drift velocity depends linearly on current and inversely on carrier density and cross‑section; it is independent of the conductor’s length. This concept bridges the microscopic motion of carriers to the macroscopic quantities used in Ohm’s law, resistance, and resistivity.
steps: The takeaway: drift velocity is the tiny average speed of charge carriers that produces the macroscopic current we measure.

Here is why: first, current is defined as charge passing a point per unit time; if each carrier carries charge e and there are n carriers per unit volume moving with average speed v_d through area A, the charge crossing…

Second, this relation shows that for a fixed current, a thicker wire (larger A) or a material with more free electrons (larger n) reduces v_d — which is why copper wires have drift velocities around 10⁻⁴ m/s.
Third, the direction of v_d for electrons is opposite to the conventional current because electrons are negatively charged; for holes in a semiconductor it aligns with conventional current.

Fourth, although each electron drifts slowly, the electric field that drives them propagates at nearly the speed of light, so a switch turns on a lamp across the room almost instantly — an analogy is a long pipe filled…
Fifth, typical exam traps: confusing drift velocity with thermal speed, or forgetting to convert cross‑section from mm² to m².
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., I = n e v_d) reveals the misconception that cross‑sectional area does not affect current — confusing current density with current.
remember: State the formula linking current I, carrier density n, cross‑sectional area A, electron charge e, and drift velocity v_d.
If the cross‑sectional area of a copper wire is doubled while the current remains the same, what happens to the drift velocity? Explain.
A student claims that drift velocity of electrons in a typical household wire is about 10⁶ m/s. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Ohm's law states that for a conductor at constant temperature…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Ohm's law states that for a conductor at constant temperature, the steady current I flowing through it is directly proportional to the potential difference V applied across its ends. The constant of proportionality is the resistance R of the conductor, giving the mathematical form V = IR. Here V is measured in volts (V), I in amperes (A), and R in ohms (Ω). The law holds for ohmic conductors — materials whose V–I graph is a straight line through the origin. Resistance arises from collisions between drifting charge carriers and the lattice; it depends on the material's resistivity ρ, length l, and cross‑sectional area A via R = ρ l/A. Temperature changes alter ρ, so Ohm's law is strictly valid only when temperature is constant. Non‑ohmic devices (e.g., filament lamps, diodes) show a curved V–I characteristic because their resistance varies with voltage or current. The law provides the foundation for analysing simple circuits, calculating power P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R, and designing electrical appliances.
steps: Ohm's law states that for a conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, with resistance as the constant of proportionality.
Here is why: first, the linear relationship means a graph of V versus I is a straight line through the origin; the slope gives the resistance.
Second, resistance quantifies how much a material opposes current — it depends on the material's resistivity, length, and cross‑sectional area.
Third, the law holds only when temperature is constant because heating changes resistivity.

Fourth, many practical components like nichrome wire in heaters obey Ohm's law, while devices like incandescent bulbs do not. Fifth, knowing V=IR lets us design circuits: for a 240 V mains supply, a 60 W bulb draws I =…
Consider a simple lab setup: a battery, a rheostat, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter across a nichrome wire.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "V = I/R with R in volts") reveals the misconception that resistance is a voltage-like quantity rather than a ratio of voltage to current.
remember: State the mathematical form of Ohm's law and name the SI units of each quantity.
A student plots a V–I graph for a conductor and obtains a straight line passing through the origin with a slope of 12….
Evaluate the claim: "Ohm's law is a fundamental law of nature like Newton's laws of motion.".

cards.title: Resistance (symbol R, SI unit ohm…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Resistance (symbol R, SI unit ohm, Ω) quantifies how much a conductor opposes the flow of electric current. By Ohm’s law, for a conductor at constant temperature, the potential difference V across its ends is directly proportional to the steady current I through it: V = I R. Hence R = V/I. Resistance depends on the material’s intrinsic property resistivity (ρ), the conductor’s length L, and its cross‑sectional area A through R = ρ L/A (covered in the next node). It also varies with temperature; for most metals R increases linearly with temperature rise. In a circuit, resistors are components designed to provide a known, stable resistance to control current, divide voltage, or dissipate power (P = I²R = V²/R). The concept links directly to electric current (node 001), drift velocity (node 002), and Ohm’s law (node 003), and it sets the stage for resistivity (node 005) and temperature dependence (node 006).
steps: Resistance is the property that converts electrical energy into heat when current flows; the one thing to remember is R = V/I for any ohmic conductor at constant temperature.
Here is why: when a potential difference V pushes charge through a wire, the charge carriers (electrons) collide with the lattice ions, losing kinetic energy as heat.
The more collisions per unit length, the larger the opposition — that is resistance.
Consider a copper wire of length L and cross‑section A. Doubling L doubles the number of collisions, so R doubles.
Halving A forces the same current through a smaller “pipe”, again doubling R. Different materials have different intrinsic collision frequencies, captured by resistivity ρ (next node).

An ohmic conductor (e.g., a metal wire at steady temperature) gives a straight‑line V‑I graph through the origin; a filament lamp curves upward because its temperature rises, increasing R — a classic exam trap.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “unit is volt per ampere” without naming ohm) reveals the misconception that derived units need not have special names — students must recognise that V/A is named ohm.
remember: State the SI unit of resistance and write the defining equation linking resistance, voltage, and current.
A student measures a current of 0.25 A through a resistor when 12 V is applied. She claims the resistance is 48 Ω. Evaluate her claim.
Two identical copper wires are connected in series. Wire A is at 20 °C, wire B at 100 °C. Compare their resistances and explain the physical reason.

cards.title: Resistivity (symbol ρ, pronounced “rho”) is an intrinsic property of a material…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Resistivity (symbol ρ, pronounced “rho”) is an intrinsic property of a material that quantifies its opposition to the flow of electric current, independent of the object's shape or size. It is defined as the resistance R of a uniform conductor of unit length (1 m) and unit cross‑sectional area (1 m²): ρ = (R\,A)/(L) where R is the measured resistance (ohm, Ω), A is the cross‑sectional area (square metre, m²), and L is the length (metre, m). The SI unit of resistivity is ohm‑metre (Ω·m). Its reciprocal, conductivity σ = 1/ρ, measures how easily charge moves. Resistivity depends on the material’s atomic structure, electron density, and temperature; for most metals it rises linearly with temperature, while for semiconductors it falls. Unlike resistance, which varies with dimensions, resistivity is a material constant used to compare substances (e.g., copper ≈ 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, nichrome ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m). Understanding resistivity links the microscopic picture of drift velocity and electron scattering to the macroscopic law V = IR, and it precedes the study of temperature dependence of resistivity and the design of circuits using specific materials.
steps: Takeaway: Resistivity is an intrinsic material property that tells how strongly a substance opposes electric current, independent of the piece’s length or thickness.
Here is why: 1.
Geometric independence: Resistance changes if you stretch or thin a wire, but resistivity stays the same because it factors out length and area (ρ = RA/L). 2.
Material sensitivity: Different substances have vastly different ρ values—copper’s low ρ makes it ideal for wiring, while nichrome’s high ρ suits heating elements. 3.
Temperature link: For metals, increased lattice vibrations at higher T scatter electrons more, raising ρ; this predictable trend lets us design temperature sensors (e.g., platinum RTDs). 4.
Conductivity inverse: High conductivity (good conductors) means low ρ; this relationship simplifies circuit analysis when we need conductance (G = σA/L). 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “resistivity is the resistance of a wire and its unit is ohm”) reveals the misconception that resistivity depends on the object's dimensions, ignoring the normalization by length and area that makes it an intrinsic property.
remember: State the definition of resistivity and give its SI unit.
Explain how resistivity differs from resistance, using the formula that relates them.
A student claims that “increasing the temperature of a metallic conductor always decreases its resistivity.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Temperature dependence of resistance (or resistivity) quantifies how the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Temperature dependence of resistance (or resistivity) quantifies how the opposition to electric current varies with temperature. For most metallic conductors the resistivity ρ increases linearly with temperature over a wide range and is expressed as ρ = ρ_0 [1 + α (T - T_0) ] where ρ₀ is the resistivity at a reference temperature T₀ (usually 0 °C or 20 °C), α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (unit °C⁻¹), and T is the absolute temperature in °C. Since resistance R of a uniform conductor is R = ρ (l)/(A) (l = length, A = cross‑sectional area), the same linear relation holds for resistance: R = R_0 [1 + α (T - T_0) ] For alloys such as nichrome α is small (≈ 0.0001 °C⁻¹), making them suitable for standard resistors. For semiconductors and insulators the dependence is exponential (ρ ∝ e^E_g/2kT) and α is negative; heating creates more charge carriers, so resistance drops sharply. The sign and magnitude of α therefore distinguish conductors, alloys, and semiconductors. The concept links directly to the microscopic picture: in metals lattice vibrations (phonons) scatter electrons more at higher T, while in semiconductors thermal excitation across the band gap dominates.
steps: The resistance of a metallic conductor rises linearly with temperature because increased lattice vibrations scatter conduction electrons more frequently.
Here is why: when a metal is heated, its atoms vibrate with larger amplitude about their equilibrium positions.
These vibrations act as scattering centres for the drifting electrons, reducing the mean free path and therefore increasing resistivity.
The linear approximation R = R_0[1 + α (T - T_0)] works well from about –50 °C to 300 °C for pure metals.
Consider a copper wire of length 2 m and cross‑section 1 mm² at 20 °C (R₀ = 0.034 Ω).
Copper’s α ≈ 0.00393 °C⁻¹.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “α has unit Ω °C⁻¹”) reveals the misconception that α is a resistance change per degree rather than a fractional change per degree.
remember: State the SI unit of the temperature coefficient of resistance α and give its typical sign for a pure metal.
A copper wire has resistance 10 Ω at 20 °C. If α = 0.0039 °C⁻¹, what is its resistance at 80 °C? Show the calculation.
Explain why the temperature coefficient of resistance for an intrinsic semiconductor is negative, whereas for a metal it is positive.

cards.title: Electromotive force (EMF) of a cell is the work done by the cell in moving a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electromotive force (EMF) of a cell is the work done by the cell in moving a unit positive charge around a complete circuit that includes the cell itself. It is the potential difference across the terminals of the cell when no current is drawn (open‑circuit condition). EMF is not a mechanical force; it represents energy supplied per unit charge and is measured in volts (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹. For a cell of EMF ε, if a charge Q passes through it, the chemical work done is W = εQ. The EMF depends on the nature of the electrodes, the electrolyte, and temperature, but it is independent of the external circuit resistance. In a closed circuit the terminal voltage V is less than ε because of the internal resistance r (V = ε – Ir), a relation that will be developed in the next node. EMF is the source of energy that drives current; it is the “pressure” that establishes an electric field in the wires. Understanding EMF is essential before analysing circuits with Kirchhoff’s rules or measuring unknown EMFs with a potentiometer.
steps: The EMF of a cell is the energy supplied per unit charge when the cell operates without delivering current.
Here is why: EMF is an intrinsic property of the electrochemical cell, determined solely by its chemistry and temperature, and it represents the maximum potential difference the cell can provide.
First, consider a simple Daniell cell: zinc and copper electrodes in their respective sulphate solutions.
The spontaneous redox reaction does chemical work on charges, raising their potential energy.
If we connect a voltmeter of very high resistance across the terminals, the reading equals the EMF because negligible current flows.
Second, the work‑energy definition ε = W/Q follows directly: moving 1 C of charge through the cell requires the cell to expend ε joules of chemical energy.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “EMF is measured in amperes because it drives current”) reveals the misconception that EMF is a current rather than an energy‑per‑charge quantity.
remember: What is the SI unit of EMF and how is it defined in terms of work and charge.
A student measures the voltage across a cell with a high‑resistance voltmeter and obtains 1.5 V. When the same cell is connected to a 2 Ω resistor, the voltmeter reads 1.2 V.….
Evaluate the statement: “The EMF of a cell is the force that pushes electrons through a circuit.”.

cards.title: Internal resistance (symbol r, SI unit ohm Ω) is the inherent opposition to…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Internal resistance (symbol r, SI unit ohm Ω) is the inherent opposition to current flow within a source of electromotive force (EMF) such as a cell or battery. It arises from the electrolyte, electrodes, and contact resistances inside the cell. When a current I flows, a potential drop Ir occurs across this internal resistance, so the terminal voltage V across the external circuit is given by V = E – Ir, where E is the EMF (open‑circuit voltage). The internal resistance is in series with the external load resistance R; the total circuit resistance is R + r. Consequently, the current delivered is I = E/(R + r). Internal resistance causes the terminal voltage to decrease as the load current increases, and it limits the maximum current a cell can supply (short‑circuit current I_sc = E/r). It is a key parameter in determining the efficiency and performance of cells, and it varies with temperature, age, and state of charge. The concept links directly to Ohm’s law (node 003), resistance (node 004), and EMF (node 007), and it is essential for applying Kirchhoff’s rules (node 009) and for potentiometric measurements (node 011).
steps: The terminal voltage of a cell is always less than its EMF when current flows because the cell’s own internal resistance drops a voltage Ir. Here is why: a real cell is not an ideal voltage source; it contains…
When the circuit is open, no current flows, so the internal drop Ir is zero and a voltmeter reads the full EMF E. As soon as a load R is connected, current I = E/(R + r) flows.
The same current passes through the internal resistance r, producing a voltage drop Ir inside the cell.

The external terminals therefore see only V = E – Ir. This explains why a fresh battery can light a bulb brightly (small r), while an old battery with large r makes the bulb dim even though its EMF may be unchanged.
Consider a 1.5 V dry cell with r = 0.5 Ω connected to a 2 Ω lamp.

The current is I = 1.5/(2 + 0.5) = 0.6 A. The terminal voltage is V = 1.5 – 0.6×0.5 = 1.2 V. The lamp receives 1.2 V, not 1.5 V. If the lamp is replaced by a 0.1 Ω wire (near short circuit), I = 1.5/(0.1 + 0.5) = 2.5 A…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “volt” or “ampere”) reveals the misconception that internal resistance is a voltage or current rather than an opposition to current flow.
remember: What is the SI unit of internal resistance and its standard symbol.
A cell of EMF 12 V and internal resistance 0.4 Ω is connected to an external resistor of 5.6 Ω. Explain why the terminal voltage across the external resistor is less than 12 V.
Evaluate the statement: “If a cell’s internal resistance is zero, the terminal voltage always equals the EMF regardless of the load.”.

cards.title: Kirchhoff’s rules are two fundamental principles for analysing electric…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kirchhoff’s rules are two fundamental principles for analysing electric circuits. Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL) states that the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a junction is zero: ΣI = 0, reflecting charge conservation. Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL) states that the algebraic sum of potential differences (emf drops across resistors and rises across sources) around any closed loop is zero: ΣV = 0, reflecting energy conservation. Together they provide a systematic method to write independent equations for unknown branch currents and voltages in networks containing resistors, cells, and internal resistances. The rules apply to both DC and AC steady‑state circuits, provided lumped‑element assumptions hold. They extend Ohm’s law (V = IR) and the concepts of emf (ε) and internal resistance (r) covered in earlier nodes, enabling solution of multi‑loop circuits that cannot be reduced by simple series‑parallel combinations.
steps: Kirchhoff’s rules let us solve any resistor network by writing charge‑ and energy‑conservation equations at junctions and loops.
Here is why: the total charge entering a junction must leave it, and the net energy change around a closed path must be zero.
Consider a circuit with two cells ε₁ = 12 V (r₁ = 1 Ω) and ε₂ = 6 V (r₂ = 0.5 Ω) connected to three resistors R₁ = 4 Ω, R₂ = 3 Ω, R₃ = 2 Ω forming two loops sharing a middle branch.
First, label branch currents I₁, I₂, I₃ with assumed directions.
Apply KCL at the central junction: I₁ = I₂ + I₃.
Next, choose two independent loops (left and right).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “I₁ + I₂ + I₃ = 0”) reveals the misconception that all currents are treated with the same sign regardless of direction, ignoring the algebraic nature of the law.
remember: State Kirchhoff’s Current Law in words and give its mathematical expression for a junction with three incoming currents I₁, I₂ and one outgoing current I₃.
A student writes the KVL equation for a loop containing a 10 V battery (internal resistance 0.2 Ω) and a 5 Ω resistor as 10 – I·0.2 – I·5 =….
Evaluate the statement: “In a circuit with two loops sharing a resistor, the current through the shared resistor can be found by applying KVL to each loop independently without….

cards.title: A Wheatstone bridge is a four‑arm resistor network
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A Wheatstone bridge is a four‑arm resistor network (P, Q, R, S) powered by a cell across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other.
