cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “growth is learning new skills”) reveals the misconception that growth and development are synonymous, confusing measurable bodily expansion with functional skill acquisition.
remember: Define growth and state two ways it differs from development.
Explain why the cephalocaudal pattern means an infant’s head grows faster than the legs.
A 10‑year‑old girl’s height is at the 90th percentile while her weight is at the 30th percentile. Evaluate whether this indicates a growth disorder.

cards.title: Maturation refers to the genetically programmed…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Maturation refers to the genetically programmed, sequential unfolding of physical, cognitive, and emotional capacities that occurs relatively independent of specific environmental training. It is driven by hereditary factors — particularly the timed expression of genes — and sets the upper limits and typical sequence of development (e.g., reflexes → voluntary motor control → symbolic thought). Unlike growth (quantitative increase in size) or learning (experience‑dependent change), maturation is qualitative, universal across cultures, and follows a predictable chronological order. It interacts with the environment: adequate nutrition, health, and stimulation are necessary for the genetic programme to express fully, but they cannot accelerate the sequence beyond its biological readiness. In lifespan psychology, maturation provides the scaffold upon which experiences (learning, culture, education) build, and it underpins the stage theories of Piaget, Erikson, and Kohlberg, each of which assumes maturational readiness for the next stage.
steps: Maturation is the biologically scripted timetable that releases new abilities in a fixed order, regardless of how much you practice.

Here is why: first, genes contain regulatory sequences that switch on at specific ages, producing proteins that remodel neural circuits and hormonal axes; second, this genetic clock operates across all humans, so a baby…

Consider a Class 12 student preparing for ISC boards: the ability to reason abstractly about ethics (Kohlberg’s post‑conventional level) depends on prefrontal cortex maturation that typically completes in late…
An exam trap is confusing “maturation” with “learning” — remember, learning is experience‑dependent and variable, while maturation is species‑typical and time‑locked.
When answering, always link the milestone to its genetic‑hormonal trigger (e.g., gonadotropin‑releasing hormone surge for puberty) and note the environmental permissive factors (nutrition, health).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “maturation is just getting bigger”) reveals the misconception that maturation and growth are synonymous, confusing structural enlargement with functional reorganization.
remember: Define maturation and state two ways it differs from growth.
Why can’t intensive coaching make a 7‑year‑old child reach Piaget’s formal‑operational stage.
Evaluate the statement: “Maturation alone determines the age at which puberty begins.”.

cards.title: Heredity‑environment interaction refers to the dynamic…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Heredity‑environment interaction refers to the dynamic, bidirectional process whereby genetic predispositions and environmental contexts continuously shape each other to produce developmental outcomes. It rejects the simple additive model (heredity + environment = trait) in favour of three interlocking mechanisms: (1) Genotype‑Environment Correlation — individuals’ genetic make‑up influences the environments they experience, classified as passive (parents provide both genes and home), evocative (a child’s temperament elicits specific responses), and active (the child selects niches that match genetic inclinations). (2) Genotype‑Environment Interaction (G×E) — the effect of an environmental exposure differs across genotypes; for example, a child with a high‑risk allele for anxiety may develop the disorder only under chronic stress, while a low‑risk peer remains resilient. (3) Epigenetic Modulation — environmental factors such as nutrition, caregiving quality, or toxin exposure can alter gene expression without changing DNA sequence, creating lasting phenotypic changes that may even be transmitted across generations. Together, these mechanisms explain why identical twins raised apart show both similarities and divergences, and why interventions timed to sensitive periods can redirect developmental trajectories. The concept underpins later topics such as Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems, where proximal processes operate within nested environmental layers that constantly interact with the child’s biological substrate.
steps: Heredity and environment do not act independently; they continuously interact to shape development.
Here is why: first, genes provide a range of possible phenotypes — a reaction norm — while the environment determines where within that range the individual falls.
Second, the three genotype‑environment correlations show that children are not passive recipients; their genetic propensities actively sculpt the experiences they encounter.

For instance, a musically inclined child (genetic propensity) may be enrolled in classical Hindustani vocal classes by parents (passive), attract a teacher’s extra attention because of quick learning (evocative), and…

Third, G×E means the same environment can have opposite effects depending on genotype; a supportive school climate may boost academic confidence in a child with a “growth‑mindset” genotype but have little impact on a…

Fourth, epigenetic changes — such as DNA methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene following early maternal deprivation — illustrate how early Indian contexts like joint‑family caregiving or institutional care can…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “genotype‑environment correlation means genes and environment are correlated statistically but not causally”) reveals the misconception that correlation implies only a statistical association, ignoring the causal pathway from genotype to…
remember: Define “genotype‑environment correlation” and name its three subtypes.
A child with a genetic predisposition for high aggression grows up in a highly supportive, non‑violent….
Critically evaluate the statement: “Epigenetic changes prove that environment can rewrite the genetic code.”.

cards.title: Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1979, revised 1994) proposes that human development is the product of dynamic, bidirectional interactions between an individual and a series of environmental systems organised by proximity and influence. The microsystem comprises immediate settings where the person directly participates — home, classroom, peer group. The mesosystem captures interconnections among microsystems, such as parent‑teacher communication or coordination between school and after‑school tuition. The exosystem includes settings that affect the individual indirectly, for example a parent’s shift schedule, municipal housing policy, or a sibling’s board exam stress. The macrosystem embodies the overarching cultural, economic, legal, and ideological context — Indian joint‑family norms, the Right to Education Act, media narratives about success. Finally, the chronosystem adds the temporal dimension: life transitions (puberty, migration), historical events (demonetisation, pandemic), and evolving societal expectations. Development is not linear; each system exerts proximal processes — recurrent, increasingly complex interactions — that drive psychological change. The theory stresses person‑context fit: a child’s temperament, genetic endowment, and agency interact with environmental affordances and constraints. It also introduces the concept of ecological transition — moving from one microsystem to another (e.g., home to school) — which can reorganise developmental trajectories. In the Indian context, the theory helps explain why a child in a rural village with limited school infrastructure but strong community support may show different cognitive‑social outcomes than an urban peer with abundant resources but high parental pressure.
steps: Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory explains development as the outcome of nested, interacting environmental layers that change over time.
Here is why: the theory moves beyond “nature vs. nurture” by showing that every context — from a mother’s lullaby to a national curriculum — simultaneously shapes and is shaped by the growing person.
First, consider the microsystem: Rohan’s daily interactions with his mother, his Class 12 teacher, and his cricket teammates are proximal processes.
These recurrent activities — helping with homework, practicing batting, negotiating curfew — directly build his self‑efficacy and social skills.
Second, the mesosystem links these microsystems.
When Rohan’s mother attends a parent‑teacher meeting and learns he struggles with physics, she arranges a weekend tutor.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing macrosystem before exosystem) reveals the misconception that broader cultural forces act more directly than specific institutional settings, confusing level of immediacy with level of influence.
remember: Name the five ecological systems in Bronfenbrenner’s model in order from the most immediate to the broadest.
Explain how a parent’s workplace policy (e.g., mandatory overtime) can affect a child’s school performance using the concept of the exosystem.
Evaluate the statement: “The macrosystem is static and does not change during a person’s lifetime.”.

cards.title: Infancy motor milestones are the predictable sequence of gross‑ and fine‑motor…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Infancy motor milestones are the predictable sequence of gross‑ and fine‑motor achievements that typically emerge from birth to 24 months, reflecting the interplay of maturation (genetically timed neural and muscular development) and experience (opportunities for movement, cultural caregiving practices). Gross‑motor milestones include head control (≈2 months), rolling (≈4 months), sitting without support (≈6 months), crawling (≈8‑10 months), pulling to stand (≈9‑12 months), cruising (≈10‑12 months) and independent walking (≈12‑15 months). Fine‑motor milestones progress from reflexive grasp (birth) to voluntary reach (≈3 months), palmar grasp (≈5 months), raking grasp (≈7 months), inferior pincer (≈9 months) and mature pincer grasp (≈12 months). These milestones are not rigid deadlines; normal variation spans several months. They are shaped by heredity‑environment interaction (see node) and the microsystem of family routines (Bronfenbrenner’s microsystem, node). Delays beyond the typical range may signal developmental concerns and warrant screening.
steps: Motor milestones in infancy unfold as a cascade where each new posture creates the sensory‑motor context for the next skill.
Here is why: the infant’s nervous system matures in a cephalocaudal (head‑to‑toe) and proximodistal (center‑outward) pattern, so head control precedes trunk control, which precedes limb coordination.
Consider a newborn in a typical Indian joint family: the baby spends many hours on a cotton mat on the floor, giving ample tummy‑time.
By 2 months the infant lifts the head briefly — a sign that cervical extensors and vestibular input have matured enough.
At 4 months the baby rolls from prone to supine, using the newly strong neck and trunk muscles.
By 6 months the infant sits unsupported, freeing the hands for exploration.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “9‑10 months”) reveals the misconception that walking follows crawling immediately, ignoring the need for sufficient balance and strength development.
remember: List the typical age range (in months) for the emergence of independent walking in infancy.
Explain why a baby who spends most waking hours in a cloth sling may show delayed crawling but normal head control.
Evaluate the statement: “If an infant has not crawled by 10 months, they will definitely have a developmental disorder.”.

cards.title: A reflex is an involuntary, rapid…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: A reflex is an involuntary, rapid, and stereotyped response to a specific sensory stimulus, mediated by a neural pathway known as the reflex arc. The arc comprises five elements: a sensory receptor, a sensory neuron, one or more interneurons (in polysynaptic reflexes), a motor neuron, and an effector (muscle or gland). In infancy, primitive reflexes (e.g., Moro, rooting, palmar grasp, Babinski) are present at birth and typically disappear as the corticospinal tracts mature, usually by 4–6 months. Postural and locomotor reflexes (e.g., righting, stepping) emerge later and support motor milestones such as sitting and walking. Clinically, the presence, symmetry, and timely disappearance of these reflexes serve as bedside markers of central nervous system integrity; persistence or asymmetry may signal neurodevelopmental disorders such as cerebral palsy. Reflex testing therefore bridges the observable motor milestones (covered in the previous node) and the cognitive structures described by Piaget’s sensorimotor stage (next node).
steps: Reflexes are the nervous system’s ready‑made survival circuits that appear before voluntary control develops.
Here is why: 1.

Hard‑wired circuitry – The reflex arc bypasses the brain, allowing a response in <50 ms. In a newborn, the withdrawal reflex protects the hand from a hot surface even though the cortex cannot yet process “heat =…
Primitive reflexes as developmental milestones – The Moro (startle) reflex appears at birth, peaks at 1 month, and vanishes by 4–5 months as the corticospinal tract myelinates.
Its disappearance coincides with the infant’s ability to voluntarily reach — a motor milestone covered in the previous node. 3.
Clinical window – A pediatrician checks the rooting reflex (turning toward cheek stroke) at the 6‑week visit.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “motor neuron → sensory neuron → interneuron”) reveals the misconception that the motor neuron initiates the reflex, confusing the direction of neural transmission with the order of anatomical structures.
remember: Name the five components of a reflex arc in the correct order from stimulus to response.
Explain why the withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic while the knee‑jerk (patellar) reflex is monosynaptic.
Assess the clinical importance of the presence or absence of the Moro reflex in a 4‑month‑old infant.

cards.title: The sensorimotor stage is Piaget’s first major period of cognitive development…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The sensorimotor stage is Piaget’s first major period of cognitive development, spanning roughly birth to 24 months. During this stage infants construct understanding by coordinating sensory input (seeing, hearing, touching) with motor schemes (grasping, sucking, looking). The stage is divided into six sequential substages: 1. Reflexes (0‑1 month) – innate automatic responses (rooting, sucking) that form the earliest schemes. 2. Primary circular reactions (1‑4 months) – repetition of actions centred on the infant’s own body (e.g., thumb‑sucking) that are pleasurable and become habitual. 3. Secondary circular reactions (4‑8 months) – repetition of actions that produce an effect in the external environment (shaking a rattle to hear sound). 4. Coordination of secondary circular reactions (8‑12 months) – intentional combination of schemes to achieve a goal (pulling a cloth to retrieve a toy); emergence of object permanence and the A‑not‑B error. 5. Tertiary circular reactions (12‑18 months) – active experimentation, varying actions to discover new outcomes (dropping objects from different heights). 6. Mental representation (18‑24 months) – internal symbols allow deferred imitation, symbolic play, and full object permanence (searching for objects in invisible displacement). Key achievements include the development of object permanence (understanding objects continue to exist when out of sight), goal‑directed behaviour, means‑end analysis, and the beginnings of mental representation that enable language and pretend play. These cognitive structures lay the groundwork for the preoperational stage (covered in node) and for attachment formation (node).
steps: The sensorimotor stage is the foundation of all later cognition because it transforms innate reflexes into purposeful, representational thought.
Here is why: infants begin with only reflexive schemes, but through repeated circular reactions they discover that their actions can produce predictable effects in the world.

First, primary circular reactions centre on the body; then secondary circular reactions extend this discovery to objects, teaching the infant that “I shake → sound happens.” By substage 4 the infant coordinates two…
In substage 5 the child becomes a little scientist, systematically varying actions (dropping a spoon from the high chair, then from the floor) to explore causality.

Finally, substage 6 marks the breakthrough: the child can hold a mental image of an absent object, enabling deferred imitation (copying an action seen yesterday) and symbolic play (using a banana as a phone).
An everyday Indian illustration: a 10‑month‑old in a joint family watches Dadi hide a steel tumbler under a cloth, lifts the cloth, and retrieves it — showing substage 4 coordination.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing “Tertiary circular reactions” before “Coordination of secondary circular reactions”) reveals the misconception that experimentation precedes goal‑directed coordination, confusing the developmental logic of means‑end before…
remember: List the six substages of Piaget’s sensorimotor stage in correct chronological order.
Explain how object permanence evolves from substage 4 to substage 6, citing the A‑not‑B error and invisible displacement.
Critically evaluate the claim: “Sensorimotor intelligence is purely reactive and lacks intentionality.”.

cards.title: Attachment is an enduring emotional bond between an infant and a primary…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Attachment is an enduring emotional bond between an infant and a primary caregiver that shapes the child’s sense of security and exploration. Mary Ainsworth operationalised this construct through the Strange Situation Procedure (SSP), a standardized laboratory protocol for infants aged 12‑18 months. The SSP consists of eight episodes, each lasting about three minutes, involving the mother, a stranger, and the infant in a unfamiliar playroom. Key episodes include two separations (mother leaves) and two reunions (mother returns), allowing observation of the infant’s separation anxiety, stranger anxiety, and, crucially, reunion behaviour. Based on reunion responses, Ainsworth identified three primary attachment patterns: Secure (Type B) — infant seeks contact, is easily soothed, and returns to play; Insecure‑Avoidant (Type A) — infant ignores or avoids mother on reunion, showing minimal distress; Insecure‑Resistant/Ambivalent (Type C) — infant displays both seeking and resisting contact, difficult to soothe. Later, Main and Solomon added a fourth category, Disorganized/Disoriented (Type D), characterised by contradictory, fearful, or stereotyped behaviours. The SSP links these patterns to caregiver sensitivity: consistent, responsive caregiving predicts secure attachment, while inconsistent, intrusive, or neglectful care predicts insecure types. The procedure remains the gold standard for assessing early attachment, though cultural variations in caregiving norms can influence classification distributions.
steps: The Strange Situation reveals attachment quality by observing how an infant uses the caregiver as a secure base during mild stress.
Here is why: the procedure creates a graded series of separations and reunions that activate the attachment system, making the infant’s internal working model of the caregiver observable.
First, the infant explores the playroom while the mother sits quietly — this tests the secure‑base effect.
Second, a stranger enters, talks to the mother, then approaches the infant — this probes stranger anxiety.
Third, the mother leaves (first separation) — separation distress appears.
Fourth, the stranger stays and tries to comfort — the infant’s response to a non‑caregiver is noted.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the Attachment Q‑Sort”) reveals the misconception that any attachment measure is interchangeable with the SSP, confusing a naturalistic observational tool with the specific lab paradigm.
remember: What is the name of the standardized laboratory procedure developed by Mary Ainsworth to assess infant‑caregiver attachment.
Why does the Strange Situation include both separation and reunion episodes rather than only observing the infant during separation.
Critically evaluate the claim that the Strange Situation measures attachment universally across all cultures.

cards.title: Gross motor skills involve large‑muscle movements such as running, jumping…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Gross motor skills involve large‑muscle movements such as running, jumping, climbing, and throwing; fine motor skills require precise coordination of small muscles, especially in the hands and fingers, for tasks like drawing, buttoning, cutting with scissors, and handwriting. During childhood (approximately 2–12 years) these abilities follow a predictable sequence: by age 3 a child can hop on one foot and copy a circle; by age 5 she can skip, catch a bounced ball, and copy a square; by age 7 she can ride a two‑wheel bicycle, tie shoelaces, and write legibly; by age 10 she shows refined coordination in sports and intricate crafts. Development is driven by maturation of the nervous system (myelination, cerebellar refinement), opportunities for practice, nutritional status (protein, iron, calcium), and cultural expectations — e.g., traditional games like kho‑kho or gilli‑danda emphasise running and striking, while activities like rangoli drawing nurture fine dexterity. Assessment tools such as the Bruininks‑Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency (BOT‑2) provide standardized norms. Gross and fine motor progress underpins later cognitive achievements: writing fluency supports academic expression, and coordinated movement enables participation in group sports that foster social cognition. This node links the infancy motor milestones (node 006) and reflex integration (node 007) to the cognitive stages described in Piaget’s preoperational and concrete operational periods (node 011).
steps: Gross and fine motor skills develop in a predictable sequence during childhood, shaped by maturation, experience, and cultural context.
Here is why: the nervous system matures in a cephalocaudal and proximodistal pattern, so control of the trunk and shoulders precedes refined finger movements.
For example, a 3‑year‑old in a Mumbai chawl first masters climbing the staircase (gross) before she can manipulate the tiny beads of a mala (fine).
Second, repeated practice in varied environments strengthens neural pathways.
A child who plays kabaddi daily develops explosive leg power and balance earlier than a peer limited to indoor study.
Third, nutrition directly affects muscle growth and myelination; iron‑deficiency anaemia, common in some Indian regions, can delay both running speed and handwriting fluency.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “fine motor comes first because we use hands constantly”) reveals the misconception that frequency of use determines developmental order, confusing functional demand with maturational sequence.
remember: A student states that “fine motor skills develop before gross motor skills because the hands are used more often.” Is this statement correct? Explain.
Why does a child who regularly plays traditional games like kho‑kho often show advanced gross motor coordination compared with a child who spends most time on sedentary screen….
Evaluate the claim: “If a 7‑year‑old cannot tie shoelaces, it indicates a developmental delay requiring immediate clinical referral.”.

cards.title: Piaget’s preoperational stage (≈2–7 years) is marked by the emergence of…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Piaget’s preoperational stage (≈2–7 years) is marked by the emergence of symbolic function: children use words, images, and pretend play to represent absent objects. Thinking remains egocentric — they struggle to adopt another’s perspective — and centrated, focusing on a single salient dimension (e.g., height of liquid) while ignoring others. Conservation of quantity, number, mass, and volume is absent; transformations are seen as changing the essence. The concrete operational stage (≈7–11 years) introduces logical operations that can be applied to concrete, tangible materials. Children master conservation, reversibility (mentally undoing an action), classification (grouping by multiple criteria), seriation (ordering along a dimension), and decentration (considering several aspects simultaneously). Thought is still bound to physical reality; abstract or hypothetical reasoning appears only in the later formal operational stage. The transition reflects a qualitative reorganisation of cognitive structures, not merely accumulation of knowledge.
steps: The central claim is that Piaget’s preoperational and concrete operational stages represent a qualitative shift from perception‑bound, egocentric thought to logical, reversible reasoning anchored in concrete objects.

Here is why: first, the preoperational child’s symbolic function allows language and pretend play, yet thinking remains centred on one striking feature — such as the height of a liquid column — leading to systematic…

Second, egocentrism prevents the child from appreciating that another person’s view of a three‑mountain scene differs from their own, a limitation demonstrated in the classic “three‑mountains” experiment.

Third, the concrete operational child overcomes these limits by decentration — simultaneously attending to height and width — and by mental reversibility, recognising that pouring liquid back restores the original…

Fourth, classification and seriation emerge: a child can now group marbles by colour and size, and arrange bangles from smallest to largest, operations impossible without the ability to coordinate multiple dimensions.

Fifth, these abilities appear in everyday Indian settings: a 5‑year‑old insists the taller steel tumbler holds more lassi, while a 9‑year‑old correctly states the quantity is unchanged after pouring into a wider bowl…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “concrete operational because she can talk about the clay”) reveals the misconception that verbal ability alone signals logical operations, confusing symbolic function with operational thought.
remember: Identify the stage a child is likely in if she believes that a ball of clay flattened into a pancake has more clay because it looks bigger.
A 6‑year‑old is shown two identical rows of five buttons….
Evaluate whether a child who can sort a mixed pile of red and blue beads into two colour groups and then re‑sort each colour group by size has reached the concrete operational….

cards.title: Gender concepts refer to the cognitive and social frameworks through which…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Gender concepts refer to the cognitive and social frameworks through which individuals understand, categorize, and enact gender. They comprise three inter‑related components: gender identity (an internal sense of being male, female, both, neither, or another gender), gender roles (culturally prescribed behaviours, attitudes, and expectations associated with each gender), and gender schemas (mental networks that organise information about gender and guide perception). Developmentally, children first acquire a basic gender label (around age 2‑3), then develop gender stability (understanding gender is constant over time) and gender constancy (recognising gender does not change with superficial alterations). Social learning theory, cognitive‑developmental theory (Kohlberg), and gender‑schema theory (Bem) explain how biology, family, peers, media, and cultural institutions interact to shape these concepts. In the Indian context, joint‑family structures, religious rituals, and regional media reinforce distinct gender scripts, making the interplay of tradition and modernity a key area of study.
steps: Gender concepts are mental frameworks that organise how children and adolescents interpret and perform gender in everyday life.
Here is why: they emerge from a dynamic interaction between biological predispositions and cultural scripts, and they progress through identifiable cognitive milestones.
First, toddlers label themselves and others as “boy” or “girl” (gender labeling, ~2‑3 years).
Next, they grasp gender stability — the idea that a boy grows into a man — around age 4‑5.
Finally, they achieve gender constancy, understanding that gender remains unchanged despite changes in clothing or hairstyle, typically by age 6‑7.

Social‑learning theory argues that children imitate same‑gender models and are reinforced for gender‑typical behaviours; in India, a boy may be praised for playing cricket while a girl is encouraged to learn classical…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “gender role”) reveals the misconception that internal sense and external expectations are the same, confusing self‑concept with socially prescribed behaviour.
remember: What is the term for a child’s internal sense of being male, female, or another gender.
Explain why a 4‑year‑old who believes a boy becomes a girl if he wears a dress has not yet achieved gender constancy.
Evaluate the claim: “Gender‑schema theory fully explains why Indian girls prefer dolls and boys prefer trucks.”.

cards.title: Lawrence Kohlberg proposed a stage theory of moral development based on how…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Lawrence Kohlberg proposed a stage theory of moral development based on how individuals reason about right and wrong. He identified three levels, each with two stages, making six stages in total. Level 1 – Pre‑conventional morality (typically ages 4‑10): - Stage 1: Obedience and Punishment Orientation – actions are judged by their immediate consequences; “wrong” means “will be punished.” - Stage 2: Individualism and Exchange – right behaviour satisfies one’s own needs; fairness is a reciprocal deal (“you scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours”). Level 2 – Conventional morality (typically ages 10‑adolescence): - Stage 3: Good Interpersonal Relationships – morality is about living up to social expectations and being a “good” person in the eyes of significant others. - Stage 4: Maintaining Social Order – emphasis on obeying laws, respecting authority, and performing duties to keep society functioning. Level 3 – Post‑conventional morality (rare before late adolescence/adulthood): - Stage 5: Social Contract and Individual Rights – rules are seen as flexible agreements that protect basic rights; laws can be changed if they violate justice. - Stage 6: Universal Ethical Principles – moral reasoning is guided by self‑chosen, abstract principles such as justice, equality, and human dignity; these principles override laws when they conflict. Kohlberg used moral dilemmas (e.g., the Heinz dilemma) to assess reasoning, not the decision itself. The theory assumes invariant sequence, hierarchical integration, and cross‑cultural universality, though later research highlighted cultural variations and the role of moral emotions.
steps: Kohlberg’s theory tells us that moral reasoning matures through a fixed sequence of six stages grouped into three levels, and that the reason behind a moral choice matters more than the choice itself.
Here is why: the theory emerged from longitudinal interviews where children, adolescents, and adults responded to hypothetical dilemmas such as Heinz stealing a drug to save his dying wife.
Kohlberg coded the justifications — not the “steal” or “don’t steal” verdict — and found a predictable progression.
First, at the pre‑conventional level, reasoning is egocentric.

A Class 5 student in Mumbai might say, “Heinz shouldn’t steal because the police will catch him and he’ll go to jail” (Stage 1) or “Heinz should steal because his wife needs the medicine and he’ll feel good helping her”…
The focus is on personal consequences or reciprocal benefit.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Conventional, Pre‑conventional, Post‑conventional”) reveals the misconception that the levels are interchangeable or that conventional reasoning appears before pre‑conventional reasoning, ignoring the invariant sequence claim.
remember: Recall: List the three levels of Kohlberg’s moral development in order from earliest to latest.
Reasoning: A 12‑year‑old says, “Heinz should steal the drug because his wife will die otherwise, and a good husband protects his family.” Identify the Kohlberg stage and explain….
Evaluate: “Kohlberg’s Stage 6 is universally attained by all adults in every culture.” State whether this claim is true or false and provide two pieces of evidence.

cards.title: Adolescence: puberty is the biologically driven transition from childhood to…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Adolescence: puberty is the biologically driven transition from childhood to reproductive maturity, typically beginning between ages 9‑14 in girls and 10‑15 in boys. It is initiated by the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑gonadal (HPG) axis: the hypothalamus releases gonadotropin‑releasing hormone (GnRH), stimulating the anterior pituitary to secrete luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle‑stimulating hormone (FSH). These gonadotropins activate the gonads — ovaries in females, testes in males — to produce sex steroids (estradiol, progesterone, testosterone). The steroids drive secondary sexual characteristics (thelarche, pubarche, menarche, spermarche, voice deepening, muscle accretion) and the adolescent growth spurt mediated by insulin‑like growth factor‑1 (IGF‑1). Puberty timing is influenced by genetics (≈50‑80 % heritability), nutrition, body‑fat percentage, chronic illness, and psychosocial stress. The process unfolds in Tanner stages (I‑V) for breast/genital development and pubic hair, providing a clinical yardstick. Puberty also reorganises brain circuitry — synaptic pruning and myelination in prefrontal cortex and limbic system — linking to the cognitive advances covered in the formal operational stage node and the psychosocial tasks of identity formation (Erikson, Marcia) in later nodes.
steps: Puberty is the coordinated hormonal surge that rewires the body and brain for adult reproductive capacity.

Here is why: the hypothalamus “wakes up” after a juvenile pause, releasing GnRH in pulsatile bursts; this pulse frequency determines whether the pituitary releases more LH or FSH, which in turn directs the gonads to…
The steroids then trigger the visible changes — breast buds, testicular enlargement, pubic hair — and the invisible brain remodelling that underpins abstract reasoning and identity exploration.
Consider a 12‑year‑old girl in Mumbai: her menarche at 11.8 years matches the urban secular trend of 0.3 year earlier per decade, linked to higher BMI and reduced infectious load.
Her brother, 13, shows voice cracking and facial fuzz at Tanner stage III, while his rural cousin of the same age remains at stage I due to lower caloric intake and higher parasitic burden.
These examples illustrate how the same biological program runs on different schedules because of nutrition, genetics, and environment.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “testosterone or estrogen starts puberty”) reveals the misconception that gonadal steroids are the trigger rather than the downstream effect of the HPG axis.
remember: What is the first hormonal signal that initiates puberty in both sexes.
Explain why two 13‑year‑old boys in the same Indian city can be at different Tanner stages.
Evaluate the statement: “Menarche is the most reliable single marker of pubertal completion in girls.”.

cards.title: The formal operational stage is Piaget’s fourth and final cognitive stage…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The formal operational stage is Piaget’s fourth and final cognitive stage, typically emerging around age 11‑12 and continuing through adulthood. It is characterised by the ability to reason abstractly, manipulate symbols without concrete referents, and engage in hypothetical‑deductive reasoning. Adolescents can formulate propositions, test them mentally, and draw logical conclusions — e.g., solving algebra problems, debating ethical dilemmas, or designing experiments. Key sub‑abilities include propositional logic (if‑then reasoning), combinatorial analysis (systematically varying factors), and metacognition (thinking about one’s own thinking). This stage builds on the concrete operational stage (node) where logic is tied to tangible objects; formal operations free thought from the immediate environment. It also interacts with puberty‑driven brain maturation (node) that expands prefrontal cortex connectivity, enabling the neural substrate for abstract thought. The stage underpins later identity formation (node) because adolescents can now envision future selves and evaluate ideological commitments.
steps: The formal operational stage equips adolescents with a mental laboratory where they can test ideas without physical trial‑and‑error.

Here is why: first, abstract reasoning lets them manipulate concepts like “justice” or “infinity” that have no concrete counterpart; a Class 12 student in Delhi can debate the fairness of a new education policy without…

Second, hypothetical‑deductive reasoning enables systematic problem‑solving: given a science fair challenge, the student can generate multiple hypotheses (“If I increase sunlight, then plant growth will rise”), predict…

Third, propositional logic allows evaluation of “if‑then” statements purely symbolically; for instance, “If all mammals breathe air, and a whale is a mammal, then a whale breathes air” is judged valid without observing…

Fourth, combinatorial thinking lets them vary several factors at once — e.g., planning a study schedule by mixing subjects, break lengths, and sleep hours to find an optimal mix. Fifth, metacognition lets them monitor…

These abilities emerge alongside puberty‑driven prefrontal maturation (node) and set the stage for Erikson’s identity versus role confusion (node), because adolescents can now imagine multiple future selves and commit…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “birth to 2 years”) reveals the misconception that formal operations appear in infancy, confusing it with the sensorimotor stage.
remember: What is the typical age range for the onset of Piaget’s formal operational stage.
Explain why a 10‑year‑old who can solve concrete arithmetic problems but cannot solve “If all A are B and all B are C, are all A C?” has not yet reached formal operations.
Evaluate the claim: “Formal operational thinking is universal and appears at the same age in every culture.”.

cards.title: Erikson’s fifth psychosocial stage, Identity vs. Role Confusion…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Erikson’s fifth psychosocial stage, Identity vs. Role Confusion, occurs roughly between ages 12‑18. The adolescent must integrate childhood identifications (family, school, culture) with new cognitive abilities (formal operational thought) and social expectations (peer groups, media, career pathways) to forge a coherent ego identity — a stable, internalised sense of who one is, what one values, and where one is headed. Successful resolution yields the virtue fidelity: the ability to sustain loyalties and commitments despite contradictory pressures. Failure produces role confusion, manifested as diffuse self‑concept, difficulty committing to goals, and vulnerability to negative peer influence. The stage builds on the earlier crises of trust, autonomy, initiative, and industry, and it sets the foundation for the next stage, Intimacy vs. Isolation. Key sub‑concepts include psychosocial moratorium (a socially sanctioned period for exploration), identity foreclosure (premature commitment without exploration), identity diffusion (lack of both exploration and commitment), and negative identity (adopting an identity opposite to societal expectations). In the Indian context, the tension between traditional family expectations (e.g., arranged career paths) and globalised peer culture intensifies the moratorium.
steps: Erikson’s fifth psychosocial stage, Identity vs. Role Confusion, is the central developmental task of adolescence where individuals synthesize earlier identifications into a coherent sense of self.

Here is why: first, the adolescent brain attains formal operational thought, allowing hypothetical‑deductive reasoning about future selves; this cognitive leap lets a student in Delhi imagine “What if I become a…
Second, society grants a psychosocial moratorium — a culturally recognised “time‑out” (e.g., gap years, hobby classes, internships) where exploration is tolerated.
In India, this appears as coaching‑center trials, summer camps, or volunteer work with NGOs.

Third, peer groups become the primary mirror; a teenager in Bengaluru may adopt the language, dress, and values of a coding club, a cricket team, or a theatre troupe, each offering a provisional identity.

Fourth, family expectations — often strong in collectivist settings — can either scaffold exploration (parents encouraging a music class) or force foreclosure (insisting on engineering without discussion).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Intimacy vs. Isolation”) reveals the misconception that the fifth stage deals with adult relationships rather than adolescent self‑definition.
remember: What is the central psychosocial conflict of Erikson’s fifth stage.
Why does formal operational thought enable the identity search.
Evaluate the claim: “A teenager who follows her parents’ career choice without question has achieved identity.”.

cards.title: James Marcia expanded Erikson’s “identity vs. role confusion” stage by…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: James Marcia expanded Erikson’s “identity vs. role confusion” stage by operationalising two dimensions: exploration (actively trying out roles, values, beliefs) and commitment (making a firm, personal decision). Crossing these yields four identity statuses: 1. Identity Diffusion – low exploration, low commitment; the adolescent shows little interest in future roles and avoids decisions. 2. Foreclosure – low exploration, high commitment; commitments are adopted from authority figures (parents, teachers) without personal search. 3. Moratorium – high exploration, low commitment; the adolescent actively experiments with alternatives but has not yet settled. 4. Identity Achievement – high exploration, high commitment; after a period of searching, the adolescent makes self‑chosen, stable commitments. These statuses are not fixed stages; individuals can move between them across domains (career, religion, politics, gender). Marcia’s interview‑based Identity Status Interview (ISI) assesses each domain separately, allowing a profile rather than a single label. The model links directly to Erikson’s crisis resolution: successful navigation yields Achievement, while unresolved crisis may leave a person in Diffusion or Foreclosure.
steps: Marcia’s four identity statuses map every adolescent’s mix of searching and deciding into a clear 2 × 2 grid.
Here is why: Erikson described the adolescent crisis qualitatively;
Marcia gave it measurable axes — exploration (trying out options) and commitment (sticking to a choice).
Consider a Class 12 student, Priya, who attends a career‑counselling fair, talks to engineers, doctors, and artists, then enrolls in a B.Tech programme after weighing pros and cons.
She shows high exploration (fair, conversations) and high commitment (enrollment) → Identity Achievement.
Now picture Rohan, whose father is a chartered accountant.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “crisis and resolution”) reveals the misconception that Marcia simply renamed Erikson’s terms instead of creating measurable axes.
remember: List the two dimensions Marcia used to derive his four identity statuses.
A 17‑year‑old says, “My parents want me to study law, so I’m preparing for….
Critically evaluate whether Marcia’s statuses can be considered developmental stages in the same sense as Piaget’s stages.

cards.title: Delinquency refers to a persistent pattern of antisocial, illegal…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Delinquency refers to a persistent pattern of antisocial, illegal, or norm‑violating behaviours exhibited by adolescents (typically ages 10‑18) that are serious enough to warrant legal intervention. It encompasses acts such as theft, vandalism, substance‑related offences, truancy, and violent aggression. The concept is linked to developmental theories: Erikson’s identity‑versus‑role‑confusion stage predicts that failure to achieve a coherent identity can lead to delinquent experimentation; Marcia’s identity statuses (especially diffusion and foreclosure) correlate with higher delinquency risk; Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems highlight how microsystem (family, peers), mesosystem (school‑family links), exosystem (parental workplace stress), and macrosystem (cultural norms, media) interact to shape delinquent trajectories. Heredity‑environment interaction studies show genetic predispositions (e.g., impulsivity) amplify risk only when combined with adverse environments (neglect, peer deviance). Delinquency is distinct from normal adolescent risk‑taking because of its chronicity, severity, and legal consequences.
steps: Delinquency is a chronic, legally relevant pattern of antisocial behaviour that emerges when adolescent identity formation collides with adverse ecological contexts.
Here is why: first, identity diffusion or foreclosure (Marcia) leaves youths without a stable self‑concept, making them vulnerable to peer‑driven deviance.
Second, family microsystems characterised by harsh discipline, low monitoring, or parental conflict weaken internal controls.
Third, peer mesosystems that reinforce rule‑breaking provide social rewards for delinquent acts.
Fourth, macrosystem influences such as media glorification of violence and socioeconomic inequality amplify risk.

Consider a 16‑year‑old in Mumbai who drops out of school, joins a street‑corner group, and begins snatching bags; his identity is diffused, his father works night shifts (exosystem stress), his mother uses authoritarian…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “any teenage rebellion is delinquency”) reveals the misconception that occasional rule‑breaking equals delinquency, ignoring the required frequency and legal consequence criteria.
remember: Define delinquency and list two criteria that distinguish it from normal adolescent risk‑taking.
Explain how Marcia’s identity diffusion status can increase delinquency risk, referencing at least one ecological system.
Critically evaluate the statement: “Genetic impulsivity alone causes delinquency.” Use the heredity‑environment interaction perspective.

cards.title: Strain (often called distress) is the negative psychological and physiological…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Strain (often called distress) is the negative psychological and physiological response when perceived demands exceed an individual’s coping resources, leading to impaired functioning, anxiety, and health risks. Eustress is the positive counterpart: a moderate, short‑lived stress response that enhances motivation, focus, and performance without overwhelming the person. Both arise from the same stress appraisal process (primary and secondary appraisal) but differ in the balance between demand and perceived control. When the demand‑resource gap is small and the person feels capable, the arousal is interpreted as challenge → eustress; when the gap is large or control is low, the same arousal is interpreted as threat → strain. The concepts are linked to the Yerkes‑Dodson inverted‑U curve (optimal arousal), Selye’s General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm‑resistance‑exhaustion), and later nodes on stressors, cognitive appraisal, and coping strategies.
steps: Takeaway: Whether a stressor becomes eustress or strain depends on the person’s appraisal of demand versus coping resources, not on the stressor itself.

Here is why: the same event — say, a Class 12 board‑exam timetable release — can trigger eustress in a student who has prepared a revision plan (high perceived control) and strain in a peer who feels unprepared (low…
First, primary appraisal evaluates the event as irrelevant, benign‑positive, or stressful.
If stressful, it is further labelled as a challenge (potential gain) or a threat (potential loss).
A challenge appraisal leans toward eustress; a threat appraisal leans toward strain.
Second, secondary appraisal assesses available coping options — time, knowledge, social support.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “eustress is any stress that feels good”) reveals the misconception that pleasant feelings alone define eustress, ignoring the cognitive appraisal of demand‑resource balance.
remember: Define eustress and give one everyday example relevant to an Indian Class 12 student.
Explain why the same stressor (e.g., a surprise class test) can produce eustress in one student and strain in another.
Evaluate the statement: “All stress is harmful; therefore schools should eliminate every source of stress for students.”.

cards.title: Stress is the psychological and physiological response to demands that exceed…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Stress is the psychological and physiological response to demands that exceed perceived coping resources. Types of stress are classified primarily by valence and duration: 1. Eustress – positive, short‑term stress that motivates and enhances performance (e.g., preparing for a cultural fest). 2. Distress – negative stress that overwhelms coping, leading to anxiety, fatigue, or illness (e.g., chronic family conflict). 3. Acute stress – immediate, brief reaction to a specific event (e.g., a sudden pop quiz). 4. Chronic stress – prolonged exposure to stressors without relief (e.g., ongoing financial pressure). 5. Episodic acute stress – frequent acute episodes due to a chaotic lifestyle (e.g., a student juggling tuition, sports, and family duties). These categories interact: eustress can become distress if intensity or duration exceeds optimal arousal (Yerkes‑Dodson upside‑down‑U). Understanding the type guides appropriate management — relaxation for distress, challenge‑setting for eustress.
steps: Takeaway: Stress is not a single experience; its impact depends on whether it is perceived as a challenge (eustress) or a threat (distress) and on how long it lasts.
Here is why: 1.
Valence matters — Eustress releases dopamine and moderate cortisol, sharpening focus for a dance rehearsal; distress floods the system with sustained cortisol, impairing memory. 2.

Duration shapes outcome — Acute stress (a surprise class test) triggers a brief fight‑or‑flight surge that subsides; chronic stress (parental unemployment) keeps the alarm system on, eroding immunity. 3.
Frequency creates a pattern — Episodic acute stress appears when a student habitually over‑commits — tuition, cricket, family functions — producing repeated spikes that mimic chronic wear. 4.
Transition risk — Without recovery, acute episodes accumulate, shifting the curve leftward so that even mild demands feel threatening. 5.
remember: List the five major types of stress discussed in this node.
Explain why eustress can improve performance while distress impairs it, referring to physiological mediators.
Evaluate the statement: “All acute stress is harmful and should be eliminated.”.

cards.title: A stressor is any stimulus or demand — physical, psychological, social…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: A stressor is any stimulus or demand — physical, psychological, social, or environmental — that initiates the stress response. Stressors are classified by source: environmental (noise, pollution, natural disasters), social (relationship conflict, peer pressure, academic deadlines), physiological (illness, sleep deprivation, hunger), and psychological (negative self‑talk, unrealistic expectations, fear of failure). They can be acute (sudden, short‑lived, e.g., a surprise test) or chronic (persistent, e.g., ongoing family financial strain). The intensity of a stressor is not fixed; it depends on the individual’s cognitive appraisal (primary: “Is this a threat?”; secondary: “Can I cope?”) and on dispositional factors such as Type A/B personality, optimism‑pessimism, and locus of control (covered in later nodes). Stressors trigger the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) and, if prolonged, can lead to strain, burnout, or health problems (immune suppression, hypertension, ulcers). Understanding stressors is the first step toward effective management strategies like relaxation training, biofeedback, meditation, and yoga.
steps: Takeaway: A stressor is any demand that activates the stress response, and its impact depends on how the individual appraises it. Here is why: 1.

Source matters – Environmental stressors like Mumbai’s monsoon flooding or Delhi’s air pollution affect everyone in the area, but only those who appraise the situation as threatening experience stress. 2.
Social demands – Board‑exam deadlines, college‑admission cut‑offs, or family expectations are classic Indian social stressors; they become chronic when they persist across months. 3.
Physiological triggers – Skipping meals during a long coaching‑class day, or recovering from dengue, act as internal stressors that lower coping capacity. 4.
Psychological origins – A student’s belief “I must score 95 % or I’m a failure” is a self‑generated stressor; it exists even without an external event. 5.

Appraisal filters the effect – Primary appraisal asks “Is this a threat?” Secondary appraisal asks “Do I have resources?” A student with high self‑efficacy (internal locus) may see the same exam as a challenge…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “stressors are only external events like exams”) reveals the misconception that internal thoughts cannot be stressors, ignoring psychological stressors.
remember: Define “stressor” and give one example each of an environmental, a social, a physiological, and a psychological stressor relevant to an Indian Class 12 student.
Explain why the same event — a surprise class test — can be a stressor for one student but not for another.
Evaluate the statement: “Chronic stressors are always more harmful than acute stressors.”.

cards.title: Hans Selye’s General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) is a three‑stage physiological…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Hans Selye’s General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) is a three‑stage physiological model that explains how an organism responds to prolonged stressors. 1. Alarm Reaction – The immediate “fight‑or‑flight” response mediated by the sympathetic‑adrenal‑medullary (SAM) axis. The hypothalamus activates the adrenal medulla, releasing adrenaline and noradrenaline, causing increased heart rate, blood pressure, and glucose mobilisation. 2. Stage of Resistance – If the stressor persists, the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑adrenal (HPA) axis dominates. Cortisol secretion rises, sustaining energy supply, suppressing non‑essential functions (immune, reproductive), and attempting to restore homeostasis. The organism appears to cope, but physiological resources are being depleted. 3. Stage of Exhaustion – Continuous demand exhausts adrenal reserves and the body’s adaptive capacity. Cortisol levels may fall or become dysregulated, leading to immune collapse, cardiovascular disease, ulcers, and psychological burnout. GAS links stressors (external or internal) to physiological strain and health outcomes. It provides the biological backbone for later concepts such as cognitive appraisal (primary/secondary), the upside‑down‑U performance curve, and stress‑management interventions. The model assumes a non‑specific response: any stressor triggers the same physiological cascade, though intensity varies with appraisal and individual differences (Type A/B, locus of control, optimism).
steps: Takeaway: Selye’s GAS describes a universal, three‑stage physiological cascade — Alarm, Resistance, Exhaustion — that turns any persistent stressor into measurable health risk.
Supporting arguments: 1.
The Alarm stage is an immediate, SAM‑driven surge preparing the body for rapid action. 2.
The Resistance stage shifts to HPA‑driven cortisol, which sustains energy but suppresses immunity and repair. 3.
The Exhaustion stage reflects depleted adrenal capacity, leading to disease if the stressor is not removed.
Narrative with Indian examples: Consider a Class 12 student, Priya, preparing for the ISC board exams.
remember: Name the three stages of Selye’s General Adaptation Syndrome in correct order.
Explain why the Resistance stage is physiologically deceptive.
Evaluate the claim: “GAS applies only to physical stressors like injury, not to psychological stressors like exam anxiety.”.

cards.title: Cognitive appraisal is the mental process through which an individual evaluates…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Cognitive appraisal is the mental process through which an individual evaluates a situation’s significance for well‑being. Primary appraisal classifies the event as irrelevant, benign‑positive, or stressful (harm/loss, threat, challenge). Secondary appraisal assesses coping resources and options — personal skills, social support, time, and perceived control — determining whether the stressor can be managed. The interaction of both appraisals shapes the emotional response (e.g., anxiety, eustress) and subsequent coping behaviour. This two‑stage model, proposed by Lazarus and Folkman (1984), explains why the same exam can be a threat for one student and a challenge for another, depending on perceived resources and stakes.
steps: Cognitive appraisal decides whether an event becomes stress or eustress by first labeling the event (primary) and then checking resources (secondary).

Here is why: the same traffic jam can be a harmless delay (primary: benign) for a passenger with a flexible schedule, but a threat (primary: threat) for a driver who must reach a hospital; the driver’s secondary…
Primary appraisal: “This exam threatens my college admission” (threat) or “It challenges me to prove my preparation” (challenge).
Secondary appraisal: “I have revised all chapters, I can ask teachers, I have a calm study space” (high resources) versus “I missed many classes, I have no notes, I feel unprepared” (low resources).
The first combination yields eustress and focused study; the second yields anxiety and avoidance.
In Indian contexts, family expectations often raise the stakes of primary appraisal, while access to tutoring or peer groups shapes secondary appraisal.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “primary appraisal only decides if an event is good or bad”) reveals the misconception that primary appraisal is a simple valence judgement rather than a nuanced classification of stress relevance.
remember: What are the three possible outcomes of primary appraisal according to Lazarus and Folkman.
Explain how secondary appraisal differs from primary appraisal in terms of focus and function.
A student views an upcoming debate competition as a chance to improve public speaking (challenge) but believes she has no time to prepare (low….

cards.title: Stress arises from the interaction between external situational factors and…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Stress arises from the interaction between external situational factors and internal dispositional factors. External situational causes include major life events (e.g., board exams, family relocation, financial crisis), daily hassles (traffic, noisy neighbourhood, deadline pressure), and environmental conditions (pollution, overcrowding). Internal dispositional causes refer to stable personality traits that shape how a person appraises and reacts to those situations. The most researched dispositional typology is Type A vs. Type B behavior pattern (Friedman & Rosenman, 1974). Type A individuals exhibit chronic time urgency, competitiveness, hostility, and a relentless drive for achievement; they appraise many situations as threats and respond with heightened physiological arousal. Type B individuals are relaxed, patient, and less reactive, appraising the same events as challenges rather than threats. The interaction is bidirectional: a Type A person may select or create more stressful environments (e.g., taking on extra tuition), while a high‑stress environment can amplify Type A tendencies. This node focuses on these two broad cause categories; optimism‑pessimism and locus of control are treated in subsequent nodes (,).
steps: Takeaway: Stress is produced when external demands meet an internal disposition that amplifies threat appraisal, especially in Type A personalities.
Supporting arguments: 1.
External situational stressors are objective events — board exams, family illness, moving cities — that require adaptation. 2.
Daily hassles (traffic jams in Mumbai, power cuts, noisy tuition centres) accumulate and predict health outcomes better than major events. 3.
Type A behavior pattern (time urgency, hostility, competitive drive) creates a cognitive bias toward threat appraisal, raising cortisol and sympathetic activation. 4.
Type B pattern buffers the same events by fostering challenge appraisal and quicker physiological recovery. 5.
remember: List three external situational stressors commonly faced by Indian Class 12 students and briefly describe each.
Explain why a Type A individual is more likely to appraise a routine traffic jam as a threat rather than a challenge.
Evaluate the statement: “External situational stressors alone determine the level of stress experienced by a student.”.

cards.title: Optimism‑pessimism is a stable dispositional dimension describing how…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Optimism‑pessimism is a stable dispositional dimension describing how individuals habitually interpret future events. Optimism reflects a generalized expectation that good outcomes will occur, leading to approach‑oriented coping, positive reappraisal, and lower physiological arousal during stressors. Pessimism reflects a generalized expectation of negative outcomes, fostering avoidance coping, catastrophising, and heightened sympathetic activation. In the stress‑process model, this disposition operates at the primary appraisal stage (evaluating threat vs. challenge) and the secondary appraisal stage (judging coping resources). Optimists tend to appraise stressors as challenges (eustress) and mobilise problem‑focused strategies; pessimists appraise them as threats (distress) and rely on emotion‑focused or defensive strategies. The construct links to Type A/B behaviour (Type A often correlates with pessimistic urgency), locus of control (optimists show internal control), and health outcomes such as immune function, cardiovascular reactivity, and burnout risk. It is measured by tools like the Life Orientation Test‑Revised (LOT‑R) and is distinct from transient mood states.
steps: Takeaway: Optimism and pessimism are stable expectancies that shape whether a stressor is appraised as a challenge or a threat, thereby directing coping choices and long‑term health trajectories.

Supporting argument 1 – Primary appraisal filter: When an optimistic student hears “board exams in two months,” the primary appraisal tags the event as a challenge (“I can prepare”) rather than a threat (“I will fail”).

A pessimistic peer tags the same event as a threat, triggering the alarm stage of GAS. Supporting argument 2 – Secondary appraisal of resources: Optimists inventory internal resources (“I have good notes, I can ask…
Pessimists discount resources (“nothing works”), leading to helplessness.
Supporting argument 3 – Coping pathway: Challenge appraisal + high perceived control → problem‑focused coping (planning, active study).
Threat appraisal + low control → emotion‑focused or avoidant coping (denial, substance use).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “optimism means always feeling happy”) reveals the misconception that optimism is a transient mood rather than a trait‑like expectancy.
remember: Define optimism and pessimism as dispositional constructs in the stress‑process model.
Explain how an optimistic primary appraisal leads to problem‑focused coping, whereas a pessimistic primary appraisal leads to emotion‑focused coping.
Evaluate the claim: “Optimism directly improves immune function independent of coping behaviour.”.

cards.title: Locus of control is a personality dimension describing the extent to which…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Locus of control is a personality dimension describing the extent to which individuals perceive events as contingent on their own actions (internal) versus outside forces such as fate, luck, or powerful others (external). Developed by Julian Rotter (1966), it operates as a generalized expectancy that shapes cognitive appraisal of stressors: internals tend to engage in primary appraisal that emphasizes challenge and secondary appraisal that highlights personal coping resources, whereas externals more often appraise situations as threats beyond their control. This dispositional factor interacts with Type A/B behavior patterns and optimism‑pessimism (covered in sibling nodes) to influence physiological stress responses — internals show lower cortisol reactivity, better immune function, and reduced risk of hypertension and ulcers. In the Indian classroom context, a student with an internal locus attributes exam performance to study strategies, while an external locus student blames the difficulty of the paper or teacher bias, leading to divergent stress‑management behaviours.
steps: Locus of control determines whether a person sees a stressor as a challenge they can master or a threat they must endure.

Here is why: Rotter’s concept shows that expectancy of control shapes the very first appraisal — primary appraisal — where an internal individual asks “What can I do?” while an external individual asks “Why is this…
This difference cascades into secondary appraisal: internals inventory personal skills, social support, and time, whereas externals perceive few coping options.

Consequently, internals activate problem‑focused coping (planning, seeking information) and exhibit lower physiological arousal (reduced HPA‑axis activation), protecting immune function and cardiovascular health.
Externals rely more on emotion‑focused or avoidant coping, sustaining cortisol elevation that suppresses lymphocytes and raises blood pressure, increasing ulcer risk.

In an Indian board‑exam scenario, an internal student creates a revision timetable, practices past papers, and sleeps adequately; an external student worries about “luck” and “paper leakage”, skips meals, and…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “locus of control means the location of stress in the body”) reveals the misconception that the term refers to a physical site rather than a cognitive belief about agency.
remember: Define locus of control and name its two main orientations.
Explain how an internal locus of control influences primary appraisal of an upcoming board examination.
Compare the secondary appraisal coping resources typically reported by internal versus external locus students facing a difficult project deadline.

cards.title: Stress‑immune interactions are studied in psychoneuroimmunology.
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Stress‑immune interactions are studied in psychoneuroimmunology. Acute stress activates the sympathetic‑adrenal‑medullary (SAM) axis, releasing catecholamines that cause rapid redistribution of leukocytes — natural killer (NK) cells and cytotoxic T‑cells surge in blood, enhancing immune surveillance. Simultaneously, the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑adrenal (HPA) axis releases cortisol, which binds glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells, inhibiting pro‑inflammatory cytokine production (IL‑1, IL‑6, TNF‑α) and suppressing lymphocyte proliferation. Chronic stress maintains elevated cortisol, leading to glucocorticoid receptor resistance, persistent low‑grade inflammation, reduced NK cytotoxicity, impaired vaccine antibody response, and delayed wound healing. Cognitive appraisal (primary/secondary) modulates HPA activation: threat appraisal amplifies cortisol; challenge appraisal blunts it. Dispositional factors — Type A behaviour, pessimism, external locus of control — heighten threat appraisal and prolong HPA output, compounding immune suppression. Conversely, optimism and internal locus of control promote adaptive coping, limiting cortisol exposure. This node links Selye’s General Adaptation Syndrome and cognitive appraisal to measurable immune outcomes, setting the stage for stress‑related hypertension and ulcer formation.
steps: Takeaway: Chronic stress suppresses immunity mainly through sustained cortisol release from the HPA axis, while acute stress briefly boosts immune surveillance via catecholamine‑driven leukocyte redistribution.
Supporting arguments: 1.
HPA‑axis cascade – Stressor → hypothalamic CRH → pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortisol → glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells → transcriptional repression of inflammatory genes. 2.

SAM‑axis surge – Stressor → sympathetic nerves → adrenal medulla → epinephrine/norepinephrine → β‑adrenergic receptors on leukocytes → rapid mobilization of NK cells and CD8⁺ T‑cells into circulation. 3.

Time‑dependent divergence – Minutes‑hours: catecholamines dominate → transient immunosurveillance boost; days‑weeks: cortisol dominates → lymphocyte apoptosis, cytokine shift to Th2, NK cytotoxicity drop. 4.
Appraisal modulation – Primary appraisal (threat vs challenge) sets HPA magnitude; secondary appraisal (coping resources) determines duration.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “adrenaline”) reveals the misconception that the fast‑acting catecholamine surge of the SAM axis drives long‑term immunosuppression, confusing acute redistribution with chronic suppression.
remember: Which hormone, released during chronic stress, is primarily responsible for suppressing immune function.
Explain why acute stress can temporarily enhance immune surveillance while chronic stress impairs it.
Critique the statement: “All stress is bad for the immune system.”.

cards.title: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a sustained elevation of systemic…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure above 140/90 mmHg (or 130/80 mmHg per newer guidelines). In the stress‑health pathway, chronic activation of the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic‑adrenal‑medullary (SAM) system raises catecholamines and cortisol, causing vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and increased cardiac output. These physiological changes interact with behavioural factors (poor diet, low physical activity, smoking) and dispositional traits (Type A behaviour, external locus of control, pessimism) covered in earlier nodes. Persistent hypertension damages endothelial lining, accelerates atherosclerosis, and raises risk for stroke, myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease, and hypertensive retinopathy. It is both a consequence of prolonged stress (linking to Selye’s GAS exhaustion stage) and a mediator that amplifies immune‑system suppression (node) and ulcer formation (node). Management therefore targets stress appraisal (primary/secondary), relaxation training, biofeedback, meditation, and yoga (nodes‑018) to lower sympathetic tone and restore vascular compliance.
steps: Chronic stress drives hypertension through a neuro‑endocrine cascade that keeps blood vessels constricted and the kidneys retaining salt.
Here is why: the HPA axis releases cortisol while the SAM system floods the bloodstream with adrenaline and noradrenaline; together they raise heart rate, contractility, and peripheral resistance.
Consider a Class 12 student preparing for board exams who habitually skips meals, sleeps five hours, and worries about results — this mirrors a Type A, high‑locus‑of‑control‑external profile.
Over weeks, the repeated “fight‑or‑flight” spikes become a new baseline, shifting the pressure‑volume curve upward.
The first supporting argument is that sustained catecholamine exposure causes vascular remodelling — smooth‑muscle hypertrophy narrows arterioles.
Second, cortisol enhances renal sodium re‑absorption via mineralocorticoid receptors, expanding blood volume.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “120/80 mmHg”) reveals the misconception that normal adult BP equals the hypertensive cut‑off, confusing optimal with pathological values.
remember: What is the typical blood‑pressure threshold used to diagnose hypertension in adolescents according to current clinical guidelines.
Explain how chronic activation of the HPA axis contributes to sustained high blood pressure.
Evaluate the statement: “Type A behaviour alone causes hypertension.”.

cards.title: Stress‑induced ulcers (primarily peptic ulcers) are mucosal erosions in the…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Stress‑induced ulcers (primarily peptic ulcers) are mucosal erosions in the stomach or duodenum that arise when chronic psychological stress disrupts the balance between aggressive factors (gastric acid, pepsin) and defensive mechanisms (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow). The hypothalamic‑pituitary‑adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic‑adrenal‑medullary (SAM) system, activated during prolonged stress, increase cortisol and catecholamines. Cortisol suppresses prostaglandin synthesis, weakening the mucosal barrier, while catecholamines reduce splanchnic blood flow, impairing repair. Simultaneously, stress‑related behaviours — irregular meals, excessive tea/coffee, smoking, alcohol — amplify acid secretion. The result is a vicious cycle: stress → physiological changes → mucosal vulnerability → ulcer formation → pain → further stress. This node links to sibling nodes on immune suppression, hypertension, and the broader health‑effects framework of the chapter.
steps: Chronic stress creates a physiological environment that erodes the stomach’s protective lining, leading to ulcers.
Here is why: the HPA axis releases cortisol, which inhibits prostaglandin synthesis; prostaglandins normally stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow.
Without them, the mucosal barrier thins.
Simultaneously, sympathetic activation shunts blood away from the gut, delaying repair.
Behavioural changes — skipping meals, drinking strong chai, smoking — add acid load.
Over weeks, these factors combine to produce mucosal breaks.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “adrenaline”) reveals the misconception that acute sympathetic catecholamines are the main drivers of mucosal defence suppression, confusing the rapid SAM response with the slower, sustained HPA effect that dominates in chronic stress.
remember: What is the primary hormonal mediator that suppresses prostaglandin synthesis during chronic stress, thereby weakening the gastric mucosal barrier.
Explain why a student who attributes ulcer pain solely to “spicy food” misses the psychophysiological contribution of stress.
Evaluate the statement: “If a person has no Helicobacter pylori infection, stress cannot cause ulcers.”.

cards.title: The upside‑down‑U curve, formally known as the Yerkes‑Dodson law…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The upside‑down‑U curve, formally known as the Yerkes‑Dodson law, describes the empirical relationship between arousal (stress level) and performance. At low arousal, attention and motivation are insufficient, yielding poor performance. As arousal increases, cognitive resources such as alertness, focus, and energy mobilisation improve, producing a rise in performance until an optimal arousal point is reached — this zone corresponds to eustress. Beyond this optimum, excessive arousal triggers anxiety, narrowed attention, physiological hyper‑reactivity (e.g., tachycardia, cortisol surge), and impaired working memory, causing performance to decline — this zone reflects distress. The exact location of the peak shifts with task complexity: simple or well‑practised tasks tolerate higher arousal (peak shifts right), whereas complex, novel, or fine‑motor tasks require lower arousal (peak shifts left). Individual differences — Type A vs. Type B behaviour pattern, optimism‑pessimism, locus of control — also modulate the curve’s shape and optimal point. The model integrates concepts from earlier nodes: stressors (node 003) raise arousal; cognitive appraisal (node 005) determines whether the arousal is interpreted as challenge or threat; and the General Adaptation Syndrome (node 004) explains the physiological trajectory when arousal becomes chronic.
steps: Takeaway: Performance improves with increasing stress up to an optimal point, after which further stress impairs performance.
Here is why: 1.
Low arousal = under‑activation.
When a student feels no pressure before a test, the brain’s reticular activating system remains quiet, leading to mind‑wandering and low encoding efficiency. 2.
Moderate arousal = eustress zone.
A manageable deadline releases catecholamines that sharpen selective attention and consolidate memory — think of the focused energy you feel the week before the ISC practicals. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Performance always improves with more stress”) reveals the misconception that stress is linearly beneficial, ignoring the distress limb where cognitive overload occurs.
remember: Define the upside‑down‑U curve (Yerkes‑Dodson law) in one sentence.
Why does moderate stress (eustress) enhance performance while high stress (distress) impairs it.
Evaluate the statement: “The optimal arousal level is the same for all tasks and all individuals.”.

cards.title: Burnout is a psychological syndrome resulting from prolonged exposure to…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Burnout is a psychological syndrome resulting from prolonged exposure to occupational or academic stressors, characterized by three inter‑related dimensions: (1) Emotional exhaustion — a sense of being overextended and depleted of emotional resources; (2) Depersonalization (or cynicism) — a detached, negative, or callous attitude toward one’s work, studies, or the people involved; and (3) Reduced personal accomplishment — a decline in feelings of competence, productivity, and achievement. Unlike acute stress (see node Strain and eustress) or the physiological alarm‑resistance‑exhaustion pattern of Selye’s GAS (node), burnout develops gradually through a mismatch between job/academic demands and the individual’s resources (coping skills, social support, autonomy). It is distinct from depression because its symptoms are context‑specific (work/school) and often improve with removal from the stressor, though chronic burnout can precipitate clinical depression.
