cards.definition: The fundamental attribution error (FAE) is a pervasive bias in social perception where observers attribute others' behaviour to internal, dispositional causes (personality, attitude) while under‑weighting external, situational factors (context, constraints). First documented by Lee Ross (1977), FAE emerges from the covariation model of Kelley: observers lack consensus, distinctiveness, and consistency information about the actor, so they default to dispositional inferences. It differs from the actor‑observer bias (where actors attribute their own actions to situations) and from the self‑serving bias (where we credit success to ourselves and blame failure on situations). Cultural research shows FAE is stronger in individualistic cultures; collectivist contexts like many Indian communities display a more balanced attribution style because situational norms are salient. FAE influences everyday judgments — teachers labeling a quiet student "uninterested" rather than anxious, employers assuming a late employee is "lazy" instead of considering transport delays — and can reinforce stereotypes and prejudice.
steps: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to over‑attribute others' actions to their personality while ignoring the situation.
Here is why: first, observers lack full situational data, so they rely on the most visible cue — the actor's behaviour.
Second, dispositional inferences are cognitively cheaper; labeling someone "lazy" requires less effort than analysing traffic, family emergencies, or systemic barriers.
Third, language reinforces trait labels (e.g., "he is rude") making them sticky.

Fourth, cultural scripts in individualistic societies promote personal responsibility, amplifying FAE; collectivist settings like joint families in India make situational demands more salient, reducing the bias.

Fifth, FAE persists even when situational constraints are obvious, as shown in the classic essay experiment where participants still rated a writer's true attitude despite knowing the position was assigned.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "FAE is when we blame ourselves for failures") reveals confusion with the self‑serving bias, which concerns self‑attributions, not judgments of others.
remember: What is the fundamental attribution error.
Why does the fundamental attribution error occur even when situational constraints are made explicit.
Evaluate the claim: "The fundamental attribution error is universal and equally strong across all cultures.".

cards.title: The self‑serving bias is a systematic tendency to attribute positive outcomes…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The self‑serving bias is a systematic tendency to attribute positive outcomes to internal, dispositional causes (ability, effort, personality) while attributing negative outcomes to external, situational causes (luck, task difficulty, others’ actions). First documented by Miller and Ross (1975), it operates as a self‑esteem maintenance mechanism. The bias has two complementary components: self‑enhancement (claiming credit for success) and self‑protection (deflecting blame for failure). It interacts with the fundamental attribution error — while the FAE leads us to over‑attribute others’ behaviour to disposition, the self‑serving bias flips the script for the self. Cultural research shows the bias is stronger in individualistic contexts (e.g., urban Indian middle‑class) and weaker in collectivist settings where group harmony tempers self‑promotion. The bias also predicts motivational consequences: persistent self‑serving attributions can sustain effort after success but may hinder learning from failure if external excuses become habitual.
steps: The self‑serving bias is a universal tendency to claim credit for success and deny responsibility for failure, protecting self‑esteem.
Here is why: 1.
Self‑enhancement – When a Class 12 student tops the pre‑board, she says “I prepared well.” This internal attribution boosts confidence and motivates further study. 2.
Self‑protection – When the same student scores low in a mock test, she says “The paper was out of syllabus.” The external attribution shields her self‑image from threat. 3.
Contrast with FAE – In we saw observers over‑attribute a peer’s poor performance to laziness (disposition).
The self‑serving bias reverses this lens for the self, showing the actor‑observer asymmetry. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “self‑serving bias means always blaming others”) reveals the misconception that the bias only operates for failure, ignoring the self‑enhancement side for success.
remember: Define self‑serving bias and name its two components.
Explain why a student who says “I got 90 % because I’m intelligent” but “I failed because the teacher hates me” is demonstrating self‑serving bias.
Compare self‑serving bias with fundamental attribution error. Give one similarity and one difference.

cards.title: The false consensus effect is a cognitive bias in social perception whereby…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The false consensus effect is a cognitive bias in social perception whereby individuals systematically overestimate the extent to which their own beliefs, attitudes, values, or behaviours are shared by others. First documented by Ross, Greene, and House (1977), it arises from two intertwined mechanisms: (1) availability heuristic — personal experiences and salient self‑generated thoughts are more accessible than alternative viewpoints, and (2) motivational validation — people desire social support for their positions, so they unconsciously assume consensus exists. Unlike the fundamental attribution error (which misattributes others’ actions to disposition) or the self‑serving bias (which credits success to self and failure to externals), false consensus specifically distorts perceived prevalence of one’s own stance. It operates across domains — political opinions, consumer preferences, moral judgments — and is amplified in homogeneous groups (e.g., regional or linguistic communities in India) where selective exposure limits contact with dissenters. Consequences include reduced perspective‑taking, increased polarisation, and flawed group decision‑making because members assume unanimity that does not exist. Researchers measure it by asking participants to estimate the percentage of peers who would make the same choice; the gap between estimate and actual distribution quantifies the bias.
steps: False consensus is the tendency to overestimate how many people share our own opinions, attitudes, and behaviours.
Here is why: first, the availability heuristic makes our own stance cognitively salient — we recall our reasons instantly, while alternative views remain vague.
Second, motivational validation drives us to seek social confirmation; believing “everyone thinks like me” protects self‑esteem and reduces cognitive dissonance.
Third, selective exposure in homogeneous Indian settings — such as a Gujarati family assuming all neighbours prefer vegetarian thali — limits encounters with dissent, reinforcing the illusion.
Fourth, the bias is measured by asking participants to predict peer choices; the discrepancy between prediction and actual distribution reveals its magnitude.

Fifth, consequences include group polarisation (members push further toward the perceived majority) and poor collective decisions (e.g., a student council assuming unanimous support for a policy that actually splits the…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is the tendency to conform to group norms”) reveals the misconception that false consensus is about behavioural conformity rather than perceptual overestimation of agreement.
remember: Define the false consensus effect in one sentence.
Explain two psychological mechanisms that give rise to the false consensus effect.
Compare false consensus with self‑serving bias. Which bias distorts perceived social agreement and which distorts causal attribution for personal outcomes.

cards.title: Automatic vigilance refers to the rapid…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Automatic vigilance refers to the rapid, non‑conscious scanning of the social environment for cues that signal potential threat, novelty, or social deviation. It operates through low‑level perceptual processes (e.g., amygdala‑mediated threat detection) and higher‑order schema activation (e.g., stereotypes about out‑groups). Unlike controlled attention, it requires minimal cognitive resources, is triggered by salient features such as angry faces, sudden movements, or norm violations, and feeds into subsequent attributional processes (e.g., Kelley’s covariation model) and bias formation (e.g., fundamental attribution error). In the ISC syllabus it is positioned after false‑consensus bias and before counterfactual thinking, linking perception of others’ behaviour to the automatic generation of “what‑if” alternatives.
steps: Automatic vigilance is a fast, non‑conscious scanning system that prioritises socially relevant threats before deliberate thought begins.
Here is why: the brain allocates limited attentional resources to stimuli that historically predicted danger or social exclusion, allowing rapid behavioural adjustment.

First, the amygdala evaluates sensory input for emotional salience — angry faces, sudden noises, or unexpected proximity — within 100–150 ms. Second, the superior temporal sulcus processes biological motion, flagging…
Third, stored social schemas (e.g., “strangers at night are risky”) amplify the signal, producing a brief physiological arousal (increased heart rate, skin conductance).

Fourth, this output biases subsequent controlled attribution: the observer is more likely to attribute the target’s behaviour to dispositional traits (fundamental attribution error) rather than situational factors.
Fifth, the same mechanism underlies the false‑consensus effect — people overestimate how many others share their vigilant reaction.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “prefrontal cortex and hippocampus”) reveals the misconception that controlled, memory‑based structures drive this early detection, confusing top‑down regulation with bottom‑up threat scanning.
remember: Define automatic vigilance and name two neural structures involved.
Explain how automatic vigilance differs from controlled social perception in terms of speed and resource demand.
Evaluate the claim: “Automatic vigilance always leads to accurate social judgements.”.

cards.title: Counterfactual thinking is a cognitive process in which individuals generate…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Counterfactual thinking is a cognitive process in which individuals generate mental simulations of alternatives to past factual events, typically structured as “if‑only” or “what‑if” statements. It operates on two primary dimensions: direction (upward vs. downward) and structure (additive vs. subtractive). Upward counterfactuals imagine better outcomes (“If I had studied harder, I would have topped the board”), often eliciting regret or motivation; downward counterfactuals imagine worse outcomes (“If I hadn’t guessed that answer, I would have failed”), usually producing relief or satisfaction. Additive counterfactuals insert a new element (“If I had taken tuition, I would have understood calculus”), whereas subtractive counterfactuals remove an existing element (“If I hadn’t fallen ill before the exam, I would have scored higher”). The theory, rooted in Kahneman and Tversky’s simulation heuristic and later refined by Roese (1997), posits that counterfactuals serve three functions: (1) preparative — they guide future behaviour by highlighting causal links; (2) affective — they regulate emotions through contrast effects; and (3) social — they influence blame, responsibility judgments, and moral reasoning. In the ISC curriculum, counterfactual thinking is positioned after automatic vigilance (which primes attention to salient stimuli) and before social influence concepts, illustrating how internal mental simulations feed into group‑level processes such as conformity and obedience.
steps: Counterfactual thinking is the mind’s “what‑if” engine that rewrites past events to extract lessons, soothe feelings, or assign blame.
Here is why: it transforms a single factual outcome into a branching set of mental simulations, each serving a distinct psychological purpose.
First, direction matters.

Upward counterfactuals (“If I had practiced the piano daily, I would have won the competition”) create a contrast that highlights a gap between reality and a better alternative, often sparking regret but also motivating…
Downward counterfactuals (“If I hadn’t attended that extra coaching class, I would have failed”) create a contrast with a worse alternative, generating relief and bolstering self‑esteem.
Indian students frequently experience both after board results: a 95 % scorer may ruminate on the missed 5 % (upward), while a 33 % passer may feel grateful for not failing (downward).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “If I hadn’t fallen ill, I would have scored higher”) reveals the misconception that any “if‑only” statement is upward additive; this example is downward subtractive because it removes a negative event and imagines a better outcome, not…
remember: Define counterfactual thinking and give one original example of an upward additive counterfactual in an Indian school setting.
Explain the difference between the preparative and affective functions of counterfactual thinking, using a single Indian‑context scenario that illustrates both.
A student says, “Counterfactual thinking is just day‑dreaming about the past.” Evaluate this claim with reference to the structural classification of counterfactuals.

cards.title: Social influence: groups refers to the processes by which the presence, norms…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Social influence: groups refers to the processes by which the presence, norms, roles, and dynamics of a collectivity alter the thoughts, feelings, and actions of its members. A group is defined in ISC Psychology as two or more individuals who (1) interact directly or indirectly, (2) perceive themselves as a unit (“we”), (3) share common goals or norms, and (4) are interdependent — outcomes for one affect others. Groups vary on dimensions such as size (dyad to large crowd), duration (temporary task force vs. lifelong family), structure (formal roles in a student council vs. informal friendship circle), and cohesiveness (strength of attraction to the group). Key sub‑concepts that link to later nodes: - Group norms — shared expectations that guide behaviour (e.g., “arrive on time for rehearsals”). - Roles — patterned behaviours attached to positions (captain, wicket‑keeper). - Social identity — the part of self‑concept derived from group membership, which fuels in‑group favouritism. - Group cohesion — the bond that keeps members together; high cohesion amplifies conformity and polarisation (covered in). - Collective efficacy — the group’s shared belief in its capability, influencing effort (relevant to social loafing,). Understanding groups as a context is essential because phenomena such as social facilitation, social loafing, group polarisation, conformity, and obedience all operate within group settings. The present node therefore establishes the structural and psychological foundations — definition, types (primary, secondary, reference), formation stages (forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning), and basic influence mechanisms (normative pressure, informational dependence) — that the subsequent concept nodes will elaborate.
steps: Groups are the fundamental social units that channel individual behaviour through shared norms, roles, and identity.
Here is why: a group is not merely a gathering; it is a psychological entity that creates a “we” from separate “I”s.
First, interaction provides the raw data — members observe each other’s actions, hear opinions, and adjust.
In a Mumbai local‑train commuters’ WhatsApp group, a single message about a delay spreads instantly, shaping everyone’s travel plan.
Second, shared identity turns interaction into belonging; students wearing the same house‑colour T‑shirt at a sports meet feel collective pride, which research shows increases effort on group tasks.
Third, common goals align effort — a village panchayat meeting to build a check‑dam coordinates labour, resources, and timelines.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “physical proximity and common language”) reveals the misconception that spatial closeness or superficial similarity constitutes a group, ignoring the psychological interdependence and shared identity required.
remember: List the four defining criteria of a psychological group as per the ISC Class 12 syllabus.
Explain why a crowd at a railway station does not qualify as a group, using the four criteria.
Evaluate the statement: “Primary groups are always more influential than secondary groups.”.

cards.title: Social facilitation refers to the change in an individual’s performance caused…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Social facilitation refers to the change in an individual’s performance caused by the real, imagined, or implied presence of others. The classic formulation (Zajonc, 1965) states that the mere presence of conspecifics increases physiological arousal, which strengthens the dominant response. For simple, well‑learned, or habitual tasks the dominant response is correct, so performance improves. For complex, novel, or poorly learned tasks the dominant response is often incorrect, so performance declines. Three major theoretical accounts explain the mechanism: (1) Drive theory – presence creates a non‑specific drive that energises dominant responses; (2) Evaluation apprehension – the fear of being judged adds arousal beyond mere presence; (3) Distraction‑conflict – attending to others splits attention, creating conflict that heightens arousal. The effect is moderated by task complexity, familiarity, and whether the others are passive audience members or active co‑actors. In Indian contexts, a classical dancer performs flawless mudras before a crowd (facilitation) but stumbles on a new choreography (impairment); a student solves routine arithmetic faster in a study group but struggles with a novel proof when peers watch. Social facilitation is distinct from social loafing (reduced effort in groups) and from conformity (changing behaviour to match group norms), though all three arise from group presence.
steps: Social facilitation is the tendency for the presence of others to enhance performance on simple or well‑learned tasks while impairing performance on complex or novel tasks.
Here is why: first, Zajonc’s drive theory proposes that any conspecific presence raises a generalised drive level; this drive amplifies the most probable (dominant) response.
When the task is easy, the dominant response is correct, so performance rises.
Second, evaluation apprehension adds a social‑evaluative component: people fear negative judgement, which further heightens arousal and sharpens the dominant response.
Third, distraction‑conflict theory argues that attending simultaneously to the task and to others creates attentional conflict, producing arousal that again strengthens the dominant response.
Fourth, task complexity is the critical moderator: simple tasks (e.g., typing a familiar paragraph) show facilitation; complex tasks (e.g., solving a new logic puzzle) show impairment.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “social facilitation always improves performance”) reveals the misconception that presence of others is uniformly beneficial, ignoring the crucial role of task complexity.
remember: Define social facilitation in one sentence.
Why does the presence of others improve performance on a simple task according to drive theory.
Compare social facilitation and social loafing in terms of direction of performance change and group size.

cards.title: Social loafing is the reduction in individual effort that occurs when people…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Social loafing is the reduction in individual effort that occurs when people work collectively compared with when they work alone. It arises from two core mechanisms: diffusion of responsibility (each member feels less personally accountable because the outcome is shared) and reduced evaluation apprehension (individual performance is less identifiable, lowering the pressure to perform). The classic demonstration is Ringelmann’s rope‑pulling experiment, where per‑person force declined as group size increased. Factors that amplify loafing include large groups, additive tasks where contributions are pooled, low task meaningfulness, and cultures that emphasise individualism over collectivism. Conversely, making individual outputs identifiable, increasing task importance, fostering group cohesion, and setting clear individual goals attenuate the effect. Social loafing is distinct from social facilitation, which describes performance changes due to the mere presence of others; loafing specifically concerns effort loss in collective tasks where individual input cannot be isolated.
steps: Social loafing is the tendency for individuals to exert less effort when working in a group than when working alone because their individual output becomes less identifiable.
Here is why: first, diffusion of responsibility makes each member feel that the group’s success or failure is shared, so personal accountability shrinks.
Second, reduced evaluation apprehension occurs because observers cannot pinpoint who contributed what, lowering the drive to impress or avoid criticism.
Third, the free‑rider effect lets some members coast on others’ efforts, especially when the task is additive (e.g., pulling a rope, clapping).
Fourth, larger groups magnify these processes — Ringelmann found that per‑person force dropped from 100 % alone to about 70 % in a six‑person team.
Fifth, cultural context matters: collectivist settings (e.g., many Indian joint‑family or community tasks) often show weaker loafing because group identity is salient.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Asch’s conformity study”) reveals the misconception that any famous group experiment illustrates loafing, confusing conformity pressure with effort loss.
remember: Define social loafing and name the classic experiment that first demonstrated it.
Explain why social loafing tends to increase as group size grows.
Critically evaluate the claim that social loafing is absent in collectivist cultures such as India.

cards.title: Group polarisation is the tendency for a group’s prevailing attitude to become…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Group polarisation is the tendency for a group’s prevailing attitude to become more extreme after discussion, moving further in the direction of the initial majority inclination. It differs from conformity (where individuals align with a group norm) and from groupthink (where dissent is suppressed). Two main mechanisms drive it: persuasive arguments theory — exposure to novel, supporting arguments strengthens the initial view — and social comparison theory — members adjust their positions to appear slightly more extreme than the perceived group average, seeking social approval. The phenomenon is observed in risk‑taking (risky shift) and caution (cautious shift) contexts. It interacts with social facilitation (performance changes in presence of others) and social loafing (reduced effort in groups) by altering the motivational climate of the group. In Indian settings, polarisation can be seen in residential‑society WhatsApp groups where initial mild concern about a civic issue escalates into a demand for drastic action after discussion.
steps: Group polarisation means that after discussion a group’s attitude becomes more extreme in the direction it already leaned.
Here is why: first, members hear new arguments that support the initial view, making the position seem more justified (persuasive arguments theory).
Second, individuals compare themselves with the perceived group norm and shift slightly beyond it to appear more committed (social comparison theory).
Consider a college festival committee in Delhi that initially feels mildly positive about inviting a controversial speaker.

During the meeting, each member shares reasons why the speaker will boost attendance; the pool of arguments grows, and each person wants to seem more enthusiastic than the average, so the final decision becomes a strong…
A third factor is the risky shift: when the pre‑discussion leaning is toward risk, the group moves to a riskier stance; conversely, a cautious lean produces a cautious shift.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it is the same as conformity”) reveals the misconception that any group influence equals conformity, ignoring the extremity shift unique to polarisation.
remember: Define group polarisation and name the two main theoretical mechanisms that explain it.
Explain why a group that initially leans toward caution may become even more cautious after discussion, using social comparison theory.
A student claims that group polarisation and groupthink are the same because both involve groups making extreme decisions. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Conformity refers to a change in behaviour or belief to match those of others…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Conformity refers to a change in behaviour or belief to match those of others, driven by social pressure. Two primary motives underlie conformity: normative influence and informational influence. Normative influence occurs when an individual conforms to gain social approval or avoid rejection; the person publicly complies but may not privately accept the group’s position. Informational influence occurs when an individual looks to others as a source of evidence about reality, especially in ambiguous or crisis situations; this often leads to genuine private acceptance because the person believes the group is correct. The dual‑process model of conformity (Deutsch & Gerard, 1955) distinguishes these processes: normative influence produces compliance, while informational influence produces internalisation. Both can operate simultaneously; for example, a student may adopt a study method because peers use it (normative) and because the method appears effective (informational). Normative influence is stronger when group cohesion is high and responses are public; informational influence is stronger when the task is difficult, ambiguous, or the individual lacks expertise. Understanding this distinction helps explain classic findings such as Asch’s line‑judgement experiments (where normative pressure dominated) and Sherif’s autokinetic effect studies (where informational influence prevailed).
steps: Conformity is driven by two distinct motives — normative influence (the need to belong) and informational influence (the need to be right) — and recognising which motive is at play predicts whether a person merely…
First, normative influence stems from the fundamental human desire for social acceptance.
When a group’s expectations are clear and the situation is public, individuals often go along to avoid ridicule or exclusion, even if they privately disagree.
This yields compliance without internalisation.
Second, informational influence arises from uncertainty.
In ambiguous, complex, or novel situations, people treat others’ behaviour as data about what is correct.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “normative influence is when you follow others because they know better”) reveals confusion with informational influence, mistaking the accuracy motive for the social‑approval motive.
remember: Define normative influence.
Explain why a person might conform due to informational influence in an ambiguous situation.
Critically evaluate the claim that normative influence always leads to public compliance without private acceptance.

cards.title: Asch’s study (1951) is a classic laboratory investigation of conformity using a…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Asch’s study (1951) is a classic laboratory investigation of conformity using a simple perceptual task. Participants were shown a standard line and three comparison lines; only one comparison matched the standard in length. The real participant was seated among 6–8 confederates who, on critical trials, unanimously gave an incorrect answer. Asch measured how often the genuine participant conformed to the majority’s wrong judgment. Across 18 critical trials, the overall conformity rate was about 37 %, with 75 % of participants conforming at least once. Key variations demonstrated factors that increase or decrease conformity: - Group size: conformity rose sharply up to three confederates, then plateaued. - Unanimity: a single dissenting confederate dropped conformity dramatically, showing the importance of social support. - Task difficulty: making the lines more similar increased conformity, indicating informational influence when the stimulus is ambiguous. Asch’s findings are central to the distinction between normative influence (conforming to gain social approval or avoid rejection) and informational influence (conforming because others are seen as a source of accurate information). The study also links to later work on minority influence (Moscovici) and obedience (Milgram), illustrating how social pressure shapes behaviour in groups.
steps: Asch’s line‑judgment experiments demonstrated that people frequently conform to a clearly wrong majority, revealing the power of normative social influence.
First, the experimental set‑up was deceptively simple: a single naïve participant judged line lengths alongside confederates who deliberately gave wrong answers on 12 of 18 trials.
This design isolates the pressure to agree with a unanimous majority while keeping the perceptual task unambiguous.
Second, the headline result — an average conformity rate of 37 % across critical trials — shows that even when the correct answer is obvious, a substantial minority will publicly endorse an error.
Importantly, 75 % of participants conformed at least once, indicating that conformity is not limited to a few “weak” individuals.
Third, Asch’s systematic variations pinpointed the conditions that amplify or reduce conformity.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “over 70 %”) reveals the misconception that most people always yield to majority pressure, confusing the “at least once” figure (75 %) with the per‑trial conformity rate.
remember: What was the approximate overall conformity rate reported in Asch’s original 1951 line‑judgment experiment.
Why did conformity drop dramatically when a single confederate gave the correct answer.
Evaluate whether Asch’s findings support the claim that conformity is primarily driven by informational influence.

cards.title: Conformity factors are the situational and personal variables that increase or…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Conformity factors are the situational and personal variables that increase or decrease the likelihood that an individual will change their behaviour or opinions to match a group norm. Key factors include group size (conformity rises with size up to about 4–5 members, then plateaus), unanimity (a single dissenter dramatically reduces conformity), group cohesion (high attraction to the group increases pressure to conform), status and expertise (high‑status or expert members exert stronger normative influence), cultural orientation (collectivist cultures such as many Indian communities show higher baseline conformity than individualist cultures), task difficulty and ambiguity (difficult or ambiguous tasks increase reliance on informational influence), public vs. private response (public responses heighten normative pressure), and individual differences such as need for affiliation, self‑esteem, and locus of control. These factors interact: for example, a cohesive, unanimous group of moderate size facing an ambiguous task will produce maximal conformity, whereas a large but divided group with a confident, low‑affiliation individual will produce minimal conformity. Understanding these factors allows prediction of when social influence will override personal judgement.
steps: Takeaway: Conformity is not a fixed trait but a dynamic outcome shaped by a constellation of group‑level and individual‑level factors that can amplify or dampen social pressure.
Here is why: Classic experiments (Asch, 1951) showed that a naïve participant often agreed with a clearly wrong majority.
Subsequent research systematically varied elements of that situation to discover why conformity rises or falls.
First, group size matters because each additional confederate adds normative pressure, but the effect saturates around four to five members — adding more people yields diminishing returns.
In an Indian classroom, a teacher asking a question may see a few students raise hands; once three or four have answered, the rest often follow even if unsure.
Second, unanimity is a powerful brake: a single ally who dissents cuts conformity dramatically (from ~33 % to ~5 % in Asch’s variations).
remember: Which of the following factors is most likely to decrease conformity in an Asch‑type line‑judgment….
Explain why a highly cohesive group of five friends in Kolkata might show more conformity on a difficult puzzle than a less cohesive group of five strangers, even though group….
Evaluate the claim: “In individualist cultures, conformity is always lower than in collectivist cultures, regardless of the situation.”.

cards.title: Obedience is a form of social influence where an individual complies with…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Obedience is a form of social influence where an individual complies with direct commands from a perceived legitimate authority figure. Stanley Milgram’s 1961–1963 experiments at Yale University demonstrated that a majority of participants (≈65 %) administered what they believed were dangerous electric shocks (up to 450 V) to a “learner” simply because an experimenter in a lab coat instructed them to continue. The paradigm used a teacher‑learner cover story: the participant (teacher) read word pairs and delivered escalating shocks for each error. Key factors that increased obedience included: (1) proximity of the authority — the experimenter physically present; (2) legitimacy and institutional backing — Yale’s prestige; (3) gradual escalation — small increments (15 V steps) creating a foot‑in‑the‑door effect; (4) absence of dissenting peers — no other “teachers” refusing; (5) depersonalisation of the victim — learner unseen/heard only through a wall. Situational variations (e.g., moving the experiment to a run‑down office, having the experimenter give orders by phone, introducing rebellious confederates) systematically reduced obedience rates, confirming that obedience is not a fixed trait but a product of specific contextual pressures. This node focuses on the original baseline study and the core situational factors; detailed factor analysis is covered in the prerequisite node.
steps: Milgram’s obedience experiments reveal that ordinary people can inflict severe harm when directed by a legitimate authority within an institutional setting.

Here is why: the baseline study placed participants in a teacher role, escalating shocks in 15‑volt increments up to 450 V while an experimenter insisted “The experiment requires that you continue.” First, proximity of…
Second, institutional legitimacy — moving the lab from Yale to a nondescript office building reduced obedience to 47.5 %.

Third, victim proximity — hearing the learner pound the wall (voice‑feedback) lowered obedience to 62.5 %; seeing the learner in the same room dropped it to 40 %; touching the learner’s hand to a shock plate fell to 30…
Fourth, peer dissent — two confederate teachers refusing to continue cut obedience to 10 %.
Fifth, gradual commitment — the step‑by‑step increase exploited the foot‑in‑the‑door principle, making refusal psychologically harder at each stage.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “300 V”) reveals the misconception that the scale stopped at the “XXX” label, confusing the visual marker with the actual top voltage.
remember: What was the maximum voltage level on the shock generator used in Milgram’s baseline obedience study.
Explain why obedience rates dropped when the experimenter gave instructions by telephone rather than in person.
Evaluate the claim: “Milgram’s findings prove that humans are naturally cruel.”.

cards.title: The cognitive component of an attitude refers to the mental representations…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The cognitive component of an attitude refers to the mental representations — beliefs, thoughts, knowledge, and expectations — that a person holds about an attitude object (a person, group, issue, or thing). These cognitions can be descriptive (e.g., “Electric cars run on batteries”) or evaluative (e.g., “Electric cars are environmentally friendly”). They may be explicit (consciously accessible and reportable) or implicit (automatically activated, often outside awareness). In the ABC model, the cognitive component supplies the informational base that interacts with the affective (emotional) and behavioural (action‑tendency) components; consistency among the three predicts attitude strength and stability. Researchers typically assess the cognitive component through self‑report scales (Likert‑type items), thought‑listing tasks, or implicit association tests. Because cognitions are propositional, they are amenable to logical analysis, persuasion, and change via information exposure — topics covered in later nodes (–009).
steps: The cognitive component of an attitude is the set of beliefs, thoughts, and information a person holds about an object, person, or issue, and it forms the knowledge base that shapes the affective and behavioural…
Here is why: first, cognitions are propositional — they can be true or false — so they provide the factual scaffolding for an attitude.
For instance, a student who believes “Online classes reduce interaction” holds a descriptive cognition that can be verified.
Second, cognitions carry evaluative weight; the same student may also think “Reduced interaction harms learning,” an evaluative cognition that colours the attitude positively or negatively.

Third, cognitions operate at two levels: explicit beliefs that the student can articulate in a survey, and implicit associations that surface in rapid categorisation tasks (e.g., pairing “online learning” with…

Fourth, the cognitive component directly influences attitude strength — attitudes supported by many consistent, confident cognitions resist change more than those based on few or contradictory thoughts.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is the feeling you get when you see the object”) reveals the misconception that cognition equals emotion, confusing the cognitive slice with the affective component.
remember: Define the cognitive component of an attitude in one sentence.
Explain how the cognitive component differs from the affective component of an attitude.
Assess whether the statement “Electric vehicles are expensive” represents a cognitive or affective element of an attitude toward electric vehicles.

cards.title: The affective component refers to the emotional or feeling‑based dimension of…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The affective component refers to the emotional or feeling‑based dimension of an attitude. It captures the valence (positive, negative, neutral) and intensity (mild to strong) of affect associated with an attitude object — a person, group, idea, or situation. In the tripartite model (cognitive‑affective‑behavioural), affect provides the motivational energy that can drive behavioural intentions. Affect can be explicit (consciously reported liking/disliking) or implicit (automatic physiological responses such as increased heart rate when viewing a feared stimulus). It interacts with the cognitive component (beliefs, knowledge) and the behavioural component (past actions, behavioural intentions) to produce a relatively stable attitude structure. Formation of affect occurs through classical conditioning (pairing a neutral stimulus with an emotional response), observational learning (modelling emotional reactions), cultural norms (shared emotional meanings), genetic predispositions (temperament), and direct information exposure (media, personal experience). Change in affect is central to persuasion (e.g., fear appeals) and cognitive dissonance reduction (altering feelings to match behaviour). In prejudice, the affective component manifests as hostility, contempt, or pity toward out‑groups, often preceding discriminatory behaviour.
steps: The affective component is the emotional core that gives an attitude its motivational force.
Here is why: affect supplies the “push” that turns a belief into action, and it can exist even when cognitive knowledge is weak or contradictory.
First, affect arises through classical conditioning — a neutral stimulus (e.g., a brand logo) paired repeatedly with a pleasant jingle acquires positive affect.
Second, modelling allows us to adopt the emotional reactions of significant others; a child who sees parents express pride during the national anthem internalises that pride.
Third, cultural norms prescribe appropriate emotional responses — collective joy during Diwali, collective grief after a national tragedy — shaping shared affective attitudes.
Fourth, genetic factors such as temperament influence baseline emotional reactivity, making some individuals more prone to strong positive or negative affect.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the thoughts you have about an object”) reveals the misconception that affect equals cognition, confusing emotional evaluation with informational content.
remember: What is the affective component of an attitude.
Explain how classical conditioning can create a positive affective response toward a previously neutral product logo.
Evaluate the claim: “If someone holds a strong negative belief about a group, they must also feel strong negative affect toward that group.”.

cards.title: The behavioural component of an attitude refers to the observable actions or…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: The behavioural component of an attitude refers to the observable actions or behavioural intentions that stem from an individual’s evaluation of an object, person, or issue. It is the “doing” part of the tri‑component model (cognitive‑affective‑behavioural) and represents the translation of beliefs (cognitive) and feelings (affective) into overt conduct. In CISCE ISC Psychology, this component is measured through self‑reports of past behaviour, behavioural intentions, or direct observation. It interacts bidirectionally: strong behavioural tendencies can reinforce cognitions and affect, while changes in cognition or affect can modify future behaviour. The behavioural component is distinct from the other two because it is publicly observable, making it the primary target for attitude‑change techniques such as persuasion and cognitive‑dissonance interventions (covered in node). It also underpins prejudice‑discrimination links: discriminatory acts are the behavioural expression of prejudiced attitudes (nodes‑013). Understanding this component allows psychologists to predict real‑world actions — voting, purchasing, helping — from measured attitudes.
steps: The behavioural component is the outward expression of an attitude — what a person actually does or intends to do. Here is why: attitudes only become socially relevant when they translate into actions that others can…

First, the behavioural component is measured differently from cognitions and affect; researchers use behavioural intention scales (“I will buy this product”) and direct observation (counting how many times a student…

Second, the classic LaPiere (1934) study showed a large gap: Chinese‑American couples were served in 250+ US establishments, yet 90 % of those same establishments later said they would not serve Chinese people.
In India, a similar gap appears when people endorse “Swachh Bharat” (cognitive) and feel pride (affective) but still litter in public spaces.

Third, the behavioural component is the lever for change: persuasion campaigns (e.g., “Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao”) target intentions to act, while cognitive‑dissonance interventions create discomfort between behaviour…

Fourth, discriminatory acts — refusing to rent a flat to a certain community — are the behavioural manifestation of prejudiced attitudes, linking this node to the prejudice‑discrimination chain (nodes‑013).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the behavioural component is just feeling happy about voting”) reveals the misconception that affect and behaviour are the same, confusing internal emotion with external action.
remember: Define the behavioural component of an attitude and give one Indian example that distinguishes it from the cognitive and affective components.
Explain why behavioural intentions measured on a Likert scale may not perfectly predict actual behaviour, citing one classic study.
Evaluate the statement: “If a person holds a strong positive attitude toward environmental protection, they will definitely recycle regularly.”.

cards.title: Modelling is a core mechanism of attitude formation described in Bandura’s…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Modelling is a core mechanism of attitude formation described in Bandura’s social learning theory. It occurs when an individual (the observer) acquires a new attitude by watching a model — a person or symbolic figure — express or act on that attitude. The process involves four mediational steps: attention (the observer notices the model’s attitude‑relevant behaviour), retention (the observed attitude is encoded in memory), reproduction (the observer later enacts similar attitude‑consistent behaviour), and motivation (the observer expects a reward or avoids punishment, often vicariously, for adopting the attitude). Modelling can be live (parents, peers), symbolic (media characters, influencers), or verbal (instructions). It interacts with the behavioural component of attitudes because the observed actions provide a template for the observer’s own behavioural expressions. Unlike direct conditioning, modelling does not require the observer to experience reinforcement personally; vicarious reinforcement — seeing the model rewarded — suffices. Cultural norms and media exposure amplify modelling effects, making it a powerful route for transmitting social attitudes such as gender roles, political leanings, or brand preferences.
steps: Attitudes are often formed by observing and imitating the attitudes expressed by significant models in one’s environment.

Here is why: first, the observer must pay attention to the model; salient, attractive, or high‑status models (e.g., a popular Bollywood actor endorsing a health drink) capture attention more effectively.
Second, the observed attitude must be retained in memory; repeated exposure (daily TV ads, parental reminders) strengthens retention.
Third, the observer must be capable of reproduction — translating the stored representation into actual attitude‑consistent behaviour, such as buying the endorsed drink.
Fourth, motivation drives performance; if the model is shown gaining social approval or pleasure, the observer anticipates similar outcomes (vicarious reinforcement).
Consider a Class 12 student in Mumbai who sees her mother respectfully greeting elders every morning.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “modelling is the same as classical conditioning”) reveals the misconception that observational learning requires direct stimulus‑response pairing, ignoring the cognitive mediational steps unique to social learning theory.
remember: What is modelling in the context of attitude formation.
Explain how the attention and retention processes contribute to attitude formation through modelling.
Critically evaluate the role of modelling versus direct experience in forming attitudes towards environmental conservation.

cards.title: Conditioning in attitude formation refers to the process by which repeated…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Conditioning in attitude formation refers to the process by which repeated associative learning creates or modifies the cognitive, affective, and behavioural components of an attitude. In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus (e.g., a brand logo) is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus that naturally evokes an emotional response (e.g., pleasant music), so the neutral stimulus alone eventually elicits the same affective reaction, becoming a conditioned stimulus that carries a positive or negative evaluation. In operant conditioning, attitudes are strengthened or weakened by consequences: behaviours expressing an attitude that are reinforced (praise, rewards) increase the likelihood of that attitude persisting, while punishment or lack of reinforcement leads to extinction. Both forms interact with the three attitude components — cognitive (beliefs about the object), affective (emotional valence), and behavioural (tendency to act) — and can generalise to similar stimuli, making conditioned attitudes relatively stable but still amenable to change through counter‑conditioning or extinction.
steps: Conditioning shapes attitudes by repeatedly linking a neutral stimulus with an emotional response, so the stimulus alone can trigger the attitude.

Here is why: first, classical conditioning creates an affective tag — a brand jingle (neutral) paired with a feel‑good festival scene (unconditioned) makes the jingle itself evoke warmth, embedding a positive affective…

Second, operant conditioning locks in the behavioural component — when a child says “I like this cereal” and receives a smile from a parent, the verbal behaviour is reinforced, strengthening the cognitive belief that…

Third, repetition and schedule of reinforcement determine durability; intermittent reinforcement (e.g., occasional discount coupons) makes the attitude more resistant to extinction than continuous reinforcement.
Fourth, stimulus generalisation spreads the attitude — a positive feeling toward one product of a brand transfers to other products sharing the logo.
Fifth, counter‑conditioning can reverse the attitude — pairing the same logo with an aversive outcome (e.g., news of a product recall) can create a new conditioned response.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Classical conditioning is when you are rewarded for saying you like a product”) reveals the misconception that classical conditioning involves voluntary behaviour and reinforcement, confusing it with operant conditioning.
remember: Define classical conditioning in the context of attitude formation.
Explain how operant conditioning can strengthen a positive attitude toward a product.
Critically evaluate the claim that conditioning alone can account for all attitude formation.

cards.title: Cultural norms are shared expectations and standards of behaviour that emerge…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Cultural norms are shared expectations and standards of behaviour that emerge from the collective practices, values, symbols, and traditions of a society. They operate at three interlocking levels: (1) descriptive norms — what most people actually do (e.g., celebrating Diwali with lights); (2) injunctive norms — what the group approves or disapproves (e.g., disapproval of littering in public spaces); and (3) prescriptive norms — explicit rules codified in customs, religious texts, or community guidelines (e.g., dietary restrictions during Navratri). In attitude formation, cultural norms supply the cognitive component (beliefs about what is typical or desirable), the affective component (emotional resonance with group identity), and the behavioural component (habitual actions that signal conformity). They interact with other formation mechanisms: modelling (observing elders), conditioning (rewards/punishments for norm‑consistent acts), genetic predispositions (temperament influencing sensitivity to social cues), and information exposure (media reinforcing normative narratives). Because norms are transmitted vertically (parent‑to‑child) and horizontally (peer‑to‑peer), they create a stable yet adaptable framework within which individual attitudes develop, shift, or resist change.
steps: Cultural norms are the invisible script that guides what a society thinks, feels, and does, and they are the primary source of shared attitudes.
Here is why: norms provide the content for beliefs (cognitive), the emotional charge of belonging (affective), and the behavioural templates that signal group membership.

First, descriptive norms tell us “what everyone does.” In many Indian towns, people queue at railway stations despite no formal rule; a newcomer infers that queuing is the correct attitude toward public order.

Second, injunctive norms convey “what we ought to do.” When a family expects a daughter to touch elders’ feet, the affective warmth attached to that gesture reinforces a respectful attitude toward authority.
Third, prescriptive norms are codified — like the Manusmriti‑derived dietary rules during festivals — and they shape attitudes by making deviation feel morally wrong, not just unusual.
These norms travel through vertical transmission (parents teaching children during daily rituals) and horizontal transmission (peer groups enforcing dress codes at college festivals).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “descriptive norms are written laws”) reveals the misconception that norms must be formalised, confusing prescriptive norms with descriptive ones. Working: Descriptive norm example — most households light diyas during…
remember: What are the three types of cultural norms and give one Indian example for each.
Explain how cultural norms contribute to the cognitive component of an attitude.
A student claims that cultural norms are static and never change. Evaluate this claim using the concept of norm transmission.

cards.title: Genetic factors in attitude formation refer to the hereditary contribution to…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Genetic factors in attitude formation refer to the hereditary contribution to individual differences in evaluative dispositions toward objects, people, or issues. Research using twin and adoption designs estimates the proportion of variance in specific attitudes (e.g., political orientation, religiousness, environmental concern) attributable to additive genetic effects, known as heritability. Identical (monozygotic) twins share 100 % of their segregating genes, whereas fraternal (dizygotic) twins share on average 50 %; greater attitude similarity in identical pairs signals genetic influence. Adoption studies further separate genetic from shared‑environment effects by comparing adoptees with biological versus adoptive parents. Importantly, heritability is a population‑level statistic — it does not imply that a given person’s attitude is fixed by DNA. Gene‑environment interplay operates through passive correlation (parents provide both genes and environment), evocative correlation (genetically influenced traits elicit specific social responses), and active correlation (individuals select environments matching their genetic propensities). Thus, genetic factors provide a probabilistic bias that interacts with modelling, conditioning, cultural norms, and information exposure to shape the final attitude.
steps: Genetic factors give each person a probabilistic starting template for attitudes, not a rigid script.
Here is why: first, twin studies consistently show higher attitude concordance in identical than fraternal twins, indicating that shared DNA increases similarity.

Second, adoption studies reveal that adoptees’ attitudes correlate more strongly with biological parents they never met than with adoptive parents who raised them, confirming a genetic signal independent of shared home…

Third, heritability estimates for attitudes such as political ideology, religiosity, and social trust typically range from 30 % to 50 %, leaving ample room for cultural norms, modelling, and information exposure to…

Fourth, gene‑environment correlations explain how the same genetic propensity can lead to different outcomes: a child genetically inclined toward openness may seek diverse books (active correlation), evoke encouraging…

Fifth, the Indian context illustrates this interplay — a teenager with a genetic bias toward collectivist values may still adopt an individualistic attitude if exposed to global media and peer groups that model autonomy.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Each person’s attitude is 40 % determined by genes”) reveals the misconception that heritability applies to individuals rather than populations.
remember: What does a heritability estimate of 0.40 for attitudes toward environmental conservation indicate.
Why do researchers compare identical and fraternal twins when estimating genetic influence on attitudes.
Critically evaluate the claim: “Attitudes are mostly genetic, so education cannot change them.”.

cards.title: Information exposure refers to the process by which attitudes are acquired or…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Information exposure refers to the process by which attitudes are acquired or modified through the receipt of factual or persuasive content from external sources such as mass media, educational materials, advertisements, or public announcements. Unlike modelling (observing others) or conditioning (associative learning), information exposure operates primarily through the cognitive component of attitudes: the individual processes the presented information, evaluates its credibility, and integrates it into existing belief structures. The affective component may shift as the new knowledge alters emotional evaluations (e.g., learning about health risks of junk food can generate disgust). The behavioural component can subsequently change when the updated cognition and affect guide actions (e.g., choosing healthier snacks). Information exposure interacts with other formation mechanisms: it can reinforce cultural norms when media reflect prevailing values, it can amplify genetic predispositions by providing content that resonates with innate tendencies, and it can set the stage for later persuasion or cognitive dissonance processes. In the ISC curriculum, information exposure is treated as a distinct, direct route to attitude formation that emphasizes the role of knowledge acquisition and media literacy in shaping social judgments.
steps: Information exposure directly shapes attitudes by supplying new knowledge that revises the cognitive, affective, and behavioural components, even without personal experience or social observation.

First, the cognitive component is updated when an individual processes factual content — for instance, a student reading a government report on air‑quality indices in Delhi revises beliefs about pollution severity.
Second, the affective component follows: the same report may evoke concern or anxiety about health, altering emotional evaluations of outdoor activities.
Third, the behavioural component can shift as the revised cognition and affect guide choices — the student may start using a mask or prefer indoor exercise.

Supporting argument one: Source credibility determines how deeply the information is integrated; a report from the Central Pollution Control Board carries more weight than an unverified social‑media post.
Supporting argument two: Message repetition across channels (news, school assemblies, posters) strengthens encoding, making the attitude more resistant to counter‑information.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the affective component changes first because news makes us feel”) reveals the misconception that emotional reactions precede cognitive appraisal, confusing the sequence of attitude formation with the immediate affective response to…
remember: What is the primary attitude component that is first affected by information exposure.
Explain why a government health advisory on dengue prevention broadcast on All India Radio is an example of information exposure rather than modelling.
Evaluate the claim: “Repeated exposure to a political party’s manifesto on television guarantees a favourable attitude toward that party.”.

cards.title: Attitude change occurs through two broad mechanisms…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Attitude change occurs through two broad mechanisms: persuasion and cognitive dissonance reduction. Persuasion is the process by which a message alters an attitude; the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) distinguishes a central route — where the receiver carefully evaluates argument quality, requiring high motivation and ability — from a peripheral route — where cues such as source attractiveness, credibility, or emotional appeals trigger change without deep processing. The Yale Attitude Change Approach adds that source credibility, message discrepancy, and audience involvement interact to determine effectiveness. Cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1957) posits that inconsistency among cognitions (beliefs, attitudes, behaviours) creates an aversive motivational state (dissonance). People reduce dissonance by changing one cognition, adding consonant cognitions, or trivialising the inconsistency. Classic paradigms include induced compliance (insufficient justification), effort justification, free‑choice paradigm, and hypocrisy induction. Factors influencing the magnitude of dissonance are the importance of the elements, the proportion of dissonant to consonant cognitions, and the perceived freedom of choice. In the Indian context, a voter exposed to a party’s manifesto (central route) may change attitude if arguments are strong, while a celebrity endorsement (peripheral route) may sway a less involved voter. Post‑purchase dissonance after buying an expensive two‑wheeler often leads to emphasising its fuel efficiency to justify the expense.
steps: The key takeaway is that attitudes change either because a message is processed deeply (central route) or because superficial cues trigger a quick shift (peripheral route), and when behaviour conflicts with existing…

Here is why: First, the Elaboration Likelihood Model shows that motivation and ability determine processing depth; a student preparing for JEE will scrutinise a coaching institute’s success rates (central), whereas a…

Second, the Yale approach adds that a credible source (e.g., a respected scientist) and a message moderately discrepant from the audience’s current view maximise change, but extreme discrepancy triggers counter‑arguing.

Third, cognitive dissonance arises when a person freely chooses a behaviour that contradicts an attitude — like a vegetarian student eating meat at a friend’s wedding — creating tension proportional to the importance of…

Fourth, dissonance reduction follows predictable paths: changing the attitude (“maybe occasional meat isn’t wrong”), adding consonant cognitions (“the host would be offended if I refused”), or minimising importance…

Fifth, the induced‑compliance paradigm demonstrates that low external justification (small reward) produces greater attitude change than high justification, a finding replicated in Indian classroom experiments where…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “central route because the endorsement is a strong argument”) reveals the misconception that any persuasive cue constitutes argument quality — confusing source attractiveness with message content.
remember: Which route of the Elaboration Likelihood Model is most likely activated when a voter with low political interest chooses a candidate because a popular film star endorses them.
In Festinger’s induced‑compliance experiment, participants paid $1 to lie about a boring task reported enjoying it more than those paid….
A student who strongly values environmental conservation buys a petrol‑guzzling SUV because it was the only vehicle available in her….

cards.title: Social learning as a cause of prejudice and discrimination refers to the…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Social learning as a cause of prejudice and discrimination refers to the process by which individuals acquire biased attitudes and discriminatory behaviours through observation, imitation, and reinforcement within their social environment. Rooted in Bandura’s social learning theory, it emphasizes four mechanisms: (1) Modelling – watching significant others (parents, teachers, peers, media figures) express stereotyped beliefs or act discriminatorily; (2) Vicarious reinforcement – seeing the model rewarded (social approval, laughter, status) for prejudiced remarks, which increases the observer’s likelihood of adopting the same attitude; (3) Identification and internalisation – the observer identifies with the model (e.g., same caste, gender, regional group) and internalises the expressed bias as part of their own self‑concept; (4) Cultural transmission – repeated exposure across generations embeds the prejudice into norms, making it appear “natural” or “common sense.” In the Indian context, caste‑based prejudice, regional stereotypes (e.g., “Biharis are criminals”), gender role expectations, and religious biases are often transmitted through family conversations, school peer groups, cinema, television serials, and social media forwards. Unlike genetic factors or direct conditioning, social learning operates without the learner experiencing direct punishment or reward; the learning is indirect, cognitive, and highly dependent on the perceived credibility and status of the model. This node focuses exclusively on social learning; other causes such as realistic competition, categorization, and stereotyping are covered in sibling nodes.
steps: Social learning is the primary pathway through which prejudice and discrimination are acquired without direct experience.

Here is why: individuals, especially children, observe the attitudes and behaviours of influential models — parents, elders, teachers, media personalities — and imitate them, especially when the model is rewarded or…
First, modelling provides a script: a father casually remarking “lower‑caste people are unclean” gives the child a ready‑made belief.
Second, vicarious reinforcement strengthens the script: the father’s peers laugh and nod, signalling social approval, so the child expects similar rewards for repeating the remark.
Third, identification makes the script personal: the child shares the father’s caste, gender, or regional identity, so adopting the bias feels like loyalty to the in‑group.

Fourth, cultural transmission repeats the script across generations and media: school textbooks, popular films, and WhatsApp forwards reiterate the same stereotype, turning it into a “common sense” norm.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “social learning is just watching TV and copying”) reveals the misconception that mere exposure equals learning, ignoring the cognitive mediational steps that determine whether observation translates into internalised prejudice.
remember: Define social learning as a cause of prejudice and name the four mediational processes identified by Bandura that operate in this context.
A student argues that “prejudice against a particular community in my village is purely genetic because everyone in my family holds it.” Using social learning theory, evaluate….
Critically assess whether media portrayal of a regional group as “corrupt” can alone create prejudice in viewers who have no personal contact with that group.

cards.title: Realistic competition is a theoretical explanation for prejudice and…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Realistic competition is a theoretical explanation for prejudice and discrimination that originates from Realistic Conflict Theory (Sherif, 1966). It proposes that intergroup hostility arises when two or more groups pursue mutually exclusive goals — such as employment, territory, political power, or economic resources — and the success of one group necessarily limits the success of the other. The theory identifies three linked components: 1. Objective scarcity — a tangible, limited resource (e.g., government jobs, water rights, college seats). 2. Perceived zero‑sum interdependence — each group believes the other’s gain is its loss. 3. Resulting negative stereotypes and discriminatory behaviour — the competing out‑group is labelled lazy, dishonest, or threatening to justify exclusion. Unlike social‑learning or categorization accounts, realistic competition stresses material conflict rather than mere perception or cultural transmission. It predicts that reducing actual competition (e.g., through superordinate goals, resource expansion, or cooperative tasks) will diminish prejudice, a hypothesis confirmed in the classic Robbers Cave experiment. In the Indian context, realistic competition helps explain communal tension over reservation quotas, water sharing between states, or job markets where migrant workers are viewed as rivals by local labour.
steps: Realistic competition explains prejudice as a rational response to genuine resource scarcity, not merely a cognitive error.
Here is why: when groups need the same limited resource — jobs, water, land, or political representation — each group’s gain reduces the other’s share.

This objective conflict creates a zero‑sum perception: “If they win, we lose.” The perception then fuels negative stereotypes (“they are taking our jobs”) and discriminatory actions (exclusion, violence).

The Robbers Cave study demonstrated this by creating two boy groups, imposing competitive tournaments, and observing rapid hostility; later, introducing superordinate goals (e.g., fixing a broken water supply) reduced…
Consider an Indian example: the Cauvery water dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Both states depend on the same river for irrigation and drinking water.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “prejudice comes from observing parents’ biases”) reveals the misconception that social learning alone explains prejudice, confusing realistic competition (node) with the social‑learning account (node).
remember: What is the central claim of Realistic Conflict Theory regarding the origin of intergroup prejudice.
Explain why the Robbers Cave study is considered evidence for realistic competition rather than for categorization‑based prejudice.
Evaluate the statement: “Realistic competition fully explains communal violence in India.”.

cards.title: Categorization is the cognitive process by which individuals classify objects…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Categorization is the cognitive process by which individuals classify objects, events, or people into groups based on shared attributes such as appearance, language, religion, or regional origin. In social psychology, it operates automatically and often unconsciously, forming the basis of social identity theory: people define themselves by “in‑group” memberships and contrast them with “out‑groups.” The process involves three linked mechanisms: (1) perceptual grouping — noticing salient cues (e.g., dress, accent); (2) prototype matching — comparing the cue to a mental prototype of a category; and (3) category activation — retrieving associated beliefs, emotions, and behavioural scripts. Categorization feeds directly into stereotyping (the next node) by supplying the categorical labels that stereotypes attach to, and it interacts with realistic competition (previous node) because scarce resources heighten the salience of group boundaries. While categorization is a universal, adaptive heuristic, it becomes a source of prejudice when categories are essentialised, over‑generalised, or used to justify discrimination.
steps: Categorization is the mental shortcut that turns a flood of social information into manageable group labels, and it is the first cognitive step that can later solidify into prejudice.

Here is why: the brain evolved to detect patterns quickly; in a diverse Indian classroom, a student instantly sorts peers into “Hindi‑speakers,” “Tamil‑speakers,” “cricket‑players,” or “debate‑team members” based on…
First, perceptual grouping picks up salient cues — a turban, a bindi, a particular accent.
Second, prototype matching compares those cues to stored category prototypes (e.g., “Punjabi” prototype includes turban, loud laughter, butter‑chicken love).
Third, category activation retrieves the bundle of associated traits, expectations, and emotional tones linked to that prototype.
This three‑stage flow is automatic, often bypassing conscious control.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “categorization is the same as stereotyping”) reveals the misconception that sorting and content‑filling are identical, ignoring the distinct cognitive stages.
remember: Define social categorization and list its three core mechanisms.
Explain how realistic competition intensifies the effects of categorization on intergroup bias.
Evaluate the claim: “Categorization is always harmful because it leads to prejudice.”.

cards.title: Stereotyping is a cognitive process whereby individuals assign a fixed…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Stereotyping is a cognitive process whereby individuals assign a fixed, oversimplified set of attributes to all members of a social group. It operates at the cognitive component of attitudes (beliefs about the group), influences the affective component (emotional reactions such as prejudice), and can drive the behavioural component (discriminatory actions). Stereotypes form through categorization (node): the mind groups people into “us” vs. “them” based on salient cues (e.g., language, dress, religion). Once a category is activated, schema‑consistent information is noticed and remembered, while contradictory evidence is ignored (confirmation bias). Cultural norms, media portrayals, and social learning (node) reinforce these schemas. Stereotypes can be explicit (conscious endorsement) or implicit (automatic, unconscious activation). They serve a heuristic function — reducing information‑processing load — but at the cost of accuracy and fairness. In the Indian context, stereotypes about caste, region, gender, and language groups shape everyday interactions, hiring decisions, and policy attitudes.
steps: Stereotyping is the mental shortcut that assigns a uniform set of traits to every member of a social group, turning a flexible category into a rigid label.

Here is why: the brain first categorizes people (node) — e.g., “people from the North‑East” — then fills the category with culturally supplied attributes (“they eat spicy food, they are good at sports”).
This filling occurs through social learning (observing family, media, peers) and cultural norms that repeatedly pair the group with certain traits.
Once the stereotype is stored, it guides attention: we notice confirming instances (a North‑Eastern student winning a race) and overlook disconfirming ones (the same student excelling in literature).

The affective component then attaches feelings — pride, fear, contempt — to the label, and the behavioural component may produce discrimination (e.g., a landlord refusing to rent to “people from that region”).

In India, the “Madrasi” stereotype (all South Indians are dark‑skinned, eat idli, speak Tamil) illustrates how language, cuisine, and appearance are collapsed into one caricature, affecting hiring in multinational firms.
remember: Define stereotyping in one sentence and name the cognitive process that precedes it.
Explain how cultural norms and social learning interact to strengthen a regional stereotype in India.
Evaluate the claim: “Stereotypes are always harmful because they are false.”.

cards.title: Recategorization is a prejudice‑reduction strategy rooted in Social Identity…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Recategorization is a prejudice‑reduction strategy rooted in Social Identity Theory and the Common Ingroup Identity Model. It works by altering the cognitive representation of social groups: instead of perceiving others as members of a distinct out‑group, individuals come to view them as part of a superordinate, inclusive category (e.g., “citizens of India”, “members of this school”). This shift reduces the salience of the original ingroup–outgroup boundary, weakening stereotype activation (see node) and the categorization process that fuels prejudice (see node). Three related processes exist: decategorization (seeing individuals, not groups), recategorization (creating a new, shared ingroup), and subcategorization (maintaining subgroups under a common umbrella). Empirical work by Gaertner, Dovidio and colleagues shows that when a superordinate identity is made salient — through common goals, shared symbols, or joint tasks — intergroup bias diminishes. In the Indian context, initiatives such as “Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat” or national integration camps operationalise recategorization by highlighting a pan‑Indian identity over linguistic, regional, or religious sub‑identities.
steps: Recategorization reduces prejudice by shifting people’s mental grouping from narrow “us vs. them” categories to a broader, shared identity.

Here is why: first, Social Identity Theory posits that self‑esteem derives from favourable ingroup comparisons; when a superordinate category includes former out‑group members, the comparison becomes cooperative rather…

Second, the Common Ingroup Identity Model specifies that making a common identity salient — through shared goals, symbols, or fate — triggers cognitive restructuring that extends ingroup favouritism to former out‑group…

Third, recategorization differs from decategorization (which tries to erase group labels) and subcategorization (which keeps subgroups distinct under a superordinate label); research shows recategorization yields more…

Fourth, classic experiments (e.g., Gaertner et al., 1993) demonstrated that participants who worked on a joint task under a common team name showed less bias than those who worked separately, even when original group…

Fifth, in India, the “Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat” programme pairs states for cultural exchange, explicitly framing participants as “Indians first” — a real‑world recategorization that has been linked to increased mutual…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “recategorization means ignoring group differences altogether”) reveals the misconception that recategorization erases subgroup identities, confusing it with decategorization.
remember: Define recategorization in the context of prejudice reduction.
Explain how recategorization differs from decategorization and subcategorization.
Assess the strength of recategorization as a standalone strategy for reducing prejudice.

cards.title: Intergroup contact refers to structured…
cards.subject: Psychology
cards.definition: Intergroup contact refers to structured, face‑to‑face interaction between members of different social groups (e.g., religious, caste, linguistic, or regional groups) designed to reduce prejudice and discrimination.
